Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

In the Vinaya Piṭaka

Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā

Vajirabuddhi-Ṭīkā

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Paññāvisuddhāya [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] dayāya sabbe;

Vimocitā yena vineyyasattā;

Taṃ cakkhubhūtaṃ sirasā namitvā;

Lokassa lokantagatassa dhammaṃ.

I pay homage with my head to that Buddha, the eye of the world, by whom all beings fit for training were liberated through compassion purified by wisdom. Having paid homage, I also pay homage with my head to the Dhamma of Him who has reached the end of the worlds.

Saṅghañca sīlādiguṇehi yutta-

Mādāya sabbesu padesu sāraṃ;

Saṅkhepakāmena mamāsayena;

Sañcodito bhikkhuhitañca disvā.

And having paid homage to the Sangha endowed with virtues such as moral discipline, and having taken the essence from all passages; by my intention which desires brevity, being urged by the bhikkhus and having seen the benefit for them,

Samantapāsādikasaññitāya[V 0.0002];

Sambuddhaghosācariyoditāya;

Samāsato līnapade likhissaṃ;

Samāsato līnapade likhītaṃ.

I shall write concisely a determination of the meaning of the obscure terms in the commentary named Samantapāsādikā, composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa.

Saññā nimittaṃ kattā ca, parimāṇaṃ payojanaṃ;

Sabbāgamassa pubbeva, vattabbaṃ vattumicchatāti. –

The name, the reason for composing, the author, the extent, and the benefit—this pentad should be stated at the very beginning of every treatise by an author who wishes to speak.

Vacanato samantapāsādiketi saññā. Dīpantare bhikkhujanassa atthaṃ nābhisambhuṇātīti nimittaṃ. Buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyenāti kattā. Samadhikasattavīsatisahassamattena tassa ganthenāti parimāṇaṃ. Ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ dhammassāti payojanaṃ.

By the words, 'Samantapāsādikā,' the name is stated. By 'it does not fully serve the purpose of the community of bhikkhus in another island,' the reason is stated. By 'the one whose name, Buddhaghosa, was given by his teachers,' the author is stated. By 'the text of which has a measure of over twenty-seven thousand,' the extent is stated. By 'for the long-endurance of the Dhamma,' the benefit is stated.

Tatrāha [M 0.0002] – “vattabbaṃ vattumicchatāti yaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha kathaṃvidho vattā”ti? Uccate –

Therein, a questioner asks: 'Regarding the statement, "should be stated by one who wishes to speak," what kind of speaker is meant?' The answer is stated:

Pāṭhatthavidūsaṃhīro, vattā suci amaccharo;

Catukkamapariccāgī, desakassa hitussukoti. (mahāni. aṭṭha. ganthārambhakathā);

A speaker is one who knows the text and its meaning, is undaunted, pure, not miserly, does not abandon the fourfold method, and is zealous for the welfare of his audience.

Tatra paṭhīyateti pāṭho. So hi anekappakāro atthānurūpo atthānanurūpo ceti. Kathaṃ? Sandhāyabhāsito byañjanabhāsito sāvasesapāṭho niravasesapāṭho nīto neyyoti. Tatra anekatthavattā sandhāyabhāsito nāma “mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā”tiādi (dha. pa. 294). Ekatthavattā byañjanabhāsito nāma “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”tyādi (dha. pa. 1, 2; netti. 90, 92; peṭako. 14). Sāvaseso nāma “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, āditta”mityādi (mahāva. 54; saṃ. ni. 4.28). Viparīto niravaseso nāma “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchantī”tyādi (mahāni. 156; paṭi. ma. 3.5). Yathā vacanaṃ, tathā avagantabbo nīto nāma “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”tyādi. Yuttiyā anussaritabbo neyyo nāma “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave”tyādi (a. ni. 1.170).

Herein, pāṭha is that which is recited. Indeed, it is of many kinds, both conforming to the meaning and not conforming to the meaning. How? There is speech with an underlying meaning, speech with a literal meaning, text with a remainder, text without a remainder, that of definitive meaning, and that of inferable meaning. Among these, speech with an underlying meaning, having many meanings, is such as: “Having killed mother and father…”. Speech with a literal meaning, having one meaning, is such as: “Mind precedes all mental states…”. Text with a remainder is such as: “All, monks, is burning…”. Its opposite, text without a remainder, is such as: “All phenomena in every way come into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One…”. That of definitive meaning is to be understood just as it is stated, such as: “Impermanent, suffering, not-self…”. That of inferable meaning is to be considered by reasoning, such as: “One person, monks…”.

Atthopi anekappakāro pāṭhattho sabhāvattho ñeyyattho pāṭhānurūpo pāṭhānanurūpo sāvasesattho niravasesattho nītattho neyyatthotyādi. Tattha yo taṃtaṃsaññāpanatthamuccārīyate pāṭho, sa [V 0.0003] pāṭhattho “sātthaṃ sabyañjana”mityādīsu (pārā. 1; dī. ni. 1.190) viya. Rūpārūpadhammānaṃ lakkhaṇarasādi sabhāvattho “sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāvetī”tyādīsu (vibha. 489; saṃ. ni. 5.3) viya. Yo ñāyamāno hitāya bhavati, sa ñātumarahattā ñeyyattho “atthavādī dhammavādī”tyevamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.9, 194; 3.238; ma. ni. 1.411) viya. Yathāpāṭhaṃ bhāsito pāṭhānurūpo “cakkhu, bhikkhave, purāṇakamma”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.146) bhagavatā vuttamato cakkhumapi kammanti. Byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ paṭibāhayamānena vutto pāṭhānanurūpo. Vajjetabbaṃ kiñci apariccajitvā parisesaṃ katvā vutto sāvasesattho “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjatī”ti [M 0.0003] (saṃ. ni. 4.60; mahāni. 107) ca, “sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno”tyādīsu (dha. pa. 129) viya. Viparīto niravasesattho “sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca (dī. ni. 2.155; mahā. 287; netti. 114). Tatra, bhikkhave, ko mantā ko saddhātā…pe… aññatra diṭṭhapadehī”tyādi (a. ni. 7.66). Saddavaseneva vedanīyo nītattho “rūpā saddā rasā gandhā, phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā”tyādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.151, 165; mahāva. 33) viya. Sammutivasena veditabbo neyyattho “cattārome, bhikkhave, valāhakūpamāpuggalā”tyādīsu viya (a. ni. 4.101; pu. pa. 157). Āha ca –

The meaning is also of various kinds: the meaning of the text (pāṭhattho), the meaning of inherent nature (sabhāvattho), the meaning to be known (ñeyyattho), the meaning in accordance with the text (pāṭhānurūpo), the meaning not in accordance with the text (pāṭhānanurūpo), the meaning with a remainder (sāvasesattho), the meaning without a remainder (niravasesattho), the definitive meaning (nītattho), the inferable meaning (neyyattho), and so on. Among these, the text that is uttered for the purpose of conveying a particular meaning is the meaning of the text, as in "with meaning and with phrasing" and so on. The inherent nature, such as the characteristic, function, etc., of material and immaterial phenomena, is the meaning of inherent nature, as in "develops right view" and so on. That which, when known, is for one's welfare, is, because of its worthiness to be known, the meaning to be known, as in "one who speaks of the meaning, one who speaks of the Dhamma" and so on. The meaning spoken in accordance with the text is the meaning in accordance with the text; as it was said by the Blessed One, "The eye, monks, is old kamma," therefore the eye is also kamma. The meaning not in accordance with the text is that which is spoken by one who obstructs the meaning by means of the letter's shadow. The meaning with a remainder is that which is spoken by not abandoning something that should be excluded, thus leaving a remainder, as in "dependent on the eye and forms, consciousness arises" and "all tremble at the rod, all fear death" and so on. The opposite is the meaning without a remainder, as in "wandered on, transmigrated, by me and by you." "Here, monks, who is the knower, who can find stability… except for those who have seen the path?" and so on. The definitive meaning is that which is to be known only by the power of the word, as in "sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and tactile objects are delightful" and so on. The inferable meaning is that which is to be known by way of convention, as in "These four, monks, are persons comparable to clouds" and so on. And it is said:

“Yo attho saddato ñeyyo, nītatthaṃ iti taṃ vidū;

Atthassevābhisāmaggī, neyyattho iti kathyate”ti.

The meaning that is to be known from the word, that they know as the definitive meaning; the meaning established by conventional agreement is called the inferable meaning.

Evaṃ pabhedagate pāṭhatthe vijānātīti pāṭhatthavidū. Na saṃhīrate parapavādīhi dīgharattaṃ titthavāsenetyasaṃhīro. Bhāvanāyāgamādhigamasampannattā vattuṃ sakkotīti vattā, saṅkhepavitthāranayena hetudāharaṇādīhi avabodhayituṃ samatthotyattho. Socayatyattānaṃ pare ceti suci, dussīlyaduddiṭṭhimalavirahitotyattho. Dussīlo hi attānamupahantunādeyyavāco ca bhavatyapattāhārācāro iva niccāturo vejjo. Duddiṭṭhi paraṃ upahanti, nāvassaṃ nissayo ca bhavatyahivāḷagahākulo iva kamalasaṇḍo. Ubhayavipanno sabbathāpyanupāsanīyo bhavati gūthagatamiva chavālātaṃ gūthagato viya ca kaṇhasappo. Ubhayasampanno pana suci sabbathāpyupāsanīyo sevitabbo ca viññūhi, nirupaddavo iva ratanākaro. Nāssa maccharotyamaccharo, ahīnācariyamuṭṭhītyattho. Suttasuttānulomācariyavādaattanomatisaṅkhātassa catukkassāpariccāgī, tadatthasseva byākhyātetyattho. Atha vā paccakkhānumānasaddatthāpattippabhedassa pamāṇacatukkassāpariccāgī.

He knows the special meanings of the text that have come by way of analysis; therefore, he is called a knower of the text's meaning. He is not shaken by the censures of others or by the practices of sectarians over a long period; therefore, he is called unshaken. Because he is endowed with learning and realization, he is able to speak; therefore, he is called a speaker. He is able to make others understand by the concise and detailed methods, with reasons, examples, and so on; this is the meaning. He purifies himself and others; therefore, he is called pure, meaning he is free from the stain of immorality and wrong view. For an immoral person, harming himself, has words that are not to be heeded, like a perpetually sick physician with improper diet and conduct. One with wrong view harms others and is not a refuge for them, like a lotus grove infested with fiercely-seizing snakes. One deficient in both ways is in every way not to be associated with, like a firebrand for burning corpses that has fallen into filth or like a black serpent that has fallen into filth. But one accomplished in both, being pure, is in every way to be associated with and attended upon by the wise, like a mine of jewels that is free from danger. For him, there is no stinginess; therefore, he is called 'not stingy,' meaning he does not have the teacher's closed fist. He does not abandon the fourfold standard designated as Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati; he is an expounder of the meaning of that alone. Or, he does not abandon the fourfold standard of proof divided into perception, inference, testimony, and implication.

“Ekaṃsavacanaṃ [V 0.0004] ekaṃ, vibhajjavacanāparaṃ;

Tatiyaṃ paṭipuccheyya, catutthaṃ pana ṭhāpaye”ti. –

“One answer is categorical, another is analytical; the third one should answer by questioning back, and the fourth, however, one should set aside.”

Evaṃ [M 0.0004] vuttacatukkassa vā apariccāgī; Hitussuko iti sotūnaṃ hitāyossuko, tesamavabodhanaṃ pati patthetī tyattho; So eso sucittā piyo; Catukkassa apariccāgittā garu; Asaṃhīrattā bhāvanīyo; Desakattā vattā; Hitussukattā vacanakkhamo; Pāṭhatthaviduttā gambhīrakathaṃ kattā; Amaccharattā no caṭṭhāne niyojakoti;

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako”. (a. ni. 7.37; netti. 113) –

Or, he does not abandon the fourfold set of answers spoken of thus. 'Eager for welfare' means he is zealous for the welfare of the listeners; he desires their understanding—this is the meaning. That teacher, because of his purity, is dear; because he does not abandon the fourfold, he is venerable; because he is unshaken, he is worthy of cultivation; because he is an expounder, he is a speaker; because he is eager for their welfare, he is patient with speech; because he knows the text and its meaning, he is a maker of profound talk; because he is not stingy, he does not engage others in what is unsuitable. “Dear, venerable, and worthy of cultivation, a speaker and patient with speech, a maker of profound talk, and one who does not engage others in what is unsuitable.”

Itiabhihito desako;

Thus is the expounder described.

Sotā idāni abhidhīyate –

Now the listener is spoken of—

Dhammācariyagaru saddhā-paññādiguṇamaṇḍito;

Asaṭhāmāyo sotāssa, sumedho amatāmukho.

A listener is one who reveres the Dhamma and the teacher, is adorned with virtues such as faith and wisdom, is not deceitful or fraudulent, is endowed with good wisdom, and is facing the Deathless.

Tattha dhammagaruttā kathaṃ na paribhavati, ācariyagaruttā kathikaṃ na paribhavati, saddhāpaññādiguṇapaṭimaṇḍitattā attānaṃ na paribhavati, asaṭhāmāyattā amatābhimukhattā ca avikkhittacitto bhavati, sumedhattā yonisomanasikarotītyattho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

In that context, due to revering the Dhamma, he does not disparage the talk; due to revering the teacher, he does not disparage the speaker. Due to being adorned with virtues such as faith and wisdom, he does not disparage himself. Due to being without deceit and fraud and due to facing the Deathless, he is not of distracted mind. Due to having good wisdom, he attends wisely. Such is the meaning. For it has been said:

“Pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Na kathaṃ paribhoti, na kathikaṃ paribhoti, na attānaṃ paribhoti, avikkhittacitto dhammaṃ suṇāti ekaggacitto, yoniso ca manasi karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.151).

“Monks, one who is endowed with five qualities, while listening to the good Dhamma, is capable of entering into the certainty of rightness in wholesome states. What five? One does not disparage the talk, does not disparage the speaker, does not disparage oneself, listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted and concentrated mind, and attends wisely.”

Taṃlakkhaṇappattattā bhāvanā bhavati savanassetyutto sotā.

Because of having attained that characteristic, there is the cultivation of hearing; for this reason, he is called a 'listener'.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

Idāni [V 0.0005] assārambho – tattha yoti aniyamaniddeso, tena visuddhajātikulagottādīnaṃ kilesamalavisuddhiyā, pūjārahatāya vā akāraṇataṃ dassetvā yo koci imissā samantapāsādikāya ādigāthāya niddiṭṭhalokanāthattahetuṃ yathāvuttahetumūlena thirataraṃ [M 0.0005] acalaṃ katvā yathāvuttahetukālaṃ accantameva pūrento avasāne yathāvuttahetuphalaṃ sampādetvā yathāvuttahetuphalappayojanaṃ sādheti, sova paramapūjārahoti niyameti.

Now, the treatise is begun. Therein, the word 'yo' is an indefinite indicator. By this, it is shown that pure birth, family, lineage, and so on, or purity from the stain of defilements, or the state of being worthy of veneration are not the cause. Rather, whosoever—having made the cause for being the Protector of the World, which was indicated by the introductory verse of this Samantapāsādikā, firmer and unshakeable by means of the root of that aforementioned cause; and constantly fulfilling the time which is the cause, as was stated; and in the final existence, having accomplished the fruit of the cause as was stated; and accomplishing the purpose which is the benefit of the fruit of that cause—that very one is supremely worthy of veneration. Thus it is determined.

Ettāvatā –

By this much—

Bhayasammohaduddiṭṭhi-paṇāmo nesa sabbathā;

Paññāpubbaṅgamo eso, paṇāmoti nidassito.

This veneration is in no way a veneration out of fear, delusion, or wrong view; this veneration, which has wisdom as its forerunner, is thus demonstrated.

Tatra hetūti atidukkarāni tiṃsapāramitāsaṅkhātāni puññakammāni. Tāni hi accantadukkhena kasirena vacanapathātītānubhāvena mahatā ussāhena karīyantīti atidukkarāni nāma. Atidukkarattā eva hi tesaṃ atidullabhaṃ loke anaññasādhāraṇaṃ nāthattasaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ phalanti, taṃ tattha hetuphalaṃ; hetumūlaṃ nāma yathāvuttassa hetuno nipphādanasamatthā mahākaruṇā, sā ādipaṇidhānato paṭṭhāya “mutto mocessāmī”tiādinā nayena yāva hetuphalappayojanā, tāva abbocchinnaṃ pavattati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Therein, 'cause' refers to the meritorious deeds known as the thirty perfections, which are exceedingly difficult to perform. For they are called 'exceedingly difficult' because they are performed with absolute suffering, with hardship, with an intensity that transcends the path of speech, and with great effort. Indeed, it is precisely because of their exceedingly difficult nature that they bear as their fruit the state of a protector, which is exceedingly rare in the world and not shared with others. Therein, that is the cause-fruit. The 'root-cause' is the great compassion capable of accomplishing the aforementioned cause. Beginning from the initial aspiration, by the method of 'Being freed, I shall free others,' and so on, it proceeds unbroken for as long as the purposes of the cause-fruit exist. Concerning which, it was said:

“Sakānanā sagrivarā sasāgarā,

Gatā vināsaṃ bahuso vasundharā;

Yugantakāle salilānalānile,

Na bodhisattassa mahātapā kuto”ti.

“The earth, with its forests, chief mountains, and oceans, has gone to destruction many times; at the end of an eon, by water, fire, and wind, how could the great compassionate striving of a Bodhisatta be destroyed?”

Yāya samannāgatattā “namo mahākāruṇikassa tassā”ti āha. Hetukālaṃ nāma catuaṭṭhasoḷasaasaṅkhyeyyādippabhedo kālo, yaṃ sandhāyāha “kappakoṭīhipi appameyyaṃ kāla”nti. Tattha accantasaṃyogatthe upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ “māsaṃ adhīte, divasaṃ [V 0.0006] caratī”tiādīsu viya. Kāmañca so kālo asaṅkhyeyyavasena pameyyo viññeyyo, tathāpi kappakoṭivasena aviññeyyataṃ sandhāya “kappakoṭīhipi appameyyaṃ kāla”nti āha. Tattha kālayatīti kālo, khipati viddhaṃsayati sattānaṃ jīvitamiti attho. Kala vikkhepe. Tattha kappīyati saṃkappīyati sāsapapabbatādīhi upamāhi kevalaṃ saṃkappīyati, na manussadivasamāsasaṃvaccharādigaṇanāya gaṇīyatīti kappo. Ekantiādigaṇanapathassa koṭibhūtattā koṭi, kappānaṃ koṭiyo kappakoṭiyo[M 0.0006]. Tāhipi na pamīyatīti appameyyo, taṃ appameyyaṃ. Karontoti nānatthattā dhātūnaṃ dānaṃ dento, sīlaṃ rakkhanto, lobhakkhandhato nikkhamanto, attahitaparahitādibhedaṃ taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ pajānanto, vividhena vāyāmena ghaṭento vāyamanto, taṃ taṃ sattāparādhaṃ khamanto, paṭiññāsammutiparamatthasaccāni saccāyanto, taṃ taṃ sattahitaṃ adhiṭṭhahanto, sakalalokaṃ mettāyanto, mittāmittādibhedaṃ pakkhapātaṃ pahāya taṃ taṃ sattaṃ ajjhupekkhanto cāti attho. Khedaṃ gatoti anantappabhedaṃ mahantaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ anubhavanaṭṭhena gato, sampattotyattho. Saṃsāradukkhañhi sārīrikaṃ mānasikañca sukhaṃ khedayati pātayatīti “khedo”ti vuccati. Lokahitāyāti idaṃ yathāvuttahetuphalappayojananidassanaṃ, “saṃsāradukkhānubhavanakāraṇanidassana”ntipi eke –

Because of being endowed with which, it is said: ‘Homage to that Greatly Compassionate One.’ The time of the causes is a time with divisions such as four, eight, and sixteen incalculable eons, referring to which it is said: ‘a time immeasurable even by crores of eons.’ Therein, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of continuous connection, as in ‘he studies for a month, he walks for a day,’ and so on. And though that time is measurable and knowable by way of incalculable eons, yet, referring to its unknowability by way of crores of eons, it is said: ‘a time immeasurable even by crores of eons.’ Therein, 'time' (kāla) is so called because it drives (kālayati), that is, it casts away (khipati) and destroys (viddhaṃsati) the life of beings; such is the meaning. The root 'kala' is used in the sense of 'to cast away.' Therein, an eon (kappa) is so called because it is conceived (kappīyati), reckoned (saṃkappīyati) only by similes like the mustard-seed mountain, etc., but it is not counted by the reckoning of human days, months, or years. A ‘koṭi’ is so called because it is the culmination (koṭi) of the path of counting beginning with ‘one,’ etc.; ‘crores of eons’ (kappakoṭiyo) are the culminations of eons. It is ‘immeasurable’ (appameyyo) because it cannot be measured (na pamīyati) even by those; that is, the immeasurable time. The meaning of ‘doing’ (karonto) is as follows, due to the diverse meanings of the roots: giving gifts, protecting virtue, departing from the aggregate of greed, knowing that and that Dhamma which is divided into one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., striving and exerting with various kinds of effort, enduring this and that offense of beings, making true the truths of promises, conventions, and ultimate reality, resolving on this and that welfare for beings, extending loving-kindness to the entire world, and abandoning partiality divided into friend, non-friend, etc., and regarding this and that being with equanimity. ‘Gone to exhaustion’ (khedaṃ gato) means having gone to, having attained, the boundless and great suffering of saṃsāra in the sense of experiencing it; such is the meaning. For the suffering of saṃsāra exhausts (khedayati) and fells (pātayati) both physical and mental happiness, hence it is called ‘exhaustion’ (kheda). ‘For the welfare of the world’—this indicates the aforementioned cause, fruit, and purpose. And some say it indicates the reason for experiencing the suffering of saṃsāra.

“‘Jātisaṃsāradukkhānaṃ, gantuṃ sakkopi nibbutiṃ;

Ciralliṭṭhopi saṃsāre, karuṇāyeva kevala’nti. –

“Although able to go to Nibbāna, the cessation of the sufferings of saṃsāra and birth, He is long afflicted in saṃsāra purely out of compassion.”

Ca vutta”nti, tamayuttaṃ. Na hi bhagavā lokahitāya saṃsāradukkhamanubhavati. Na hi kassaci dukkhānubhavanaṃ lokassa upakāraṃ āvahati. Evaṃ panetaṃ dasseti tiṃsapāramitāpabhedaṃ hetuṃ, pāramitāphalabhūtaṃ nāthattasaṅkhātaṃ phalañca. Yathā cāha “mamañhi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccantī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.129; 5.2). Tattha bhagavā yathāvuttahetūhi sattānaṃ vineyyabhāvanipphādanapaññābījāni vapi, hetuphalena paripakkindriyabhāvena parinipphannavineyyabhāve satte vinayi, saṃsāradukkhato mocayīti attho. Na evaṃ saṃsāradukkhena lokassa upakāraṃ kiñci akāsi, tasmā karonto atidukkarāni lokahitāyāti sambandho. Imissā yojanāya sabbapaṭhamassa bodhisattassa uppattikālato paṭṭhāya bodhisattassa nāthattasaṅkhātapāramitāhetuphalādhigamo veditabbo. Yo nāthoti hi sambandho adhippeto. Imassa panatthassa –

And it has been said thus.” That is unsuitable. For the Blessed One does not experience the suffering of saṃsāra for the welfare of the world. Indeed, the experience of suffering by anyone does not bring benefit to the world. Rather, it shows this: the cause, which is the division of the thirty perfections, and the fruit, known as the state of a protector, which is the result of the perfections. And as He said: “Indeed, Ānanda, by relying on me, the good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth,” and so on. Therein, the Blessed One, by the aforementioned causes, sowed for beings the seeds of wisdom that accomplish the state of being trainable; by the fruit of the cause, which is the state of having mature faculties, He trained beings whose trainable nature had been brought to perfection, and liberated them from the suffering of saṃsāra—this is the meaning. It is not that He benefited the world through the suffering of saṃsāra; therefore, the connection is: “while doing extremely difficult deeds for the welfare of the world.” By this construction, from the time of the arising of the very first Bodhisatta, the Bodhisatta's attainment of the cause and fruit of the perfections, known as the state of a protector, should be understood. For the intended connection is with “who is a protector.” But of this meaning—

“Yadeva [V 0.0007] paṭhamaṃ citta-muppannaṃ tava bodhaye;

Tvaṃ tadevassa lokassa, pūjike parivasittha”. –

“Whatever first thought arose in you for the sake of enlightenment; that very thought you have attended to in a worshipful manner for this world.”

Iti vacanaṃ sādhakaṃ. Paṭhamacittassa pāramitābhāvo rukkhassa aṅkurato paṭṭhāya uppattiupamāya sādhetabbo. Etthāha – “khedaṃ gatoti vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ[M 0.0007], yathāvuttanayena guṇasādhanāsambhavato”ti? Na, antarā anivattanakabhāvadīpanato. Dukkarāni karonto khedaṃ gato eva, na antarā khedaṃ asahanto nivattatīti dīpeti. Lokadukkhāpanayanakāmassa vā bhagavato attano dukkhānubhavanasamatthataṃ dasseti.

This statement is proof. The state of the first thought being a perfection should be established by the simile of the arising of a tree, starting from the sprout. Here one might say: ‘Is the statement “gone to exhaustion” meaningless, since the quality cannot be established in the manner explained?’ No, because it shows the state of not turning back midway. It shows that one who undertakes difficult deeds indeed goes to exhaustion, but does not turn back midway, being unable to endure the exhaustion. Alternatively, it demonstrates the Blessed One’s capacity to endure his own suffering, he who desires to remove the suffering of the world.

“Yassa kassaci varadossaṃ, yāvāhaṃ sabbasattadukkhāni;

Sabbāni sabbakālaṃ yugaṃ, padmasseva bujjhantomhī”ti. –

“For as long as I am to be a giver of the supreme boon to any being whatsoever, I awaken to all the sufferings of all beings, at all times and all at once, like a lotus.”

Evaṃadhippāyassa attamattadukkhānubhavanasamatthatāya kāyeva kathāti atisayaṃ atthaṃ dassetīti attho. Atha vā khedaṃ gatoti byāpāraṃ paricayaṃ gatotipi attho sambhavati. Kammādīsu sabyāpāraṃ purisaṃ disvā santi hi loke vattāro “khinnoyaṃ kamme, khinnoyaṃ satte”tiādi. Imissā yojanāya nāthoti iminā buddhattādhigamasiddhaṃ koṭippattaṃ nāthabhāvaṃ patvā ṭhitakālo dassitoti veditabbo. Keci “mahākāruṇikassāti vadanto buddhabhūtassāti dassetī”ti likhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ viya, bodhisattakālepi tabbohārasabbhāvato. Tasmā so ettakaṃ kālaṃ dukkarāni karonto avasāne dukkarapāramitāpāripūriyā tāsaṃ phalabhūtaṃ nāthabhāvaṃ patvā lokahitāya byāpāraṃ gatoti ayamattho nidassito hoti. “Bodhiṃ gato”ti vuttepi subyattaṃ hetuphalaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Buddhabhāvappattasseva ca nāthassa namo kato hoti visesavacanasabbhāvato, na bodhisattassa. Evaṃ santepi vinayādhikāro idhādhippeto. So ca pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya yāvamaraṇakālā hoti. Taṃ ativiya parittaṃ kālaṃ lajjino atisukaraṃ sīlamattaṃ ekakassa attano hitāya attamattadukkhāpanayanādhippāyena paripūrento ko nāma idhalokaparalokātikkamasukhaṃ na gaccheyya, nanu bhagavā sakalalokadukkhāpanayanādhippāyena kappakoṭīhipi appameyyaṃ kālaṃ karonto atidukkaranirassādaṃ khedaṃ gatoti aññāpadesena guṇaṃ vaṇṇeti ācariyo.

The meaning is that it shows the supreme meaning: for one with such an intention, because of his capability to endure only his own suffering, what is there to say of suffering in the body? Alternatively, the meaning 'gone to fatigue' (khedaṃ gato) can also possibly mean 'has become accustomed to exertion'. For, upon seeing a person engaged in work and so on, there are indeed speakers in the world who say, ‘This one strives in work, this one strives in the affairs of beings,’ and so on. In this interpretation, it should be understood that by the word ‘Protector’ (nātha), the time is shown when he was established, having attained the state of a Protector which is the pinnacle, accomplished through the attainment of Buddhahood. Some write, ‘By saying “the Greatly Compassionate One,” he indicates one who has become a Buddha,’ but that does not seem correct, because that designation existed even during the time of the Bodhisatta. Therefore, this meaning is pointed out: that Bodhisatta, having performed difficult deeds for such a long time, in his final existence, through the fulfillment of the perfection of difficult practice, attained the state of a Protector—which is the fruit of those perfections—and engaged in exertion for the welfare of the world. Even when it is said, ‘He has attained enlightenment,’ the cause and effect are shown very clearly. And homage is made only to the Protector who has attained the state of Buddhahood, not to the Bodhisatta, because of the existence of a specific term. Even so, the section on the Vinaya is intended here. And that extends from the time of his going forth until the time of his death. During that very brief time, for a conscientious person, while fulfilling mere virtue which is very easy to do for the welfare of oneself alone, with the intention of removing only one's own suffering—who indeed would not attain the happiness that transcends this world and the next? Indeed, the Blessed One, with the intention of removing the suffering of the entire world, for an immeasurable time of countless crores of aeons, performing extremely difficult deeds, reached a state of joyless fatigue—thus the teacher praises his virtue by way of indirect reference.

Lokahitāyāti ettha lokiyati ettha dukkhanti loko, luyate vā jātijarāmaraṇadukkhehīti loko, iminā sattalokaṃ jātilokañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tasmā tassa sattalokassa [V 0.0008] idhalokaparalokahitaṃ atikkantaparalokānaṃ vā ucchinnalokasamudayānaṃ lokānaṃ[M 0.0008], idha jātiloke okāsaloke vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasaṅkhātañca hitaṃ sampiṇḍetvā lokassa, lokānaṃ, loke vā hitanti sarūpekadesekasesaṃ katvā “lokahita”miccevāha. Nāthoti sabbasattānaṃ āsayānusayacariyādhimuttibhedānurūpadhammadesanasamatthatāya “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi…pe… taṃ suṇāthā”ti (ma. ni. 3.420) evaṃ yācanaṭṭhenāpi nāthateti nātho. Bhikkhūnaṃ vītikkamānurūpaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanena diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikāya ca karuṇāya upagantvā tapati, suttantavasena vā tesaṃ sabbasattānaṃ anusayite kilese karuṇāya ca paññāya ca upagantvā tapati, abhidhammavasena vā te te saṅkhāre aniccādilakkhaṇavasena upaparikkhitvā attano kilese paññāya upecca paricchinditvā tapatīti tapanaṭṭhenāpi nāthateti nātho. Sadevake loke appaṭipuggalattā kenaci appaṭihatadhammadesanattā paramacittissariyappavattito ca issariyaṭṭhenāpi nāthateti nātho. “Dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṃsesī”ti (mahāva. 90) vacanato sampahaṃsanasaṅkhātena āsīsaṭṭhena, paṇidhānato paṭṭhāya “kathaṃ nāmāhaṃ mutto mocayissāmī”tiādinā nayena āsīsaṭṭhena vā nāthateti nāthoti veditabbo, sammāsambuddho. Catūhipi nāthaṅgehi catuvesārajjacatupaṭisambhidādayo sabbepi buddhaguṇā yojetabbā, ativitthārikabhayā pana na yojitā.

Herein, regarding 'for the welfare of the world,' 'world' (loka) is so called because suffering is established therein (lokiyati), or because it is afflicted (luyate) by the sufferings of birth, aging, and death. By this term, both the world of beings and the world of birth are included. Therefore, having combined the welfare in this world and the next for that world of beings; the welfare for the worlds of those who have transcended the next world, for whom the cause of the world has been cut off; and also the welfare designated as a pleasant abiding in the present life, here in the world of birth or in the spatial world—the commentator has said simply 'for the welfare of the world,' having made a partial ellipsis of a similar form from the phrases 'welfare of the world,' 'of the worlds,' or 'in the world.' He is the Protector (Nātha) because he is capable of teaching the Dhamma in accordance with the various dispositions, underlying tendencies, conduct, and inclinations of all beings, and thus he is sought (nāthate) in the sense of being requested, as when he says: 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma… listen to it.' He is the Protector because he torments (tapati): by laying down training rules for bhikkhus in accordance with their transgressions, having approached with compassion for their welfare in this life and the next, he torments the defilements. Or, by way of the Suttas, having approached the latent defilements of all those beings with compassion and wisdom, he torments them. Or, by way of the Abhidhamma, having investigated those various formations by way of the characteristics of impermanence and so on, and having approached and discerned his own defilements with wisdom, he torments them. Thus, he is the Protector also in the sense of tormenting (tapanaṭṭha). He is the Protector also in the sense of sovereignty (issariyaṭṭha), because he is an unparalleled person in the world with its devas, because his teaching of the Dhamma is unopposed by anyone, and because of the exercise of supreme mastery of mind. From the statement, 'He instructed, encouraged, roused, and gladdened them with a talk on the Dhamma,' he is the Protector in the sense of aspiration (āsīsaṭṭha), which is designated as gladdening. Or, starting from his original resolution, in the manner of 'How, being liberated myself, shall I liberate others?', he is the Protector in the sense of aspiration. Thus, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is to be understood as the Protector. All the Buddha’s qualities, such as the four grounds of confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and so on, should be connected by way of these four aspects of a Protector. However, for fear of excessive elaboration, they are not connected here.

Namoti paramatthato buddhaguṇabahumānapabbhārā cittanati, cittanatippabhavā ca vacīkāyanati. Atthu meti pāṭhasesena sambandho. Mahākāruṇikassāti ettha sabbasattavisayattā mahussāhappabhavattā ca mahatī karuṇā mahākaruṇā. Tattha paṇidhānato paṭṭhāya yāvaanupādisesanibbānapurappavesā niyuttoti mahākāruṇiko, bhagavā. Ettha ca mahākāruṇikassāti iminā yathāvuttahetumūlaṃ dasseti. Nikkaruṇo hi paradukkhesu udāsino buddhatthāya paṇidhānamattampi atibhāriyanti maññanto appameyyaṃ kālaṃ atidukkaraṃ hetuṃ pūretvā nāthattasaṅkhātaṃ hetuphalappayojanabhūtaṃ lokahitaṃ kathaṃ karissati. Tasmā sabbaguṇamūlabhūtattā mahākaruṇāguṇameva vaṇṇento “namo mahākāruṇikassā”ti āha. Ettāvatā hetuanurūpaṃ phalaṃ, phalānurūpo [M 0.0009] hetu, dvinnampi anurūpaṃ mūlaṃ, tiṇṇampi anurūpaṃ payojananti ayamattho dassito hoti.

‘Homage’ is, in the ultimate sense, an inclination of the mind (cittanati) bent in great esteem for the Buddha’s qualities; and from that inclination of mind arises the inclination of speech and body. The connection is to be made with the remainder of the text as: ‘May my homage be.’ Here, in ‘to the Greatly Compassionate One,’ great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is ‘great’ because its object is all beings and because it arises from great endeavor. In that regard, he was engaged from his original aspiration right up to his entry into the city of Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates; thus he is the Greatly Compassionate One, the Blessed One. And here, by the words ‘to the Greatly Compassionate One,’ he indicates the root of the aforementioned cause. For how could one without compassion, who is indifferent to the suffering of others and who would consider even the mere aspiration for Buddhahood to be too burdensome, fulfill the extremely difficult cause for an immeasurable time and accomplish the welfare of the world—which is the purpose of the cause and the fruit, designated as Protectorship? Therefore, because great compassion is the root of all qualities, praising this very quality, he says, ‘Homage to the Greatly Compassionate One.’ By this much, the following meaning is shown: the fruit is appropriate to the cause, the cause is appropriate to the fruit, the root is appropriate to both, and the purpose is appropriate to all three.

Evaṃ acchariyapuriso, nātho nāthaguṇe ṭhito;

Namoraho anāthassa, nāthamānassa sampadaṃ.

Thus, the wonderful person, the Protector established in the qualities of a Protector, is worthy of homage, bringing to fulfillment the aspiration of the unprotected who esteem him as their refuge.

Ettha [V 0.0009] siyā “anekesu bhagavato guṇesu vijjamānesu kasmā ‘mahākāruṇikassā’ti ekameva gahita”nti? Uccate –

Here, it might be asked: “Among the many virtues of the Blessed One that exist, why is only ‘to the Greatly Compassionate One’ taken?” The reply is given:

Dosahīnassa satthassa, codanā tu na vijjate;

Dosayuttamasatthañca, tasmā codanā apattakāti.

For a treatise that is free from faults, no accusation exists; and a faulty work is not a true treatise. Therefore, the accusation is inapplicable.

Na mayā codanā katā, kintu pucchā eva katā. Apica –

No accusation was made by me, but rather, only a question was asked. Furthermore:

“Phalaṃ satipi rukkheḍḍhe, na patatyavikampite;

Codanā yā’tthu satthānaṃ, pucchanātyatthaphalaṃ mahatā.

Though there is fruit on a prosperous tree, it does not fall if unshaken; likewise, whether it be an accusation or a question directed at the treatises, the fruit of its meaning is exceedingly great.

“Nabhottuṃ kurute sammā, gahituṃ nāḍḍhate ghaṭaṃ;

Akkhepe hi kate tadi-cchissāṇābuddhibandhanaṃ.

One does not make proper use of the teaching, nor does one strive with effort to grasp it. For when a reproach is made against a faultless teacher, for one who desires such fault-finding, it becomes a fetter to their authority and wisdom.

“Yathā himapado paddho, pabuddho gandhalimpiyā;

Bhinnatthaviramassevaṃ, satthakatātthalimpiyā”ti. –

Just as a lotus bestowed by the moon awakens when anointed with scent, so too a treatise free from broken meaning is well-made by being anointed with its meaning.

Evaṃ cekaṃ –

And thus it is said:

Sammāpi codanā taṃ khalu, guravo vivākyā vivaddha;

Yatisissā āghaṭṭitāti-vākyenābhyadhikaṃ gopaya.

Even when an exhortation is proper, it indeed affects teachers who have diverse speech and growing ascetic-disciples. Therefore, guard against excessive speech.

Saravatī āceraṃ kiliṭṭhā, tadicchissajitāttānaṃ;

Jayatyattānamācero, sadassasseva sārathīti. –

A disciple who is accustomed to seeing the teacher's fault, having speech that pierces like an arrow, afflicts the teacher and is thereby defeated himself. Just as a charioteer conquers his own horse, the teacher conquers the disciple who is dependent on him. Thus it should also be said.

Atroccate –

Herein, what is fitting is said:

Yassa hi vākyasahassaṃ, vākye vākye satañca jivhā;

Nāmaṃ dasabalaguṇapadesaṃ, vattuṃ kappenapi na sakkā.

For one who has a thousand mouths, and in each mouth a hundred tongues, it would not be possible, even in a whole aeon, to speak the name that indicates the virtues of the Ten-Powered One.

Yathā [M 0.0010][V 0.0010] –

For example:

Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassāti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.425; udā. aṭṭha. 53; cariyā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) –

Even if the Buddha, speaking of nothing else, were to speak the praise of a Buddha for a whole life-aeon, that long-lasting aeon would be exhausted in the interim, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Cottattā na sakkā bhagavataṃ guṇānamavasesābhidhātuṃ.

And because it has been so stated, it is not possible to declare the virtues of the Blessed Ones without remainder.

Apica –

Furthermore:

Yathā tvaṃ sattānaṃ, dasabala tathā ñāṇakaruṇā;

Guṇadvandaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, tava guṇagaṇā nāma tiguṇāti. –

O Ten-Powered One, just as you are excellent among beings, so too is the pair of wisdom and compassion excellent. Your wisdom and compassion, a collection of virtues, are called exceedingly excellent virtues.

Sabbaguṇaseṭṭhattā mūlattā ca ekameva vuttaṃ. Atha vā “chasu asādhāraṇañāṇesu aññatarattā taggahaṇena sesāpi gahitāva sahacaraṇalakkhaṇenā”ti ca vadanti. Visesato panettha abhidhammassa kevalaṃ paññāvisayattā abhidhammaṭṭhakathārambhe ācariyena “karuṇā viya sattesu, paññā yassa mahesino”ti paññāguṇo vaṇṇito tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayacaayādhimuttibhedānurūpaparicchindanapaññāya, sattesu mahākaruṇāya ca adhikārattā. Suttantaṭṭhakathārambhe “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ, paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti bhagavato ubhopi paññākaruṇāguṇā vaṇṇitā. Idha pana vinaye āsayādinirapekkhaṃ kevalaṃ karuṇāya pākatikasattenāpi asotabbārahaṃ suṇanto, apucchitabbārahaṃ pucchanto, avattabbārahañca vadanto sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesīti karuṇāguṇoyeveko vaṇṇitoti veditabbo.

Only the one virtue of compassion was stated because it is the most excellent of all virtues and because it is the root cause. Alternatively, some say: 'Because it is one among the six unshared knowledges, by taking it the others are also indeed taken by the method of concomitance.' Here, however, in particular, because the Abhidhamma is the domain of wisdom alone, at the beginning of the Abhidhamma commentary the Teacher praised the virtue of wisdom, saying: 'The wisdom of the Great Sage towards beings is like compassion.' Because it is the domain of the wisdom that discerns in accordance with the various inclinations, latent tendencies, conduct, and dispositions of those beings, and of the great compassion towards all beings, at the beginning of the Suttanta commentaries both the virtues of wisdom and compassion of the Blessed One were praised: 'His heart cooled by compassion, the darkness of delusion dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.' But here in this Vinaya, without regard for inclinations and so on, solely through compassion—hearing what is not fit to be heard even by an ordinary being, asking what is not fit to be asked, and saying what is not fit to be said—he laid down the training rule. Therefore, it should be understood that only the one virtue of compassion was praised by the Teacher.

Paññādayā attaparatthahetū,

Tadanvayā sabbaguṇā jinassa;

Ubho guṇā te guṇasāgarassa,

Vuttā idhācariyavarena tasmā.

Wisdom and compassion are the causes for the welfare of oneself and others; all the qualities of the Conqueror follow from them. Therefore, both those qualities of the Conqueror, the ocean of virtues, have been stated here by the noble Teacher.

Ettāvatā [V 0.0011] aṭṭhakathādigāthā,

Samāsato vuttapadatthasobhā;

Ayampi vitthāranayoti cāhaṃ,

Uddhaṃ ito te paṭisaṃkhipāmi.

Thus far, the preliminary verse of the commentary is beautiful with the meaning of its words stated briefly. This method of explanation is the detailed one; and without continuing in this manner, I will summarize them from this point onward.

Dutiyagāthāya [M 0.0011] asambudhanti dhammānaṃ yathāsabhāvaṃ abujjhanto. Buddhanisevitanti buddhānubuddhapaccekabuddhehi gocarabhāvanāsevanāhi yathārahaṃ nisevitaṃ. Bhavā bhavanti vattamānabhavato aññaṃ bhavaṃ gacchati upagacchati, paṭipajjatīti attho. Atha vā bhavoti sassatadiṭṭhi. Tassa paṭipakkhattā abhavoti ucchedadiṭṭhi. Bhavoti vā vuddhi. Abhavoti hāni. Bhavoti vā duggati. Abhavoti sugati. “Appamāṇā dhammā, asekkhā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. tikamātikā 13, 11) viya hi vuddhiatthattā akārassa. Bhāvayatīti bhavo, jāti. Bhavatīti vā bhavo. Savikārā bahuvidhakhandhuppatti dīpitā. Abhavoti vināso, jātibhāvaṃ maraṇabhāvañca gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha arahantānaṃ maraṇampi khaṇikavasena gahetabbaṃ. Bhavesu abhavo bhavābhavo, taṃ bhavābhavaṃ, bhavesu abhāvapaññattiṃ gacchatīti attho. Jīvalokoti sattaloko, saṅkhāralokaokāsalokānaṃ bhavābhavagamanāsambhavato sattalokaṃ jīvalokoti viseseti. Avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsinoti ettha navapi lokuttaradhammā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Apacayagāmitā hi catumaggadhammassa odhiso avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃso, so assa atthi, tadārammaṇaṃ hutvā tattha sahāyabhāvūpagamanena nibbānassāpi. Yathāha “yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo…pe… idaṃ vuccati nibbāna”nti. Arahattassāpi tathā rāgādikkhayavacanasabbhāvato. Phalasāmaññena tiṇṇampi phalānaṃ atthīti navavidhopesa “avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsī”ti vuccati. Atha vā sahacaraṇalakkhaṇakaāraṇatāya paṭipakkhagocaraggahaṇatā. Anabhihitopi hi dhammassa tatrābhihitova bujjhitabbo iti vacanato kāraṇagocaraggahaṇena cattāripi phalāni gahitāni. Narakādīsu apatamānaṃ dhāreti sugatiyaṃ uppādanenāti dhammo. Puna sugatimhi ajananakārī akusaladhamme nivāretvā poseti pavatteti vaḍḍhetīti dhammo. So pana kāmarūpārūpabhedato tividho accantasukhāvahanato, tatopi uttamattā dhammavaro.

In the second verse, regarding `asambudhanti`: not knowing the true nature of phenomena as it is. Regarding `Buddhanisevitaṃ`: it is suitably resorted to by Buddhas, Anubuddhas, and Paccekabuddhas through resorting to a suitable range and resorting to development. Regarding `bhavābhavaṃ`: one goes from the present existence to another existence, approaches it, and undertakes it; this is the meaning. Alternatively, `bhava` is the eternalist view; being its opposite, `abhava` is the annihilationist view. Or, `bhava` is growth, and `abhava` is decline. Or, `bhava` is a woeful destination, and `abhava` is a happy destination. For, just as in such phrases as 'immeasurable dhammas, dhammas of the adept,' the letter 'a' has the meaning of augmentation. 'It causes to become' (`bhāvayati`), therefore it is `bhavo` (becoming), i.e., birth. Or, 'it becomes' (`bhavati`), therefore it is `bhavo`. The arising of the manifold aggregates with their alterations is shown. `Abhavo` is destruction; it is said that one goes to the state of birth and the state of death. Here, even the death of Arahants should be taken as momentary death. `Abhavo` (non-becoming) in `bhavesu` (in existences) is `bhavābhava`. `Taṃ bhavābhavaṃ` means one goes to the conceptual designation of non-existence in existences; this is the meaning. `Jīvaloka` (the world of the living) is the world of beings; because going to existence and non-existence is not possible for the world of formations and the world of space, it specifies the world of beings with the term `jīvaloka`. Regarding `avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsino` (destroyer of the net of defilements starting with ignorance): here, the nine supramundane dhammas are included. Indeed, for the Dhamma of the four paths, the state of proceeding by destroying defilements is, specifically, the destruction of the net of defilements starting with ignorance. This exists for it. It also exists for Nibbāna, by being its object and by resorting to a state of companionship with it. As it is said: 'Friend, the destruction of lust... this is called Nibbāna.' Likewise, for the fruit of Arahantship also, this quality exists because of the presence of the term expressing the destruction of lust and so on. By the commonality of fruit, it also exists for the other three fruits. Therefore, this ninefold Dhamma is called 'the destroyer of the net of defilements starting with ignorance.' Alternatively, because it is a cause known by the characteristic of association, there is the grasping of the opposing object. For, according to the saying, 'Even what is not stated of the Dhamma there should be understood as stated,' the four fruits are also included by grasping the cause (the path) and the object (Nibbāna). It is 'Dhamma' because it sustains a being, preventing them from falling into hell and other woeful states, by causing them to arise in a happy destination. Again, it is 'Dhamma' because it prevents unwholesome dhammas that cause non-arising in a happy destination, and it nurtures, promotes, and increases wholesome states. That Dhamma, however, is threefold by the distinction of the sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere. Because it brings ultimate happiness and because it is supreme even among those, it is the excellent Dhamma (`dhammavaro`).

Etthāha – “catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasaccānaṃ ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamidaṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ sandhāvitaṃ saṃsarita’nti (dī. ni. 2.155; mahāva. 287) vacanato catusaccadhammaṃ asambudhaṃ bhavā bhavaṃ gacchati jīvalokoti siddhaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ asambudhaṃ gacchati, tasseva [V 0.0012] “tassā”ti ante taṃniddesena niyamanato catusaccadhammopi avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsī [M 0.0012] dhammavaroti cāpajjati. Aññathā “namo avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsino dhammavarassa tassā”ti taṃniddesena samānavibhattikaraṇaṃ na yujjati atippasaṅganiyamanato, “avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsino dhammavarassā”ti vacanaṃ visesanavacanaṃ. Tasmā dukkhasamudayasaccānaṃ tabbhāvappasaṅgo natthīti ce? Na, taṃniddesena samānavibhattiṭṭhāne avisesitattā. Api ca maggasaccanirodhasaccesu phalānaṃ apariyāpannattā nava lokuttaradhammā saṅgahitāti vacanavirodho, phalānaṃ asaṅgahe verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ na kevalaṃ ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca, api ca ariyaphaladhammehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttañhetaṃ “rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ…pe… dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti (vi. va. 887) vacanavirodho cāti pubbāparaviruddhā esā gāthā sāsanaviruddhā cā”ti? Vuccate – sabbametamayuttaṃ vuttagāthatthājānanato. Ettha hi ācariyena pavattipavattihetuvisayavibhāgo ca dassito. Kathaṃ? Tattha asambudhanti asambodho, so atthato avijjā, tāya ca taṇhupādānāni gahitāni, tayopi te dhammā samudayasaccaṃ, bhavābhavanti ettha dukkhasaccaṃ vuttaṃ. Sugatiduggatippabhedo hi bhavo atthato pañcupādānakkhandhā honti. “Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti (mahāva. 1) vacanato dukkhappavatti pavatti nāma, dukkhasamudayo pavattihetu nāma, avijjāsaṅkhātassa ca pavattihetussa aggahitaggahaṇena nirodhamaggasaccadvayaṃ visayo nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ “tattha katamā avijjā? Dukkhe aññāṇaṃ…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇa”nti (vibha. 226).

Herein, the objector says: 'Monks, due to not fully understanding and not penetrating the Four Noble Truths, this long course has been run through and wandered through by me as well as by you' (Dī. Ni. 2.155; Mahāva. 287). From this statement, it is established that the world of beings, not understanding the Dhamma of the Four Truths, goes from existence to existence. Therefore, because that which is not understood is what one transmigrates through, and because this very thing is specified at the end by the demonstrative pronoun 'tassa', it follows that the Dhamma of the Four Truths is also the excellent Dhamma that destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance. Otherwise, making it have the same case ending with the demonstrative pronoun 'tassa' in the phrase 'Homage to that excellent Dhamma that destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance' would not be suitable, due to the over-extended specification; the phrase 'to the excellent Dhamma that destroys the net of defilements such as ignorance' is a qualifying phrase. Therefore, if one were to say, 'Is there not the consequence of the truths of suffering and its origin being that excellent Dhamma?' The reply is: No, because in the instance of having the same case ending with that demonstrative pronoun, it is not specified. Furthermore, because the fruits are not included in the truths of the path and cessation, there is a contradiction with the statement that the nine supramundane Dhammas are included. If the fruits are not included, there would be a contradiction with the statement in the commentary on the Verañja section: 'not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the scriptural Dhamma along with the dhammas of the Noble Fruits.' And there would be a contradiction with the statement, 'Come for refuge to this Dhamma... free from passion, unshakable, sorrowless...' (Vimānavatthu 887). Therefore, this verse is contradictory to what comes before and after, and it is also contradictory to the Dispensation.'

It is replied: All of this is unsuitable, due to not knowing the meaning of the aforementioned verse. For herein, the teacher has shown the distinction between the domains of the process of existence, the cause of that process, and the object. How? Therein, 'asambudhaṃ' means non-understanding; that, in essence, is ignorance. And by that, craving and clinging are taken. Those three dhammas are the truth of the origin. Herein, by 'bhavābhavaṃ' (from existence to existence), the truth of suffering is stated. For existence, which is differentiated into good and bad destinations, is in essence the five aggregates subject to clinging. In accordance with the statement, 'Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering' (Mahāva. 1), the process of suffering is called 'the process of existence'; the origin of suffering is called 'the cause of the process of existence'. And by grasping what was not previously grasped of the cause of the process of existence, which is designated as ignorance, the two truths of cessation and the path are called the 'object'. For it is said: 'Therein, what is ignorance? It is not knowing suffering... not knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering' (Vibh. 226).

Ettha ca nirodhasaccaṃ buddhena gocarāsevanāya āsevitaṃ, maggasaccaṃ bhāvanāsevanāya. Ettāvatā asambudhaṃ buddhanisevitaṃ yanti upayogappatto yo visayo nirodho ca maggo ca, tassa yathāvuttāvijjādikilesajālattayaviddhaṃsino namo dhammavarassāti ayaṃ gāthāya attho. Pariyattidhammopi kilesaviddhaṃsanassa suttantanayena upanissayapaccayattā kilesaviddhaṃsanasīlatāya “avijjādikilesajālaviddhaṃsī”ti vattuṃ sambhavati. Evañhi sati rāgavirāgāti gāthattho, so dhammaṃ deseti…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetīti suttattho ca asesato gahito hoti. Atha [M 0.0013] vā imāya gāthāya kevalaṃ pariyattidhammova gahito hoti, yaṃ sandhāyāha “so dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ…pe… brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.190; pārā. 1), tampi asambudhaṃ buddheheva nisevitaṃ gocarāsevanāya anaññanisevitaṃ. Yathāha “bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā…pe… bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.146).

And herein, the Truth of Cessation is frequented by the Buddha through the practice of its domain, and the Truth of the Path through the practice of development. To this extent, this is the meaning of the verse: Homage to that excellent Dhamma, the destroyer of the aforementioned triple net of defilements beginning with ignorance, which is the object—namely, Cessation and the Path—that is reached by application, not comprehended by others, and frequented by the Buddhas. The scriptural Dhamma also, because it is a decisive support condition for the destruction of defilements according to the Suttanta method, and because of its nature of destroying defilements, can be called the 'destroyer of the net of defilements beginning with ignorance.' For when this is so, the meaning of the verse beginning 'dispassion for lust,' and the meaning of the Sutta 'He teaches the Dhamma... He proclaims the holy life,' are grasped completely, without remainder. Alternatively, by this verse, only the scriptural Dhamma is taken, in reference to which it is said, 'He teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning... He proclaims the holy life' (Dī. Ni. 1.190; Pārā. 1). That too, not being comprehended by others, is frequented only by the Buddhas through the practice of its domain, and not frequented by any other. As it is said: 'Our Dhammas, venerable sir, are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, with the Blessed One as their refuge... having heard from the Blessed One, the monks will bear it in mind' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.146).

Tatiyagāthāya [V 0.0013] sīlādayo kiñcāpi lokiyalokuttarā yathāsambhavaṃ labbhanti, tathāpi ante “ariyasaṅgha”nti vacanato sīlādayo cattāro dhammakkhandhā lokuttarāva. Ettha ca “sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇappabhutīhī”ti vattabbe sarūpekasesaṃ katvā “vimuttiñāṇappabhutīhī”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca kiñcāpi vimuttīti phaladhammāva sutte adhippetā, tathāpi “maggā vuṭṭhahitvā maggaṃ paccavekkhati. Pahīne kilese paccavekkhati. Phalaṃ paccavekkhati. Nibbānaṃ paccavekkhatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.410) vacanato maggādipaccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ vimuttiñāṇanti veditabbaṃ. Vimutti vimokkho khayoti hi atthato ekaṃ. “Khaye ñāṇaṃ anuppāde ñāṇanti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142; dī. ni. 3.304) ettha khayo nāma maggo, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayoti phalanibbānānaṃ adhivacana”nti sutte āgatameva. Pahīnakilesānaṃ khayo pākatiko khayo eva. Pabhuti-saddena tisso vijjā cha abhiññā catasso paṭisambhidāti evamādayo guṇā saṅgahitā. Samannāgamaṭṭhena aparihīnaṭṭhena ca yutto. Khettaṃ janānaṃ kusalatthikānanti “anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti suttato kusalassa viruhanaṭṭhānattā, suttantanayena upanissayapaccayattā ca kāmaṃ kusalassa khettaṃ hoti saṅgho, na kusalatthikānaṃ janānaṃ. Tasmā na yujjatīti ce? Na, suttatthasambhavato. Sutte “anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341) hi vuttaṃ. Kassa lokassa? Puññatthikassa khettaṃ saṅgho, puññupanissayattā puññakkhettaṃ hoti saṅgho, kusalatthikānanti ca vuccanti. Lokepi hi devadattassa khettaṃ yaññadattassa khettaṃ sāliyavupanissayattā sālikhettaṃ yavakhettanti ca vuccati. Ariyasaṅghanti vigatakilesattā ariyaṃ parisuddhaṃ ariyānaṃ, ariyabhāvaṃ vā pattaṃ sīladiṭṭhisāmaññena saṅghatattā saṅghaṃ. “Ariya-saddena sammutisaṅghaṃ nivāretī”ti keci likhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ vimuttiñāṇaguṇaggahaṇena visesitattā. Sirasāti [M 0.0014] iminā kāmaṃ kāyanatiṃ dasseti, tathāpi uttamasaṅghe guṇagāravena uttamaṅgameva niddisanto “sirasā namāmī”tyāha. Sirassa pana uttamatā uttamānaṃ cakkhusotindriyānaṃ nissayattā, tesaṃ uttamatā ca dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyahetutāya veditabbā. Etthāha – anusandhikusalo

In the third verse, although virtues such as morality, etc., may be obtained as worldly or supramundane according to what is possible, yet at the end, due to the phrase “the noble Saṅgha,” the four Dhamma-aggregates, beginning with morality, are only supramundane. And here, though it should be said “with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge of liberation, etc.,” by way of a residual of the same form, it is stated as “with the knowledge of liberation, etc.” And here, although in the Suttas “liberation” is intended to mean only the fruition-states, still, according to the statement, “Having arisen from the path, one reviews the path. One reviews the abandoned defilements. One reviews the fruition. One reviews Nibbāna,” the knowledge that reviews the path, etc., should be understood as the knowledge of liberation. For liberation (vimutti), emancipation (vimokkha), and destruction (khaya) are one in meaning. In the phrase, “knowledge in destruction, knowledge in non-arising,” here ‘destruction’ is the path, while ‘destruction of lust, destruction of hatred’ are designations for fruition and Nibbāna, as has indeed come in the Suttas. For those whose defilements are abandoned, destruction is natural destruction indeed. By the word ‘etc.’, qualities such as the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the four analytical knowledges are included. It is appropriate by the meaning of being endowed and by the meaning of being unimpaired. Regarding ‘a field for people seeking wholesome states’: from the Sutta, “the unsurpassed field of merit for the world,” because it is a place for the growth of the wholesome, and by the Sutta method, because it is a decisive support condition, the Saṅgha is indeed a field for the wholesome, not for people seeking wholesome states. If it is said, ‘Therefore, it is not fitting’? No, because the meaning of the Sutta is possible. For in the Sutta it is said, “the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” For which world? The Saṅgha is a field for one who seeks merit; because it is a support for merit, the Saṅgha is a field of merit, and they are called ‘those who seek wholesome states.’ For in the world too, Devadatta’s field and Yaññadatta’s field are called a rice field and a barley field because they are a support for rice and barley. The ‘noble Saṅgha’ (ariyasaṅgha): because of being free from defilements, it is noble (ariya), pure; or it is of the noble ones (ariyānaṃ); or it is a Saṅgha that has attained the state of a noble one (ariyabhāva), so called because it is grouped together by a commonality of virtue and view. Some write, “By the word ‘noble’ (ariya), it excludes the conventional Saṅgha,” but that is not good, because it is already specified by the inclusion of the quality of the knowledge of liberation. By this word ‘with the head’ (sirasā), it indeed shows inclination with the body; yet, with reverence for the qualities of the supreme Saṅgha, the commentator, wishing to point out only the highest limb, said, “I bow with the head.” But the supremacy of the head is due to its being the support of the supreme faculties of the eye and ear, and their supremacy should be understood as being the cause for unsurpassed seeing and unsurpassed hearing. Here, one skilled in making connections says:

“Upogghāto padañceva, padattho padaviggaho;

Codanāpratyavajjānaṃ, byākhyā tantassa chabbidhā”ti. –

Introduction, the word, the meaning of the word, the analysis of the word, objection, and reply—the explanation of a treatise is sixfold.

Evamavatvā kasmā ratanattayapaṇāmaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttanti? Vuccate – satācārattā. Ācāro kiresa sappurisānaṃ, yadidaṃ saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayapūjāvidhānaṃ. Tasmā “satācārato bhaṭṭhā mā mayaṃ homā”ti [V 0.0014] karīyati, catugambhīrabhāvayuttañca vinayapiṭakaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmassa mahāsamuddaṃ ogāhantassa viya paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatassāpi mahantaṃ bhayaṃ hoti, bhayakkhayāvahañcetaṃ ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇajanitaṃ paṇāmapūjāvidhānaṃ. Yathāha “evaṃ buddhaṃ sarantāna”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.249). Apicācariyo satthupūjāvidhānena asatthari satthābhinivesassa lokassa yathābhūtaṃ satthari eva sammāsambuddhe satthusambhāvanaṃ uppādeti, asatthari satthusambhāvanaṃ pariccajāpeti, “tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ attano dahatī”ti vuttadosaṃ pariharati. Antarāyabahulattā khandhasantatiyā vippakatāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya attano āyuvaṇṇasukhabalānaṃ parikkhayasambhavāsaṅkāya “abhivādanasīlissa…pe… āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ bala”nti (dha. pa. 109) vuttānisaṃse yāva saṃvaṇṇanāpariyosānā pattheti. Api cettha buddhassa bhagavato paṇāmapūjāvidhānaṃ sammāsambuddhabhāvādhigamatthaṃ buddhayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhaṃ janeti. Lokiyalokuttarabhedassa, lokuttarasseva vā saddhammassa pūjāvidhānaṃ paccekabuddhabhāvādhigamatthaṃ paccekabuddhayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhaṃ janeti. Saddhammapaṭivedhamattābhilāsino hi te. Paramatthasaṅghapūjāvidhānaṃ paramatthasaṅghabhāvādhigamatthaṃ sāvakayānaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ ussāhaṃ janeti, maṅgalādīni vā sātthāni anantarāyāni ciraṭṭhitikāni bahumatāni ca bhavantīti evaṃladdhikānaṃ cittaparitosanatthaṃ “pūjā ca pūjaneyyāna”nti bhagavatā pasatthamaṅgalaṃ karoti. Vuccate ca –

Without saying thus, why is the homage to the Triple Gem stated first? It is said: because of the practice of the virtuous. This is indeed the practice of good people, namely, the performance of homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of an exposition. Therefore, it is done with the thought, 'Let us not fall away from the practice of the virtuous.' And for one who wishes to expound the Vinaya Piṭaka, which is endowed with fourfold profundity, even if endowed with proficiency in wisdom, there is great fear, like one entering the great ocean. This homage and veneration, born from the recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem, brings about the destruction of fear. As it is said: 'Thus, for those recollecting the Buddha...' and so on. Furthermore, the teacher, by the method of venerating the Teacher, causes the world, which wrongly adheres to a non-teacher as the Teacher, to generate the true recognition of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One as the Teacher indeed. He causes them to abandon the recognition of a non-teacher as the Teacher and avoids the fault stated as, 'He claims the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own.' Because the continuity of the aggregates is fraught with many dangers, and fearing the possible decline of one’s own life, beauty, happiness, and strength while the Vinaya exposition is still unfinished, one aspires, until the very end of the exposition, for the benefits stated: 'For one who is habitually respectful... life, beauty, happiness, and strength.' Here also, the homage and veneration to the Blessed One, the Buddha, generates effort in those who practice the Buddhayāna for the attainment of perfect self-enlightenment. The method of veneration of the true Dhamma, whether worldly or supramundane—or solely the supramundane—generates effort in those who practice the Paccekabuddhayāna for the attainment of Paccekabuddhahood. For they desire only the penetration of the true Dhamma. The method of veneration of the ultimate Sangha generates effort in those who practice the Sāvakayana for the attainment of the state of the ultimate Sangha. Or, for the contentment of the minds of those who hold the view that auspicious acts are beneficial, free from obstacles, long-lasting, and highly esteemed, he performs the auspicious act praised by the Blessed One as, 'Homage to those worthy of homage.' And it is said:

“Maṅgalaṃ [M 0.0015] bhagavā buddho, dhammo saṅgho ca maṅgalaṃ;

Maṅgalādīni sātthāni, sīghaṃ sijjhanti sabbaso.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, is auspicious; the Dhamma and the Sangha are auspicious. Through auspicious acts, beneficial results are quickly and completely accomplished.

“Satthu pūjāvidhānena, evamādī bahū guṇe;

Labhatīti vijānanto, satthupūjāparo siyā”ti.

Knowing that one obtains many such virtues by the method of venerating the Teacher, one should be devoted to venerating the Teacher.

Ettha ca satthupadhānattā dhammasaṅghānaṃ pūjāvidhānaṃ satthupūjāvidhānamicceva daṭṭhabbaṃ sāsanato lokato ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Here, because the Teacher is primary, the method of venerating the Dhamma and the Sangha should be regarded as precisely the method of venerating the Teacher, both from the perspective of the Dispensation and of the world. Therefore, this is said:

“Satthā”ti dhammo sugatena vutto;

Nibbānakāle yamato sa satthā;

Suvatthigāthāsu “tathāgato”ti;

Saṅgho ca vutto yamato sa satthā.

The Dhamma was called 'Teacher' by the Sugata; for which reason, at the time of his Parinibbāna, it is the Teacher. In the Suvatthi verses, the Sangha is also spoken of as 'Tathāgata'; for which reason, it is the Teacher.

Kiñca [V 0.0015] bhiyyo –

Furthermore:

Dhammakāyo yato satthā, dhammo satthā tato mato;

Dhammaṭṭhito so saṅgho ca, satthusaṅkhyaṃ nigacchati.

Since the Teacher is the Dhamma-body, the Dhamma is therefore considered the Teacher; and that Sangha, being established in the Dhamma, also attains the designation of 'Teacher'.

Santi hi loke vattāro kosagataṃ asiṃ gahetvā ṭhitaṃ purisaṃ visuṃ aparāmasitvā “asiṃ gahetvā ṭhito eso”ti. Tenevāha cāriyamātraccevā –

For indeed, in the world there are speakers who, without considering the sheath separately, say of a man standing holding a sword in its sheath, 'This one stands holding a sword.' Therefore, the teacher Ācariyamātracceva said:

“Namatthu buddharatnāya, dhammaratnāya te namo;

Namatthu saṅgharatnāya, tiratnasamavānayī”ti.

May there be homage to the Buddha-jewel; homage to your Dhamma-jewel. May there be homage to the Sangha-jewel. The three jewels bring forth equal benefit.

Apica sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇanimittānuttaravimokkhapātubhāvābhisaṅkhātaṃ khandhasantānamupādāya “buddho”ti yadi paññāpiyati, dhammo paṇāmārahoti kā eva kathā, saṅgho ca “saṅghe gotami dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi saṅgho cā”ti vuttattā bhājananti dīpeti. Atha vā “buddhasubodhito dhammo ācariyaparamparāya suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittatelamiva aparihāpetvā yāvajjatanā ābhatattā eva mādisānampi sotadvāramanuppatto”ti saṅghassa ācariyo atīva ādarena paṇāmaṃ karoti “sirasā namāmī”ti.

Moreover, if the continuum of aggregates is designated as 'Buddha' with reference to the manifestation of unsurpassed liberation, which is characterized by unobstructed knowledge in all phenomena, then what need is there to say that the Dhamma is worthy of homage? And it is shown that the Sangha is a worthy recipient because it was said, 'Gotamī, give to the Sangha. When you give to the Sangha, I myself will be venerated, as will the Sangha.' Or alternatively, because 'the Dhamma, well-understood by the Buddha, has been brought down through the lineage of teachers to the present day without diminution, like oil poured into a golden vessel, and has thus reached the ear-door of even persons such as I,' the teacher pays homage with extreme reverence, saying, 'I bow with my head.'

Evaṃ [M 0.0016] anekavidhaṃ paṇāmappayojanaṃ vadanti, ācariyena pana adhippetappayojanaṃ attanā eva vuttaṃ “iccevamaccantanamassaneyya”ntiādinā catutthagāthāya. Iccevanti ettha iti-saddo ratanattayapūjāvidhānaparisamattattho. Yadi evaṃ yathāvihitamattameva pūjāvidhānaṃ arahati ratanattayaṃ, na tato uddhanti āpajjatīti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ “evamaccantanamassaneyya”nti āha. Tattha evanti iminā yathāvuttavidhiṃ dasseti. Yathāvuttena vidhinā, aññena vā tādisena accantameva muhuttamapi aṭṭhatvā abhikkhaṇaṃ nirantaraṃ niyamena namassanārahaṃ namassamānassa hitamahapphalakaraṇatoti attho. Evaṃvidhaṃ dullabhaṭṭhena mahapphalaṭṭhena ca siddhaṃ ratanabhāvaṃ ratanattayaṃ namassamāno yaṃ puññābhisandaṃ alatthaṃ alabhiṃ. Akusalamalaṃ tadaṅgādippahānena punātīti puññaṃ. Kilesadarathappaṭippassaddhiyā sītalattā cittaṃ abhisandetīti abhisando. Puññañca taṃ abhisando cāti puññābhisando, taṃ puññābhisandaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “puññamahattaṃ”nti bhaṇanti, “vipula”nti vacanato so attho na yujjatīti ācariyo. Atha vā puññānaṃ abhisando puññābhisando[V 0.0016], taṃ puññābhisandaṃ. Sanda savaneti dhātu. Tasmā puññasotaṃ puññussayanti attho yujjati, taṃ pana vipulaṃ, na parittanti dassitaṃ vipula-saddena.

Thus, teachers say the purpose of homage is of many kinds; however, the intended purpose was stated by the teacher himself with the fourth verse beginning, 'iccevamaccantanamassaneyya'. Herein, in 'iccevaṃ', the word 'iti' has the meaning of the completion of the procedure of venerating the Triple Gem. If it were so, the Triple Gem would be worthy of only the prescribed procedure of veneration and nothing beyond it. To prevent this undesirable implication, he said, 'evamaccantanamassaneyya'. Therein, by 'evaṃ', he indicates the aforementioned procedure. The meaning is: because it brings about welfare and great fruit for one who, by the aforementioned procedure or by another similar one, pays homage to that which is worthy of homage—constantly, without stopping even for a moment, repeatedly, uninterruptedly, and regularly. Paying homage to the Triple Gem, established in its nature as a gem of this kind by being difficult to obtain and by being of great fruit, whatever accumulation of merit I have obtained. Because it purifies the stain of the unwholesome by means of abandonment, beginning with momentary abandonment, it is called 'puñña' (merit). Because, through the calming of the torment of defilements, it is cool and soothes the mind, it is called 'abhisanda'. It is 'puñña' and it is 'abhisanda'; therefore, it is 'puññābhisanda' (an accumulation of merit). In the Gaṇṭhipada commentaries, however, they say it means 'the greatness of merit', but the teacher states that this meaning is not suitable because of the word 'vipula' (abundant). Alternatively, 'puññābhisando' is a stream or accumulation of merits. The root 'sanda' is in the sense of 'flowing'. Therefore, the meaning 'a current of merit' or 'an accumulation of merit' is suitable. That it is, however, abundant and not limited, is shown by the word 'vipula'.

Pañcamagāthā yasmiṃ vinayapiṭake pāḷito ca atthato ca anūnaṃ lajjīpuggalesu pavattanaṭṭhena ṭhite sakalaṃ tividhampi sāsanaṃ tesveva puggalesu patiṭṭhitaṃ hoti. Kassa sāsananti ce? Aṭṭhitassa bhagavato. Bhagavā hi ṭhitihetubhūtāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā abhāvena aṭṭhitoti vuccati. Ucchedadiṭṭhiko hi paraloke nirapekkho kevalaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogamanuyuñjanto tiṭṭhati, na paralokahitāni puññāni kattuṃ byāvaṭo hoti, sassatadiṭṭhiko tāni kattuṃ āyūhati. Bhagavā pana tathā atiṭṭhanto anāyūhanto majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanto sayañca oghaṃ tari, pare ca tāresi. Yathāha “appatiṭṭhaṃ khvāhaṃ, āvuso, anāyūhaṃ oghamatari”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.1). Catubrahmavihāravasena sattesu suṭṭhu sammā ca ṭhitassāti atthavasena vā susaṇṭhitassa. Susaṇṭhitattā hesa kevalaṃ sattānaṃ dukkhaṃ apanetukāmo hitaṃ upasaṃharitukāmo sampattiyā ca pamodito apakkhapatito ca hutvā vinayaṃ deseti, tasmā imasmiṃ [M 0.0017] vinayasaṃvaṇṇanādhikāre sāruppāya thutiyā thomento āha “susaṇṭhitassā”ti. Gaṇṭhipade pana “manāpiye ca kho, bhikkhave, kammavipāke paccupaṭṭhite”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.35; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.386) suttassa, “susaṇṭhānā surūpatā”ti (khu. pā. 8.11) suttassa ca vasena susaṇṭhitassāti attho vutto, so adhippetādhikārānurūpo na hoti. Amissanti kiṃ vinayaṃ amissaṃ, udāhu pubbācariyānubhāvanti? Nobhayampi. Amissā eva hi vinayaṭṭhakathā. Tasmā bhāvanapuṃsakavasena amissaṃ taṃ vaṇṇayissanti sambandho. Pubbācariyānubhāvanti aṭṭhakathā “yasmā pure aṭṭhakathā akaṃsū”ti vacanato tesaṃ ānubhāvo nāma hoti. Kiñci apubbaṃ disvā santi hi loke vattāro “kassesa ānubhāvo”ti. Atha vā bhagavato adhippāyaṃ anugantvā taṃtaṃpāṭhe atthaṃ bhāvayati vibhāvayati, tassa tassa vā atthassa bhāvanā vibhāvanāti ānubhāvo vuccati aṭṭhakathā.

In the fifth verse: When the Vinaya Piṭaka, complete both in text and in meaning, is established among conscientious individuals by way of its functioning, the entire threefold Teaching is established in those very individuals. If it is asked, 'Whose teaching is it?' The answer is: 'Of the unestablished Blessed One.' For the Blessed One is called 'unestablished' (aṭṭhita) due to the absence of the annihilationist view, which is a cause for being established. For one with an annihilationist view, being indifferent to the next world, remains engaged only in the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures; he is not engaged in making merit for the welfare of the next world. One with an eternalist view strives to do those things. But the Blessed One, not being established and not striving in that way, practicing the Middle Path, crossed the flood himself and caused others to cross. As he said: 'Friend, not being established and not striving, I indeed crossed the flood' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.1). Alternatively, `susaṇṭhitassa` is said by way of the meaning 'of one who is well and rightly established among beings through the power of the four divine abodes'. For, being well-established, desiring only to remove the suffering of beings and to bring them welfare, rejoicing in their success, and being impartial, he teaches the Vinaya. Therefore, in this section on the commentary of the Vinaya, praising with suitable praise, he said `susaṇṭhitassa` ('of the well-established one'). In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, the meaning of `susaṇṭhitassa` is stated by way of the sutta, 'When, monks, agreeable and disagreeable results of action present themselves...' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.35; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.386) and the sutta, 'well-proportioned, of good form' (Khu. Pā. 8.11); that meaning is not in accordance with the intended section. Regarding `amissaṃ` ('unmixed'): What is unmixed? The Vinaya, or the influence of the ancient teachers? Neither of the two. For the Vinaya commentary itself is unmixed. Therefore, the connection should be made thus: 'I shall expound it as unmixed', by way of the neuter gender of the abstract noun. Regarding `pubbācariyānubhāva` ('the influence of the ancient teachers'): because it will be said, 'Since in the past they composed the commentaries', the commentary is called their 'influence'. For, having seen something unprecedented, there are those in the world who say, 'Whose influence is this?' Alternatively, because it follows the intention of the Blessed One and develops and clarifies the meaning in each respective text, or because it is the development and clarification of each respective meaning, the commentary is called 'influence' (`ānubhāva`).

Pubbācariyānubhāve sati kiṃ puna taṃ vaṇṇayissanti iminā ārambhenāti tato vuccanti chaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamanavamagāthāyo. Tattha ariyamaggañāṇambunā niddhotamalattā visuddhavijjehi, teneva niddhotāsavattā visuddhapaṭisambhidehi, visuddhapaṭisambhidattā ca saddhammasaṃvaṇṇanakovidehīti yojanā veditabbā. Keci “pubbācariyāti vutte lokācariyāpi, sāsane rāhulācariyādayopi saṅgayhanti, te apanetuṃ kāmañcātiādi vutta”nti vadanti. “Taṃ vaṇṇayissa”nti vuttattā pubbaṭṭhakathāya ūnabhāvo dassitoti ce? Na, cittehi nayehi saṃvaṇṇitoti [V 0.0017] dassetuṃ “kāmañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Saddhammaṃ saṃvaṇṇetuṃ kovidehi, tāya saṃvaṇṇanāya vā kovidehi saddhammasaṃvaṇṇanakovidehi.

The commentary, which is the powerful work of the ancient teachers, being already in existence, what is the purpose of undertaking again to explain it with the words, 'I shall explain that'? Because this criticism might be raised, after that fifth verse, the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are spoken. Therein, the construction should be understood thus: by those possessing pure knowledge, because their stains have been washed away by the water of the noble path-knowledge; by those possessing pure analytical knowledge, because their cankers have been washed away by that very same water; and, because they possess pure analytical knowledge, by those skilled in expounding the good Dhamma. Some say: 'When "ancient teachers" is stated, it could include worldly teachers, and in the Dispensation, teachers such as the Elder Rāhula and others. To exclude them, the verse beginning with `kāmañca` was spoken.' If it is said: 'Because it is stated, "I shall explain it," is a deficiency in the ancient commentary thereby shown?' It should not be so said. The verse beginning with `kāmañca` was spoken to show this meaning: 'It was well expounded by the ancient commentators with various wondrous methods.' The compound `saddhammasaṃvaṇṇanakovidehi` means: skilled in expounding the good Dhamma, or skilled in that exposition.

Sallekhiyeti kilesajātaṃ bāhullaṃ vā sallikhati tanuṃ karotīti sallekho, sallekhassa bhāvo sallekhiyaṃ, tasmiṃ sallekhiye. Nosulabhūpamehīti asulabhūpamehi. Mahāvihārassāti mahāvihāravaṃsassa. Paññāya accuggataṭṭhena dhajo upamā etesanti dhajūpamā, tehi dhajūpamehi. Sambuddhavaraṃ anuayehi anugatehi sambuddhavaranvayehi, buddhādhippāyānugehīti adhippāyo. Idha vara-saddo “sāmaṃ saccāni buddhattā sambuddho”ti vacanato paccekabuddhāpi saṅgayhanti. Tasmā te apanetuṃ vutto.

Regarding `sallekhiye`: one effaces (`sallikhati`) or makes austere (`tanuṃ karoti`) the mass of defilements or an abundance of requisites; therefore, this is `sallekho` (effacement). The state of one who practices effacement is `sallekhiyaṃ`. `Tasmiṃ sallekhiye` means: in that state of effacement. `Nosulabhūpamehi` means `asulabhūpamehi`: by those for whom a simile is not easily found. `Mahāvihārassa` means `mahāvihāravaṃsassa`: of the lineage of the Mahāvihāra. A banner is their simile (`dhajo upamā etesaṃ`) because they are highly exalted in wisdom (`paññāya accuggataṭṭhena`); hence they are `dhajūpamā` (like a banner); `tehi dhajūpamehi` means by those who are like a banner. `Sambuddhavaranvayehi` means: by those who follow (`anugatehi`) in the way (`anuayehi`) of the Sammāsambuddha's noble intention (`sambuddhavaraṃ`). The meaning is: by those who follow the Buddha's intention (`buddhādhippāyānugehi`). Here, according to the etymology, 'Because he has understood the truths by himself, he is a `sambuddho`,' the term `sambuddha` could also include Paccekabuddhas. Therefore, the word `vara` (noble) is stated in order to exclude them.

Aṭṭhakathāya [M 0.0018] ūnabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni attano karaṇavisesaṃ tassa payojanañca dassetuṃ “saṃvaṇṇanā”tiādimāha. Na kiñci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇātīti kiñci payojanaṃ phalaṃ hitaṃ na sādhetīti attho “na taṃ tassa bhikkhuno kiñci atthaṃ anubhotī”tiādīsu (pārā. 538) viya. Ajjhesanaṃ buddhasirivhayassāti iminā yasmā sahampatibrahmunā ajjhiṭṭhena dhammo desito bhagavatā, sāriputtassa ajjhesanaṃ nissāya vinayo paññatto, tasmā ayampi ācariyo taṃ ācariyavattaṃ pūjento imaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ buddhasirittherassa yācanaṃ nissāya akāsīti dasseti. Samanussarantoti tassābhāvaṃ dīpeti ādarañca.

Without showing a deficiency in the ancient commentary, he now says 'saṃvaṇṇanā' and so on, in order to show the special reason for his own composition and its purpose. 'Not achieving any benefit' means not accomplishing any useful purpose, result, or good, just as in passages such as 'that monk does not experience any benefit from it' (Pārā. 538). By 'at the request of the one named Buddhasiri,' he shows that because the Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One at the request of Brahmā Sahampati, and the Vinaya was established based on Sāriputta's request, therefore this teacher too, honoring that duty of a teacher, made this commentary at the request of the Elder Buddhasiri. By 'Samanussaranto' ('remembering'), he indicates that Elder's good qualities and his respectedness.
