Tato paraṃ dve gāthāyo kattabbavidhidassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tena tāsu aṭṭhakathāsu vuttavinicchayapaccayavimatiṃ vinodeti, ekaṭṭhakathāya kusalassa vā “ayaṃ nayo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthī”ti paṭikkhepaṃ nivāreti, ayuttatthapariccāgena tattha abhiniviṭṭhānaṃ abhinivesaṃ pariccajāpeti, theravādadassanena vinayavinicchayaṃ pati vinayadharānaṃ kāraṇopapattito uhāpohakkamaṃ dasseti, ayuttattheravādapaṭikkhepena puggalappamāṇataṃ paṭikkhipatīti ime cānisaṃsā kattabbavidhidassanena dassitā honti. Saṃvaṇṇanaṃ tañca samārabhanto tassā saṃvaṇṇanāya mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ sarīraṃ katvā samārabhissaṃ, mahāpaccariyampi yo vutto vinicchayo, tatheva kurundīnāmādīsu loke vissutāsu aṭṭhakathāsu ca yo vutto vinicchayo, tatopi vinicchayato mahāaṭṭhakathānayena, vinayayuttiyā vā yuttamatthaṃ tassa sarīrassa alaṅkāraṃ viya gaṇhanto samārabhissaṃ. Kiṃ saṃvaṇṇanameva, na aññanti dassanatthaṃ puna saṃvaṇṇanāggahaṇaṃ. Atha vā antogadhattheravādaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ katvā samārabhissanti yojanā veditabbā. Theravādā hi bahiaṭṭhakathāya vicaranti. Ettha ādi-saddena cūḷapaccariandhakaariyaṭṭhakathāpannavārādayopi saṅgahitā[V 0.0018]. Tattha paccarī nāma sīhaḷabhāsāya uḷumpaṃ kira, tasmiṃ nisīditvā katattā tameva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Kurundīvallivihāro nāma atthi, tattha katattā kurundī nāma jātā.

After that, two verses are spoken to show the procedure to be followed. By this, it dispels doubt regarding the basis for the decisions stated in those commentaries; for one skilled in a single commentary, it prevents the rejection, 'This method is not in the commentary'; by abandoning an unsuitable meaning, it causes those attached to it to abandon their adherence; by showing the Theravāda, it demonstrates to the experts in the Vinaya the procedure of what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected regarding a Vinaya decision, based on the suitability of the reason; and by rejecting an unsuitable Theravāda, it rejects taking a person as the standard. Thus, these benefits are shown by demonstrating the procedure to be followed. And undertaking that explanation, I will do so having made the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā its body. Furthermore, whatever decision is stated in the Mahāpaccarī, and likewise whatever decision is stated in the commentaries renowned in the world beginning with the Kurundī and others, from those decisions too, I will undertake this work, taking the suitable meaning—in accordance with the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā or with what is proper according to the Vinaya—like an ornament for that body. To show the answer to the question, 'Is it only the explanation and nothing else?', the word 'explanation' is mentioned again. Alternatively, the connection should be understood thus: 'I will undertake this work by making the Theravāda that is included within into an explanation.' For the Theravādas circulate outside the commentary. Here, by the word 'ādi' (beginning with), the Cūḷapaccarī, Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā, Ariya-aṭṭhakathā, Paṇṇavāra, and so on are also included. Among them, the name 'Paccarī', it is said, is 'a raft' in the Sinhalese language; because it was composed while seated on that, this very name arose. There is a monastery named Kurundīvalli; because it was composed there, the name 'Kurundī' arose.

Samma samārabhissanti kattabbavidhānaṃ sajjetvā ahaṃ ṭhito, tasmā taṃ me nisāmentūti gāthāya taṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ me mama, mayā vā vuccamānanti pāṭhaseso[M 0.0019]. Nisāmentu passantu paññācakkhunā suṇantu vā saddhāvīriyapītipāmojjābhisaṅkhārena saṅkharitvā pūjayantā sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ. Kassa dhammaṃ? Dhammappadīpassa tathāgatassa. Kiṃ dasseti? Padīpaṭṭhāniyo hi dhammo hitāhitappakāsanato, padīpadharaṭṭhāniyo dhammadharo tathāgato, tasmā parinibbutepi tasmiṃ tathāgate tattha sokaṃ akatvā sakkacca dhammaṃ paṭimānayantā nisāmentūti dasseti. Atha vā “dhammakāyā tathāgatā”ti (dī. ni. 3.118) vacanato dhammo ca so padīpo cāti dhammappadīpo, bhagavā.

I stand ready, having prepared the arrangement of what should be done, thinking, 'They will begin rightly.' Therefore, in the verse 'let them listen to that of me,' the remainder of the reading to be supplied is: 'that explanation of mine (mama), or that explanation spoken by me (mayā).' Let them behold with the eye of wisdom, or let them hear, having conditioned themselves with the conditioning of faith, energy, joy, and gladness, honoring the Dhamma respectfully. Whose Dhamma? The Dhamma of the Tathāgata who is the Dhamma-lamp. What does this show? Indeed, the Dhamma stands in the place of a lamp because it reveals what is beneficial and not beneficial. The Tathāgata, the bearer of the Dhamma, is in the place of a lamp-bearer. Therefore, it shows that even though that Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, without making sorrow there, they should listen, respectfully honoring the Dhamma. Alternatively, because it is said, 'The Tathāgatas are the Dhamma-body,' he is the Dhamma and he is the lamp; thus, he is the Dhamma-lamp. The Blessed One is meant.

Yo dhammavinayo yathā buddhena vutto, so tatheva buddhaputtehi sāvakehi ñāto avabuddho, yehi tesaṃ buddhaputtānaṃ matiṃ adhippāyaṃ accajantā niravasesaṃ gaṇhantā. Pureti purā, porāṇattherā vā. Aṭṭhakathāti aṭṭhakathāyo, upayogabahuvacanaṃ.

The Dhamma-Vinaya which was spoken by the Buddha in a certain way, was known and understood in that very same way by the disciples, the sons of the Buddha, who grasped it completely, without abandoning the intention and opinion of those sons of the Buddha. `Pure` means `purā` (formerly), or the ancient elders. `Aṭṭhakathā` stands for `aṭṭhakathāyo` (commentaries); it is the accusative plural.

Yaṃ atthajātaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbampi pamādalekhakānaṃ pamādalekhamattaṃ vajjayitvā. Kiṃ sabbesampi pamāṇaṃ? Na, kintu sikkhāsu sagāravānaṃ idha vinayamhi paṇḍitānaṃ, mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana saccepi alikepi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ, taṃ pamādalekhanti veditabbaṃ. Pamādalekhaṃ vajjayitvā pamāṇaṃ hessatīti sambandho.

Regarding whatever body of meaning is stated in the commentaries, all of that, having excluded what is merely the careless writing of careless scribes—is the word of all of them the standard? No. But rather, the word of the wise in this Vinaya who are respectful towards the trainings is the standard. However, in the Great Commentary, whether speaking truth or speaking falsely, only a `dukkaṭa` (wrongdoing) is stated; that should be known as a careless writing. The connection to be made is this: having excluded the careless writing, it will be the standard.

Tato cāti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaatthajātato tantikkamaṃ pāḷikkamaṃ. Suttantā suttāvayavā. Antoti hidaṃ abbhantarāvayavasambhāvanādīsu dissati. Suttantesu bhavā suttantikā, tesaṃ suttantikānaṃ, suttantaganthesu āgatavacanānanti attho. Atha vā amīyatīti anto, sādhīyatīti adhippāyo. Kena sādhīyati? Suttena, suttassa anto suttanto, ko so? So so atthavikappo, tasmiṃ suttante niyuttāni vacanāni suttantikāni. Tesaṃ suttantikānaṃ vacanānamatthaṃ. Tassa tassa āgamasuttassa abhidhammavinayasuttassa cānurūpaṃ paridīpayantī, ayaṃ tāvettha samāsato atthavibhāvanā – “itipi so bhagavā”tiādīnaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.41; 5.479; a. ni. 6.10; pārā. 1) suttantikānaṃ vacanānamatthaṃ āgamasuttantānurūpaṃ. “Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ siyā [M 0.0020] kusalaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti (cūḷava. 220) evamādīnaṃ [V 0.0019] abhidhammasuttantikānaṃ vacanānamatthaṃ abhidhammasuttantānurūpanti evamādi. Hessatīti bhavissati, karīyissatīti adhippāyo. Vaṇṇanāpīti ettha api-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, so tasmāti padena yojetabbo. Kathaṃ? Paṇḍitānaṃ pamāṇattāpi vitthāramaggassa samāsitattāpi vinicchayassa asesitattāpi tantikkamassa avokkamitattāpi suttantikavacanānaṃ suttantaṭṭhakathānurūpaṃ dīpanatopi tasmāpi sakkaccaṃ anusikkhitabbāti. Ettha “tantikkamaṃ avokkamitvā”ti vacanena siddhepi “aṭṭhakathācariyā verañjakaṇḍādīsu ‘suttantikānaṃ bhāro’ti gatā, mayaṃ pana vatvāva gamissāmā”ti dassetuṃ “suttantikāna”nti vuttaṃ kira.

And from that, that is, from the nature of the meaning stated in the commentaries, comes the textual sequence, the Pāḷi sequence. Suttantas are parts of the suttas. Indeed, this word 'anta' is seen in the meanings of 'internal', 'part', 'praise', and so on. Those that are in the suttantas are suttantikas. Of those suttantikas, the meaning is 'of the words that have come in the sutta texts'. Alternatively, because it is accomplished, it is called 'anta'; the intended meaning is 'it is achieved'. By what is it achieved? By the sutta. The end of the sutta is the suttanta. What is that? It is this or that particular meaning. The words connected with that suttanta are suttantikas. The meaning of those suttantika words. Explaining in accordance with each respective sutta of the Āgamas and also of the Abhidhamma and Vinaya suttas—this, first of all, is the brief clarification of the meaning here. The meaning of the suttantika words such as 'Indeed, that Blessed One is...' is in accordance with the Āgama suttantas. The meaning of the Abhidhamma suttantika words such as 'A legal question concerning a dispute may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate' is in accordance with the Abhidhamma suttantas, and so forth. 'Hessati' means 'it will be'; the intended meaning is 'it will be done'. Here, in 'vaṇṇanāpi', the word 'api' has the meaning of collection, and it should be connected with the word 'tasmā'. How? Because it is an authority for the wise, because the extensive path is summarized, because the decision is made without remainder, because the textual sequence is not transgressed, and because it illuminates the meaning of the suttantika words in accordance with the sutta commentary—therefore, it should also be carefully studied. Here, although it is established by the statement 'without transgressing the textual sequence,' it is said 'of the suttantikas' in order to show this: 'The commentary teachers, in the Verañjakaṇḍa and so on, proceeded, saying, "It is the responsibility of the Suttantikas," but we, however, will proceed only after having explained,' it is said.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Commencement of the Text is concluded.

Bāhiranidānakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the External Introduction

Tadaṅgavinayādibhedena [M 0.0021] vinayassabahuttā vinayo tāva vavatthapetabbo. “Buddhena dhammo vinayo ca vutto”ti pubbe vuttattā idāni “vuttaṃ yenā”ti na vattabbanti ce? Tassa evamādivacanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti sambandho. Dhāritaṃ yena cābhataṃ. Yatthappatiṭṭhitañcetanti vacanaṃ sakalampi vinayapiṭakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Attapaccakkhavacanaṃ na hotīti āhacca bhāsitaṃ na hotīti adhippāyo. Na hi bhagavato atītādīsu appaccakkhaṃ kiñci atthi. Yadi attapaccakkhavacanaṃ na hoti, padasodhammāpattiṃ na janeyyāti ce? Na, sāvakabhāsitassapi padasodhammāpattijananato. Niyamābhāvā atippasaṅgoti ce? Na, padasodhammasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṅgītittayaṃ āruḷho”ti visesitattā. Tathā aṭṭhakathāyampi saṅgītiṃ āruḷhattā “khandhānañca paṭipāṭi…pe… saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddesa) evamādivacanaṃ, yañca saṅgītiāruḷhakkamānugataṃ, taṃ padasodhammāpattiṃ janetīti āyasmā upatisso.

Since the Vinaya is manifold by way of its divisions such as the Tadaṅga Vinaya, the Vinaya should first be classified. If it is said that since 'The Dhamma and Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha' was stated previously, now it should not be said 'by whom was it spoken?'—the connection is that this was said in reference to such initial statements. And 'by whom it was upheld and brought forth, and where it was established'—this statement refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. 'It is not a statement of personal experience' means it is not spoken from direct personal knowledge. For indeed, there is nothing whatsoever for the Blessed One in the past and so forth that is not directly perceived. If it is said, 'If it is not a statement of personal experience, would it not give rise to the padasodhamma offense?' No, because even that which is spoken by disciples gives rise to the padasodhamma offense. If it is said, 'Is there an over-extension due to the absence of a fixed rule?' No, because in the commentary on the Padasodhammasikkhāpada, it is specified as 'that which has been included in the three Councils'. Similarly, in the commentary also, because it has been included in the Councils, statements like 'the sequence of the aggregates... and so on... is called saṃsāra' (DhsA. Nidānakathā; VibhA. 226, Saṅkhārapadaniddesa), and whatever follows the order of that which has been included in the Councils—these give rise to the padasodhamma offense, according to Venerable Upatissa.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the First Great Council

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma cāti ettha ca-saddo atirekattho, tena aññāpi atthīti dīpeti. Tampi sālavanaṃ upagantvā mittasuhajje apaloketvā nivattanato upavattananti pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ kira. Yamakasālānanti ekā kira sālapanti sīsabhāge, ekā pādabhāge. Tatrāpi eko [V 0.0020] taruṇasālo sīsabhāgassa āsanne hoti, eko pādabhāgassa, mūlakhandhaviṭapapattehi aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā ṭhitasālānantipi vuttaṃ. Anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyāti itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ “katakicco pītija hāsa ceto averamukhenābhatakuṇḍalenā”tiādīsu viya. Parinibbāne parinibbānahetu, tasmiṃ ṭhāne vā mā socittha cittena, mā paridevittha vācāya “paridevanaṃ vilāpa”nti vacanato. Mahāsamaṇenāti nissakkatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Sūriyaṃ’sūbhi paṭukarā’bhā’riṇassa tāṇā ityatreva. Yañca bhagavato anuggahaṃ, tassa anuggahassāti ācariyā. Ekacce pana “yaṃ yasmā ahaṃ anuggahito”ti vadanti. Nibbasanānīti niṭṭhitavasanakiccāni, mayā paribhuñjitvā apanītāni[M 0.0022]. Yadi suyuttāni dhāressasīti pucchati, kavacasadisāni sāṇāni. Issariyasadisā nava anupubbavihārādayo. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo nirodhasamāpatti ca paṭilābhakkamena “anupubbavihārā”ti vuttā.

In `Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti nāma ca`, the particle `ca` has an additional meaning, thereby indicating that there are others as well. Because of returning after having gone to that Sāla grove and having informed friends and companions, the name 'Upavattana' indeed became well-known. Regarding the twin Sāla trees: it is said one row of Sāla trees was at the head-part, and one at the foot-part. Therein also, one young Sāla tree was near the head-part and another near the foot-part; it is also said that they were Sāla trees standing intertwined with one another by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves. Regarding `anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā`, the instrumental case is in the sense of denoting a particular state, just as in such examples as: 'Having done what was to be done, with a joyful mind born of rapture, a face free from enmity, and adorned with earrings.' `Parinibbāne` means 'on account of the Parinibbāna' or 'in that place.' Then, in accordance with the statement 'lamentation is wailing,' it is said: 'Do not grieve with the mind, do not lament with speech.' Regarding `Mahāsamaṇena`, this is the instrumental case in the sense of the ablative, just as in `Sūriyaṃsūbhi paṭukarā’bhā’riṇassa tāṇā` (The protection for the sage is the radiance that makes things clear from the sun's rays). Regarding `Yañca bhagavato anuggahaṃ`, the teachers say it means 'of that favor.' Some, however, say it means 'because of which I was favored.' `Nibbasanāni` means: those for which the function of being worn is finished, having been used and set aside by me. 'If you are well-practiced, will you be able to bear them?'—thus he asks. The hempen cloths are like armor. The nine successive abidings, etc., are like sovereignty. The eight attainments and the attainment of cessation are called 'successive abidings' in the order of their attainment.

Anāgate sannikaṭṭhe, tathātīte cirantane;

Kāladvayepi kavīhi, purāsaddo payujjate.

In the near future, and likewise in the distant past; in both these times, the word 'purā' is employed by the wise.

Satthusāsanameva pariyatti satthusāsanapariyatti, sā suttageyyādivasena navaṅgā. Tipiṭakameva sabbapariyattippabhedaṃ dhārentīti tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadharā. “Vinā na sakkā”ti na vattabbaṃ “tipiṭakasabbapariyattippabhedadhare”ti vuttattā, evaṃ santepi atthi viseso tehi sammukhāpi asammukhāpi sutaṃ, therena pana asammukhāpaṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthīti. Na vāyanti ettha vāti vibhāsā, aññāsipi na aññāsipīti attho. Tatra uccinane. Bahusaddo vipullattho “anantapāraṃ bahu veditabbamitya”treva. Pubbe “tipiṭakasabbapaayattippabhedadhare”ti vuttattā “bahu cānena…pe… pariyatto”ti na yujjatīti ce? Na, tipiṭakassa anantattā, tasmā amhe upādāya tena bahu pariyattoti adhippāyo. Itarathā ānandatthero tehi appassutoti āpajjati, “asammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ nāma natthī”ti vacanavirodho ca. Aḍḍhamāso atikkantoti ettha eko divaso naṭṭho, so pāṭipadadivaso, kolāhaladivaso nāma so, tasmā idha na gahito. Saṃvegavatthuṃ kittetvā kīḷanato sādhukīḷanaṃ nāma. Svepīti api-saddo apekkhāmantānuññāya. Subhasuttaṃ “aciraparinibbute bhagavatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.444) vuttattā caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassesu antogadhaṃ na hotīti ce? Na, bhagavato kāle laddhanayattā kathāvatthu viya. Chaḍḍitā patitā uklāpā chaḍḍitapatitauklāpā. Āṇā eva appaṭihataṭṭhena cakkanti āṇācakkaṃ. Ekato ettha nipatantīti ekanipātanaṃ. Ākāsena āgantvā nisīdīti eketi etaṃ dutiyavāre gamanaṃ sandhāyāti āyasmā upatisso[V 0.0021]. Paṭhamaṃ vā ākāsena gantvā parisaṃ patvā bhikkhupantiṃ apīḷento pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā āsane eva attānaṃ dassesi. Ubhayathā ca āpāthaṃ gato, tena ubhayampi yujjati, aññathā dvīsu ekaṃ abhūtaṃ āpajjati.

The Teacher's teaching itself is the textual tradition (pariyatti); the textual tradition of the Teacher's teaching. That textual tradition has nine members by way of Sutta, Geyya, and so on. Because they bear the Tipiṭaka, which comprises all the divisions of the textual tradition, they are called 'bearers of all the divisions of the textual tradition of the Tipiṭaka'. It should not be said, "It is not possible without him," because it is stated, "bearers of all the divisions of the textual tradition of the Tipiṭaka." Even so, there is a distinction: by them it was heard both in the presence and in the absence of the Buddha, but for the Elder, there is nothing that was received in the absence of the Buddha. The word `vā` here has the meaning of `vibhāsā` (option). The meaning is: 'sometimes one knew, and sometimes one did not know.' There, in selecting, the word 'much' (`bahu`) has an extensive meaning, just as in "The limitless and boundless is to be known extensively." If one were to object, saying: "Because it was said before 'bearers of all the divisions of the textual tradition of the Tipiṭaka', is the statement 'much has been learned by him... the textual tradition' not suitable?" No, it is not so, because of the limitlessness of the Tipiṭaka. Therefore, the intention is that, in comparison to us, much was learned by him. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder Ānanda was less learned than them, and there would also be a contradiction with the statement, 'There is nothing that was received in the absence of the Buddha.' Here, in the phrase "half a month has passed," one day is lost. That is the first day of the lunar fortnight; it is called the day of commotion, and therefore it is not included here. Because of playing after having proclaimed a matter for spiritual urgency, it is called `sādhukīḷanaṃ` (good play). In `svepi` (even tomorrow), the particle `api` functions in the sense of expectation, consideration, and consent. If one were to say: "Because the Subha Sutta was spoken 'soon after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna,' is it not included in the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma?" No, it is not so, because its method was obtained during the time of the Blessed One, just like the Kathāvatthu. Discarded, fallen rubbish is 'discarded-and-fallen-rubbish'. The command itself, in the sense of being unopposed, is the wheel; therefore, it is the 'wheel of command' (`āṇācakkaṃ`). Because they fall down together here, it is called `ekanipātanaṃ` (falling together). The Venerable Upatissa says that this statement, 'Some say: "Having come through the sky, he sat down,"' refers to his coming on the second occasion. Or, on the first occasion, having gone through the sky and reached the assembly, without disturbing the row of monks, he dived into the earth and showed himself on his own seat. And in both ways, it is plausible; therefore, both accounts are suitable. Otherwise, of the two statements, one would become untrue.

Atha [M 0.0023] kho āyasmā mahākassapo āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ pucchi…pe… āyasmā upālitthero vissajjesīti idaṃ pubbe “paṭhamaṃ āvuso upālī”tiādinā (cūḷava. 439) vuttapucchāvissajjanaṃ saṅkhipitvā saṅgītikārakehi dassitavacananti gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ. Tathā hotu, kimatthaṃ panettha “nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchi, vatthumpi pucchī”ti evaṃ pubbe dassitānukkamena avatvā “vatthumpi pucchi, nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchī”ti evaṃ anukkamo katoti? “Vatthumūlakattā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā uppaṭipāṭiyā vutta”nti vadanti eke. Ettha pana vicāraṇā verañjakaṇḍe sampatte karīyati. Rājāgāraketi evaṃnāmake uyyāne. Abhiramanārahaṃ kira rājāgārampi. Tattha, yassa vasenetaṃ evaṃ nāmaṃ labhati. Atha kho “āyasmā mahākassapo”tiādinā pubbe vuttameva saṅkhipitvā dasseti saṅgītikārako vasīgaṇo. Yadi evaṃ yathā nidānampi pucchi, puggalampi pucchīti ettha pucchākkamo dassito, tathā ānandattherassa vissajjanakkamopi kimatthaṃ na dassitoti ce? Iminānukkamena saṅgahaṃ pañcapi nikāyā anāruḷhāti dassanatthaṃ. Kathaṃ pana āruḷhāti? Āyasmā mahākassapo pañcapi nikāye anukkameneva pucchi, ānandatthero pana anukkameneva pucchitampi apucchitampi tassa tassa suttassa sabhāvaṃ antarā uppannaṃ vatthuṃ uddesaniddesakkamaṃ mātikāvibhaṅgakkamanti evamādisabbaṃ anurūpavacanaṃ pakkhipitvā vissajjesi, tenevāha “eteneva upāyena pañcapi nikāye pucchī”ti. Atha vā “ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ rājāgārake”ti vattabbe “rājāgārake ambalaṭṭhikāya”nti uppaṭipāṭivacanenapi imamatthaṃ dīpeti. “Ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ viharati rājāgārake”ti hi vuttaṃ.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli… and the Venerable Elder Upāli answered. This statement—the previously mentioned question-and-answer section beginning with “First, friend Upāli,” which was summarized and presented by the compilers of the Council—is written in the Gaṇṭhipada. So be it. But why here, instead of stating in the previously shown sequence—“he asked about the origin, he asked about the person, he asked about the subject matter”—was the sequence made thus: “he asked about the subject matter, he asked about the origin, he asked about the person”? Some say, “It was stated out of sequence because the subject matter is the root of the laying down of a training rule.” Here, however, the investigation will be done when the Verañjakaṇḍa is reached. `Rājāgārake` refers to a park so named. It is said that a royal resting place worthy of great delight was also made there, and it is because of this that the park obtained such a name. Then, beginning with “the Venerable Mahākassapa,” the compiler, the group of masters, presents in a condensed form what was previously stated. If so, one might ask: just as the sequence of questioning was shown here—“he asked about the origin, he asked about the person”—why was the sequence of the Venerable Ānanda’s answers not also shown? It was not shown in order to demonstrate that the five Nikāyas were not compiled according to this sequence. But how were they compiled? The Venerable Mahākassapa questioned sequentially through the five Nikāyas. The Venerable Ānanda, however, in his replies, inserted all appropriate words—including both what was asked sequentially and what was not asked, the inherent nature of each respective discourse, the subject matter that arose in between, the sequence of headings and expositions, the sequence of the matrix and analysis, and so on—and thus he answered. Therefore, it is said, “In this way, he questioned the five Nikāyas.” Alternatively, this point is also clarified by the out-of-sequence phrasing “in Rājāgāraka at Ambalaṭṭhikā,” when it should be said, “at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Rājāgāraka.” For it was said, “He dwells at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Rājāgāraka.”

Gahakāranti imassa attabhāvagehassa kārakaṃ taṇhāvaḍḍhakiṃ gavesanto yena ñāṇena sakkā so daṭṭhuṃ, tassatthāya dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhāro ettakaṃ kālaṃ anekajātisaṃsāraṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ avindanto vicarinti attho. Dukkhā jāti punappunanti idaṃ gahakārakagavesanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Sabbā te phāsukāti tava sabbā anavasesakilesaphāsukā mayā bhaggā. Gahakūṭaṃ nāma avijjā. Somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇaṃ somanassamayaṃ. Na hi somanassamayaṃ ñāṇaṃ khandhasabhāvabhedato. Daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanāti yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ, taṃ [M 0.0024] pana tattha tattha pakāsayissāma. Aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhamme ca vinaye cāti ettha pāṇātipāto akusalanti evamādīsu [V 0.0022] maraṇādhippāyassa jīvitindriyupacchedakappayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā akusalaṃ, na pāṇasaṅkhātajīvitindriyassa upacchedakasaṅkhāto atipāto. Tathā adinnassa parasantakassa ādānasaṅkhātā viññatti abyākato dhammo, tabbiññattisamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā akusalo dhammoti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.27) evamādinā aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite dhamme paṭibalo vinetuṃ. Jātarūparajataṃ parasantakaṃ theyyacittena gaṇhantassa yathāvatthuṃ pārājikathullaccayadukkaṭesu aññataraṃ, bhaṇḍāgārikasīsena diyyamānaṃ gaṇhantassa pācittiyaṃ, attatthāya gaṇhantassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyaṃ, kevalaṃ lolatāya gaṇhantassa anāmāsadukkaṭaṃ, rūpiyachaḍḍakasammatassa anāpattīti evaṃ aññamaññasaṅkaravirahite vinayepi paṭibalo vinetunti attho. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti, etena phalavasena javanavasena ca cittassa vuddhiṃ dasseti. “Avisiṭṭha”nti pāṭho, sādhāraṇanti attho.

The meaning is this: I, seeking the house-builder—craving, the carpenter, the maker of this house of self-existence—have wandered for such a long time through the saṃsāra of many births, not finding that knowledge by which that house-builder can be seen, for the sake of which I made the aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. The statement, 'Birth again and again is suffering,' is the reason for seeking the house-builder. Regarding 'All your rafters': All your rafters, which are the defilements without remainder, have been broken by me. The ridge-pole of the house (`gahakūṭa`) is ignorance. Knowledge accompanied by joy is called 'made of joy'. Indeed, knowledge is not 'made of joy', because of the distinction in the intrinsic nature of the aggregates. The phrase concerning the purpose of making firm and making lax is stated in a general way; we shall clarify this in the respective places. Herein, regarding 'in the Dhamma and the Vinaya, which are free from mutual confusion': In such statements as 'killing living beings is unwholesome,' the unwholesome factor is the volition that gives rise to the application of cutting off the life-faculty with the intention of causing death, not the act of killing itself, which is defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty designated as a living being. Similarly, the intimation known as taking another's property that is not given is an indeterminate state, but the volition of theft which gives rise to that intimation is an unwholesome state. In this way, he is able to train in the Dhamma, which is free from mutual confusion. For a monk who takes gold or silver belonging to another with a thieving mind, depending on the circumstances, one of the following offenses is incurred: Pārājika, Thullaccaya, or Dukkaṭa. For one who takes what is given by a treasurer, a Pācittiya offense is incurred. For one who takes it for one's own sake, a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense is incurred. For a monk who handles it merely out of frivolity, an Anāmāsa Dukkaṭa (offense of touching) is incurred. For a monk designated as one who discards money, there is no offense. Thus, the meaning is that he is also able to train in the Vinaya, which is free from mutual confusion. ‘Develops’ (`bhāveti`) means ‘increases’ (`vaḍḍheti`). By this, he shows the growth of the mind by way of the fruit of attainment and by way of impulsion. The reading is `avisiṭṭha`; the meaning is 'common'.

Desentassa vasenettha, desanā piṭakattayaṃ;

Sāsitabbavasenetaṃ, sāsanantipi vuccati.

Herein, by way of the one who teaches, the three Piṭakas are called 'desanā' (discourse); by way of those who are to be instructed, this is also called 'sāsanā' (instruction).

Kathetabbassa atthassa, vasenāpi kathāti ca;

Desanā sāsanā kathā, bhedampevaṃ pakāsaye.

And by way of the meaning that is to be expounded, it is also called 'kathā' (exposition); thus should one make clear the distinction between desanā, sāsanā, and kathā.

Sāsanassa napuṃsakattā “yathā…pe… dhammasāsanānī”ti vuttaṃ. Duccaritasaṃkilesaṃ nāma atthato cetanā, tathākārappavattacittuppādo vā. Aniccādilakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā pavattattā vipassanācittāni visayato lokiyā’bhisamayo asammohato lokuttaro, lokuttaro eva vā abhisamayo visayato nibbānasaṅkhātassa atthassa, itarassa maggādikassa asammohatotipi eke. Ettha “paṭivedho”ti vuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ gambhīranti ce? Gambhīrassa udakassa pamāṇaggahaṇakāle dīghena pamāṇena bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃ alabbhaneyyabhāvadassanatthaṃ idānīti vuttanti eke. Yassa catthāya maggaphalatthāya. Tañca atthaṃ nānubhonti nādhigacchanti kañci attanā adhippetaṃ, itivādapamokkhañca. Kasmā? Atthassa anupaparikkhitvā gahitattā. Adhigataphalattā paṭividdhākuppo. Puna khīṇāsavaggahaṇena [M 0.0025] arahantameva dasseti, na sekkhaṃ. So hi yathā bhaṇḍāgāriko rañño kaṭakamakuṭādiṃ gopetvā icchiticchitakkhaṇe upaneti, evaṃ sahetukānaṃ sattānaṃ maggaphalatthāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tāsaṃyeva tattha vinayapiṭake pabhedato vuttattā, vāyamitvā tā eva pāpuṇātīti ācariyā. Kimatthaṃ tissova vijjā tattha vibhattāti? Sīlasampattiyā etaparamupanissayabhāvato. “Aparehipi sattahaṅgehi samannāgato bhikkhu vinayadharo [V 0.0023] hoti. Āpattiṃ jānāti, anāpattiṃ, lahukaṃ āpattiṃ, garukaṃ āpattiṃ, anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati…pe… dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati…pe… āsavānañca khayā…pe… upasampajja viharatī”ti (pari. 327) suttamettha sādhakaṃ. Vinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā sīlasampattiṃ nissāya āsavakkhayañāṇena saheva viya dibbacakkhupubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāni paṭilabhati. Visuṃ etesaṃ parikammakiccaṃ natthīti dassanatthaṃ tāsaṃyevāti vuttanti ca vadanti eke. Abhidhamme pana tissovijjā cha abhiññā catasso ca paṭisambhidā aññe ca sammappadhānādayo guṇavisesā vibhattā. Kiñcāpi vibhattā, tathāpi visesato paññājātikattā catasso paṭisambhidā pāpuṇātīti dassanatthaṃ tāsaṃ tatthevāti avadhāraṇavipallāso kato. Attanā duggahitena dhammenāti pāṭhaseso. Kattari cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, hetutthe ca, attanā duggahitahetūti adhippāyo. Kasmā panāti “anulomiko”ti vuttatthaṃ dīpeti.

Because 'sāsana' is neuter, it is said 'yathā…pe… dhammasāsanānī'. The defilement of misconduct is, in essence, volition, or the arising of consciousness occurring in such a manner. Because they proceed by penetrating the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, the insight-consciousnesses are a mundane realization in terms of their object; the supramundane realization is by way of non-delusion. Or, the supramundane realization alone, in terms of its object, is the realization of the meaning designated as Nibbāna, while for the other, such as the path, it is a realization by way of non-delusion—so say some. Here, knowledge is what is called 'penetration'. If it is asked, 'How is it profound?' Just as when taking the measure of deep water, there must be a long measure, so too, to show the state of being unobtainable, it is said 'now'—so say some. And for the sake of which goal—for the sake of the path and fruition—they do not experience that benefit, nor do they attain any goal intended by themselves, or deliverance from such censure. Why? Because of having grasped it without investigating the meaning. Because the fruit has been attained, their penetration is unshakable. Furthermore, by the mention of 'one whose taints are destroyed', it indicates only the Arahant, not the trainee. For just as a treasurer, having guarded the king’s bracelets, crowns, and so forth, presents them at the desired moment, so too did he teach the Dhamma for the sake of beings who have the conditions, for the sake of the path and fruition. Since those very knowledges are explained in detail there in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the teachers say that by striving, one attains those very ones. Why are only the three knowledges analyzed there? Because the perfection of virtue is the ultimate supporting condition for this. 'Moreover, a monk endowed with seven other qualities is a bearer of the Vinaya. He knows an offense…pe… he recollects manifold past lives…pe… with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings…pe… and having realized for himself with direct knowledge, he enters and remains in the emancipation of mind and emancipation by wisdom that are taintless in the here-and-now through the destruction of the taints' (Pari. 327). This sutta is the proof here. Having mastered the Vinaya and relying on the perfection of virtue, one attains the knowledges of the divine eye and recollection of past lives as if together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. To show that there is no separate preparatory work for these, it is said 'of those very ones'—so say some. In the Abhidhamma, however, the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, and other special qualities such as the right exertions are analyzed. Although they are analyzed, nevertheless, to show that one attains the four analytical knowledges specifically because they are of the nature of wisdom, a reversal of emphasis was made with the phrase 'of those, right there' (`tāsaṃ tattheva`). 'By the Dhamma poorly grasped by oneself'—this is the remainder of the text. And this is an instrumental expression in the agentive sense, and also in the sense of cause; the intended meaning is 'because it was poorly grasped by oneself'. The phrase 'But why?' (`Kasmā pana`) explains the meaning stated as 'conducive'.

Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanānayo.

The method of the explanation of the discourse on the First Great Council.

Dutiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Second Council

Pannabhārāti patitakkhandhabhārā. “Bhārā have pañcakkhandhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.22) hi vuttaṃ. “Sammukhā bhavissāma na bhavissāmā”ti vattāro. Tesu daharā kira. Jamminti lāmakaṃ.

“Pannabhārā” means those whose burden of the aggregates has been laid down. For it is said, “Indeed, the five aggregates are a burden.” There are those who say, “We shall be present, we shall not be present.” Among them, some are said to be young. “Jammi” means inferior.

Dutiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanānayo.

The method of the explanation of the discourse on the Second Council.

Tatiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Third Council

Brahmalokā [M 0.0026] cavitvāti ettha cattāro maggā pañcānantariyāni niyatamicchādiṭṭhīti imeyeva niyatā, na mahaggatā, tasmā paṇidhivasena heṭṭhupapattipi hoti. Aticchathāti aticca icchatha, gantvā bhikkhaṃ pariyesathāti adhippāyo. Keṭubhaṃ nāma kabyakaraṇavidhiyuttaṃ satthaṃ. Kiriyākappaṃ ityeke, kattākhyādilakkhaṇayuttasatthaṃ. Asandhimittāti tassā nāmaṃ. Tassā kira sarīre sandhayo na paññāyanti, madhusitthakena kataṃ viya sarīraṃ hoti. Tasmā “evaṃnāmikā jātā”tipi vadanti. Māgadhakena patthena cattāro patthā āḷhakaṃ, cattāri āḷhakāni [V 0.0024] doṇaṃ, catudoṇā mānikā, catumānikā khārikā, vīsatikhāriko vāhoti. Kethumālāti “sīsato uṭṭhahitvā ṭhito obhāsapuñjo”ti vadanti. Rājiddhiadhikārappasaṅgenetaṃ vatthu vuttaṃ, nānukkamena. Anukkamena pana buddhasāsanāvahāraṃ vatthuṃ dīpento “rājā kirā”tiādimāha. Kilesadamanena dantaṃ. Kāyavācāhi guttaṃ. “Pācīnamukho”tipi pāṭho atthi. Pubbe jeṭṭhabhātikattā teneva paricayena pattaggahaṇatthāya ākāraṃ dasseti. Abhāsīti “bhāsissāmī”ti vitakkesi. Apare “aññātanti vuttepi sabbaṃ abhaṇī”ti vadanti. Amatanti nibbānasaṅkhātāya nivattiyā saguṇādhivacanaṃ, tassā appamādo padaṃ maggo. Maccūti pavattiyā sadosādhivacanaṃ, tassā pamādo padaṃ maggoti evaṃ cattāri saccāni sandassitāni honti. Saṅghasaraṇagatattā saṅghanissitā pabbajjā, bhaṇḍukammassa vā tadāyattattā. Nigrodhattherassānubhāvakittanādhikārattā pubbe vuttampi pacchā vattabbampi sampiṇḍetvā āha “puna rājā asokārāmaṃ nāma mahāvihāraṃ kāretvā saṭṭhisahassāni…pe… caturāsītivihārasahassāni kārāpesī”ti. “Puthujjanakalyāṇakassa vā paccavekkhitaparibhogo”ti vacanato sekkhāva paramatthato dāyādā, tathāpi thero mahindakumārassa pabbajjatthaṃ ekena pariyāyena lokadhammasiddhena evamāha “yo koci mahārāja…pe… orasaṃ putta”nti. Vuttañhi vede –

In the phrase 'having fallen from the Brahma world': the four paths, the five heinous crimes, and fixed wrong view—these alone are fixed; the exalted states are not. Therefore, by the power of aspiration, rebirth in a lower realm also occurs. Regarding `Aticchatha`, the word division is `aticca icchatha`; the intention is: 'Having gone, seek alms.' The treatise called Keṭubha is one connected with the method of poetic composition; some say it is Kiriyākappa, a treatise endowed with characteristics such as agent and verb. 'Asandhimittā' is her name. It is said that in her body the joints were not apparent; her body was as if made with beeswax. Therefore, they also say, 'She was born with such a name.' By the Magadhan measure: four `patthas` are an `āḷhaka`; four `āḷhakas` are a `doṇa`; four `doṇas` are a `mānikā`; four `mānikās` are a `khārikā`; and twenty `khārikas` are a `vāha`. 'Kethumālā'—they say, 'a mass of light that, having risen from the head, is stationary.' This account is told in connection with the section on the king’s psychic power, not in sequence. However, explaining in sequence the account that conveys the Buddha’s Dispensation, he said, 'The king, it is said…' and so on. Tamed by the subduing of defilements. Guarded in body and speech. There is also the reading, 'facing east.' Because he was the elder brother in a previous existence, with that same familiarity he makes a gesture for the sake of receiving the bowl. Regarding `abhāsi` (he spoke): he thought, 'I will speak.' Others say: 'Even when "it is known" was said, he recited everything.' 'Deathless' is a designation according to its own quality for the cessation from the round of existence, which is called Nibbāna; its path is heedfulness. 'Death' is a designation according to its own fault for the continuation of the round of existence; its path is heedlessness. Thus, the Four Truths are well shown. The going forth is dependent on the Sangha because of having gone to the Sangha for refuge, or because the act of tonsure is dependent on it. Because this is the section proclaiming the spiritual power of the Elder Nigrodha, what was said before and what is to be said later are combined, and it is stated: 'Again, King Asoka, having built a great monastery named Asokārāma… had eighty-four thousand monasteries built.' From the statement, 'Or the use after reflection by a virtuous worldling,' it follows that only the trainees are heirs in the ultimate sense. Nevertheless, for the sake of Prince Mahinda's going forth, the Elder spoke thus with a discourse established by worldly and doctrinal convention: 'Whoever, O great king… one's own son...' For it is said in the Veda—

“Aṅgā aṅgā sambhavasi, hadayā adhijāyase;

Attā ve putto nāmāsi, sa jīva saradosata”nti.

From my very limbs you are produced, from my heart you are born; you, son, are indeed my very self. May you live for a hundred autumns.

Tasmā [M 0.0027] iminā pariyāyena oraso putto mātāpitūhi pabbajito ce, atthato te sayaṃ pabbajitā viya honti. Dhammakathikā kasmā nārocenti? Rājā “theraṃ gaṇhitvā āgacchathā”ti amacce pesesi, dhammakathikā therassa āgamanakāle parivāratthāya pesitā, tasmā. Apica tena vuttavidhināva vadanti caṇḍattā, caṇḍabhāvo cassa “ambaṃ chinditvā veḷuyā vatiṃ karohī”ti vuttaamaccavatthunā vibhāvetabbo. Kasmā pana dhammakathikā rājāṇāpanaṃ karontīti? “Sāsanaṃ paggahetuṃ samattho”ti vuttattā. Dīpakatittiroti kūṭatittiro. Ayaṃ pana kūṭatittirakamme niyuttopi suddhacitto, tasmā tāpasaṃ pucchi. Sāṇipākāranti sāṇipākārena. Vibhajitvā vadatīti vibhajjavādī “atthi khvesa brāhmaṇa pariyāyo”tiādinā (pārā. 5). Apica sassatavādī ca bhagavā “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ asaṅkhata”ntiādi (itivu. 43)-vacanato. Ekaccasassatiko ca “sappaccayā [V 0.0025] dhammā, appaccayā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7) vacanato. Antānantiko ca –

Therefore, by this method, if their own son is ordained by his parents, it is, in effect, as if they themselves were ordained. Why do the Dhamma-preachers not announce it? The king sent his ministers, saying, “Invite the elder and come.” The Dhamma-preachers were sent to attend the elder upon his arrival; for that reason, they do not announce. Moreover, they speak only according to the method he stated, because of his harshness. And his harsh nature should be understood through the story of the minister who was told, “Cut down the mango tree and make a fence with bamboo.” But why do the Dhamma-preachers carry out the king’s command? Because it was said, “He is able to support the Teaching.” Dīpakatittiro means a cunning partridge. But this one, although engaged in the work of a cunning partridge, had a pure mind; therefore, he asked the ascetic. Sāṇipākāraṃ means with a hemp-cloth enclosure. He is called an Analyst (vibhajjavādī) because he speaks by analyzing, as in the passage beginning, “Surely, brahmin, there is this way…” Furthermore, the Blessed One is also an eternalist (sassatavādī), because of the statement, “There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unconditioned…” And a partial-eternalist (ekaccasassatiko) because of the teaching, “There are conditioned phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena.” And a finitist-infinitist (antānantiko)—

“Gamanena na pattabbo, lokassanto kudācanaṃ;

Na ca appatvā lokantaṃ, dukkhā atthi pamocanaṃ”. (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45);

“By traveling, the end of the world is never to be reached; nor without reaching the end of the world is there liberation from suffering.”

“Anamataggoyaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃsāro pubbakoṭi na paññāyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.124; cūḷani. kappamāṇavapucchāniddesa 61) vacanato. Amarāvikkhepikapakkhampi īsakaṃ bhajati bhagavā “sassato lokoti abyākatametaṃ asassato lokoti abyākatameta”ntiādiabyākatavatthudīpanato sammutisaccadīpanato ca. Tañhi ajjhattabahiddhādivasena na vattabbaṃ. Yathāha “ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ na vattabbaṃ ajjhattārammaṇantipī”tiādi (dha. sa. 1437). Tathā adhiccasamuppannikapakkhampi bhajati “laddhā mudhā nibbutiṃ bhuñjamānā”ti (khu. pā. 6.7; su. ni. 230) vacanato. Tattha hi mudhāti adhiccasamuppannavevacanaṃ. Saññīvādādiko ca bhagavā saññībhavaasaññībhavanevasaññīnāsaññībhavavasena. Ucchedavādī ca “ahañhi, brāhmaṇa, ucchedaṃ vadāmi rāgassā”ti (pārā. 6) vacanato. Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī ca “khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti (mahāva. 23; dī. ni. 2.215; saṃ. ni. 3.35) vacanato, “natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti (mahāva. 16) vacanato, diṭṭheva dhamme nirodhasamāpattidīpanato [M 0.0028] ca. Evaṃ tena tena pariyāyena tathā tathā veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vibhajitvā vadatīti vibhajjavādī bhagavāti.

“Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned.” The Blessed One also slightly inclines toward the side of the Amarāvikkhepikas (eel-wrigglers) because of his exposition of the undeclared points and of conventional truth, as when it is said: “Is the world eternal?—this is undeclared. Is the world not eternal?—this is undeclared,” and so on. For that conventional truth should not be spoken of in terms of internal, external, and so on. As it is said: “The base of nothingness should not be spoken of as having an internal object,” etc. Similarly, he inclines toward the side of the accidentalists because of the saying: “Having obtained Nibbāna by chance, they enjoy it.” For in that context, ‘by chance’ (mudhā) is a synonym for ‘arisen by chance’ (adhiccasamuppanna). And the Blessed One is a proponent of the view of perception and so on, by way of the existence with perception, the existence without perception, and the existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He is also an annihilationist because of the saying: “For I, brahmin, declare the annihilation of lust.” He is also a proponent of Nibbāna in this very life because of the sayings: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived,” and “Now there is no further becoming,” and because he shows the attainment of cessation in this very life. Thus, by this and that reason, in this and that manner, according to the inclinations of those to be taught, he speaks having analyzed; therefore, the Blessed One is an analyst (vibhajjavādī).

Tatiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanānayo.

The Method of the Explanation of the Account of the Third Council.

Pupphanāmo sumanatthero. Mahāpadumattheroti eke. Mahiṃsakamaṇḍalaṃ andharaṭṭhanti vadanti. Dhammacakkhu nāma tayo maggā. Sotāpattimagganti ca eke. Pañcapi raṭṭhāni pañca cīnaraṭṭhāni nāma. Rājagaheti deviyā katavihāre. Silakūṭamhīti pabbatakūṭe. Vaḍḍhamānanti alaṅkaraṇacuṇṇaṃ. Ariyadese atīva sammataṃ kira. Ekarasena nāthakaraṇā iti damiḷā. Sārapāmaṅganti uttamaṃ pāmaṅgaṃ. Petavatthuādinā saṃvejetvā abhisamayatthaṃ saccasaṃyuttañca. Meghavanuyyānaṃ nāma mahāvihāraṭṭhānaṃ. “Dvāsaṭṭhiyā leṇesū”ti pāṭho. Dasabhātikanti abhayakumārādayo dasa, te idha [V 0.0026] na vuttā. Vutthavasso pavāretvāti cātumāsiniyā pavāraṇāyāti attho. Paṭhamapavāraṇāya vā pavāretvā ekamāsaṃ tattheva vasitvā kattikapuṇṇamāsiyaṃ avoca, aññathā “puṇṇamāyaṃ mahāvīro”ti vuttattā na sakkā gahetuṃ. Mahāvīroti buddhopacārena dhātuyo vadati. Jaṅghappamāṇanti “thūpassa jaṅghappamāṇa”nti vadanti. Mātulabhāgineyyā cūḷodaramahodarā. Dharamānassa viya buddhassa rasmi sarasarasmi, rañño lekhāsāsanaṃ appesi, evañca mukhasāsanamavoca. Doṇamattā magadhanāḷiyā dvādasanāḷimattā kira. “Paricchinnaṭṭhāne chijjitvā”ti pāṭho. Sabbadisāhi pañca rasmiyo āvaṭṭetvāti pañcahi phalehi nikkhantattā pañca, tā pana chabbaṇṇāva. Kattikajuṇhapakkhassa pāṭipadadivaseti juṇhapakkhassa paṭhamadivaseti attho. Mahābodhiṭṭhāne parivāretvā ṭhitanāgayakkhādidevatākulāni. Gopakā nāma rājaparikammino tathābhāvakiccā. Tesaṃ kulānaṃ nāmantipi keci. Udakādivāhā kāliṅgā. Kāliṅgesu janapadesu jātisampannaṃ kulaṃ kāliṅgakulanti keci.

The elder named Puppha is Sumana Thera. Some say he is the elder Mahāpaduma. They say the Mahiṃsaka region is the Andha country. The five countries are called the five Cīna countries. At Rājagaha, in the monastery built by the queen. Silakūṭa means on a mountain peak. Vaḍḍhamāna means ornamental powder. It is said to be highly esteemed in the noble land. The Damiḷas say it means powders bound with a single resinous substance. Sārapāmaṅga means the supreme pāmaṅga. Having inspired a sense of urgency by means of the Petavatthu and so on, for the purpose of realization, he also taught the Saccasaṃyutta. The place called Meghavana Park is the site of the Mahāvihāra. The reading is “in sixty-two caves.” Dasabhātika means the ten princes beginning with Prince Abhaya; they are not mentioned here. Vutthavasso pavāretvā means at the Pavāraṇā at the end of the four-month rains retreat. Or, having performed the first pavāraṇā, staying there for one month, he spoke on the full moon of Kattika; otherwise, since it is said “on the full moon, the great hero,” it cannot be taken differently. The word Mahāvīra refers to the relics by way of metaphorical extension from the Buddha. Jaṅghappamāṇa means “the measurement of the thūpa’s drum,” they say. Cūḷodara and Mahodara were uncle and nephew. Like a ray of the living Buddha, there is a ray dripping with essence; he sent the king's written message, and also delivered an oral message. A doṇa measure is said to be twelve nāḷis by the Magadhan nāḷi. The reading is, 'having been cut at a defined place.' Having turned the five rays in all directions means: there are five because they emerge from the five fruits, but they are of six colors. Kattikajuṇhapakkhassa pāṭipadadivasa means the first day of the bright fortnight of Kattika. At the Mahābodhi site, the families of nāgas, yakkhas, and other deities stood surrounding it. Gopakas are royal attendants who perform such duties. Some also say this is merely the name of their families. Those who carry water and so on are called Kāliṅgas. Some say that in the Kāliṅga countries, a family of high birth is called a Kāliṅga family.

Paṭhamapāṭipadadivaseti dutiyauposathassa pāṭipadadivaseti attho. Tattha ṭhitehi samuddassa diṭṭhattā taṃ ṭhānaṃ samuddasālavatthu. Soḷasa jātisampannakulāni aṭṭha brāhmaṇāmaccakulāni. Mahāariṭṭhatthero cetiyagirimhi [M 0.0029] pabbajito. Amaccassa pariveṇaṭṭhāneti sampatikālavasenāha. Mahindatthero dvādasavassiko hutvā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ sampatto, tattha dve vassāni vasitvā vinayaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi, dvāsaṭṭhivassiko hutvā parinibbuto. Vinayo saṃvaratthāyāti vinayapiṭakaṃ, tassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ vā. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ sappaccayanāmarūpapariggaho. Maggādipaccavekkhaṇe asati antarā parinibbānaṃ nāma natthi sekkhassa maraṇaṃ vā, satiyeva hoti. Tasmā āha “vimuttiñāṇadassana”nti. Anupādāparinibbānatthāyāti kañci dhammaṃ anupādāya aggahetvā īsakampi anavasesetvā parinibbānatthāyāti attho. Upanisāti “vinayo saṃvaratthāyā”tiādikā kāraṇaparamparā. Ettāvatā attahitanipphattiṃ dassetvā idāni parahitanipphattiṃ dassetuṃ “etadatthaṃ sotāvadhāna”nti āha. Tassattho – attano vinayakathanaṃ vinayamantanañca uggahetuṃ paresaṃ sotassa odahanaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ. Tato uggahitavinayakathāmantanānaṃ tesaṃ upanisā yathāvuttakāraṇaparamparā siddhāyevāti na puna dassitāti veditabbā. Aññathā etadatthā upanisāti iminā vacaneneva anupādāparinibbānassa saṅgahitattā anupādāparinibbānato uddhaṃ sotāvadhānāsambhavato etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānanti ante na sambhavatīti niratthakaṃ bhaveyya, na ca niratthakaṃ parahitanipphattiyā mūlakāraṇadassanatthattāti veditabbaṃ.

The phrase Paṭhamapāṭipadadivase means: on the first day after the second Uposatha. Because the ocean was seen by those standing there, that place is called Samuddasālavatthu. The sixteen families of noble birth are eight families of brahmins and eight families of ministers. The Elder Mahāariṭṭha went forth at Cetiyagiri. The minister’s residence is referred to in terms of the present time. The Elder Mahinda, being of twelve vassas, arrived at the island of Tambapaṇṇi; having stayed there for two years, he established the Vinaya. Being of sixty-two vassas, he attained Parinibbāna. 'The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint' means the Vinaya Piṭaka, or the learning of it. The knowledge and vision of things as they really are is the full comprehension of name-and-form with its conditions. When there is no reviewing of the path and so on, there is no so-called intermediate Parinibbāna, nor is there death for a trainee; it occurs only when there is such reviewing. Therefore, it is said, “the knowledge and vision of liberation.” The phrase anupādāparinibbānatthāya means for the purpose of Parinibbāna without clinging: that is, for the purpose of attaining Parinibbāna without clinging to any phenomenon, without grasping it, and without leaving even the slightest remainder. The term upanisā means the causal sequence beginning with “the Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint.” Having thus far shown the accomplishment of one's own welfare, now, in order to show the accomplishment of others' welfare, it is said, “for this purpose, there is the application of the ear.” Its meaning is this: `sotāvadhāna` is the application of the ear for others to learn one's own recitation and discussion of the Vinaya. Therefore, for those who have learned the recitation and discussion of the Vinaya, the proximate cause for them—the causal sequence as stated above—is already accomplished, and so it is not shown again; this should be understood. Otherwise, if another meaning were taken, since Parinibbāna without clinging is already included by this very statement, 'for this purpose is the proximate cause,' and since the application of the ear is impossible beyond Parinibbāna without clinging, then the phrase 'for this purpose, there is the application of the ear' at the end would be impossible, and thus it would be meaningless. But it is not meaningless, because it serves to show the root cause for the accomplishment of others' welfare; this should be understood.

Evaṃ [V 0.0027] yathā yathā yaṃ yaṃ, sambhaveyya padaṃ idha;

Taṃ taṃ tathā tathā sabbaṃ, payojeyya vicakkhaṇoti.

Thus, whatever term might arise here in whatever way, all of that should be applied accordingly by the discerning one.

Bāhiranidānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the external introduction is concluded.

Pārājikavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Pārājika

Verañjakaṇḍo

The Verañja Chapter

Verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Verañja Chapter

“Tena [M 0.0030][V 0.0028] samayena buddho bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena vesāliyā avidūre kalandagāmo nāma hotī”ti vinayanidāne ārabhitabbe verañjakaṇḍassa ārambho kimatthoti ce? Vuccate – mūlato pabhuti vinayanidānaṃ dassetuṃ. Yadi evaṃ “paṭhamaṃ āvuso upāli pārājikaṃ kattha paññattanti, vesāliya”nti vacanena virujjhatīti ce? Na virujjhati. Kasmā? Kattha paññattanti hi nidānapucchā. Evaṃ santepi “paṭhamassa pārājikassa kiṃnidāna”nti pucchite sādhāraṇamahānidānavissajjanaṃ ayuttaṃ viyāti? Nāyuttaṃ, sabbesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ pāṭekkaṃ nidānassa puṭṭhattā tassa vissajjetabbattā ca sabbasādhāraṇamahānidānaṃ paṭhamamāha. Ekantena pucchāvissajjanakkamena pārājikādīni saṅgahaṃ āropitāni. Kathaṃ āropitānīti ce? Āyasmatā mahākassapena anukkamena sabbopi vinayo pucchito, puṭṭhena ca āyasmatā upālittherena yathāsambhavaṃ nirantaraṃ vissajjitameva. Apucchitānipi vinītavatthuādīni yujjamānāni vatthūni antokatvā vissajjanakkameneva gaṇasajjhāyamakaṃsūti veditabbaṃ. Aññathā verañjakaṇḍaṃ paṭhamapārājikasseva nidānanti vā anadhikārikaṃ vā nippayojanaṃ vā pāṭekkaṃ sikkhāpadanidānapucchānantaraṃ tadeva vissajjetabbanti vā āpajjati, tasmā ādito pabhuti vinayanidānaṃ dassetuṃ “tena samayenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

“At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time, not far from Vesālī, there was a village named Kalandagāma.” If it is asked, ‘What is the purpose of commencing the Verañja Chapter when the Vinaya’s origin should be commenced?’ It is said: to show the Vinaya’s origin from the very beginning. If so, does this not contradict the statement, “Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika rule promulgated?—At Vesālī”? It does not contradict. Why? Because the question “Where was it promulgated?” is an inquiry about the origin. Even so, when asked, “What was the origin of the first Pārājika?” is it not as if the reply with the common great origin is inappropriate? It is not inappropriate, because the origin is asked for separately for each training rule, and since that must be answered, the common great origin is stated first. The Pārājika and other rules have been compiled entirely according to the sequence of questions and answers. How were they compiled? The Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the entire Vinaya in sequence, and the Venerable Upāli Thera, when questioned, answered appropriately and without interruption. It should be understood that even unasked matters, such as disciplinary cases and other relevant topics, were included, and they made a communal recitation according to the sequence of answers. Otherwise, it would follow that the Verañja Chapter is the origin of only the first Pārājika, or that it is unrelated, or that it is without purpose, or that after a question about the origin of each training rule separately, that very thing must be given as the answer. Therefore, to show the origin of the Vinaya from the beginning, “At that time,” and so forth, has been commenced.

Idāni nidānabhaṇane payojanaṃ vakkhāma – vinayassaāṇādesanattā bhagavato tāva āṇārahabhāvadīpanaṃ[V 0.0029], āṇābhūtassa ca vinayassa anaññavisayabhāvadīpanaṃ, āṇāya ṭhitānaṃ sāvakānaṃ mahānubhāvadīpanañcāti tividhamassa payojanaṃ. Kathaṃ? Āṇāsāsanāraho hi bhagavā pahīnakilesattā, adhigataguṇavisesattā, lokajeṭṭhaseṭṭhattā, tādibhāvappattattā ca, arasarūpatādīhi aṭṭhahi akkosavatthūhi akampanato bhagavato tādibhāvappatti veditabbā, aṭṭhannampi tesaṃ akkosavatthūnaṃ attani sambhavapariyāyadīpanapāḷiyā pahīnakilesatā veditabbā[M 0.0031]. Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ tissannañca vijjānaṃ adhigamaparidīpanena adhigataguṇavisesatā veditabbā. “Nāhaṃ taṃ brāhmaṇa passāmi sadevake…pe… muddhāpi tassa vipateyyā”ti ca “jeṭṭho seṭṭho lokassā”ti ca vacanena jeṭṭhaseṭṭhatā veditabbā, idañca bhagavato āṇārahabhāvadīpanappayojanaṃ. “Āgamehi tvaṃ sāriputta, āgamehi tvaṃ sāriputta, tathāgatova tattha kālaṃ jānissatī”ti vacanaṃ anaññavisayabhāvadīpanaṃ. “Sādhāhaṃ, bhante, pathaviṃ parivatteyya”nti ca “ekāhaṃ, bhante, pāṇiṃ abhinimminissāmī”ti ca “sādhu, bhante, sabbo bhikkhusaṅgho uttarakuruṃ piṇḍāya gaccheyyā”ti ca imehi therassa tīhi sīhanādehi āṇāya ṭhitānaṃ sāvakānaṃ mahānubhāvatādīpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sāvatthiyādīsu aviharitvā kimatthaṃ bhagavā verañjāyameva tadā vihāsīti ce? Naḷeruyakkhassa pītisañjananatthaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa bhikkhāvasena akilamanatthaṃ, verañjabrāhmaṇassa pasādasañjananatthaṃ, mahāmoggallānattherassa ānubhāvadīpanaṭṭhānabhūtattā, sāriputtattherassa vinayapaññattiyācanahetubhūtaparivitakkanaṭṭhānabhūtattā ca. Tesu pacchimaṃ balavakāraṇaṃ, tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tena samayenāti yena kālena āyasmato…pe… tena kālenā”ti. Purimesu catūsu asaṅgahakāraṇesu paṭhamena bhagavā mettābhāvanādinā amanussānaṃ cittasaṃrakkhaṇena bhikkhūnaṃ ādaraṃ janeti. Dutiyena parisāvacarena bhikkhunā evaṃ parisā saṅgahetabbā, evaṃ appicchena santuṭṭhena ca bhavitabbanti vā dasseti. Tatiyena paccaye nirapekkhena kulānuggaho kātabboti. Catutthena evaṃ mahānubhāvenāpi paccayatthaṃ na loluppaṃ kātabbaṃ, kevalaṃ paradattupajīvinā bhavitabbanti dasseti. “Tenātiādipāṭhassa…pe… vinayassatthavaṇṇana”nti vacanato añño tenātiādipāṭho, añño vinayo āpajjati.

Now, we will explain the purpose of the discourse on the origin. Since the Vinaya is a teaching by command, its purpose is threefold: to demonstrate the Blessed One’s worthiness to command, to demonstrate that the Vinaya, being a command, is not the domain of any other, and to demonstrate the great power of disciples who abide by his command. How so? The Blessed One is worthy to command because he has abandoned defilements, attained special qualities, is the eldest and best in the world, and has reached the state of 'Tādi' (the 'Such-like' state). His attainment of the 'Tādi' state is to be understood from his unshakenness in the face of the eight grounds for abuse, such as being without taste, without form, and so forth. The abandonment of defilements is to be understood through the passage explaining the conditions for the arising of those eight grounds of abuse in oneself. The attainment of special qualities is shown by the explanation of the four jhānas and the three true knowledges. His being the eldest and best in the world is known through statements like, “I, brahmin, do not see in this world with its devas… his head would split apart,” and “Eldest and best of the world.” This demonstrates the purpose of showing the Blessed One’s worthiness to command. The statement, “Wait, Sāriputta, wait, Sāriputta! The Tathāgata himself will know the time for that,” demonstrates that this is not the domain of any other. The great power of disciples who abide by his command is to be understood through these three lion’s roars of the Elder: “Good, venerable sir, I could turn over the earth,” “Good, venerable sir, I alone could create a hand,” and “Good, venerable sir, the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus could go for alms in Uttarakuru.” Why did the Blessed One dwell in Verañjā at that time instead of Sāvatthī and other places? For the purpose of arousing joy in the Naḷeru Yaksha, for the non-weariness of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus regarding alms-food, for arousing confidence in the brahmin of Verañjā, because it served as a basis for demonstrating the power of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and because it provided a ground for the Venerable Sāriputta’s reflection, which became the cause for requesting the establishment of the Vinaya. Among these, the last is the strongest reason. Hence, the commentary states, “At that time—the time when the Venerable… at that time.” As for the first four reasons for patronage: by the first, the Blessed One generates respect for the bhikkhus by protecting the minds of non-humans through the development of loving-kindness and other practices. By the second, he shows that the assembly should be supported in this way by a bhikkhu who frequents the assembly, or that one should be of few wishes and easily contented. By the third, he shows that support should be given to families while being unconcerned with requisites. By the fourth, he demonstrates that even one of such great power should not be greedy for requisites, but should live solely on what is given by others. From the statement, “The passage beginning 'tena'… up to the exposition of the meaning of the Vinaya,” it would follow that the passage beginning “tena” is one thing, and the Vinaya is another.

“Tenātiādipāṭhamhā, ko añño vinayo idha;

Tassatthaṃ dassayantova, kare vinayavaṇṇana”nti. –

From the passage beginning with 'Tena,' what other Vinaya is here? Explaining its meaning, should one compose the exposition of the Vinaya?

Ce? Nanu vuttaṃ pubbeva “idañhi buddhassa bhagavato attapaccakkhavacanaṃ na hotī”tiādi, tasmā upālittherena vuttassa tenātiādipāṭhassa atthaṃ nānappakārato dassayanto karissāmi vinayassa [V 0.0030] bhagavato attapaccakkhavacanabhūtassa atthavaṇṇananti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yadi evaṃ “tena [M 0.0032] samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatīti evamādivacanapaṭimaṇḍitanidānaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kena dhārita”ntiādivacanaṃ virujjhati “tena samayenā”tiādivacanassa vinayapiṭakapariyāpannabhāvadīpanatoti ce? Na, aññatthepi tabbohārasiddhito “nānāvidhabhittikammapaṭimaṇḍitavasano puriso”tiādīsu viya. Vinayassādibhāvena saṅgītikārakehi anuññātattā vinayapariyāpannatāpi yujjati tassa vacanassa. Etthāha – yathā suttante “ekaṃ samaya”nti ca, abhidhamme ca “yasmiṃ samaye”ti aniyamato vuttaṃ, tathā avatvā idha “tena samayenā”ti paṭhamaṃ taṃniddesova kasmā vuttoti? Vuccate – tassa tassa sikkhāpadapaññattisamayassa, yassa vā sikkhāpadapaññattihetubhūtassa samayassa hetu bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi, tassa ca samayassa atītassa tesaṃ saṅgītikārakānaṃ vasīnaṃ suviditattā. Kathaṃ? “Ye te bhikkhū appicchā te ujjhāyantī”tiādivacanato, “atha kho te bhikkhū bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesu”nti ca “atha kho bhagavā etasmiṃ nidāne sannipātāpetvā”ti ca “bhikkhūnaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ tadanu…pe… dasa atthavase paṭicca saṅghasuṭṭhutāyā”ti ca “evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti ca khandhakesu ca “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajja”ntiādivinayakkamassa vacanato yo so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo, tassa tassa vinayakkamassa so paññattisamayo ca suvidito tesaṃ pañcasatānaṃ dhammadharānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, nāyaṃ nayo suttantābhidhammesu sambhavati. Tasmā suviditattā tena samayena hetubhūtena viharatīti viharatipadena ekasambandhattā ca paṭhamaṃ yaṃniddesādino asambhavato ca vinayapiṭake taṃniddesova paṭhamaṃ vutto. Kathaṃ? Ettha “yena kho pana samayena vesāliyā avidūre kalandagāmo nāma hotī”ti vā “yena kho pana samayena vesālī…pe… hotī”ti vā asambhavato yaṃniddesena avatvā taṃniddesasseva sambhavato “tena kho pana samayena…pe… kalandagāmo nāma hotī”ti vuttanti, kevalaṃ suviditattā vā. Aniyamaniddesavacananti ettha kiñcāpi yathāvuttanayena niyamaniddesavacanamevetaṃ taṃniddesattā, tathāpi sampatikālavasena taditaresaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aviditattā “aniyamaniddesavacana”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “ayañhi sabbasmimpi vinaye yuttī”ti, taṃ tabbahulena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

If it is asked: Was it not previously stated, 'This is not the Buddha’s own personally realized statement,' and so on? Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: while explaining in various ways the meaning of the text beginning with 'tena' spoken by the Elder Upāli, 'I shall make an exposition of the meaning of the Vinaya, which is the Blessed One's own personally realized statement.' If so, does the statement beginning, 'By whom was the Vinaya Piṭaka, whose introduction is adorned with such words as, “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā,” maintained?' contradict the indication that the statement beginning 'tena samayena' is included in the Vinaya Piṭaka? No, because that usage is established in other contexts as well, just as in phrases like, 'a man whose dwelling is adorned with various wall paintings.' Because it was permitted by the compilers of the council as the beginning of the Vinaya, the inclusion of that statement in the Vinaya is also justified. Here, an objector said: Just as in the Suttanta, 'at one time,' and in the Abhidhamma, 'at whatever time,' are stated indefinitely, why, without saying it like that, was 'at that time'—the definite indication with 'taṃ'—stated first here? It is answered: Because that past time—the time of the enactment of each training rule, or the time which was the cause for the enactment of the training rule, for which reason the Blessed One dwelt in that very place—was well-known to those masters, the compilers of the council. How so? From statements such as, 'Those monks who were of few desires were critical…'; and, 'Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One…'; and, 'Then the Blessed One, on this occasion, having had the Saṅgha assembled…'; and, '…for the monks, what is suitable in that regard… for the complete well-being of the Saṅgha…'; and, 'And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule…'; and also in the Khandhakas, from the Vinaya procedure beginning with, 'I allow, monks, the going forth by the three refuges…'—whatever was the time of the enactment of the training rule, that time of enactment for each and every Vinaya procedure was well-known to those five hundred monks, the bearers of the Dhamma. This method is not possible in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma. Therefore, because it was well-known, and because of the single connection with the word 'viharati' (as in, 'he dwells at that time which was the cause'), and because of the impossibility of beginning with an indefinite pronoun like 'yaṃ', only the definite pronoun 'taṃ' was stated first in the Vinaya Piṭaka. How is it impossible? Here, because it is impossible to say, 'On the occasion when near Vesālī there was a village named Kalandaka,' or 'On the occasion when at Vesālī… there was,' and so, not speaking with the indefinite pronoun 'yaṃ', and because only the definite pronoun 'taṃ' is possible, it was said, 'At that time… there was a village named Kalandaka.' Or, it was said thus simply because it was well-known. Regarding the phrase 'indefinite indication statement': although, according to the method stated, this is indeed a definite indication statement because it is a definite pronoun ('taṃ'), nevertheless, by way of the present time, because it is not known to other monks apart from those compilers, it was called an 'indefinite indication statement.' As for the statement that was made, 'This reasoning applies throughout the entire Vinaya,' it should be understood that this was stated as applying for the most part.

Yadi [M 0.0033] sabbaṃ tenāti padaṃ aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ bhaveyya, tena hi bhikkhave bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadanti ettha idampi pubbe siddhatthaṃ tenāti padaṃ aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ bhaveyya. “Tena samayena buddho bhagavā uruvelāyaṃ viharatī”tiādīsu vuttaṃ tenāti padañca aniyamaniddesavacanaṃ bhaveyya, na ca hoti, tasmā yesaṃ tena taṃniddesena niddiṭṭhattho avidito, tesaṃ [V 0.0031] vasenāha “aniyamaniddesavacanameta”nti. Atha vā tato paṭhamaṃ tadatthādassanato pacchāpi taṃsambandhena yaṃniddesadassanato ca “aniyamaniddesavacanameta”nti vuttaṃ. Atha vā pubbaṇhādīsu ayaṃ nāmāti aniyametvā kālaparidīpanassa samayasaddassa upapadabhāvenapi evaṃ vattumarahati “yadidaṃ aniyamaniddesavacana”nti. Atha vā “tenā”ti vutte tena ghaṭena paṭenāti sabbatthappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ niyamaṃ karoti “samayenā”ti. Kena pana samayena? Parabhāge atthato siddhena sāriputtassa parivitakkasamayena. Etthāha – vitakkasamayo ce idhādhippeto, “parato idha pana hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena cā”tiādivacanaṃ virujjhatīti? Na, bāhullena vuttattā. Suttantābhidhammesu viya avatvā idha vinayapiṭake karaṇavacanena kasmā niddesoti hi codanā. Tasmā tassā vissajjane bāhullena karaṇavacanappayojanaṃ vattukāmo ācariyo āha “yo so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo”tiādi. Na sampati vuccamānasseva karaṇavacanassa payojanaṃ vattukāmo, imassa pana hetuatthova sambhavati, na karaṇattho, tasmā āha “aparabhāge atthato siddhenā”tiādi. Samayañcāti āgamanapaccayasamavāyaṃ tadanurūpakālañca upādāyāti attho. Paccayasāmaggiñca āgamanakālañca labhitvā jānissāmāti adhippāyo.

If the word 'tena' were in all cases a term of indefinite reference, then in the text 'tena hi bhikkhave bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadanti', this word 'tena', whose meaning was previously established, would also be a term of indefinite reference. In passages such as, 'At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Uruvelā,' the word 'tena' would also be a term of indefinite reference, but it is not so. Therefore, on account of those for whom the meaning indicated by that word 'tena'—a reference with the pronoun 'ta'—is not known, the commentator said, 'This is a term of indefinite reference.' Alternatively, it is said, 'This is a term of indefinite reference,' because that meaning is not indicated first, and also because later, in connection with it, a reference with 'ya' is to be shown. Alternatively, without specifying 'this is the name' among times such as the forenoon, it is also appropriate to say thus—'that which is a term of indefinite reference'—due to its being an adjunct to the word 'samaya', which indicates time. Alternatively, when 'tena' is said, to prevent its application in all cases, such as 'by that pot' or 'by that cloth', the specification 'by the occasion' (samayena) is made. But by what occasion? By the occasion of Sāriputta’s reflection, which is established by its meaning in the subsequent portion. Here an objector says: If the occasion of reflection is intended here, would not the subsequent statement—'Here, however, the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are possible. For that occasion of laying down the training rule is difficult to discern even for Sāriputta and others; by that occasion which has become the cause and has become the instrument...'—be contradicted? No, it is not contradicted, because it is stated in a general sense. Indeed, the objection is: Why is there a reference with the instrumental case here in the Vinaya Piṭaka, without stating it as is done in the Suttanta and Abhidhamma? Therefore, in answering that objection, the commentator, wishing to state the purpose of the instrumental case in a general sense, said, 'that occasion of laying down the training rule,' etc. He does not wish to state the purpose of the instrumental case for that which is being spoken of right now; for this, however, only the meaning of cause is possible, not the meaning of instrument. Therefore, he said, 'in the subsequent portion, established by its meaning,' etc. And 'samayaṃ' means taking into account the concurrence of conditions for arrival and the suitable time in accordance with that; this is the meaning. The intention is: 'We shall know, having obtained the assemblage of conditions and the time of arrival.'

Etthāha – yathā “ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo samayo cā”ti ettha khaṇasamayānaṃ eko attho, tathā kālañca samayañca upādāyāti kālasamayānaṃ eko attho siyā, apica āgamanapaccayasamavāyo cettha samayo kālassāpi āgamanapaccayattā samayaggahaṇeneva so gahitoti visuṃ kālo kimatthaṃ gahitoti ca? Vuccate – appeva nāma svepīti kālassa paṭhamaṃ niyamitattā na samayo kālattho[M 0.0034]. Tasmiṃ sveti niyamitakāle itaresaṃ āgamanapaccayānaṃ samavāyaṃ paṭicca upasaṅkameyyāma yathāniyamitakālepi pubbaṇhādippabhedaṃ yathāvuttasamavāyānurūpaṃ kālañca upādāyāti sveti paricchinnadivase pubbaṇhādikālaniyatabhāvaṃ dasseti, tasmā kālasamayānaṃ na ekatthattā kālassa visuṃ gahaṇampi sātthakanti veditabbaṃ. Yasmā khaṇe khaṇe tvaṃ bhikkhu jāyasi ca jīyasi ca mīyasi ceti bhikkhuniyā santike abhikkhaṇaṃ gacchatīti (pāci. 198) ca khaṇe khaṇe bhāsati satthusāsananti ca khaṇasaddo anekattho, tathā samayasaddo ca, tasmā ekamekena niyamento “ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo cā”ti āha. Khaṇasamayānaṃ attho ekattho yujjati khaṇo okāsalābho, aṭṭhakkhaṇavajjito navamo khaṇoti attho. Attano attano ucchedādayo diṭṭhigatasaṅkhāte samaye ettha pavadantīti samayappavādako. Sveva tindukācīrasaṅkhātāya timbarurukkhapantiyā parikkhittattā [V 0.0032] tindukācīraṃ. Ekasālaketi eko sālarukkho. “Kuṭikā”tipi vadanti. Atthābhisamayāti attano hitapaṭilābhā. Dhīroti ca paṇḍito vuccati, nāñño. Sammā mānābhisamayāti suṭṭhu mānassa pahānena, samucchedavasena suṭṭhu mānappahānenāti attho. Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭhotiādīsu “catunnaṃ saccānaṃ catūhi ākārehi paṭivedho”tiādīsu khandhapañcakasaṅkhātassa dukkhassa dukkhākāratāyaṭṭho. Saṅkhataṭṭho kāraṇuppattiattho, dukkhāya vedanāya santāpaṭṭho. Sukhāya vedanāya vipariṇāmaṭṭho. Pīḷanaṭṭhādikova abhisamayaṭṭhoti attho daṭṭhabbo. Gabbhokkantisamayotiādīsupi pathavīkampanaālokapātubhāvādīhi devamanussesu pākaṭo. Dukkarakārikasamayopi kāḷo samaṇo gotamo na kāḷotiādinā pākaṭo. Sattasattāhāni ca aññāni ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo.

Here, an objector says: Just as in 'Indeed, O monks, there is but one moment and one occasion,' the words 'moment' and 'occasion' have one meaning, so too, in 'taking into account time and occasion,' the words 'time' and 'occasion' might have one meaning. Furthermore, another objection is raised: Herein, 'occasion' is the concurrence of conditions for arrival. Since 'time' is also a condition for arrival, its meaning is included by the term 'occasion'. This being so, for what purpose is 'time' mentioned separately? The reply is given: Because time is first determined by 'Perhaps even tomorrow,' 'occasion' does not have the meaning of 'time'. In that determined time, 'tomorrow,' we might approach depending on the concurrence of the other conditions for arrival. And by the phrase 'taking into account... the time'—a time suitable for the aforementioned concurrence and having divisions such as the forenoon, even within a generally determined time—it is shown that within the specified day of 'tomorrow', a specific time such as the forenoon is being determined. Therefore, because 'time' and 'occasion' do not have a single meaning, it should be understood that the separate mention of 'time' is also meaningful. Because the word 'moment' has many meanings—as in 'In every moment, O monk, you are born, you age, and you die'; and 'He goes frequently to the nun's presence'; and 'He speaks the Teacher's Dispensation moment by moment'—and similarly, the word 'occasion' also has many meanings, therefore, delimiting one by means of the other, the Blessed One said, 'Indeed, O monks, there is but one moment and one occasion.' The meaning of 'moment' and 'occasion' is fittingly a single meaning. 'Moment' is the gaining of an opportunity; it means the ninth moment, which is other than the eight inopportune moments. They are called 'proponents of views' (samayappavādaka) because herein they proclaim their respective doctrines, such as annihilationism, which are designated as wrong views. That very place is called Tindukācīra because it is surrounded by a row of Timbaru trees, also known as Tinduka trees. 'Ekasālaka' means there is one Sāla tree; some also say 'there is a hut'. 'Attainment of the goal' (atthābhisamaya) is due to the attainment of one's own welfare. He is called 'wise' (dhīra) and 'learned' (paṇḍita), not anything else. 'Right overcoming of conceit' (sammā mānābhisamaya) means through the thorough abandonment of conceit, that is, through the thorough abandonment of conceit by way of eradication. In such passages as 'Suffering has the meaning of oppression,' and 'the penetration of the four truths through four aspects,' it refers to the characteristic of suffering as it pertains to the suffering designated as the five aggregates. The meaning of 'conditioned' is the meaning of arising from a cause. For painful feeling, it has the meaning of torment; for pleasant feeling, it has the meaning of change. The meaning of 'realization' (abhisamaya) should be understood as precisely the meaning of oppression and so on. Also in such instances as 'the time of conception in the womb,' it was made manifest to devas and humans by the earthquake, the appearance of light, and so on. The time of performing the ascetic practices was also made manifest by such statements as 'The ascetic Gotama is dark [from austerities], not dark [by nature],' and so on. The seven weeks and other such periods constitute the occasion for dwelling in bliss in the present life.

Accantameva taṃ samayanti ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva pattasanniṭṭhānā, tāva accantasampayogena tasmiṃ samaye. Karuṇāvihārena vihāsīti karuṇākiccavihārena tasmiṃ samaye vihāsīti attho. Taṃ samayañhi karuṇākiccasamayaṃ. Ñāṇakiccaṃ karuṇākiccanti dve bhagavato kiccāni, abhisambodhi ñāṇakiccaṃ, mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā veneyyasattāvalokanaṃ [M 0.0035] katvā tadanurūpakaraṇaṃ karuṇākiccaṃ. “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīya”nti (ma. ni. 1.273; udā. 12, 28) hi vuttaṃ, taṃ bhagavāpi karotiyeva. Atha vā āgantukehi bhikkhūhi ādisamāyogañca. Tattha karuṇākiccaṃ vihāraṃ dassento “karuṇāvihārena vihāsī”ti āha. Adhikaraṇañhi kālatthoti ettha hi-kāro kāraṇattho. Tattha hi abhidhamme kālasamūhakhaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātavasena pañcavidho samayaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo. Kālasamūhaṭṭho samayo kathaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ hoti? Adhikaraṇamuppattiṭṭhānaṃ pubbaṇhe jātoti yathā, evaṃ kālaṭṭho samayasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Kathaṃ rāsaṭṭho? Yavarāsimhi jātoti yathā. Tasmā yasmiṃ kāle puñje vā cittaṃ samuppannaṃ, tasmiṃ kāle puñje vā phassādayo uppajjantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Adhikaraṇañhīti ettha abhidhamme niddiṭṭhaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kālaṭṭho samūhaṭṭho ca hoti, “yasmiṃ samaye”ti vuttaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idāni bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇañca dassento “tattha vuttāna”miccādimāha. Tattha abhidhamme vuttānaṃ bhāvo nāma kinti? Uppatti vijjamānatā, sā tesaṃ tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ, sā pana samayassa bhāvena bhāvo lakkhīyati ñāyati, tasmā tattha bhummavacananiddeso katoti vuttaṃ hoti.

They come together with it absolutely from the beginning of the undertaking until the attainment of completion; for that long, there is an absolute connection at that time. 'He dwelt with a compassionate abiding' means he dwelt with the abiding that is the function of compassion at that time; this is the meaning. For that occasion is indeed the occasion of the function of compassion. The Blessed One has two functions: the function of knowledge and the function of compassion. Supreme enlightenment is the function of knowledge, while the function of compassion is entering the attainment of great compassion, surveying beings fit to be trained, and acting in accordance with them. For it is said, 'Monks, for you who have gathered, two things are to be done' (MN 1.273; Ud 12, 28); this the Blessed One also indeed does. Alternatively, it refers to the initial association with visiting monks. In that context, showing the abiding that is the function of compassion, he said, 'he dwelt with a compassionate abiding.' In 'for the basis has the meaning of time,' the particle 'hi' has the meaning of reason. Indeed, there in the Abhidhamma, the meaning of 'samaya' (occasion) should be understood in five ways: as time, as a collection, as a moment, as a conjunction, and as a cause. How is 'samaya' with the meaning of time and collection a basis?
