The basis is the place of arising, as in 'arisen in the morning'; in this way, the word 'samaya' should be understood as having the meaning of time. How with the meaning of a heap? As in 'arisen in a heap of barley.' Therefore, it is said that in whatever time or collection consciousness arises, in that time or collection contact and other factors arise. In 'for the basis,' the basis pointed out in the Abhidhamma is both that which has the meaning of time and that which has the meaning of collection; it should be understood that this was said with reference to the basis spoken of as 'at which time.' Now, also showing the characteristic of a state by means of a state, he says, 'of those stated therein,' etc. Therein, in the Abhidhamma, what is called the 'state' (bhāva) of those things stated? It is arising, existence. That is the state of those phenomena of contact and so on, stated therein. That state, however, is discerned and known by the state of the occasion. Therefore, it is said that the specification in the locative case has been made there.

Tattha khaṇo nāma aṭṭhakkhaṇavinimutto navamo khaṇo, tasmiṃ sati uppajjati. Samavāyo nāma [V 0.0033] cakkhundriyādikāraṇasāmaggī, tasmiṃ sati uppajjati. Hetu nāma rūpādiārammaṇaṃ. Tasmā tasmiṃ khaṇakāraṇasamavāyahetumhi sati tesaṃ phassādīnaṃ bhāvo vijjamānatā hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha pana hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavatīti ettha atthadvayamekassa sambhavatīti idha vinaye vuttassa samayasaddassa kattukaraṇatthe tatiyā hetumhi ca ityuttattā. So dubbiññeyyoti “tathāgatova tattha kālaṃ jānissatī”ti vuttattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena samayenāti tassa samayassa kāraṇā “annena vasati vijjāya vasatī”ti yathā, annaṃ vā vijjaṃ vā labhāmīti tadatthaṃ vasatītyattho. Evaṃ “tena samayena viharatī”ti vutte hetvatthe tatiyā daṭṭhabbā, tasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā samayañca vītikkamañca olokayamāno tattha tattha vihāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatiyapārājikādīsu “icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, addhamāsaṃ[M 0.0036], paṭisallīyitu”nti (pārā. 162) evamādīsu daṭṭhabbā, tasmā dutiyā kāladdhāne accantasaṃyogeti dutiyātra sambhavati “māsamadhīte divasamadhīte”ti yathā. Idha pana hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavatīti ettha yassa karaṇavacanassa hetuattho sambhavati, tena samayena hetubhūtena taṃ taṃ vatthuvītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ vītikkamasamayasaṅkhātaṃ vā sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi. Yassa karaṇattho sambhavati, tena karaṇabhūtena samayena sampattena sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsīti adhippāyo.

Therein, 'moment' refers to the ninth moment, free from the eight moments; when that exists, it arises. 'Confluence' refers to the harmony of conditions such as the eye faculty; when that exists, it arises. 'Cause' refers to the object such as form. Therefore, when that moment, confluence of conditions, and cause exist, the state, the existence, of contact and so forth is said to be. Here, however, the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument both arise. Thus, because two meanings arise for a single term, it is because it is said that for the word 'samaya' as stated in this Vinaya, the instrumental case is used in the sense of agent and instrument, and also in the sense of cause. That it is difficult to understand is said to be because it is stated, 'Only the Tathāgata will know the time for that.' 'By that occasion' means 'because of that occasion,' just as in 'he dwells by food, he dwells by knowledge,' the meaning is that he dwells for the purpose of obtaining food or knowledge. Thus, when it is said, 'he dwells at that time,' the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of cause. Therefore, it is said that observing the occasion for the laying down of the training rule and the transgression, he dwelled here and there. This should be seen in the third Pārājika and so forth, as in 'I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for half a month,' and so on. Therefore, according to the rule 'the accusative is used for continuous connection with time and distance,' the accusative case is possible here, as in 'he studies for a month, he studies for a day.' Here, however, where it is said that the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument both arise: where the meaning of cause arises for an instrumental expression, the Blessed One dwelled here and there, considering that cause which had become the occasion—whether it was what is called the transgression of that particular object, or what is called the occasion of transgression, and the cause for formulating a training rule. Where the meaning of instrument arises, the Blessed One dwelled here and there, establishing the training rules by means of that occasion which had arrived and become the instrument. This is the intended meaning.

Gaṇṭhipade pana “sudinnādīnaṃ vītikkamova kāraṇaṃ nāma, tassa niyamabhūto kālo pana karaṇameva taṃ kālaṃ anatikkamitvāva sikkhāpadassa paññapetabbattā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ niddosaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “idaṃ karaṇaṃ pubbabhāgattā paṭhamaṃ vattabbampi pacchā vutta”nti, taṃ duvuttaṃ. Hetuatthato hi yathā pacchā karaṇattho yojiyamāno anukkameneva yogaṃ gacchati, tathā ca yojito. Yaṃ pana aṭṭhakathācariyo pacchā vuttaṃ idaṃ karaṇatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ yojetvā paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ hetuatthaṃ pacchā yojesi, taṃ yojanāsukhattāti veditabbanti ācariyena likhitaṃ. Ito paṭṭhāya yattha yattha “ācariyena likhita”nti vā “ācariyassa takko”ti vā vuccati, tattha tattha ācariyo nāma ānandācariyo kalasapuravāsīti gahetabbo. Etthāha – yathā suttante “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā”ti vuccati, tathā “tena samayena bhagavā verañjāya”nti vattabbaṃ, atha savevacanaṃ vattukāmo thero, tathāgato sugatotiādīnipi vattabbāni, atha imasseva padadvayassa gahaṇe kiñci payojanaṃ atthi, taṃ vattabbanti? Vuccate – kesañci buddhassa bhagavato paramagambhīraṃ ajjhāsayakkamaṃ ajānataṃ “apaññatte sikkhāpade anādīnavadasso…pe… abhiviññāpesī”tiādikaṃ (pārā. 36) “atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ sudinnaṃ paṭipucchī”tiādikañca (pārā. 39) “sādiyi tvaṃ bhikkhūti. Nāhaṃ bhagavā sādiyi”ntiādikañca (pārā. 72) [V 0.0034] tathā purāṇavohārikaṃ bhikkhuṃ pucchitvā tena vuttaparicchedena dutiyapārājikapaññāpanañca devadattassa pabbajjānujānanañcāti evamādikaṃ vinayapariyattiṃ disvā buddhasubuddhataṃ paṭicca saṅkā sambhaveyya, “tathā kiṃ pana tuyhaṃ chavassa kheḷāsakassā”ti [M 0.0037] (cūḷava. 336) evamādikaṃ pharusavacanapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vinayapariyattiṃ nissāya khīṇāsavattaṃ paṭicca saṅkā sambhaveyya, tadubhayasaṅkāvinodanatthaṃ āyasmatā upālittherena idameva padadvayaggahaṇaṃ sabbattha katanti veditabbaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – kāmaṃ sabbañeyyabuddhattā buddhoyeva, bhaggasabbadosattā bhagavāva, so satthāti. Paratopi vuttaṃ “jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchanti…pe… anatthasaṃhite setughāto tathāgatāna”nti (pārā. 16). Suttante ca vuttaṃ “saṇhenapi kesi vinemi pharusenapī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.111).

In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: 'For Sudinna and others, the transgression itself is the cause. The time which is the determinant for it, however, is indeed the instrument, because the training rule had to be laid down without exceeding that time.' That is faultless. But what was said—'This instrument, though it should be stated first as it is in the preliminary part, was stated afterwards'—is poorly stated. For, when the meaning of the instrument is applied after the meaning of cause, it connects only in sequential order, and it has been so applied. However, as for the Aṭṭhakathā master first applying this later-stated instrumental meaning and afterwards applying the first-stated causal meaning, it should be understood that this was for the sake of ease of application. From here on, wherever it is said, 'written by the teacher' or 'the teacher’s reasoning,' the teacher should be understood as the teacher Ānanda, a resident of Kalasapura. Here, an objector says: Just as in the Suttanta it is stated, 'At one time, the Bhagavā…,' so too it should be stated, 'At that time, the Bhagavā was at Verañjā…' Or else, if the Elder wishes to speak with synonyms, terms such as 'the Tathāgata,' 'the Sugata,' and so on, should also be said. However, is there any purpose in taking just these two words? That should be stated. It is said: For some who do not know the supremely profound course of intention of the Buddha, the Bhagavā, a doubt might arise concerning the Buddha's perfect enlightenment upon seeing such Vinaya scripture as: 'When the training rule was not laid down... he made it fully known...'; and 'Then the Bhagavā questioned the venerable Sudinna...'; and 'Did you consent, bhikkhu? I did not consent, Bhagavā...'; and furthermore, the laying down of the second Pārājika after questioning a bhikkhu who was formerly a judge and by the definition given by him; and the permitting of Devadatta's ordination. Furthermore, a doubt might arise concerning his state of having destroyed the cankers, relying on Vinaya scripture connected with harsh speech, such as, 'What use are you, you corpse, you phlegm-eater?' It should be understood that to dispel both these doubts, the venerable Elder Upāli made this very taking of the pair of words everywhere. By this, it is shown: Indeed, because of having awakened to all that is knowable, he is the Buddha, and because of having broken all faults, he is the Bhagavā; he is the Teacher. Elsewhere it is also said: 'Tathāgatas ask even though they know… for the sake of eliminating what is unbeneficial, the Tathāgatas strike down obstacles.' And in the Suttanta it is said: 'Kesi, I train with gentleness and also with harshness…'

Asādhāraṇahetumhīti ettha kusalamūlāni na akusalānaṃ kadāci mūlāni honti, tathā akusalamūlāni kusalānaṃ, abyākatamūlāni na kadāci kusalānanti ayameva nayo labbhati, yasmā kusalā hetū taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo (paṭṭhā. 1.1.401 ādayo), tasmā kusalāni kusalānaṃyevātiādinayo na labbhati. Puci vuccate kuṭṭhā, te mandayati nāsayatīti pucimando. Sattānaṃ hitasukhanipphādanādhimuttatanti ettha sāmaññato vuttasatte dvidhā bhinditvā dassetuṃ “manussānaṃ upakārabahulata”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Bahujanahitāyāti bahuno janassa hitatthāya. Paññāsampattiyā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikahitūpadesako hi bhagavā. Sukhāyāti sukhatthāya. Cāgasampattiyā upakārakasukhasampadāyako hi esa. Mettākaruṇāsampattiyā lokānukampāya mātāpitaro viya. Lokassa rakkhitagopitā hi esa. Devamanussānanti ettha bhabbapuggale veneyyasatteyeva gahetvā tesaṃ nibbānamaggaphalādhigamāya attano uppattiṃ dasseti. “Atthāyā”ti hi vutte paramatthatthāya nibbānāya, “hitāyā”ti vutte taṃsampāpakamaggatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, maggato uttari hitaṃ nāma natthīti. Sukhāyāti phalasamāpattisukhatthāya tato uttari sukhābhāvato. Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātenāti ettha samādhiṃ paññañca aggahetvā diṭṭhisīlamattaggahaṇaṃ sabbasekkhāsekkhasāmaññattā. Kosambakasuttepi (ma. ni. 1.492) “sīlasāmaññagato viharati, diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharatī”ti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhiggahaṇena paññāpi gahitāti ce? Na, sotāpannādīnampi paññāya paripūrakāribhāvappasaṅgato, tasmā ekalakkhaṇānampi tāsaṃ paññādiṭṭhīnaṃ avatthantarabhedo atthi dhitisamādhindriyasammāsamādhīnaṃ viya[M 0.0038]. Aññāsīti ettha sotadvārānusārena ñātā, atthā sutāti hi vuccanti “sutametaṃ, bho gotama, pāpakā samācārā dissanti ceva suyyanti cā”tiādīsu viya. “Bhikkhu kho, upāli[V 0.0035], saṅghaṃ bhindatī”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 354) viya avadhāraṇatthe vā. Verañjāyaṃ bhavo vijjamāno. Itthambhūtassa evaṃ bhūtassa. Kathaṃ bhūtassa? Sakyaputtassa sakyakulā pabbajitassa, evaṃ hutvā ṭhitassa kittisaddo abbhuggatoti abhisaddena yoge upayogavacanāni hontīti attho.

Herein, in the text asādhāraṇahetumhi, wholesome roots are never roots of unwholesome states; likewise, unwholesome roots are never roots of wholesome states, and indeterminate roots are never roots of wholesome states—this very method is obtained. Because wholesome causes are a condition, by way of root-condition, for material phenomena co-arisen with them, therefore, the method such as 'wholesome states are a condition only for wholesome states' is not obtained. Leprosy (kuṭṭha) is called puci. Because it weakens (mandayati) and destroys (nāsayati) them (te), it is therefore called pucimanda. Herein, in the text sattānaṃ hitasukhanipphādanādhimuttatanti, in order to show the beings spoken of in a general sense by dividing them in two—namely as humans and devas—it is said, 'for the great benefit of humans,' and so on. Bahujanahitāya means for the benefit of many people. Indeed, through the accomplishment of wisdom, the Blessed One is an instructor on the welfare pertaining to the present life and to the future life. Sukhāya means for the sake of happiness. Indeed, through the accomplishment of generosity, this one is a provider of beneficial happiness. Through the accomplishment of loving-kindness and compassion, out of compassion for the world, he is like a mother and father. Indeed, this one is the protector and guardian of the world. Herein, in devamanussānaṃ, taking only those beings to be trained, individuals who are capable, he shows his own arising for their attainment of Nibbāna, the path, and the fruit. Indeed, when 'for the goal' (atthāya) is said, it means for the ultimate goal, for Nibbāna; when 'for the welfare' (hitāya) is said, it means for the sake of the path that leads to that attainment, for there is no welfare higher than the path. Sukhāya means for the sake of the happiness of the attainment of fruition, because there is no happiness higher than that. Herein, in diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena, the taking of merely view and virtue, without taking concentration and wisdom, is done because of the commonality to all trainees and non-trainees. In the Kosambaka Sutta as well it is said, 'He dwells having attained commonality of virtue, he dwells having attained commonality of view.' If it is said, 'By the taking of view, is wisdom also taken?' No, because of the unwanted consequence of it being a fulfiller of the wisdom of stream-enterers and so on. Therefore, although they have a single characteristic, there is a difference of state between that wisdom and view, just as there is a difference of state between fortitude (dhiti), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), and right concentration (sammāsamādhi). Herein, in aññāsi ('he understood'), it means 'known in accordance with the ear-door'. For meanings are indeed said to be 'heard' (sutā), as in such passages as, 'This has been heard by me, venerable Gotama, that evil practices are both seen and heard,' and so on. Or, the particle kho is in the sense of emphasis, as in, 'A bhikkhu, Upāli, indeed divides the Saṅgha,' and so on. 'Being in Verañjā' (verañjāyaṃ bhavo) means 'existing' (vijjamāno). 'Of one who has become such' (itthambhūtassa) means 'of one who has become thus' (evaṃ bhūtassa). Of one who has become how? Of the son of the Sakyans, gone forth from the Sakyan clan; the sound of fame of one who is established, having become thus, has arisen. The meaning is that in connection with the prefix abhi-, accusative case endings are used.

Kāmupādānapaccayā eva mettaṃ bhāveti, brahmaloke nibbattatīti iminā kāmupādānahetu kammaṃ katvā kāmabhave eva nibbattatītivādīnaṃ vādo paṭikkhittoti vadanti, “brahmaloke paṇītā kāmā”ti sutvā, kappetvā vā pacchā “tattha sampattiṃ anubhavissāmī”ti kāmupādānapaccayā tadupagaṃ karotīti brahmalokepi kāmanīyaṭṭhena kāmā, “tadārammaṇattā taṇhā kāmupādānanti vuttā”ti ca vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Kammañca cakkhussa janakakāraṇaṃ, kammassa mūlakāraṇaṃ taṇhā, tasmā na mūlakāraṇaṃ hoti janakaṃ. Rūpataṇhādayo dukkhasaccaṃ khandhapariyāpannattā, “yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkha”nti (dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 1.131; vibha. 190) vacanato ca. Tassa mūlakāraṇabhāvena samuṭṭhāpikāti tassa kāraṇabhūtassa imassa khandhapañcakassa samuṭṭhāpikāti yojetabbaṃ. “Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vacanato tassa eva kāraṇantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Apica “rūpādi viya taṇhāpi taṇhāya uppattippahānaṭṭhāna”nti vacanato rūpādi viya taṇhāpi dukkhasaccaṃ kataṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “rūpataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.400; vibha. 203) ca “etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.401; ma. ni. 1.134) ca. Visuddhimagge “sabbākārena pana upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhañceva ariyasaccañca aññatra taṇhāyā”ti vacanato idha rūpataṇhādayo dukkhasaccanti vacanaṃ virujjhatīti ce? Na, aññamaññāsaṅkarabhāvena dassetuṃ tattha tattha vuttattā. Yadi taṇhā upādānakkhandhapariyāpannā na bhaveyya, saccavibhaṅge “tattha katame saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā. Seyyathidaṃ, rūpupādānakkhandho [M 0.0039]..pe… viññāṇupādānakkhandho”ti (vibha. 202) ettha “ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ saṅkhārupādānakkhandho”ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, na ca vuttaṃ, tasmā dukkhasaccapariyāpannā taṇhāti ce? Na, hetuphalasaṅkaradosappasaṅgato. Na saṅkaradosoti ce? Saccavibhaṅgapāḷiyañhi pañcahi koṭṭhāsehi samudayasaccaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ.

They say that by this [statement from the commentary], 'One develops loving-kindness only with clinging to sensual pleasures as condition and is reborn in the Brahma-world,' the view of those who hold that 'having performed kamma due to the cause of clinging to sensual pleasures, one is reborn only in the sensual realm' is refuted. Having heard, 'In the Brahma-world, there are refined sensual pleasures,' or having conceived it, one later [thinks], 'I will experience that fortune there,' and due to clinging to sensual pleasures, undertakes that which leads to it. Therefore, even in the Brahma-world, [things] are called 'sensual pleasures' in the sense of being desirable, and they also say, 'Because it has that as its object, craving is called clinging to sensual pleasures.' This should be investigated. And kamma is the generative cause of the eye; craving is the root cause of kamma. Therefore, the generative cause is not the root cause. Craving for form and so on are the truth of suffering because they are included in the aggregates, and because of the statement, 'Not to get what one wants, that too is suffering' (Dī. Ni. 2.387; Ma. Ni. 1.131; Vibh. 190). Regarding the phrase 'the originator by being its root cause,' it should be construed thus: [craving is] the originator of this pentad of aggregates, for which that [kamma] is the cause. Because of the teaching, 'From the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance' (Ma. Ni. 1.103), it is also suitable to say that it is the cause of that very [kamma]. Furthermore, because of the statement, 'Like form, etc., craving itself is a basis for the arising and abandoning of craving,' craving, like form, etc., is also made the truth of suffering. For this has been said: 'Craving for form is a dear form, a pleasant form in the world; it is here that this craving, when arising, arises' (Dī. Ni. 2.400; Vibh. 203), and 'It is here that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned' (Dī. Ni. 2.401; Ma. Ni. 1.134). If it is said: Because of the statement in the Visuddhimagga, 'But in every way, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering and a noble truth, except for craving,' does the statement here, 'craving for form, etc., are the truth of suffering,' conflict with it? No, because it is stated in various places in order to show their state of non-intermingling. If [it is argued]: If craving were not included in the aggregates of clinging, then in the Saccavibhaṅga, in the passage, 'Therein, what, in brief, are the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering? That is to say, the aggregate of clinging to form... the aggregate of clinging to consciousness' (Vibh. 202), it would have been necessary to say, 'the aggregate of clinging to formations, excluding craving.' But this was not said. Therefore, craving is included in the truth of suffering.' If it is argued thus, [the reply is:] No, because it would lead to the fault of confusing cause and effect. If it is said, 'There is no fault of confusion'? Indeed, in the Saccavibhaṅga text, the truth of the origin is set forth in five parts.

Kathaṃ? Taṇhāti eko vāro, taṇhā ca avasesā ca kilesāti dutiyo, taṇhā ca avasesā ca kilesā avasesā ca akusalā dhammāti tatiyo, taṇhā ca avasesā ca kilesā [V 0.0036] avasesā ca akusalā dhammā tīṇi ca kusalamūlāni sāsavānīti catuttho, taṇhā ca avasesā ca kilesā avasesā ca akusalā dhammā tīṇi ca kusalamūlāni sāsavāni avasesā ca sāsavā kusalā dhammāti pañcamo vāroti. Āma niddiṭṭhaṃ, tathāpi abhidhammabhājaniyeyeva, na aññasmiṃ, so ca nayo ariyasaccaniddese na labbhati. Tathā hi tattha “cattāri saccāni”ccevāha, suttantabhājaniyapañhapucchakesu viya “cattāri ariyasaccānī”ti na vuttaṃ, tasmā suttantabhājaniyova pamāṇaṃ tattha ca taṇhāya vuttattā. Yathāha “tattha katamaṃ dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobhavikā…pe… seyyathidaṃ, kāmataṇhā”tiādi (vibha. 203). “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) iminā pariyāyena vuttattā tattha vuttampi pamāṇameva. “Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati pathavīkasiṇa”nti (dha. sa. 186 ādayo) vacanato “kasiṇānī”ti jhānāni vuttāni. Keci “uggahanimittapaṭibhāganimitte sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. “Dvattiṃsākārāpi paṇṇattiṃ vissajjetvā paṭikūlāti sati paṭṭhapetabbā”ti vacanato satigocarā rūpādayo ca veditabbā.

How? 'Craving is the truth of the origin': this is the first section. 'Craving and the remaining defilements are the truth of the origin': this is the second section. 'Craving, the remaining defilements, and the remaining unwholesome states are the truth of the origin': this is the third section. 'Craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots with influxes are the truth of the origin': this is the fourth section. 'Craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots with influxes, and the remaining wholesome states with influxes are the truth of the origin': this is the fifth section. Yes, it has been specified, yet it is specified only in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, not elsewhere. And that method is not found in the Exposition of the Noble Truths. For indeed, there it is said only 'the four truths'; unlike in the Suttanta-bhājanīya and Pañhāpucchaka, it is not stated as 'the four noble truths'. Therefore, the Suttanta-bhājanīya is the authority, and there craving is stated. As it is said: 'Therein, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence... namely, sensual craving,' etc. (Vibh. 203). Because it is stated by way of 'What is impermanent, that is suffering' (SN 3.15), what is stated there is also an authority. From the statement, 'Having entered and abided in the first jhāna on the earth kasiṇa' (Dhs. 186, etc.), the jhānas are called 'kasiṇas'. Some say, 'This is said with reference to the learning sign and the counterpart sign,' but that is not correct. From the statement, 'Regarding the thirty-two parts, having abandoned the concept (paññatti), mindfulness should be established on them as repulsive,' it should be understood that the objects of mindfulness are form and so on.

Saddhāhirottappabāhusaccavīriyārambhopaṭṭhitasatisampajaññatāti ime satta saddhammā nāma. Sabhāvatoti dukkhato. Na cavatīti deve sandhāya. Ñāteyyanti ñātabbaṃ. Daṭṭheyyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā pana “nāhaṃ gamanena lokassa antaṃ ñāteyya”nti vadāmīti attho. Lokanti khandhalokaṃ. Gamanena na pattabboti sarīragamanena, agatigamanena vā na pattabbo, ariyagamanena lokantaṃ patvāva dukkhā atthi pamocananti vuttaṃ hoti. Samitāvīti samitakileso. Āhāraṭṭhitikāti paccayaṭṭhitikā. Ye keci [M 0.0040] paccayaṭṭhitikā, sabbe te lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena eko lokoti adhippāyo. Saṅkhārā hi sakasakapaccayāyattatāya sattā visattā sattā nāma. Pariharanti paricaranti. Disāti upayogabahuvacanaṃ. Bhanti paṭibhanti. Ke te? Teyeva virocamānā pabhassarā candimasūriyā. Aṭṭha lokadhammā saṅkhārāva. “Sinerussa samantato”ti vacanato yugandharādayo sineruṃ parikkhipitvā parimaṇḍalākārena ṭhitāti vadanti. Parikkhipitvā accuggato lokadhātu ayaṃ. “Ma-kāro padasandhikaro”ti vadanti. Aññathāpi lakkhaṇādibhedato saṅkhāralokaṃ, āsayānusayabhedato sattalokaṃ, cakkavāḷādiparimāṇato okāsalokañca sabbathāpi viditattā lokavidū.

Faith, moral shame, moral dread, much learning, energetic arousal, established mindfulness, and clear comprehension—these are called the seven good qualities. By nature (sabhāvato) means by suffering (dukkhato). 'He does not fall' (na cavati) is said in reference to the deities. 'To be known' (ñāteyya) means what should be known. 'To be seen' (daṭṭheyya) means what should be seen. Or alternatively, the meaning is: 'I do not say that the end of the world is to be known by going.' 'World' (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandhalokaṃ). 'It is not to be reached by going' means: it is not to be reached by physical going or by going the wrong way; only by the going of the noble ones, having reached the end of the world, is there liberation from suffering. Thus it is said. 'One who has quelled' (samitāvī) means one whose defilements are quelled. 'Subsisting on food' (āhāraṭṭhitikā) means dependent on conditions. Whatever beings subsist on conditions, all those beings, in the sense of perishing and disintegrating, are one world. This is the intention. Indeed, formations are dependent on their own respective conditions; beings (sattā) are so-called because they are attached (sattā) and clinging (visattā). Pariharanti means paricaranti (they move about). The word 'disā' is an accusative plural. 'They shine' (bhanti) means paṭibhanti (they shine forth). What are they? They are those very moon and sun, resplendent and radiant. The eight worldly conditions are merely formations. Following the text 'around Sineru', they say that the Yugandhara and other mountains, having encircled Mount Sineru, stand in a circular formation. Having encircled it, this world-sphere stands exceedingly high. They say, 'The letter 'ma' serves as a word-connector.' Alternatively, because of having known in all ways: the world of formations through the distinctions of characteristics, etc.; the world of beings through the distinctions of disposition and latent tendency; and the spatial world through the measure of the Cakkavāḷa, etc.—He is called Lokavidū, the Knower of the World.

Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ parittaṃ lokiyaṃ, tena sabbaṃ lokaṃ kathaṃ abhivati? Asadisānubhāvattā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya. Tañhi attano visaye bhagavato sabbaññutaññāṇagatikaṃ[V 0.0037], lahutarappavatti ca bhavaṅgacittadvayānantaraṃ uppattito. Na kassaci evaṃlahutaraṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, api āyasmato sāriputtassa, tassa kiresa cittavāro pañcadasabhavaṅgānantaranti. Aggisikhadhūmasikhā ca nāgā kira sīhaḷadīpe. Atthassa dīpakaṃ padaṃ atthapadaṃ. Ekatthadīpakaṃ padaṃ, sabbametaṃ vākyanti attho. Aṭṭha disā nāma aṭṭha vimokkhā, samāpattiyo vā. Satthavāho satthāti nipātito yathā pisitāso pisāco. Udake maṇḍūko ahaṃ āsiṃ, na thale maṇḍūko, vārimattameva gocaro, tassa me tava dhammaṃ suṇantassa sīsaṃ daṇḍena sannirumbhitvāti pāṭhaseso. Anādaratthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. “Ettakenapi evarūpā iddhi bhavissatī”ti sitaṃ katvā. Vimokkhoti cettha maggo, tadanantarikaṃ ñāṇaṃ nāma phalañāṇaṃ, tasmiṃ khaṇe buddho nāma. Sabbassa buddhattāti kattari. Bodhetāti hetukattari. Seṭṭhatthadīpakaṃ vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ nāma, tathā uttamaṃ. Sacchikāpaññattīti sabbadhammānaṃ sacchikaraṇavasena sayambhutā paññatti, attanā eva vā ñātā sacchikatātipi sacchikāpaññatti. Bhagī bhagavā cīvarapiṇḍapātādīnaṃ. Bhajī araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni. Bhāgī atthadhammavimuttirasassa. Rāgādikilesagaṇabhaggamakāsi. Bhāvitattano bhāvitakāyo. Bhavassa antaṃ nibbānaṃ maggādhigamena taṃ gatoti bhavantago.

The knowledge and vision of liberation is of the sense-sphere, limited, and mundane; by that, how can it overcome the entire world? Because of its incomparable power, it is like the knowledge of omniscience. Indeed, that knowledge, in its own domain, is similar to the Blessed One's knowledge of omniscience and has a very swift occurrence, because it arises immediately after two moments of life-continuum consciousness. For no one does such a swift mind arise, not even for the Venerable Sāriputta; for him, it is said, this thought-process arises after fifteen moments of life-continuum. It is said that in the island of Sīhaḷa there are Nāgas named Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha. A word that illuminates the meaning is an 'atthapada'. A word that illuminates one meaning. The meaning is: all this is a sentence. The eight directions are the eight liberations, or the eight attainments. The word 'satthavāho' is irregularly formed as 'satthā', just as 'pisitāso' is formed as 'pisāco'. 'I was a frog in the water, not a frog on land; my resort was only the water. While I was listening to your Dhamma, my head was pinned down with a stick'—the remainder of the text is to be supplied. Or, it is the genitive case in the sense of disregard. Having smiled, thinking, 'Even by just this, such psychic power will arise.' And here, 'vimokkha' is the path. The knowledge immediately following that is called the knowledge of fruition. At that moment, one is called a 'buddha'. The phrase 'sabbassa buddhattā' ('from having understood all') is in the agent sense (kattari). The word 'bodheti' ('he causes to understand') is in the causal agent sense (hetukattari). A word that illuminates the highest meaning is called 'seṭṭha', and likewise 'uttama'. 'Sacchikāpaññatti' is a designation that has arisen of itself by way of directly realizing all phenomena, or a designation known and directly realized by oneself. The Blessed One is an apportioner (bhagī) of robes, almsfood, and so on. He resorts to (bhajī) remote forest lodgings. He is a partaker (bhāgī) of the taste of the meaning, the Dhamma, and liberation. He effected the breaking (bhaggaṃ akāsi) of the host of defilements such as lust. He has a developed self (bhāvitatta) and a developed body (bhāvitakāya). He has gone (gato) to the end of existence (bhavassa antaṃ), which is Nibbāna, by the attainment of the path; therefore, he is 'bhavantago'.

“Lobhaṃ[M 0.0041], bhikkhave, ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahathā”tiādinā (itivu. 1) nayena ekakādivasenāgate gahetvā vadati. Saṃkilesataṇhādiṭṭhiduccaritasaṃkilesavasena aniccadukkhamanattāsubhesu niccantiādivipariyesā. Cīvarahetu vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, piṇḍapāta senāsanaitibhavābhavahetu vā (a. ni. 4.9). Cetokhilā satthari kaṅkhati, dhamme, saṅghe, sikkhāya, sabrahmacārīsu kupitoti (dī. ni. 3.319; vibha. 941) āgatā pañca. Kāme avītarāgo hoti…pe… kāye, rūpe, yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā, aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ caratīti (dī. ni. 3.320; vibha. 941) āgatā pañca vinibandhā. Vivādamūlāni kodho upanāho makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyaṃ thambho sārambho sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitā ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggitā (a. ni. 6.36; dī. ni. 3.325). Vibhaṅge pana “kodho makkho issā sāṭheyyaṃ pāpicchatā sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitā”ti (vibha. 944) āgataṃ. Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, evaṃ chandarāgo, ajjhosānaṃ, pariggaho, macchariyaṃ, ārakkho, ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ, daṇḍādānasatthādāna…pe… akusalā dhammā sambhavantīti (dī. ni. 2.104; 3.359; a. ni. 9.23; vibha. 963) vuttānaṃ. Rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbadhammataṇhāti cha, tā kāmabhavavibhavataṇhāvaseneva [V 0.0038] aṭṭhārasa, tā eva ajjhattikassupādāya aṭṭhārasa, bāhirassupādāya aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa, tā atīte chattiṃsa, anāgate chattiṃsa, paccuppanne chattiṃsāti evaṃ aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritānīti. Māretīti māro, pamādo “pamādo maccuno pada”nti (dha. pa. 21) vacanato. Sammāājīvavināsanato vā kilesā vuccanti “māro”ti, vadhakūpamattā khandhāva mārā. Abhisaṅkhārā jātidukkhābhinibbattāpanato, jātassa jarādisambhavato ca mārā. Ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitamāraṇato maccu māro. Aṇimatā nāma paramāṇu viya adassanūpagamanaṃ. Laghimatā sarīrena, cittena vā sīghagamanaṃ. Mahimatā candimasūriyādīnampipāṇinā parāmasanādi. Patti nāma yathicchitadesappatti. Pakāsanatā, lābhakassatthasādhanaṃ vā pākammaṃ. Īsattaṃ nāma sayaṃvasitā. Vasittaṃ nāma aparavasitā. Yatthakāmāvasāyitaṃ nāma yatthicchati yadicchati yāvadicchati, tattha tāva tadatthasādhanaṃ. Pīḷanasaṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhena [M 0.0042] vā dukkhamariyasaccantiādimhi idaṃ codanāpubbaṅgamaṃ atthavissajjanaṃ – dukkhādīnaṃ aññepi rūpataṇhādayo atthā atthi, atha kasmā cattāro eva vuttāti ce? Aññasaccadassanavasena āvibhāvato.

“Monks, abandon one thing, greed,” and so on. Thus, he speaks by taking up the teachings that have come by way of the singular, etc. By way of the defilements of craving, wrong views, and misconduct, there are the perversions of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the unsatisfactory as satisfactory, the not-self as self, and the foul as fair. “Monks, for a monk, craving arises on account of robes, or on account of alms-food, lodging, this existence and that existence.” The five mental barrennesses mentioned are: one doubts the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, and is hostile toward one's fellows in the holy life. The five bonds mentioned are: one is not free from passion for sensual pleasures… for the body, for form; having eaten to one's belly's fill as much as one wishes, one practices the holy life aspiring for rebirth in some group of devas. The roots of dispute are: anger, hostility, denigration, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, misapprehension of one's own views, tenacious grasping, and being hard to relinquish. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated: “anger, denigration, envy, fraud, evil desires, and misapprehension of one's own views.” Dependent on craving, there is seeking; dependent on seeking, there is gain; dependent on gain, there is decision-making; thus, desire and lust, clinging, possessiveness, stinginess, guarding; and on account of guarding, the taking up of rods and weapons… unwholesome states arise. Craving for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these six, by way of craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence, become eighteen. These same eighteen, with respect to the internal and with respect to the external, become thirty-six. These thirty-six in the past, future, and present total one hundred and eight proliferations of craving. Because it kills (māreti), it is called Māra. Negligence (pamādo) is also Māra, according to the saying, “Negligence is the path of death.” Or, because they destroy right livelihood, the defilements are called “Māra.” The aggregates are Māra, being like executioners. Volitional formations are Māra because they produce the suffering of birth, and because for one who has been born, aging and so on occur. Death is Māra because it kills the life comprised within a single existence. Aṇimatā is the attainment of invisibility, like a minute atom. Laghimatā is swift movement with the body or with the mind. Mahimatā is the power of being able to touch even the moon and sun with the hand. Patti is the power of reaching a desired place. Pākammaṃ is the accomplishment of the purpose for one who desires it. Īsattaṃ is mastery over oneself. Vasittaṃ is mastery over others. Yatthakāmāvasāyitaṃ is the ability to accomplish that purpose as wished, wherever one wishes, for whatever one wishes, and as much as one wishes. In the context of the Noble Truth of Suffering, it is defined by the meaning of oppression, conditionedness, torment, and change. This explanation is preceded by a question: “If there are other meanings of suffering, such as craving for form, etc., why are only four mentioned?” The answer is: Because they become manifest through the showing of the other truths.

“Tattha katamaṃ dukkheñāṇaṃ, dukkhaṃ ārabbha yā uppajjati paññā”tiādināpi (vibha. 794) nayena ekekasaccārammaṇavasenāpi saccañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) nayena ekaṃ saccaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā sesesu kiccanipphattivasenāpi vuttaṃ. Tattha yadā ekekaṃ saccaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tadā samudayadassanena tāva sabhāvato pīḷanalakkhaṇassāpi dukkhassa yasmā taṃ āyūhanalakkhaṇena samudayena āyūhitaṃ saṅkhataṃ, tasmāssa so saṅkhataṭṭho āvi bhavati. Yasmā pana maggo kilesasantāpaharo susītalo, tasmāssa maggadassanena santāpaṭṭho āvi bhavati nandassa accharādassanena sundariyā anabhirūpabhāvo viya. Avipariṇāmadhammassa pana nirodhassa dassanena tassa vipariṇāmaṭṭho āvi bhavatīti vattabbameva natthi. Sabhāvato āyūhanalakkhaṇassapi samudayassa dukkhadassanena nidānaṭṭho āvi bhavati asappāyabhojanato uppannabyādhidassanena bhojanassa byādhinidānabhāvo viya. Visaṃyogabhūtassa nirodhassa dassanena saṃyogaṭṭho. Niyyānabhūtassa ca maggassa dassanena palibodhaṭṭhoti. Tathā nissaraṇassāpi nirodhassa avivekabhūtassa samudayassa dassanena vivekaṭṭho āvi bhavati. Maggadassanena asaṅkhataṭṭho. Iminā hi anamatagge saṃsāre maggo na diṭṭhapubbo, sopi ca sappaccayattā saṅkhato evāti appaccayadhammassa asaṅkhatabhāvo ativiya pākaṭo hoti. Dukkhadassanena panassa amataṭṭho āvi bhavati. Dukkhañhi visaṃ, amataṃ nibbānanti. Tathā niyyānalakkhaṇassāpi [V 0.0039] maggassa samudayadassanena “nāyaṃ hetu nibbānassa pattiyā, ayaṃ hetū”ti hetvattho āvi bhavati. Nirodhadassanena dassanaṭṭho paramasukhumarūpāni passato “vippasannaṃ vata me cakkhū”ti cakkhussa vippasannabhāvo viya. Dukkhadassanena adhipateyyaṭṭho anekarogāturakapaṇajanadassanena issarajanassa uḷārabhāvo viyāti evamettha lakkhaṇavasena, ekassa aññasaccadassanavasena ca itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ āvibhāvato [M 0.0043] ekekassa cattāro atthā vuttā. Upadhiviveko nikkilesatā.

The knowledge of the truths is also spoken of by the method beginning, “Herein, what is the knowledge in suffering? The wisdom that arises concerning suffering,” by way of taking each single truth as an object. It is also spoken of by the method beginning, “Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering, he also sees the origin of suffering,” by way of making one truth the object and accomplishing the function regarding the remaining truths. Therein, when one makes each single truth the object, then, by seeing the origin, for suffering—which by its intrinsic nature has the characteristic of oppression—because it is accumulated and conditioned by the origin which has the characteristic of accumulation, therefore its meaning as 'conditioned' becomes manifest. And because the path removes the fever of defilements and is very cool, therefore, for this suffering, by seeing the path, its meaning as 'fever' becomes manifest, like the unattractiveness of Sundarī becoming manifest to Nanda by seeing the celestial nymphs. But by seeing cessation, which has an unchangeable nature, it is not even to be said that for that suffering, its meaning as 'changeable' becomes manifest. For the origin, which by its intrinsic nature has the characteristic of accumulation, by seeing suffering, its meaning as 'source' becomes manifest, like the state of food being the source of illness becoming manifest by seeing the illness that has arisen from unsuitable food. By seeing cessation, which is disjunction, its meaning as 'conjunction' becomes manifest. And by seeing the path, which is the escape, its meaning as 'obstruction' becomes manifest. Likewise, for cessation, which is also the escape, by seeing the origin, which is non-seclusion, its meaning as 'seclusion' becomes manifest. By seeing the path, its meaning as 'unconditioned' becomes manifest. For in this beginningless saṃsāra, the path has not been seen before; and that path too, being with a condition, is indeed conditioned. Thus, the unconditioned nature of the unconditioned state becomes exceedingly clear. But by seeing suffering, for this cessation, its meaning as 'deathless' becomes manifest. For suffering is poison, and Nibbāna is the deathless. Likewise, for the path, which also has the characteristic of escape, by seeing the origin, its meaning as 'cause' becomes manifest in the thought: 'This is not the cause for attaining Nibbāna; this is the cause.' By seeing cessation, its meaning as 'seeing' becomes manifest, like the clarity of the eye becoming manifest to one who sees extremely subtle forms, in the thought: 'Oh, how clear is my eye!' By seeing suffering, its meaning as 'sovereignty' becomes manifest, like the exalted state of a sovereign person becoming manifest by seeing a host of wretched people afflicted by many diseases. Thus here, by way of characteristics, and by way of the manifestation of the other three truths through seeing one, four meanings for each are stated. Seclusion from the substrata is the state of being without defilements.

Paṭipakkhaṃ atthayantīti paccatthikā. Pati viruddhā amittā paccāmittā. Sacchikatvā pavedetīti ettāvatā bhagavato sabbaññutaṃ dīpeti. Tena ñāṇasampattiṃ dīpetvā idāni karuṇāsampattiṃ dīpetuṃ “so dhammaṃ desesī”tiādimāha. Atha vā kiṃ so pavedesīti? Ñāṇaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ tilokahitabhūtameva. So dhammaṃ desesīti kīdisaṃ? “Ādikalyāṇa”ntiādi. Anena vacanena vattuṃ arahabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sāsanadhammoti ovādapariyatti. Kiccasuddhiyāti kilesappahānanibbānārammaṇakiccasuddhiyā. Sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ nāma sikkhattayaṃ, navakoṭisahassānītiādikaṃ vā. Maggameva brahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Tassa pakāsakaṃ piṭakattayaṃ idha sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ nāma. Chasu atthapadesu saṅkhepato kāsanaṃ saṅkāsanaṃ. Ādito kāsanaṃ pakāsanaṃ. Ubhayampi vitthāretvā desanaṃ vivaraṇaṃ. Puna vibhāgakaraṇaṃ vibhajanaṃ. Opammādinā pākaṭakaraṇaṃ uttānīkaraṇaṃ. Sotūnaṃ cittaparitosajananena, cittanisānena ca paññāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Byañjanapadesu akkharaṇato akkharaṃ, “ekakkharapadamakkhara”nti eke. Vibhattiantaṃ padaṃ. Byañjayatīti byañjanaṃ, vākyaṃ. Padasamudāyo vā vākyaṃ. Vibhāgapakāso ākāro nāma. Phusatīti phassotiādi nibbacanaṃ nirutti, niruttiyā niddiṭṭhassa apadeso niddeso nāma. Phusatīti phasso, so tividho – sukhavedanīyo dukkhavedanīyo adukkhamasukhavedanīyoti. Etesu ayaṃ yojanā – akkharehi saṅkāsayati, padehi pakāsayati, byañjanehi vivarati, ākārehi vibhajati, niruttīhi uttāniṃ karoti, niddesehi paññāpeti. Akkharehi vā saṅkāsayitvā padehi pakāseti, byañjanehi vivaritvā ākārehi vibhajati, niruttīhi uttāniṃ katvā niddesehi paññāpeti. Akkharehi vā ugghāṭetvā padehi vineti ugghaṭitaññuṃ, byañjanehi vivaritvā ākārehi vineti vipañcitaññuṃ, niruttīhi netvā niddesehi vineti neyyanti veditabbaṃ. Atthoti bhāsitattho. Tassevatthassa paṭivijjhitabbo sako sako bhāvo paṭivedho nāma. Taṃ ubhayampi attho nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “atthagambhīratāpaṭivedhagambhīratāhi sāttha”nti. Dhammoti vā desanāti vā byañjanameva. Niddosabhāvena parisuddhaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ, sikkhattayapariggahito [M 0.0044] maggo ca, ubhayampi brahmacariyapadena [V 0.0040] saṅgahitaṃ. Paṭipattiyāti paṭipattihetu. Āgamabyattitoti punappunaṃ adhīyamānā khandhādayo pākaṭā honti. Duruttasatthāni adhīyamānāni sammohamevāvāhanti.

They desire opposition, therefore they are called adversaries. Opposing, they are enemies, adversaries. Having realized and declared it, thus the Blessed One’s omniscience is illuminated. By that, having illuminated the perfection of knowledge, now to illuminate the perfection of compassion, he said, “He taught the Dhamma,” and so on. Or else, what did he declare? Knowledge—all of it solely for the welfare of the three worlds. “He taught the Dhamma”—what kind? “Good in the beginning,” and so on. By this statement, the state of being worthy to speak is illuminated. The Dhamma of the Teaching is instruction and scripture. “Purified in purpose” means by the purification of the task of abandoning defilements with Nibbāna as the object. The holy life of the Teaching is the threefold training, or the ninety billion, and so on. The path itself is the holy life—the path-holy life. Its exposition is the three baskets, here called meaningful and well-phrased. Among the six terms of meaning, a concise showing is indication. A showing from the beginning is exposition. The teaching that elaborates on both is explanation. Further, making a division is analysis. Making apparent through similes and so on is clarification. Paññāpana should be understood as that which generates delight in the minds of listeners and sharpens the mind. Among the terms of phrasing, because it does not perish, it is a syllable. Some say, 'A word of a single syllable is a syllable.' A word is a term with a case-ending. Because it expresses the meaning, it is a phrase, a sentence. Or, a collection of words is a sentence. A distinct exposition is called a characteristic. The derivation “it touches, thus it is contact,” and so on, is etymology. The detailed reference to what is indicated by etymology is called exposition. “It touches,” thus it is contact; this is threefold: contact accompanied by pleasant feeling, contact accompanied by painful feeling, and contact accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Herein, this is the application: with syllables, he indicates; with words, he expounds; with phrases, he explains; with characteristics, he analyzes; with etymologies, he clarifies; with expositions, he makes known. Or, having indicated with syllables, he expounds with words; having explained with phrases, he analyzes with characteristics; having clarified with etymologies, he makes known with expositions. Or, it should be understood thus: having revealed with syllables, he guides the quick-witted with words; having explained with phrases, he guides the discerning with characteristics; having led with etymologies, he guides the trainable with expositions. “Meaning” is the expressed meaning. The penetration of that very meaning, its own nature to be realized, is called realization. Both are called meaning. Hence it is said, “Meaningful because of profundity of meaning and profundity of realization.” “Dhamma” or “teaching” is just the phrasing. The holy life of the Teaching, purified by its faultless nature, and the path embraced by the threefold training—both are included under the term “holy life.” “By practice” means for the sake of practice. “From skill in the scriptures” means that, by repeated study, the aggregates and so on become apparent. Studying poorly spoken teachings brings only confusion.

2-3. Kacci khamanīyaṃ sītuṇhādi. Kacci yāpanīyaṃ yathāladdhehi jīvitasādhanehi jīvitaṃ. Appābādhanti appopasaggaṃ, appātaṅkanti apparogaṃ. Kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ sarīrakicce. Kacci balaṃ samaṇakicce. Kacci phāsuvihāro yathāvuttanayena appābādhatāya, anukkaṇṭhanādivasena vā. Sattasaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya pacchimavayo, uttarāmukhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Lokavivaraṇe jāte idha kiṃ olokesi, natthettha tayā sadisopīti āha “tvaṃ sadevakassa lokassa aggo”tiādi. Āsabhiṃ uttamaṃ. Upapattivasena devā. Rūpānaṃ paribhogavasena, patthanāvasena vā uppannā rāgasampayuttā somanassavedanānurūpato uppajjitvā hadayatappanato ambarasādayo viya “rūparasā”ti vuccanti. Tathāgatassa pahīnāti adhikāravasenāha. Tathāgatassapi hi kassaci te pahīnāti matthakacchinnatālo viya katā. Kathaṃ? Rūparasādivacanena vipākadhammadhammā gahitā, te vijjamānāpi matthakasadisānaṃ taṇhāvijjānaṃ maggasatthena chinnattā āyatiṃ tālapantisadise vipākakkhandhe nibbattetuṃ asamatthā jātā. Tasmā tālāvatthu viya katā. “Kusalasomanassāpi ettha saṅgahitā”ti vadanti. Paṭhamamaggena pahīnā kammapathaṭṭhāniyā, dutiyena ucchinnamūlā oḷārikā, tatiyena tālāvatthukatā kāmarāgaṭṭhāniyā. Catutthena anabhāvaṃkatā rūparāgārūparāgaṭṭhāniyā. Aparihānadhammataṃ pana dīpento “āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā”ti āha. Tadaṅgappahānena vā pahīnā vipassanākkhaṇe, jhānassa pubbabhāgakkhaṇe vā, vikkhambhanappahānena ucchinnamūlā jhānakkhaṇe. “Vivicceva kāmehī”ti (pārā. 11) hi vuttaṃ. Samucchedappahānena tālāvatthukatā tatiyavijjādhigamakkhaṇe. Itthambhūtā pana te rūparasādayo anabhāvaṃkatā āyatimanuppādadhammāti ekamevidaṃ atthapadaṃ. Paṭhamāya vā abhinibbhidāya pahīnā, dutiyāya ucchinnamūlā, tatiyāya tālāvatthukatā. Itthambhūtā yasmā anabhāvaṃkatā nāma honti, tasmā āyatiṃanauppādadhammāti veditabbā. Atha vā dukkhañāṇena pahīnā, samudayañāṇena ucchinnamūlā[M 0.0045], nirodhañāṇena tālāvatthukatā, maggañāṇena anabhāvaṃkatā, paccavekkhaṇañāṇena āyatiṃ anuppādadhammāti veditabbā. Lokiyamaggena vā pahīnā, dassanamaggena ucchinnamūlā, tividhena bhāvanāmaggena tālāvatthukatātiādi. Brāhmaṇassa avisayattā dhammarasā na uddhaṭā.

2–3. Is it bearable, regarding cold, heat, and so on? Is life sustainable with the means for living as they are obtained? Are there few afflictions, that is, few troubles, and few diseases, that is, few illnesses? Is there lightness when performing bodily duties? Is there strength for performing the duties of a recluse? Is there a comfortable dwelling, in the way described, by being of few afflictions or by way of being without discontent and so on? From the age of sixty-seven onward is the last stage of life; it is said to be 'facing north'. When the world-revealing miracle occurred, what was looked at here? There is not even one like you here—thus it was said: “You are the foremost in the world with its devas,” and so on. A noble and supreme (speech). Devas are so by way of their rebirth. Having arisen in accordance with feelings of mental pleasure associated with lust—which themselves have arisen either through the enjoyment of forms or through longing for them—they are called 'tastes of form' because they delight the heart, like the taste of mangoes and so on. 'For the Tathāgata, they are abandoned'—this is said by way of relevance. Indeed, for the Tathāgata or for anyone else, they are abandoned; thus, they are made like a palm tree with its crown cut off. How so? By the term 'tastes of form,' resultant phenomena and their conditioning phenomena are included. Though they exist, because craving and ignorance, which are like the crown, have been cut by the sword of the path, they have become incapable of producing in the future the series of resultant aggregates, which are like a row of palm trees. Therefore, they are made like a palm-stump. Some say, 'Wholesome feelings of mental pleasure are also included here.' By the first path, those pertaining to the courses of action are abandoned. By the second, the gross ones are uprooted. By the third, those pertaining to sensual lust are made like a palm-stump. By the fourth, those pertaining to lust for form and lust for the formless are brought to non-existence. Then, showing their nature of not declining, he said, 'They are of a nature not to arise in the future.' Or, they are abandoned by substitution of opposites at the moment of insight or at the moment of the preliminary stage of absorption; they are uprooted by suppression at the moment of absorption—for indeed, it is said: 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures…' (Vin-piṭaka, Pārājika 11). By eradication, they are made like a palm-stump at the moment of attaining the third knowledge. Thus, these tastes of form and so on, having been brought to non-existence, are of a nature not to arise in the future—this is a single expression of meaning. Or, by the first breakthrough, they are abandoned; by the second, they are uprooted; by the third, they are made like a palm-stump. Because those of such a nature are called 'brought to non-existence,' they should be understood as being of a nature not to arise in the future. Alternatively, by the knowledge of suffering, they are abandoned; by the knowledge of the origin, they are uprooted; by the knowledge of cessation, they are made like a palm-stump; by the knowledge of the path, they are brought to non-existence; by the knowledge of reviewing, they are of a nature not to arise in the future—thus they should be known. Or, by the mundane path, they are abandoned; by the path of vision, they are uprooted; by the threefold path of development, they are made like a palm-stump, and so on. Because the tastes of the Dhamma were beyond the scope of the brahmin, they were not brought up.

11. Dhammadhātunti ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dhammadhātu nāma. Anukampavacanānurūpaṃ “puṇṇacando viyā”ti vuttaṃ, sūriyavacanaṃ “suppaṭividdhattā”tivacanānurūpaṃ, pathavīsamacittatāya kāraṇaṃ [V 0.0041] “karuṇāvipphāra”nti vadanti. Paṭicchādetabbe hi attano guṇe “āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriya”ntiādinā pakāsento attano karuṇāvipphāraṃ pakāsetīti gahetabbo. Varabhūrimedhaso varaputhulañāṇo, bhūrīti vā bhūmi, bhūmi viya patthaṭavarapaññoti attho. Abujjhi etthātipi adhikaraṇena rukkho bodhi. Sayaṃ bujjhati, bujjhanti vā tena taṃsamaṅginoti maggo bodhi, evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇampi. Bujjhīyatīti nibbānaṃ bodhi. Tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ upanissayavato yathāsambhavaṃ tisso vijjā veditabbā. Ekaggatāvasena tikkhabhāvo. Tikkhopi ekacco saro lakkhaṃ patvā kuṇṭho hoti, na tathā idaṃ. Satindriyavasenassa kharabhāvo, saddhindriyavasena vippasannabhāvo, antarā anosakkitvā kilesapaccatthikānaṃ suṭṭhu abhibhavanato vīriyindriyavasenassa sūrabhāvo ca veditabbo. Maggavijāyanatthaṃ gabbhaggahaṇakālo saṅkhārupekkhānantaramanulomattā.

11. Here, the term “dhammadhātu” refers to the knowledge of omniscience. In accordance with the compassionate speech, it is said, “like the full moon.” The mention of the sun is in accordance with the phrase “because of being thoroughly penetrated.” The reason for the earth-like equanimity of mind is said to be “the pervasion of compassion.” For although one’s own virtues should be concealed, by declaring, “my energy is aroused,” and so forth, it should be understood that one reveals the pervasion of one’s compassion. The noble one of vast wisdom (`varabhūrimedhaso`) means one possessing broad knowledge; or `bhūri` means expanse or ground, signifying wisdom as vast and broad as the earth. Here, because he “awakened” (`abujjhi`) there, by locative construction the tree is “awakening” (`bodhi`). One awakens by oneself, or those endowed with it awaken by means of it; thus the path is `bodhi`. So too is the knowledge of omniscience. That which is to be awakened to is Nibbāna, which is `bodhi`. For one who has the supporting condition for the three knowledges, the three knowledges should be understood as arising accordingly. The sharpness is due to one-pointedness. Though some arrows may become dull upon reaching the target, this is not so here. The firmness is due to the faculty of mindfulness, the clarity due to the faculty of faith, and the heroic quality due to the faculty of energy, because it thoroughly overcomes the adversaries, the defilements, without wavering in between. The time of conception for the purpose of giving birth to the path is immediately after equanimity toward formations, because of its conformity.

Chandoti ca saṅkappoti ca avatthantarabhedabhinno rāgova –

Desire and intention are just lust, not different except by a difference in their state—

“Senahātthyaṅgamupeti,

Rattahadayo rāgena;

Sammagate rattakāmamupeti,

Kāmapatitaṃ lokassa mātrālamatī”ti –

“A man with an impassioned heart, through affection, approaches a woman's body. When there is a desire to unite through lust, he approaches a state of inflamed sensual desire. A woman mingling with a man of the world reaches a state of falling into sensual desire.”

Ādīsu viya –

As in the preceding examples—

Vibhaṅgeyeva kiñcāpi attho vuttoti ettha ayamadhippāyo – vibhaṅgapāḷiṃ ānetvā idha vuttopi sabbesaṃ upakārāya na hoti, tasmā taṃ aṭṭhakathānayeneva pakāsayissāmīti. Itoti kāmehi. Kāyavivekādīsu [M 0.0046] upadhiviveko tatiyo, tasmā tatiyaṃ chaḍḍetvā dve gahetvā tadaṅgādīsu vikkhambhanavivekaṃ gahetvā “tayo evā”ti vuttā. Evaṃ sati cittavikkhambhanā ekatthā evāti viseso na siyāti ce? Appanāvārattā na panevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāyavivekaggahaṇena pubbabhāgaggahaṇaṃ ñāyati, tasmā cittavivekoti tadaṅgaviveko vutto, vikkhambhanena appanākāleti gahetabbaṃ asaṅkarato. Atha vā cittavivekena tadaṅgavikkhambhanā gahitā, itarena vikkhambhanaviveko evātipi yuttaṃ, kilesakāmattā vā dvīsu kammesu pariyāpanno puriso viya. Yathā avijjamānena avijjamānapaññattivasena loke “saphalo rukkho”ti [V 0.0042] vuccati, tatheva vijjamānena vijjamānapaññattivasena sāsane “savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ jhāna”nti vuccatīti adhippāyo.

Regarding the phrase, 'Even though the meaning is stated in the Vibhaṅga,' the intention here is this: even if the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi were brought and stated here, it would not be for the benefit of all; therefore, I will explain it only by the method of the commentary. The word 'ito' refers to 'from sensual pleasures'. Among bodily seclusion and so forth, seclusion from the substrata is the third. Therefore, having discarded the third, taken the two, and, from among seclusion-by-substitution and so forth, taken seclusion by suppression, it is said, 'only three'. If it is taken thus, one might say: 'Then mental seclusion and seclusion by suppression would indeed be of one meaning, so there would be no distinction.' However, it should not be regarded thus, because this is the section on absorption. By the taking of bodily seclusion, the taking of the preliminary part is understood. Therefore, by 'mental seclusion', seclusion-by-substitution is stated; by 'suppression', seclusion at the time of absorption is stated. Thus, it should be taken without confusion. Alternatively, by mental seclusion, both seclusion-by-substitution and seclusion by suppression are taken; by the other, seclusion by suppression itself is taken. This too is suitable. Or, it is like a person engaged in two actions because of defilement-desires. Just as in the world, by means of a designation of what is non-existent, it is said, 'a tree with fruit', so too in the Teaching, by means of a designation of what is existent, it is said, 'jhāna with initial application, with sustained application'. This is the intention.

Vūpasamāti ettha kesaṃ vūpasamāti, kiṃ paṭhamajjhānikānaṃ, udāhu dutiyajjhānikānanti? Ettha yadi paṭhamajjhānikānaṃ, natthi tesaṃ vūpasamo. Na hi paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārarahitaṃ atthi. Yadi dutiyajjhānikānaṃ, nattheva vūpasamo tattha tadabhāvāti ce? Tenetaṃ vuccati “samatikkamā”ti, samatikkamopi na tesaṃyeva. Kintu sakalassapi paṭhamajjhānadhammarāsissāti ce? Tenetaṃ vuccati “oḷārikassa pana samatikkamā”tiādi. Sabbepi paṭhamajjhānadhammā oḷārikāva dutiyajjhānato, na kevalaṃ vitakkavicāradvayamevāti ce? Na vitakkavicārāyeva tehi sampayuttānaṃ oḷārikabhāvatoti tesveva ādīnavadassanena dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe tesaṃ abhāvo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvā”ti, yassa dhammassānubhāvena, yogena vā idaṃ jhānaṃ “sampasādana”nti vuccati “ekodibhāva”nti ca, tassa dassanatthaṃ saddhāsamādhayo vibhaṅge vuttā. Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpade (pāci. 257 ādayo) sappiādayo viyāti vutte ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā na virujjhati. Samaṃ passatīti līnuddhaccaṃ pahāya khīṇāsavassa chasu dvāresu iṭṭhāniṭṭhachaḷārammaṇāpāthe parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanākārabhūtā upekkhā chaḷaṅgupekkhā. Nīvaraṇādipaṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanāgahaṇe majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā nāma. Vicinane majjhattabhūtā upekkhā vipassanupekkhā nāma. Tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā brahmavihārupekkhā bojjhaṅgupekkhā tatramajjhattupekkhā jhānupekkhā pārisuddhupekkhā [M 0.0047] ca atthato ekā tatramajjhattupekkhāva, avatthābhedena bhedo nesaṃ. Saṅkhārupekkhāvipassanupekkhānampi ekatā paññāvasena, kiccavasena pana duvidhatā veditabbā.

Here, regarding the word 'calming' (vūpasama), is it the calming of the factors belonging to the first jhāna, or of those belonging to the second jhāna? If it is of the factors belonging to the first jhāna, there is no calming of them, for the first jhāna is not devoid of initial and sustained application. If it is of the factors belonging to the second jhāna, there is certainly no calming there due to their absence. If this is so, it is for this reason that 'through transcending' is said. And this transcending is not of them alone. But if one should ask, 'Is it of the entire collection of phenomena of the first jhāna?' For that reason, this is said, beginning with 'through the transcending of the coarse.' And if one should ask, 'Are not all phenomena of the first jhāna coarse in comparison to the second jhāna, not just the pair of initial and sustained application?' No. It is because of the coarse nature of the factors associated with them that initial and sustained application are themselves considered coarse. Therefore, by seeing the danger in those very factors, their absence occurs at the moment of the second jhāna. For this reason, it was said, 'due to their non-appearance at the moment of the second jhāna.' To show by which factor's power, or through association with which, this jhāna is called 'internal serenity' and 'one-pointedness,' faith and concentration are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga. When it is said, 'like ghee and so forth' in the training rule on fine foods, this explanation of the meaning is not contradicted. 'He sees equally' means: having abandoned sinking and restlessness, for one whose cankers are destroyed, when the six-fold agreeable and disagreeable objects appear at the six doors, the equanimity that has the characteristic of not abandoning its pure natural state is the six-limbed equanimity. The equanimity that has become neutral in the taking up of contemplation and investigation of the hindrances and so forth is called equanimity towards formations. The equanimity that has become neutral in investigation is called insight-equanimity. Among these, the six-limbed equanimity, the divine abiding equanimity, the enlightenment factor equanimity, equanimity as neutrality, jhāna-equanimity, and purity-equanimity are one in meaning; they are simply equanimity as neutrality. Their difference is due to a difference in occasion. The oneness of equanimity towards formations and insight-equanimity is by way of wisdom, but their twofold nature should be understood by way of function.

Chaḷaṅgupekkhā kāmāvacarā, brahmavihārupekkhā rūpāvacarātiādinā bhūmivasena. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā khīṇāsavasseva, brahmavihārupekkhā tiṇṇampi puthujjanasekkhāsekkhānanti evaṃ puggalavasena. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā somanassupekkhāsahagatacittasampayuttā, brahmavihārupekkhā upekkhāsahagatacittasampayuttā evāti evaṃ cittavasena. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā chaḷārammaṇā, brahmavihārupekkhā dhammārammaṇāvāti ārammaṇavasena. Vedanupekkhā vedanākkhandhena saṅgahitā, itarā nava saṅkhārakkhandhenāti khandhasaṅgahavasena. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā brahmavihārabojjhaṅgajhānupekkhā pārisuddhitatramajjhattupekkhā ca atthato ekā, tasmā ekakkhaṇe ekāva siyā, na itarā, tathā saṅkhārupekkhāvipassanupekkhāpi. Vedanāvīriyupekkhānaṃ ekakkhaṇe siyā uppattīti. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā abyākatā, brahmavihārupekkhā kusalābyākatā, tathā sesā. Vedanupekkhā pana siyā [V 0.0043] akusalāpi. Evaṃ kusalattikavasena. Dasapetā saṅkhepena cattārova dhammā vīriyavedanātatramajjhattañāṇavasena. “Dukkhadomanassasukhasomanassāna”nti evaṃ pahānakkamena avatvā vibhaṅge vuttanayena kasmā vuttānīti ce? Suttānurakkhaṇatthaṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītanti ettha “ārammaṇavasena aggahetvā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītākārena anubhavatīti gahetabba”nti vadanti. Kasmā? Ekaṃyeva kasiṇaṃ ārabbha sabbesaṃ pavattito. Tatiyajjhānato paṭṭhāya upakārā hutvā āgatāti satisīsena desanā katā, vigatavalāhakādinā sommatāya rattiyā valāhakādinā kālussiye satipi divā viya anupakārikā na hoti rattiṃ, tasmā “attano upakārakattena vā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sūriyappabhābhibhavā, rattiyā alābhāti ime dve hetū aparisuddhatāya kāraṇaṃ. Sommabhāvena, attano upakārakattena cāti ime dve sabhāgatāya kāraṇa”nti vadanti, tassā aparisuddhāya jātiyāti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā kāraṇavacananti eke.

Six-factored equanimity pertains to the sense-sphere, while Brahmavihāra equanimity pertains to the form-sphere; this is to be understood by way of plane. Six-factored equanimity belongs only to one whose taints are destroyed, while Brahmavihāra equanimity belongs to all three—the ordinary person, the trainee, and the non-trainee; this is to be understood by way of individual. Six-factored equanimity is associated with consciousness accompanied by joy or equanimity, while Brahmavihāra equanimity is associated only with consciousness accompanied by equanimity; this is to be understood by way of consciousness. Six-factored equanimity has six objects, whereas Brahmavihāra equanimity has only the mental phenomenon as its object; this is to be understood by way of object. Equanimity as feeling is included in the feeling aggregate, while the other nine are included in the formations aggregate; this is to be understood by way of inclusion in the aggregates. Six-factored equanimity, Brahmavihāra-, enlightenment factor-, jhāna-, purity-, and neutrality-equanimity are one in meaning; therefore, in a single moment, only one can be, not the others. Likewise, equanimity towards formations and insight equanimity are also one. The arising of feeling-equanimity and energy-equanimity can occur in a single moment. Six-factored equanimity is indeterminate, while Brahmavihāra equanimity is wholesome and indeterminate; likewise for the rest. But feeling-equanimity can also be unwholesome; this is to be understood by way of the wholesome triad. These ten, in brief, are only four phenomena by way of energy, feeling, neutrality, and knowledge. If it is asked why, in the Vibhaṅga, they are stated in that way and not in the order of abandonment as 'suffering, displeasure, pleasure, and joy,' it is for the sake of preserving the Sutta. Regarding 'agreeable, disagreeable, and the opposite,' here they say: 'It should be understood as experiencing in the manner of agreeable, disagreeable, and the opposite, without grasping by way of the object.' Why? Because all of them proceed with a single kasiṇa as the object. Starting from the third jhāna, it becomes helpful, and thus the teaching is given with mindfulness as its head. Just as on a pleasant night, even when there is obscurity from clouds and the like, the night is not unhelpful as it would be during the day; therefore, it is said, 'or by its own helpfulness.' They say: 'Being overpowered by the sun's radiance and the non-obtaining of the night—these two causes are the reason for impurity. Its pleasant nature and its own helpfulness—these two are the reason for suitability.' This means 'of its impure birth'; therefore, some say it is a word expressing cause.

Jhānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the discourse on jhāna is concluded.

Pubbenivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on Previous Abodes

12. Cittekaggatāsabhāgattā [M 0.0048] jhānānaṃ “kesañci cittekaggatatthānī”ti āha. Kusalānaṃ bhavokkamanasabhāgattā “kesañci bhavokkamanatthānī”ti. Asabhāgattā sesaṭṭhānesu “pādakatthānī”ti avatvā “pādakānī”ti āha. Tena pādakabhūtānampi yathāsambhavaṃ cittekaggatā bhavokkamanatāvahataṃ, itaresaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ pādakatāvahatañca dīpeti. Asabhāgattā javanavipassanāpādakāni samānāni abhiññāpādakāni ca honti, abhiññāpādakāni ca vipassanāpādakāni hontītipi dīpeti, tathā pādakābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Abhiññāya hi catutthameva pādakaṃ, na itarāni. Tesu catutthassa tatiyaṃ pādakaṃ, tatiyassa dutiyaṃ, dutiyassa paṭhamanti. Atha vā “cattāri jhānānī”ti yathālābhato vuttaṃ.

12. Because of the jhānas' shared nature of one-pointedness of mind, he said, 'for some, they are in the position of one-pointedness of mind.' Because of the wholesome states' shared nature of descending into existence, he said, 'for some, they are in the position of descending into existence.' Because of their dissimilar nature, in the remaining instances, without saying 'they are in the position of a foundation,' he said 'foundations.' By this, he clarifies that for those jhānas that have become a foundation, there is, as is possible, the bringing about of one-pointedness of mind and descending into existence; and for the others, as is possible, the bringing about of the state of being a foundation. Because of their dissimilar nature, he clarifies that the foundations for impulsion-insight and the foundations for direct knowledge are similar, and also that the foundations for direct knowledge are foundations for insight. Likewise, he clarifies the absence of a foundation. Indeed, for direct knowledge, only the fourth jhāna is the foundation, not the others. Among them, the third is the foundation for the fourth, the second for the third, and the first for the second; thus it should be understood. Alternatively, 'the four jhānas' is said according to what is obtained.

Vinayanidānanimittaṃ, verañjanivāsakappanaṃ;

Satthu yasmā tasmā bhagavā, vijjattayamāha verañje.

Because the Teacher's making a dwelling in Verañjā is the cause of the Vinaya Nidāna, therefore the Blessed One declared the threefold knowledge in Verañjā.

Vuttañhetaṃ “vinaye suppaṭipanno bhikkhu sīlasampattiṃ nissāyā”tiādi (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā). Sīlavato hi sīlapaccavekkhaṇatthaṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭhānesu nisinnassa nisajjanato paṭṭhāya attano atītakiriyānussaraṇabahulatāya pubbenivāsānussativijjā appakasirena [V 0.0044] samijjhati. Tathā attānaṃ paṭicca sattānaṃ cutipariggahaṇasīlatāya cutūpapātañāṇaṃ appakasirena samijjhati, udakādīsu sukhumatta dassanasīlatāya dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ samijjhati. Yasmā sattavidhamethunasaṃyogaparivajjanena, kāmāsavādiparivajjanena vā brahmacariyaṃ akhaṇḍādibhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmāssa āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ appakasirena samijjhatīti ettha vinayanidāne vijjattayameva dassitaṃ, tasmā āha “yesañca guṇānaṃ dāyakaṃ ahosi, tesaṃ ekadesaṃ dassento”ti, aññathā vijjattayapaṭilābhamattappasaṅgo siyāti.

For it has been said: 'A bhikkhu well-practiced in the Vinaya, relying on the perfection of virtue,' and so on. Indeed, for a virtuous one, when seated in places for seclusion by day and night for the purpose of reviewing his virtue, from the moment of his sitting, due to the frequency of recollecting his past actions, the knowledge of the recollection of past lives is perfected with little difficulty. Similarly, due to the practice of comprehending the passing away of beings in relation to oneself, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is perfected with little difficulty. Because the holy life attains an unbroken state by avoiding the sevenfold sexual union, or by abandoning the taints of sensuality and so on, therefore, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is perfected for him with little difficulty. Thus, here in the introduction to the Vinaya, only the threefold knowledge is shown. Therefore, he said: 'Showing a part of those qualities of which it was the giver,' otherwise, the implication would be merely the attainment of the threefold knowledge.

So evanti iminā kiñcāpi catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāpi saṅgahaṃ gacchati, na kevalaṃ purimajjhānattikameva, tathāpi kevalaṃ purimajjhānattikameva gaṇhanto “evanti catutthajjhānakkamanidassanametaṃ, iminā paṭhamajjhānādhigamādinā kamena catutthajjhānaṃ paṭilabhitvāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha, taṃ kasmāti [M 0.0049] ce? Sambhārabhūmittā. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (visuddhi. 2.381) “ettha ca purimāni tīṇi jhānāni yasmā pītipharaṇena ca sukhapharaṇena ca sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvā lahumudukammaññakāyo hutvā iddhiṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā iminā pariyāyena iddhilābhāya saṃvattanato sambhārabhūmiyoti veditabbāni. Catutthajjhānaṃ pana iddhilābhāya pakatibhūmi evā”ti. Idameva vā atthaṃ sandhāyāha “pubbe imāni cattāri jhānāni kesañci abhiññāpādakānī”ti. Yadi evaṃ catutthajjhānampi antokatvā evanti kimatthaṃ na vuttaṃ. Tañhi pakatibhūmīti ce? Na vattabbaṃ, catutthajjhānato parassa samāhitādibhāvappattassa cittassa atthibhāvappasaṅgato. Yasmā yasmiṃ sati “pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya cittaṃ abhininnāmesi”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā tasmiṃ catutthajjhānacitte pakatibhūmibhāvappatte abhiññāpādake jāte parikammacittaṃ “pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya abhininnāmesi”nti āha. Abhinīhārakkhamaṃ hotīti ettha taṃ iddhividhādhigamatthāya parikammacittaṃ abhinīharati. Kasiṇārammaṇato apanetvā iddhividhābhimukhaṃ pesesi. Gaṇṭhipade pana “abhiññāpādakajjhānato iddhividhañāṇādīnaṃ nīharaṇattha”nti vuttattā abhinīhārakkhamanti attho pakappito.

Thus, although by this word 'thus' the preliminary practice for all four jhānas is included, not just the first three jhānas, yet, taking only the first three jhānas, he says, '“Thus” is an indication of the progression to the fourth jhāna; by this means, it is said that having attained the first jhāna and so on in sequence, one obtains the fourth jhāna.' If it is asked why, it is because they are the preparatory ground. For it has been said in the commentary: 'Herein, the first three jhānas, because by pervading with rapture and pervading with pleasure, and by entering into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness, one’s body becomes light, soft, and workable, and one attains psychic power, should therefore, in this way, be understood as the preparatory ground because they lead to the attainment of psychic power. The fourth jhāna, however, is indeed the natural ground for the attainment of psychic power.' Or, referring to this same meaning, he says, 'Formerly, these four jhānas were for some the basis for the higher knowledges.' If so, why was it not said 'thus,' including the fourth jhāna as well? If it is because that is the natural ground, it should not be said so, because of the consequence that there would exist a mind that has attained a state of concentration, etc., beyond the fourth jhāna. Since, when that fourth jhāna is present, it is said, 'He inclined his mind toward the knowledge of the recollection of past lives,' therefore, when that fourth-jhāna-mind has attained the state of being the natural ground and has become the basis for higher knowledge, he says that one 'inclined the preparatory mind toward the knowledge of the recollection of past lives.' In the phrase 'it is capable of being directed,' here one directs that preparatory mind for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. Having removed it from the kasiṇa object, one sends it forth toward the kinds of psychic power. In the Ganthipada, however, because it is said, 'for the purpose of bringing forth the knowledges of the kinds of psychic power, and so on, from the jhāna that is the basis for higher knowledge,' the meaning 'capable of being directed' is construed.

So evaṃ samāhite evaṃ āneñjappatteti yojanā veditabbā dutiyavikappe, nīvaraṇadūrībhāvena vitakkādisamatikkamenāti paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ kiccasaṅgaṇhanato. Ayaṃ yojanā paṭhamavikappe na sambhavati “parisuddhetiādīsu panā”ti vacanena “eva”nti padassa anuppabandhanivāraṇato. Teneva “upekkhāsatipārisuddhibhāvena parisuddhe”tiādimāha. Icchāvacarānanti “aho vatāhaṃ āpattiñceva āpanno assaṃ, na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyu”ntiādinā [V 0.0045] (ma. ni. 1.60) nayena uppannaicchāvasena pavattānaṃ kopaapaccayānaṃ abhāvena anaṅgaṇeti attho. Ettha ca pana yathāvuttappakārā icchāpi paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamāya antarāyikā “sampajānamusāvādo kho panāyasmanto antarāyiko dhammo”ti (mahāva. 134) vuttattā, pageva icchāvacarā kopaapaccayā, tasmā vuttaṃ “jhānapaṭilābhapaccanīkānaṃ pāpakānaṃ icchāvacarāna”ntiādi. Katthaci pana “jhānapaṭilābhapaccayānaṃ icchāvacarāna”nti potthakesu pāṭho dissati, so pamādalekho, gaṇṭhipade ca “aho vata satthā mamaññeva paṭipucchitvā dhammaṃ deseyyā”ti [M 0.0050] yo tadattho likhito, so dullikhito. Na hi jhānapaṭilābhapaccayā kopādayo anaṅgaṇasutte (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) vuttā, “na ca yuttito sambhavanti jhānalābhino tadabhāvā”ti ācariyo vadati, taṃ vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Ettha vijjattayassa uttaruttaravisesadassanatthaṃ “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādinā punappunaṃ aṭṭhaṅganidassanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Uttaruttaravisesā cebhāsaṃ attadukkhaparadukkhadassanatadupasamattadīpanato veditabbā. Bhagavā hi pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena attano anantasaṃsāradukkhaṃ passitvā, cutūpapātañāṇena parassa ca lokassa āsavakkhayañāṇena tadubhayavūpasamattañca passitvā taṃ deseti, paṭhamena vā attadukkhadassanato attasinehapariccāgaṃ dīpeti. Dutiyena paradukkhadassanato paresu kopapariccāgaṃ, tatiyena ariyamaggadassanato mohapariccāgañca dīpeti. Evaṃ nānāguṇavisesadīpanato imasseva lokiyābhiññādvayassa idha gahaṇaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

The construction 'Thus concentrated, thus having attained imperturbability' should be understood in the second alternative, because it summarizes the function of the first jhāna and so on by way of being far from the hindrances and transcending initial thought, etc. This construction is not possible in the first alternative because the words 'in being purified, etc.' prevent the sequential connection of the word 'thus.' For that reason, he says, 'being purified by the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness,' and so on. 'Those who move in desire' means without blemish due to the absence of anger and resentment that proceed by the power of an arisen wish, according to the method of 'Oh, that I might have committed an offense, and that the bhikkhus might not know me,' and so on. And here, even a wish of the aforesaid kind is an obstacle to the attainment of the first jhāna and so on, because it is said: 'Venerable sirs, intentional false speech is an obstructive factor.' How much more so desire-ridden anger and resentment? Therefore, it is said, 'of evil, desire-ridden things that are hostile to the attainment of jhāna,' and so on. In some places, however, the reading 'of desire-ridden things that are conditions for the attainment of jhāna' is seen in the books; that is a careless writing. And in the Ganthipada, the meaning written for that term as 'Oh, that the Teacher, having questioned only me, would teach the Dhamma!' is badly written. For anger and so on are not spoken of in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta as conditions for the attainment of jhāna. The teacher says, 'And they are not logically possible, because of their absence in one who has attained jhāna.' That should be investigated. Here, it should be understood that to show the progressively superior distinction of the three knowledges, the demonstration of the eight factors has been made repeatedly by the phrase 'with the mind thus concentrated,' and so on. And their progressively superior distinctions should be understood from its illuminating the seeing of one's own suffering, the seeing of others' suffering, and the pacification of both. For the Blessed One teaches that, having seen his own endless suffering in saṃsāra with the knowledge of the recollection of past lives; having seen the suffering of others and of the world with the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings; and having seen the pacification of both with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Or, with the first knowledge, by seeing one's own suffering, he illuminates the abandonment of self-affection. With the second, by seeing others' suffering, he illuminates the abandonment of anger towards others. With the third, by seeing the noble path, he illuminates the abandonment of delusion. Thus, it should be understood that because it illuminates various special qualities, the inclusion here of just these two mundane higher knowledges has been made.

Yasmā atītajāti eva nivāso, tasmā “atītajātīsū”ti na vattabbanti ce? Na, jātiyā ekadesepi nivāsavohārasiddhidassanato. Pāḷiyaṃ kiñcāpi “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”tiādivacanena sakalajātiyā anussaraṇameva pubbenivāsānussati viya dissati, na evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tadekadesānussaraṇampi pubbenivāsānussati evāti dassanatthaṃ, bhummavacanaṃ kataṃ okāsādisaṅgahatthañca. “Chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsū”ti ādi-saddena anivutthalokadhātudīparaṭṭhanagaragāmādiggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “tesaṃ chinnavaṭumakānaṃ lokuttarasīlādīni na bhagavatā bodhisattakāle viññātānī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthāpattito lokiyāni viññātānīti āpajjati, taṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇādhikāre “ariyānaṃ upavādakā”ti vacanena samentaṃ viya dissati. Na hi ariye apassantassa evaṃ hoti. Kimatthaṃ panettha anussati vuttā, nanu esa vijjādhikāroti ce? Ādikammikassa sativasena nibbattito, atītadhammānaṃ satiyā visesādhikārattā ca. Vuttañhi “anussarāmī”ti.

If one were to say: 'Because only a past birth is a dwelling, therefore, should “in past births” not be stated?' No, it should indeed be stated, because the convention of 'dwelling' is established even in a part of a birth. Although in the Pāḷi, by the statement beginning with 'one birth, two births,' the recollection of the entire birth appears to be like the recollection of former dwellings, it should not be understood thus. The recollection of even a part of that birth is indeed the recollection of former dwellings. In order to show this, the locative case was used, and also for the purpose of including location and so forth.
