Was it not that, having disregarded Māgaṇḍikā, he taught the Dhamma for the welfare of her parents? To show this meaning, the Elder explained the attainment of Arahantship by Bījaka and his mother. The statement, 'Now at that time, not far from Vesālī, there is a village named Kalandagāma, at which time Sudinna engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife,' or 'at which time the Blessed One laid down the first Pārājika rule,' is not suitable here. Why? Because the commentary statement, 'Here, however, the meaning of cause and the meaning of instrument are possible,' is not found here. For that village was long-established, not just at that very time. But since that village, though long-established, deserves to be spoken of as existing at all times from the time of its establishment, for that reason it was said, 'Now at that time, not far from Vesālī, there is a village named Kalandagāma.'

25-6. Anuññātosi pana tvanti samaṇavattadassanatthaṃ bhagavā pucchati. Mātāpitūhi ananuññātanti ettha janakeheva ananuññātadassanatthaṃ pucchīti vuttaṃ. Na kho sudinna tathāgatāti “pabbājetu maṃ bhagavā”ti yācanāvasena panevamāha, na bhagavā sayaṃ saraṇāni datvā pabbājesi. Dukkhassāti ettha “kalabhāgampī”ti pāṭhaseso. Vikappadvayepīti dutiyatatiyavikappesu. Purimapadassāti kiñcīti padassa. Uttarapadenāti dukkhassāti padena. Samānavibhattīti sāmivacanaṃ. Yathā kiṃ? “Kassaci dukkhassā”ti vattabbe “kiñci dukkhassā”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Akāmakā vinā bhavissāmāti tayā saddhiṃ amaritvā akāmā jīvissāma. Sacepi na marāma, akāmakāva tayā viyogaṃ pāpuṇissāma, tayi jīvamāne eva no maraṇaṃ bhaveyya, maraṇenapi no tayā viyogaṃ mayaṃ akāmakāva pāpuṇissāma.

25-6. The Blessed One asks, 'But are you permitted?' to show the proper conduct of a recluse. Here, 'Not permitted by mother and father' is said to show that he was not permitted by his very parents. 'Not so, Sudinna, the Tathāgatas'—this he said by way of a request, 'May the Blessed One ordain me.' The Blessed One did not ordain him by giving the refuges himself. Here, regarding 'of suffering,' the remainder of the reading is 'even a portion.' 'In both alternatives' refers to the second and third alternatives. 'Of the former word' refers to the word 'something.' 'By the latter word' refers to the word 'of suffering.' 'Same grammatical case' refers to the genitive case. How so? It should be understood that instead of saying, 'of some suffering,' it is said, 'of something's suffering.' 'Unwillingly, we shall be without you' means: 'Not dying together with you, we shall live on unwillingly.' Even if we do not die, we shall unwillingly be separated from you. While you are still living, it would be our death; and even by our death, we would unwillingly be separated from you.

30. Katipāhaṃ balaṃ gāhetvāti kasmā panāyaṃ tathā pabbajjāya tibbacchando anuññāto samāno katipāhaṃ ghareyeva vilambitvā kāyabalañca aggahesīti? Anumatidānena mātāpitūsu sahāyakesu ca tuṭṭho tesaṃ cittatuṭṭhatthaṃ. Kesuci aṭṭhakathāpotthakesu keci ācariyā “ayaṃ sudinno jīvakavatthuto pacchā paṃsukūlikadhutaṅgavasena paṃsukūliko jāto”ti saññāya “gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṃsukūlikadhutaṅgavasena paṃsukūliko hotī”ti likhanti, taṃ “acirūpasampanno”ti vacanena virujjhati. “Tathā sudinno hi bhagavato dvādasame vasse pabbajito[V 0.0063], vīsatime vasse ñātikulaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho sayaṃ pabbajjāya aṭṭhavassiko hutvā”ti, “bhagavato hi buddhattaṃ pattato paṭṭhāya yāva idaṃ vatthaṃ, etthantare vīsati vassāni na koci gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyi, sabbe paṃsukūlikāva ahesu”nti ca vuttena aṭṭhakathāvacanena virujjhati, pabbajjāya aṭṭhavassiko, na upasampadāya. Upasampadaṃ pana jīvakavatthuto (mahāva. 326) pacchā [M 0.0069] alattha, tasmā avassiko ñātikulaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho siyāti ce? Na, “alattha kho sudinno kalandaputto bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampada”nti ekato anantaraṃ vuttattā. Pabbajjānantarameva hi so upasampanno terasadhutaṅgaguṇe samādāya vattanto aṭṭha vassāni vajjigāme viharitvā nissayamuttattā sayaṃvasī hutvā “etarahi kho vajjī dubbhikkhā”tiāditakkavasena yena vesālī tadavasari, tasmā “paṃsukūlikadhutaṅgavasena paṃsukūliko hotī”ti ettakoyeva pāṭho yesu potthakesu dissati, sova pamāṇato gahetabbo. “Āraññiko hotī”ti iminā pañca senāsanapaṭisaṃyuttāni saṅgahitāni nesajjikaṅgañca vihārasabhāgattā, “piṇḍapātiko”ti iminā pañca piṇḍapātapaṭisaṃyuttāni, “paṃsukūliko”ti iminā dve cīvarapaṭisaṃyuttāni saṅgahitānīti. Ñātigharūpagamanakāraṇadīpanādhippāyato sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ visuṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Mā atiharāpesu”nti kālabyattayavasena vuttaṃ. Dhammassantarāyakaratarattā “imaṃ naya”nti anayoyeva.

30. Why, though so eager for the going forth and having been given permission, did he still delay at home for a few days to build up his physical strength? Being pleased with his parents and friends for giving their consent, he did so for the sake of their mental satisfaction. In some commentary manuscripts, certain teachers, thinking, 'This Sudinna, after the account of Jīvaka, became a wearer of rag-robes by means of the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes,' write: 'Having rejected a householder's robe, he becomes a wearer of rag-robes by means of the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes.' This is contradicted by the statement 'soon after his full ordination.' It is also contradicted by the commentary statement which says: 'Indeed, Sudinna went forth in the Blessed One’s twelfth year, and in the twentieth year he entered his relatives’ village for alms, having been ordained for eight years,' and 'Indeed, from when the Blessed One attained Buddhahood until this story, in this interval of twenty years, no one accepted a householder's robe; all were wearers of rag-robes.' He was eight years since his going forth, not since his full ordination. But if it is said that he received full ordination after the account of Jīvaka and therefore entered his relatives’ village for almsfood, not yet having completed a vassa, this is not so. For it is stated immediately and together: 'Sudinna the Kalandakaputta received the going forth in the Blessed One's presence; he received the full ordination.' For right after his going forth he was fully ordained. Having undertaken the thirteen ascetic qualities, he dwelt for eight years in a Vajjian village. Then, being free from dependence and self-reliant, he went to Vesālī, thinking, 'Now the Vajjian country is afflicted by famine,' and so on. Therefore, only that reading which is found in the manuscripts, namely, 'he becomes a wearer of rag-robes by means of the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes,' should be taken as authoritative. By the phrase 'he was a forest-dweller,' the five practices connected with lodging are included, as well as the sitter's practice, since it is of the same nature as a dwelling. By 'he was an alms-eater,' the five practices connected with almsfood are included. By 'he was a wearer of rag-robes,' the two practices connected with robes are included. It should be understood that the practice of going for alms in sequence is mentioned separately to show the reason for visiting his relatives’ home. 'Do not let them carry it too far' is said with an inversion of tense. Because it is a greater obstacle to the Dhamma, 'this method' is indeed a wrong method.

Yebhuyyena hi sattānaṃ, vināse paccupaṭṭhite;

Anayo nayarūpena, buddhimāgamma tiṭṭhati.

Indeed, for most beings, when destruction is at hand, what is unprofitable in the guise of what is profitable approaches and establishes itself in the mind.

36. Apaññatte sikkhāpadeti ettha duvidhaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ. Kathaṃ? “Evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti evaṃ sauddesānuddesabhedato duvidhaṃ. Tattha pātimokkhe sarūpato āgatā pañca āpattikkhandhā sauddesapaññatti nāma. Sāpi duvidhā sapuggalāpuggalaniddesabhedato. Tattha yassā paññattiyā anto āpattiyā saha, vinā vā puggalo dassito, sā sapuggalaniddesā. Itarā apuggalaniddesāti veditabbā. Sapuggalaniddesāpi duvidhā dassitādassitāpattibhedato. Tattha adassitāpattikā nāma aṭṭha pārājikā dhammā. “Pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti hi puggalova tattha dassito, nāpatti. Dassitāpattikā nāma bhikkhunīpātimokkhe “sattarasa saṅghādisesā dhammā nissāraṇīyaṃ saṅghādisesa”nti hi tattha āpatti dassitā saddhiṃ puggalena, tathā apuggalaniddesāpi dassitādassitāpattitova duvidhā. Tattha adassitāpattikā nāma sekhiyā dhammā. Sesā dassitāpattikāti [V 0.0064] veditabbā. Sāpi duvidhā aniddiṭṭhakārakaniddiṭṭhakārakabhedato. Tattha aniddiṭṭhakārakā nāma sukkavissaṭṭhi musāvāda omasavāda [M 0.0070] pesuñña bhūtagāma aññavādaka ujjhāpanaka gaṇabhojana paramparabhojana surāmeraya aṅgulipatodaka hasadhamma anādariya talaghātakajatumaṭṭhaka sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena pañcadasavidhā honti. Sesānaṃ puggalaniddesānaṃ vasena niddiṭṭhakārakā veditabbā.

36. Herein, the establishment of a training rule is twofold. How so? As in, 'And so, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule,' it is thus twofold, distinguished as with recitation and without recitation. Therein, the five classes of offenses that appear in the Pātimokkha in their own form are called 'establishment with recitation' (sauddesapaññatti). That is also twofold, distinguished as with personal indication and without personal indication. Therein, an establishment in which a person is indicated, either with or without the offense, is one with personal indication (sapuggalaniddesā). The other is to be understood as being without personal indication (apuggalaniddesā). That with personal indication is also twofold, distinguished as with the offense shown and with the offense not shown. Therein, the eight Pārājika rules are those with the offense not shown (adassitāpattikā). For in the phrase, 'He is defeated, not in communion,' only the person is indicated, not the offense. Those with the offense shown (dassitāpattikā) are the seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha; for in the text, 'seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules... a Saṅghādisesa requiring expulsion,' the offense is shown together with the person. Similarly, those without personal indication are also twofold, distinguished by way of the offense being shown and the offense not being shown. Therein, the Sekhiya rules are those with the offense not shown (adassitāpattikā). The remaining are to be understood as those with the offense shown (dassitāpattikā). That is also twofold, distinguished as with an unspecified agent and with a specified agent. Therein, those with an unspecified agent (aniddiṭṭhakārakā) are of fifteen kinds, by way of the training rules concerning: intentional emission of semen, lying, abusive speech, slander, destroying plant life, prevarication, complaining, group eating, eating in succession, alcoholic drinks, tickling with the fingers, playing in the water, disrespect, a blow with the hand, and using a lacquered object. The remaining are to be understood as having a specified agent (niddiṭṭhakārakā) by way of their personal indications.

Anuddesapaññattipi padabhājanantarāpattivinītavatthupaṭikkhepapaññattiavuttasiddhivasena chabbidhā honti. Tattha “yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (pārā. 61) evamādikā padabhājaniye sandissamānāpatti padabhājanasikkhāpadaṃ nāma. “Na tveva naggena āgantabbaṃ, yo āgaccheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādikā (pārā. 517) antarāpattisikkhāpadaṃ nāma. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, divā paṭisallīyantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyitu”nti (pārā. 75) evamādikā vinītavatthusikkhāpadaṃ nāma. “Lohituppādako, bhikkhave, anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo, upasampanno nāsetabbo”ti (mahāva. 114) evamādikā paṭikkhepasikkhāpadaṃ nāma. Khandhakesu paññattadukkaṭathullaccayāni paññattisikkhāpadaṃ nāma. “Yā pana bhikkhunī naccaṃ vā gītaṃ vā vāditaṃ vā dassanāya gaccheyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 834) iminā vuttena “yā pana bhikkhunī nacceyya vā gāyeyya vā vādeyya vā pācittiya”nti evamādikaṃ yaṃ kiñci aṭṭhakathāya dissamānaṃ āpattijātaṃ, vinayakammaṃ vā avuttasiddhisikkhāpadaṃ nāma. Chabbidhampetaṃ chahi kāraṇehi uddesārahaṃ na hotīti anuddesasikkhāpadaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – pañcahi uddesehi yathāsambhavaṃ visabhāgattā thullaccayadubbhāsitānaṃ, sabhāgavatthukampi dukkaṭathullaccayadvayaṃ asabhāgāpattikattā, antarāpattipaññattisikkhāpadānaṃ nānāvatthukāpattikattā, paṭikkhepasikkhāpadānaṃ kesañci vinītavatthupaññattisikkhāpadānañca adassitāpattikattā, adassitavatthukattā bhedānuvattakathullaccayassa, adassitāpattivatthukattā avuttasiddhisikkhāpadānanti. Ettāvatā “duvidhaṃ sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ uddesānuddesabhedato”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ samāsato pakāsitaṃ hoti.

The establishment of rules without recitation (anuddesapaññatti) is also sixfold: by word-analysis, by intermediate-offense, by settled-case, by prohibition, by enactment, and by what is unstated but implied. Among these, the offense found in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājaniya), such as, ‘What has been mostly eaten is a grave offense,’ is called a word-analysis training rule. A rule such as, ‘One should certainly not approach naked; whoever should approach, it is an offense of wrong-doing,’ is called an intermediate-offense training rule. A rule such as, ‘I allow, bhikkhus, one who is in seclusion during the day to remain in seclusion after closing the door,’ is called a settled-case training rule. A rule such as, ‘Bhikkhus, one who has shed the blood [of a Tathāgata], if unordained, should not be ordained; if ordained, he should be expelled,’ is called a prohibition training rule. The offenses of wrong-doing and grave offenses laid down in the Khandhakas are called enactment training rules. By what is stated in the rule, ‘Whatever bhikkhunī should go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music, it is an offense of expiation,’ whatever class of offense or Vinaya procedure is found in the commentary—such as, ‘Whatever bhikkhunī should dance, or sing, or play an instrument, it is an offense of expiation’—is called an unstated-but-implied training rule. It should be understood that this sixfold group of training rules is not suitable for recitation for six reasons, and thus is called a training rule without recitation. These are as follows: grave offenses and wrong speech are, as the case may be, dissimilar to the five recitations; the pair of wrong-doing and grave offenses, even with a similar basis, are of a dissimilar offense-type; the training rules for intermediate offenses and enactments have various bases and various offenses; for the prohibition training rules, and for some of the settled-case and enactment training rules, the offense is not shown; for the grave offense of following a schismatic, the basis is not shown; and for the unstated-but-implied training rules, the offense and basis are not shown. Thus far, what was stated as ‘The laying down of a training rule is twofold, distinguished as with-recitation and without-recitation,’ has been explained in brief.

Tattha apaññatte sikkhāpadeti sauddesasikkhāpadaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ekacce ācariyā evaṃ kira vaṇṇayanti “cattāro pārājikā kativassābhisambuddhena bhagavatā paññattātiādinā pucchaṃ katvā tesu paṭhamapārājiko [M 0.0071] vesāliyaṃ paññatto pañcavassābhisambuddhena hemantānaṃ paṭhame māse dutiye pakkhe dasame divase aḍḍhateyyaporisāya chāyāya [V 0.0065] puratthābhimukhena nisinnena aḍḍhaterasānaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ majjhe sudinnaṃ kalandaputtaṃ ārabbha paññatto”ti, taṃ na yujjati, kasmā? –

Herein, it should be understood that the phrase ‘when the training rule had not been laid down’ is said with reference to a training rule with recitation. Some teachers, it is said, explain it thus: Having posed the question, ‘The four Pārājikas—in which year of his rains-residences after becoming fully enlightened were they laid down by the Blessed One?’ and so on, they say: ‘Among these, the first Pārājika was laid down at Vesālī in the fifth year of his rains-residences after becoming fully enlightened, in the first month of the winter season, in the second fortnight, on the tenth day, when the shadow was two and a half man-lengths, while he was seated facing east in the midst of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus, on account of Sudinna, the son of the householder Kalanda.’ This is not tenable. Why?

Yasmā dvādasamaṃ vassaṃ, verañjāyaṃ vasi jino;

Tasmiñca suddho saṅghoti, neva pārājikaṃ tadā.

Because the Conqueror dwelt at Verañjā during the twelfth rains-residence, and in that year the Saṅgha was pure, therefore the Pārājika was not laid down then.

Therassa sāriputtassa, sikkhāpaññattiyācanā;

Tasmiṃ siddhāti siddhāva, garukāpatti no tadā.

The Elder Sāriputta's request for the laying down of the training rules was manifest at that time; thus it is indeed established that a grave offense was not laid down then.

Ovādapātimokkhañca, kiṃ satthā catuvassiko;

Paṭikkhipi kimāṇañca, samattaṃ anujāni so.

Did the Teacher, being of four years, reject the Ovāda-pātimokkha? And did he permit the Āṇā-pātimokkha in its entirety?

Ajātasattuṃ nissāya, saṅghabhedamakāsi yaṃ;

Devadatto tato saṅgha-bhedo pacchimabodhiyaṃ.

Relying on Ajātasattu, Devadatta created a schism in the Saṅgha; from that, the schism in the Saṅgha occurred in the latter period of the enlightenment.

Ārādhayiṃsu maṃ pubbe, bhikkhūti munibhāsitaṃ;

Suttameva pamāṇaṃ no, sova kālo anappakoti.

‘Formerly, the bhikkhus pleased me’—so the Sage has said. For us, the Sutta alone is the authority, and that period was not insignificant.

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “atha bhagavā ajjhācāraṃ apassanto pārājikaṃ vā saṅghādisesaṃ vā na paññapesī”ti, taṃ sakalasikkhāpadaṃ sandhāyāha. Na kevalaṃ sauddesasikkhāpadamattaṃ, tena sauddesānuddesapaññattibhedaṃ sakalaṃ pārājikaṃ sandhāyāhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi nābhiparāmasanampi kāyasaṃsaggo, tathāpi etaṃ visesaniyamanato, acchandarāgādhippāyato ca visuṃ vuttaṃ. Chandarāgarattasseva hi kāyasaṃsaggo idhādhippeto. Asucipāne pana hatthiniyā tāpasapassāvapānena vālakābyo nāma uppajjati, vālakābyassa vatthu vattabbaṃ. Maṇḍabyassa nābhiyā parāmasaneneva kira. Rūpadassane pana vejjakā āhu –

As for the statement that was said, ‘Then the Blessed One, not seeing misconduct, did not lay down a Pārājika or a Saṅghādisesa,’ that was said referring to the entire training rule. It was not said referring merely to the training rule with recitation. Therefore, it is said that it was spoken referring to the entire Pārājika, which is distinguished by enactments with and without recitation. Although touching the navel is also lustful bodily contact, nevertheless, this was stated separately due to the special restriction and because it is not intended with lustful desire. Indeed, here bodily contact is intended only for one who is impassioned with lustful desire. Regarding the drinking of impurity, a being named Vālakābya arises from a female elephant drinking an ascetic's urine. It is said that for Maṇḍabya, a being arose merely from the touching of the navel. As for seeing a form, physicians say:

“Thīnaṃ sandassanā sukkaṃ, kadāci calitovare;

Taṃ gāmadhammakaraṇaṃ, dvayasamaṃ saṅgamiya;

Gabbhādīti ayaṃ nayo, thīnaṃ purisadassanāsītyūpaneyya”.

From a woman's sight of men, semen sometimes moves in a private chamber; having come to that act of village-practice with the equal desire of two, she conceives a womb. This is the method. It should be understood that this happens from a woman's sight of a man.

Tathāpyāhu [M 0.0072][V 0.0066] –

Furthermore, they say:

“Pupphike edhiyya suddhe, passaṃ narañca itthi taṃ;

Gabbhañca nayetyutta-miti tasmā kāso itī”ti.

When the menses is pure, a woman, seeing a man and causing the emission of seed, may also bring about that conception. Thus it is said. Therefore, the teacher Kāsa says:

Rājorodho viyāti sīhaḷadīpe ekissā itthiyā tathā ahosi, tasmā kira evaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi yāva brahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchi, na taṃ manussānaṃ visayo ahosi tesaṃ rūpaṃ viya. Teneva bhikkhū pucchiṃsu “kacci no tvaṃ āvuso sudinna anabhirato”ti.

In the phrase ‘like one in the royal harem’: In the island of Sīhaḷa, it happened thus to a certain woman; therefore, it is said, it was spoken thus. Although the sound rose up as far as the Brahma world, it was not the domain of humans, just as their form is not their domain. For that very reason, the bhikkhus asked, ‘Friend Sudinna, are you not discontented?’

39. Kalīti kodho, tassa sāsanaṃ kalisāsanaṃ, kalaho. Gāmadhammanti ettha janapadadhammaṃ janapadavāsīnaṃ siddhiṃ. Attāti cittaṃ, sarīrañca. Asuttantavinibaddhanti vinayasutte anāgataṃ, suttābhidhammesupi anāgataṃ, pāḷivinimuttanti attho. Kusumamālanti nānāguṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Ratanadāmanti atthasampattiṃ sandhāya vadati. Paṭikkhipanādhippāyā bhaddāli viya. Padaniruttibyañjanāni nāmavevacanāneva “nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ niruttī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1315) viya. Nippariyāyena virati sikkhāpadaṃ nāma. Akusalapakkhe dussīlyaṃ nāma cetanā. Kusalapakkhepi cetanāpariyāyato vibhaṅge “sikkhāpada”nti vuttaṃ. Saṅghasuṭṭhutāyāti ettha lokavajjassa paññāpane saṅghasuṭṭhutā hoti pākaṭādīnavato. Paññattivajjassa paññāpane saṅghaphāsutā hoti pākaṭānisaṃsattā. Tattha paṭhamena dummaṅkūnaṃ niggaho, dutiyena pesalānaṃ phāsuvihāro. Paṭhamena samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighāto, dutiyena diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ. Tathā paṭhamena appasannānaṃ pasādo, dutiyena pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvo. “Pubbe katapuññatāya codiyamānassa bhabbakulaputtassā”ti vuttattā “sudinno taṃ kukkuccaṃ vinodetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi, teneva pabbajjā anuññātā”ti vadanti, upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Tathā paṭhamena saddhammaṭṭhiti, dutiyena vinayānuggaho hotīti veditabbo.

39. Kali means anger; a dispute under its influence is a `kalisāsana`, a quarrel. Here, in the phrase gāmadhamma, it means the custom of the country-folk, the affair of the country-dwellers. Attā means mind and body. Asuttantavinibaddha means not found in the Vinaya Sutta, and also not found in the Sutta and Abhidhamma; the meaning is 'liberated from the Pāḷi text'. Kusumamālā is said with reference to various virtues. Ratanadāma is spoken with reference to the accomplishment of meaning. Those with the intention to reject are like Bhaddāli. Padaniruttibyañjanāni are merely synonyms for names, as in "name, naming, appellation, explanation," etc. Directly, abstinence is called a training rule. In the unwholesome sphere, what is called dussīlya (immorality) is volition. In the wholesome sphere too, in the Vibhaṅga, volition is figuratively called a "training rule". Here, regarding saṅghasuṭṭhutā (well-being of the Saṅgha): in the laying down of a rule concerning a worldly fault, there is the well-being of the Saṅgha because of the obvious disadvantage. In the laying down of a rule concerning a prescribed fault, there is the comfort of the Saṅgha (saṅghaphāsutā) because of the obvious benefit. There, by the first, there is the restraining of the unruly; by the second, the comfortable abiding of the virtuous. By the first, there is the warding off of future defilements; by the second, of those in the present life. Furthermore, by the first, there is the arising of faith in the faithless; by the second, an increase for the faithful. Because it is said, "of a capable clansman who, due to merit made in the past, is being admonished," they say, "Sudinna, having dispelled that remorse, realized arahantship; for that very reason, the going forth was permitted." This should be examined. Furthermore, by the first, there is the establishment of the true Dhamma; by the second, the support of the Vinaya—thus it should be understood.

Apicettha vatthuvītikkame yattha ekantākusalabhāvena, taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhubhāvāya paññattaṃ lokavajjato, yattha paññattijānane eva atthāpatti, na aññadā, taṃ saddhammaṭṭhitiyā vāpi pasāduppādabuddhiyā dhammadesanāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ, itarañca sekhiyaṃ, idaṃ lokavajjaṃ nāma. Vatthuno paññattiyā vā vītikkamacetanāyābhāvepi paṭikkhittassa karaṇe, kattabbassa akaraṇe vā [M 0.0073] sati yattha āpattippasaṅgo, taṃ sabbaṃ ṭhapetvā surāpānaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti veditabbaṃ. Āgantukavattaṃ, āvāsika, gamika, anumodana, bhattagga, piṇḍacārika, āraññaka, senāsana[V 0.0067], jantāghara, vaccakuṭi, saddhivihārika, upajjhāya, antevāsika, ācariyavattanti etāni aggahitaggahaṇanayena gaṇiyamānāni cuddasa, etāni pana vitthārato dveasīti mahāvattāni nāma honti. Sattahi āpattikkhandhehi saṃvaro saṃvaravinayo paññattisikkhāpadameva. Tattha paññattivinayo samathavinayatthāya samathavinayo saṃvaravinayatthāya saṃvaravinayo pahānavinayatthāyāti yojanā veditabbā. Yaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhu, taṃ saṅghaphāsūti ekamiva vuttaṃ saṅghasuṭṭhutāya sati saṅghaphāsu bhavissatīti dīpanatthaṃ. Pakarīyanti ettha te te payojanavisesasaṅkhātā atthavasāti atthavasaṃ “pakaraṇa”nti vuccati. Dasasu padesu ekekaṃ mūlaṃ katvā dasakkhattuṃ yojanāya padasataṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha pacchimassa padassa vasena atthasataṃ purimassa vasena dhammasataṃ atthajotikānaṃ niruttīnaṃ vasena niruttisataṃ, dhammabhūtānaṃ niruttīnaṃ vasena niruttisatanti dve niruttisatāni, atthasate ñāṇasataṃ, dhammasate ñāṇasataṃ dvīsu niruttisatesu dve ñāṇasatānīti cattāri ñāṇasatāni veditabbāni. Ettha saṅghasuṭṭhutāti dhammasaṅghassa suṭṭhubhāvoti attho. “Atthapadānīti aṭṭhakathā. Dhammapadānīti pāḷī”ti vuttaṃ kira.

Moreover, here, that training rule wherein the transgression of the basis is entirely due to an unwholesome state and which is laid down for the well-being of the Saṅgha as a worldly fault; and that training rule wherein an offense occurs only upon knowing the regulation and not otherwise, which is connected with the teaching of the Dhamma for the stability of the true Dhamma or for the purpose of inspiring faith, as well as the other Sekhiya rules—this group of training rules is called a 'worldly fault' (lokavajjaṃ). Wherein, even in the absence of an intention to transgress the object or the regulation, there is the liability of an offense in the doing of what is forbidden or in the non-doing of what ought to be done—all of that, excepting the rule on drinking intoxicants, should be known as a 'regulation-based fault' (paṇṇattivajjaṃ). The duties for newcomers, residents, those departing, giving thanks, the refectory, the alms-round, forest-dwelling, lodgings, the steam-bath, the toilet, the co-resident, the preceptor, the pupil, and the teacher—these, when counted by the method of taking up what has not been taken up, are fourteen. These, however, in detail, are called the eighty-two great duties. Restraint from the seven classes of offenses is the Discipline of Restraint, which is precisely the prescribed training rule itself. Therein, the Discipline of Regulation is for the sake of the Discipline of Settlement; the Discipline of Settlement is for the sake of the Discipline of Restraint; and the Discipline of Restraint is for the sake of the Discipline of Abandoning—thus the connection should be understood. What is for the well-being of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha—this is said as if they were one, to illustrate that when there is well-being for the Saṅgha, there will be comfort for the Saṅgha. Herein, those various specific purposes, designated as 'reasons of benefit' (atthavasā), are undertaken; therefore, 'reasons of benefit' (atthavasaṃ) is called a 'treatise' (pakaraṇaṃ). In the ten terms, having made each one the root and applying it ten times, a hundred terms are stated. Therein, by way of the latter term, a hundred meanings; by way of the former term, a hundred Dhammas; by way of expressions that illuminate the meaning, a hundred expressions; by way of expressions that have become Dhamma, a hundred expressions—thus, two hundred expressions. In the hundred meanings, a hundred knowledges; in the hundred Dhammas, a hundred knowledges; in the two hundred expressions, two hundred knowledges—thus, four hundred knowledges should be understood. Herein, 'well-being of the Saṅgha' (saṅghasuṭṭhutā) means the good state of the Dhamma-Saṅgha. It is said, it seems: 'Terms of meaning are the commentary; terms of Dhamma are the Pāḷi.'

Methunaṃ dhammanti evaṃ bahulanayena laddhanāmakaṃ sakasampayogena, parasampayogena vā attano nimittassa sakamagge vā paramagge vā paranimittassa sakamagge eva pavesapaviṭṭhaṭhituddharaṇesu yaṃ kiñci ekaṃ paṭisādiyanavasena seveyya pārājiko hoti asaṃvāsoti. Keci pana “pavesādīni cattāri vā tīṇi vā dve vā ekaṃ vā paṭiseveyya, pārājiko hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘so ce pavesanaṃ sādiyati, paviṭṭhaṃ, ṭhitaṃ, uddharaṇaṃ sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassā’tiādī”ti (pārā. 59) vadanti, tesaṃ matena catūsupi catasso pārājikāpattiyo āpajjati. Teyeva evaṃ vadanti “āpajjatu methunadhammapārājikāpatti methunadhammapārājikāpattiyā tabbhāgiyā”ti, “attano vītikkame pārājikāpattiṃ, saṅghādisesāpattiñca āpajjitvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya gahaṭṭhakāle methunādipārājikaṃ āpajjitvā puna pabbajitvā upasampajjitvā ekaṃ saṅghādisesāpattiṃ ekamanekaṃ vā paṭikaritvāva so puggalo yasmā nirāpattiko hoti, tasmā so gahaṭṭhakāle [M 0.0074] sāpattikovāti antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassāpi attheva āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ. Vuṭṭhānadesanāhi pana asujjhanato ‘payoge payoge āpatti pārājikassā’ti na vuttaṃ gaṇanapayojanābhāvato. Kiñcāpi na vuttaṃ, atha kho padabhājane ‘āpatti pārājikassā’ti vacanenāyamattho siddho”ti yuttiñca vadanti. Yadi evaṃ mātikāyampi “yo pana bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya pārājika”nti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, pārājikassa anavasesavacanampi na yujjeyya. Sabbepi hi āpattikkhandhe bhikkhugaṇanañca anavasesetvā [V 0.0068] tiṭṭhatīti anavasesavacananti katvā paveseva āpatti, na paviṭṭhādīsu, tamevekaṃ sandhāya “yassa siyā āpattī”ti pārājikāpattimpi anto katvā nidānuddese vacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tasmā mātikāyaṃ “pārājika”nti avatvā “pārājiko hotī”ti puggalaniddesavacanaṃ tena sarīrabandhanena upasampadāya abhabbabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. “Āpatti pārājikassā”ti padabhājane vacanaṃ antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannassāpi pārājikassa asaṃvāsassa sato puggalassa atheyyasaṃvāsakabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Na hi so saṃvāsaṃ sādiyantopi theyyasaṃvāsako hoti, tasmā “upasampanno bhikkhu”tveva vuccati. Tenevāha “asuddho hoti puggalo aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpanno, tañce suddhadiṭṭhi samāno anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā akkosādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti omasavādena dukkaṭassā”ti (pārā. 389). Anupasampannassa tadabhāvato siddho so “upasampanno bhikkhu”tveva vuccatīti. Tena padasodhammaṃ sahaseyyañca na janeti, bhikkhupesuññādiñca janetīti veditabbaṃ. Bhikkhunīnaṃ saṅghādisesesu pana bhikkhusaṅghādisesato vuṭṭhānavidhivisesadassanatthaṃ “ayampi bhikkhunī…pe… āpannā”ti (pāci. 679) puggalaniddesaṃ katvāpi pārājikato adhippāyantaradassanatthaṃ “nissāraṇīyaṃ saṅghādisesa”nti (pāci. 679) āpattināmaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Ettāvatā sapuggalaniddese dassitādassitāpattidukaṃ vitthāritaṃ hoti. Apuggalaniddesesu sekhiyesu āpattiyā dassanakāraṇaṃ sekhiyānaṃ aṭṭhakathāyameva vuttaṃ. Tadabhāvato itaresu āpattidassanaṃ kataṃ. Apuggalaniddesesupi dassitādassitāpattidukañca vitthāritaṃ hotīti.

Regarding 'sexual intercourse' (methunaṃ dhammaṃ): should one engage in this act, which has obtained its name by common usage, either by one's own effort or by another's effort, with one's own organ in one's own path or in another's path, or with another's organ only in one's own path; and should one, by way of consenting, engage in any single moment among the stages of insertion, having been inserted, remaining, and withdrawal, he is defeated (pārājiko) and not in communion (asaṃvāso). Some, however, say: "Should one engage in four, three, two, or one of the stages beginning with insertion, he is defeated." For this has been said: "If he consents to the insertion, to what has been inserted, to what is remaining, to the withdrawal, it is an offense of pārājika," and so on. According to their view, one falls into four pārājika offenses in the four moments. Those same ones say thus: "Let the pārājika offense of sexual intercourse be incurred; it is of a similar kind to a pārājika offense of sexual intercourse." And: "Because a person—who, due to his own transgression, having fallen into a pārājika offense and a saṅghādisesa offense, having renounced the training, and during his time as a householder having committed a pārājika offense such as sexual intercourse, then having gone forth and been ordained again, becomes without offense only after having made amends for one saṅghādisesa offense once or many times—therefore, that person was an offender during his time as a householder. Therefore, even for one who has committed the final offense, there is indeed rehabilitation from the offense." But because there is no purification by the confessions for rehabilitation, it is not said, 'for each act, an offense of pārājika,' because there is no benefit in counting. Although it is not said, nevertheless, this meaning is established by the statement in the Padabhājana, 'an offense of pārājika,' and they state this reasoning. If so, then in the Mātikā it should also be said, 'Whatever monk should engage in sexual intercourse, a pārājika,' and the statement 'without remainder' for one who is pārājika would not be suitable. For it stands without leaving a remainder of all the aggregates of offenses and the counting as a monk. Therefore, having understood the statement 'without remainder' thus, the offense is only in the insertion, not in having entered and so on. Referring to that one alone, the statement in the Nidānuddesa, 'for whom there may be an offense,' should be understood as having included the pārājika offense. Therefore, in the Mātikā, instead of saying 'pārājika' (the offense), the statement indicating the person, 'he becomes one who is defeated' (pārājiko hoti), is for the purpose of showing, by that bodily connection (like a severed head), the state of being unfit for ordination. The statement in the Padabhājana, 'an offense of pārājika,' is for the purpose of showing that even a person who has committed the final offense, being one who is defeated and not in communion, is not in the state of being a 'thief in communion.' For he does not become a 'thief in communion' even while consenting to communion; therefore, he is called 'an ordained monk.' For that very reason, He said: "A person is impure who has committed a certain pārājika offense; if one of pure view, having made him give no opportunity, speaks with the intention to insult, it is an offense of wrong-doing for contemptuous speech." Because this is absent for an unordained person, it is established that he is called 'an ordained monk.' By this, it should be understood that he does not give rise to the Padasodhamma offense or the Sahaseyya offense, but he does give rise to the offense of slandering a monk, and so on. But in the case of the Saṅghādisesa offenses of nuns, for the purpose of showing the special procedure of rehabilitation from the Saṅghādisesa of monks, even after making the designation of the person, "This nun... has fallen into," the taking up of the offense's name, "a Saṅghādisesa requiring expulsion," was also done for the purpose of showing a different intention from a pārājika. By this much, the pair of offenses—shown and not shown—in the case of designation with a person has been explained in detail. Among the designations without a person, in the Sekhiya rules, the reason for not showing the offense is stated in the commentary on the Sekhiyas themselves. Due to its absence there, the showing of the offense is done in the others. And in the designations without a person, the pair of offenses—shown and not shown—has also been explained in detail.

Paṭhamapaññattikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of the first declaration is finished.

Sudinnabhāṇavāraṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Recitation Section on Sudinna is finished.

Makkaṭīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Female Monkey

40-1. Dutiyapaññattiyaṃ [M 0.0075] “idha mallā yujjhantī”tiādīsu viya paṭisevatīti vattamānavacanaṃ pacurapaṭisevanavasena vuttaṃ, “tañca kho manussitthiyā, no tiracchānagatāyā”ti paripuṇṇatthampi paṭhamaṃ paññattiṃ attano micchāgāhena vā lesaoḍḍanatthāya vā evamāha. Paripuṇṇatthataṃyeva niyametuṃ “nanu āvuso tatheva taṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ, teneva makkaṭīvatthu vinītavatthūsu pakkhittaṃ avisesattā, tathā vajjiputtakavatthu. Vicāraṇā panettha tatiyapaññattiyaṃ āvi bhavissati. “Nanu, āvuso, bhagavatā anekapariyāyenā”tiādi na kevalaṃ sauddesasikkhāpadeneva siddhaṃ, “tiracchānagatādīsupi pārājika”nti anuddesasikkhāpadenapi siddhanti [V 0.0069] dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atha vā yadi sauddesasikkhāpadaṃ sāvasesanti paññapesi, iminā anuddesasikkhāpadenāpi kiṃ na siddhanti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmī”ti tadeva sikkhāpadaṃ paṭhamapaññattameva lesatthikānaṃ alesokāsaṃ katvā āmeḍitatthaṃ katvā paññapessāmīti attho. Aññathā “aññavādake vihesake pācittiya”ntiādīsu (pāci. 101) viya vatthudvayena āpattidvayaṃ āpajjati, na cāpajjati, so evattho aññenāpi vacanena suppakāsito, suparibyattakaraṇatthena daḷhataro katoti adhippāyo. Tatiyapaññattiyampi aññesu ca evaṃ visuddho.

In the second declaration, the present tense verb 'paṭisevati' (engages in), as in 'Here, the Mallas fight' and similar cases, is stated by way of frequent indulgence. Regarding the first declaration, which has a complete meaning, he spoke thus—'but that is with a human woman, not with an animal'—either due to his own wrong grasp or for the purpose of finding a loophole. To establish its very completeness of meaning, it was said, 'Is it not so, friend, that it is exactly like that?' For that very reason, the story of the female monkey was included among the disciplined cases due to its non-distinction; likewise the story of the Vajjiputtaka. The investigation here will become clear in the third declaration. The statement 'Is it not, friend, that by the Blessed One in many ways...' was said to show that it is established not only by the training rule with its full wording but also by the abbreviated training rule, namely, 'a pārājika offense even with animals, etc.' Or else, it was said to show this: if one were to declare that the training rule with its full wording is incomplete, is it not established by this abbreviated training rule as well? In 'Therefore, monks, I will lay down a training rule for the monks...,' the meaning is: I will lay down that very same training rule, the very first declaration, having made it so there is no opportunity for those seeking loopholes and having reiterated the meaning. Otherwise, as in cases like 'for one who speaks evasively or causes vexation, it is a pācittiya offense,' one would incur two offenses for two grounds, but one does not incur them. That very same meaning is well-explained by another statement as well; it is made firmer by making it thoroughly distinct. This is the intention. In the third declaration and in other decisions as well, the clarification should be made in this way.

Yassa sacittakapakkhetiādimhi pana gaṇṭhipadanayo tāva paṭhamaṃ vuccati, sacittakapakkheti surāpānādiacittake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sacittakesu pana yaṃ ekantamakusaleneva samuṭṭhāpitañca. Ubhayaṃ lokavajjaṃ nāma. Surāpānasmiñhi “surā”ti vā “pātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vā jānitvā pivane akusalameva, tathā bhikkhunīnaṃ gandhavaṇṇakatthāya lepane, bhesajjatthāya lepane adosattā “avicāraṇīya”nti ettakaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha na vaṭṭatīti “jānitvā”ti vuttavacanaṃ na yujjati paṇṇattivajjassāpi lokavajjabhāvappasaṅgato. Imaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgaṃ pariharitukāmatāya vajirabuddhittherassa gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ “idha sacittakanti ca acittakanti ca vicāraṇā vatthuvijānaneyeva hoti, na paññattivijānane. Yadi paññattivijānane hoti, sabbasikkhāpadāni lokavajjāneva siyuṃ, na ca sabbasikkhāpadāni lokavajjāni[M 0.0076], tasmā vatthuvijānaneyeva hotī”ti, idaṃ yujjati. Kasmā? Yasmā sekhiyesu paññattijānanameva pamāṇaṃ, na vatthumattajānananti, yaṃ pana tattheva vuttaṃ “pasuttassa mukhe koci suraṃ pakkhipeyya, anto ce paviseyya, āpatti, tattha yathā bhikkhuniyā adhakkhakaṃ ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ parassa āmasanādikāle kāyaṃ acāletvā citteneva sādiyantiyā āpatti ‘kiriyāva hotī’ti vuttā yebhuyyena kiriyasambhavato, tathā ayampi tadā kiriyāva hotī”ti, taṃ suvicāritaṃ anekantākusalabhāvasādhanato. Surāpānāpattiyā ekantākusalatā pana majjasaññinopi sakiṃ payogena pivato hotīti katvā vuttā.

However, in the section beginning with 'yassa sacittakapakkhe', the method of the Gaṇṭhipada is first stated. The term 'sacittakapakkhe' is stated with reference to the non-volitional training rules such as the drinking of intoxicants. However, among the volitional training rules, that which is certainly caused to arise by the unwholesome alone, and the non-volitional one—both are called a worldly fault. Indeed, in the training rule on drinking intoxicants, because of drinking while knowing either 'it is an intoxicant' or 'it is not allowable to drink,' it is indeed unwholesome. Similarly, for bhikkhunīs, anointing for the purpose of fragrance and complexion is indeed unwholesome. Because anointing for the purpose of medicine is without fault, only this much is said: 'It is not to be investigated.' Therein, the spoken phrase 'knowing it is not allowable' is not suitable, because of the consequence that even a fault by prescription would become a worldly fault. Due to the desire to avoid this undesirable consequence, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada of the Elder Vajirabuddhi: 'Here, the investigation into "volitional" and "non-volitional" is only in the matter of knowing the object; it is not in the matter of knowing the prescription. If it were in the matter of knowing the prescription, all training rules would be only worldly faults, but not all training rules are worldly faults. Therefore, it is only in the matter of knowing the object.' This is suitable. Why? Because in the Sekhiya rules, knowledge of the prescription alone is the standard, not the mere knowledge of the object. However, what is stated in that very Gaṇṭhipada: 'If someone were to pour an intoxicant into the mouth of one who is asleep, and if it should enter inside, there is an offense. Therein, just as it is said of a bhikkhunī who, at the time of being touched, etc., by another man below the collarbone and above the circle of the knee, does not move her body but consents with the mind alone, that the offense "is only an action" because for the most part it can arise from a functional-consciousness root, so too this offense, at that time, is only an action'—that statement is well-considered because it establishes its nature as not exclusively unwholesome. However, the exclusively unwholesome nature of the offense of drinking an intoxicant is stated on the grounds that it occurs even for one who, not perceiving it as an intoxicant, drinks it with a single effort.

Ayaṃ panettha attho – sikkhāpadasīsena āpattiṃ gahetvā yassa sikkhāpadassa sacittakassa cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajjaṃ. Sacittakācittakasaṅkhātassa acittakassa ca sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, tampi surāpānādi lokavajjanti imamatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā “yassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva hoti, taṃ lokavajja”nti vuttaṃ. Sacittakapakkheti hi idaṃ vacanaṃ acittakaṃ sandhāyāha. Na hi ekaṃsato sacittakassa sacittakapakkheti [V 0.0070] visesane payojanaṃ atthi. Yasmā panettha paṇṇattivajjassa paññattijānanacittena sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalameva, vatthujānanacittena sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ siyā kusalaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākataṃ, tasmā “tassa sacittakapakkhe cittaṃ akusalamevā”ti na vuccatīti “sesaṃ paṇṇattivajja”nti vuttaṃ. Adhimāne vītikkamābhāvā, supinante abbohārikattā supinante vijjamānāpi vītikkamachāyā abbohārikabhāvenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idaṃ pana vacanaṃ daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanattā ca vuttaṃ, tena yaṃ vuttaṃ bāhiranidānakathādhikāre “daḷhīkammasithilakaraṇappayojanāti yebhuyyatāya vutta”ntiādi, taṃ suvuttamevāti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, this is the meaning: having taken an offense under the heading of a training rule, for whichever intentional training rule the mind is solely unwholesome, that is a worldly fault. And for the non-volitional training rule, which is designated as having intentional and non-volitional aspects, in its intentional aspect the mind is solely unwholesome; that too, such as the drinking of intoxicants, is a worldly fault. Having summarized this meaning, it was said: “For whichever, in its intentional aspect, the mind is solely unwholesome, that is a worldly fault.” For this statement, “in the intentional aspect,” is said in reference to the non-volitional. Indeed, for what is exclusively intentional, there is no purpose in the specification “in the intentional aspect.” Because herein, for a prescribed fault, with the mind that knows the prescription, the mind in the intentional aspect is solely unwholesome; but with the mind that knows the object, the mind in the intentional aspect may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate. Therefore, it is not said, “For that, the mind in the intentional aspect is solely unwholesome,” and thus it was said by the commentator, “The remainder is a prescribed fault.” Because there is no intention to transgress in conceit, and because actions in a dream are non-transactional, it is meant that even though the shadow of a transgression exists in a dream, it is non-transactional. This statement, however, was also said for the purpose of strengthening a former prescription and relaxing a later one. Therefore, what was said in the section on the Bāhiranidānakathā, such as, “It is said for the most part for the purpose of strengthening and relaxing,” that should be understood as well-said.

Makkaṭīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Female Monkey is concluded.

Vajjiputtakavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Vajjiputtaka Monk

43-4. Vajjīsu [M 0.0077] janapadesu vasantā vajjino nāma, tesaṃ puttā. Yāvadatthanti yāvatā attho adhippāyoti vuttaṃ hoti, tattha yaṃ vuttaṃ “sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃanāvikatvā”ti, taṃ kāmaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhāne, tadekaṭṭhe ca dubbalyāvikaraṇe paññatte sati yujjati, na aññathā. Tathāpi idāni paññapetabbaṃ upādāya vuttaṃ, kathañhi nāma chabbaggiyā bhikkhū atirekacīvaraṃ dhāressanti (pārā. 459), āḷavakā bhikkhū kuṭiyo kārāpenti appamāṇikāyo (pārā. 342), bhikkhuniyo dve vassāni chasu dhammesu asikkhitasikkhaṃ sikkhamānaṃ vuṭṭhāpenti (pāci. 1077), saṅghena asammataṃ vuṭṭhāpentītiādi (pāci. 1084) viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi tato pubbe adhiṭṭhānaṃ vikappanaṃ vā anuññātaṃ. Yadabhāvā atirekacīvaranti vadeyya, pamāṇaṃ vā na paññattaṃ, yadabhāvā appamāṇikāyoti vadeyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Ullumpatu maṃ, bhante, saṅgho anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti (mahāva. 71, 126) upasampadaṃ yācitvā upasampannena upasampannasamanantarameva “upasampannena bhikkhunā methuno dhammo na paṭisevitabbo, asakyaputtiyo”ti (mahāva. 129) ca paññattena assamaṇādibhāvaṃ upagantukāmena nanu paṭhamaṃ ajjhupagatā sikkhā paccakkhātabbā, tattha dubbalyaṃ vā āvikātabbaṃ siyā, te pana “sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseviṃsū”ti anupaññattiyā okāsakaraṇatthaṃ vā taṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “So āgato na upasampādetabbo”ti kiñcāpi ettheva vuttaṃ, tathāpi itaresupi pārājikesu yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya [V 0.0071] dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā yo pārājikavatthuṃ adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyati, manussaviggahaṃ vā jīvitā voropeti, paṭivijānantassa uttarimanussadhammaṃ vā ullapati, so āgato na upasampādetabbo. Anupaññatti hi daḷhīkammasithilakammakaraṇappayojanā. Sā hi yassa pārājikaṃ hoti aññā vā āpatti, tassa niyamadassanappayojanātilakkhaṇānupaññattikattā. Evañhi ante avatvā ādimhi vuttā “gāmā vā araññā vā”ti (pārā. 91) anupaññatti viya. Paripuṇṇe panetasmiṃ sikkhāpade –

43-4. Those dwelling in the Vajjian country are called Vajjis, and their sons are the Vajjiputtakas. 'As much as is desired' means as much as is intended. Therein, the statement, 'without having renounced the training and without having declared weakness,' is applicable when a rule for renouncing the training and, in the same context, for declaring weakness has been laid down, but not otherwise. Nevertheless, it is stated here with reference to what is to be laid down, and this should be understood as being like the following cases: How indeed could the group-of-six monks wear an extra robe? The Āḷavakan monks have huts built without measure; the nuns ordain a probationer who has not trained for two years in the six rules; they ordain one not approved by the Sangha, and so on. For before that, neither determination nor sharing of robes had been permitted, in the absence of which one could speak of an 'extra robe'. Nor had a measure for huts been laid down, in the absence of which one could speak of them as being 'without measure'. This consistency of examples should be understood in this way. After requesting ordination by saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Saṅgha, out of compassion, lift me up,' and having been ordained, should not a monk who wishes to attain the state of being a non-ascetic, etc.—in light of the rule laid down immediately after ordination, 'A monk who has been ordained should not engage in sexual intercourse; he is not a son of the Sakyan'—first renounce the training he had undertaken, or declare his weakness therein? But as for them, it should be understood that the statement, 'without renouncing the training and without declaring weakness, they engaged in sexual intercourse,' was said to create an opportunity for a supplementary ruling. Although it is said right here, 'He, having come back, should not be ordained,' it should be understood to apply to the other Pārājika offenses as is applicable. For one who, without renouncing the training and without declaring weakness, takes what is not given, amounting to theft, or deprives a human being of life, or falsely claims superhuman attainments while knowing it to be so, such a person, having come back, should not be ordained. For a supplementary ruling has the purpose of strengthening or relaxing a rule. For it has the purpose of showing the fixed nature of the offense—be it a Pārājika or another offense—and thus it is a supplementary ruling that serves as a characteristic. Thus, without being stated at the end, it is stated at the beginning, like the supplementary ruling, 'from a village or from the wilderness.' But in this complete training rule—

“Nidānā mātikābhedo, vibhaṅgo taṃniyāmako;

Tato āpattiyā bhedo, anāpatti tadaññathā”ti. –

From the origin, the division of the mātikā; the Analysis is its determinant; from that, the division of the offense; and non-offense is otherwise.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0078] nayo veditabbo. Tattha sudinnavatthu makkaṭivatthu vajjiputtakavatthu cāti tippabhedaṃ vatthu imassa sikkhāpadassa nidānaṃ nāma, tato nidānā “yo pana, bhikkhu, bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno…pe… asaṃvāso”ti imissā mātikāya bhedo jāto. Tattha hi “antamaso tiracchānagatāyā”ti itthiliṅgavacanena “saccaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tañca kho itthiyā no purise no paṇḍake no ubhatobyañjanake cā”ti makkaṭipārājiko viya aññopi lesaṃ oḍḍetuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tādisassa alesokāsassa dassanatthaṃ idaṃ vuccati. Makkaṭivatthusaṅkhātā nidānā “antamaso tiracchānagatāyapī”ti mātikāvacanabhedo na itthiyā eva methunasiddhidassanato kato, tasmā vibhaṅgo taṃniyāmako tassā mātikāya adhippetatthaniyāmako vibhaṅgo. Vibhaṅge hi “tisso itthiyo. Tayo ubhatobyañjanakā. Tayo paṇḍakā. Tayo purisā. Manussitthiyā tayo magge…pe… tiracchānagatapurisassa dve magge”tiādinā (pārā. 56) nayena sabbalesokāsaṃ pidahitvā niyamo kato.

This method should be understood. Herein, the story of Sudinna, the story of the monkey, and the story of the Vajjiputtaka—these three kinds of stories are the origin of this training rule. From that origin, the division of this mātikā has arisen: 'Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus… is not in communion.' Here indeed, because of the feminine word 'even with a female animal,' another, like the one who committed a pārājika with a monkey, is able to raise a pretext, saying: 'Truly, friend, the training rule was laid down by the Blessed One, but that was laid down for a woman, not for a man, not for a eunuch, not for a hermaphrodite.' Therefore, this is stated to show that there is no opportunity for such a pretext. From the origin known as the Makkāṭivatthu, the distinction in the mātikā wording, 'even with a female animal,' was not made solely on account of seeing the accomplishment of the sexual act with a female. Therefore, the Analysis is its determinant; the Analysis is the determinant of the intended meaning of that mātikā. For in the Analysis, by the method beginning with, 'Three kinds of women, three kinds of hermaphrodites, three kinds of eunuchs, three kinds of men. For a human woman, three passages… for a male animal, two passages,' having closed all loopholes, a definitive rule is established.

Etthāha – yadi evaṃ sādhāraṇasikkhāpadavasena vā liṅgaparivattanavasena vā na kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, bhikkhunīnampi “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti vibhaṅge vattabbaṃ siyā. Tadavacanena bhikkhunī purisaliṅgapātubhāvena bhikkhubhāve ṭhitā evaṃ vadeyya “nāhaṃ upasampadakāle bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannā, tasmā na appaccakkhātasikkhāpi methunadhammena pārājikā homī”ti? Vuccate – tathā na vattabbaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Bhikkhunīnampi “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti vutte bhikkhunīnampi sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ atthīti āpajjati, tañcāniṭṭhaṃ. Idaṃ aparaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgoti “sabbasikkhāpadāni sādhāraṇāneva, nāsādhāraṇānī”ti. Apicāyaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannovāti dassanatthaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, taṃyeva upajjha”ntiādi (pārā. 69) vuttaṃ, apica yo tathā lesaṃ oḍḍetvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto vajjiputtakā viya pārājiko hoti. Te hi “bhikkhūnaṃ [V 0.0072] sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti vacanābhāve sati “āpattiṃ tumhe, bhikkhave, āpannā pārājika”nti vuttā bhagavatā. Ettha pana “bhikkhave”ti vuttattā keci bhikkhuliṅge ṭhitā, “idāni cepi mayaṃ, bhante ānanda, labheyyāma bhagavato santike [M 0.0079] pabbajjaṃ labheyyāma upasampada”nti vuttattā keci vibbhantāti veditabbā. Tato āpattiyā bhedoti tato vibhaṅgato “akkhāyite sarīre pārājikaṃ, yebhuyyena khāyite thullaccaya”ntiādi āpattiyā bhedo hoti. Anāpatti tadaññathāti tato eva vibhaṅgato yenākārena āpatti vuttā, tato aññenākārena anāpattibhedova hoti. “Sādiyati āpatti pārājikassa, na sādiyati anāpattī”ti hi vibhaṅge asati na paññāyati. Ettāvatā samāsato gāthāttho vutto hoti. Ettha ca pana –

Here, the questioner says: If it were so, either by way of a common training rule or by way of gender transformation, it should be stated in the Vibhaṅga not only for bhikkhus but also for bhikkhunīs that they are "one who has undertaken the training and livelihood." Due to that not being stated, might a bhikkhunī, being established in the state of a bhikkhu through the manifestation of the male organ, say thus: "At the time of my ordination, I did not undertake the training and livelihood of bhikkhus; therefore, even without having renounced the training, I do not become one who has committed a pārājika offense through sexual intercourse"?

It is said: It should not be stated thus, because of the undesirable implication. If it were said for bhikkhunīs also, "one who has undertaken the training and livelihood," it would imply that for bhikkhunīs also there is the renunciation of the training, and that is undesirable. This is another undesirable implication: "All training rules are common only; there are no uncommon ones."

Moreover, to show that this one has indeed undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus, it was said, "I allow, O bhikkhus, that same preceptor," and so on. Furthermore, whoever, having raised a pretext in that way, engages in sexual intercourse, becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense, like the Vajjiputtakas. For they, while there was an absence of the statement "one who has undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus," were told by the Blessed One, "You, O bhikkhus, have committed a pārājika offense."

But here, because it was said "O bhikkhus," it should be understood that some were established in the state of a bhikkhu; and because it was said, "If now, venerable Ānanda, we might receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, might receive the full ordination," it should be understood that some had disrobed.

Then, regarding "the distinction of the offense": from that Vibhaṅga, the distinction of the offense arises, such as, "in a body not eaten by animals, it is a pārājika offense; in a body mostly eaten, it is a thullaccaya offense," and so on.

Regarding "no offense otherwise": from that very Vibhaṅga, in whatever manner an offense is stated, in a manner other than that, there is indeed a distinction of no-offense. For, if the Vibhaṅga were absent, it would not be discerned that "Consenting, there is a pārājika offense; not consenting, there is no offense."

By this much, the meaning of the verse has been stated in brief. And here, moreover—

“Nidānamātikābhedo, vibhaṅgassa payojanaṃ;

Anāpattipakāro ca, paṭhamo nippayojano”ti. –

The division of the origin story and the matrix, the purpose of the analysis, and the section on non-offenses; the first is without purpose.

Imaṃ nayaṃ dassetvāva sabbasikkhāpadānaṃ attho pakāsitabbo. Kathaṃ? Bhagavatā pana yenākārena yaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpitaṃ, tassa ākārassa samatthaṃ vā asamatthaṃ vāti duvidhaṃ nidānaṃ, ayaṃ nidānabhedo. Mātikāpi nidānāpekkhā nidānānapekkhāti duvidhā. Tattha catutthapārājikādisikkhāpadāni nidānāpekkhāni. Na hi vaggumudātīriyā bhikkhū sayameva attano attano asantaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ musāvādalakkhaṇaṃ pāpetvā bhāsiṃsu. Aññamaññassa hi te uttarimanussadhammassa gihīnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsiṃsu, na ca tāvatā pārājikavatthu hoti. Tattha tena lesena bhagavā taṃ vatthuṃ nidānaṃ katvā pārājikaṃ paññapesi, tena vuttaṃ “nidānāpekkha”nti. Iminā nayena nidānāpekkhāni ñatvā tabbiparītāni sikkhāpadāni nidānānapekkhānīti veditabbāni, ayaṃ mātikābhedo.

Having shown this method, the meaning of all the training rules should be explained. How? In whatever manner a training rule was laid down by the Blessed One, the origin story of that manner is twofold: complete or incomplete. This is the division of the origin story. The matrix is also twofold: dependent on the origin story or not dependent on the origin story. Herein, the training rules such as the fourth Pārājika are dependent on the origin story. For the monks on the bank of the Vaggumudā did not, of their own accord, speak by falsely claiming a superhuman state that they did not possess, which is characteristic of false speech. Rather, they spoke in praise of each other's superhuman state to householders, and merely by that, the ground for a Pārājika offense does not arise. There, on that pretext, the Blessed One, having made that matter the origin story, laid down the Pārājika. Therefore, it is said to be 'dependent on the origin story.' By this method, having known the training rules that are dependent on the origin story, the rules opposite to them should be understood as not dependent on the origin story. This is the division of the matrix.

Nānappakārato mūlāpattippahonakavatthupayogacittaniyāmadassanavasena mātikāya vibhajanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ tesaṃ appahonakatāya vā tadaññataravekallatāya vā vītikkame sati āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ, asati anāpattidassanatthañcāti sabbattha tayo atthavase paṭicca mātikāya vibhajanaṃ vibhaṅgo ārabhīyatīti veditabbo. Ettha pana “bhikkhakoti bhikkhu, bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti [V 0.0073] bhikkhu, bhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhū”ti kevalaṃ byañjanatthadīpanavasena pavatto vā, “samaññāya bhikkhū”ti bhikkhubhāvasambhavaṃ anapekkhitvāpi kevalaṃ bhikkhu nāma pavattiṭṭhānadīpanavasena pavatto vā, “ehi bhikkhūti bhikkhu, saraṇagamanehi upasampannoti bhikkhu, ñatticatutthena kammena upasampannoti bhikkhū”ti upasampadānantarenāpi bhikkhubhāvasiddhidīpanavasena [M 0.0080] pavatto vā, “bhadro bhikkhu, sāro bhikkhu, sekkho bhikkhu, asekkho bhikkhū”ti bhikkhukaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgatabhikkhudīpanavasena pavatto vā vibhaṅgo ajjhupekkhito sabbasāmaññapadattā, tathā aññabhāgiyasikkhāpadādīsu sadvāravasena, adhikaraṇadassanādivasena pavatto ca ajjhupekkhito itarattha tadabhāvatoti veditabbo.

It should be understood that in all training rules, the Vibhaṅga is undertaken depending on three purposes: to show, in various ways, the nature of the division of the mātikā by way of showing the object, effort, and mind sufficient for a root offense; to show the types of offenses when there is a transgression due to their insufficiency or a deficiency in one or another of them; and to show non-offense when there is no transgression. Here, however, the Vibhaṅga is overlooked when it proceeds merely by way of showing the meaning of the words, such as: ‘A bhikkhu is a beggar... a bhikkhu is one who wears a torn-cloth robe’; or when it proceeds merely by way of showing the basis for the occurrence of the name ‘bhikkhu’ even without considering the possibility of the state of a bhikkhu, such as: ‘Bhikkhus by designation’; or when it proceeds by way of showing the accomplishment of the state of a bhikkhu immediately upon higher ordination, such as: ‘A bhikkhu is one who is told, “Come, bhikkhu,”... a bhikkhu is one who is fully ordained by a formal act with a motion and three announcements’; or when it proceeds by way of showing a bhikkhu who is endowed with the qualities that make one a bhikkhu, such as: ‘A virtuous bhikkhu... a non-trainee bhikkhu’. This is because it is a term common to all training rules. Likewise, in the Aññabhāgiya training rules and so on, that which proceeds by way of their own doors, by way of showing legal cases, and so on, is also overlooked, because in other training rules, such a Vibhaṅga does not exist. Thus it should be understood.

Tattha tisso itthiyotiādi vatthuniyamadassanavasena pavatto, manussitthiyā tayo magge methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantassa āpatti pārājikassātiādi payoganiyamadassanavasena pavatto, bhikkhussa sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhitetiādi cittaniyamadassanavasena pavatto, sādiyati āpatti pārājikassa, na sādiyati anāpattītiādi vatthupayoganiyame sati cittaniyamabhāvābhāvavasena āpattānāpattidassanatthaṃ pavatto, mataṃ yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ āpatti thullaccayassātiādi vatthussa appahonakatāya vītikkame āpattibhedadassanatthaṃ pavatto, na sādiyati anāpattīti cittaniyamavekalyena vītikkamābhāvā anāpattidassanatthaṃ pavattoti. Evaṃ itaresupi sikkhāpadesu yathāsambhavanayo ayanti payojano vibhaṅgo.

Therein, the passage beginning 'three women' is set forth by way of showing the determination of the object. The passage beginning 'for one engaging in sexual intercourse in the three passages of a human woman, there is an offense of pārājika' is set forth by way of showing the determination of the effort. The passage beginning 'when a bhikkhu's mind for engaging arises' is set forth by way of showing the determination of the mind. The passage beginning 'if he consents, it is an offense of pārājika; if he does not consent, there is no offense' is set forth to show offense and no-offense by way of the presence or absence of the determination of the mind when the determination of the object and effort exist. The passage beginning 'a corpse mostly eaten... it is an offense of thullaccaya' is set forth to show the distinction of offenses in a transgression due to the object's insufficiency. The passage 'if he does not consent, there is no offense' is set forth to show no-offense because of the absence of transgression due to a deficiency in the determination of the mind. In this way, this method is to be understood as is appropriate in the other training rules as well. Thus, the purpose of the Vibhaṅga is to be seen.

Anāpattivāro pana mūlāpattito, tadaññekadesato, sabbāpattito ca anāpattidīpanavasena tividho. Tattha yo paṭhamo, so vibhaṅgo viya tayo atthavase paṭicca pavatto. Katame tayo? Mātikāpadānaṃ sātthakaniratthakānaṃ tadaññathā uddharaṇānuddharaṇavasena sappayojananippayojanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ, tadaññathā paṭipattikkamadassanatthaṃ, āpattippahonakaṭṭhānepi vissajjanatthañcāti. Kathaṃ? Eḷakalomasikkhāpade “bhikkhuno paneva addhānamaggappaṭipannassa eḷakalomāni uppajjeyyuṃ, ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbānī”ti (pārā. 572) etāni kevalaṃ vatthumattadīpanapadānīti niratthakāni nāma, tesaṃ anāpatti. “Addhānamaggaṃ appaṭipannassa uppanne eḷakalome anāpatti, ākaṅkhamānena paṭiggahite”tiādinā nayena tadaññathā anuddharaṇena nippayojanabhāvo dīpito hoti, yadidaṃ mātikāyaṃ “methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”ti, idaṃ sātthakaṃ. Tassa [M 0.0081] sappayojanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ “anāpatti ajānantassa asādiyantassā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā jānanasādiyanabhāvena āpatti, asevantassa anāpatti, tasmā vuttaṃ mātikāyaṃ “yo pana bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyya, pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti [V 0.0074] adhippāyo. “Parapariggahitaṃ parapariggahitasaññitā garuparikkhāro theyyacittaṃ avaharaṇa”nti vuttānaṃ pañcannampi aṅgānaṃ pāripūriyā petatiracchānagatapariggahite āpattippahonakaṭṭhānepi vissajjanatthaṃ “anāpatti petapariggahite”tiādi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Anāpatti imaṃ jāna, imaṃ dehi, imaṃ āhara, iminā attho, imaṃ kappiyaṃ karohīti bhaṇatītiādi pana tadaññathā paṭipattikkamadassanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā “nidānamātikābhedo”tiādinā vuttagāthāya attho pakāsito hoti.

The section on non-offenses, however, is threefold by way of explaining non-offenses: from the root offense, from a portion other than that, and from all offenses. Among these, the first, like the Vibhaṅga, has proceeded depending on three purposes. What are the three? For the purpose of showing the meaningfulness and meaninglessness of the mātikā-terms by way of citation and non-citation in a different manner; for the purpose of showing the sequence of practice in a different manner; and for absolution even in a situation sufficient for an offense. How so? In the training rule concerning sheep's wool, the words: 'If sheep's wool should arise for a bhikkhu who has entered upon a long road, it is to be accepted by the bhikkhu if he is desirous.' These terms merely show the subject matter and are thus called meaningless; for them, there is no offense. By the method beginning with, 'For one who has not entered upon a long road, if sheep's wool arises, there is no offense; if it is accepted by one who is desirous,' by not citing it in a different manner, its purposelessness is shown. As for the statement in the mātikā, 'should engage in the act of sexual intercourse,' this is meaningful. For the purpose of showing its purposefulness, it was said: 'There is no offense for one who is unknowing, for one who is not consenting.' Because there is an offense through the state of knowing and consenting, and no offense for one who does not engage, it was therefore said in the mātikā: 'Whatever bhikkhu should engage in the act of sexual intercourse, he is defeated, not in communion.' This is the intention. For the five factors stated—'possessed by another,' 'the perception of it as possessed by another,' 'a heavy requisite,' 'a thievish intention,' and 'removal'—for the purpose of absolution even in a situation sufficient for an offense regarding what is possessed by a departed one or an animal, it is said: 'There is no offense regarding what is possessed by a departed one,' and so on. However, 'There is no offense for one who says, “Know this, give this, bring this, there is a need for this, make this allowable,”' and so on, should be understood as having been said for the purpose of showing the sequence of practice in a different manner. By this much, the meaning of the verse stated, beginning with 'The distinction of the introduction and the mātikā,' has been explained.

Ettha paṭhamapaññatti tāva paṭhamabodhiṃ atikkamitvā paññattattā, āyasmato sudinnassa aṭṭhavassikakāle paññattattā ca rattaññumahattaṃ pattakāle paññattā. Dutiyaanupaññatti bāhusaccamahattaṃ pattakāle uppannā. So hāyasmā makkaṭipārājiko yathā mātugāmapaṭisaṃyuttesu sikkhāpadesu tiracchānagatitthī anadhippetā, tathā idhāpīti saññāya “saccaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, tañca kho manussitthiyā, no tiracchānagatitthiyā”ti āha. Tatiyānupaññatti lābhaggamahattaṃ pattakāle uppannā. Te hi vajjiputtakā lābhaggamahattaṃ pattā hutvā yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā nhāyitvā varasayanesu sayitvā tatiyānupaññattiyā vatthuṃ uppādesuṃ, te ca vepullamahattaṃ patte saṅghe uppannā, sayañca vepullamahattaṃ pattāti “vepullamahattampettha labbhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Idaṃ paṭhamapārājikasikkhāpadaṃ tividhampi vatthuṃ upādāya catubbidhampi taṃ kālaṃ patvā paññattanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the first enactment was laid down at the time of reaching the greatness of seniority, because it was enacted after the first enlightenment had been passed and because it was enacted when the Venerable Sudinna was of eight years' standing. The second supplementary enactment arose when the greatness of great learning was reached. That venerable one who committed a pārājika offense with a monkey, with the thought, 'Just as in the training rules connected with women a female animal is not intended, so too here she is not intended,' said, 'Indeed, friend, a training rule was enacted by the Blessed One, and that was for a human woman, not for a female animal.' The third supplementary enactment arose when the greatness of the highest gain was reached. For those Vajjian monks, having reached the greatness of the highest gain, and having eaten to their heart's content, bathed, and slept on excellent beds, gave rise to the basis for the third supplementary enactment. And they arose in a Saṅgha that had reached a state of abundance, and they themselves had reached a state of abundance. Therefore, it was said: 'Herein, the greatness of abundance is also obtained.' This first Pārājika training rule should be understood as having been enacted based upon three kinds of incidents and having reached those four kinds of times.

Tattha yo panāti anavasesapariyādānapadaṃ. Bhikkhūti tassa atippasaṅganiyamapadaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannoti tassa visesanavacanaṃ. Na hi sabbopi bhikkhunāmako yā bhagavatā yāya kāyaci upasampadāya upasampannabhikkhūnaṃ heṭṭhimaparicchedena sikkhitabbasikkhā vihitā, “ettha saha jīvantī”ti yo ca ājīvo vutto, taṃ ubhayaṃ samāpannova hoti. Kadā pana samāpanno ahosi? Yāya kāyaci upasampadāya upasampannasamanantarameva [M 0.0082] tadubhayaṃ jānantopi ajānantopi tadajjhupagatattā samāpanno nāma hoti. Saha jīvantīti yāva sikkhaṃ na paccakkhāti, pārājikabhāvañca na pāpuṇāti, yaṃ pana vuttaṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhāsamāpanno sājīvaṃ avītikkamanto sājīvasamāpanno hotī”ti, taṃ ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena vuttaṃ. Na hi sikkhaṃ aparipūrento kāmavitakkādibahulo vā ekaccaṃ sāvasesaṃ sājīvaṃ vītikkamanto vā sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno nāma na hoti. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena pana catukkaṃ labbhati atthi bhikkhu sikkhāsamāpanno sīlāni paccavekkhanto na sājīvasamāpanno acittakaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamanto, atthi na sikkhāsamāpanno [V 0.0075] kāmavitakkādibahulo sājīvasamāpanno nirāpattiko, atthi na sikkhāsamāpanno na ca sājīvasamāpanno anavasesaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, atthi sikkhāsamāpanno ca sājīvasamāpanno ca sikkhaṃ paripūrento sājīvañca avītikkamanto, ayameva catuttho bhikkhu ukkaṭṭho idha adhippeto siyā. Na hi bhagavā anukkaṭṭhaṃ vattuṃ yuttoti ce? Na, “tatra yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”tivacanavirodhato. Ukkaṭṭhaggahaṇādhippāye sati “sikkhāti tisso sikkhā”ti ettakameva vattabbanti adhippāyo. Sikkhattayasamāpanno hi sabbukkaṭṭhoti.

Herein, 'whoever' is a term that includes everything without exception. 'Bhikkhu' is a term that restricts that over-extension. 'One who has undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus' is a qualifying term for that. For not every person merely called a bhikkhu is one who has undertaken both the training that should be learned, prescribed by the Blessed One for bhikkhus ordained by any kind of ordination according to the lowest limit, and the livelihood that was spoken of as 'they live together herein'. But when did one become one who has undertaken it? Immediately upon being ordained by any kind of ordination, whether knowing or not knowing, by virtue of having accepted it, one is said to be one who has undertaken both. One lives together with this training and livelihood for as long as one does not renounce the training and does not reach the state of pārājika. As for what is stated in the Andhaka Commentary, 'one who fulfills the training is one who has undertaken the training, and one who does not transgress the livelihood is one who has undertaken the livelihood' — this was said by way of the highest standard. For it is not the case that one who does not fulfill the training, or who is abundant in sensual thoughts, or who transgresses some part of the livelihood that has a remainder, is not one who has undertaken the training and livelihood. But according to the highest standard, a fourfold distinction is found: there is a bhikkhu who has undertaken the training, reflecting on the precepts, but has not undertaken the livelihood, transgressing a training rule unintentionally; there is one who has not undertaken the training, being abundant in sensual thoughts, but has undertaken the livelihood, being without offense; there is one who has neither undertaken the training nor the livelihood, having incurred an offense without remainder; and there is one who has both undertaken the training and the livelihood, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood. This fourth bhikkhu, the highest, might be intended here. If it is said, 'For it is not fitting for the Blessed One to speak of what is not the highest,' the reply is no, because of the contradiction with the statement, 'Herein, that which is the training in higher virtue, this is the training intended in this context.' If the intention were to take the highest, the meaning is that only this much should be said: 'Training means the three trainings.' For one who has undertaken the threefold training is the highest of all.

“Methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”ti parato vacanaṃ apekkhitvā adhisīlasikkhāva vuttāti ce? Na, tassāpi abhabbattā. Na hi adhisīlasikkhaṃ paripūrento sājīvañca avītikkamanto methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevituṃ bhabbo, taṃ sikkhaṃ aparipūrento sājīvañca vītikkamanto eva hi paṭiseveyyāti adhippāyo, tasmā evamettha attho gahetabbo. Yasmā sikkhāpadasaṅkhāto sājīvo adhisīlasikkhameva saṅgaṇhāti, netaraṃ adhicittasikkhaṃ adhipaññāsikkhaṃ vā, tasmā “tatra yāyaṃ adhisīlasikkhā, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā adhisīlasikkhāya saṅgāhako sājīvo sikkhāsājīvoti vutto. Iti sājīvavisesanatthaṃ sikkhāggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthameva vibhaṅge sikkhaṃ aparāmasitvā “tasmiṃ sikkhati, tena vuccati sājīvasamāpanno”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0083], tena ekamevidaṃ atthapadanti dīpitaṃ hoti. Tañca upasampadūpagamanantarato paṭṭhāya sikkhanādhikārattā “sikkhatī”ti ca “samāpanno”ti ca vuccati. Yo evaṃ “sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti saṅkhyaṃ gato, tādisaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca aparabhāge sājīvasaṅkhātameva sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya, tasmiṃyeva ca dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyāti ayamattho yujjati. Kintu aṭṭhakathānayo paṭikkhitto hoti. So ca na paṭikkhepārahoti tena tadanusārena bhavitabbaṃ.

If it were said that only the training in higher virtue is meant, in consideration of the subsequent statement, 'he should engage in sexual intercourse'? That should not be said, for that too is impossible for him. For one who is fulfilling the training in higher virtue and not transgressing the livelihood is not able to engage in sexual intercourse. Indeed, only one who is not fulfilling that training and is transgressing the livelihood would engage in it; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus. Because the livelihood, designated as the training rule, includes only the training in higher virtue—not the other, the training in higher mind or the training in higher wisdom—it is therefore said: 'Therein, that which is the training in higher virtue, this is the training intended in this context.' Therefore, the livelihood that includes the training in higher virtue is called 'training-livelihood'. Thus, the taking up of the word 'training' is done to specify the livelihood. For the very purpose of clarifying that meaning, it is said in the Vibhaṅga, without referring to 'training': 'He trains in that, therefore he is called one who has undertaken the livelihood.' By that, it is shown that this is a single term of meaning. And that, starting from immediately after attaining full ordination, is called 'he trains' and 'he has undertaken' because of the authorization to train. This meaning is suitable: that one who has thus come to be designated as 'one who has undertaken the training and livelihood,' having depended on such a condition, might subsequently, without renouncing the training itself designated as livelihood, and without revealing weakness in it, engage in sexual intercourse. However, the commentarial method is thereby rejected. And that is not worthy of rejection; therefore, one should proceed in accordance with it.

Adhippāyo panettha pariyesitabbo, so dāni vuccati – sabbesupi sikkhāpadesu idameva bhikkhulakkhaṇaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, yadidaṃ “bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno”ti. Khīṇāsavopi sāvako āpattiṃ āpajjati acittakaṃ, tathā sekkho. Puthujjano pana sacittakampi, tasmā sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanabhikkhūnaṃ sāmaññamidaṃ bhikkhulakkhaṇanti katvā kevalaṃ sikkhāsamāpanno, kevalaṃ sājīvasamāpanno ca ubhayasamāpanno cāti sarūpekadesekasesanayena “sikkhāsājīvasamaāpanno”tveva sampiṇḍetvā ukkaṭṭhaggahaṇena anukkaṭṭhānaṃ gahaṇasiddhito aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ukkaṭṭhova vutto. Tameva sampādetuṃ “tasmiṃ sikkhati, tena vuccati sājīvasamāpanno”ti ettha sikkhāpadassa [V 0.0076] avacane parihāraṃ vatvā yasmā pana so asikkhampi samāpanno, tasmā sikkhāsamāpannotipi atthato veditabboti ca vatvā “yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno taṃ appaccakkhāya yañca sājīvaṃ samāpanno tattha dubbalyaṃ anāvikatvā”ti vuttanti ayamaṭṭhakathāyaṃ adhippāyo veditabbo. Etasmiṃ pana adhippāye adhisīlasikkhāya eva gahaṇaṃ sabbatthikattā, sīlādhikārato ca vinayassāti veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyanto sīlaṃ samādiyatīti vuccati, evaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paccakkhanto sīlasaṅkhātaṃ sikkhaṃ paccakkhātīti vattuṃ yujjati, tasmā tattha vuttaṃ “yaṃ sikkhaṃ samāpanno, taṃ appaccakkhāyā”ti. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya paṭisevitamethunassa upasampadaṃ anujānanto na samūhanati nāma. Na hi so bhikkhu hutvā paṭisevi, “yo pana bhikkhū”ti ca paññattaṃ. Ettāvatā samāsato “sikkhāsājīvasamānno”ti ettha vattabbaṃ vuttaṃ.

The intention here should be sought, and it is now stated: In all the training rules, this is the common characteristic of a bhikkhu, namely, 'one who has undertaken the training and livelihood of bhikkhus.' Even a disciple whose cankers are destroyed incurs an unintentional offense, as does a trainee. An ordinary person, however, incurs even an intentional one. Therefore, having considered this to be the common characteristic of bhikkhus—trainees, non-trainees, and ordinary persons—and having summarized 'one who has undertaken merely the training,' 'one who has undertaken merely the livelihood,' and 'one who has undertaken both' into just 'one who has undertaken the training and livelihood' by the method of elliptical compounding, because the inclusion of the lesser cases is established by taking the highest case, only the highest case is mentioned in the commentary. To establish that very meaning, having stated the explanation for the non-mention of the training rule in the passage 'He trains in that, therefore he is called one who has undertaken the livelihood,' and having said, 'And since that person has also undertaken the training, therefore he should also be understood in meaning as "one who has undertaken the training,"' and having said, 'Whatever training he has undertaken, without having rejected that, and whatever livelihood he has undertaken, without having revealed weakness therein'—this is the intention in the commentary that should be understood. In this intention, however, it should be understood that the taking is of the training in higher virtue itself, because of its relevance in all cases and because the Vinaya has virtue as its domain.
