Naṭṭhakāyappasādanti ettha upahatindriyassa āpattisambhavato idhāpi āpattīti ce? Neti dassanatthaṃ “matacammaṃ vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Matacammañhi anupādinnaṃ, upādinne eva pārājikāpatti. Apidhāya appaṭicchādetvā. Yathā dantā na dissanti, tathā pidhāyeva nisīditabbanti adhippāyo.

55. The word 'Paṭisevatināmā' is not in the mātikā; therefore, he said, 'in the case of paṭiseveyya,' and so forth. The phrase 'Eso methunadhammo nāmā' is in all the Pāḷi books; in the commentary, 'eso vuccati methunadhammo nāmā' is cited. The connection, 'one's own organ by means of a woman's organ,' being difficult to understand, was shown by the commentator. The connection, 'a woman's organ by means of one's own organ,' was not shown because it is easy to understand. In 'having left the four places,' this refers to touching the inner surface; for one who withdraws without touching, there is no offense. 'Middle' means the tip. 'Upper middle' means the tip of the upper part. Concerning 'Naṭṭhakāyappasāda,' if one should say that an offense occurs here too, since an offense is possible for one with impaired faculties, in order to show this is not so, 'or a dead hide,' etc., was said. Indeed, a dead hide is non-appropriated, and the pārājika offense applies only to what is appropriated. `Apidhāya` means not having covered. The intention is that one should sit only having covered the mouth in such a way that the teeth are not seen.

Gonasoti goṇapiṭṭhiko maṇḍalasappo, yassa piṭṭhe lohitakāni maṇḍalāni dissanti. Kalalaparicayavāricāramacchaggahaṇena kiñcāpi samudde mahāmukhā hatthisarīrampi ekappahārena gilituṃ samatthā tato mahantatarā ca gahitā honti, tesaṃ mukhādīsu methunadhammo na sambhavatīti tattha ṭhānaparicchedo natthīti eke, vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. Etameva hīti anantaraṃ sandhāya. Saddhiṃ yojanāya akkharayojanāya. “Paññattaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato samasikkhatā nāmāti vuttattā sabbasikkhāpadaṃ sabbabhikkhūhi sikkhitabbaṃ. Na hi kassaci ūnamadhikaṃ vā atthī”ti tassa gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Parivāre pana –

A 'gonasa' is a snake with a variegated back, a snake with circular markings, on whose back red circles are seen. By the inclusion of the term 'fish', which refers to those accustomed to mud and those that move in water: although in the ocean there are large-mouthed creatures able to swallow even an elephant's body in one gulp and to seize even larger creatures, the act of sexual intercourse is not possible in their mouths and so on. Thus, some say that in their case there is no determination of a location; this should be accepted after investigation. The phrase 'Etameva hi' was said with reference to the immediately following verse. It is an explanation together with the grammatical construction and the construction of the letters. 'Because it is said, "The training rule that has been laid down... is called equal training because it must be trained in equally by all conscientious persons," all training rules must be trained in by all monks. For there is neither less nor more for anyone.' Thus it is said in his Ganthipada. But in the Parivāra—

“Na ukkhittako na ca pana pārivāsiko,

Na saṅghabhinno na ca pana pakkhasaṅkanto;

Samānasaṃvāsakabhūmiyā ṭhito,

Kathaṃ nu sikkhāya asādhāraṇo siyā”ti. (pari. 479) –

He is not one suspended, nor one on probation; he has not split the Saṅgha, nor has he gone over to another faction. Established on the ground of common communion, how then could he be not common to the training?

Vuttaṃ. Tadaṭṭhakathāya ca “ayaṃ pañhā nahāpitapubbakaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Ayañhi khurabhaṇḍaṃ pariharituṃ na labhati, aññe labhanti. Tasmā sikkhāya asādhāraṇo”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ yathā saṃsandati sameti, tathā veditabbaṃ[M 0.0101]. Bhikkhunīnaṃyeva sādhāraṇāni sikkhāpadānipi bhikkhu sikkhati, evamaññopi anhāpitapubbako bhikkhu taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ sikkhati eva tadatthakosallatthanti [V 0.0091] katvā sabbampi sikkhāpadaṃ samasikkhatā nāmāti. Yaṃ taṃ vuttanti sambandho. “Tisso itthiyo”tiādivibhaṅgotaṃniyāmakotilakkhaṇattā vatthuniyamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena amanussitthippasaṅgena kate suvaṇṇarajatādimaye paṭikkhipati. Ito paṭṭhāya ye ca “tayo atthavase paṭicca vibhaṅgo pavattatī”ti pubbe vuttā, te yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā veditabbā.

It is said. And in its commentary it is said: “This question was stated with reference to one who was formerly a barber. For he is not allowed to carry barber's equipment, while others are allowed. Therefore, it is said, ‘he is not common to the training.’” All that should be understood as it connects and accords. Even the training rules common only to nuns are trained in by a bhikkhu; likewise, another bhikkhu who was not formerly a barber also certainly trains in that training rule for the sake of skill in its meaning. Having considered this, all the training rules are called ‘equal training.’ The connection should be made with what was said. The analysis beginning with “Three women,” etc., is stated for the purpose of defining the subject matter, as it has the characteristic of being a definition. By this, it rejects images made of gold, silver, and so on, that are made in the context of a non-human woman. From here onward, those three grounds on account of which the analysis proceeds, which were previously stated, should be understood by applying them as appropriate.

Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse of the First Tetrad

57. Āpatti pārājikā assa hotīti ettha yasmā sā akusalā āpatti tassa bhikkhuno sīlasambhavaṃ abhibhavati, rāgābhibhave tasmiṃ pārājikāti laddhanāmā pubbabhāge āpannā dukkaṭathullaccayādayo āpattiyo abhibhavitvā vināsetvā sayamevekā assa. Vatthunā sabhāgāhi vā asabhāgāhi vā aññāhi pārājikattena samānajātikāhi āpattīhi sayaṃ nābhibhavīyatīti eke. Taṃ taṃ pubbe vicāritameva. Yadā pana catassopi pārājikāpattiyo ekato honti, tadā tā tassa bhikkhuno bhikkhubhāvaṃ abhibhavanti, abhikkhuṃ karonti, anupasampannaṃ karonti, samaññāyapi bhikkhu na hoti. Omasavādapācittiyaṃ na janetīti eke. Dutiyena atthavikappena pārājikassa dhammassa patti sampatti āpattīti attho saṅgahito hotīti katvā āpattisampattivādīnaṃ saṅgahito hoti, yujjati cesā parasāpekkhā. Sāpattiko nāma so bhikkhu hoti, aññathā tassa khaṇabhaṅgena anāpattiko bhaveyya, na ca hotīti. Kadā pana hotīti? Yadā kālaṃ karoti, yadā ca sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya sāmaṇerādibhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhati. Yadi evaṃ sikkhāya paccakkhātāya pārājikāpatti paccakkhātā hoti sikkhā cāti ubhayaṃ tassa ekato atthi, saṅghādisesādiāpatti sikkhāpaccakkhānena kiṃ na paccakkhātā, puna upasampannena desāpetabbā. Sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ jātaṃ, abhikkhu āpattito vuṭṭhāti, gahaṭṭho vuṭṭhāti, sāmaṇero vuṭṭhāti, tato [M 0.0102] vinayavirodhā na vuṭṭhāti. Hañci pana vuṭṭhāti gahaṭṭho, sāmaṇero vā sīlasampannova jhānalābhī assa, sotāpattiphalassa vā arahattaphalassa vā lābhī assa, pārājikāpattiyā sāpattiko arahā assa. Ukkhittako uppabbajito vā parivāsāraho mānattāraho uppabbajito vā sīlasampanno jhānalābhī assa, sotāpattiphalassa, arahattaphalassa vā lābhī assa, sāpattiko santarāyiko arahā assa, so puna upasampanno parivāsaṃ, mānattaṃ vā datvā abbhetabbo ukkhittako osāretabboti samāno ayaṃ upalabbhoti.

57. Herein, regarding 'the offense would be a pārājika': because that unwholesome offense destroys that bhikkhu’s state of virtue, and because when that virtue is overcome by lust, it receives the name 'pārājika'; having overcome and destroyed the offenses such as dukkaṭa and thullaccaya incurred in the preliminary stage, it alone would exist. Some say that it itself is not overcome by other offenses of the same kind in meaning as 'pārājika', whether they are similar or dissimilar to the object. That very matter has already been investigated before. But when all four pārājika offenses occur together, they overcome that bhikkhu’s state as a bhikkhu, they make him a non-bhikkhu, they make him unordained, and he is not a bhikkhu even by designation. Some say he does not incur the pācittiya for contemptuous speech. By the second alternative meaning, the meaning 'the reaching, the completion of the pārājika rule is an offense' is included. Therefore, the view of those who hold that one is endowed with the offense is included. And this is suitable, as it is dependent on another term. That bhikkhu is called one who has an offense; otherwise, through momentary destruction, he would become one without an offense, but he is not. But when does he become one without an offense? If it is asked: when he dies, and when, having renounced the training, he remains in the state of a novice and so on. If so, with the renunciation of the training, is the pārājika offense renounced, and the training too? If so, both are present for him at once. Are not the saṅghādisesa and other offenses renounced by renouncing the training? Must they not be confessed again by one who has been reordained? The renunciation of the training has become a rising from the offense. A non-bhikkhu rises from the offense; a layman rises; a novice rises. That rising, being contrary to the Vinaya, is not a rising. But if he does rise, a layman or a novice, being endowed with virtue, could be a recipient of jhāna, or a recipient of the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of arahantship. An Arahant could be one with an offense due to a pārājika offense. A suspended one or one who has disrobed, who is worthy of probation or penance; or one who has disrobed, if he were endowed with virtue, a recipient of jhāna, or a recipient of the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of arahantship, he would be an Arahant who has an offense and an obstacle. If such a one is reordained, having been given probation or penance, he is to be rehabilitated. A suspended one is to be reinstated. This being so, this case is found.

Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo – pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ āpanno yāva bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti sādiyati [V 0.0092] saṃvāsaṃ, santarāyikattā uposathadivasādīsu gahaṭṭhassa viya sayameva sīlaṃ samādiyantassapi na sīlasamādānaṃ ruhati, pageva jhānādīni. So ce bhikkhubhāvaṃ na sādiyati na paṭijānāti saṃvāsaṃ na sādiyati, kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āvikatvā rājavericorādibhayena kāsāvaṃ na pariccajati, anupasampannova hoti sahaseyyādiṃ janeti, sīlassa ca jhānādīnañca bhāgī hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Herein is the determination: A bhikkhu who has committed a pārājika offense, as long as he acknowledges his status as a bhikkhu and approves of communal living, due to the obstacle, even if he himself undertakes the precepts like a householder on observance days and so forth, the undertaking of precepts does not take root, let alone jhānas and so forth. But if he does not acknowledge his status as a bhikkhu and does not approve of communal living, but merely, having disclosed his offense to the bhikkhus, does not discard the saffron robe out of fear of kings, enemies, thieves, and so forth, he is indeed an unordained person and generates offenses such as sharing a bed. And he has a share in virtue and jhānas and so forth. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Āpannena visuddhāpekkhena santī āpatti āvikātabbā, āvikatā hissa phāsu hoti, paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamāyā”tiādi (mahāva. 134-135).

"One who has incurred an offense and desires purity, the existing offense should be disclosed. For when it is disclosed, it is comfortable for him, for the attainment of the first jhāna," and so on (Mahāvagga 134-135).

Tattha santī āpattīti sāvasesānavasesappabhedā sabbāpi āpatti āpannā adhippetā. Evaṃ santepi pageva gahaṭṭhādibhūmiyaṃ ṭhito jhānādīnaṃ bhāgī assa suddhante ṭhitattā, yo pana ukkhittako anosārito, garudhammaṃ vā āpajjitvā avuṭṭhito sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya gahaṭṭhādibhūmiyaṃ ṭhito, na so jhānādīnaṃ bhāgīyeva bhavati na suddhante ṭhitattā, sakaraṇīyattā ca, teneva bhagavatā “so puna upasampanno osāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tassa puggalassa te bhikkhukāle āpannā antarāyikā dhammā vippaṭisāraṃ janayitvā avippaṭisāramūlakānaṃ pāmojjādīnaṃ sambhavaṃ nivārenti, no sakāsāvesuyeva. No ce nivārenti, sambhavati. Garukaṃ āpajjitvā bhikkhūnaṃ āvikatvā ce uppabbajito, pakatatto hutvā [M 0.0103] uppabbajitoti katvā jhānādīnaṃ bhāgī assa “āvikatā hissa phāsu hotī”ti vuttattā. Pageva bhikkhukāle, na tveva ukkhittako sakaraṇīyattāti eke. Tadanuvattanako pana taṃ laddhiṃ pahāya bhāgī assa. Na, bhikkhave, sagahaṭṭhāya parisāya (mahāva. 154) sikkhāpaccakkhātakassa antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannakassa nisinnaparisāyāti (mahāva. 183) ettha gahaṭṭho nāma pakatiyā gihiliṅge ṭhito. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya bhikkhuliṅge ṭhito sikkhāpaccakkhātako. So sakāsāvesu sāpekkhattā sāmaṇerabhāvaṃ patthayamāno teneva liṅgena tīhi saraṇagamanehi sāmaṇero hoti. Antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno saṃvāsaṃ sādiyantopi pacchā pubbe vuttakkamena asādiyitvā sāmaṇerabhāvaṃ patthayamāno sikkhāpaccakkhātako viya tīhi saraṇagamanehi sāmaṇero hoti, na puna kāsāvaṃ paṭiggāhāpetabbo bhikkhūhi paṭhamaṃ dinnaliṅgeyeva ṭhitattā. Yo pana pārājiko codiyamāno parājitvā “handa, bhante, sāmaṇero bhavāmi, saraṇāni dethā”ti vadati, “sādhu gaṇhāhī”ti na vattabbo, gihiliṅge ṭhapetvā puna kāsāyāni paṭiggāhāpetvā pabbājetabbo. “Idaṃ pana sabbaṃ attano matiyā vuttattā vicāretvā gahetabba”nti ācariyo vadati. Pavesanaṃ nāma aṅgajātaṃ pavesentassa aṅgajātena samphusanaṃ. Paviṭṭhaṃ nāma yāva mūlā pavesentassa vippakatakāle vāyāmakālo. Sukkavissaṭṭhisamaye aṅgajātaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāma. Uddharaṇaṃ nāma nīharaṇakālo. Gaṇṭhipade pana “vāyāmato oramitvā ṭhānaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ asaṅkarato dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Pavesanapaviṭṭhauddharaṇakālesupi sukkavissaṭṭhi hotiyeva.

Herein, by 'there are offenses' is meant all offenses that have been incurred, of the kinds with and without a remainder. Even so, one who was previously established on the plane of a householder and so on may be a partaker of jhāna and so on, because of being established in a pure state. But as for one who has been suspended and not rehabilitated, or who, having incurred a grave offense, has not arisen from it, he is not a partaker of jhāna and so on, because of being established in an impure state and because there is something that must be done for him. For this reason the Blessed One has said: 'If he is reordained, he should be rehabilitated.' Therefore, for that person, those obstructive states incurred during his time as a bhikkhu generate remorse and prevent the arising of gladness and so on, which are rooted in non-remorse, but this does not apply to the robes themselves. If they do not prevent it, it is possible for them to arise. If, having committed a grave offense, he disrobes without having disclosed it to the bhikkhus, he may be a partaker of jhāna and so on, on the grounds that he has disrobed as a normal person, because it is said: 'Disclosure brings him ease.' Previously, during his time as a bhikkhu, he is not a partaker if he is suspended, some say, because there is something to be done for him. But one who follows him, having abandoned that view, may be a partaker. In the passages 'Not, bhikkhus, in an assembly that includes a householder...' and '...for one who has renounced the training, for one who has committed a final offense, in a seated assembly', a 'householder' is one who stands in the mark of a layman by nature. One who has renounced the training but stands in the mark of a bhikkhu is a 'renouncer of the training.' He, having attachment to his robes and desiring the state of a novice, becomes a novice in that same mark by taking the three refuges. One who has committed a final offense, even if he consents to communion, if he later does not consent in the way stated before and desires the state of a novice, he becomes a novice by taking the three refuges, just like a renouncer of the training; but he should not be made to receive the saffron robe again by the bhikkhus, since he stands in the mark given to him at first. But one who, being accused of a pārājika offense, is defeated and says, 'Come, venerable sirs, I will become a novice; give me the refuges,' should not be told, 'Good, take them.' He should be established in the mark of a layman, made to receive the saffron robes again, and then be given the going forth. The teacher says: 'But all this is said according to my own opinion; it should be investigated before being accepted.' 'Insertion' is the contact of the sexual organ with another for one who is inserting it. 'Entered' is the period of effort for one who inserts it up to the root, during the time of an incomplete act. At the time of the emission of semen, the sexual organ is said to be 'stationed.' 'Withdrawal' is the time of removal. But in the Gaṇṭhipada it is said: 'Having desisted from the effort, the state is called "stationed."' This is said to show it without confusion. Emission of semen certainly occurs also during the times of insertion, penetration, and withdrawal.

Paṭhamacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the First Tetrad is finished.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Sixty-Nine and Two-Hundred Tetrads

59-60. “Mataṃ yebhuyyena akkhāyita”nti vacanato amataṃ yebhuyyena khāyitampi pārājikavatthumevāti dasseti. Sabbaso khāyitaṃ, uppāṭitaṃ vā thullaccayavatthumevāti dasseti, tathā “yebhuyyena khāyita”nti [M 0.0104] vacanato mataṃ sabbakhāyitaṃ, uppāṭitaṃ vā dukkaṭavatthūti dasseti. Na ca sāvasesaṃ paññapenti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Idañhi sikkhāpadaṃ lokavajjaṃ, na paṇṇattivajjaṃ. Tattha sikkhāpadanti pārājikaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tattha thullaccayampi hi lokavajjaṃ, na paṇṇattivajjaṃ. Atha vā ubhayampi anavasesaṃ paññattaṃ. Pārājikakhette hi heṭṭhimakoṭiṃ pāpetvā ṭhapite tato paraṃ thullaccayanti paññattameva hoti. Tattha thullaccayakhettampi pārājikakhettaṃ viya heṭṭhimaparicchedena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Upaḍḍhakkhāyite thullaccayanti yattha nimittaṃ khāyitaṃ, taṃ dukkaṭavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Etthāha – paṇṇattivajjaṃ kiṃ sāvasesameva bhagavā paññāpetīti? Na. Ekaṃsato pana yathāsambhavaṃ tattha tattha pakāsayissāma, kimatthaṃ pana bhagavā upaḍḍhakkhāyite pārājikaṃ na paññāpesīti ayaṃ tāva apucchā buddhavisayattā vinayapaññattiyā. Idaṃ panettha kāraṇapatirūpakaṃ “upaḍḍhabhāvassa dubbinicchayattā”ti. Yebhuyyena khāyitaṃ nāma vaccamaggapassāvamaggamukhānaṃ catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāse atikkamma yāva tatiyakoṭṭhāsapariyosānā khāditaṃ, tatiyakoṭṭhāsaṃ atikkamma yāva catutthakoṭṭhāsapariyosānā dukkaṭavatthu.

59-60. Based on the statement, 'The dead part is mostly not eaten,' it shows that even if the living part is mostly consumed, it is a case entailing expulsion. It shows that if it is entirely consumed or torn out, it is a case entailing a grave offense. Similarly, based on the statement 'mostly consumed,' it shows that if the dead part is entirely consumed or torn out, it is a case entailing a wrong-doing. And they do not prescribe with a remainder. For what reason? For this training rule is a worldly blame, not a prescribed blame. Therein, by 'training rule,' expulsion is intended. Therein, a grave offense is also indeed a worldly blame, not a prescribed blame. Alternatively, both are prescribed without remainder. For in the field of expulsion, once the lower limit has been reached and established, what is beyond that is prescribed as a grave offense. Therein, it should be understood that the field of a grave offense is also described with a lower boundary, like the field of expulsion. Regarding 'a grave offense for what is half-consumed': where the mark is consumed, that should be understood as a case of wrong-doing. Here one says: 'Does the Blessed One prescribe a prescribed blame only with a remainder?' No. But we will explain it definitely as it occurs in each respective case. 'But for what reason did the Blessed One not prescribe expulsion when half is consumed?' This, to begin with, is an improper question, because the legislation of the Vinaya is the domain of a Buddha. This here is an apparent reason: 'because the state of being half is difficult to determine.' 'Mostly consumed' means: among the four parts of the anal passage, urinary passage, and mouth, having surpassed two parts, it is consumed up to the end of the third part. Surpassing the third part up to the end of the fourth part is a case of wrong-doing.

Yadipi nimittaṃ sabbaso khāyitanti “jīvamānakasarīraṃyeva sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti, taṃ vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Allasarīreti abhinave, akuthite vā manussānaṃ jīvamānasarīre akkhināsādīsu thullaccayameva. Tiracchānagatānaṃ hatthiassādīnaṃ nāsāya vatthikose ca thullaccayanti “amaggena amaggaṃ paveseti, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti imāya pāḷiyā atthavisesenettha vuttaṃ. Upakacchakādīsu dukkaṭaṃ, sabbesampi tiracchānagatānaṃ akkhikaṇṇavaṇesu dukkaṭaṃ, avasesasarīrepi dukkaṭamevāti idaṃ vinītavatthusmiṃ “ehi, bhante, methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevā”ti[V 0.0094]. “Alaṃ bhagini netaṃ kappatī”ti (pārā. 79) iminā tāva methunarāgābhāvo dassito hoti. “Ehi, bhante, ūruntarikāya ghaṭṭehi…pe… so bhikkhu tathā akāsī”ti iminā tāva mocanassādo dassito hoti, tenevāha bhagavā “āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti. “Yo pana methunarāgena ūruntarikāya ghaṭṭeti, tassa dukkaṭa”nti siddhanti katvā vuttaṃ.

Even if the mark is completely consumed, and some say, 'This is stated with reference to a living body only,' that should be taken after investigation. Regarding a fresh body—that is, a new or unspoiled living human body—in the eyes, nose, and so on, it is only a grave offense. The statement that for animals such as elephants and horses, in the nose and in the genital sheath, it is a grave offense, is stated here with a specific meaning derived from this Pāḷi text: 'One enters a non-path with a non-path; it is a grave offense.' For the armpits and similar areas, it is a wrong-doing; for all animals, in the eyes, ears, or wounds, it is a wrong-doing; and even for the rest of the body, it is only a wrong-doing. In the Vinītavatthu, it is said: 'Come, venerable one, let us engage in sexual intercourse.' 'Enough, sister, this is not allowable'—by this, first, the absence of sexual lust is shown. 'Come, venerable one, rub between the thighs… and so the bhikkhu did so'—by this, first, the pleasure of emission is shown. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'It is an offense entailing suspension.' 'But whoever, with sexual lust, rubs between the thighs, for him it is a wrong-doing'—this is established and thus stated.

Manussānaṃ [M 0.0105] akkhikaṇṇavaṇādi thullaccayavatthu, tiracchānagatānaṃ dukkaṭavatthūti ettha duviññeyyo pāḷileso, tasmā “na ca, bhikkhave, rattacittena aṅgajātaṃ chupitabbaṃ, yo chupeyya, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vacanato rattacittena akkhikaṇṇavaṇaṃ chupantassa dukkaṭanti siddhanti ayaṃ cammakkhandhake pāḷilesoti veditabbo. “Jīvamānakapurisassāti jīvamānakasaddo mate vattabbameva natthīti ñāpanatthaṃ vutto”ti vadanti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ panāti idaṃ kiñcāpi “katvā mahāaṭṭhakathaṃ sarīra”nti vuttaṃ, atha kho sesaaṭṭhakathāsu “methunarāgena mukhenā”ti vacanābhāvato tattheva bhāvato taṃ vacanaṃ pāḷivacanena saṃsanditvā dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “taṃ sabbampīti mahāaṭṭhakathāyameva methunarāgena itthiyā nimittaṃ appavesento chupati, thullaccaya”nti ca vuttaṃ. “Methunarāgena mukhenā”tipi katthaci, pāḷiyaṃ avisesena “na ca, bhikkhave, rattacittena aṅgajātaṃ chupitabba”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā “taṃ sabba”nti vuttaṃ. Purimaṃ pasaṃsantīti tiracchānagati…pe… vuttanayeneva thullaccayaṃ, kāyasaṃsaggarāgena dukkaṭantiādiaṭṭhakathāvacanehi saṃsandanato. “Taṃ sabbampi…pe… purimaṃ pasaṃsantī”ti idaṃ saṅgītito pacchā sīhaḷadīpakehi ācariyehi pāḷiyā, aṭṭhakathāyañca vuttavacanaṃ saṃsanditvā vuttavinicchayoti vuttaṃ. Ettha itarathā hīti pakatimukhena. Kasmā dukkaṭanti ce? “Aṅgulibījādīni pavesentassa dukkaṭa”nti vuttattā yuttaṃ. Tiracchānagatitthiyā passāvamagganti ettha mahāaṭṭhakathāyampi pubbe “nimitta”nti vatvā ettha “passāvamagga”nti vuttattā avasesanimitte dukkaṭanti yuttaṃ viya dissati. Vuttanayenevāti methunarāgena. Thullaccayanti ca khandhake passāvanimittavasenevāgatattā upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ.

In the statement, 'For humans, the eyes, ears, wounds, etc., are grounds for a grave offense, while for animals, they are grounds for a wrong-doing,' the subtle point of the Pāḷi is difficult to understand. Therefore, because of the Pāḷi, 'And, monks, one with a lustful mind should not touch the sexual organ; whoever should touch it, it is a grave offense,' it is established that for one who touches an eye, ear, or wound with a lustful mind, it is a wrong-doing. This subtle point of the Pāḷi in the Cammakkhandhaka should be understood thus. Regarding 'of a living man,' they say that the word 'living' is stated to make it known that there is nothing at all to be said regarding one who is dead. But regarding the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, although it is said, 'making the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā the body [of the work],' nevertheless, because of the absence of the statement 'with sexual lust, through the mouth' in the other commentaries, and because of its presence only there, that statement is given to show its correspondence after comparing it with the word of the Pāḷi. But in the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is also said: 'Regarding "all that," it is stated only in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "If, with sexual lust, one touches a woman's sexual organ without inserting [one's own], it is a grave offense."' The phrase 'with sexual lust, through the mouth' is also stated in some Pāḷi text. In the Pāḷi, it is stated generally, 'And, monks, one with a lustful mind should not touch the sexual organ.' Therefore, 'all that' is stated. The phrase 'they praise the former' is stated because of its correspondence with the words of the commentary, such as: 'For an animal... a grave offense in the aforementioned way; a wrong-doing for lust of bodily contact.' It is said that this [passage], 'All that... they praise the former,' is a decision stated by the teachers from the island of Sri Lanka after the Council, having harmonized the words stated in both the Pāḷi and the commentary. Here, 'otherwise, indeed' means through the natural orifice. If one should ask, 'Why is it a wrong-doing?' [The answer is:] Because it is stated, 'For one who inserts a finger, testicles, and so on, it is a wrong-doing,' it is appropriate. Regarding 'the urinary passage of a female animal': because even in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, having previously said 'sexual organ,' it here says 'urinary passage,' the statement that for the remaining sexual organs it is a wrong-doing seems to be appropriate. The phrase 'in the aforementioned way' means with sexual lust. And the phrase 'a grave offense' should be understood after investigation, since in the Khandhaka it is mentioned only in connection with the urinary organ.

Ekūnasattatidvisatacatukkakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Sixty-Nine, the Two Hundred, and the Fourfold is concluded.

Santhatacatukkabhedakakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse Analyzing the Fourfold Section on Felt Rugs

61-2. Itthinimittaṃ khāṇuṃ katvāti itthinimittassa anto khāṇuṃ pavesetvā samatalaṃ vā katvā atirittaṃ vā khāṇuṃ ghaṭṭentassa dukkaṭaṃ pavesābhāvā. Īsakaṃ anto pavesetvā [V 0.0095] ṭhitaṃ khāṇumeva ce aṅgajātena [M 0.0106] chupati, pārājikaṃ. “Uppalagandhā uppalabhāvā”tipi dīpavāsino paṭhanti kira. Suttaṃ bhikkhumhīti sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhiteti (pārā. 57) ettha viya. “Suttabhikkhumhī”ti ca paṭhanti, taṃ ujukameva.

Regarding the phrase, 'having made a stump into a woman's sign': for one who, having inserted a stump inside a woman's sign and made it level, or who rubs a protruding stump, it is a wrong-doing because of the absence of insertion. If, having inserted it a little inside, he touches with the male organ the very stump that remains there, it is a pārājika offense. The inhabitants of the island, it is said, also recite, 'The scent of a water lily, the nature of a water lily.' The phrase `suttaṃ bhikkhumhī` is like in the case of `sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhite` ('when a thought of intercourse has arisen'). And they also recite `suttabhikkhumhī`; that is indeed straightforward.

Santhatacatukkabhedakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse Analyzing the Fourfold Section on Felt Rugs is concluded.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Analysis of Terms is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Miscellaneous Discourses

Pakiṇṇake yāni sikkhāpadāni “kiriyānī”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ vasena kāyo, vācā ca saha viññattiyā veditabbā. Akiriyānaṃ vasena vinā viññattiyā veditabbā, cittaṃ panettha appamāṇaṃ bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānassa kiriyattā, acittakattā ca. Tattha kiriyā āpattiyā anantaracittasamuṭṭhānā veditabbā. Aviññattijanakampi ekaccaṃ bāhullanayena “kiriya”nti vuccati, yathayidaṃ paṭhamapārājikaṃ viññattiyā abhāvepi “so ce sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassā”ti hi vuttaṃ “na sādiyati anāpattī”ti ca. Viññattisaṅkhātāpi kiriyā vinā sevanacittena na hoti cittajattā, vikārarūpattā, cittānuparivattikattā ca. Tasmā kiriyāsaṅkhātamidaṃ viññattirūpaṃ itaraṃ cittajarūpaṃ viya janakacittena vinā na tiṭṭhati, itaraṃ saddāyatanaṃ tiṭṭhati, tasmā kiriyāya sati ekantato tajjanakaṃ sevanacittaṃ atthiyevāti katvā na sādiyati anāpattīti na yujjati. Yasmā viññattijanakampi samānaṃ sevanacittaṃ na sabbakālaṃ viññattiṃ janeti, tasmā vināpi viññattiyā sayaṃ uppajjatīti katvā “sādiyati, āpatti pārājikassā”ti vuttaṃ. Nuppajjati ce, na sādiyati nāma, tassa anāpatti, teneva bhagavā “kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhū”ti citteneva āpattiṃ paricchindati, na kiriyāyāti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā cha āpattisamuṭṭhānāni, tāni eva āpattikarā dhammā nāmāti ca, catūhākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati kāyena vācāya kāyavācāhi kammavācāya āpajjatīti ca etāni suttapadāni avirodhitāni honti, aññathā virodhitāni. Kathaṃ? Yañhi āpattiṃ kammavācāya āpajjati, na tattha kāyādayoti āpannaṃ, tato [M 0.0107] kammavācāya saddhiṃ āpattikarā dhammā sattāti āpajjati, atha tatthāpi kāyādayo ekato vā nānāto vā labbhanti. “Catūhi ākārehī”ti na yujjati, “tīhākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjatī”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti evaṃ virodhitāni honti. Kathaṃ avirodhitānīti? Saviññattikāviññattikabhedabhinnattā kāyādīnaṃ. Yā kiriyā āpatti, taṃ ekaccaṃ kāyena saviññattikena āpajjati[V 0.0096], ekaccaṃ saviññattiyā vācāya, ekaccaṃ saviññattikāhi kāyavācāhi āpajjati. Yā pana akiriyā āpatti, taṃ ekaccaṃ kammavācāya āpajjati, tañca kho avasiṭṭhāhi aviññattikāhi kāyavācāhiyeva, na vinā “no ce kāyena vācāya paṭinissajjati, kammavācāpariyosāne āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti (pārā. 414, 421) vacanato. Avisesena vā ekaccaṃ āpattiṃ kāyena āpajjati, ekaccaṃ vācāya, ekaccaṃ kāyavācāhi. Yaṃ panettha kāyavācāhi, taṃ ekaccaṃ kevalāhi kāyavācāhi āpajjati, ekaccaṃ kammavācāya āpajjatīti ayamattho veditabboti evaṃ avirodhitāni honti.

In the miscellaneous section, the training rules called 'actions' should be understood, in relation to them, as body and speech together with intimation. The 'non-actions' should be understood, in relation to them, as being without intimation. Herein, the mind is not the measure, because an offense originating from reporting what is factual is an action, and because it is without intention. Therein, the action of an offense should be understood as arising from the immediately preceding mind. Even a certain training rule that does not produce intimation is called an 'action' by way of generality; just as for this first pārājika, even in the absence of intimation, it is said: 'If he consents, it is a pārājika offense,' and 'If he does not consent, there is no offense.' Even the action designated as intimation does not occur without the mind of indulgence, because it is born of the mind, because it is a derived form, and because it follows after the mind. Therefore, this form of intimation, designated as an action, does not endure without its generating mind, like other mind-born matter; another, such as the sound-base, does endure. Therefore, it is not logical to say, 'if he does not consent, there is no offense,' on the grounds that when there is an action, the mind of indulgence that generates it must necessarily be present. Because the mind of indulgence, although capable of generating intimation, does not always generate intimation, therefore, on the grounds that it arises by itself even without intimation, it is said, 'If he consents, it is a pārājika offense.' If it does not arise, it is called 'not consenting,' and for him there is no offense. For that very reason, the Blessed One determines the offense by the mind alone, asking, 'What was your intention, monk?'—not by the action; this should be understood. Thus far, there are six origins of offenses, and those very things are called 'offense-causing factors.' And the scriptural statements that 'one commits an offense in four ways: by body, by speech, by body and speech, or by a formal act' are not contradictory; otherwise, they are contradictory. How so? For whatever offense one commits by a formal act, it follows that body, etc., are not involved there. Therefore, the offense-causing factors, together with the formal act, would be seven. Furthermore, if in that case body, etc., are also found either together or separately, then 'by four ways' is not correct; it should be said, 'one commits an offense by three ways.' Thus they are contradictory. How are they not contradictory? Because of the division of body, etc., into the distinction of 'with intimation' and 'without intimation'. Of the offenses that are actions, some are committed by the body with intimation, some by speech with intimation, and some by both body and speech with intimation. But of the offenses that are non-actions, some are committed by a formal act, and that too only by the remaining body and speech that are without intimation, not without them—because of the statement: 'If he does not renounce by body or speech, at the conclusion of the formal act, he commits an offense of saṅghādisesa.' Or, without distinction, some offenses are committed by body, some by speech, and some by body and speech. Among these committed by body and speech, some are committed solely by body and speech, and some are committed by a formal act. This meaning should be understood. Thus they are not contradictory.

Tatrāyaṃ samāsato atthavibhāvanā – kāyena āpajjatīti kāyena saviññattikena akattabbaṃ katvā ekaccaṃ āpajjati, aviññattikena kattabbaṃ akatvā āpajjati, tadubhayampi kāyakammaṃ nāma. Akatampi hi loke “kata”nti vuccati “idaṃ dukkaṭaṃ mayā, yaṃ mayā puññaṃ na kata”nti evamādīsu, sāsane ca “idaṃ te, āvuso ānanda, dukkaṭaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ na pucchī”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 443), evamidha vinayapariyāye kāyena akaraṇīyampi “kāyakamma”nti vuccati, ayameva nayo vācāya āpajjatītiādīsu. Tattha samuṭṭhānaggahaṇaṃ kattabbato vā akattabbato vā kāyādibhedāpekkhameva āpattiṃ āpajjati, na aññathāti dassanatthaṃ. Kiriyāggahaṇaṃ kāyādīnaṃ saviññattikāviññattikabhedadassanatthaṃ. Saññāggahaṇaṃ āpattiyā aṅgānaṅgacittavisesadassanatthaṃ, tena yaṃ cittaṃ kiriyālakkhaṇe, akiriyālakkhaṇe vā sannihitaṃ, yato vā kiriyā vā akiriyā vā hoti, na taṃ avisesena āpattiyā aṅgaṃ vā anaṅgaṃ vā hoti, kintu yāya saññāya “saññāvimokkha”nti vuccati, tāya sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ aṅgaṃ, itaraṃ anaṅganti dassitaṃ hoti. Idāni [M 0.0108] yena cittena sikkhāpadaṃ sacittakaṃ hoti, yadabhāvā acittakaṃ, tena tassa avisesena sāvajjattā lokavajjabhāvova vuccati, kintu sāvajjaṃyeva samānaṃ ekaccaṃ lokavajjaṃ ekaccaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti dassanatthaṃ lokavajjaggahaṇaṃ. Cittameva yasmā “lokavajja”nti vuccati, tasmā manokammampi siyā āpattīti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ kammaggahaṇaṃ. Yaṃ panettha akiriyālakkhaṇaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ kusalattikavinimuttaṃ siyāti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ kusalattikaggahaṇaṃ. Yā panettha abyākatā āpatti, taṃ ekaccaṃ avedanampi saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpanno āpajjatīti katvā vedanāttikaṃ ettha na labbhatīti aniṭṭhappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ vedanāttikaggahaṇaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Sikkhāpadañhi sacittakapuggalavasena “ticittaṃ tivedana”nti laddhavohāraṃ acittakenāpannampi “ticittaṃ tivedana”micceva vuccati. Tatridaṃ suttaṃ “atthāpatti acittako āpajjati acittako vuṭṭhāti [V 0.0097] (pari. 324). Atthāpatti kusalacitto āpajjati kusalacitto vuṭṭhātī”tiādi (pari. 470). Anugaṇṭhipade pana “saññā sadā anāpattimeva karoti, cittaṃ āpattimeva, acittakaṃ nāma vatthuavijānanaṃ, nosaññāvimokkhaṃ vītikkamajānanaṃ, idametesaṃ nānatta”nti vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the exposition of the meaning in brief: ‘Commits with the body’ means that one commits a certain offense by doing with the body accompanied by expression what ought not to be done, or by not doing with the body which is without expression what ought to be done. Both of these are called bodily action. For even what is not done is called ‘done’ in the world, as in such phrases as, ‘This was wrongly done by me, in that I did not perform a meritorious act,’ and so on. And in the Dispensation, as in, ‘This, friend Ānanda, was wrongly done by you, in that you did not ask the Blessed One,’ and so on (Cūḷavagga 443). Thus, here in the Vinaya terminology, even an omission by the body is called ‘bodily action.’ This same method applies to ‘commits with speech,’ and so on. Therein, the inclusion of ‘origin’ (samuṭṭhāna) is to show that one commits an offense only with reference to the distinction of body, etc., according to whether something should be done or not done, and not otherwise. The inclusion of ‘action’ (kiriya) is to show the distinction of body, etc., as being with expression (saviññattika) and without expression (aviññattika). The inclusion of ‘perception’ (saññā) is to show the distinction of the mind as a factor or non-factor of the offense. By this, it is shown that a mind that is present in the characteristic of action or non-action, or from which an action or non-action arises, is not indiscriminately a factor or non-factor of the offense. Rather, the mind associated with that perception by which it is called ‘perception-release’ (saññāvimokkha) is a factor, while the other is not a factor. Now, regarding the mind by which a training rule becomes intentional (sacittaka), and in the absence of which it is unintentional (acittaka)—by that, due to its being blameworthy without distinction, it is called a ‘worldly fault’ (lokavajja). However, the inclusion of ‘worldly fault’ is to show that while it is indeed blameworthy, some is a worldly fault and some is a fault by enactment (paṇṇattivajja). Since the mind itself is called a ‘worldly fault,’ the inclusion of ‘action’ (kamma) is to prevent the undesirable implication that mental action (manokamma) could also be an offense. Here, the inclusion of the ‘wholesome triad’ (kusalattika) is to prevent the undesirable implication that an action characterized by non-action might be excluded from the wholesome triad. Here, the inclusion of the ‘feeling triad’ (vedanāttika) is to prevent the undesirable implication that the feeling triad is not obtained here, considering that one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti) incurs certain indeterminate offenses even without feeling. This should be understood. For a training rule, having obtained the designation ‘of three minds, of three feelings’ in relation to a person with a mind, is still called ‘of three minds, of three feelings’ even when incurred by one without a mind (acittakena). In this regard, there is this passage: ‘There is an offense that one without a mind (acittako) commits and from which one without a mind emerges (Pari. 324). There is an offense that one with a wholesome mind commits and from which one with a wholesome mind emerges,’ and so on (Pari. 470). However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is said: ‘Perception always brings about non-offense, while the mind brings about only an offense. What is called “unintentional” (acittaka) is not knowing the object; knowing the transgression is not “perception-release.” This is their distinction.’

Sabbasaṅgāhakavasenāti sabbasikkhāpadānaṃ saṅgahavasena. Bhikkhuniyā cīvaradānādi kiriyākiriyato. Jātarūparajatapaṭiggahaṇādi siyā kiriyato. Upanikkhittāpaṭikkhepe siyā akiriyato. Desitavatthukapamāṇātikkantakuṭikaraṇe siyā kiriyato, adesitavatthukapamāṇātikkantakaraṇe siyā kiriyākiriyato. Yaṃ cittaṅgaṃ labhatiyevāti kāyacittaṃ vācācittanti evaṃ. Vināpi cittenāti ettha vināpi cittena sahāpi cittenāti adhippāyo. Yo so saviññattiko, aviññattiko ca vutto kāyo, tassa kammaṃ kāyakammaṃ, tathā vacīkammaṃ. Tattha saviññattiko kāyo uppattiyā kammaṃ sādheti, itaro anuppattiyā. Tathā vācāti veditabbaṃ, sikkhāpadanti “yo tattha nāmakāyo padakāyo”ti vacanato vītikkame yujjatīti vuttaṃ. “Hasituppādavoṭṭhabbanānipi āpattisamuṭṭhāpakacittāni. Idampi na mayā paricchinnanti hasamāno passati yadā, tadā voṭṭhabbanaṃ javanagatika”nti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Abhiññācittāni paññattiṃ ajānitvā iddhivikubbanādikāle gahetabbāni.

‘By way of encompassing all’ means by way of encompassing all the training rules. The giving of a robe, etc., to a bhikkhunī arises from action and non-action. The accepting of gold and silver, etc., may arise from action. The non-rejection of what is placed nearby may arise from non-action. The making of a hut exceeding the measure on a designated site may arise from action; the making of one exceeding the measure on an undesignated site may arise from action and non-action. Regarding ‘whatever mental component is indeed obtained,’ it is thus: consciousness associated with the body and consciousness associated with speech are obtained. Herein, regarding ‘even without consciousness,’ the meaning is: ‘either without consciousness or together with consciousness.’ The body that is said to be with expression (saviññattika) and without expression (aviññattika)—its action is bodily action; similarly, verbal action. Therein, the body with expression accomplishes the action of commission; the other, of omission. It should be understood that speech is likewise. As for ‘training rule,’ it is said that it is applicable in the case of transgression on account of the statement, ‘Whatever is the name-body, the phrase-body.’ It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: ‘The smile-arising consciousness and the determining consciousness are also minds that originate an offense. When, while smiling, one perceives, “This too has not been determined by me,” then the determining consciousness has the nature of an impulsion.’ The supernormal knowledge consciousnesses are to be taken at the time of performing psychic transformations and so on, through not knowing the concept.

Ettha [M 0.0109] pana yo pana bhikkhu bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno…pe… methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto atthi koci pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso, atthi koci na pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso. Dukkaṭathullaccayavatthūsu paṭisevanto atthi koci na pārājiko. Pakkhapaṇḍako apaṇḍakapakkhe upasampanno paṇḍakapakkhe methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto so pārājikaṃ āpattiṃ nāpajjatīti na pārājiko nāma. Na hi abhikkhuno āpatti nāma atthi. So anāpattikattā apaṇḍakapakkhe āgato kiṃ asaṃvāso hoti na hotīti? Hoti, “abhabbo tena sarīrabandhanenā”ti (pārā. 55; mahāva. 129) hi vuttaṃ. “Yo pana, bhikkhu, bhikkhūnaṃ…pe… asaṃvāso”ti (pārā. 44) vuttattā yo pana bhikkhubhāvena methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati, so eva abhabbo. Nāyaṃ apārājikattāti ce? Na, “byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo”ti (mahāva. 86) vuttaṭṭhāne yathā abhikkhunā kammavācāya sāvitāyapi kammaṃ ruhati kammavipattiyā asambhavato, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ yutti – upasampannapubbo eva ce kammavācaṃ sāveti, saṅgho ca tasmiṃ upasampannasaññī, evañce kammaṃ ruhati, na aññathāti no khantīti ācariyo. Gahaṭṭho vā titthiyo vā paṇḍako [V 0.0098] vā anupasampannasaññī kammavācaṃ sāveti, saṅghena kammavācā na vuttā hoti, “saṅgho upasampādeyya, saṅgho upasampādeti, upasampanno saṅghenā”ti (mahāva. 127) hi vacanato saṅghena kammavācāya vattabbāya saṅghapariyāpannena, saṅghapariyāpannasaññitena vā ekena vuttā saṅghena vuttāva hotīti veditabbo, ayameva sabbakammesu yutti. Tathā atthi methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto koci nāsetabbo “yo bhikkhunīdūsako, ayaṃ nāsetabbo”ti vuttattā eva, so anupasampannova, sahaseyyāpattiādiṃ janeti, tassa omasane ca dukkaṭaṃ hoti. Abhikkhuniyā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto na nāsetabbo “antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpanno, bhikkhave, anupasampanno…pe… nāsetabbo”ti pāḷiyā abhāvato. Teneva so upasampannasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, na sahaseyyāpattādiṃ janeti, kevalaṃ asaṃvāsoti katvā gaṇapūrako na hoti, ekakammaṃ ekuddesopi hi saṃvāsoti vutto. Samasikkhatāpi saṃvāsoti katvā so tena saddhiṃ natthīti padasodhammāpattiṃ pana janetīti kāraṇacchāyā dissati. Yathā bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa ekakammādino [M 0.0110] saṃvāsassa abhāvā bhikkhunī asaṃvāsā bhikkhussa, tathā bhikkhu ca bhikkhuniyā, padasodhammāpattiṃ pana janeti. Tathā “antimavatthuṃ ajjhāpannopi ekacco yo nāsetabbo”ti avuttoti iminā nidassanena sā kāraṇacchāyā gahaṇaṃ na gacchati.

Here, however, regarding any bhikkhu who has entered upon the training and livelihood of bhikkhus… engaging in sexual intercourse—there is a certain one who becomes pārājika and is not in communion; there is a certain one who does not become pārājika but is not in communion. Engaging in the objects of dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses, there is a certain one who is not pārājika. A pakkhapaṇḍaka ordained in a period when he is not a paṇḍaka, who then engages in sexual intercourse in a period when he is a paṇḍaka, does not fall into a pārājika offense; thus, he is not called 'pārājika.' For there is no such thing as an offense for one who is not a bhikkhu. Since he has no offense, when he has returned to the period of not being a paṇḍaka, is he not in communion, or is he not? He is. For it is said, 'He is incapable by that bodily constitution.' Because it is said, 'Whatever bhikkhu… is not in communion,' whoever engages in sexual intercourse with the status of a bhikkhu, he alone is incapable. If one were to say: Is this one not incapable because he is not pārājika? No. In the place where it is said, 'The Saṅgha should be informed by a competent, capable bhikkhu,' just as the formal act is valid even when recited by one who is not a bhikkhu—because of the impossibility of a failure of the act—so this case should be understood as analogous. Herein, this is the reasoning: The teacher says, 'It is our view that if one who was previously ordained recites the formal act, and the Saṅgha perceives him as ordained, only then is the act valid, not otherwise.' If a householder, a sectarian, or a paṇḍaka who is perceived as unordained recites the formal act, it is as if the formal act has not been spoken by the Saṅgha. For according to the text, 'The Saṅgha should ordain, the Saṅgha ordains, one is ordained by the Saṅgha,' it should be understood that when the formal act is to be spoken by the Saṅgha, if it is spoken by one included in the Saṅgha, or by one perceived as being included in the Saṅgha, it is indeed considered as spoken by the Saṅgha. This very same reasoning applies in all formal acts. Likewise, there is a certain one engaging in sexual intercourse who is to be expelled, because it is said, 'Whoever is a corrupter of bhikkhunīs, he is to be expelled.' He is in fact unordained; he gives rise to the offense of lying down together, etc., and for insulting him, there is a dukkaṭa offense. One who engages in sexual intercourse with a non-bhikkhunī is not to be expelled, because of the absence of a Pāḷi text stating, 'Bhikkhus, one who has committed the final offense, being unordained… is to be expelled.' For that very reason, he is counted as ordained; he does not give rise to the offense of lying down together, etc. Being merely not in communion, he does not complete a quorum. For having a common formal act and a common recitation is called 'communion.' Because having the same training is also 'communion,' and that communion does not exist with him, he therefore gives rise to the padasodhamma offense—thus a semblance of a reason appears. Just as, due to the absence of communion—such as a common formal act—of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with a bhikkhunī, a bhikkhunī is not in communion with a bhikkhu, and likewise a bhikkhu with a bhikkhunī, yet he gives rise to the padasodhamma offense. Likewise, because it is not said, 'Even one who has committed the final offense, a certain one is to be expelled,' by this example, that semblance of a reason is not accepted.

Api ca “bhikkhu suttabhikkhumhi vippaṭipajjati, paṭibuddho sādiyati, ubho nāsetabbā”ti (pārā. 66) ca, “tena hi, bhikkhave, mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsethā”ti (pārā. 384) ca vacanato yo saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisitvā anuvijjakena anuvijjiyamāno parājāpito, sopi anupasampannova, na omasavādapācittiyaṃ janetīti veditabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi “upasampannaṃ upasampannasaññī khuṃsetukāmo”ti pāḷi natthi, kiñcāpi kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ “yaṃ akkosati, tassa upasampannatā, anaññāpadesena jātiādīhi akkosanaṃ, ‘maṃ akkosatī’ti jānanā, atthapurekkhāratādīnaṃ abhāvoti imānettha cattāri aṅgānī”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, tathāpi duṭṭhadosasikkhāpade “asuddho hoti puggalo aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpanno, tañce suddhadiṭṭhi samāno okāsaṃ kārāpetvā akkosādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti omasavādassā”ti (pārā. 389) vacanato asuddhe upasampannasaññāya eva omasantassa pācittiyaṃ. Asuddhadiṭṭhissa dukkaṭaṃ. “Suddho hoti puggalo, aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ anajjhāpanno, tañce suddhadiṭṭhi samāno okāsaṃ kārāpetvā akkosādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti omasavādassā”ti (pārā. 389) vacanato pana [V 0.0099] kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ “tassa upasampannatā upasampannasaññitā”ti na vuttaṃ anekaṃsikattā tassa aṅgassāti veditabbaṃ.

Moreover, according to the statements: 'A bhikkhu who disagrees with a bhikkhu learned in the Suttas, and one who, being awakened, approves, both should be expelled,' and 'Therefore, bhikkhus, expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā,' it should be understood that one who, having entered the midst of the Saṅgha and being investigated by an investigator, is defeated, is also indeed not an ordained person; he does not generate a pācittiya offense of abusive speech. Although there is no Pāḷi text stating, 'intending to scold one who is ordained, perceiving him as ordained,' and although in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī it is stated, 'Herein, these are the four factors: the one whom he scolds, that one's state of being ordained; the scolding by means of birth and so on, without referring to another; the knowledge "he is scolding me"; and the absence of putting benefit first, etc.,' nevertheless, in the training rule concerning a corrupt fault, according to the statement: 'A person is impure, having committed some pārājika offense, and if one with the view that he is pure, having arranged an opportunity, speaks with the intention to scold, there is an offense of abusive speech,' for one who disparages an impure person with the very perception that he is ordained, there is a pācittiya offense. For one who has the view that the other is impure, there is a dukkaṭa offense. However, according to the statement: 'A person is pure, not having committed any pārājika offense, and if one with the view that he is pure, having arranged an opportunity, speaks with the intention to scold, there is an offense of abusive speech,' it should be understood that in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī it is not said 'his state of being ordained and the perception of him as ordained' because that factor is not unequivocal.

Api cettha sikkhāpaccakkhātakacatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ, atthi puggalo sikkhāpaccakkhātako na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno, atthi sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno na sikkhāpaccakkhātako, atthi sikkhāpaccakkhātako ceva sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno ca, atthi neva sikkhāpaccakkhātako na sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Tattha tatiyo bhikkhunīsikkhāpaccakkhātako veditabbo. Sā hi yāva na liṅgaṃ pariccajati, kāsāve saussāhāva samānā sāmaññā cavitukāmā sikkhaṃ paccakkhantīpi bhikkhunī eva sikkhāsājīvasamāpannāva. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “na, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā sikkhāpaccakkhāna”nti (cūḷava. 434). Kadā ca pana sā [M 0.0111] abhikkhunī hotīti? Yadā sāmaññā cavitukāmā gihinivāsanaṃ nivāseti, sā “vibbhantā”ti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “yadeva sā vibbhantā, tadeva abhikkhunī”ti (cūḷava. 434). Kittāvatā pana vibbhantā hotīti? Sāmaññā cavitukāmā kāsāvesu anālayā kāsāvaṃ vā apaneti, naggā vā gacchati, tiṇapaṇṇādinā vā paṭicchādetvā gacchati, kāsāvaṃyeva vā gihinivāsanākārena nivāseti, odātaṃ vā vatthaṃ nivāseti, saliṅgeneva vā saddhiṃ titthiyesu pavisitvā kesaluñcanādivataṃ samādiyati, titthiyaliṅgaṃ vā samādiyati, tadā vibbhantā nāma hoti. Tattha yā bhikkhuniliṅge ṭhitāva titthiyavataṃ samādiyati, sā titthiyapakkantako bhikkhu viya pacchā pabbajjampi na labhati, sesā pabbajjamevekaṃ labhanti, na upasampadaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ kiñcāpi “yā sā, bhikkhave, bhikkhunī sakāsāvā titthāyatanaṃ saṅkantā, sā āgatā na upasampādetabbā”ti vacanato yā paṭhamaṃ vibbhamitvā pacchā titthāyatanaṃ saṅkantā, sā āgatā upasampādetabbāti anuññātaṃ viya dissati. Saṅgītiācariyehi pana “catuvīsati pārājikānī”ti vuttattā na puna sā upasampādetabbā, tasmā eva sikkhāpaccakkhānaṃ nānuññātaṃ bhagavatā. Antimavatthuajjhāpannā pana bhikkhunī eva. Pakkhapaṇḍakīpi bhikkhunī eva. Kinti pucchā.

Furthermore, in this regard, the tetrad concerning one who renounces the training should be understood: there is a person who renounces the training but has not entered upon the training and livelihood; there is one who has entered upon the training and livelihood but does not renounce the training; there is one who both renounces the training and has entered upon the training and livelihood; and there is one who neither renounces the training nor has entered upon the training and livelihood. Among these, the third should be understood as a bhikkhunī who renounces the training. For as long as she does not abandon the outward sign, even if she renounces the training while still wearing the saffron robe with enthusiasm and desiring to fall away from the monastic life, she is still a bhikkhunī who has entered upon the training and livelihood. For the Blessed One has said: 'Bhikkhus, there is no renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī.' But when does she become a non-bhikkhunī? When, desiring to fall away from the monastic life, she puts on the clothing of a laywoman, she is reckoned as 'disrobed.' For the Blessed One has said: 'As soon as she has disrobed, then she is a non-bhikkhunī.' And to what extent is one disrobed? Desiring to fall away from the monastic life, without attachment to the saffron robes, she either removes the saffron robe, or goes naked, or goes covering herself with grass or leaves, or wears the saffron robe itself in the manner of lay clothing, or wears white cloth, or, while still bearing her own sign, enters among the sectarians and undertakes observances such as plucking out hair, or adopts the outward sign of sectarians—then she is called 'disrobed.' In this case, a bhikkhunī who, while still maintaining the sign of a bhikkhunī, undertakes the practices of sectarians is like a bhikkhu who has defected to the sectarians—she does not later obtain even the going forth. The others obtain only the going forth, not full ordination. Although in the Pāli it appears as if it were permitted—based on the statement, 'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī who, while wearing the saffron robe, has gone over to the abode of sectarians, if she returns, is not to be given full ordination,' which implies that one who first disrobes and then goes over to the abode of sectarians, if she returns, is to be given full ordination—nevertheless, as the teachers of the Recital have said, 'There are twenty-four offenses entailing expulsion,' she is therefore not to be given full ordination again. For this very reason, renunciation of the training was not permitted by the Blessed One. However, a bhikkhunī who has committed the final offense is still a bhikkhunī. A pakkhapaṇḍakī is also still a bhikkhunī. The word 'what' here signifies a question.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Decided Cases

67. Vinītāni vinicchitāni vatthūni vinītavatthūni. Tesaṃ tesaṃ “tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhū”tiādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ pāṭekkaṃ nāmagaṇanaṃ uddharitvā uddharitvā ūnādhikadosasodhanaṭṭhena uddānā ca tā matrādisiddhigāthāhi chandovicitilakkhaṇena gāthā cāti “uddānagāthā [V 0.0100] nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, de, sodhane iti dhātussa rūpaṃ uddānāti veditabbaṃ. Imā pana uddānagāthā dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi saṅgītikāle ṭhapitā, katthāti ce? Padabhājanīyāvasāne. “Vatthugāthā nāma ‘tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhū’tiādīnaṃ imesaṃ vinītavatthūnaṃ nidānānī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayena vinītavatthūni eva “vatthugāthā”ti vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Idamettha samāsato adhippāyanidassanaṃ [M 0.0112] – “āpattiṃ tvaṃ, bhikkhu, āpanno pārājika”nti mūlāpattidassanavasena vā, “anāpatti, bhikkhu, pārājikassa, āpatti saṅghādisesassa, dukkaṭassā”ti āpattibhedadassanavasena vā, “anāpatti, bhikkhu, asādiyantassā”ti anāpattidassanavasena vā yāni vatthūni vinītāni vinicchitāni, tāni vinītavatthūni nāma. Tesaṃ vinītavatthūnaṃ nidānavatthudīpikā tanti vatthugāthā nāma. Uddānagāthāva “vatthugāthā”ti vuttāti eke. Tesaṃ “iminā lakkhaṇena āyatiṃ vinayadharā vinayaṃ vinicchinissantī”ti vacanena virujjhati. Na hi uddānagāthāyaṃ kiñcipi vinicchayalakkhaṇaṃ dissati, uddānagāthānaṃ visuṃ payojanaṃ vuttaṃ “sukhaṃ vinayadharā uggaṇhissantī”ti, tasmā payojananānattatopetaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ viggaho – vatthūni eva gāthā vatthugāthā. Vinītavatthuto visesanatthamettha gāthāggahaṇaṃ. Uddānagāthāto visesanatthaṃ vatthuggahaṇanti veditabbaṃ. Keci pana “gāthānaṃ vatthūnīti vattabbe vatthugāthāti vutta”nti vadanti. Makkaṭivatthuṃ aññe tattha bhikkhū ārocesuṃ, idha sayameva. Tattha kāraṇassa “bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ paññatta”nti vuttattā vajjiputtakāpi aññe eva. “Tattha ānandatthero, idha te evā”ti aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Ācariyassa adhippāyo pubbe vutto, tasmā upaparikkhitabbaṃ.

67. Cases that have been judged and decided are vinītavatthūni (decided cases). For each of these cases, such as 'Now at that time, a certain monk...', the name and number are extracted again and again, and for the purpose of cleansing the faults of deficiency and excess, there are summaries (uddāna). And those summaries are also verses marked by the characteristic of chandoviciti with verses accomplished through matrā and so on; therefore, they are called 'summary verses' (uddānagāthā). The word uddāna should be understood as the form derived from the root 'de' in the sense of 'sodhana' (cleansing). These summary verses were placed by the Elder Compilers of the Dhamma at the time of the communal chanting. If asked where, they were placed at the end of the Padabhājanīya. It is said in the gaṇṭhipada (gloss): 'The vatthugāthā (case verses) are the introductions to these decided cases, such as "Now at that time, a certain monk..."' Therefore, following the method stated there, it should be understood that the decided cases themselves are what are called vatthugāthā. This is a concise demonstration of the meaning herein: those cases that have been judged and decided—whether by way of showing the root offense, as in, 'Monk, you have committed a Pārājika offense'; or by way of showing the distinction of offenses, as in, 'Monk, there is no Pārājika offense, but there is a Saṅghādisesa offense, a Dukkaṭa offense'; or by way of showing non-offense, as in, 'Monk, there is no offense for one who does not consent'—are called vinītavatthūni (decided cases). The canonical text that illuminates the introductory case of these decided cases is called vatthugāthā. Some say that the summary verses themselves are called vatthugāthā. This contradicts the statement: 'By this characteristic, future upholders of the Vinaya will decide upon the Vinaya.' For no characteristic of decision is seen in a summary verse. A separate purpose for summary verses has been stated: 'So that upholders of the Vinaya may learn them with ease.' Therefore, this distinction should be understood from the difference in purpose. Herein, this is the analysis: the cases themselves are the verses; hence, vatthugāthā. Here, the inclusion of the term 'gāthā' serves to distinguish them from the vinītavatthu. It should be understood that the inclusion of the term 'vatthu' serves to distinguish them from the uddānagāthā. Some, however, say: 'When it should be said "the cases of the verses" (gāthānaṃ vatthūni), it is stated as vatthugāthā.' In the monkey case, other monks reported it there; here, he himself reported it. In that case, the reason for reporting it oneself is because of the statement, 'The training rule was laid down by the Blessed One'; the Vajjiputtaka monks are also different ones. It is said in a certain gaṇṭhipada: 'There, it was the Elder Ānanda; here, it was they themselves.' The teacher's intention has been stated before; therefore, it should be investigated.

67-8. Ñatvāti apucchitvā sayameva ñatvā. Pokkharanti sarīraṃ bheripokkharaṃ viya. Lokiyā avikalaṃ “sundara”nti vadanti, tasmā vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti paṭhamenatthena visiṭṭhakāyacchavitāyāti attho, dutiyena vaṇṇasundaratāyāti. “Uppalagabbhavaṇṇattā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā, tasmā uppalavaṇṇāti nāmaṃ labhī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Nīluppalavaṇṇā kāyacchavīti vacanaṃ pana sāmacchaviṃ dīpeti. Loke pana “uppalasamā pasatthasāmā”ti vacanato “yā sāmā sāmavaṇṇā sāmatanumajjhā, sā pāricariyā sagge mama vāso”ti vacanato sāmacchavikā itthīnaṃ pasatthā. “Yāvassā naṃ andhakāra”ntipi pāṭho. Kilesakāmehi vatthukāmesu yo na limpati.

67-8. `Ñatvāti` means having known by oneself without asking. `Pokkhara` means the body, just as in `bheripokkhara`. Worldly people call one with a complete body 'beautiful'; therefore, by the first meaning, `vaṇṇapokkharatā` is to be understood as the excellence of the body's complexion, and by the second, as the beauty of the complexion. It is said in the Gaṇṭhipada: 'Because her complexion was like the inside of a lotus, that is, a golden complexion, she received the name Uppalavaṇṇā.' The phrase 'a body complexion the color of a blue lotus', however, indicates a dark complexion. In the world, however, from the saying, 'Like a lotus is the praised dark complexion,' and from the saying, 'She who is dark, of dark complexion, with a slender dark waist—that dark woman is a dwelling in heaven for my service,' a woman with a dark complexion is praised among women. There is also the reading: `Yāvassā naṃ andhakāra`. He who is not smeared by the defilements of sensual pleasure in the objects of sensual pleasure.

69. Itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhūtanti itthisaṇṭhānaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, tañca kho purisindriyassa antaradhānena [V 0.0101] itthindriyassa pātubhāvena. Evaṃ purisindriyapātubhāvepi. Etena yathā brahmānaṃ purisindriyaṃ nuppajjati, kevalaṃ purisasaṇṭhānameva [M 0.0113] uppajjati, yathā ca kassaci paṇḍakassa vināpi purisindriyena purisasaṇṭhānaṃ uppajjati, na tathā tesanti dassitaṃ hoti, taṃ pana itthindriyaṃ, purisindriyaṃ vā antaradhāyantaṃ marantānaṃ viya paṭilomakkamena sattarasamacittakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya antaradhāyati. Paccuppanne indriye niruddhe itaraṃ visabhāgindriyaṃ pātubhavati. Yasmā mahāniddaṃ okkantasseva kirassa visabhāgindriyaṃ pātubhavati, tasmā “rattibhāge niddaṃ okkantassā”ti vuttaṃ. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, taṃyeva upajjhaṃ tameva upasampada”nti vacanato pavattinīyeva upajjhāyā, upasampadācariyā bhikkhunīyeva ācariyāti katvā tāsaṃ upajjhāyavattaṃ, ācariyavattañca iminā bhikkhunāsadāsāyaṃ pātaṃ bhikkhunupassayaṃ gantvā kātabbaṃ, tāhi ca imassa vihāraṃ āgamma saddhivihārikavattādi kātabbaṃ nu khoti ce? “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhikkhunīhi saṅgamitu”nti vacanena vinābhāvadīpanato kevalaṃ na puna upajjhā gahetabbā, na ca upasampadā kātabbāti dassanatthameva “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, taṃyeva upajjha”ntiādi vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha bhikkhunīhi saṅgamitunti bhikkhūhi vinā hutvā bhikkhunīhi eva saddhiṃ samaṅgī bhavituṃ anujānāmīti attho, tasmā iminā pāḷilesena “tassā eva gāmantarādīhi anāpattī”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ siddhaṃ hoti, āgantvā saṅgamituṃ sakkā, yañca bhagavatā gamanaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ nissāya kuto gāmantarādipaccayā āpatti. Na hi bhagavā āpattiyaṃ niyojetīti yuttameva taṃ, aññathā “yā āpattiyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi asādhāraṇā, tāhi āpattīhi anāpattī”ti pāḷivacanato na gāmantarādīhi anāpattīti āpajjati. Sādhāraṇatā āpattiyeva “yā āpattiyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi asādhāraṇā, yā ca bhikkhunīhi saṅgamantiyā gāmantaranadīpārarattivippavāsagaṇaohīyanāpattiyo, tāhi āpattīhi anāpattī”ti na vuttattāti ce? Na vuttaṃ aniṭṭhappasaṅgato. Bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ saṅkantāyapi tassā tā pahāya aññāhi saṅgamantiyā gāmantarādīhi anāpatti eva sabbakālanti imassa aniṭṭhappasaṅgato tathā na vuttanti attho. Tattha gāmantarāpattādivatthuṃ sañcicca tasmiṃ kāle ajjhācarantīpi sā liṅgapātubhāvena kāraṇena anāpajjanato anāpatti. Anāpajjanaṭṭheneva vuṭṭhāti nāmāti veditabbā. Tathā yogī anuppanne [M 0.0114] eva kilese nirodheti. Abandhanopi patto “ūnapañcabandhano”ti vuccati, sabbaso vā pana na sāveti appaccakkhātā hoti sikkhā, evamidha anāpannāpi āpatti vuṭṭhitā nāma hotīti veditabbā.

69. The female characteristic appears—this means the female form appears. And this occurs through the disappearance of the male faculty and the appearance of the female faculty. It is to be understood similarly in the case of the appearance of the male faculty. By this, it is shown that it is not the same for these individuals as it is for Brahmās, for whom the male faculty does not arise but only the male form arises, or as it is for some eunuchs, for whom the male form arises even without the male faculty. Furthermore, that female faculty or male faculty, while disappearing, disappears in reverse order starting from the seventeenth thought-moment, just as for those who are dying. When the present faculty has ceased, the other, dissimilar faculty appears. Because the dissimilar faculty is said to appear only when one has entered deep sleep, it was therefore said, 'upon entering sleep during the night.'

If one were to ask: 'Based on the statement, “I allow, O monks, that same preceptor, that same ordination,” is the preceptor the female preceptor (pavattinī) and the teacher the bhikkhunī who was the ordination teacher? And for this reason, should the duties towards the preceptor and teacher be performed by this monk by always going to the bhikkhunī residence in the evening and morning? And should those bhikkhunīs, having come to this monk's monastery, perform the duties of a co-resident, and so on?'

It should be understood that the statement beginning with, “I allow, O monks, that same preceptor...” was spoken only to show this: a preceptor should not be taken again, and ordination should not be performed again. This is because it indicates a state of being without the need for the statement, “I allow, O monks, to associate with bhikkhunīs.” Therein, 'to associate with bhikkhunīs' means: I allow them to be in harmony together with bhikkhunīs only, being without bhikkhus. Therefore, by this hint in the Pāli, the commentary's statement, “For her, there is no offense regarding going to another village, etc.,” is established. It is possible to come and associate. And since that going was permitted by the Blessed One, on account of that, how could there be an offense conditioned by going to another village, etc.? Indeed, the Blessed One does not enjoin one in an offense, so that is proper. Otherwise, from the Pāli statement, “Whatever offenses of monks are not shared with bhikkhunīs, for those offenses there is no offense,” it would follow that regarding going to another village, etc., it is not a no-offense but is indeed an offense.

If one were to say: 'Because they are shared offenses, it is indeed an offense, for it was not stated thus: “Whatever offenses of monks are not shared with bhikkhunīs, and whatever offenses there are for a bhikkhunī associating with them—such as going to another village, crossing a river, staying away overnight, and being left behind by a group—for those offenses there is no offense.”'? It was not stated thus due to an undesirable consequence. The meaning is: it was not stated in that way because of the undesirable consequence of this meaning: that even for her who has gone with bhikkhunīs, if she abandons them and associates with others, there would always be no offense regarding going to another village, etc.

Therein, even though she, at that time, intentionally transgresses the basis for an offense of going to another village, etc., because she does not incur it for the reason of the appearance of the new characteristic, it is a no-offense. It should be understood that she is said to be 'rehabilitated from the offense' precisely in the sense of not having incurred it. Just as a yogī eradicates defilements that have not yet arisen; just as a bowl that is not yet bound is called 'lacking the five bindings'; or just as when one does not declare it at all, the training is unrenounced; so too here, it should be understood that an offense that has not been incurred is called 'rehabilitated'.

Yasmā pana sā purisena sahaseyyāpattiṃ anāpajjantīpi sakkoti bhikkhunīhi saṅgamituṃ[V 0.0102], tasmā anāpattīti katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ubhinnampi sahaseyyāpatti hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ parivāre “aparehipi catūhākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati saṅghamajjhe gaṇamajjhe puggalassa santike liṅgapātubhāvenā”ti (pari. 324). Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ parivāre “atthāpatti āpajjanto vuṭṭhāti vuṭṭhahanto āpajjatī”ti (pari. 324), tassa sahaseyyādiṃ āpajjati asādhāraṇāpattīhi vuṭṭhāti, tadubhayampi sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Dūre vihāro hoti pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchimaṃ, vihārato paṭṭhāya gāmaṃ pavisantiyā gāmantaraṃ hotīti attho. Saṃvidahanaṃ parimocetvāti addhānagamanasaṃvidahanaṃ akatvāti attho. Tā kopetvāti pariccajitvāti attho. “Paripuṇṇavassasāmaṇerenāpī”ti vacanato aparipuṇṇavassassa upajjhāyaggahaṇaṃ natthīti viya dissati. Vinayakammaṃ katvā ṭhapitoti vikappetvā ṭhapito. Avikappitānaṃ dasāhātikkame nissaggiyatā veditabbā. Puna paṭiggahetvā sattāhaṃ vaṭṭatīti pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ sannidhiṃ bhikkhunīhi paṭiggāhāpetvā paribhuñjitu”nti (cūḷava. 421) vacanato vuttaṃ. Anapekkhavissajjanenāti vatthuṃ anapekkhavissajjanena vā paṭiggahaṇena vā puna paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjissāmīti. Pakkhamānattakāle punadeva liṅgaṃ parivattati chārattaṃ mānattameva dātabbanti sace, bhikkhukāle appaṭicchannāya āpattiyā, no paṭicchannāyāti no laddhīti ācariyo.

However, because that person, even while not incurring the offense of lying down together with a man, is able to associate with bhikkhunīs, therefore, because it would otherwise be no offense, it is said in the commentary: 'For both, there is the offense of lying down together.' This is also stated in the Parivāra: 'One incurs an offense in four other ways: in the midst of the Sangha, in the midst of a group, in the presence of an individual, and by the manifestation of the sexual organ' (Pari. 324). Regarding what is stated in the Parivāra, 'One who is incurring an offense rises from it, and one who is rising from it incurs an offense' (Pari. 324), it should be understood that this is said with reference to both: incurring an offense such as lying down together, and rising from non-common offenses. A monastery is considered 'far' if it is five hundred bow-lengths away; the meaning is that starting from the outermost monastery, for a bhikkhunī entering the village, the `gāmantara` offense is incurred. 'Having set aside the arrangement' means not having made an arrangement for a long journey. 'Having angered them' means having abandoned them. From the statement, 'Even by a sāmaṇera of completed years,' it appears that for a sāmaṇera who has not completed his years, the taking of a preceptor is not permitted. 'Having performed a Vinaya act and set it aside' means having formally determined it and set it aside. For items that have not been formally determined, it should be understood that after ten days have passed, they become subject to forfeiture. Regarding 'having received it again, it is allowable for seven days,' this is said based on the statement, 'I allow, O bhikkhus, for bhikkhus to have a store received by bhikkhunīs and then use it' (Cūḷavagga 421). The phrase 'by relinquishment without expectation' is explained as relinquishing the object without expectation, or receiving it with the thought, 'I will receive it again and use it.' If, during the period of `pakkhamānatta`, the sexual characteristic changes again, `mānatta` for six nights is to be given. This applies in the case of an offense that was unconcealed at the time of being a bhikkhu, not a concealed one. 'This is our view,' says the teacher.

Parivāsadānaṃ pana natthīti bhikkhuniyā chādanāsambhavato vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sace bhikkhunī asādhāraṇaṃ pārājikāpattiṃ āpajjitvā purisaliṅgaṃ paṭilabhati, bhikkhūsu upasampadaṃ na labhati, pabbajjaṃ labhati, anupabbajitvā bhikkhubhāve ṭhito sahaseyyāpattiṃ na janeti. Vibbhantāya bhikkhuniyā purisaliṅge pātubhūte bhikkhūsu upasampadaṃ na labhati, pārājikaṃ. Avibbhantamānassa gahaṭṭhasseva sato bhikkhunīdūsakassa sace itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavati, neva bhikkhunīsu upasampadaṃ labhati, na [M 0.0115] puna liṅgaparivatte jāte bhikkhūsu vāti. Bhikkhuniyā liṅgaparivatte sati bhikkhu hoti, so ce sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya vibbhamitvā itthiliṅgaṃ paṭilabheyya, bhikkhunīsu upasampadaṃ paṭilabhati ubhayattha pubbe pārājikabhāvaṃ appattattā. Yā pana bhikkhunī paripuṇṇadvādasavassā purisaliṅgaṃ paṭilabheyya, upasampanno bhikkhu eva. Puna sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya āgato na upasampādetabbo aparipuṇṇavīsativassattā. Puna liṅgaparivatte sati bhikkhunīsu upasampadaṃ labhati. Evaṃ ce katadvādasasaṅgahassa dārakassa liṅgaparivatte sati gihigatā itthī hoti, paripuṇṇadvādasavassā upasampādetabbā kira. Bhikkhuniyā itthiliṅgantaradhānena, bhikkhussa vā purisaliṅgantaradhānena pakkhapaṇḍakabhāvo bhaveyya, na sā bhikkhunī bhikkhunīhi nāsetabbā bhikkhu vā bhikkhūhi puna pakatibhāvāpattisambhavā[V 0.0103]. Pakatipaṇḍakaṃ pana sandhāya “paṇḍako nāsetabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Pakkhapaṇḍako hi saṃvāsanāsanāya nāsetabbo, itaro ubhayanāsanāyāti attho. Yadi tesaṃ puna pakatibhāvo bhaveyya, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, taṃyeva upajjhaṃ tameva upasampadaṃ tāniyeva vassāni bhikkhunīhi saṅgamitu”nti ayaṃ vidhi sambhavati. Sace nesaṃ liṅgantaraṃ pātubhaveyya, so ca vidhi, yā āpattiyo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīhi sādhāraṇā, tā āpattiyo bhikkhunīnaṃ santike vuṭṭhātuṃ asādhāraṇāhi anāpattīti ayampi vidhi sambhavati. Yaṃ vuttaṃ parivāre “saha paṭilābhena purimaṃ jahati, pacchime patiṭṭhāti, viññattiyo paṭippassambhanti, paññattiyo nirujjhanti, saha paṭilābhena pacchimaṃ jahati, purime patiṭṭhāti, viññattiyo”tiādi, taṃ yathāvuttavidhiṃ sandhāya vuttanti amhākaṃ khantīti ācariyo. Itthiliṅgaṃ, purisaliṅgaṃ vā antaradhāyantaṃ kiṃ sakalampi sarīraṃ gahetvā antaradhāyati, udāhu sayameva. Kiñcettha – yadi tāva sakalaṃ sarīraṃ gahetvā antaradhāyati, ayaṃ puggalo cuto bhaveyya. Tasmā sāmaññā cuto bhaveyya, puna upasampajjanto opapātiko bhaveyya. Atha sayameva antaradhāyati, sopi bhāvo tassa virujjhati. Itthindriyādīni hi sakalampi sarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitānīti khaṇanirodho viya tesaṃ antaradhānaṃ veditabbaṃ, tasmā yathāvuttadosappasaṅgābhāvo veditabbo. Aññamaññaṃ saṃsaṭṭhappabhānaṃ dīpānaṃ ekappabhānirodhepi itarissā ṭhānaṃ viya sesasarīraṭṭhānaṃ tattha hotīti veditabbaṃ.

However, it should be understood that the granting of probation is not done, because concealment is not possible for a bhikkhunī. If a bhikkhunī commits an unshared pārājika offense and then acquires the male characteristic, she does not receive higher ordination among the bhikkhus but does receive the going forth. Having gone forth again, while established in the state of a bhikkhu, he does not incur the offense of lying down together. If a bhikkhunī who has disrobed manifests the male characteristic, she does not receive higher ordination among the bhikkhus; it is a pārājika impediment. If the female characteristic appears for a layman who has violated a bhikkhunī and has not disrobed, she receives higher ordination neither among the bhikkhunīs, nor among the bhikkhus if her characteristic changes again. If a bhikkhunī’s characteristic changes and she becomes a bhikkhu, and if he then renounces the training, disrobes, and regains the female characteristic, she receives higher ordination among the bhikkhunīs—because in either case, she had not previously reached the state of pārājika. But if a bhikkhunī who has completed twelve years acquires the male characteristic, he is indeed a fully ordained bhikkhu. If he later renounces the training and returns, he should not be given higher ordination, as he has not completed twenty years of age. But if his characteristic changes again, she receives higher ordination among the bhikkhunīs. Similarly, if a boy of twelve years undergoes a change of characteristic and becomes a woman who has lived the household life, she, having completed twelve years of age, should, it is said, be given higher ordination. If through the disappearance of a bhikkhunī’s female characteristic, or through the disappearance of a bhikkhu’s male characteristic, the state of a fortnightly paṇḍaka should arise, that bhikkhunī should not be expelled by the bhikkhunīs, nor should that bhikkhu be expelled by the bhikkhus—because of the possibility of returning to the natural state. However, with reference to a natural paṇḍaka, it was said, 'A paṇḍaka should be expelled.' Indeed, a fortnightly paṇḍaka should be expelled by expulsion from co-residence, while the other should be expelled by means of both expulsions—of the characteristic and of co-residence. This is the meaning. If their natural state should arise again, this procedure is possible: 'I allow, O bhikkhus... to associate with the bhikkhunīs with that same preceptor, that same higher ordination, and those same years of seniority.' If another characteristic should appear for them, that procedure is also possible, and this procedure is also possible: that for whichever offenses of bhikkhus are shared with bhikkhunīs, one is to rise from those offenses in the presence of bhikkhunīs, but for the unshared ones, there is no offense. What was said in the Parivāra—'Simultaneously with the acquisition, one abandons the former and is established in the latter; announcements cease, regulations are annulled...' and so on—that was said with reference to the aforementioned procedure. The teacher says: This is our preference. When the female or male characteristic is disappearing, does it disappear taking the entire body with it, or does only the characteristic itself disappear? What is the case here? If it were to disappear taking the entire body with it, that person would be deceased. Therefore, they would have fallen from the monastic life, and upon re-ordaining, they would be of spontaneous birth. Now, if only the characteristic itself disappears, that state of being is also untenable for that person. For the female faculties and so on stand pervading the entire body. Their disappearance should be understood as being like momentary cessation; therefore, the absence of the consequence of the aforementioned fault should be known. It should be known that just as for lamps with intermingled lights, even when one light ceases, a basis for the other remains; so too, the rest of the body subsists there as a basis.

71-2. Muccatu [M 0.0116] vā mā vā dukkaṭamevāti mocanarāgābhāvato. Avisayoti asādiyanaṃ nāma evarūpe ṭhāne dukkaranti attho. Methunadhammo nāma ubhinnaṃ vāyāmena nipajjati “tassa dvayaṃdvayasamāpattī”ti vuttattā, tasmā tvaṃ mā vāyāma, evaṃ te anāpatti bhavissati, kiriyañhetaṃ sikkhāpadanti vuttaṃ hoti, “āpattiṃ tvaṃ bhikkhu āpanno pārājika”nti vacanato akiriyampetaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ yebhuyyena “kiriya”nti vuccatīti siddhaṃ hoti.

Whether one is released or not, it is only a dukkaṭa offense because of the absence of lust for release. In the context of 'not an object,' the meaning is that not consenting in such a situation is a dukkaṭa offense. The act of sexual intercourse is accomplished by the effort of both, because it is said, 'Of that is the attainment of two by two.' Therefore, 'You, do not make an effort; thus for you there will be no offense.' Indeed, it is said that this training rule has action as its origin.
