Because of the passage, 'You, monk, have committed a pārājika offense,' it is established that although this training rule also has non-action as its origin, it is called 'of action-origin' by the general rule.

73-4. “Pārājikabhayena ākāsagatameva katvā pavesanādīni karontassa sahasā tālukaṃ vā passaṃ vā aṅgajātaṃ chupati ce, dukkaṭamevā”ti vadanti. Kasmā? Na methunarāgattāti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Dantānaṃ bāhirabhāvo oṭṭhānaṃ bāhirabhāvo viya thullaccayavatthu hotīti vuttaṃ “bahi nikkhantadante jivhāya ca thullaccaya”nti. Taṃ puggalaṃ visaññiṃ katvāti vacanena so puggalo khittacitto nāma hotīti dassitaṃ hoti. Yo pana puggalo na visaññīkato, so ce attano aṅgajātassa dhātughaṭṭanacariṇijjhiṇikādisaññāya sādiyati, methunasaññāya [V 0.0104] abhāvato visaññīpakkhameva bhajatīti tassa anāpatticchāyā dissati. “Methunametaṃ maññe kassaci amanussassā”ti ñatvā sādiyantassa āpatti eva. Paṇḍakassa methunadhammanti paṇḍakassa vaccamagge vā mukhe vā, bhummatthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. Avedayantassapi sevanacittavasena āpatti santhateneva sevane viya.

They say: 'For one who, out of fear of a pārājika offense, performs insertion and so forth only into empty space, if his sexual organ suddenly touches the palate or the flank, it is only a dukkaṭa offense.' Why? Because it is not due to sexual lust. This should be investigated. The state of the teeth being outside, like the state of the lips being outside, is a basis for a thullaccaya offense; thus it is said, 'For teeth protruding outside and for the tongue, a thullaccaya offense.' By the phrase 'having made that person unconscious,' it is shown that that person is called one with a distracted mind. But as for a person who has not been made unconscious, if he consents with the perception of his own sexual organ's customary rubbing, moving, and shifting of elements, he enters the side of the unconscious due to the absence of the perception of intercourse; thus for him, a shadow of no-offense is seen. For one who consents even after knowing, 'This, I think, is the intercourse of some non-human being,' there is an offense indeed. In the phrase 'sexual intercourse with a paṇḍaka,' the genitive case 'of a paṇḍaka' is used in the locative sense, referring to 'in the anus or in the mouth.' Even for one who does not feel sensation, there is an offense by the power of the mind that wishes to engage, just as in the act of engaging itself.

Upahatindriyavatthusmiṃ “etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, so ārocesī”ti duvidho pāṭho atthi. Tattha “ārocesu”nti vuttapāṭho “vediyi vā so bhikkhave”ti vuttattā sundaraṃ, aññathā “āpattiṃ tvaṃ bhikkhū”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. “Vediyā vā”ti dīpavāsino paṭhanti kira, methunadhammassa pubbapayogā hatthaggāhādayo, tasmā “dukkaṭamevassa hotī”ti iminā purimapadena sambandho. Yasmā pana dukkaṭamevassa hoti, tasmā yāva sīsaṃ na pāpuṇāti puggalo, tāva dukkaṭe tiṭṭhatīti sambandho veditabbo. Sīsaṃ nāma maggapaṭipādanaṃ. “Sīsaṃ na pāpuṇātīti pārājikaṃ na hoti tāva pubbapayogadukkaṭe tiṭṭhatī”ti aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ[M 0.0117]. Uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhenāti ettha bhāvaniṭṭhāpaccayo veditabbo. Daṭṭhena daṃsena khādanenāti hi atthato ekaṃ.

Regarding the case of one with impaired faculties, there are two readings: “etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ” (they reported this matter), and “so ārocesī” (he reported it). Among these, the reading stated as “ārocesuṃ” is preferable, because it is said, “vediyi vā so bhikkhave” (or he might feel, O bhikkhus); otherwise, it would have to be said, “āpattiṃ tvaṃ bhikkhū” (you, bhikkhu, have committed an offense). The residents of the island, it is said, recite “vediyā vā”. The preliminary acts of sexual intercourse are such as the taking of the hand; therefore, the connection is with the preceding phrase, “For him, there is only a dukkaṭa.” And since for him there is only a dukkaṭa, the connection should be understood thus: as long as a person does not reach the “head,” he remains in a dukkaṭa. “Head” means causing entry into the passage. It is written in a certain glossary: “‘Not reaching the head’ means a pārājika offense does not occur; until then, he remains in the dukkaṭa of a preliminary act.” Here, in the phrase “uccāliṅgapāṇakadaṭṭhena” (by the bite of a caterpillar), the suffix should be understood as indicating an abstract state. For indeed, “daṭṭhena” (by the bite), “daṃsena” (by the sting), and “khādanena” (by the chewing) are one in meaning.

76-7. Saṅgāmasīse yuddhamukhe yodhapuriso viyāyaṃ bhikkhūti “saṅgāmasīsayodho bhikkhū”ti vuccati. Rukkhasūcidvāraṃ upilavāya, ekena vā bahūhi vā kaṇṭakehi thakitabbaṃ kaṇṭakadvāraṃ. Dussadvāraṃ sāṇidvārañca dussasāṇidvāraṃ. “Kilañjasāṇī”tiādinā vuttaṃ sabbampi dussasāṇiyameva saṅgahetvā vuttaṃ. Ekasadisattā “eka”nti vuttaṃ. Ākāsataleti hammiyataleti attho. Ayañhettha saṅkhepoti idāni vattabbaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Kiñci karontā nisinnā hontīti vuttattā nipannānaṃ āpucchanaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. “Yathāparicchedameva ca na uṭṭhāti, tassa āpattiyevā”ti kiñcāpi avisesena vuttaṃ, anādariyadukkaṭāpatti eva tattha adhippetā. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti? “Rattiṃ dvāraṃ vivaritvā nipanno aruṇe uggate uṭṭhahati, anāpattī”ti vuttattā, mahāpaccariyaṃ visesetvā “anādariyadukkaṭāpi na muccatī”ti vuttattā ca, tena itarasmā dukkaṭā muccatīti adhippāyo. Yathāparicchedameva ca na uṭṭhāti, tassa āpattiyevāti ettha na anādariyadukkaṭaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathāparicchedamevāti avadhāraṇattā paricchedato abbhantare na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Puna “supatī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne viya sanniṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Evaṃ nipajjantoti nipajjanakāle āpajjitabbadukkaṭameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasmā yathāparicchedena uṭṭhahantassa dve dukkaṭānīti vuttaṃ hotīti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyampi “yadi rattiṃ dvāraṃ asaṃvaritvā nipanno ‘divā vuṭṭhahissāmī’ti, anādariye āpatti [V 0.0105] dukkaṭassā”ti vuttaṃ, etthāpi “nipanno”ti vuttattā “aruṇe uṭṭhite uṭṭhāhī”ti na vuttattā ca jānitabbaṃ. “Mahāpaccariyaṃ anādariyadukkaṭameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttadukkaṭa”nti eke vadanti. Tassa anāpattīti atthato anipannattā vuttaṃ. “Sace pana rattiṃ saṃvaritvā nipanno, aruṇuṭṭhānasamaye koci vivarati, dvārajagganādīni akatvā nipannassa āpattiyeva. Kasmā? Āpattikhettattā”ti vadanti.

This monk is like a warrior at the head of the battle, at the forefront of the fight; thus, he is called 'a warrior monk at the head of the battle.' A wooden-bolt door is closed by bolting; a thorn-door is to be closed with one or many thorns. A cloth door and a hemp-curtain door are a cloth-and-hemp-curtain door. What is said by 'a mat-curtain,' and so forth, is said as being included within 'cloth-and-hemp-curtain door.' Because they are of one kind, it is called 'one.' 'Ākāsatala' means the upper storey of a building. 'This here is the summary' is said with reference to what is to be said now. Some say: 'Because it is said, "They are sitting, doing something," asking leave of those who are lying down is not allowable.' Although it is stated without specification, 'And if he does not get up exactly at the designated time, for him there is an offense indeed,' only the offense of wrong-doing due to disrespect is intended there. How is this understood? Because it is said, 'If one lies down at night with the door open and rises at dawn, there is no offense,' and because the Mahāpaccarī specifies, 'Even from the wrong-doing of disrespect, one is not exempt,' the implication is that one is exempt from the other wrong-doing. The phrase 'If he does not rise according to the fixed limit, for him there is only an offense' does not refer to the wrong-doing of disrespect here. 'Exactly at the designated time' is an emphatic statement; therefore, it is said that an offense does not occur within the designated time. Again, as in the place where 'sleeps' is said, it is stated having taken a conclusion. Thus, 'when lying down' refers only to the wrong-doing that is to be incurred at the time of lying down; therefore, it is said that for one who does not rise according to the designated time, there are two wrong-doings. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is also said: 'If one lies down at night without securing the door, thinking, "I will rise by day," there is an offense of wrong-doing due to disrespect.' Here also, it should be understood because 'lying down' is said, and because 'Rise when dawn has broken!' is not said. Some say: 'The Mahāpaccarī refers only to the wrong-doing of disrespect, not to the wrong-doing mentioned in the commentary.' 'There is no offense for him' is said because, in essence, he is not lying down. They say: 'But if one lies down at night with the door secured, and at dawn someone opens it, for the one lying down without performing the watching of the door and other duties, an offense is incurred. Why? Because it is a field of offense.'

Yasmā yakkhagahitakopi visaññībhūto viya khittacitto nāma hoti, assa pārājikāpattito anāpatti, pageva aññato, tasmā “yakkhagahitako viya visaññībhūtopi na muccatī”ti yaṃ mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pubbe [M 0.0118] sañcicca divā nipanno pacchā yakkhagahitakopi visaññībhūtopi na muccati nipajjanapayogakkhaṇe eva āpannattāti adhippāyena vuttaṃ. Bandhitvā nipajjāpitova muccatīti na yakkhagahitakādīsveva, sopi yāva sayameva sayanādhippāyo na hoti, tāva muccati. Yadā kilanto hutvā niddāyitukāmatāya sayanādhippāyo hoti, tadā saṃvarāpetvā, jaggāpetvā vā ābhogaṃ vā katvā niddāyitabbaṃ, aññathā āpatti. Sabhāgo ce natthi, na passati vā, na gantuṃ vā sakkoti. Cirampi adhivāsetvā pacchā vedanāṭṭo hutvā anābhogeneva sayati, tassa “anāpatti vedanāṭṭassā”ti vacanena anāpatti, tassāpi avisayattā āpatti na dissatīti visaññībhāveneva supantassa “anāpatti khittacittassā”ti vacanena na dissati. Ācariyā pana evaṃ na kathayantīti avisesena “na dissatī”ti na kathayanti, yadi saññaṃ appaṭilabhitvā sayati, avasavattattā āpatti na dissati, sace saññaṃ paṭilabhitvāpi kilantakāyattā sayanaṃ sādiyanto supati, tassa yasmā avasavattattaṃ na dissati, tasmā āpatti evāti kathayantīti adhippāyo.

Since even one seized by a yakkha, though as if unconscious, is called 'one with a deranged mind,' there is no Pārājika offense for him, let alone a lesser one. Therefore, the statement in the Mahāpaccarī, 'Even one who is unconscious like one seized by a yakkha is not exempt,' was spoken with this intention: one who, having intentionally lain down during the day beforehand, is afterwards seized by a yakkha and becomes unconscious, is not exempt, because the offense was already incurred at the very moment of the preliminary act of lying down. The statement, 'One who is made to lie down after being bound is exempt,' is not only for the case of one seized by a yakkha and so on. Even he is exempt only as long as he does not have the intention to lie down of his own accord. When, being weary, he has the intention to lie down out of a desire to sleep, he should sleep only after having someone restrain him, or keep him awake, or after making a mental note; otherwise, an offense is incurred. If there is no companion, or he does not see one, or is unable to go, he may endure for a long time and later, afflicted by pain, lie down without making a mental note. For him, there is no offense, by the statement, 'There is no offense for one afflicted by pain.' For one who sleeps in a state of unconsciousness, no offense is seen, in accordance with the statement, 'There is no offense for one with a deranged mind.' However, the teachers do not state it thus. They do not say 'it is not seen' without distinction. If one sleeps without having regained awareness, an offense is not seen, due to being not in control. But if, even after having regained awareness, he consents to sleeping due to bodily exhaustion, since a lack of control is not apparent in his case, they state that an offense is indeed incurred. This is the intention.

Mahāpadumattheravāde yakkhagahitako khittacittako muccati. Bandhitvā nipajjāpito asayanādhippāyattā, vedanāṭṭattā ca muccatīti adhippāyo. Evaṃ sante pāḷiaṭṭhakathā, theravādo ca sameti, tasmā tesaṃ tesaṃ vinicchayānaṃ ayameva adhippāyoti no khantīti ācariyo, anugaṇṭhipade pana yakkhagahitakopi visaññībhūtopi na muccati nāma, pārājikaṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbo so antarantarā saññāpaṭilābhatoti adhippāyo. “Bandhitvā nipajjāpito vā”ti kurundīvacanena ekabhaṅgena nipannopi na muccatīti ce? Muccatiyeva. Kasmā? Atthato anipannattā. Kurundīvādena mahāaṭṭhakathāvādo sameti. Kasmā? Avasavattasāmaññato. Kiñcāpi sameti, ācariyā pana evaṃ na kathayanti. Na kevalaṃ teyeva, mahāpadumattheropīti [V 0.0106] dassanatthaṃ “mahāpadumattherenā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāpadumattheravāde “pārājikaṃ āpajjituṃ abhabbo yakkhagahitako nāmā”ti ca vuttaṃ, tattha ācariyā pana evaṃ vadanti “sace okkantaniddo ajānantopi pāde mañcakaṃ āropeti, āpattiyevāti vuttattā yo pana patitvā tattheva sayati na vuṭṭhāti, tassa āpatti antarantarā jānantassāpi ajānantassāpi hotī”ti[M 0.0119]. Sabbaṭṭhakathāsu vuttavacanāni sampiṇḍetvā dassetuṃ “idha ko muccati ko na muccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yakkhagahitako vā visaññībhūto vā na kevalaṃ pārājikaṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbo eva, sabbopi āpajjati. Evaṃ “bandhitvā nipajjāpitova muccatī”ti vacanena tassapi avasavattattā “āpatti na dissatī”ti evaṃ na kathayanti. Yasmā ummattakakhittacittavedanāṭṭesu aññataro na hoti, tasmā “āpattiyevā”ti kathayanti. Idaṃ kira sabbaṃ na saṅgītiṃ āruḷhaṃ. “Pavesanaṃ sādiyatītiādinā vuttattā akiriyāpi hotīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ, yadā pana sādiyati, tadā sukhumāpi viññatti hoti evāti idha kiriyā evā”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

In the view of the Elder Mahāpaduma, one seized by a yakkha or one with a deranged mind is exempt. The meaning is that one who is bound and made to lie down is exempt due to not having the intention to lie down and due to being afflicted by pain. This being so, the Pāḷi Aṭṭhakathā and the Elder's view are in agreement. Therefore, the teacher says, 'Of those various decisions, this very meaning is suitable; this is our preference.' However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, one seized by a yakkha or one who has become unconscious is indeed not exempt; the meaning is that he is capable of falling into a pārājika offense because he intermittently regains perception. If it is said that by the statement in the Kurundī, 'or one who is bound and made to lie down,' even one lying on one side is not exempt? He is indeed exempt. Why? Because in essence, he is not lying down. The view of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā agrees with the view of the Kurundī. Why? Because of the commonality of not being under one's own control. Although they agree, the teachers, however, do not state it thus. To show that it is not only they, but that even the Elder Mahāpaduma does not state it, the words 'by the Elder Mahāpaduma' were said. And in the view of the Elder Mahāpaduma, it is said: 'One named a 'yakkhagahitaka' (one seized by a yakkha) is incapable of falling into a pārājika offense.' Regarding that, however, the teachers say thus: 'Because it is said, "If one who has fallen into deep sleep, even without knowing, places his feet onto the bed, it is indeed an offense," as for the monk who, having fallen, lies down in that very place and does not get up, for him an offense occurs intermittently, whether he is aware or unaware.' To show a summary of the statements made in all the Aṭṭhakathās, it was said: 'Here, who is exempt, and who is not exempt?' One seized by a yakkha or one who has become unconscious is not merely capable of falling into a pārājika offense; every such one falls into an offense. Thus, they do not say that based on the statement 'Only one who is bound and made to lie down is exempt,' an offense is not seen for him due to his being not in control. They say, 'Since he is not one among the insane, the deranged, or the pain-afflicted, it is indeed an offense.' It seems all this was not submitted to the council. In the Anugaṇṭhipada it is said: 'Because it is stated by the words "consents to the entry," etc., some say that it can also be an offense not originating from an action. That should not be accepted. For when one consents, at that time even a subtle intimation indeed occurs. Therefore, here it is only an action.'

Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Pārājika is finished.

2. Dutiyapārājikaṃ

2. The Second Pārājika

Dhaniyavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Dhaniya

84. Dutiye rājūhi eva pariggahitattā “rājagaha”nti laddhanāmake samīpatthena, adhikaraṇatthena ca paṭiladdhabhummavibhattike gijjhakūṭe pabbate catūhi vihārehi viharantoti adhippāyo. Tassa “vassaṃ upagacchiṃsū”ti iminā sambandho veditabbo. Tayo eva hi ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā gaṇakammaṃ karonti, na tato ūnā adhikā vā akiriyattā. Tattha vinayapariyāyena saṅghagaṇapuggalakammakosallatthaṃ idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ – atthi saṅghakammaṃ saṅgho eva karoti, na gaṇo na puggalo, taṃ apalokanakammassa kammalakkhaṇekadesaṃ ṭhapetvā itaraṃ catubbidhampi kammaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atthi saṅghakammaṃ saṅgho ca karoti, gaṇo ca karoti, puggalo ca karoti. Kiñcāti? Yaṃ pubbe ṭhapitaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ parivāraṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yasmiṃ vihāre dve tayo janā vasanti[V 0.0107], tehi nisīditvā katampi saṅghena katasadisameva. Yasmiṃ pana vihāre eko bhikkhu hoti, tena bhikkhunā uposathadivase pubbakaraṇapubbakiccaṃ katvā nisinnena katampi katikavattaṃ saṅghena katasadisameva hotī”ti (pari. aṭṭha. 495-496). Punapi vuttaṃ “ekabhikkhuke pana [M 0.0120] vihāre ekena sāvitepi purimakatikā paṭippassambhati evā”ti. Atthi gaṇakammaṃ saṅgho karoti, gaṇo karoti, puggalo karoti, taṃ tayo pārisuddhiuposathā aññesaṃ santike karīyanti, tassa vasena veditabbaṃ. Atthi gaṇakammaṃ gaṇova karoti, na saṅgho na puggalo, taṃ pārisuddhiuposatho aññamaññaṃ ārocanavasena karīyati, tassa vasena veditabbaṃ. Atthi puggalakammaṃ puggalova karoti, na saṅgho na gaṇo, taṃ adhiṭṭhānuposathavasena veditabbaṃ. Atthi gaṇakammaṃ ekaccova gaṇo karoti, ekacco na karoti, tattha añattikaṃ dve eva karonti, na tayo. Sañattikaṃ tayova karonti, na tato ūnā adhikā vā, tena vuttaṃ “tayo eva hi ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā gaṇakammaṃ karonti, na tato ūnā adhikā vā akiriyattā”ti. Tasmā tayova vinayapariyāyena sampahulā, na tato uddhanti veditabbaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “kiñcāpi kammalakkhaṇaṃ tayova karonti, atha kho tehi kataṃ saṅghena katasadisanti vuttattā ekena pariyāyena tayo janā vinayapariyāyenapi saṅgho”ti vuttaṃ, idaṃ sabbampi vinayakammaṃ upādāya vuttaṃ, lābhaṃ pana upādāya antamaso ekopi anupasampannopi “saṅgho”ti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati kira. Pavāraṇādivasassa aruṇuggamanasamanantarameva “vutthagassā”ti vuccanti, ukkaṃsanayena “pāṭipadadivasato paṭṭhāyā”ti vuttaṃ, teneva “mahāpavāraṇāya pavāritā”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā antarāyena apavāritā “vutthavassā”ti na vuccantīti āpajjati. Thambhādi kaṭṭhakammanti veditabbaṃ. Keci tanukaṃ dārutthambhaṃ antokatvā mattikāmayaṃ thambhaṃ karonti, ayaṃ pana tathā na akāsi, tena vuttaṃ “sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ karitvā”ti. Telamissāya tambamattikāya.

84. In the second [Pārājika], the intention is this: while dwelling on the mountain Gijjhakūṭa near Rājagaha—which obtained the name 'Rājagaha' because it was taken possession of only by kings, and where the locative case is used with the meaning of proximity and location—by means of four modes of dwelling. Its connection with 'they entered the rains residence' should be understood. Indeed, only three perform a group-act after presenting a motion, neither fewer nor more, because otherwise it is not a valid act. Here, for the sake of skill in the formal acts of the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual according to the Vinaya method, this miscellaneous section should be understood: There is a formal act of the Saṅgha that only the Saṅgha performs, not a group and not an individual; that should be understood as the other fourfold formal act, setting aside the Apalokanakamma (act of announcement), which has only a partial characteristic of a formal act. There is a formal act of the Saṅgha that the Saṅgha performs, a group performs, and an individual performs. What is that? That which was established previously. Indeed, this was stated in the Parivāra commentary: 'In a monastery where two or three persons reside, what is done by them having sat down together is just like what is done by the Saṅgha. But in a monastery where there is one bhikkhu, on the Uposatha day, the agreement made by that bhikkhu, having done the preliminary duties and preliminary functions and having sat down, is just like what is done by the Saṅgha.' Again, it was stated: 'But in a monastery with a single bhikkhu, even when the announcement is made by that one, the previous agreement is certainly pacified.' There is a group-act that the Saṅgha performs, the group performs, and the individual performs; this should be understood by way of the three purity Uposathas that are performed in the presence of others. There is a group-act that only a group performs, not the Saṅgha and not an individual; this should be understood by way of the purity Uposatha that is performed by means of mutual announcement. There is an individual-act that only an individual performs, not the Saṅgha and not a group; this should be understood by way of the determination-Uposatha. There is a group-act that one kind of group performs and another does not. Therein, an act without a motion is performed by only two, not three. An act with a motion is performed by only three, not fewer or more than that; therefore it was said, 'Indeed, only three perform a group-act after presenting a motion, neither fewer nor more, because otherwise it is not a valid act.' Therefore, it should be understood that according to the Vinaya method, only three constitute a 'multitude' (sambahulā), and not more than that. But in the Anugaṇṭhipada it is said: 'Although only three perform the characteristic of the formal act, nevertheless, because it is said that what is done by them is like what is done by the Saṅgha, in one sense, three persons are also the Saṅgha according to the Vinaya method.' All this was said in reference to a Vinaya act. But in reference to gains, it seems that at the very least even one unordained person attains the designation of 'Saṅgha'. On the day of Pavāraṇā, immediately after the sunrise, they are called 'those who have completed the rains residence'; by way of the superior method, it is said 'from the first day onwards'. For that very reason, it was said, 'they have performed the invitation of the great Pavāraṇā'. Otherwise, it would follow that those who have not performed the invitation due to an obstacle are not called 'those who have completed the rains residence'. A post, etc., should be understood as 'timber work'. Some make a clay post, having placed a thin wooden post inside, but this one did not do so; therefore it was said, 'having made the hut entirely of clay'. With copper-colored clay mixed with oil.

85. “Mā pacchimā janatā pāṇesu pātabyataṃ āpajjī”ti iminā anuddesasikkhāpadena yattha iṭṭhakapacana pattapacana kuṭikaraṇa vihārakārāpana navakammakaraṇa khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇa vihārasammajjana paṭaggidāna kūpapokkharaṇīkhaṇāpanādīsu pātabyataṃ jānantena bhikkhunā kappiyavacanampi na vattabbanti dasseti, teneva pariyāyaṃ avatvā tesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ anāpattivāresu “anāpatti asatiyā ajānantassā”ti vuttaṃ. “Antarāpattisikkhāpada”ntipi etassa nāmameva. “Gacchathetaṃ, bhikkhave, kuṭikaṃ bhindathā”ti iminā kataṃ labhitvā tattha vasantānampi dukkaṭamevāti ca siddhaṃ. Aññathā hi [M 0.0121] bhagavā na bhindāpeyya. Esa nayo bhedanakaṃ chedanakaṃ uddālanakanti etthāpi, āpattibhedāva. Tato eva hi [V 0.0108] bhedanakasikkhāpadādīsu viya “aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti na vuttaṃ, tathā aññassatthāya karoti, cetiyādīnaṃ atthāya karoti, dukkaṭamevāti ca siddhaṃ, aññathā kuṭikārasikkhāpadādīsu viya “aññassatthāya vāsāgāraṃ ṭhapetvā sabbattha, anāpattī”ti nayameva vadeyya, na bhindāpeyya. Sabbamattikāmayabhāvaṃ pana mocetvā kaṭṭhapāsāṇādimissaṃ katvā paribhuñjati, anāpatti. Tathā hi chedanakasikkhāpadādīsu bhagavatā nayo dinno “aññena kataṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ paṭilabhitvā chinditvā paribhuñjatī”tiādīsu. Keci pana “vayakammampīti etena mūlaṃ datvā kārāpitampi atthi, tena taṃ aññena katampi na vaṭṭatīti siddha”nti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Kasmā? Sambhāre kiṇitvā sayameva karontassāpi vayakammasambhavato. Kiṃ vā pāḷilese sati aṭṭhakathālesanayo. Iṭṭhakāhi giñjakāvasathasaṅkhepena katā vaṭṭatīti ettha pakatiiṭṭhakāhi cinitvā kattabbāvasatho giñjakāvasatho nāma. Sā hi “mattikāmayā”ti na vuccati, “iṭṭhakakuṭikā”tveva vuccati, tasmā thusagomayatiṇapalālamissā mattikāmayāpi apakkiṭṭhakamayāpi “sabbamattikāmayā”tveva vuccatīti no khantīti ācariyo, bhasmādayo hi mattikāya daḷhibhāvatthameva ādīyanti, apakkiṭṭhakamayāpi giñjakāvasathasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, na ca āyasmā dhaniyo ekappahāreneva kumbhakāro viya kumbhaṃ taṃ kuṭikaṃ niṭṭhāpesi, anukkamena pana sukkhāpetvā sukkhāpetvā mattikāpiṇḍehi cinitvā niṭṭhāpesi, apakkiṭṭhakamayā kuṭi viya sabbamattikāmayā kuṭi ekābaddhā hoti, na tathā pakkiṭṭhakamayā, tasmā sā kappatīti eke. Sabbamattikāmayāya kuṭiyā bahi ce tiṇakuṭikādiṃ katvā anto vasati, dukkaṭameva. Sace tattha tattha chiddaṃ katvā bandhitvā ekābaddhaṃ karoti, vaṭṭati. Anto ce tiṇakuṭikādiṃ katvā anto vasati, vaṭṭati. Kārako eva ce vasati, karaṇapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati, na vasanapaccayā. Sace anto vā bahi vā ubhayattha vā sudhāya limpati, vaṭṭati. Yasmā sabbamattikāmayā kuṭi sukarā bhindituṃ, tasmā tattha ṭhapitaṃ pattacīvarādi aguttaṃ hoti, corādīhi avaharituṃ sakkā, tena vuttaṃ “pattacīvaraguttatthāyā”ti.

85. “‘Lest the later generation should fall into the destruction of life.’ By this supplementary training rule, it is shown that where there are activities such as firing bricks, firing bowls, building a hut, having a monastery built, undertaking new work, repairing what is broken and dilapidated, sweeping the monastery, giving kindling, having wells and ponds dug, and so on, a bhikkhu who knows that destruction of life is involved should not even speak words that are allowable. For this reason, without stating the method, in the no-offense clauses of those training rules it is said: ‘There is no offense for one who is unmindful, for one who does not know.’ ‘Training rule on an intermediate offense’ is also a name for this. By the words, ‘Go, bhikkhus, break this hut,’ it is established that it is a dukkaṭa offense even for those who, having obtained what was made, live in it. Otherwise, the Blessed One would not have had it broken. This is the method also in the cases of breaking, cutting, and uprooting; it is just a difference of offense. For this reason, in the training rules on breaking and so on, it is not said: ‘Having obtained what was made by another, he uses it; it is an offense of dukkaṭa.’ Similarly, if he does it for the sake of another, or for the sake of a cetiya and so on, it is established that it is a dukkaṭa offense. Otherwise, as in the training rules on building a hut, he would have stated the principle, ‘Except for establishing a dwelling for another's sake, in all cases there is no offense,’ and he would not have had it broken. But if, having removed its nature of being entirely of clay by making it mixed with wood, stone, and so on, one uses it, there is no offense. For in the training rules on cutting and so on, the Blessed One has given the method in such passages as: ‘Having obtained what was made by another that exceeds the measure, he uses it after cutting it down.’ Some, however, say: ‘By this, “even commissioned work,” it is established that even what is commissioned by giving a price is not allowable, though it was made by another.’ This is not sound. Why? Because commissioned work is possible even for one who does it himself after buying the materials. Or rather, when there is a hint in the Pāli, what need is there for a hint from the commentary? Here, what is made of bricks, in short a brick-house, is allowable. A dwelling that is to be made by laying ordinary bricks is called a brick-house. For it is not called ‘of clay,’ but is called a ‘brick hut.’ Therefore, what is made of clay mixed with chaff, cow-dung, grass, and leaves, and also what is made of unbaked bricks, is called ‘entirely of clay.’ ‘This is our view,’ says the teacher, for ashes and so on are added to clay only for the sake of strengthening it. What is made of unbaked bricks also does not reach the category of a brick-house. And the venerable Dhaniya did not finish that hut in a single go like a potter making a pot, but he finished it by building it up with lumps of clay, letting it dry again and again. A hut of unbaked bricks, like a hut entirely of clay, is a single solid mass; a hut of baked bricks is not so. Therefore, some say it is allowable. If one makes a grass hut, etc., outside a hut entirely of clay and lives inside it, it is a dukkaṭa offense. If, having made holes here and there and having bound it, one makes it a single solid mass, it is allowable. If one makes a grass hut, etc., inside and lives inside it, it is allowable. If the maker himself lives in it, he commits a dukkaṭa offense on account of making it, not on account of living in it. If one plasters it with stucco on the inside or the outside or both, it is allowable. Because a hut entirely of clay is easy to break, a bowl, robe, etc., placed there is not secure; it can be carried off by thieves and others. Therefore it was said: ‘for the sake of the protection of the bowl and robes.’

Pāḷimuttakavinicchayavaṇṇanā

Explanation of Vinaya Decisions Not in the Pāli Text

Tena [M 0.0122] kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū uccāvace patte dhārenti, uccāvacāni pattamaṇḍalāni dhārentī”ti (cuḷava. 253) evamādīni vatthūni nissāya “na, bhikkhave, uccāvacā pattā dhāretabbā, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā nayena akappiyaparikkhāresu [V 0.0109] ca dukkaṭaṃ paññattaṃ. Kasmā? Tadanulomattā. Yatthāpi na paññattaṃ, tattha “na, bhikkhave, uccāvacāni chattāni dhāretabbāni, yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”tiādinā (cūḷava. 269-270) nayena dukkaṭaṃ sambhavati, tasmā “tatrāyaṃ pāḷimuttako”ti ārabhitvā sabbaparikkhāresu vaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ, savikāraṃ vā karontassa āpatti dukkaṭanti dīpentena “na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Etthāha – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ṭhapetvā paharaṇiṃ sabbaṃ lohabhaṇḍaṃ, ṭhapetvā āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ dārupattaṃ dārupādukaṃ sabbaṃ dārubhaṇḍaṃ, ṭhapetvā katakañca kumbhakārikañca sabbaṃ mattikābhaṇḍa”nti (cūḷava. 293) vuttattā yathāṭhapitaṃ vajjetvā itaraṃ sabbaṃ vaṇṇamaṭṭhampi savikārampi avisesena vaṭṭatīti? Vuccate – taṃ na yuttaṃ yathādassitapāḷivirodhato, tasmā “ṭhapetvā paharaṇi”nti evaṃ jātivasena ayaṃ pāḷi pavattā, yathādassitā pāḷi vaṇṇamaṭṭhādivikārapaṭisedhanavasena pavattāti evaṃ ubhayampi na virujjhati, tasmā yathāvuttameva. Āraggena nikhādanaggena, “āraggeriva sāsapo”ti (ma. ni. 2.458; dha. pa. 401; su. ni. 630) ettha vuttanayato āraggena.

Now at that time, the bhikkhus of the group of six were using various kinds of bowls and various kinds of bowl-mats. Based on such stories, it was laid down by the method beginning: ‘Bhikkhus, various kinds of bowls are not to be used. Whoever should use them, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.’ In this way, a dukkaṭa was also prescribed for unallowable requisites. Why? Because of its conformity with that. Even where it was not prescribed, a dukkaṭa arises by the method beginning: ‘Bhikkhus, various kinds of sunshades are not to be used. Whoever should use them, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.’ Therefore, beginning with, ‘Herein, this is a point not in the Pāli text,’ it should be understood that it was said, ‘It is not allowable,’ by the one who explains that for a person who makes any requisite polished or altered, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. Here, an objector says: ‘Since it is said, “I allow, bhikkhus, all metal goods except a weapon; all wooden goods except a long chair, a couch, a wooden bowl, and wooden sandals; all clay goods except a water-clearing nut pot and pottery,” does it mean that, having excluded what was set aside, all the rest, whether polished or altered, is allowable without distinction?’ The reply is: That is not proper, because it contradicts the Pāli as shown. Therefore, this Pāli passage, ‘except a weapon,’ proceeds by way of type, while the Pāli passage shown proceeds by way of prohibiting alterations such as polishing. Thus, both do not conflict. Therefore, it should be understood just as was stated. Āraggena: with the point of a stylus. From the method stated in the phrase ‘like a mustard seed on an awl-point,’ āraggena means with the point of an awl.

Paṭṭamukhe vāti paṭṭakoṭiyaṃ. Pariyanteti cīvarapariyante. Veṇiuhumuniyupeññāma. Agghiyanti cetiyaṃ. Gayamuggaranti tulādaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ, gayā sīse sūcikā hoti, mukhapattā ladrā. Ukkiranti nīharanti karonti ṭhapenti. Koṇasuttapiḷakā nāma gaṇṭhikapaṭṭādikoṇesu suttamayapiḷakā. Yaṃ ettha cīvaraṃ vā patto vā “na vaṭṭatī”ti vutto, tattha adhiṭṭhānaṃ ruhati, vikappanāpi ruhatīti veditabbaṃ. Deḍḍubhoti udakasappo. Acchīti kuñjarakkhi. Gomuttakanti gomuttasaṇṭhānā rājiyo. Kuñcikāya senāsanaparikkhārattā suvaṇṇarūpiyamayāpi vaṭṭatīti chāyā dissati, “kuñcikāya vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato aññe kappiyalohādimayāva kuñcikā kappanti pariharaṇīyaparikkhārattā. Ārakaṇṭako potthakādikaraṇasatthakajāti. “Āmaṇḍakasārako āmalakaphalamayo”ti vadanti[M 0.0123]. Tālapaṇṇabījanīādīsu “vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi tāni kuñcikā viya pariharaṇīyāni, atha kho “uccāvacāni na dhāretabbānī”ti paṭikkhepābhāvato vuttaṃ. Kevalañhi tāni “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vidhūpanañca tālavaṇṭañcā”tiādinā (cūḷava. 269) vuttāni. Gaṇṭhipade pana “telabhājanesu vaṇṇamaṭṭhakammaṃ vaṭṭatīti senāsanaparikkhārattā”ti vuttaṃ. Rājavallabhāti rājakulūpakā. Sīmāti idhādhippetā bhūmi, baddhasīmā ca. “Yesaṃ santakā tesaṃ sīmā, tattha parehi na kattabba”nti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Bhūmi ca sīmā ca yesaṃ santakā, tehi eva vāretabbā. Yesaṃ pana aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ sīmā katā, te vāretuṃ na issarā”ti vadanti[V 0.0110]. “Saṅghabhedādīnaṃ kāraṇattā ‘mā karothā’ti paṭisedhetabbā evā”ti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ kira.

`Paṭṭamukhe vāti`: at the end of the cloth strip. `Pariyanteti`: at the edge of the robe. `Veṇiuhumuniyupeññāma`: stitching in the manner of a braid. `Agghiyanti`: stitching in the shape of a cetiya. `Gayamuggaranti`: stitching in the shape of a balance-beam; the `gayā` is small at the head and large at the tip. `Ukkiranti, nīharanti, karonti, ṭhapenti`: they take out, they bring forth, they make, they place. `Koṇasuttapiḷakā nāma`: small thread-tassels at the corners of the belt-end, etc. Regarding whatever robe or bowl is said herein to be 'not allowable,' it should be understood that for such, a formal determination is valid, and a disposal is also valid. `Deḍḍubhoti`: a water snake. `Acchīti`: an elephant’s eye. `Gomuttakanti`: stripes in the shape of the path of cow's urine. Because a key is a requisite for the lodging, an impression is seen that even one made of gold and silver is allowable. But since it is said, ‘Polished work on a key is not allowable,’ other keys made only of allowable metals and so on are suitable, because it is a requisite to be carried about. `Ārakaṇṭako`: a type of curved-tip knife for incising palm-leaf books, etc. They say: ‘An `āmaṇḍakasāraka` is a container made from the āmalaka fruit.’ Regarding palm-leaf fans, etc., it is said: ‘Polished work is allowable.’ Although they, like a key, are requisites to be carried about, yet it is said so because of the absence of a prohibition, ‘Various kinds are not to be used.’ For they are simply mentioned in the passage beginning: ‘I allow, bhikkhus, a whisk-fan and a palm-leaf fan.’ But in the Gaṇṭhipada it is said: ‘Polished work on oil containers is allowable because they are requisites of the lodging.’ `Rājavallabhāti`: those who frequent the royal family. `Sīmāti`: here the intended meaning is land, and also a consecrated boundary. In the Anugaṇṭhipada it is said: ‘The boundary belongs to those who own it; it should not be made there by others.’ They say: ‘The land and the boundary belong to those who own them; they alone should prevent others. But those who have made a boundary on the land of others are not able to prevent them.’ It is said, it seems, in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā: ‘They should indeed be prevented with the words, “Do not do this,” because it is a cause for schism in the Sangha and so on.’

86-7. Dārukuṭikaṃ kātuṃ, kattunti ca atthi. Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikanti phalāphalaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āṇāpehīti vacanaṃ aniṭṭhe eva vuccatīti katvā bandhaṃ āṇāpesi. Issariyamattāyāti samiddhiyaṃ mattāsaddoti ñāpeti.

To make a wooden hut; and there is also the reading `kattuṃ`. `Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ` should be understood as being like `phalāphalaṃ` (fruit and non-fruit). The word `Āṇāpehi` (Command) is spoken only in regard to something undesirable; having considered this, he commanded the binding. Regarding `Issariyamattāya`: this shows that the word `mattā` is used in the sense of prosperity.

88. “Evarūpaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitvā”ti ca pāṭho. Lomena tvaṃ mutto, mā punapi evarūpamakāsīti idaṃ kiṃ byāpādadīpakaṃ, dārūsupi lobhakkhandhadīpakaṃ vacanaṃ sotāpannassa sato tassa rājassa patirūpaṃ. Nanu nāma “pubbe kataṃ sukataṃ bhante, vadeyyātha punapi yenattho”ti pavāretvā atīva pītipāmojjaṃ uppādetabbaṃ tena siyāti? Saccametaṃ sotāpannattā atīva buddhamāmako dhammamāmako saṅghamāmako ca, tasmā bhikkhūnaṃ akappiyaṃ asahanto, sikkhāpadapaññattiyā ca okāsaṃ kattukāmo “supayuttāni me dārūnī”ti tuṭṭhacittopi evamāhāti veditabbaṃ. Imehi nāma evarūpe ṭhāne. “Āgatapadānurūpenāti aññehi vā padehi, ito thokatarehi vā āgatakāle tadanurūpā yojanā kātabbā”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Na kevalaṃ imasmiṃyeva sikkhāpade, aññesupi āgacchanti, tasmā tattha tattha āgatapadānurūpena yojanā veditabbā”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Ujjhāyanattho adinnassādinnattāva, te ujjhāyiṃsu.

88. “Having spoken such words” is also a reading. Is this statement, 'You are released by a hair's breadth; do not do such a thing again,' which indicates ill will and, regarding the logs, indicates a mass of greed, fitting for that king, being a stream-enterer? Indeed, should he not, having invited them by saying, 'Venerable sirs, what was done by you before was well done. Again, whatever you have need of, you should speak of that,' have given rise to exceeding joy and delight? This is true. Because he was a stream-enterer, he was exceedingly devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Sangha. Therefore, being unable to endure what was unseemly for the monks, and wishing to create an occasion for the laying down of a training rule, even though his mind was pleased, he spoke thus—this should be understood. In such a case, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada (Explanatory Notes): 'According to the words that have come, whether with other words or with slightly fewer than these, when they come, a corresponding construction should be made.' It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada (Supplementary Explanatory Notes): 'Not only in this training rule, but they also occur in others; therefore, in each and every case, the construction should be understood according to the words that have come.' The complaining was on account of taking what was not given; they complained.

Rudradāmako nāma rudradāmakādīhi uppādito. Bārāṇasinagarādīsu tehi tehi rājūhi porāṇasatthānurūpaṃ lakkhaṇasampannā uppāditā nīlakahāpaṇā. Tesaṃ kira tibhāgaṃ agghati rudradāmako, tasmā tassa [M 0.0124] pādo thullaccayavatthu hoti. Māsako pana idha appamāṇaṃ. Kahāpaṇo kiñcikāle ūnavīsatimāsako hoti, kiñci kāle atirekavīsatimāsako. Tasmā tassa kahāpaṇassa catutthabhāgo pañcamāsako viya atirekapañcamāsako vā ūnapañcamāsako vā pādoti veditabbaṃ. Imassatthassa dīpanatthaṃ “tadā rājagahe vīsatimāsako kahāpaṇo hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rajatamayo suvaṇṇamayo tambamayo ca kahāpaṇo hoti. Suvaṇṇabhūmiyaṃ viya pādopi yattha tambamayova kato hoti, tattha sova pādoti ācariyo. Yasmā pādo ekanīlakahāpaṇagghanako, tasmā tassa pādassa catutthabhāgova siyā pādoti eke. Idaṃ na yujjati. Yo ca tattha pādāraho bhaṇḍo, tassa catutthabhāgasseva pārājikavatthubhāvappasaṅgato. Yadi pādārahaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ pārājikavatthu, siddhaṃ “sova pādo pacchimaṃ pārājikavatthū”ti[V 0.0111]. Na hi sabbattha bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā nīlakahāpaṇagghena agghāpenti. Yasmā tassa tasseva kahāpaṇagghena agghāpenti, tasmā tassa tassa janapadassa pādova pādoti tadagghanakameva pādagghanakanti siddhaṃ, “so ca kho porāṇassa nīlakahāpaṇassa vasena, na itaresanti yattha pana nīlakahāpaṇā vaḷañjaṃ gacchanti, tatthevā”ti keci vadanti, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ.

A coin named Rudradāmaka was issued by Rudradāmaka and others. In cities such as Bārāṇasī, nīlakahāpaṇas, endowed with marks according to ancient treatises, were issued by those various kings. It is said that a Rudradāmaka is worth a third part of those; therefore, a quarter of it constitutes an object of a thullaccaya offense. Here, however, a māsaka is not a standard measure. A kahāpaṇa is sometimes less than twenty māsakas and sometimes more than twenty māsakas. Therefore, a fourth part of that kahāpaṇa—whether it be like five māsakas, more than five māsakas, or less than five māsakas—should be understood as a pāda. To clarify this meaning, the text beginning, “At that time in Rājagaha, a kahāpaṇa was twenty māsakas,” was stated. There, a kahāpaṇa can be made of silver, gold, or copper. Where the pāda is also made only of copper, as in Suvaṇṇabhūmi, the teachers say that this itself is the pāda. Some say, “Since a pāda is worth one nīlakahāpaṇa, therefore only a fourth part of that pāda would be a pāda.” This is not correct, because it would lead to the consequence that only a fourth part of an item worth a pāda would become an object of a pārājika offense. If an item worth a pāda is an object of a pārājika offense, then the statement, “that very pāda is the lowest threshold for a pārājika offense,” is established. For they do not everywhere value an item according to the worth of a nīlakahāpaṇa. Since they value it according to the worth of the kahāpaṇa of that very region, it is therefore established that the pāda of that very region is the pāda; thus, an item of that value is an item worth a pāda. Some say that the statement, “And that is with reference to the ancient nīlakahāpaṇa, not others,” applies only where nīlakahāpaṇas are in circulation. This should be accepted after investigation.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Word-by-word Analysis

92. Gāmā vā araññā vāti lakkhaṇānupaññattikattā paṭhamapaññattiyā ādimhi vuttā. Yato vā apakkantā, so amanusso nāma. “Amanussagāmaṃ apārupitvā, gāmappavesanañca anāpucchā pavisituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Yato gāmato āgantukāmā eva apakkantā, taṃ gāmaṃ evaṃ pavisituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti eke. Keci pana “yakkhapariggahabhūtopi āpaṇādīsu dissamānesu eva ‘gāmo’ti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, adissamānesu pavesane anāpattī”ti vadanti. “Gāmo eva upacāro gāmūpacāroti evaṃ kammadhārayavasena gahite kurundaṭṭhakathādīsu vuttampi suvuttameva hotī”ti vadanti. “Tassa gharūpacāro gāmoti āpajjatī”ti vacanaṃ paṭikkhipati. “Gāmassupacāro ca gāmo ca gāmūpacāro cā”ti vadanti, taṃ virujjhati, na. “Imesaṃ lābhādīsu lakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘gharaṃ gharūpacāro’tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ na mayaṃ paṭikkhipāmā”ti ca vadanti. “Kataparikkhepo [M 0.0125] cāti gharassa samantato tattako upacāro nāmā”ti gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “yo yo aṭṭhakathāvādo vā theravādo vā pacchā vuccatīti ito anāgataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, nātītaṃ. Yadi atītampi sandhāya vuttaṃ, mahāpadumatheravādova pamāṇaṃ jātanti āpajjati, tasmā anāgatameva sandhāya vuttanti ācariyā kathayantī”ti vuttaṃ. Sesampīti gāmūpacāralakkhaṇampi.

92. “Whether from a village or from the wilderness”—this is stated at the beginning of the first enactment because it is a subsequent designation marking the basis of a pārājika offense. A village from which people have departed, even with the intention of returning, is called an 'uninhabited village' (amanusso). “It is permissible to enter an uninhabited village without covering oneself with the outer robe and without asking permission for entering the village,” as stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. Some say, “When they have departed from a village with the intention of returning, it is not permissible to enter that village in this way.” But others say, “Even a village that has become possessed by yakkhas is counted as a 'village' only when shops and so on are visible; when they are not visible, there is no offense in entering.” They also say, “When 'gāmūpacāro' is taken as a kammadhāraya compound meaning 'the village itself is the vicinity' (gāmo eva upacāro), then what is said in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā and other texts is indeed well-said.” This rejects the statement that implies, “The vicinity of a house is a village.” They say, “'Gāmūpacāro' means 'the vicinity of the village and the village'.” Does that contradict? It does not. And they also say, “Referring to the characteristics of these in regard to gain and so on, it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā 'a house, the vicinity of a house,' etc. We do not reject that statement.” Regarding “having made a boundary,” it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada: “The area of such an extent all around a house is called the 'vicinity'.” But in the Anugaṇṭhipada it is stated: “This statement, 'Whatever commentary view or elders' view is stated later,' is said with reference to what is yet to come, not to the past. If it were said with reference to the past as well, it would imply that the view of the great elder Mahāpaduma would become the standard. Therefore, the teachers explain that it is said with reference only to what is yet to come.” By “and the rest,” the characteristic of the village vicinity is also to be understood.

Tatrāyaṃ nayoti tassa gāmūpacārassa gahaṇe ayaṃ nayo. Vikālegāmappavesanādīsūti ettha “gāmappavesanañhi bahi eva āpucchitabba”nti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Taṃ aṭṭhakathāya na sametī”ti vadanti. “Gāmasaṅkhātūpacāraṃ sandhāya vutta”nti gahite sametīti mama takko. “Ādi-saddato ghare ṭhitānaṃ dinnalābhabhājanādīnī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Gāmūpacāre ṭhitānaṃ pāpuṇitabbalābhaṃ sañcicca adentānaṃ pārājika”nti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi kurundiādīsu pāḷiyaṃ vuttavacanānulomavasena vuttattā “pamādalekhā”ti na vattabbaṃ, mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 0.0112] vuttavinicchayo saṅgītito paṭṭhāya āgato. “Yañcetaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāya”ntiādi sīhaḷadīpe aṭṭhakathācariyehi vuttaṃ “vinicchayanayo”ti ca. Leḍḍupāteneva paricchinditabboti parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ, na upacāraṃ. So hi tato aparena leḍḍupātena paracchinno. Imasmiṃ adinnādānasikkhāpadeti niyamena aññattha aññathāti atthato vuttaṃ hoti. Tena vā niyamena yathārutavasenāpi attho idha yujjati. Abhidhamme panātiādinā aññathāpi atthāpattisiddhaṃ dasseti.

Herein is the method for understanding that village vicinity. Regarding entering a village at an improper time and so forth, it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: “Indeed, permission to enter a village should be asked for only from outside.” They say, “This does not accord with the Aṭṭhakathā.” It is my reasoning that if it is taken as referring to the vicinity designated as the village, it does accord. It is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: “By the word ‘ādi’ (etc.) are meant bowls and so on, which are the gains given to those staying in a house.” It is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: “For monks staying in the village vicinity who intentionally do not give a gain that should be received, it is a pārājika offense.” Although, because it is stated in the Kurundī and other commentaries in accordance with the words spoken in the Pāḷi, it should not be called a ‘careless writing’, the judgment stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā has come down from the time of the Saṅgīti. The passage beginning “And this which is in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā…” was stated by the commentary teachers in the island of Sri Lanka, and it was also called “the method of judgment.” By “it should be demarcated only by the toss of a clod,” the place suitable for an enclosure is shown, not the vicinity. For that vicinity is indeed demarcated from there by another toss of a clod. In this precept on taking what is not given, by this rule, it is said in terms of meaning that it is one way here, and otherwise elsewhere. Or, by that rule, the meaning is suitable here even according to the literal sense. By the passage beginning “But in the Abhidhamma…”, it is shown that the meaning is also established in another way by implication.

“Pariccāgādimhi akate ‘idaṃ mama santaka’nti aviditampi parapariggahitameva puttakānaṃ pitu accayena santakaṃ viya, taṃ atthato apariccatte saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Thenassa kammaṃ theyyaṃ, thenena gahetabbabhūtaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ. Theyyanti saṅkhātanti theyyasaṅkhāta”nti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Taṃ theyyaṃ yassa thenassa kammaṃ, so yasmā theyyacitto avaharaṇacitto hoti, tasmā “theyyasaṅkhāta”nti padaṃ uddharitvā “theyyacitto avaharaṇacitto”ti padabhājanampi tesaṃ porāṇānaṃ yujjateva, tathāpi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. “Yañca pubbabhāge ‘avaharissāmī’ti pavattaṃ cittaṃ, yañca gamanādisādhakaṃ, parāmasanādisādhakaṃ vā majjhe pavattaṃ, yañca ṭhānācāvanapayogasādhakaṃ[M 0.0126], tesu ayameveko pacchimo cittakoṭṭhāso idha adhippeto ‘theno’ti apare”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Ūnamāsakamāsapādādīsu “avaharaṇacittesu ekacittakoṭṭhāsoti ācariyā vadantī”ti vuttaṃ.

“Even when relinquishment, etc., has not been made, and even if it is not known [by the heir] as ‘this is my property’, it is indeed property appropriated by another, just like the property of sons after the passing of their father. In essence, not having been relinquished, it is included [under appropriation].” This is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada. “The act of a thief is theft. The goods that are to be taken by the thief are designated as ‘theft’; therefore, it is called ‘designated as theft’.” This is stated in the ancient Gaṇṭhipada. That theft is the act of whichever thief; because he has a thieving mind, a mind to misappropriate, therefore, having extracted the term ‘designated as theft’, the word-analysis by those ancient teachers as ‘a thieving mind, a mind to misappropriate’ is indeed suitable. Nevertheless, it should be understood only by the method stated in the commentary. “And whichever thought has arisen in the preliminary stage as ‘I will steal’; and whichever thought has arisen in the middle, which accomplishes going, handling, etc.; and whichever thought accomplishes the effort of moving [it] from its place—among these, only this one, the last portion of thought, is intended here as ‘the thief’, according to others.” This is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. Regarding [items worth] less than a māsaka, a māsaka, a pāda, etc., it is said: “The teachers say that among minds intent on misappropriating, it is one portion of thought.”

Pañcavīsatiavahārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Twenty-Five Kinds of Misappropriation

Pañcavīsati avahārā nāma vacanabhedeneva bhinnā, atthato pana abhinnā. Ākulā duviññeyyavinicchayāti ācariyānaṃ mukhe santike sabbākārena aggahitavinicchayānaṃ duviññeyyā. Dukatikapaṭṭhānapāḷi (paṭṭhā. 5.1.1 ādayo, dukatikapaṭṭhānapāḷi) viya ākulā duviññeyyavinicchayā, kevalaṃ taṃ ācariyā pubbāparavirodhamakatvā saṅgītito paṭṭhāya āgatanayamavināsetvā vaṇṇayantīti “paṭṭhānapāḷimivāti apare vadantī”ti ca vuttā. Porāṇāti saṅgītiācariyā. Ayamettha sāmīci eva, sace na deti, āpatti natthi, pārājikabhayā pana yathā sikkhākāmo deti, evaṃ dātabbameva. Yāni panettha vatthūni, tāni sīhaḷadīpe ācariyehi saṅghādīnamanumatiyā aṭṭhakathāsu pakkhittāni, “anāgate brahmacārīnaṃ hitatthāya potthakāruḷhakālato pacchāpī”ti vuttaṃ. Āṇattikaṃ āṇattikkhaṇepi gaṇhāti, kālantarenāpi atthasādhako, kālantaraṃ sandhāyāti idametesaṃ nānattaṃ. Bhaṭṭheti apagate. Antarasamudde [V 0.0113] aturumuhude. Pharati sādheti. Navadhototi navakato. Pāsāṇasakkharanti pāsāṇañca sakkharañca.

The twenty-five kinds of theft are distinguished only by verbal expression, but in meaning they are not different. They are confused and difficult to discern in their determination; that is, for those who have not grasped the determination in all aspects in the presence of the teachers, they are difficult to discern. Like the Dukatikapaṭṭhānapāḷi, they are confused and difficult to discern in their determination. However, the teachers, without making any contradiction between earlier and later, explain them without destroying the method that has come down from the Saṅgīti. Thus, it is said, 'Others say it is like the Paṭṭhānapāḷi.' The ancients are the teachers of the Saṅgīti. This is indeed the proper course here. If one does not give, there is no offense, but out of fear of a pārājika, one should certainly give, just as one who desires training would. The cases here, however, were inserted into the commentaries by the teachers in Sri Lanka with the approval of the Saṅgha and others, with it being said, 'For the benefit of future holy-life practitioners, even after the time of their being written into books.' Theft by command (`āṇattika`) is taken even at the moment of the command; theft for one's own purpose (`atthasādhaka`) occurs after a time interval. This is their difference, with reference to the time interval. `Bhaṭṭheti` means 'when gone away'. `Antarasamudde` means `aturumuhude`. `Pharati` means `sādheti` (accomplishes). `Navadhoto` means 'newly made'. `Pāsāṇasakkharaṃ` means 'stone and gravel'.

Bhūmaṭṭhakathādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Bhūmaṭṭhakathā and so forth.

94. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana saccepi alikepi dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ, taṃ pamādalikhitanti veditabbanti yathetarahi yuttiyā gahetabbā. Tattha “catuvaggena ṭhapetvā upasampadapavāraṇaabbhānādisabbaṃ saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati”cceva vattabbe “upasampadapavāraṇakathinabbhānādīnī”ti likhantīti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ ācariyā “pamādalekhā”tveva vaṇṇayanti, tena vuttaṃ “pamādalikhita”nti. Yaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ musā, tattha tattha pācittiyanti vuttaṃ. Dukkaṭassa vacane payojanābhāvā “adinnādānassa pubbapayoge”ti vuttaṃ. Aññesampi pubbapayoge pācittiyaṭṭhāne pācittiyameva. Pamādalikhitanti ettha [M 0.0127] idha adhippetameva gahetvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanti gahite sameti viya. Ācariyā pana “pācittiyaṭṭhāne pācittiya”nti vatvā dukkaṭe visuṃ vattabbe “saccālike”ti sāmaññato vuttattā “pamādalekhā”ti vadantīti veditabbāti. “Kusalacittena gamane anāpattī”ti vuttattā “dānañca dassāmī”ti vacanena anāpatti viya.

94. However, in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā, it is stated that even in the case of truth or falsehood, it is only a dukkaṭa. That should be understood as 'written through negligence'; now, this should be accepted by reason. There, when it should have been stated, 'It is permissible for a group of four to perform all Saṅgha acts, except for ordination, invitation, rehabilitation, and so on,' it is written as 'ordination, invitation, Kathina, rehabilitation, and so on.' This should be understood. The teachers explain this indeed as 'negligent writing'; therefore, it is said to be 'written through negligence'. Wherever a statement is false, it is said that there is a pācittiya offense. Since there is no purpose in stating a dukkaṭa, it is said, 'in the preliminary act of taking what is not given.' For the preliminary acts of others as well, in a case for a pācittiya, it is only a pācittiya. Regarding 'written through negligence,' if it is taken that what is intended here is indeed what is stated in the commentary, it appears to be consistent. However, the teachers, having stated 'where a pācittiya applies, a pācittiya is incurred,' say that it is 'negligent writing' because the dukkaṭa, which should be stated separately, is stated generally as 'in the case of truth or falsehood.' This should be understood. Because it is said, 'There is no offense when going with a wholesome mind,' it is like there is no offense in the statement, 'And I will give a gift.'

Pācittiyaṭṭhāne dukkaṭā na muccatīti pācittiyena saddhiṃ dukkaṭamāpajjati. Bahukāpi āpattiyo hontūti khaṇanabyūhanuddharaṇesu dasa dasa katvā āpattiyo āpanno, tesu uddharaṇe dasa pācittiyo desetvā muccati, jātivasena “ekameva desetvā muccatī”ti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā purimena sameti. “Samodhānetvā dassitapayoge “dukkaṭa”nti vuttattā samānapayogā bahudukkaṭattaṃ ñāpeti. Khaṇane bahukānīti samānapayogattā na paṭippassambhati. Aṭṭhakathācariyappamāṇenāti yathā panettha, evaṃ aññesupi evarūpāni aṭṭhakathāya āgatavacanāni saṅgītito paṭṭhāya āgatattā gahetabbānīti attho. “Idha dutiyapārājike gahetabbā, na aññesū”ti dhammasiritthero kirāha. Gaṇṭhipade pana “purimakhaṇanaṃ pacchimaṃ patvā paṭippassambhati, teneva ekameva desetvā muccatī”ti vuttaṃ, “visabhāgakiriyaṃ vā patvā purimaṃ paṭippassambhatī”ti ca vuttaṃ.

In the case of a pācittiya, one is not freed from a dukkaṭa; one incurs a dukkaṭa together with the pācittiya. Even if there are many offenses—for instance, a monk who has incurred ten offenses each for digging, scraping, and removing—among those, for the offenses of removing, he is freed by confessing the ten pācittiyas. By the power of the category, it is said in the Kurundī, 'One is freed by confessing only one'; therefore, this agrees with the earlier statement. Because it is said 'a dukkaṭa' in the effort shown by combining instances, this indicates a state of many dukkaṭas due to the similar action. In digging, the many offenses do not cease due to the similar action. The meaning of 'by the authority of the commentary teachers' should be understood thus: just as here in this second pārājika, so too in other training rules, such statements that have come down in the commentary should be accepted because they have come down from the time of the Council onwards. The Elder Dhammasiri reportedly said, 'It should be accepted here in the second pārājika, not in others.' But in the Gaṇṭhipada it is said, 'The earlier digging ceases upon reaching the later, and for that very reason one is freed by confessing only one.' And it is also said, 'Or, upon reaching a dissimilar action, the earlier action ceases.'

Evaṃ ekaṭṭhāne ṭhitāya kumbhiyā ṭhānācāvanañcettha chahākārehi veditabbanti sambandho. Kumbhiyāti bhummavacanaṃ. Uddhaṃ ukkhipanto kesaggamattampi bhūmito moceti, pārājikanti ettha mukhavaṭṭiyā [V 0.0114] phuṭṭhokāsaṃ bundena mocite “ṭhānācāvanañcettha chahākārehi veditabba”nti iminā sameti, tathā avatvā “bhūmito mutte kesaggamattampi atikkante bhūmito mocitaṃ nāma hotī”ti daḷhaṃ katvā vadanti, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Ettha ekacce evaṃ atthaṃ vadanti “pubbe khaṇantena avasesaṭṭhānāni viyojitāni, tasmiṃ vimutte pārājika”nti. Saṅkhepamahāpaccariyādīsu vuttavacanassa pamādalekhabhāvo “attano bhājanagataṃ vā karoti, muṭṭhiṃ vā chindatī”ti vacanena dīpito.

Thus, the connection should be made that 'here, the moving of a pot situated in one place from its spot should also be understood in six ways.' The word 'kumbhiyā' is a locative term. Lifting it upwards, if one frees it from the ground even by a hair's breadth, it is a pārājika. Here, when the place touched by the rim is freed by the base, it agrees with this statement: 'the moving from its place here should also be understood in six ways.' Without stating it thus, they firmly declare, 'When it is freed from the ground and has passed beyond it even by a hair's breadth, it is called "moved from the ground."' This should be accepted after investigation. Here, some explain the meaning thus: 'Previously, by the one digging, the remaining places were separated; when that pot is freed, it is a pārājika.' That the statement made in the Saṅkhepa, Mahāpaccarī, and so forth, is a careless writing is shown by the text: 'He either makes it his own vessel, or cuts off a fistful.'

Yaṃ pana “pītamatte pārājika”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ yathetarahi “pañcaviññāṇā uppannavatthukā uppannārammaṇā”ti padassa “uppannavatthukāhi anāgatapaṭikkhepo”ti [M 0.0128] aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ “asambhinnavatthukā asambhinnārammaṇā purejātavatthukā purejātārammaṇā”ti vacanamapekkhitvā atītānāgatapaṭikkhepoti parivatteti, tathā tādisehi parivatta’nti veditabbaṃ. Na hi aṭṭhakathācariyā pubbāparaviruddhaṃ vadanti. Yaṃ pana ācariyā “idaṃ pamādalikhita”nti apanetvā paṭikkhipitvā vacanakāle vācenti, uddisanti, tameva ca imināpi ācariyena “pamādalikhita”nti paṭikkhittaṃ. Yañca suttaṃ dassetvā te paṭikkhipanti, tameva ca dassentena iminā paṭikkhittaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “taṃ pana tatthevā”tiādi.

As for the statement, 'a pārājika upon mere drinking,' it should be understood as being reinterpreted by such means, just as now the commentary's statement for the phrase 'the five consciousnesses have an arisen basis and an arisen object'—namely, 'the rejection of the future by means of an arisen basis'—is reinterpreted as 'the rejection of the past and future' by considering the statement 'with an unmixed basis and unmixed object, with a pre-arisen basis and pre-arisen object.' Indeed, the Aṭṭhakathā teachers do not speak in a way that contradicts earlier and later statements. Furthermore, the statement that the teachers set aside and reject at the time of recitation or teaching, saying, 'This is a careless writing,' that very statement has also been rejected by this teacher. And that which they reject after showing a sutta, that very thing is shown and rejected by this teacher. Therefore, it was said, 'but that is right there,' and so forth.

Anāpattimattameva vuttanti neva avahāro na gīvā anāpattīti byañjanatova bhedo, na atthatoti dassanatthaṃ. Taṃ pamādalikhitaṃ katarehīti ce? Pubbe vuttappakārehi, lekhakehi vā, esa nayo sabbattha. “Na hi tadeva bahūsu ṭhānesu yuttato pārājikamahutvā katthaci hotī”ti sabbaṃ anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Duṭṭhapitaṃ vā ṭhapetīti ettha tato paggharissatīti ṭhānācāvanaṃ sandhāya katattā pārājikaṃ taṃ pana gaṇhatu vā mā vā tattheva “bhindatī”tiādivacanato veditabbaṃ. “Tatthevāti ṭhānācāvanaṃ akarontova ṭhānā acāvetukāmova kevalaṃ ‘bhindatī’ti aṭṭhakathāvacanato ca ñāpetabba”nti aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Tathā “paggharitehi tintapaṃsuṃ gahetvā udake pakkhipitvā pacitvā gahetuṃ sakkā, tasmā gahaṇameva sandhāya vutta”nti apare. “Rittakumbhiyā upari karoti, bhaṇḍadeyya”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ āṇattiyā virujjhati, “yadā sakkosi, tadā taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti atthasādhako āṇattikāle eva pārājikaṃ. Apica āvāṭakādīni thāvarapayogāni ca ettha sādhakāni. Natthi kālakatapayogāni pārājikavatthūnīti tasmā upaparikkhitabbanti eke. Yattha yattha “apare”ti vā “eke”ti vā vuccati, tattha tattha suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā yuttaṃ gahetabbaṃ, itaraṃ chaḍḍetabbaṃ. Vadantīti ācariyā vadanti. Na, aññathā gahetabbatthatoti pāḷipariharaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evameke vadantīti taṃ [V 0.0115] na gahetabbaṃ. Kasmā? “Passāvaṃ vā chaḍḍetī”ti ca “aparibhogaṃ vā karotī”ti ca atthato ekattā, aṭṭhakathāya “muggarena pothetvā bhindatī”ti vuttattāpi.

The statement 'Only "no offense" is mentioned' is for the purpose of showing that the ruling 'neither taking nor swallowing is no offense' is a difference only in wording, not in meaning. If it is asked, 'By whom was that carelessly written?' one should answer: 'By those of the type previously mentioned, or by scribes.' This is the method in all cases. For it is not the case that the very same thing, while not being a Pārājika in many suitable instances, becomes a Pārājika in a certain instance; all this is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. In the phrase, 'Or one places it having been damaged,' here, because it is done with reference to moving it from its place so that it will flow out from there, it is a Pārājika. Whether one takes that object or not, it should be understood from the statement 'he breaks' and so forth, right there. In a certain Gaṇṭhipada it is said: 'As for "right there," it should be understood that while not moving it from its place, and while desiring not to move it from its place, one merely "breaks" it, solely from the commentary's statement to that effect.' Similarly, others say: 'From that which has flowed out, it is possible to take wet earth, put it in water, strain it, and then take the substance; therefore, it is said with reference only to the act of taking.' It is said, 'He does it over an empty pot; it would be a gift of a vessel.' That contradicts the case of an order. In the case of 'When you are able, then steal that item,' which fulfills the purpose, the Pārājika occurs at the very time of the order. Furthermore, pits and other permanent applications are proof in this matter. Some say: 'There are no temporary applications that are grounds for a Pārājika offense; therefore, this should be examined.' Wherever it is said 'others' or 'some,' in that very place one should examine it well, accept what is suitable, and reject the other. 'They say' means the teachers say. 'No, it is not to be taken otherwise'—this is said for the purpose of preserving the Pāli. The statement, 'Thus some say,' should not be accepted. Why? Because 'or one discards urine' and 'or one makes it unusable' are one in meaning, and also because it is said in the commentary, 'having struck it with a club, he breaks it.'

Ayaṃ [M 0.0129] panettha sārotiādikathāya “amhākaṃ ācariyassa vacana”nti dhammasiritthero āha. Saṅgahācariyānaṃ vādoti eke. Pubbe vuttāpi te eva, tasmā vohāravasenāti achaḍḍetukāmampi tathā karontaṃ “chaḍḍetī”ti voharanti. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ attho gahetabboti evaṃ sante “ṭhānācāvanassa natthitāya dukkaṭa”nti aṭṭhakathāvacanena ativiya sameti, tattha ṭhānācāvanacittassa natthitāya ṭhānā cutampi na “ṭhānā cuta”nti vuccatīti attho gahetabbo. Itarathāpīti theyyacittābhāvā ṭhānā cāvetukāmassapi dukkaṭaṃ yujjati.

In the discussion beginning with 'This is the essence here,' the Elder Dhammasiri said, 'It is the word of our teacher.' Some say it is the doctrine of the Saṅgaha teachers. Even the teachers previously mentioned are those very same ones; therefore, by way of conventional usage, even one who does not wish to abandon but acts in such a way is spoken of as 'abandoning.' Thus, the meaning of these terms should be understood. This being so, it agrees exceedingly well with the commentary's statement, 'Due to the absence of moving from the place, there is a dukkaṭa.' There, because of the absence of the thought of moving from the place, even if it is moved from the place, it is not called 'moved from the place'; this is the meaning to be understood. In the other case as well, due to the absence of the thought of theft, a dukkaṭa offense is appropriate even for one who wishes to move it from its place.

96. Sayameva patitamorasseva ito cito ca karoto thullaccayaṃ. Ākāsaṭṭhavinicchaye tappasaṅgena tasmiṃ vehāsādigatepi asammohatthaṃ evaṃ gahetabbanti vuttaṃ. “Evamaññatrāpi sāmise”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Ṭhānācāvanaṃ akaronto cāletī”ti vacanato ṭhānācāvane thullaccayaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Keci aphandāpetvā ṭhānācāvanācāvanehipi dukkaṭathullaccaye vadanti. “Te ṭhānācāvanaṃ akarontoti imaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ dassetvā paṭisedhetabbā”ti keci vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

96. Just as for a peacock that has fallen by itself, for one who moves it here and there, there is a thullaccaya offense. In the determination concerning things in space, it is said that it should be understood thus for the sake of non-bewilderment, by connection with that, even regarding an object situated in the air, etc. 'Likewise elsewhere too, in a case involving a material object,' is said in the Gaṇṭhipada. Because of the statement, 'He moves it without causing it to be moved from its place,' it comes to be said that there is no thullaccaya offense in moving it from its place. Some say that without causing it to shake, by both moving it from its place and not moving it from its place, there are dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses. Some say, 'They should be refuted by showing this commentary statement: “Not causing it to be moved from its place.”' This should be investigated.

97. Chedanamocanādi uparibhāgaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Avassaṃ ṭhānato ākāsagataṃ karoti. Ettha “ekakoṭiṃ nīharitvā ṭhapite vaṃse ṭhitassa ākāsakaraṇaṃ sandhāyā”ti keci vadanti. Te pana atha “mūlaṃ acchetvā valayaṃ ito cito ca sāreti, rakkhati. Sace pana mūlato anīharitvāpi hatthena gahetvā ākāsagataṃ karoti, pārājika”nti aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ dassetvā paṭisedhetabbā. Bhittinissitanti bhittiyā upatthambhitaṃ sandhāya vuttanti eke. Bhittiṃ nissāya ṭhapitanti nāgadantādīsu ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Chinnamatteti upari uggantvā ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

97. Cutting and releasing, etc., are said with reference to the upper part. It certainly causes it to be in the air from its place. Here, some say, ‘It refers to causing to be in the air something standing on a bamboo that has had one end removed and left standing.’ But they should be refuted by showing the commentary statement: ‘If, without cutting the root, one moves the ring back and forth, he protects himself. But if even without removing it from the root, he takes it with his hand and causes it to be in the air, it is a defeat offense.’ ‘Supported by a wall’ is said with reference to something propped up by a wall, according to some. ‘Leaning against a wall’ refers to standing supported by things like coat-hooks. ‘Just by being cut’ is said with reference to what stands projecting upwards.

98. Upari ṭhitassa piṭṭhiyāti ettha adho osāraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā osārentassa uparimassa piṭṭhiyā heṭṭhimena ṭhitokāsaṃ atikkantamatte pārājikaṃ, uddhaṃ ukkhipantassa udakato muttamatte. “Evaṃ gahite [M 0.0130] bhūmaṭṭhe vuttena sametī”ti vadanti. Matamacchānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānameva ṭhānaṃ kira. Theyyacittena māretvā gaṇhato ūnapādagghanake dukkaṭaṃ, sahapayogattā pācittiyaṃ natthīti eke. Madanaphalavasādīnīti ettha sīhaḷabhāsā kira vasa iti visanti attho, garuḷākārena katuppeyitaṃ vā.

98. Regarding the phrase ‘for one standing above, on the back,’ this is said with reference to lowering it. For one lowering something, it is a pārājika offense as soon as the lower edge of the upper one’s surface passes its original position; for one lifting something upward, it is as soon as it is released from the water. Some say, ‘When taken in this way, this agrees with what was said in the case of something on the ground.’ The place where dead fish are is indeed their ‘place.’ If, with the intention of stealing, one kills and takes something worth less than a quarter, there is a dukkaṭa offense; some say there is no pācittiya offense because it is a conjoined effort. Regarding ‘intoxicating fruits, vasa, etc.,’ here, ‘vasa’ is said to be a Sinhala word meaning ‘poison,’ or it refers to something prepared in the form of a garuḍa.

99. Pubbe [V 0.0116] pāse baddhasūkaraupamāya vuttā eva. “Thale ṭhapitāya nāvāya na phuṭṭhokāsamattamevā”ti pāṭho. “Vāto āgammāti vacanato vātassa natthikāle payogassa katattā avahāro natthi, atthikāle ce kato, avahārovā”ti vadanti. “Bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ pana kesanti ce? Yesaṃ hatthe kahāpaṇāni gahitāni, tesaṃ vā, nāvāsāminā nāvāya aggahitāya nāvāsāmikassa vā”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

99. Previously, this was already stated by way of the simile of a pig caught in a snare. There is a reading: ‘For a boat placed on land, it is not merely the space it touches.’ They say: ‘Because of the thought “The wind will come,” if the effort is made when there is no wind, it is not a theft; but if it is done when there is wind, it is indeed a theft.’ It is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: ‘If it is asked, “But to whom should the payment for the goods be given?” It should be given to those from whose hands the coins were taken, or, if the boat is not taken by the boat-owner, to the boat-owner.’

104. Nirambitvā upari. Akataṃ vā pana patiṭṭhapetīti apubbaṃ vā paṭṭhapetīti attho.

104. The phrase ‘Without support above, or one establishes what was not made’ means one establishes what is new.

106. Gāmaṭṭhe vā “gāmo nāmā”ti na vuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ gāmalakkhaṇassa sabbaso vuttattā.

106. In the commentary on the village section, the phrase ‘a village, namely...’ was not stated at the beginning, because the characteristic of a village had already been fully stated.

107. Araññaṭṭhe araññaṃ nāmāti puna na kevalaṃ pubbe vuttalakkhaṇaññeva araññanti idhādhippetaṃ, kintu parapariggahitameva cetaṃ hoti, taṃ idhādhippetanti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva atthepi araññaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Aggepi mūlepi chinnāti ettha “na veṭhetvā ṭhitā, chinnamatte patanakaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vadanti. Tacchetvā ṭhapitoti araññasāmikehi parehi laddhehi tacchetvā ṭhapito. Addhagatopīti cirakālikopi. “Na gahetabboti araññasāmikehi anuññātenapī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Challiyā pariyonaddhaṃ hotīti iminā sāmikānaṃ nirapekkhataṃ dīpeti. Tena vuttaṃ “gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Yadi sāmikānaṃ sāpekkhatā atthi, na vaṭṭati.

107. In the commentary on the wilderness section, the term ‘wilderness’ is not intended here again to mean merely the wilderness with the previously stated characteristic; rather, it is stated to show that what is intended here is a wilderness that has been claimed by others. For that very reason, the term ‘wilderness’ is used in the explanation as well. Regarding ‘cut at the top and at the root,’ they say: ‘It does not mean standing entangled; it is said in reference to a tree that would fall as soon as it is cut.’ ‘Adzed and placed’ means it was adzed and placed by others who have obtained it from the owners of the wilderness. ‘Even having reached a long time’ means even after a considerable period. Regarding ‘It should not be taken,’ it is stated in the Gaṇṭhipada: ‘It should not be taken even if permitted by the owners of the wilderness.’ By the phrase ‘it is wrapped with bark,’ the owners’ lack of concern is indicated. Therefore it is said, ‘It is allowable to take.’ If the owners have concern, it is not allowable.

108. Tattha “bhājanesu pokkharaṇītaḷākesu ca gāvo pakkosatīti ito paṭṭhāya tayo dasa vārā ādimeva dassetvā saṃkhittā”ti [M 0.0131] anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Nibbahanaudakaṃ nāma taḷākarakkhaṇatthāya adhikodakanikkhamanadvārena nikkhamanaudakaṃ. “Gahetuṃ na labhatīti sāmīcikammaṃ na hotī”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Ito paṭṭhāya “vutta”nti vutte anugaṇṭhipadeti gahetabbaṃ. Anikkhante udaketi pāṭhaseso, sukkhamātikāpayogattā bhaṇḍadeyyampi na hotīti adhippāyo. Taḷākaṃ nissāya khettassa katattāti “sabbasādhāraṇaṃ taḷākaṃ hotī”ti paṭhamaṃ vuttattā taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Yasmā taḷākagataṃ udakaṃ sabbasādhāraṇampi mātikāya sati taṃ atikkamitvā gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā taṃ sandhāya kurundiyādīsu avahāroti vutta”nti apare āhūti. Iminā lakkhaṇena na sametīti yasmā sabbasādhāraṇadeso nāma tañca taḷākaṃ sabbasādhāraṇaṃ, katikābhāvā ca mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva yuttanti āhācariyo.

108. Therein, it is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: ‘From the passage “in vessels, ponds, and lakes, one calls the cows” onwards, the three ten-fold sections, having been shown only at the beginning, are summarized.’ ‘Outflow-water’ (nibbahanaudaka) is the water that flows out through an outlet for excess water for the purpose of protecting the reservoir. It is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: ‘One is not able to take it; thus, it is not proper conduct.’ From this point onwards, when ‘it is said’ (vuttaṃ) is stated, it should be understood as ‘in the Anugaṇṭhipada.’ ‘When the water has not flowed out’ is a remainder of the text; the meaning is that because of the effort made in a dry channel, it is not even a case where payment for the goods is required. Because the field was made depending on the reservoir, and because it was first said, ‘the reservoir is for common use,’ it is stated with reference to that. Others say: ‘Because, although the water in the reservoir is for common use, when a channel exists, it is not allowable to take it by going beyond that channel; therefore, with reference to that, it is said in the Kurundī and other commentaries that it is a theft.’ The teacher said: ‘It does not accord with this characteristic, because what is called a place for common use is that very reservoir, which is for common use, and because there is no agreement, what is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is indeed correct.’

109. “Tato [V 0.0117] paṭṭhāya avahāro natthīti theyyāyapi gaṇhato, tasmā yathāmuṇḍamahājetabbattā, arakkhitabbattā, sabbasādhāraṇattā ca aññampi saṅghasantakaṃ idaṃ na hotī”ti gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

109. It is said in the Gaṇṭhipada: ‘From that point onwards, there is no theft, even for one who takes it with the intention to steal; therefore, because it is a thing to be won by shaven-headed monks in any way whatsoever, because it is unguarded, and because it is common to all, this is not other property of the Sangha either.’

110. Ujukameva tiṭṭhatīti ettha “samīpe rukkhasākhādīhi sandhāritattā īsakaṃ khalitvā ujukameva tiṭṭhati ce, avahāro. Chinnaveṇu viya tiṭṭhati ce, anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ suvuttaṃ, tassa vinicchaye “sace tāni rakkhantī”ti vuttattā. No aññathāti sampatte ce vāte vātamukhasodhanaṃ karoti, pārājikanti attho.

110. Herein, regarding ‘it stands upright’: It is said, ‘If, because of being supported by nearby tree branches and so on, it stumbles slightly and yet stands upright, it is a theft. If it stands like a cut bamboo, there is no offense.’ That is well said, because in the legal decision concerning crops, it is said, ‘if they guard them.’ Regarding ‘not otherwise’: If, when the wind has come, one clears the path of the wind, it is a pārājika offense; this is the meaning.

111. Aññesu pana vicāraṇā eva natthīti tesu appaṭikkhipitattā ayameva vinicchayoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Etena dhuranikkhepaṃ katvāpi corehi āhaṭaṃ codetvā gaṇhato anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

111. However, in other commentaries there is no deliberation on this; because it is not rejected in them, it is said that this very decision is the one. It is said: ‘By this, it is shown that even having laid down the burden, for one who demands and takes what was brought by thieves, there is no offense.’

112. Eseva nayoti uddhāreyeva pārājikaṃ, kasmā? Aññehi pattehi sādhāraṇassa saññāṇassa vuttattā. Padavārenāti corena nīharitvā dinnaṃ gahetvā gacchato. Gāmadvāranti vohāramattameva, gāmanti attho āṇattiyā daṭṭhabbattā, dvinnampi uddhāre eva pārājikaṃ. Asukaṃ [M 0.0132] nāma gāmaṃ gantvāti vacanena yāva tassa gāmassa parato upacāro, sabbametaṃ āṇattameva hoti. “Ṭhatvā vā nisīditvā vā vissamitvā purimatheyyacittaṃ vūpasamitvā gamanatthañce bhaṇḍaṃ na nikkhittaṃ, yathāgahitameva, padavārena kāretabboti, nikkhittañce, uddhārenā”ti ca likhitaṃ. Kevalaṃ “likhita”nti vutte gaṇṭhipade gahetabbaṃ. Theyyacittena paribhuñjantoti ṭhānācāvanaṃ akatvā nivatthapārutanīhārena “pubbevedaṃ mayā gahita”nti theyyacittena paribhuñjanto. “Naṭṭhe bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ kirā”ti likhitaṃ. “Añño vā”ti vacanena yena ṭhapitaṃ, tena dinne anāpattīti dīpitaṃ hoti gopakassa dāne viya, “kevalaṃ idha bhaṇḍadeyyanti apare”ti vuttaṃ. “Añño vā”ti vacanato yena ṭhapitaṃ. So vātipi labbhatīti vicāretvā gahetabbo. Vā-saddena yassa hatthe ṭhapitaṃ, so vā deti rājagahe gaṇako viya dhaniyassa, tasmā pārājikaṃ yuttaṃ viya.

112. This is the method: a Pārājika offense is incurred in the very lifting. Why? Because a common perception with other bowls is stated. 'By the sequence of steps' refers to a monk who is going, having taken what was brought out and given by a thief. 'Village entrance' is merely a conventional expression; the meaning is 'village'. Because it is to be understood by command, for both, the Pārājika offense is in the very lifting. By the words, 'Having gone to such-and-such village,' as far as the vicinity beyond that village extends, all this is the designated place of command. It is written: 'Whether standing, sitting, or resting, if the previous thieving intention has subsided and the goods have not been put down for the purpose of going, it should be effected by the sequence of steps, just as it was taken. But if it has been put down, then by lifting.' When it is merely said 'it is written,' it should be understood as 'in the Gaṇṭhipada.' 'One who uses it with a thieving intention' means: without having moved it from its place, one uses it with a thieving intention by the mode of wearing and draping it, thinking, 'This was taken by me before.' It is written: 'If it is lost, it is, it seems, a case for restitution of goods.' By the words 'Or another,' it is shown that if it is given by the one by whom it was placed, there is no offense, as in the case of the gift from the park-keeper.
