It is said: 'Others say, "In this case, it is merely a case for restitution of goods."' Because of the words 'Or another,' it is the one by whom it was placed. That he alone receives it should be understood after deliberation. By the word 'or,' he in whose hand it was placed, or he gives it, like the forester in Rājagaha to Dhaniya. Therefore, a Pārājika offense seems fitting.

Tava thūlasāṭako laddhoti vuttakkhaṇe musāvāde dukkaṭaṃ. Tassa nāmaṃ likhitvāti ettha “tena ‘gahetvā ṭhapeyyāsī’ti āṇattattā nāmalekhanakāle anāpatti kusasaṅkamanasadisaṃ na hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Na jānantīti na suṇantīti attho. Sace jānitvāpi cittena na sampaṭicchanti [V 0.0118] eseva nayo. Jānantena pana rakkhituṃ anicchante paṭikkhipitabbameva etanti vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Ummaggenāti purāpāṇaṃ khaṇitvā katamaggenāti attho.

At the moment of saying, ‘You have received a coarse robe,’ there is a Dukkaṭa offense for false speech. Regarding the phrase ‘having written his name,’ it is said here: ‘Since he was instructed, “Take and place it,” there is no offense at the time of writing the name; it is not like the transfer by kusa-grass token.’ ‘They do not know’ means ‘they do not hear.’ If, even knowing, they do not accept it with their mind, this is the same principle. However, by one who knows but does not wish to guard it, it must indeed be refused; this rule should be known. ‘By the tunnel’ means by a path made by digging an ancient pit; this is the meaning.

Nissitavārikassa pana sabhāgā bhattaṃ denti, tasmā yathā vihāre panti, tatheva kātabbanti sampattavāraṃ aggahetuṃ na labhanti, “tassa vā sabhāgā adātuṃ na labhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Attadutiyassāti na hi ekenānītaṃ dvinnaṃ pahoti, sace pahoti pāpetabboti dassetuṃ “yassa vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Paripucchaṃ detīti pucchitapañhassa vissajjanaṃ karotī”ti likhitaṃ. Saṅghassa bhāraṃ nāma “saddhammavācanā evā”ti vuttaṃ, “navakammikopi vuccatī”ti ca, “ito bhaṇḍato vaṭṭantaṃ puna anto pavisatīti mahāaṭṭhakathāpadassa kurundīsaṅkhepaṭṭhakathāhi adhippāyo vivarito”ti likhitaṃ.

However, for a dependent monk on duty, his fellow monks provide food; therefore, just as there is a line in the monastery, so it should be done. Thus, they are not permitted to refuse the turn when it arrives, and it is said: 'Or his fellow monks are not permitted to withhold it.' Regarding one with a companion: since what is brought by one is not sufficient for two, if it is sufficient, it should be made to reach them—to show this, 'or to whomsoever,' etc., is said. It is written in the Gaṇṭhipada: '"Giving an inquiry" means "he gives the answer to a question asked."' The burden of the Saṅgha, it is said, is 'only the recitation of the True Dhamma,' and it is also said to be 'one who undertakes new works.' It is written: '"From this bundle of goods, rolling, it enters inside again"—the meaning of this phrase from the Mahāaṭṭhakathā is explained by the Kurundī and Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathās.'

113. Gacchante yāne vāti ettha “suṅkaṭṭhānassa bahi ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti upatissatthero vadati kira. “Gacchante yāne vātiādi suṅkaṭṭhānabbhantare [M 0.0133] gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Bahi ṭhitassa vattabbameva natthi, “anto ṭhatvā”ti adhikāre vuttattā ceti yuttaṃ – yānādīsu ṭhapite tassa payogaṃ vināyeva gatesu pārājiko na hoti. Kasmā na bhaṇḍadeyyanti ce? Suṅkaṭṭhānassa bahi ṭhitattā. Araññaṭṭhe “assatiyā atikkamantassapi bhaṇḍadeyyamevā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.107) vuttaṃ tesaṃ sapariggahitattā. Idha pana “atra paviṭṭhassā”ti vacanato na bahi ṭhitassa, taṃ kira suṅkasaṅketaṃ. Aññaṃ harāpetīti tattha “sahatthā”ti vacanato anāpatti. Nissaggiyāni hontīti aṭṭhakathāto pācittiyaṃ, upacāraṃ okkamitvā pariharaṇe sādīnavattā dukkaṭaṃ.

113. Regarding the phrase 'or on a moving vehicle,' the Elder Upatissa, it is said, states: 'This was said in reference to being situated outside the customs post.' It is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: '“Or on a moving vehicle,” and so on, should be understood as within the customs post.' For one situated outside, there is nothing to be said, because it is stated in the section on 'standing inside'; this is correct. When goods placed in vehicles and so on are carried away without his effort, there is no Pārājika offense. If it is asked, 'Why are they not dutiable goods?' It is because of being situated outside the customs post. In the section on the forest, it is said: 'For one who crosses over due to mindlessness, they are indeed dutiable goods,' because those goods are possessed. Here, however, because of the phrase 'for one who has entered here,' it is not a customs post for one standing outside; that, it is said, is the demarcated customs area. Regarding 'he has another carry it,' there, because of the phrase 'with one's own hand,' there is no offense. Regarding 'they become forfeitable,' according to the Commentary, it is a Pācittiya offense. Having entered the vicinity, for avoiding it, due to the fault involved, there is a Dukkaṭa offense.

Suṅkaṭṭhāne suṅkaṃ datvāva gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti idaṃ dāni vattabbānaṃ mātikāti dhammasiritthero. “Anurādhapurassa catūsu dvāresu suṅkaṃ gaṇhanti, tesu dakkhiṇadvārassa purato maggo thūpārāmato ānandacetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā jetavanavihārassantarapākārassāsanne niviṭṭho, yo na gāmaṃ pavisanto upacāraṃ okkanto hoti. Thūpārāmato ca mahācetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rājavihāraṃ gacchanto na okkamatī”ti kira mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgataṃ. Ettha cāti suṅkaghāte “dvīhi leḍḍupātehīti ācariyaparamparābhatā”ti likhitaṃ. Dvīhi leḍḍupātehīti suṅkaghātassa paricchede aṭṭhapite yujjati, ṭhapite pana atirekayojanampi suṅkaghātaṃ hotīti tato paraṃ dve leḍḍupātā upacāroti gahetabbo. So panetthāpi duvidho bāhirabbhantarabhedato. Tattha dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhātaṃ bāhiropacāraṃ sandhāya pāḷiyaṃ, mahāaṭṭhakathāyañca dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Abbhantaraṃ sandhāya [V 0.0119] kurundiyanti no khanti. “Atra paviṭṭhassa suṅkaṃ gaṇhantūti hi niyamitaṭṭhānaṃ ekantato pārājikakhettaṃ hoti, tañca parikkhittaṃ, eko leḍḍupāto dukkaṭakhettaṃ, aparikkhittañce, dutiyo leḍḍupātoti no adhippāyo”ti ācariyo vadati.

The Elder Dhammasiri said that this phrase, 'Having paid the toll at the toll station, one is permitted to go,' is now the matrix for the statements to be made. It is said to be stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: 'At the four gates of Anuradhapura, they collect the toll. The road in front of the southern gate, having circumambulated the Ānandacetiya from the Thūpārāma, is established near the inner wall of the Jetavana monastery. One who, while entering the village, does not enter the vicinity; and one going to the royal monastery, having circumambulated the Mahācetiya from the Thūpārāma, does not enter it.' Here, regarding the toll-collection point, it is written: 'by two stone-throws, as handed down by the lineage of teachers'. The phrase 'by two stone-throws' is suitable when the boundary of the toll-collection point is not established. When it is established, however, the toll-collection point can be even more than a yojana; therefore, beyond that, two stone-throws should be understood as the vicinity. That vicinity, here too, is twofold, by the division of external and internal. Therein, with reference to the external vicinity, designated as the second stone-throw, a Dukkaṭa offense is stated in the Pāḷi and in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. With reference to the internal vicinity, in the Kurundī it is said to be a theft; this is our preference. The teacher says: 'The place designated by "Let them collect the toll from one who has entered here" is definitely the field of a Pārājika offense, and it is enclosed. One stone-throw is the field of a Dukkaṭa offense. If it is unenclosed, the second stone-throw is our intention.'

114. Dhanaṃ pana gataṭṭhāne vaḍḍhatīti ettha “vaḍḍhiyā saha avahārakassa bhaṇḍadeyya”nti likhitaṃ. “Taṃ vaḍḍhiṃ dassāmī”ti aggahesi, tattha kammaṃ akarontassa vaḍḍhatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Kevalaṃ āṭhapitakhettassa na vaḍḍhati. “Yaṃ dhanaṃ vaḍḍhi, taṃ dentassa avahārakassa vaḍḍhiyā adāne pārājikaṃ hotī”ti vadanti.

114. Here, regarding 'wealth, however, increases in the place it has gone,' it is written: 'The goods should be given to the thief along with the increase.' If he took it, thinking, 'I will give that increase,' it is said because it increases for one who does not perform work there. It does not increase for a field merely established. They say: 'When wealth has increased, for the thief who is giving it, not giving the increase becomes a pārājika offense.'

Nāmenāti [M 0.0134] sappanāmena vā sāmikena katena vā.

'By name' means either by the snake's name or by a name given by its owner.

116. Rājagharassa antovatthumhi, parikkhittarājaṅgaṇaṃ vā antovatthu. Aparikkhitte rājaṅgaṇe ṭhitassa sakalanagaraṃ ṭhānaṃ. Goṇassa “aparikkhitte ṭhitassa akkantaṭṭhānameva ṭhāna”nti vuttattā khaṇḍadvāranti attanā khaṇḍitacchiddaṃ. Tattheva ghātetīti “jīvitindriyārammaṇattā vadhakacittassa pācittiyaṃ hotīti? Na hoti. Kasmā? Adinnādānapayogattā. Tampi theyyacittaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇaṃva hoti. Idha tadubhayaṃ labhati saddhiṃ pubbabhāgāparabhāgehī”ti vuttaṃ.

116. Within the inner area of the royal residence, or an enclosed royal courtyard, is the inner area. For one standing in an unenclosed royal courtyard, the entire city is the place. Regarding an ox, since it is said, 'For one standing in an unenclosed area, the very spot it treads is its place,' 'khaṇḍadvāra' (broken gate) means a breach broken by oneself. As for killing it right there: 'Does a pācittiya offense occur because the killing thought has the life faculty as its object?' 'No, it does not. Why? Because it is an act of taking what is not given. That thought of theft also has mental formations as its object. Here, one obtains both, together with the preliminary and subsequent parts,' it is said.

118. Tassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikanti yadi yo āṇatto avassaṃ taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ harati, āṇattikkhaṇe eva pārājikaṃ. “Idha tiṇṇaṃ kasmā pārājikaṃ, nanu ‘tumhe, bhante, tayo harathā’ti vuttattā thullaccayaṃ, itaresañca paṭipāṭiyā ekekassāṇattattā ekekena ca dukkaṭena bhavitabbaṃ. Kathaṃ, eko kira māsagghanakaṃ parissāvanaṃ thenetvā desetvā nirussāho eva vā hutvā puna māsagghanakaṃ sūciṃ tatheva katvā puna māsagghanakanti evaṃ siyāti? Na evaṃ, taṃ yathā uppalathenako yena vatthu pūrati tāva saussāhattā pārājiko āsi, evamime saussāhāva na desayiṃsu vā”ti likhitaṃ, pāḷiyaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyañca saṃvidahitvā gatesu ekassuddhāre sabbesaṃ pārājikaṃ vinā viya āṇattiyā kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, atha kho “tassāyaṃ attho”ti vatvā pacchā vuttavinicchayesu ca ekabhaṇḍaekaṭṭhānādīsu ca sambahulā ekaṃ āṇāpentīti āṇattimeva niyametvā vuttaṃ, tasmā āṇatti icchitabbā viya, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “‘Ekabhaṇḍaṃ ekaṭṭhāna’nti ca pāṭho ‘ekakulassa bhaṇḍa’nti vacanato”ti vadanti.

118. 'Upon its removal, it is a pārājika for all' means that if the one who was instructed inevitably takes those goods, it is a pārājika for all at the very moment of instruction. It is written: 'Here, why is it a pārājika for the three? Should it not be a thullaccaya, since it was said, "Venerable sirs, you three take it"? And for the others, since each was instructed in turn, should it not be a dukkaṭa for each? How so? Is it like the case where one steals a water-strainer worth a māsaka and confesses it, or becomes unenthusiastic, then does the same with a needle worth a māsaka, and again with something worth a māsaka? It is not so. Just as the lotus-thief incurred a pārājika because he remained enthusiastic until the required value was completed, similarly, these monks were enthusiastic and did not confess.' In the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā, although it is said that among those who go after conspiring, upon the removal by one, it is a pārājika for all, as if without an instruction, nevertheless, having said 'this is its meaning,' in the subsequently stated legal decisions and in cases of a single item at a single location, etc., it was stated by defining it specifically as an instruction, because many monks instruct one. Therefore, an instruction seems to be required; this should be investigated. They say that the reading 'a single item, a single location' exists on the authority of the phrase 'the goods of a single family.'

119-120. Ocarake [V 0.0120] vuttanayenevāti avassaṃhāriye bhaṇḍe. Taṃ saṅketanti tassa saṅketassa. Atha vā taṃ saṅketaṃ atikkamitvā pacchā vā. Apatvā pure vā. Esa nayo taṃ nimittanti etthāpi. Akkhinikhaṇanādikammaṃ lahukaṃ ittarakālaṃ, taṅkhaṇe eva bhaṇḍaṃ avaharituṃ na sakkā, kiñci bhaṇḍaṃ dūraṃ hoti, kiñci bhāriyaṃ, taṃ gahetuṃ yāva gacchati yāva ukkhipati, tāva nimittassa pacchā hoti. Sace taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ adhigataṃ [M 0.0135] viya āsannaṃ, lahukañca, sakkā nimittakkhaṇe avaharituṃ, tameva sandhāya vuttaṃ kinti? Na, pubbe vuttampi “tato paṭṭhāya teneva nimittena avaharatī”ti vuccati āraddhattā. Yadi evaṃ “purebhattapayogo eso”ti vāro pamāṇaṃ hoti, na ca taṃ pamāṇaṃ mahāpadumattheravādassa pacchā vuttattā, na saṅketakammaṃ viya nimittakammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha hi kālaparicchedo atthi, idha natthi, idameva tesaṃ nānattaṃ.

119-120. By the method stated in the section on the spy, regarding goods that must certainly be taken. In the phrase 'that agreement' (taṃ saṅketaṃ), it means 'of that appointed time.' Or alternatively, having surpassed that appointed time, taking it afterwards; or not having reached it, taking it beforehand. This is the method also in the phrase 'that sign.' An act such as winking the eye is swift and of short duration; at that very moment, it is not possible to steal the goods. Some goods are far, some are heavy. By the time one goes to take them or lifts them, it is already after the sign. If those goods are nearby as if already obtained, and are light, it is possible to steal them at the moment of the sign. Was it said with reference to just that? No. Even regarding the previously mentioned case, it is said: 'From then on, one steals with that very sign,' because the act has been initiated. If so, the opinion, 'This is a pre-meal undertaking,' becomes the authority. But that is not the authority, because it was stated after the view of the Elder Mahāpaduma. The act by sign should not be regarded like the act by agreement. For in that case, a time-limit exists; here, there is not. This itself is the difference between them.

121. Tañca asammohatthanti eko “purebhattādīsu vā, akkhinikhaṇanādīni vā disvā gaṇhā”ti, eko gahetabbaṃ bhaṇḍanissitaṃ katvā “purebhattaṃ evaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadati, evaṃvidhesu asammohatthaṃ evaṃvidhaṃ saṅketaṃ nimittañca dassetunti ca, yathādhippāyanti dutiyo tatiyassa tatiyo catutthassāti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā ce vadantīti attho. Sace dutiyo catutthassa vadeti, na yathādhippāyoti ca. “Paṭiggahitamatteti avassaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, pubbeva thullaccaya”nti ca likhitaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhakānaṃ dukkaṭaṃ sabbatthokāsābhāvato na vuttaṃ. Pārājikāpajjanenetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ āpajjitvā āpajjanti kira. Atthasādhakāṇatticetanākhaṇe eva pārājiko hotīti adhippāyo. Tattha maggaṭṭhāniyaṃ kataraṃ, kataraṃ phalaṭṭhāniyanti “atthasādhakacetanā nāma maggānantaraphalasadisā”ti vuttattā phalaṭṭhāniyā cetanāti siddhaṃ. Āṇatti ce maggaṭṭhāniyā siyā, cetanāsahajattā na sambhavati, tathā bhaṇḍassa avassaṃhāritā ca na sambhavati. Āṇattikkhaṇe eva hi taṃ avassaṃhāritaṃ jātanti avahārakassa paṭiggaṇhañce, tampi na sambhavati anāgatattā. Cetanā ce maggaṭṭhāniyā hoti, āṇattiādīsu aññataraṃ, bhaṇḍassa avassaṃhāritā eva vā phalaṭṭhāniyā ce, attho na sambhavati. Pārājikāpatti eva hi phalaṭṭhāniyā bhavitumarahati, na aññanti evaṃ tāva idha opammasaṃsandanaṃ sambhavati cetanā maggaṭṭhāniyā, tassā pārājikāpattibhāvo phalaṭṭhāniyo. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā paṭisambhidāmagge “saddhāya ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Saddhāya saddatthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti ettha añño saddho, añño saddhāya saddatthoti siddhaṃ, yathā ca “eko amohasaṅkhāto dhammo sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo [M 0.0136] adhipatisahajātaaññamaññanissayaindriyamaggasampayuttaatthiavigatapaccayena paccayo”ti ettha amoho dhammo añño, aññe [V 0.0121] tassa hetupaccayatādayoti siddhaṃ. Yathā ca vinayapiṭake yāni cha āpattisamuṭṭhānāni, evaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ “satta āpattikkhandhā”ti vuccanti, tesaṃ aññā āpattisamuṭṭhānatā, añño āpattikkhandhabhāvoti siddhaṃ. Iminā āpattikkhandhanayena āpattādhikaraṇassa kati ṭhānānīti? Satta āpattikkhandhā ṭhānānīti. Kati vatthūnīti? Satta āpattikkhandhā vatthūnīti. Kati bhūmiyoti? Satta āpattikkhandhā bhūmiyoti evamādayopi dassetabbā. Tathā hi tassā evaṃ maggaṭṭhāniyāya atthasādhikāya cetanāya yasmā aññā pārājikāpattitā anatthantarabhūtā ākāravisesasaṅkhātā phalaṭṭhāniyā atthi, tasmā “atthasādhakacetanā nāma maggānantaraphalasadisā”ti vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā kevalaṃ dhammaniyāmattaṃyeva upamattena ācariyena evaṃ vuttantipi sambhavatīti na tattha opammasaṃsandanaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ, “idaṃ sabbaṃ kevalaṃ takkavasena vuttattā vicāretvā gahetabba”nti ācariyo.

121. And that is for the purpose of non-confusion—one says, “Take it, having seen things like pre-meal items or the winking of an eye, etc.,” another, making it dependent on the article to be taken, says, “At the pre-meal time, take the article of such a color and shape.” Thus, it is to show such a sign and such a mark for the purpose of non-confusion in such cases. And as for ‘as intended,’ if the second speaks to the third, the third to the fourth, and so on in sequence—this is the meaning. If the second speaks to the fourth, it is not as intended. A dukkaṭa offense for the receivers is not stated because there is no opportunity everywhere. It is said that they incur the pārājika offense, having first incurred this dukkaṭa offense in the process. The intention is that one becomes subject to a pārājika offense at the very moment of the volition of the instruction that accomplishes the purpose. Therein, which is path-like, which is fruit-like? Since it is said, “The volition that accomplishes the purpose is similar to the fruit immediately following the path,” it is established that the volition is fruit-like. If the instruction were path-like, it would not be possible, because it is co-nascent with volition; and likewise, the certainty of the article being carried away would not be possible. For at the very moment of the instruction, it would have to be certainly taken; and if the taker accepts, that too is not possible, because it is in the future. If the volition were path-like, and either the instruction or something else, or the certainty of the article being carried away itself, were fruit-like, the meaning would not be possible. For the pārājika offense itself ought to be fruit-like, not anything else. Thus, here the connection of the simile is possible: volition is path-like, and its state of being a pārājika offense is fruit-like. Like what? Just as in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “Knowledge in faith is the discrimination of phenomena. Knowledge in the meaning of the word 'faith' by faith is the discrimination of meaning”—here, faith is one thing, and the meaning of the word 'faith' by faith is another—this is established. And just as: “One phenomenon called non-delusion is a condition for associated phenomena by way of root condition, dominance, co-nascence, mutuality, support, faculty, path, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions”—here, the phenomenon of non-delusion is one thing, and its being a root condition, etc., are other things—this is established. And just as in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the six origins of offenses are, as appropriate, called “the seven aggregates of offenses”—here, their being an origin of offenses is one thing, and their state of being an aggregate of offenses is another—this is established. By this method of the aggregates of offenses: “How many grounds are there for the legal issue of an offense?” “The seven aggregates of offenses are the grounds.” “How many bases?” “The seven aggregates of offenses are the bases.” “How many levels?” “The seven aggregates of offenses are the levels”—thus, these and others should also be shown. For indeed, from that very volition which is path-like and accomplishes the purpose, there is another state of being a pārājika offense, which is not different in essence, is designated as a particular mode, and is fruit-like. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said, “The volition that accomplishes the purpose is similar to the fruit immediately following the path.” Or else, it is also possible that the teacher spoke thus merely by way of simile, simply as a regularity of phenomena, and therefore the connection of the simile should not be sought there. The teacher says, “All this is stated merely on the basis of reasoning—it should be accepted after investigation.”

Bhūmaṭṭhakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bhūmaṭṭhakathā and so forth is concluded.

Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Divisions of Offenses

122. “Vibhaṅganayadassanato”ti vuttattā taṃ sampādetuṃ “idāni tattha tatthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha aṅgavatthubhedena cāti avahāraṅgajānanabhedena vatthussa haritabbabhaṇḍassa garukalahukabhāvabhedenāti attho. Atha vā aṅgañca vatthubhedena āpattibhedañca dassentoti attho. Atirekamāsako ūnapañcamāsakoti ettha vā-saddo na vutto, tīhipi eko eva paricchedo vuttoti. Anajjhāvuṭṭhakaṃ nāma araññapālakādinā na kenaci mamāyitaṃ. Chaḍḍitaṃ nāma anatthikabhāvena atirekamattādinā sāmikena chaḍḍitaṃ. Naṭṭhaṃ pariyesitvā chinnālayattā chinnamūlakaṃ. Assāmikavatthūti acchinnamūlakampi yassa sāmiko koci no hoti, nirapekkhā vā pariccajanti, yaṃ vā pariccattaṃ devatādīnaṃ, idaṃ sabbaṃ assāmikavatthu nāma. Devatādīnaṃ vā buddhadhammānaṃ vā pariccattaṃ parehi [M 0.0137] ce ārakkhakehi pariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitameva. Tathārūpe hi adinnādāne rājāno coraṃ gahetvā hananādikaṃ kareyyuṃ, anārakkhake pana āvāse, abhikkhuke anārāmikādike ca yaṃ buddhadhammassa santakaṃ, taṃ “āgatāgatehi bhikkhūhi rakkhitabbaṃ gopetabbaṃ mamāyitabba”nti vacanato abhikkhukāvāsasaṅghasantakaṃ viya parapariggahitasaṅkhyameva gacchatīti chāyā dissati. Issaro hi yo koci bhikkhu tādise parikkhāre corehipi gayhamāne vāretuṃ paṭibalo ce, balakkārena acchinditvā yathāṭhāne ṭhapetunti. Apariggahite parasantakasaññissa chasu ākāresu vijjamānesupi anāpatti viya dissati[V 0.0122], “yaṃ parapariggahitañca hotī”ti aṅgabhāvo kiñcāpi dissati, parasantake tathā paṭipannake sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Attano santakaṃ corehi haṭaṃ, corapariggahitattā parapariggahitaṃ hoti, tasmā paro cetaṃ theyyacitto gaṇhati, pārājikaṃ. Sāmiko eva ce gaṇhati, na pārājikaṃ, yasmā codetvā, acchinditvā ca so “mama santakaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti gahetuṃ labhati. Paṭhamaṃ dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā ce pacchā theyyacitto gaṇhati, esa nayo. Sāmikena dhuraṃ nikkhittakāle so ce coro kālaṃ karoti, añño theyyacittena gaṇhati, na pārājiko. Anikkhittakāle eva ce kālaṃ karoti, taṃ theyyacittena gaṇhantassa bhikkhuno pārājikaṃ mūlabhikkhussa santakabhāve ṭhitattā. Corabhikkhumhi mate “matakaparikkhāra”nti saṅgho vibhajitvā ce taṃ gaṇhati, mūlasāmiko “mama santakamida”nti gahetuṃ labhati.

122. Because it was said, “By seeing the method of analysis,” in order to fulfill that, “now here and there,” etc., was begun. Therein, regarding “by the division of factors and objects,” the meaning is: by the division of knowing the factors of theft, and by the division of the object—the article to be taken away—into heavy and light states. Alternatively, the meaning is: showing both the factors and the division of offenses by way of the division of the object. Herein, regarding “an excess of a māsaka or less than five māsakas,” the word “or” (vā) is not stated; it should be understood that by all three phrases, only one single category is spoken of. “Unoccupied” (anajjhāvuṭṭhakaṃ) means not cherished by anyone, such as a forest guard, etc. “Discarded” (chaḍḍitaṃ) means abandoned by the owner due to not wanting it, or by one who has an excess, etc. A “lost” (naṭṭhaṃ) item, after having been searched for, has its root cut off because attachment to it has been severed. Regarding an “ownerless object” (assāmikavatthu): even if its root of attachment is not cut off, it is that for which there is no owner whatsoever; or which people relinquish without concern; or that which is dedicated to deities, etc. All this is called an “ownerless object.” If something dedicated to deities, etc., or to the Buddha and Dhamma, is taken possession of by other guardians, it is indeed considered as possessed by others. Indeed, for such a theft, kings, having seized the thief, would inflict punishments such as execution. Furthermore, in an unprotected residence, in one without a bhikkhu, or in a place without monastery attendants, etc., whatever property belongs to the Buddha and Dhamma—because of the saying, “It should be guarded, protected, and cherished by whatever bhikkhus come and go”—it is reckoned as “possessed by others,” just like the property of the Sangha in a residence without a bhikkhu. This is the semblance that appears. Indeed, if any bhikkhu in authority is capable of preventing such requisites from being taken even by thieves, he should forcibly seize them back and restore them to their proper place. In the case of an unpossessed item, for one who perceives it as belonging to another, even though the six factors are present, it appears as if there is no offense. Although the status as a factor, “and what is possessed by another,” is seen, it should be understood that this was said in reference to those who act thus with regard to another's property. If one's own property is stolen by thieves, because it has been taken possession of by the thieves, it becomes “possessed by others.” Therefore, if another person takes it with thieving intent, it is a pārājika offense. But if the owner himself takes it, it is not a pārājika, because he is permitted to take it by demanding it back or by seizing it, thinking, “I am taking my own property.” If, having first put down the burden, he afterwards takes it with thieving intent, this is the method. At the time when the owner has abandoned the claim, if that thief dies, and another takes it with thieving intent, he is not a pārājika offender. But if the thief dies at the very time before the claim is abandoned, for a bhikkhu who takes it with thieving intent, it is a pārājika, because it remains in the state of being the property of the original bhikkhu. When the thief-bhikkhu dies, if the Sangha, having divided it thinking it is the “requisites of the deceased,” takes it, the original owner is permitted to take it, saying, “This is my property.”

Etthāha – bhūmaṭṭhādinimittakammapariyosānā eva avahārabhedā, udāhu aññepi santīti. Kiñcettha yadi aññepi santi, tepi vattabbā. Na hi bhagavā sāvasesaṃ pārājikaṃ paññapeti. No ce santi, ye ime tulākūṭakaṃsakūṭamānakūṭaukkoṭanavañcananikatisāciyogaviparāmosaālopasāhasākārā ca suttaṅgesu sandissamānā, te idha āgatesu ettha samodhānaṃ gacchantīti ca lakkhaṇato vā tesaṃ samodhānagatabhāvo vattabboti? Vuccate – lakkhaṇato siddhova. Kathaṃ? “Pañcahi ākārehī”tiādinā nayena aṅgavatthubhedena. Āpattibhedo hi pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 128-130) vutto eva, aṭṭhakathāyañca “kūṭamānakūṭakahāpaṇādīhi vā vañcetvā gaṇhati, tassevaṃ gaṇhato avahāro theyyāvahāro”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.138; kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā) [M 0.0138] āgatattā tulākūṭagahaṇādayo theyyāvahāre samodhānaṃ gatāti siddhaṃ. Viparāmosaālopasāhasākārā ca aṭṭhakathāyāgate pasayhāvahāre samodhānaṃ gacchanti. Imaṃyeva vā pasayhāvahāraṃ dassetuṃ “gāmaṭṭhaṃ araññaṭṭha”nti mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā “gāmaṭṭhaṃ nāma bhaṇḍaṃ catūhi ṭhānehi nikkhittaṃ hotī”tiādinā nayena vibhāgo vutto. Tenedaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – gahaṇākārabhedasandassanatthaṃ visuṃ kataṃ. Na hi bhūmitalādīhi gāmāraññaṭṭhaṃ yaṃ kiñcīti. Tattha yaṃ tulākūṭaṃ, taṃ rūpakūṭaṅgagahaṇapaṭicchannakūṭavasena catubbidhampi vehāsaṭṭhe samodhānaṃ gacchati. Hadayabhedasikhābhedarajjubhedavasena tividhe mānakūṭe “svāyaṃ hadayabhedo mariyādaṃ chindatī”ti ettha samodhānaṃ gacchati. Hadayabhedo hi sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. “Phandāpeti attano bhājanagataṃ karotī”ti ettha sikhābhedopi labbhati. So “tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Khettaminanakāle rajjubhedo samodhānaṃ gacchati. “Dhammaṃ caranto sāmikaṃ parājetī”ti ettha ukkoṭanaṃ samodhānaṃ gacchatīti te ca tathā vañcananikatiyopi.

Here it is asked: Are the distinctions of theft only those beginning with 'situated on the ground' and ending with 'an act as a sign,' or are there others as well? And here, if there are others, they too should be stated. For the Blessed One does not lay down the Pārājika rule with anything remaining. If there are not, then as for these—such as theft by false weights, false coins, false measures, extortion, deception, fraud, crooked practice, snatching, plundering, and violent acts—which are seen in the collections of Suttas, are they included here among those that have been mentioned? Or should their state of being included be stated according to their characteristic? It is stated: It is indeed established by way of characteristic. How? By the method beginning with 'in five ways,' through the distinction of factor and object. For the distinction of offenses is indeed stated in the Pāli, and in the commentary, because it is stated, 'One takes by deceiving with false weights, false measures, false coins, and so on; for one taking thus, the taking is theft-taking,' it is established that taking by false weights and so on are included in theft-taking. Snatching, plundering, and violent acts are included in theft by force, which is mentioned in the commentary. Or, to show this very theft by force, having laid down the matrix 'situated in a village, situated in a forest,' the detailed explanation is stated by the method beginning with, 'An article situated in a village is placed in four locations.' By that, this is said: It was done separately in order to show the distinction in the manner of taking. For there is nothing situated in a village or forest that is apart from those beginning with 'on the ground.' Among these, as for theft by false weights, it is of four kinds—by way of fraud by appearance, fraud by parts, fraud by handling, and concealed fraud—all are included under [theft of] an object in the air. Among the three kinds of theft by false measures—by way of breaking the heart, breaking the peak, and breaking the rope—'breaking the heart' is included in 'this one breaks the boundary.' For 'breaking the heart' is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so on. 'Breaking the peak' is also found in 'he makes it shake and go into his own vessel.' It is said that this is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so on. 'Breaking the rope' is included when measuring a field. 'Extortion' is included in 'practicing the law, he defeats the owner.' And likewise, deception and fraud are also included.

Āpattibhedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the classification of offenses is concluded.

Anāpattibhedavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Classification of Non-Offenses

131. Na [V 0.0123] ca gahite attamano hoti, tassa santakaṃ vissāsagāhena gahitampi puna dātabbanti idaṃ “tena kho pana samayena dve bhikkhū sahāyakā honti. Eko gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi…pe… anāpatti, bhikkhu, vissāsaggāhe”ti (pārā. 146) iminā asamentaṃ viya dissati. Ettha hi “so jānitvā taṃ codesi assamaṇosi tva”nti vacanena anattamanatā dīpitā. Puna “anāpatti, bhikkhu, vissāsaggāhe”ti vacanena attamanatāyapi sati vissāsaggāho ruhatīti dīpitanti ce? Taṃ na, aññathā gahetabbatthato. Ayañhettha attho – pārājikāpattiyā anāpatti vissāsasaññāya gāhe sati, sopi bhikkhu sahāyakattā na kuddho codesi, piyo eva samāno “kacci assamaṇosi tvaṃ, gaccha, vinicchayaṃ katvā [M 0.0139] suddhante tiṭṭhāhī”ti codesi. Sacepi so kuddho eva codeyya, “anāpattī”ti idaṃ kevalaṃ pārājikābhāvaṃ dīpeti, na vissāsaggāhasiddhaṃ. Yo pana parisamajjhe lajjāya adhivāseti, na kiñci vadatīti attho. “Punavattukāmatādhippāye pana sopi paccāharāpetuṃ labhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sace coro pasayha gahetukāmopi “adhivāsetha, bhante, idha me cīvarānī”ti vatvā cīvarāni therena dinnāni, adinnāni vā sayaṃ gahetvā gacchati, thero puna pakkhaṃ labhitvā codetuṃ labhati, pubbe adhivāsanā adhivāsanasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati bhayena tuṇhībhūtattā, “yaṃ cīvaraṃ idha sāmiko paccāharāpetuṃ labhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sāmikassa pākatikaṃ kātabbaṃ, “idaṃ kira vatta”nti vuttaṃ. Sace saṅghassa santakaṃ kenaci bhikkhunā gahitaṃ, tassa tena saṅghassa vā dhammassa vā upakāritā atthi, gahitappamāṇaṃ apaloketvā dātabbaṃ. “So tena yathāgahitaṃ pākatikaṃ katvā anaṇo hoti, gilānādīnampi eseva nayo”ti vuttaṃ.

131. And he is not pleased when it is taken; what belongs to him, even if taken with trust, must be given back again. This statement seems inconsistent with the passage: 'At that time, two monks were friends. One entered the village for alms... no offense, monk, in taking with trust' (Pārā. 146). For herein, by the words 'knowing this, he accused him, saying, "You are not a true ascetic,"' displeasure is shown. Again, if one were to say that by the words 'no offense, monk, in taking with trust,' it is shown that taking with trust is valid even when there is displeasure, that should not be said, because the meaning should be taken differently. Herein, this is the meaning: there is no pārājika offense when the taking occurs with the perception of trust. That monk also, because he was a friend, did not accuse out of anger; being indeed dear, he accused him, saying, 'Are you perhaps not a true ascetic? Go, and having the matter judged, establish yourself in purity.' Even if he were to accuse him out of anger, the statement 'no offense' merely indicates the absence of a pārājika offense; it does not show that the taking with trust is accomplished. But as for one who, in the midst of the assembly, acquiesces out of shame and says nothing, that is the meaning. It is said, 'But with the intention of asking for it back, he too can have it returned.' If a thief, even if intending to take by force, says, 'Venerable sir, please consent regarding my robes here,' and then takes the robes, whether given by the elder or not given, and goes, the elder, upon finding support, can demand them back. The previous acquiescence does not count as acquiescence because he remained silent out of fear. It is said, 'The robe which the owner can have returned here...' It should be restored to its original state for the owner. It is said, 'This, it seems, is the duty.' If something belonging to the Sangha is taken by any monk, and with it there is benefit for that Sangha or for the Dhamma, the amount taken should be given after informing the Sangha. It is said: 'He, having thereby restored it to its original state according to what was taken, becomes free of debt. For the sick and others, this is the same method.'

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Padabhājanīya is finished.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition on Miscellaneous Topics

Sāhatthikāṇattikanti ekabhaṇḍaṃ eva. “Bhāriyañhidaṃ tvampi ekapassaṃ gaṇha, ahampi ekapassaṃ gaṇhāmīti saṃvidahitvā ubhayesaṃ payogena ṭhānācāvane kate kāyavācācittehi hoti[V 0.0124]. Aññathā ‘sāhatthikaṃ vā āṇattikassa aṅgaṃ na hoti, āṇattikaṃ vā sāhatthikassā’ti iminā virujjhatī”ti likhitaṃ. Dhammasiritthero pana “na kevalaṃ bhāriye eva vatthumhi ayaṃ nayo labbhati, pañcamāsakamattampi dve ce janā saṃvidahitvā gaṇhanti, dvinnampi pāṭekkaṃ, sāhatthikaṃ nāma taṃ kammaṃ, sāhatthikapayogattā ekasmiṃyeva bhaṇḍe, tasmā ‘sāhatthikaṃ āṇattikassa aṅgaṃ na hotī’ti vacanamimaṃ nayaṃ na paṭibāhati. ‘Sāhatthikavatthuaṅganti sāhatthikassa vatthussa aṅgaṃ na hotī’ti tattha vuttaṃ. Idha pana payogaṃ sandhāya vuttattā yujjatī”ti āha kira, taṃ ayuttaṃ kāyavacīkammanti vacanābhāvā, tasmā sāhatthikāṇattikesu payogesu aññatarena vāyamāpatti samuṭṭhāti[M 0.0140], tathāpi turitaturitā hutvā vilopanādīsu gahaṇagāhāpanavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā kālena attano kālena parassa dhammaṃ ārabbha sīghaṃ sīghaṃ uppattiṃ sandhāya “ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 21) vuttā, evaṃsampadamidanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the case of `sāhatthikāṇattika`, there is only one item. 'Having agreed, saying, "This is heavy. You also take one side, and I also will take one side," when it is moved from its place by the effort of both, it is done by body, speech, and mind. Otherwise, it contradicts this statement: "The act by one's own hand is not a factor of the act by command, nor is the act by command a factor of the act by one's own hand."' Thus it is written. The Elder Dhammasiri, however, is said to have stated: 'This principle is not obtained only in the case of a heavy object. If two persons, having agreed, take even an object worth only five māsakas, for both of them the act is individually considered `sāhatthika`. Because the effort is `sāhatthika` concerning a single item, therefore the statement, "The `sāhatthika` is not a factor of the `āṇattika`," does not obstruct this principle. It is said there, "It is not a component of the `sāhatthika` object." But here, since it is said with reference to the effort, it is appropriate.' That is incorrect, because of the absence of the statement 'bodily and verbal action.' Therefore, among the efforts of `sāhatthika` and `āṇattika`, this offense arises through one or the other only. Nevertheless, this is said with reference to taking and causing to take in a great hurry, such as during looting. Just as, with reference to the very rapid arising of phenomena—at times one's own, at times another's—they are called 'phenomena with internal and external objects' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Tikamātikā 21), so the completion of this example should be understood.

Tatthapi ye anuttarādayo ekantabahiddhārammaṇā viññāṇañcāyatanādayo ekantaajjhattārammaṇā, itare aniyatārammaṇattā “ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā”ti vuccanti, na ekakkhaṇe ubhayārammaṇattā. Ayaṃ pana āpatti yathāvuttanayena sāhatthikā āṇattikāpi hotiyeva, tasmā anidassanametanti ayuttaṃ. “Yathā aniyatārammaṇattā ‘ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā’ti vuttā, tathā aniyatapayogattā ayampi āpatti ‘sāhatthikāṇattikā’ti vuttāti nidassanameveta”nti ekacce ācariyā āhu. “Ime panācariyā ubhinnaṃ ekato ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ natthi. Atthi ce, ‘ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā’tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 2.21.1 ajjhattārammaṇatika) paṭṭhānapāṭhena bhavitabbanti saññāya āhaṃsu, tesaṃ matena ‘siyā ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā’ti vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ siyā, na ca niratthakaṃ, tasmā attheva ekato ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇo dhammo. Puna ‘ayaṃ so’ti niyamena ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā dhammā viya niddisitabbābhāvato na uddhaṭo siyā. Tattha anuddhaṭattā eva dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ubhinnampi ajjhattabahiddhādhammānaṃ ekato ārammaṇakaraṇadhammavasena ‘ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇā’ti avatvā ‘kālena ajjhattabahiddhā pavattiyaṃ ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇa’nti vuttaṃ, tasmā gaṇṭhipade vuttanayova sāroti no takko”ti ācariyo. Tattha “kāyavacīkamma”nti avacanaṃ panassa sāhatthikapayogattā ekapayogassa anekakammattāva, yadi bhaveyya, manokammampi vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, yathā tattha manokammaṃ vijjamānampi abbohārikaṃ jātaṃ, evaṃ tasmiṃ sāhatthikāṇattike vacīkammaṃ abbohārikanti veditabbaṃ, taṃ pana kevalaṃ kāyakammassa upanissayaṃ jātaṃ, cittaṃ viya tattha aṅgameva jātaṃ, tasmā [V 0.0125] vuttaṃ “sāhatthikapayogattā”ti, “aṅgabhāvamattameva hi sandhāya ‘sāhatthikāṇattika’nti vuttanti no takko”ti ca, vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

Herein also, those dhammas, such as the supramundane consciousnesses, have exclusively external objects; those, such as the consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness, have exclusively internal objects. The others, because of having indeterminate objects, are called 'dhammas with internal-and-external objects,' not because they have both objects in a single moment. This offense, however, by the method already stated, is indeed both committed by one's own hand and by command; therefore, it is inappropriate to say this is not an example. Some teachers say: 'Just as they are called 'dhammas with internal-and-external objects' because of having indeterminate objects, so too this offense is called 'committed by one's own hand and by command' because of having an indeterminate application; therefore, this is indeed an example.' But these teachers, with the perception that 'There is no taking as object both internal and external dhammas together. If there were, it should be stated by the Paṭṭhāna text beginning with: 'Dependent on a dhamma with an internal-and-external object, a dhamma with an internal-and-external object arises through the root condition...'', have spoken thus. According to their opinion, the statement 'it might be with internal-and-external objects' would be meaningless. And it is not meaningless, but is indeed meaningful. Therefore, there certainly is a dhamma that has both internal and external phenomena as its object together. Furthermore, because there is no way to point it out definitively, saying 'this is it', like the dhammas that are exclusively internal or external objects, it might not have been extracted. Precisely because it was not extracted there, in the commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, instead of saying 'with internal-and-external objects' by way of a dhamma that takes both internal and external dhammas as its object together, it is said: 'with an internal-and-external object' when it occurs at times internally and at times externally. Therefore, the method stated in the Gaṇṭhipada is the essential one; this is our reasoning,' said the teacher. Herein, the non-mention of 'bodily and verbal action' is because of its being an application by one's own hand and because a single application has multiple actions. If it were so, mental action should also be mentioned. Just as mental action, though existing there, becomes conventionally unmentionable, so too in that offense committed by one's own hand and by command, verbal action should be understood as conventionally unmentionable. That verbal action, however, has become merely a decisive support for the bodily action, just as the mind therein has become merely a factor. Therefore, it is said 'because of the application by one's own hand.' And also: 'Indeed, it is called 'committed by one's own hand and by command' with reference only to its being merely a factor; this is our reasoning.' This should be accepted after investigation.

Kāyavācā [M 0.0141] samuṭṭhānā, yassā āpattiyā siyuṃ;

Tattha kammaṃ na taṃ cittaṃ, kammaṃ nassati khīyati.

For whichever offense the origins may be body and speech, therein that mind is not the kamma; the kamma perishes and is destroyed.

Kiriyākiriyādikaṃ yañca, kammākammādikaṃ bhave;

Na yuttaṃ taṃ viruddhattā, kammamekaṃva yujjati.

And whatever, such as action and non-action, would be kamma, non-kamma, and so on—that is not suitable due to contradiction; only one kamma is appropriate.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Decided Cases

132. Anāpatti, bhikkhu, cittuppādeti ettha kevalaṃ cittaṃ, tasseva uppādetabbāpattīhi anāpattīti attho. Etthāha – upanikkhittasādiyanādīsu, sabbesu ca akiriyasikkhāpadesu na kāyaṅgacopanaṃ vā vācaṅgacopanaṃ vā, apicāpatti, kasmā imasmiṃyeva sikkhāpade anāpatti, na sabbāpattīhīti? Na, kasmā.

132. In the phrase 'There is no offense, bhikkhu, in the arising of a thought,' the meaning is: there is no offense through the offenses that are to be produced by that mere thought alone. Here, one asks: In cases such as enjoying what is placed nearby, and in all training rules concerning inaction, there is no movement of the body's limbs, and yet there is an offense. Why in this training rule alone is there no offense, and not [exemption] from all offenses? No. Why?

Kattabbā sādhikaṃ sikkhā, viññattiṃ kāyavācikaṃ;

Akatvā kāyavācāhi, aviññattīhi taṃ phuse.

The training should be undertaken exceedingly well; without making a bodily or verbal intimation, how could one, by means of body and speech without intimation, incur that [offense]?

Na lesabhāvattā. Sappāye ārammaṇe aṭṭhatvā paṭiladdhāsevanaṃ hutvā tato paraṃ suṭṭhu dhāvatīti sandhāvati. Tato abhijjhāya sahagataṃ, byāpādasahagataṃ vā hutvā visesato dhāvatīti vidhāvati.

It is not [incurred] because it is a mere hint. Not being established in a suitable object, but having attained repeated practice, it then runs well—thus it 'runs on' (sandhāvati). Then, being accompanied by covetousness or ill-will, it runs in a special way—thus it 'runs about' (vidhāvati).

137. Vaṇaṃ katvā gahetunti ettha kiñcāpi iminā sikkhāpadena anāpatti, itthirūpassa nāma yattha āmasantassa dukkaṭanti keci. “Kāyapaṭibaddhaggahaṇaṃ yuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāya vaṭṭatīti vutta”nti vadanti. Ubhayaṃ vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

137. Regarding 'having made a wound and grasped': Here, although there is no offense under this training rule, some say that for touching the form of a woman anywhere whatsoever, there is a dukkaṭa offense. Others say: 'The grasping of what is connected to the body is proper; with reference to that, it is said to be allowable.' Both [opinions] should be accepted after investigation.

Kusasaṅkāmanavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of Moving the Kusa Grass Marker

138. Mahāpaccariyādīsu yaṃ vuttaṃ “paduddhāreneva kāretabbo”ti, taṃ suvuttaṃ. Kintu tassa [V 0.0126] parikappāvahārakamattaṃ na dissatīti dassanatthaṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ. Uddhāre vāyaṃ āpanno, tasmā disvā gacchanto “paduddhāreneva kāretabbo”ti idaṃ tattha duvuttanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? “Sāṭakatthiko sāṭakapasibbakameva gahetvā bahi nikkhamitvā sāṭakabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘pacchā gaṇhissāmī’ti evaṃ parikappetvā gaṇhati, na uddhāre evāpajjati. Yadā bahi ṭhatvā [M 0.0142] ‘sāṭako aya’nti disvā gacchati, tadā paduddhāreneva kāretabbo”ti na vuttametaṃ, kintu kiñcāpi parikappo dissati, pubbabhāge avahārakkhaṇe na dissatīti na so parikappāvahāro, ayamattho mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttova, tasmā “ñāyamevā”ti vadanti. Kammantasālā nāma kassakānaṃ vanacchedakānaṃ gehāni. Ayaṃ tāvāti sace upacārasīmantiādi yāva theravādo mahāaṭṭhakathānayo, tattha keci panātiādi na gahetabbaṃ theravādattā yuttiabhāvato, na hi sāhatthike evaṃvidhā atthasādhakacetanā hoti. Āṇattike eva atthasādhakacetanā. “Sesaṃ mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttenatthena sametī”ti vuttaṃ.

138. What is stated in the Mahāpaccariya and other commentaries, 'It should be decided by the lifting of the foot,' is well-said. However, this was stated to show that the mere state of its being a theft with forethought (parikappāvahāra) is not apparent. This monk incurs the offense at the very moment of lifting; therefore, it is said that this statement, 'For one who sees and goes, it should be decided by the lifting of the foot,' is ill-said therein. How so? It is not that this was said: 'A man who wants a cloth takes only the cloth-bag and goes outside. Knowing it to be a cloth, he plans, "I will take it later." When taking it thus, he does not incur the offense at the very moment of lifting. When, standing outside, he sees, "This is a cloth," and goes, then it should be decided by the lifting of the foot.' But although forethought is apparent, it is not apparent at the moment of stealing in the preliminary stage; therefore, it is not a theft with forethought (parikappāvahāra). This meaning was indeed stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā; therefore, they say, 'This is the correct method.' `Kammantasālā` (workshops) are the houses of farmers and woodcutters. Regarding `Ayaṃ tāva`, the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is the Theravāda view. Therein, the view beginning with `keci pana` should not be accepted, because it is the Theravāda view and because of the absence of reason. Indeed, in an act by one's own hand (sāhatthika), such an intention that accomplishes the object (atthasādhakacetanā) does not arise. Only in an act by command (āṇattika) does an intention that accomplishes the object arise. It is said, 'The rest agrees with the meaning stated in the Mahāpaccariya.'

Kusasaṅkāmanakaraṇe sace paro “nāyaṃ mama santako”ti jānāti, itarassa hatthato muttamatte pārājikāpatti khīlasaṅkāmane viya. “Attano santakaṃ sace jānāti, na hotī”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sante pañcakāni saṅkarāni hontīti upaparikkhitabbaṃ.

In the act of moving the kusa-marker, if another person knows, 'This is not my property,' a Pārājika offense is incurred at the very moment it is released from the other's hand, just as in the moving of a boundary post. They say, 'If one knows it to be one's own property, an offense is not incurred.' This being the case, the pentads become confused; therefore, this should be investigated.

140. Parānuddayatāyāti ettha parānuddayatāya koṭippattena bhagavatā kasmā “anāpatti petapariggahe tiracchānagatapariggahe”ti (pārā. 131) vuttanti ce? Parānuddayatāya eva. Yassa hi parikkhārassa ādāne rājāno coraṃ gahetvā na hananādīni kareyyuṃ, tasmimpi nāma samaṇo gotamo pārājikaṃ paññapetvā bhikkhuṃ abhikkhuṃ karotīti mahājano bhagavati pasādaññathattaṃ āpajjitvā apāyupago hoti. Apetapariggahitā rukkhādī ca dullabhā, na ca sakkā ñātunti rukkhādīhi pāpabhīruko upāsakajano paṭimāgharacetiyabodhigharavihārādīni akatvā mahato puññakkhandhato parihāyeyya. “Rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ nissāya pabbajjā”ti (mahāva. 128) vuttanissayā ca anissayā honti. Parapariggahitasaññino hi bhikkhū rukkhamūlapaṃsukūlāni na sādiyissantīti, pabbajjā ca na sambhaveyyuṃ, sappadaṭṭhakāle chārikatthāya rukkhaṃ aggahetvā maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyyuṃ, acchinnacīvarādikāle sākhābhaṅgādiṃ aggahetvā naggā hutvā titthiyaladdhimeva suladdhi viya dīpentā vicareyyuṃ, tato titthiyesveva loko pasīditvā diṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ patvā saṃsārakhāṇuko bhaveyya, tasmā bhagavā parānuddayatāya [M 0.0143] eva “anāpatti petapariggahe”tiādimāhāti veditabbaṃ.

140. Herein, regarding compassion for others: If it were asked, 'Why did the Blessed One, who has reached the pinnacle of compassion for others, declare, "There is no offense in taking what is possessed by spirits or what is possessed by animals"?' It was precisely because of compassion for others. For, in the case of taking a requisite for which kings would not seize a thief and inflict killing and other punishments, people might think, 'Indeed, for such a requisite, the ascetic Gotama lays down a pārājika offense and makes a bhikkhu a non-bhikkhu!' Thinking thus, the great populace might have their faith in the Blessed One corrupted and be bound for a state of loss. Furthermore, trees and so on that are unpossessed by spirits are difficult to find, and it is not possible to know for certain; therefore, the lay devotee populace, fearing evil, might not build image-houses, cetiya-houses, bodhi-tree-houses, monasteries, and so on from trees and the like, and would thus fall away from a great mass of merit. The stated supports, 'The going forth is dependent on a dwelling at the foot of a tree and on rag-robes,' would become non-supports. For bhikkhus, perceiving these as possessed by others, would not make use of tree-root dwellings and rag-robes, and thus the going forth would not be possible. When bitten by a snake, unable to take wood from a tree for ash, they might die. At a time when their robes are stolen, unable to take a broken branch or the like, they would wander about naked, appearing to present the very doctrine of the heretics as if it were a good doctrine. Consequently, the world, placing faith only in heretics and adopting wrong views, would become like a stump in saṃsāra. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke, 'There is no offense in taking what is possessed by spirits,' and so on, precisely out of compassion for others.

141. Aparampi [V 0.0127] bhāgaṃ dehīti “gahitaṃ viññattisadisattā neva bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ na pārājika”nti likhitaṃ, idaṃ pakatijane yujjati. “Sace pana sāmiko vā tena āṇatto vā ‘aparassa sahāyabhikkhussa bhāgaṃ esa gaṇhāti yācati vā’ti yaṃ aparabhāgaṃ deti, taṃ bhaṇḍadeyya”nti vadanti.

141. Regarding the words, 'Give another portion too,' it is written: 'What is taken, being similar to a request, is neither compensation for goods nor a pārājika offense.' This applies to an ordinary person. However, they say: 'But if the owner, or one authorized by him, gives another portion with the thought, "This bhikkhu is taking or asking for a portion for another companion bhikkhu," then that other portion which is given is compensation for goods.'

148-9. Khādantassa bhaṇḍadeyyanti corassa vā sāmikassa vā sampattassa dinnaṃ sudinnameva kira. Avisesenāti “ussāhagatānaṃ vā”ti avatvā vuttaṃ, na hi katipayānaṃ anussāhatāya saṅghikamasaṅghikaṃ hoti. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyampi “yadi saussāhāva gacchanti, theyyacittena paribhuñjato avahāro hotī”ti vuttattā tadubhayamekaṃ. Chaḍḍitavihāre upacārasīmāya pamāṇaṃ jānituṃ na sakkā, ayaṃ pana bhikkhu upacārasīmāya bahi ṭhatvā ghaṇṭipaharaṇādiṃ katvā paribhuñjati khādati, tena evaṃ khāditaṃ sukhāditanti attho. “Itaravihāre tattha dittavidhināva paṭipajjitabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Sukhāditaṃ antovihārattā”ti likhitaṃ, āgatānāgatānaṃ santakattāti “cātuddisassa saṅghassa demī”ti dinnattā vuttaṃ. Evaṃ avatvā “saṅghassa demī”ti dinnampi tādisameva. Tathā hi bahi ṭhito lābhaṃ na labhati bhagavato vacanenāti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'compensation for goods for one who is eating': what is given to one who has arrived, whether a thief or an owner, is indeed well-given. 'Without distinction' means it is stated without saying 'or to those who have made an effort,' for indeed, due to the lack of effort of a few, what belongs to the Sangha does not become what does not belong to the Sangha. In the Great Commentary, it is also said: 'If they go having made an effort, for one who partakes with a thieving mind, there is misappropriation.' Therefore, these two statements are the same. In an abandoned monastery, it is not possible to know the extent of the precinct boundary. This bhikkhu, however, stands outside the precinct boundary, and after doing things such as striking a bell, he partakes and eats. Therefore, the meaning is that what is eaten in this way is well-eaten. It is said: 'In other monasteries, one should practice according to the method prescribed therein.' It is written: 'It is well-eaten because it is within the monastery.' The reason it is said to belong to those who have come and those who are yet to come is that it was given with the words, 'I give to the Sangha of the four directions.' Even if given without saying this, but just 'I give to the Sangha,' it is still the same. For it should be understood that, by the word of the Blessed One, one standing outside does not receive a gain.

153. “Matasūkaro”ti vacanato tameva jīvantaṃ bhaṇḍadeyyanti katvā dātuṃ na labhati. Vajjhaṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Maddanto gacchati, bhaṇḍadeyyanti ettha kittakaṃ bhaṇḍadeyyaṃ, na hi sakkā “ettakā sūkarā madditvā gatā gamissantī”ti jānitunti? Yattake sāmikānaṃ dinne te “dinnaṃ mama bhaṇḍa”nti tussanti, tattakaṃ dātabbaṃ. No ce tussanti, atikkantasūkaramūlaṃ datvā kiṃ opāto khaṇitvā dātabboti? Na dātabbo. Atha kiṃ codiyamānassa ubhinnaṃ dhuranikkhepena pārājikaṃ hotīti? Na hoti, kevalaṃ kappiyaparikkhāraṃ datvā tosetabbova sāmiko, eseva nayo aññesupi evarūpesūti no takkoti ācariyo. “Tadaheva vā dutiyadivase vā maddanto gacchatī”ti vuttaṃ. Gumbe khipati, bhaṇḍadeyyamevāti [M 0.0144] avassaṃ pavisanake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ettha ekasmiṃ vihāre paracakkādibhayaṃ āgataṃ. Mūlavatthucchedanti “sabbasenāsanaṃ ete issarā”ti vacanato itare anissarāti dīpitaṃ hoti.

153. Because of the phrase 'a dead pig,' it is not permissible to give that very living pig as compensation. It is explained that what is fit for slaughter is allowable. In the text 'trampling, it goes, it is compensation,' how much is the compensation? For it is not possible to know, 'this many pigs, having trampled, have gone or will go.' As much as, when given to the owners, they are satisfied, thinking, 'my property has been given,' that much should be given. If they are not satisfied, having given the value of the pigs that have passed, should a pit be dug and given? It should not be given. Then, for the one being accused, is there a pārājika offense through the laying down of the burden by both? There is not. The owner should only be satisfied by being given suitable requisites. This is the method also in other such cases; this is our reasoning, said the teacher. It is said: 'On that very day or on the second day, it goes trampling.' The phrase 'throws into a thicket, it is indeed compensation' is said with reference to that which will certainly enter. Here, in one monastery, danger from another's army and so on has come. Regarding the cutting of the root-object, because of the phrase 'these are masters of all the lodgings,' it is explained that others are not masters.

156. Ārāmarakkhakāti vissaṭṭhavasena gahetabbaṃ. Adhippāyaṃ ñatvāti ettha yassa dānaṃ paṭiggaṇhantaṃ bhikkhuṃ, bhāgaṃ vā sāmikā na rakkhanti na daṇḍenti, tassa dānaṃ appaṭicchādetvā [V 0.0128] gahetuṃ vaṭṭatīti idha sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Tampi “na vaṭṭati saṅghike”ti vuttaṃ. Ayameva bhikkhu issaroti yattha so icchati, tattha attañātahetuṃ labhati kira attho. Apica “daharo”ti vadanti. Savatthukanti saha bhūmiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Garubhaṇḍaṃ hotī”ti vatvā “tiṇamattaṃ pana na dātabba”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ kintu garubhaṇḍanti ce, arakkhiyaagopiyaṭṭhāne, vinassanakabhāve ca ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kappiyepi cāti vatvā, avatvā vā gahaṇayutte mātādisantakepi theyyacittuppādena. Idaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ “rājāpimesaṃ abhippasanno”ti (pārā. 86) vacanato lābhaggamahattaṃ, vepullamahattañca pattakāle paññattanti siddhaṃ.

156. Regarding a monastery guard, it should be taken by way of being released. In 'Having known the intention': Here, the conclusion is that when owners do not guard and do not punish a bhikkhu who is receiving a gift or a share from someone, it is permissible to take that person's gift without concealing it. That too, 'it is not permissible in the case of what belongs to the Sangha,' is stated. In 'This very bhikkhu is the master': Wherever he wishes, there he obtains it for the reason of knowing his own benefit; this is said to be the meaning. Furthermore, they say, 'It is not forbidden.' 'With its basis' means 'together with the land,' so it is said. Having said, 'It is a grave item,' it is also said, 'But a mere blade of grass should be given.' If it is asked, 'But is that not a grave item?'—it is said with reference to what is in an unguarded, unprotected place and is in a state of perishing. Whether saying 'Even in the case of what is allowable' or not, an offense arises with the arising of a thieving mind even regarding what belongs to one's mother and so on, which is suitable for taking. However, this training rule was laid down at the time when the bhikkhus had reached the greatness of the highest gains and the greatness of abundance, on account of the passage, 'The king, too, is very pleased with them.' Thus, the meaning is established.

Dutiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Second Pārājika is concluded.

3. Tatiyapārājikaṃ

3. The Third Pārājika

Paṭhamapaññattinidānavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Origin of the First Enactment

162. Tīhi suddhenāti ettha tīhīti nissakkavacanaṃ vā hoti, karaṇavacanaṃ vā. Nissakkapakkhe kāyavacīmanodvārehi suddhena. Tathā duccaritamalehi visamehi papañcehītiādinā nayena sabbakilesattikehi bodhimaṇḍe eva suddhenāti yojetabbaṃ. Karaṇapakkhe tīhīti kāyavacīmanodvārehi suddhena. Tathā tīhi sucaritehi, tīhi vimokkhehi, tīhi bhāvanāhi, tīhi sīlasamādhipaññāhi suddhenāti sabbaguṇattikehi yojetabbaṃ. Vibhāvitanti desanāya vitthāritaṃ, vibhūtaṃ vā kataṃ vihitaṃ, paññattaṃ vā hoti. Saṃvaṇṇanāti vattamānasamīpe vattamānavacanaṃ.

162. Herein, regarding 'by the one pure in three ways,' the word 'tīhi' (by three) is either an ablative or an instrumental expression. In the ablative case, it means pure from the doors of body, speech, and mind. Similarly, by the method beginning with 'from the stains of misconduct, from unevenness, and from mental proliferation,' it should be connected as 'pure at the very Bodhi-seat from all threefold defilements.' In the instrumental case, 'by three' means pure by the doors of body, speech, and mind. Likewise, it should be connected as 'pure by all threefold qualities,' such as by the three kinds of good conduct, the three liberations, the three kinds of development, and the three trainings in virtue, concentration, and wisdom. 'Vibhāvitaṃ' means expanded upon by the teaching, or made manifest, arranged, or designated. 'Saṃvaṇṇanā' is a present tense expression used in the sense of the near present.

Na [M 0.0145] kevalaṃ rājagahameva, idampi nagaraṃ. Saparicchedanti sapariyantanti attho. Saparikkhepanti eke. “Haṃsavaṭṭakacchadanenāti haṃsaparikkhepasaṇṭhānenā”ti likhitaṃ. Kāyavicchindaniyakathanti attano attabhāve, parassa vā attabhāve chandarāgappahānakaraṃ vicchindanakaraṃ dhammakathaṃ katheti. Asubhā ceva subhākāravirahitattā. Asucino ca dosanissandanapabhavattā. Paṭikūlā ca jigucchanīyattā pittasemhādīsu āsayato. Asubhāya vaṇṇanti [V 0.0129] asubhākārassa, asubhakammaṭṭhānassa vā vitthāraṃ bhāsati. Sāmiatthe hetaṃ sampadānavacanaṃ. Asubhanti asubhanimittassa āvibhāvāya paccupaṭṭhānāya vitthārakathāsaṅkhātaṃ vaṇṇaṃ bhāsabhīti attho. Tesaṃyeva ādimajjhapariyosānānaṃ dasahi lakkhaṇehi sampannaṃ kilesacorehi anabhibhavanīyattā jhānacittaṃ mañjūsaṃ nāma.

Not only Rājagaha, but this city too. 'Having a boundary' means having a limit. Some say it means having an enclosure. It is written: 'By “with the covering of a goose-enclosure” is meant with the shape of a goose-enclosure.' 'A discourse that cuts off the body' means he speaks a Dhamma discourse that causes the abandoning and cutting off of sensual desire concerning one's own or another's existence. It is indeed unattractive because it is devoid of the appearance of beauty. And it is impure because it originates from the outflow of corruption. And it is repulsive because it is disgusting and from its being a receptacle for bile, phlegm, and the like. 'He speaks in praise of the unattractive' means he speaks in detail about the aspect of the unattractive or the meditation subject of the unattractive. For this is a dative expression in the sense of relation. The meaning is that he speaks a description, which is a detailed discourse, for the manifestation and presence of the sign of the unattractive. Because the jhāna-consciousness is endowed with the ten characteristics of their very beginning, middle, and end, and because it cannot be overpowered by the thieves that are the defilements, it is called a 'casket'.

Tatrimānīti etthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – yasmiṃ vāre paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ uppajjati, taṃ sakalampi javanavāraṃ anulomaparikammaupacāragotrabhuappanāppabhedaṃ ekattanayena “paṭhamaṃ jhāna”nti gahetvā tassa paṭhamajjhānassa appanāpaṭipādikāya khippādibhedāya abhiññāya adhigatāya kiccanipphattiṃ upādāya āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi ādīti veditabbā. Tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccanipphattivasena upekkhānubrūhanā majjheti veditabbā. Pariyodāpakañāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā pariyosānanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha ādicittato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānassa uppādakkhaṇaṃ, etasmiṃ antare paṭipadāvisuddhīti veditabbā. Uppādaṭhitikkhaṇesu upekkhānubrūhanā, ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu sampahaṃsanāti veditabbā. Lakkhīyati etenāti lakkhaṇanti katvā “visuddhipaṭipattipakkhandane”tiādinā pubbabhāgo lakkhīyati, tividhena ajjhupekkhanena majjhaṃ lakkhīyati, catubbidhāya sampahaṃsanāya pariyosānaṃ lakkhīyatīti. Tena vuttaṃ “dasa lakkhaṇānī”ti.

Herein, this is the summary meaning of 'Tatrimāni': In whichever javana-process the first jhāna arises for a single moment of consciousness, that entire javana-process—comprising the distinctions of conformity, preparation, access, change-of-lineage, and absorption—is taken as 'the first jhāna' by way of unity. The purification of the path should be known as the beginning, as it arises on account of the accomplishment of the function of the attained direct knowledge, which establishes the absorption of that first jhāna and is distinguished by quickness, etc. The strengthening of equanimity should be known as the middle, by way of the accomplishment of the function of specific neutrality. Rejoicing should be known as the conclusion, by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that brings purity. Herein, from the initial consciousness up to the arising-moment of the first jhāna, this interval should be known as the purification of the path. The strengthening of equanimity is to be known in the arising and abiding moments; rejoicing is to be known in the abiding and dissolution moments. Construing 'characteristic' as 'that by which it is characterized,' the initial part is characterized by 'the purification of the path and leaping forward,' etc.; the middle is characterized by the threefold looking on with equanimity; the conclusion is characterized by the fourfold rejoicing. Therefore, it is said, 'ten characteristics.'

Pāribandhakatoti nīvaraṇasaṅkhātapāribandhakato visuddhattā gotrabhupariyosānaṃ pubbabhāgajavanacittaṃ “cittavisuddhī”ti vuccati. Tathā visuddhattā taṃ cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samādhinimittasaṅkhātaṃ appanāsamādhiṃ tadatthāya upagacchamānaṃ ekasantativasena pariṇāmentaṃ paṭipajjati nāma. Evaṃ paṭipannassa tassa tattha samathanimitte [M 0.0146] pakkhandanaṃ tabbhāvūpagamanaṃ hotīti katvā “tattha cittapakkhandana”nti vuccati. Evaṃ tāva paṭhamajjhānuppādakkhaṇe eva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi veditabbā. Evaṃ visuddhassa appanāppattassa puna visodhane byāpārābhāvā ajjhupekkhanaṃ hoti. Samathappaṭipannattā puna samādhāne byāpārābhāvā ca samathappaṭipannassa ajjhupekkhanaṃ hoti. Kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekantena upaṭṭhitattā puna ekattupaṭṭhāne byāpārāsambhavato ekattupaṭṭhānassa ajjhupekkhanaṃ hoti. Tattha jātānanti tasmiṃ citte jātānaṃ samādhipaññānaṃ yuganaddhabhāvena anativattanaṭṭhena nānākilesehi vimuttattā. Saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ vimuttirasenekarasaṭṭhena anativattanekasabhāvānaṃ tesaṃ dvinnaṃ upagataṃ tajjaṃ tassāruppaṃ tadanurūpaṃ vīriyaṃ tathā cittaṃ yogī vāheti pavattetīti katvā tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena ca visesabhāgiyabhāvattā āsevanaṭṭhena ca sampahaṃsanā hotīti attho veditabbo. Apicettha “anantarātītaṃ [V 0.0130] gotrabhucittaṃ ekasantativasena pariṇāmentaṃ paṭipajjati nāmā”ti likhitaṃ. Tattha hi pariṇāmentaṃ paṭipajjatīti etāni vacanāni atītassa na sambhavanti, yañca tadanantaraṃ likhitaṃ “appanāsamādhicittaṃ upagacchamānaṃ gotrabhucittaṃ tattha pakkhandati nāmā”ti. Imināpi taṃ na yujjati, “paṭipattikkhaṇe eva atīta”nti vuttattā “gotrabhucittaṃ tattha pakkhandatī”ti vacanameva virujjhatīti ācariyo. “Ekacittakkhaṇikampi lokuttaracittaṃ āsevati bhāveti bahulīkarotī”ti vuttattā “ekacittakkhaṇikassāpi jhānassa etāni dasa lakkhaṇānī”ti vuttaṃ. “Tato paṭṭhāya āsevanā bhāvanā evā”tipi vuttaṃ. “Adhiṭṭhānasampannanti adhiṭṭhānena sahagata”nti likhitaṃ. Tassattho – yañca “ādimajjhapariyosānasaṅkhāta”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ tesaṃ tiṇṇampi kalyāṇakatāya samannāgatattā tividhakalyāṇakatañca. Evaṃ tividhacittaṃ tadadhigamamūlakānaṃ guṇānaṃ, uparijhānādhigamassa vā padaṭṭhānaṭṭhena adhiṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā cittassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvena sampannattā adhiṭṭhānasampannaṃ nāmāti.

Regarding 'Pāribandhakato': the javana-consciousness of the preliminary part, which ends in the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) state, is called 'purity of mind' (cittavisuddhi) because it is purified from the obstruction known as the hindrances. Similarly, because it is purified, that consciousness, approaching the absorption concentration—which is the middle stage and is called the sign of concentration—for the purpose of that concentration, is said to proceed, inclining by means of a single continuity of consciousness. For one who has thus proceeded, there occurs the plunging into that sign of serenity and the approaching of that state. Because of this, it is called 'the mind’s plunging in therein' (tattha cittapakkhandana). Thus, firstly, the purity of the path should be understood by way of its coming about at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna. For one who is thus purified and has reached absorption, because there is no exertion in purifying again, there is equanimity. Because of having reached serenity, and because there is no exertion in concentrating again, for one who has reached serenity, there is equanimity. Having abandoned association with defilements, and because of being established in oneness, since exertion in establishing oneness again is not possible, for one established in oneness, there is equanimity. Regarding 'Tattha jātānaṃ': there is the purification (sampahaṃsanā) of the concentration and wisdom arisen in that mind by their nature of not surpassing one another through being yoked together, and because of their being liberated from various defilements. There is the purification of the faculties, beginning with faith, by their single function which is the taste of liberation. And because the yogī wields the effort—which is suitable to, appropriate for, and conforming to those two (concentration and wisdom) of a similar nature that do not surpass one another—and the mind that has occurred thus, there is purification also in the sense of wielding the effort suitable to them. And because of its nature as a special portion and in the sense of cultivation, there is purification. This is the meaning to be understood. Furthermore, it is written here: 'The immediately past change-of-lineage consciousness is said to proceed, inclining by means of a single continuity.' Indeed, in this context, these words 'proceeds, inclining' are not possible for a past consciousness. And that which is written immediately after: 'The change-of-lineage consciousness, approaching the absorption-concentration mind, is said to plunge therein.' By this too, that [first statement] is not suitable. Because it is said, 'It is past at the very moment of proceeding,' the very statement 'the change-of-lineage consciousness plunges therein' is contradicted. Thus says the teacher. Because it is said, 'Even a supramundane consciousness of a single mind-moment one cultivates, develops, and makes much of,' it is stated, 'Even for a jhāna of a single mind-moment, these ten characteristics apply.' And it is also said, 'From then on, it is only cultivation and development.' It is written: 'Endowed with a foundation' means 'accompanied by a foundation.' Its meaning is this: That which is called 'designated as beginning, middle, and end' is also possessed of threefold excellence because of being endowed with the excellence of those three. Thus, the threefold mind is a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) by its nature as a proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the qualities that have its attainment as their root, or for the attainment of higher jhānas. Therefore, because the mind is endowed with the state of being a foundation, it is called 'endowed with a foundation'.

Addhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyitunti ettha ācariyā evamāhu “bhikkhūnaṃ aññamaññavadhadassanasavanasambhave satthuno sati tassa upaddavassa abhāve upāyājānanato ‘ayaṃ asabbaññū’ti hetupatirūpakamahetuṃ vatvā dhammissarassāpi tathāgatassa kammesvanissariyaṃ asambujjhamānā asabbadassitamadhiccamohā bahujanā avīciparāyanā bhaveyyuṃ, tasmā so bhagavā [M 0.0147] pageva tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aññamaññaṃ vadhamānabhāvaṃ ñatvā tadabhāvopāyābhāvaṃ pana suvinicchinitvā tattha puthujjanānaṃ sugatilābhahetumevekaṃ katvā asubhadesanāya vā rūpasaddadassanasavanehi nippayojanehi viramitvā pageva tato viramaṇato, sugatilābhahetukaraṇato, avassaṃ paññāpitabbāya tatiyapārājikapaññattiyā vatthāgamadassanato ca attano sabbadassitaṃ parikkhakānaṃ pakāsento viya tamaddhamāsaṃ veneyyahitanipphattiyā phalasamāpattiyā avakāsaṃ katvā viharitukāmo ‘icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, addhamāsaṃ paṭisallīyitu’ntiādimāhā”ti. Ācariyā nāma buddhamittattheradhammasirittheraupatissattherādayo gaṇapāmokkhā, aṭṭhakathācariyassa ca santike sutapubbā. Tato aññe eketi veditabbā. “Sakena kāyena aṭṭīyanti…pe… bhavissantī”ti idaṃ parato “ye te bhikkhū avītarāgā, tesaṃ tasmiṃ samaye hoti eva bhayaṃ, hoti lomahaṃso, hoti chambhitatta”nti iminā na yujjati, idañca bhagavato asubhakathārammaṇappayojanena na sametīti ce? Na, tadatthājānanato. Sakena kāyena aṭṭīyantānampi tesaṃ ariyamaggena appahīnasinehattā khīṇāsavānaṃ viya maraṇaṃ paṭicca abhayaṃ na hoti, bhayañca pana asubhabhāvanānuyogānubhāvena mandībhūtaṃ [V 0.0131] anaṭṭīyantānaṃ viya na mahantaṃ hutvā cittaṃ mohesi. Apāyupage te satte nākāsīti evamattho veditabbo. Atha vā idaṃ purimassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā tesaṃ tasmiṃ samaye hoti eva bhayaṃ, chambhitattaṃ, lomahaṃso ca, tasmā “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā asubhakathaṃ kathetī”tiādi vuttanti.

Regarding 'to go into seclusion for half a month,' the teachers say thus: 'If, when it was possible for the Teacher to see and hear the monks killing one another, He did not know the means to prevent that calamity, then many people, not understanding the Tathāgata's lack of mastery over their kamma, even though he is the Lord of the Dhamma, and deluded by assuming he does not see all, would say, "This one is not omniscient," speaking a non-reason that is a counterfeit of a reason, and they would be destined for the Avīci hell. Therefore, that Blessed One, having known beforehand that those monks would kill one another, and having well decided that there was no means to prevent it, and having made the attainment of a good destination the sole cause for the worldlings among them; and by causing them to refrain from the unprofitable seeing of forms and hearing of sounds through the discourse on foulness; and by that very refraining beforehand; and by creating the cause for attaining a good destination; and by showing the arising of the occasion for the third Pārājika rule which must certainly be laid down; as if displaying His own state of seeing all to those who are discerning, the Blessed One, desiring to dwell for that half-month, having made an opportunity for the attainment of fruition which accomplishes the welfare of those to be trained, said the words beginning with, "I wish, monks, to go into seclusion for half a month."' The 'teachers' are to be understood as the heads of schools such as the Elder Buddhamitta, the Elder Dhammasiri, the Elder Upatissa, and others, and also those who have previously heard from the commentary teacher. Others apart from these should be known as 'certain teachers' (eke). If one were to say: 'The statement, "They are disgusted with their own bodies... they will be," does not agree with the later statement, "For those monks who are not free from passion, at that time there is indeed fear, there is horripilation, there is stiffness." And this first statement also does not agree with the Blessed One's purpose related to the object of the discourse on foulness.' To this, the reply is: No, because of not knowing the meaning of that passage. Even for those who are disgusted with their own bodies, because their affection has not been abandoned by the noble path, they are not fearless regarding death like the Arahants. But their fear, weakened by the power of practicing the meditation on foulness, does not become great and delude the mind, as it does for those who are not disgusted. The meaning should be understood thus: it did not cause those beings to go to the lower realms. Alternatively, this latter statement is a statement of the reason for the former. Because for them at that time there certainly was fear, stiffness, and horripilation, therefore it was said, 'At that time, the Blessed One gave a discourse on foulness,' and so on.

Atha vā sakena kāyena aṭṭīyantānampi tesaṃ hoti eva bhayaṃ, mahānubhāvā vītarāgāti khīṇāsavānaṃ mahantaṃ visesaṃ dasseti, atiduppasaheyyamidaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ, yato evaṃvidhānampi avītarāgattā bhayaṃ hotītipi dasseti. Tadaññe tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pañcasatānaṃ aññatarā. Tenedaṃ dīpeti “taṃ tathā āgataṃ asihatthaṃ vadhakaṃ passitvā tadaññesampi hoti eva bhayaṃ, pageva tesanti katvā bhagavā paṭhamameva tesaṃ asubhakathaṃ kathesi, parato tesaṃ nāhosi. Evaṃ mahānisaṃsā nesaṃ asubhakathā āsī”ti. Yo panettha pacchimo nayo[M 0.0148], so “tesu kira bhikkhūsu kenacipi kāyavikāro vā vacīvikāro vā na kato, sabbe satā sampajānā dakkhiṇena passena nipajjiṃsū”ti iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena sameti.

Alternatively, even those who are repulsed by their own bodies feel such fear. This shows the great distinction of the Arahants, who are of great power and free from passion. This fear of death is extremely hard to endure, and it also shows that even those of such a nature experience fear due to not being free from passion. 'Others' refers to certain ones among those five hundred monks. By this, it is illustrated: "Having seen that executioner with a sword in hand approaching, even others felt such fear; what then is to be said of them? Thinking thus, the Blessed One first taught them the discourse on the unattractive, and afterward, they had no fear. Thus, the discourse on the unattractive was of great benefit to them." As for the latter interpretation here, it accords with this commentary statement: "Among those monks, it is said that not a single one made any bodily or verbal disturbance. All lay down mindfully and clearly aware on their right sides."

Apare panāhūti kuladdhipaṭisedhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “Ayaṃ kira laddhī”ti vacanaṃ “māradheyyaṃnātikkamissatī”ti vacanena virujjhatīti ce? Na virujjhati. Kathaṃ? Ayaṃ bhikkhū aghātento māravisayaṃ atikkamissati akusalakaraṇato ca. Ghātento pana māradheyyaṃ nātikkamissati balavattā kammassāti sayaṃ mārapakkhikattā evaṃ cintetvā pana “ye na matā, te saṃsārato na muttā”ti attano ca laddhi, tasmā taṃ tattha ubhayesaṃ magge niyojentī evamāha, teneva “mārapakkhikā mārena samānaladdhikā”ti avatvā “mārassā nuvattikā”ti vuttā. “Iminā kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yasmā mārassa anuvatti, tasmā evaṃ cintetvāpi attano laddhivasena evamāhā”ti keci likhanti. Mama santike ekato upaṭṭhānamāgacchanti, attano attano ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike uddesādiṃ gaṇhāti.

The phrase 'But others said' was spoken to refute a wrong view. If one should say, 'Does the statement, "This, it seems, is the view," contradict the statement, "He will not overcome Māra’s domain"?'—it does not contradict. How so? If this person does not kill the monks, he will overcome Māra’s sphere and by not performing an unwholesome action. But by killing them, he will not overcome Māra’s domain because of the strength of the kamma. Thus, being on Māra's side, and having thought in this way, and since it is also their own view that 'those who have not died are not liberated from saṃsāra,' they spoke thus, urging him onto the path of both. For that very reason, instead of saying, 'They are of Māra's faction, having the same view as Māra,' it is said, 'They are followers of Māra.' What is meant by this? Some write: 'Because they are a follower of Māra, therefore, even having thought thus, they spoke in this way in accordance with their own view.' They come into my presence together for attendance, and each receives recitation and so on from their own teachers and preceptors.

Ānāpānassatisamādhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Concentration through Mindfulness of Breathing

165. Ayampi kho, bhikkhaveti iminā kiṃ dasseti? Yesaṃ evamassa “bhagavatā ācikkhitakammaṭṭhānānuyogapaccayā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ jīvitakkhayo āsī”ti, tesaṃ taṃ micchāgāhaṃ nisedheti. Kevalaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pubbe katakammapaccayāva jīvitakkhayo āsi, idaṃ pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ tesaṃ kesañci arahattappattiyā, kesañci anāgāmisakadāgāmisotāpattiphalappattiyā[V 0.0132], kesañci paṭhamajjhānādhigamāya, kesañci vikkhambhanatadaṅgappahānena attasinehapaayādānāya upanissayo hutvā, kesañci sugatiyaṃ uppattiyā upanissayo ahosīti sātthikāva me asubhakathā, kintu “sādhu, bhante bhagavā, aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ ācikkhatū”ti ānandena yācitattā aññaṃ pariyāyaṃ ācikkhāmi, yathā vo pubbe ācikkhitaasubhakammaṭṭhānānuyogā, evaṃ ayampi kho bhikkhaveti yojanā veditabbā. “Assāsavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ satī”ti vuttaṃ. Sā hi taṃ assāsaṃ, passāsaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ katvā pubbabhāge, aparabhāge pana assāsapassāsapabhavanimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā upaṭṭhātīti ca tathā vuttā.

165. What does the phrase 'And this too, monks' indicate? It refutes the wrong view of those who might think, 'It was because of their devotion to the meditation subject taught by the Blessed One that the lives of those monks came to an end.'
