It was solely due to the past kamma they had performed that the destruction of their lives occurred. This meditation subject, however, became a supporting condition for some to attain Arahantship; for others, to attain the fruits of non-returning, once-returning, or stream-entry; for others, to attain the first jhāna; for others, to abandon affection for the self through suppression and momentary eradication; and for others, for rebirth in a happy destination. Thus, my discourse on the unattractive is indeed beneficial. But because the Venerable Ānanda requested, saying, 'Good, venerable sir, Blessed One, please teach another method,' I explain another method. The connection should be understood thus: Monks, just as you were devoted to the previously taught meditation subject of the unattractive, so too should this be practiced. It is said, 'Mindfulness is established by way of the in-breath.' For in the preliminary stage, that mindfulness is established by taking the in-breath or the out-breath as its object; but in the later stage, it is established by taking the sign arising from the in-breath and out-breath as its object. Thus it is also explained.

Asubhe [M 0.0149] pavattaṃ asubhanti vā pavattaṃ bhāvanākammaṃ asubhakammaṃ, tadeva aññassa punappunaṃ uppajjanakassa kāraṇaṭṭhena ṭhānattā asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, ārammaṇaṃ vā asubhakammassa padaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ṭhānanti asubhakammaṭṭhānanti idha asubhajjhānaṃ, teneva “oḷārikārammaṇattā”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhavasenāti vitakkādiaṅgapaṭilābhavasena. Ārammaṇasantatāyāti anukkamena santakālaṃ upādāya vuttakāyadarathappaṭipassaddhivasena nibbuto. Parikammaṃ vāti kasiṇaparikammaṃ kira nimittuppādapariyosānaṃ. Tadā hi nirassādattā asantaṃ, appaṇihitañca. Yathā upacāre nīvaraṇavigamena, aṅgapātubhāvena ca santatā hoti, na tathā idha, idaṃ pana “ādisamannāhārato”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyavikappe asecanakoti atittikaro, tena vuttaṃ “ojavanto”ti. Cetasikasukhaṃ jhānakkhaṇepi atthi, evaṃ santepi “ubhopi jhānā vuṭṭhitasseva gahetabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Samathena sakasantāne avikkhambhite. Itarathā pāpakānaṃ jhānena sahuppatti siyā. Khandhādīnaṃ lokuttarapādakattā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ, visesena yassa nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ hoti, taṃ sandhāya vā. “Aniccānupassītiādicatukkavasena anupubbena ariyamaggavuḍḍhippatto samucchindati, sesānametaṃ natthī”ti likhitaṃ.

The act of development that occurs in relation to the unattractive, or the act of development that occurs as 'unattractive', is the 'unattractive action'. That very action, because it stands as a cause for another consciousness that arises again and again, is the 'meditation subject of unattractive action'. Or, the object stands as a proximate cause for the unattractive action, thus it is the 'meditation subject of unattractive action'. Here, the unattractive jhāna is called the 'meditation subject of unattractive action'. For that very reason, it is said, 'Because of its gross object'. 'By way of penetration' means by way of the attainment of the factors beginning with applied thought. Regarding 'due to the continuity of the object', it is said, it seems, with reference to a peaceful time in sequence: by way of the calming of bodily distress, one is quenched. Or, 'preliminary work' is indeed the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, which culminates in the arising of the sign. For at that time, because of the absence of gratification, it is not peaceful and not sublime. Just as in access concentration it is peaceful through the removal of the hindrances and the manifestation of the factors, it is not so here. But this meditation, however, is spoken of as being peaceful and sublime 'from the initial application onwards'. In the second alternative, `asecanaka` means 'that which does not cause satiety'; therefore, it is said to be 'rich in flavor'. Mental happiness exists even at the moment of jhāna. Even so, it is said, 'Both bodily and mental happiness are to be grasped only by one who has emerged from jhāna'. When evil states in one's own continuity are unsuppressed by serenity. Otherwise, the co-arising of evil states with the jhāna would occur. Because the aggregates and so on are a basis for the supramundane, it is 'partaking of penetration'. Or, it is said with reference to one for whom it is especially 'partaking of penetration'. It is written: 'By way of the tetrad beginning with "contemplating impermanence," one who has successively attained growth in the noble path cuts off defilements. For the others, this is not so'.

Tathābhāvapaṭisedhano cāti soḷasavatthukassa titthiyānaṃ natthitāya vuttaṃ. Sabbapaṭhamānaṃ pana catunnaṃ padānaṃ vasena lokiyajjhānameva tesaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ lokuttarapadaṭṭhānaṃ natthi eva. “Phalamuttamanti phale uttama”nti vuttaṃ. Ututtayānukūlanti gimhe araññe, hemante rukkhamūle, vasantakāle suññāgāre gato. Semhadhātukassa araññaṃ, pittadhātukassa rukkhamūlaṃ, vātadhātukassa suññāgāraṃ anukūlaṃ. Mohacaritassa araññaṃ anukūlaṃ mahāaraññe cittaṃ na saṅkuṭati, dosacaritassa rukkhamūlaṃ, rāgacaritassa suññāgāraṃ. Ṭhānacaṅkamāni uddhaccapakkhikāni, sayanaṃ līnapakkhikaṃ, pallaṅkābhujanena nisajjāya daḷhabhāvaṃ, ujukāyaṃ paṇidhānena assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattanasukhaṃ “parimukhaṃ sati”nti iminā ārammaṇapariggahūpāyaṃ dasseti. Kārīti karaṇasīlo[V 0.0133]. Etassa vibhaṅge “assasati passasatī”ti avatvā “sato kārī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā “assasati passasatī”ti [M 0.0150] vutte “paṭhamacatukkaṃ eva labbhati, na sesānī”ti ca “dīghaṃassāsavasenāti alopasamāsaṃ katvā”iti ca “ekatthatāya avikkhepa”nti ca “asambhogavasena pajānato”ti ca “tena ñāṇenā”ti ca “pajānatoti vuttañāṇenā”ti ca “satokārīti satisampajaññāhikārī”ti ca “paṭinissaggānupassino assāsāva paṭinissaggānupassiassāsā”ti ca likhitaṃ. Uppaṭipāṭiyā āgatampi yujjateva, tena ṭhānena paṭisiddhaṃ. Tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyanato kira potako sampatijātova khipitasaddaṃ karoti, chandapāmojjavasena cha purimā tayoti nava. Ekenākārenāti assāsavasena vā passāsavasena vā evaṃ ānāpānassatiṃ bhāvayato kāye kāyānupassanāsatikammaṭṭhānabhāvanā sampajjati.

And 'the refutation of such a state' is stated because of the non-existence of the sixteen-fold basis for the adherents of other sects. However, by means of the first four phrases, they have only mundane jhāna, and in that there is no supramundane basis at all. 'The highest fruit' means 'the highest in fruit.' 'Suitable for the three seasons' means having gone to the forest in summer, to the foot of a tree in winter, and to an empty dwelling in the rainy season. For one with a phlegmatic constitution, the forest is suitable; for one with a bilious constitution, the foot of a tree is suitable; for one with a windy constitution, an empty dwelling is suitable. For one of a deluded temperament, the forest is suitable; in a great forest, the mind does not shrink. For one of a hating temperament, the foot of a tree is suitable; for one of a lustful temperament, an empty dwelling is suitable. Standing and walking are allied with restlessness; lying down is allied with sluggishness. By sitting with legs crossed there is firmness; by setting the body erect there is ease in the occurrence of the in-breaths and out-breaths. By 'mindfulness to the fore,' he shows the method for grasping the object. 'Kārī' means one whose nature is to do. In its analysis, instead of saying 'he breathes in, he breathes out,' it is said, 'being mindful, he is one who acts.' Therefore it is written that when it is said 'he breathes in, he breathes out,' 'only the first tetrad is obtained, not the remaining ones'; and 'by way of a long in-breath,' having formed a compound without elision; and 'non-distraction through unification'; and 'of one who knows by way of non-enjoyment'; and 'by that knowledge'; and 'knowing by the knowledge that has been stated'; and 'one who acts mindfully means one who acts with mindfulness and clear comprehension'; and 'the in-breaths of one contemplating relinquishment are themselves the in-breaths of one contemplating relinquishment.' Even what has come in reverse order is indeed suitable, but it is refuted by that point. It is said that a fledgling, just after being born, makes a sneezing sound from striking the palate and causing it to cease. By way of zeal and gladness there are six; with the former three, there are thus nine. 'In one way' means either by way of the in-breath or by way of the out-breath. Thus, for one developing mindfulness of breathing in this way, in the body, the development of the meditation subject, which is mindfulness as contemplation of the body, is accomplished.

Kāyoti assāsapassāsā. Upaṭṭhānaṃ sati. Dīghanti sīghaṃ gataṃ assāsapassāsaṃ. Addhānasaṅkhāteti kālasaṅkhāte viya kālakoṭṭhāseti attho, dīghakāle vāti attho. Eko hi assāsamevūpalakkheti, eko passāsaṃ, eko ubhayaṃ, tasmā “vibhāgaṃ akatvā”ti vā vuttaṃ, chandoti evaṃ assāsato, passāsato ca assādo uppajjati, tassa vasena kattukamyatāchando uppajjati. Tato pāmojjanti. Assāsapassāsānaṃ duviññeyyavisayattā cittaṃ vivattati, gaṇanaṃ pahāya phuṭṭhaṭṭhānameva manasi karontassa kevalaṃ upekkhāva saṇṭhāti. Cattāro vaṇṇāti “pattassa tayo vaṇṇā”tiādīsu viya cattāro saṇṭhānāti attho.

`Body` means the in-breaths and out-breaths. `Establishment` means mindfulness. `Long` means the in-breath and out-breath that has come to be designated as such. `Reckoned as duration` means reckoned as time, like a division of time; this is the meaning, or it means for a long time. Indeed, one person observes only the in-breath, another only the out-breath, another both; therefore it is also said, 'without making a division.' `Desire`: thus, from the in-breath and out-breath gratification arises; through its power, the desire which is the wish to act arises. From that, gladness arises. Because the in-breaths and out-breaths are an object that is difficult to discern, the mind turns away; for one who has abandoned counting and attends only to the point of contact, mere equanimity becomes established. `Four colors` means four shapes, as in such phrases as 'three colors of a bowl'; this is the meaning.

Tathābhūtassāti ānāpānassatiṃ bhāvayato. Saṃvaroti satisaṃvaro. Atha vā paṭhamena jhānena nīvaraṇānaṃ, dutiyena vitakkavicārānaṃ, tatiyena pītiyā, catutthena sukhadukkhānaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā rūpasaññāya, paṭighasaññāya, nānattasaññāya vā pahānaṃ. “Sīlanti veramaṇi sīlaṃ, cetanā sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.39 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) vuttavidhināpettha attho daṭṭhabbo. “Atthato tathā tathā pavattadhammā upadhāraṇasamādhānasaṅkhātena sīlanaṭṭhena sīlanti vuccantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā “ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā sikkhā”ti etthāpi cetanāsīlameva, katthaci viratisīlampīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Aññathā paṇṇattivajjesupi sikkhāpadesu viratippasaṅgo ahosi[M 0.0151], pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatīti katvā tassāpi viratippasaṅgo. Tasmiṃ ārammaṇeti ānāpānārammaṇe. Tāya satiyāti tattha uppannasatiyā. “Tena manasikārenāti āvajjanenā”ti likhitaṃ. Etena nānāvajjanappavattidīpanato nānājavanavārehipi sikkhati nāmāti dīpitaṃ hoti, yena pana manasikārena [V 0.0134] vā. Ñāṇuppādanādīsūti ettha ādisaddena yāva pariyosānaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Tatrāti tasmiṃ ānāpānārammaṇe. Evanti idāni vattabbanayenā”ti likhitaṃ. Tatrāti tesaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vā. Tañhi “pubbe apariggahitakāle”ti iminā suṭṭhu sameti. “Paṭhamavādo dīghabhāṇakānaṃ. Te hi ‘paṭhamajjhānaṃ labhitvā nānāsane nisīditvā dutiyatthāya vāyāmato upacāre vitakkavicāravasena oḷārikacittappavattikāle pavattaassāsapassāsavasena oḷārikā’ti vadanti. ‘Majjhimabhāṇakā jhānalābhissa samāpajjanakāle, ekāsanapaṭilābhe ca uparūpari cittappavattiyā santabhāvato paṭhamato dutiyassupacāre sukhumataṃ vadantī’”ti likhitaṃ.

`Of one who has become thus` means of one who develops mindfulness of breathing. `Restraint` means restraint by mindfulness. Or, by the first jhāna there is the abandoning of the hindrances; by the second, of initial and sustained thought; by the third, of rapture; by the fourth, of pleasure and pain; by the attainment of the base of boundless space, of perceptions of form, perceptions of resistance, and perceptions of diversity. Here the meaning should also be seen in accordance with the method stated: 'Morality is abstinence morality, volition morality, restraint morality, non-transgression morality.' It is said: 'Essentially, things that occur in such and such a way are called "morality" in the sense of disciplining, which is designated as upholding and concentrating.' So too here, in 'this is the training intended in this sense,' it is volition-morality, but in some cases the meaning should be seen as abstinence-morality too. Otherwise, the consequence would be that abstinence applies even to training rules concerning what is blameworthy by convention, and since one 'dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint,' the consequence would be that this too is abstinence. `In that object` means in the object of breathing. `With that mindfulness` means with the mindfulness that has arisen there. It is written: '`With that attention` means with adverting.' By this it is shown that one trains also by means of various series of impulsion moments, or by whatever attention. In `in the production of knowledge, etc.,` the word 'etc.' should be understood as extending up to the very end. It is written: '`Therein` means in that object of breathing. `Thus` means by the method now to be stated.' Or, `therein` means of those in-breaths and out-breaths. For this fits well with 'at a time when they were not previously grasped.' 'The first opinion is that of the Dīgha Reciters. For they say: "Having attained the first jhāna and sitting in various postures, while striving for the second, at the time of the coarse mental process due to initial and sustained thought in access concentration, the in-breaths and out-breaths that occur are coarse." The Majjhima Reciters say: "For one who has attained jhāna, at the time of entering the attainment and when the attainment in a single posture is gained, because of the tranquil state of the successively higher mental processes, they speak of subtlety in the access to the second from the first."' This is written.

Vipassanāyaṃ panāti catudhātuvavatthānamukhena abhiniviṭṭhassa ayaṃ kamo, aññassa cāti veditabbaṃ. Ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito aññanti dassanaṃ sandhāya “sakalarūpapariggahe”ti vuttaṃ. Rūpārūpapariggaheti ettha aniccatādilakkhaṇārammaṇikabhaṅgānupassanato pabhuti balavatī vipassanā. Pubbe vuttanayenāti sabbesaṃyeva pana matena apariggahitakāletiādinā. Sodhanā nāma vissajjanaṃ. Assāti “passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāra”nti padassa.

Regarding 'But in the case of insight': this is the sequence for one who has entered upon it by way of the determination of the four elements, and for another as well; this should be understood. With reference to the seeing, 'Material form is only this much, there is nothing else besides this,' the words 'in the grasping of all material form' were stated. Here, in 'the grasping of material and immaterial form,' insight is powerful from the contemplation of dissolution onwards, which has the characteristics of impermanence and so on as its object. As for 'By the method stated before': this refers to the method beginning with 'at a time when they were not grasped,' according to the opinion of all. 'Purification' is the name for answering. 'Of it' refers to the phrase, 'calming the bodily formation.'

Purato namanā ānamanā. Tiriyaṃ namanā vinamanā. Suṭṭhu namanā sannamanā. Pacchā namanā paṇamanā. Jāṇuke gahetvā ṭhānaṃ viya iñjanāti ānamanādīnaṃ āvibhāvatthamuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yathārūpehi ānamanādi vā kampanādi vā hoti, tathārūpe passambhayanti sambandho. Iti kirāti iti ce. Evaṃ santeti santasukhumampi ce passambhati. Pabhāvanāti uppādanaṃ. Assāsapassāsānaṃ vūpasantattā ānāpānassatisamādhissa bhāvanā na hoti. Yasmā taṃ natthi, tasmā na samāpajjati, samāpattiyā abhāvena na vuṭṭhahanti. Iti kirāti evametaṃ tāva vacananti tadetaṃ[M 0.0152]. Saddova saddanimittaṃ, “sato assasati sato passasatī”ti padāni patiṭṭhapetvā dvattiṃsapadāni cattāri catukkāni veditabbāni.

Bending forward is inclining. Bending sideways is deviating. Bending well is contracting. Bending backward is bowing. 'Shaking, like standing while holding the knees,' is stated to make manifest inclining and so forth; this should be understood. The connection is to be understood thus: For whatever reason there is inclining, etc., or trembling, etc., one calms them accordingly. 'Iti kirā' means 'If one were to say thus.' 'Evaṃ sante' means 'This being so, if one calms even what is peaceful and subtle...' 'Bringing into being' means production. Because the in-breaths and out-breaths have been tranquillized, the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing does not occur. Since that is absent, one does not attain it; and because of the absence of attainment, one does not emerge from it. Regarding 'Iti kirā': this statement is thus for the time being. Sound itself is the sign of sound. Beginning with the phrases 'mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out,' the thirty-two phrases should be understood as four tetrads.

Appaṭipīḷananti tesaṃ kilesānaṃ anuppādanaṃ kiñcāpi cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīnipi atthato pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle saṅgahaṃ gacchanti “yassa siyā āpattī”ti (mahāva. 134) vacanato. Tathāpi “na tāva, sāriputta, satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti uddisati pātimokkhaṃ, yāva na idhekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā saṅghe pātubhavantī”ti ettha anadhippetattā “ābhisamācārika”nti vuttaṃ. “Yaṃ panettha āpattiṭṭhāniyaṃ na hoti, taṃ amissamevā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Non-affliction' means the non-arising of those defilements. Although duties concerning shrine-yards and so on are, in terms of meaning, included in the morality of Pātimokkha restraint, according to the saying, 'for whomever there might be an offense,' still, because it is not intended in the passage, 'Not yet, Sāriputta, does the Teacher lay down a training rule for the disciples or recite the Pātimokkha, so long as certain states that are grounds for the taints have not appeared in the Sangha,' it is called 'concerned with proper conduct.' It is said: 'Whatever here is not a basis for an offense, that is unmixed.'

Yathāvuttenāti [V 0.0135] yogānuyogakammassa padaṭṭhānattā. Sallahukavutti aṭṭhaparikkhāriko. Pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti ettha jhānampi nimittampi tadatthajotikāpi pariyatti idha kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Gamanāgamanasampannatādi senāsanaṃ. Saṃkiliṭṭhacīvaradhovanādayo khuddakapalibodhā. “Antarā patitaṃ nu kho”ti vikampati.

'As was said' means because it is the proximate cause for the task of application and endeavor. Of light livelihood, possessing the eight requisites. 'The meditation subject with five connections': here, jhāna, the sign, and the scriptural text that illuminates its meaning are called the meditation subject. A lodging endowed with suitability for coming and going, etc. Washing soiled robes and so on are minor impediments. One is uncertain, thinking, 'Has it perhaps fallen in between?'

Ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatenāti niyakajjhatte vikkhepagatena. Sāraddhā asamāhitattā. Upanibandhanathambhamūlaṃ nāma nāsikaggaṃ, mukhanimittaṃ vā. Tatthevāti nāsikaggādinimitte. “Dolāphalakassa ekapasse eva ubho koṭiyo majjhañca passatī”ti vadanti.

'Having become internally scattered' means having become scattered in one's own interior. They are agitated because of being unconcentrated. The tying-up post is the name for the nose-tip, or the sign at the mouth. 'Just there' means on the sign at the nose-tip and so on. They say: 'One sees both ends and the middle of a swing-board on one side only.'

Idha panāti kakacūpame. Desatoti phusanakaṭṭhānato. “Nimittaṃ paṭṭhapetabbanti nimitte sati paṭṭhapetabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Garūhi bhāvetabbattā garukabhāvanaṃ. Ekacce āhūti ekacce jhāyino āhu.

'But here' refers to the Simile of the Saw. 'From the region' means from the place of contact. It is said: '`A sign should be established` means mindfulness should be established on the sign.' Because it should be developed by teachers, it is a weighty development. 'Some say' means some meditators say.

“Saññānānatāyā”ti vacanato ekaccehi vuttampi pamāṇameva, saṅgītito paṭṭhāya aṭṭhakathāya anāgatattā tathā vuttaṃ. “Mayhaṃ tārakarūpaṃ nu kho upaṭṭhātī”tiādiparikappe asatipi dhātunānattena etāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ uppatti viya kevalaṃ bhāvayato tathā tathā upaṭṭhāti. “Na nimitta’nti vattuṃ na vaṭṭati sampajānamusāvādattā”ti vuttaṃ. Kammaṭṭhānanti idha vuttapaṭibhāganimittameva.

Because of the statement, 'due to the diversity of perception,' what has been said by some is also a valid measure; it is stated thus because of its not having come down in the commentary since the time of the council. Even when there is no such initial thought as, 'Does a star-like form appear to me?' and so on, due to the diversity of elements, it appears in various ways to one who is merely developing it, like the arising of these elements. It is said: 'It is not proper to say, "It is not a sign," because it would be a deliberate falsehood.' As for 'meditation subject,' here it is just the aforementioned counterpart sign.

Nimitte [M 0.0153] paṭibhāge. Nānākāranti “cattāro vaṇṇā vattantī”ti vuttanānāvidhataṃ. Vibhāvayanti jānaṃ pakāsayaṃ. Assāsapassāseti tato sambhūte nimitte, assāsapassāse vā nānākāraṃ. Nimitte hi cittaṃ ṭhapentova nānākāratañca vibhāveti, assāsapassāse vā sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhatīti vuccati. Tārakarūpādivaṇṇato. Kakkhaḷattādilakkhaṇato.

In the counterpart sign. 'Of various kinds' means the aforementioned diversity stated as, 'four colors occur.' Discerning means knowing and making manifest. Regarding 'in-breaths and out-breaths': this refers to the various kinds in the sign arisen from them, or in the in-breaths and out-breaths. For, while placing the mind on the sign, one indeed discerns the diversity; or, it is said, one binds one's own mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths. From the color of a star-like form and so on. From the characteristic of hardness and so on.

Aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittanti āsannabhavaṅgattāti kāraṇaṃ vatvā sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā chaṭṭhe, sattame vā appanāya sati maggavīthiyaṃ phalassa okāso na hoti, tasmā. Idha hotūti ce? Na, lokiyappanāpi hi appanāvīthimhi lokuttarena samānagatikāvāti paṭiladdhajjhānopi bhikkhu diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthāya jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā sattāhaṃ nisīditukāmo catutthe, pañcame vā appetvā nisīdati, na chaṭṭhe, sattame vā. Tattha hi [V 0.0136] appanā. Tato paraṃ appanāya ādhārabhāvaṃ na gacchati. Āsannabhavaṅgattā catutthaṃ, pañcamaṃ vā gacchati thale ṭhitaghaṭo viya javanānamantare ṭhitattāti kira ācariyo.

As for 'it is rejected in the commentaries': having stated the reason 'because of nearness to the bhavaṅga,' it is rejected in the Sinhala commentaries. Why? Because when absorption occurs at the sixth or seventh javana, there is no opportunity for fruition in the path process; therefore. If one should say, 'Let it occur here,' the answer is no. For indeed, even mundane absorption, in the absorption process, has the same course as the supramundane. Thus, a bhikkhu who has attained jhāna, wishing to sit for seven days for the sake of a blissful abiding in this very life, enters jhāna and sits, having caused absorption to arise at the fourth or fifth javana, not at the sixth or seventh. For absorption occurs therein. Beyond that, it does not become a basis for absorption. The teacher, it seems, said: 'Because of nearness to the bhavaṅga, it goes to the fourth or fifth, being situated between the javanas like a pot standing on the ground.'

Puthuttārammaṇāni anāvajjitvā jhānaṅgāneva āvajjanaṃ āvajjanavasī nāma. Tato paraṃ catunnaṃ, pañcannaṃ vā paccavekkhaṇacittānaṃ uppajjanaṃ, taṃ paccavekkhaṇavasī nāma. Teneva “paccavekkhaṇavasī pana āvajjanavasiyā eva vuttā”ti vuttaṃ. Samāpajjanavasī nāma yattakaṃ kālaṃ icchati tattakaṃ samāpajjanaṃ, taṃ pana icchitakālaparicchedaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ samatthatāti. “Adhiṭṭhānavasiyā vuṭṭhānavasino ayaṃ nānattaṃ adhiṭṭhānānubhāvena javanaṃ javati, vuṭṭhānānubhāvena pana adhippetato adhikaṃ javatī”tipi vadanti. Apica pathavīkasiṇādiārammaṇaṃ āvajjitvā javanañca javitvā puna āvajjitvā tato pañcamaṃ jhānaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ayaṃ kira ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo. Bhagavato pana āvajjanasamanantarameva jhānaṃ hotīti sabbaṃ anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

Not adverting to various objects but adverting only to the jhāna factors is called mastery in adverting. After that, the arising of four or five reviewing consciousnesses is called mastery in reviewing. For that very reason it is said: 'Mastery in reviewing, however, is stated by way of mastery in adverting.' Mastery in attaining is attaining absorption for as long as one wishes; this, it should be understood, is the ability to establish the desired time limit. Some also say: 'This is the difference between mastery in determination and mastery in emerging: by the power of determination, the impulsion runs; but by the power of emerging, it does not run on for longer than was intended.' Moreover, having adverted to an object such as the earth kasiṇa, and having run through the impulsion, and having adverted again, thereafter the fifth jhāna consciousness arises—this, it seems, is the highest limit. But for the Blessed One, jhāna arises immediately after adverting—all this is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada.

“Vatthunti hadayavatthuṃ. Dvāranti cakkhādi. Ārammaṇanti rūpādī”ti likhitaṃ. Yathāpariggahitarūpārammaṇaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ passati, aññathāpi passati. Kathaṃ? “Yathāpariggahitarūpavatthudvārārammaṇaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathāpariggahitarūpesu vatthudvārārammaṇāni yassa viññāṇassa, taṃ viññāṇaṃ yathāpariggahitarūpavatthudvārārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0154] tampi passati, ekassa vā ārammaṇasaddassa lopo daṭṭhabboti ca mama takko vicāretvāva gahetabbo.

It is written: 'Basis' means the heart-basis. 'Door' means the eye and so on. 'Object' means form and so forth. One sees a consciousness that has a form-object as it is apprehended, or one sees it otherwise. How? It is said: 'Or as a form-basis-door-object as it is apprehended.' One also sees that consciousness for which there are a basis, door, and objects in regard to forms as they are apprehended. Or, the elision of the one word 'object' should be noted. And this is my reasoning; it should be accepted only after careful consideration.

Tato paraṃ tīsu catukkesu dve dve padāni ekamekaṃ katvā gaṇetabbaṃ. Samathena ārammaṇato vipassanāvasena asammohato pītipaṭisaṃvedanamettha veditabbaṃ. “Dukkhametaṃ ñāṇa”ntiādīsu pana “ārammaṇato asammohato”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, idha tato vuttanayato uppaṭipāṭiyā vuttaṃ. Tattha hi yena mohena taṃ dukkhaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, na upaṭṭhāti, tassa vihatattā vā evaṃ pavatte ñāṇe yathāruci paccavekkhituṃ icchiticchitakāle samatthabhāvato vā dukkhādīsu tīsu asammohato ñāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Nirodhe ārammaṇato taṃsampayuttā pītipaṭisaṃvedanā asammohato na sambhavati mohappahānābhāvā, paṭisambhidāpāḷivirodhato ca. Tattha “dīghaṃ assāsavasenā”tiādi ārammaṇato dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti tadārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattāti ettha adhippāyo. “Āvajjato”tiādi asammohato pītipaṭisaṃvedanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Aniccādivasena jānato, passato, paccavekkhato [V 0.0137] ca. Tadadhimuttatāvasena adhiṭṭhahato, adhimuccato, tathā vīriyādiṃ samādahato khaṇikasamādhinā.

Thereafter, in the three tetrads, the phrases should be taken two by two as single items. Here, the experiencing of joy should be understood by way of serenity as to the object, and by way of insight as to non-delusion. But in such passages as 'This is the knowledge of suffering,' what was stated as 'as to the object and as to non-delusion' is stated here in the reverse order from the method stated there. For there, either because that delusion by which suffering is concealed has been struck down so that it does not appear, or because of the ability to review as one wishes at any desired time when such knowledge has arisen, the knowledge regarding the three truths—suffering, etc.—is said to be 'as to non-delusion.' In the case of the truth of cessation, an associated experiencing of joy 'as to the object' is not possible 'as to non-delusion,' because delusion has not been abandoned and because this would contradict the Paṭisambhidāmagga text. There, 'by way of a long in-breath,' etc., is stated to show 'as to the object.' The intention here is that by that mindfulness, by that knowledge, that joy is experienced because its object is experienced. 'By adverting,' etc., is stated to show the experiencing of joy 'as to non-delusion': for one who knows, sees, and reviews by way of impermanence, etc.; for one who resolves and is intent by way of being disposed towards that; and likewise for one who applies energy, etc., with momentary concentration, that joy is experienced.

Abhiññeyyanti ñātapariññāya. Pariññeyyanti tīraṇapariññāya. Sabbañhi dukkhasaccaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ, pariññeyyañca. Tatra cāyaṃ pītīti likhitaṃ. Abhiññeyyantiādi maggakkhaṇaṃ sandhāyāhāti vuttaṃ. Maggena asammohasaṅkhātavipassanākiccanipphattito maggopi abhiññeyyādiārammaṇaṃ karonto viya vutto. Vipassanābhūmidassanatthanti samathe kāyikasukhābhāvā vuttaṃ. Dvīsu cittasaṅkhārapadesūti cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃvedī…pe… sikkhati passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃvedī…pe… sikkhatīti etesu. Modanādi sabbaṃ pītivevacanaṃ. Aniccānupassanādi kilese, tammūlake khandhābhisaṅkhāre. Evaṃ bhāvitoti na catukkapañcakajjhānanibbattanena bhāvito. Evaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ katvā bhāvito. Vipassanāmaggapaccavekkhaṇakālesupi pavattaassāsamukheneva sabbaṃ dassitaṃ upāyakusalena bhagavatā.

'To be directly known' is by means of full understanding as the known. 'To be fully understood' is by means of full understanding as investigation. For the entire truth of suffering is to be directly known and to be fully understood. And in that context it is written: 'This is joy.' It is said that 'to be directly known,' etc., is stated with reference to the path moment. Because the path accomplishes the function of insight, which is called non-delusion, the path, too, is spoken of as if it were making 'to be directly known,' etc., its object. This is stated to show the stage of insight, because in serenity there is no bodily pleasure. In the two passages on the mental formation: that is, in 'experiencing the mental formation… he trains' and 'calming the mental formation… he trains.' Gladness and so on are all synonyms for joy. Contemplation of impermanence, etc., abandons the defilements and the aggregate-formations rooted in them. 'Thus developed' means not developed by producing the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, but rather developed by making it complete in all aspects. Even during the times of insight, path, and reviewing, everything is shown by the Blessed One, skilled in means, by way of the occurring in-breath.

168. Kasmā idaṃ vuccati amhehīti adhippāyo.

168. The intention is: 'Why is this said by us?'

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis

172. Ussukkavacananti [M 0.0155] pākaṭasaddasaññā kira, samānakapadanti vuttaṃ hoti. “Sutvā bhuñjantī”ti ettha viya sañcicca voropetukāmassa sañciccapadaṃ voropanapadassa ussukkaṃ, sañcetanā ca jīvitā voropanañca ekassevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na kevalaṃ cetasikamatteneva hoti, payogopi icchitabbo evāti dassetuṃ vuttānīti kira upatissatthero. “Jānitvā sañjānitvā cecca abhivitaritvā”ti vattabbe “jānanto…pe… vītikkamo”ti voropanampi dassitaṃ, tasmā byañjane ādaraṃ akatvā attho dassito. Vītikkamasaṅkhātatthasiddhiyā hi purimacetanā atthasādhikā hoti. Sabbasukhumaattabhāvanti rūpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na arūpaṃ. Attasaṅkhātānañhi arūpānaṃ khandhavibhaṅge (vibha. 1 ādayo) viya idha oḷārikasukhumatā anadhippetā. Mātukucchisminti yebhuyyavacanaṃ, opapātikamanussepi pārājikameva, arūpakāye upakkamābhāvā taggahaṇaṃ kasmāti ce? Arūpakkhandhena saddhiṃ tasseva rūpakāyassa jīvitindriyasambhavato. Tena sajīvakova manussaviggahopi nāma hotīti siddhaṃ. Ettha mātukucchisminti manussamātuyā vā tiracchānamātuyā vā. Vuttañhi parivāre (pari. 480) –

172. The term 'Ussukkavacana,' it is said, refers to the perception of an overt sound, and it is said to be a synonymous term. Just as in the phrase 'hearing, they eat,' for one who intends to deprive of life, the word 'sañcicca' (deliberately) is synonymous with the word 'voropana' (depriving of life). It is said that the intention and the act of depriving of life are one and the same. The Elder Upatissa, it is said, stated that these words were spoken to show that it is not merely by a mental factor alone, but that application is also certainly required. When it should have been said, 'knowing, perceiving, intending, and utterly transgressing,' by saying 'knowing...transgression,' the act of depriving of life is also shown. Therefore, without paying respect to the letter, the meaning is shown. For, by the accomplishment of the purpose designated as transgression, the prior intention is what accomplishes the purpose. The phrase 'all subtle self-existence' is said in reference to material form, not the immaterial. For, in the case of the immaterial things reckoned as self, the state of being gross and subtle is not intended here, as in the Analysis of the Aggregates. 'In the mother’s womb' is a general expression; even in the case of a spontaneously arisen human, it is a pārājika offense. If one should ask, 'Since there is no means of attack on an immaterial body, why is that mentioned?' Because the life faculty arises for that very material body together with the immaterial aggregates. Therefore, it is established that a human form is indeed one with life. Here, 'in the mother’s womb' means in the womb of either a human mother or an animal mother. For it is said in the Parivāra—

“Itthiṃ [V 0.0138] hane ca mātaraṃ, purisañca pitaraṃ hane;

Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā, na tenānantaraṃ phuse;

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti.

“One might kill a woman who is a mother, and one might kill a man who is a father; having killed a mother and a father, one does not thereby reach an immediately resultant kamma. This question has been considered by the skillful.”

Paṭhamanti paṭisandhicittameva. Ekabhavapariyāpannāya hi cittasantatiyā paṭisandhicittaṃ paṭhamacittaṃ nāma. Cuticittaṃ pacchimaṃ nāma. Aññathā anamatagge saṃsāre paṭhamacittaṃ nāma natthi vinā anantarasamanantaranatthivigatapaccayehi cittuppattiyā abhāvato. Bhāve vā navasattapātubhāvadosappasaṅgo. Ayaṃ sabbapaṭhamo manussaviggahoti kiñcāpi imaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ na sakkā, taṃ ādiṃ katvā santatiyā yāva maraṇā uppajjanakamanussaviggahesu aparimāṇesu “sabbapaṭhamo”ti dissati. Yadā pana yo manussaviggaho pubbāpariyavasena santatippatto hoti, tadā taṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ [M 0.0156] sakkā. Santatiṃ vikopento hi jīvitā voropeti nāma. Ettha ca nānattanaye adhippete sati “sabbapaṭhamo”ti vacanaṃ yujjati, na pana ekattanaye santatiyā ekattā. Ekattanayo ca idhādhippeto “santatiṃ vikopetī”ti vacanato, tasmā “sabbapaṭhamo”ti vacanaṃ na yujjatīti ce? Na, santatipaccuppannabahuttā. Yasmā pana santati nāma anekesaṃ pubbāpariyuppatti vuccati, tasmā “ayaṃ sabbapaṭhamo”ti vutto, evamettha dvepi nayā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, aññathā “santatiṃ vikopetī”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ na sijjhati. Kiñcāpi ettha “santatiṃ vikopetī”ti vacanato santatipaccuppannameva adhippetaṃ, na addhāpaccuppannaṃ viya dissati, tathāpi yasmā santatipaccuppanne vikopite addhāpaccuppannaṃ vikopitameva hoti, addhāpaccuppanne pana vikopite santatipaccuppannaṃ vikopitaṃ hotīti ettha vattabbaṃ natthi. Tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tadubhayampi voropetuṃ sakkā, tasmā tadeva sandhāya ‘santatiṃ vikopetī’ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabba”nti āha. “Santatiṃ vikopetī”ti vacanato pakatiyā āyupariyantaṃ patvā maraṇakasatte vītikkame sati anāpatti vītikkamapaccayā santatiyā akopitattā. Vītikkamapaccayā ce āyupariyantaṃ appatvā antarāva maraṇakasatte vītikkamapaccayā āpatti, kammabaddho cāti no takkoti ācariyo. “Maraṇavaṇṇaṃ vā saṃvaṇṇeyya, maraṇāya vā samādapeyya, ayampi pārājiko hoti asaṃvāso”ti vacanato vā cetanākkhaṇe eva pārājikāpatti ekantākusalattā, dukkhavedanattā, kāyakammattā, vacīkammattā, kiriyattā cāti veditabbaṃ.

The first is merely the rebirth-linking consciousness. For in the continuity of consciousness belonging to a single existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness is called the first consciousness. The death consciousness is called the last. Otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence, there is no first consciousness, because without the conditions of immediate contiguity, contiguous contiguity, absence, and disappearance, the arising of consciousness is impossible. Or, were it to exist, there would be the fault of implying the manifestation of a new being. This is the very first human form—though it is impossible to deprive it of life, starting from this as the beginning, in the countless human forms arising in the continuity until death, it is seen as 'the very first.' But when a human form has reached continuity through prior and subsequent existence, then it is possible to deprive that one of life. For one who disrupts the continuity is said to deprive of life. Here, when the approach of diversity is intended, the statement 'the very first' is appropriate, but not in the approach of unity, because of the oneness of the continuity. And if it is said that since the approach of unity is intended here—as shown by the statement 'one who disrupts the continuity'—therefore, the statement 'the very first' is inappropriate? No, because of the multiplicity of the present-continuity. But since continuity is called the prior and subsequent arising of many things, therefore it is said, 'this is the very first.' Thus, here both approaches are included. Otherwise, the statement 'one who disrupts the continuity' would not be established. Though here, from the statement 'one who disrupts the continuity,' only the present-continuity is intended, and it is not apparent as the present-in-time, still, since when the present-continuity is disrupted, the present-in-time is also disrupted, and when the present-in-time is disrupted, the present-continuity is disrupted, there is nothing further to say here. Therefore, the commentary states: 'It is possible to deprive of both; therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to that: “one who disrupts the continuity”.' From the statement 'one who disrupts the continuity,' it follows that if there is a transgression against a being who, having naturally reached the end of its lifespan, is about to die, there is no offense, because the continuity was not disrupted by the transgression. But if, due to a transgression, a being does not reach the end of its lifespan and dies in the interim, there is an offense, and it is bound by kamma—this is our reasoning, says the teacher. Or, from the statement 'Or if one praises death, or incites another to death, this too is a Pārājika offense, entailing non-communion,' it should be understood that the Pārājika offense occurs at the very moment of intention—because it is entirely unwholesome, associated with painful feeling, is bodily action, is verbal action, and because of its nature as an action.

Sattaṭṭhajavanavāramattanti sabhāgārammaṇavasena vuttaṃ, teneva “sabhāgasantativasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ[V 0.0139]. Attano paṭipakkhena samannāgatattā samanantarassa paccayaṃ hontaṃ yathā pure viya ahutvā dubbalassa. Tanti jīvitindriyavikopanaṃ.

“The measure of seven or eight javana-moments,” this is said by way of a similar object. For that very reason, it is also said, “by way of a similar continuity,” and so on. Because it is endowed with its own opposing factor, being a condition for the immediately succeeding state, it is not as it was before and becomes weak. Tanti is the disruption of the life faculty.

Ītinti sattavidhavicchikādīni yuddhe ḍaṃsitvā māraṇatthaṃ vissajjenti. Pajjarakanti sarīraḍāhaṃ. Sūcikanti sūlaṃ. Visūcikanti sukkhamātisāraṃvasayaṃ. Pakkhandiyanti rattātisāraṃ. Dvattibyāmasatappamāṇe mahākāye nimminitvā ṭhitanāguddharaṇaṃ, kujjhitvā olokite paresaṃ kāye visamaraṇaṃ vā ḍāhuppādanaṃ vā payogo nāma.

As for Īti, they release scorpions of seven kinds and the like in battle, having them bite to cause death. As for Pajjaraka, it is burning of the body. As for Sūcikā, it is a stake. As for Visūcikā, it is severe dry dysentery. As for Pakkhandiyā, it is bloody dysentery. Creating a massive body measuring two or three hundred fathoms, lifting up a standing nāga, or by angrily gazing causing death by poison or generating burning in the body of another—this is called 'application'.

Kecīti [M 0.0157] mahāsaṅghikā. Ayaṃ itthī. Kulumbassāti gabbhassa. Kathaṃ sā itarassāti ce? Tassa duṭṭhena manasānupakkhite so ca gabbho sā ca iddhīti ubhayampi saheva nassati, ghaṭaggīnaṃ bhedanibbāyanaṃ viya ekakkhaṇe hoti. “Tesaṃ suttantikesu ocariyamānaṃ na sametī”ti likhitaṃ, “tesaṃ mataṃ gahetvā ‘thāvarīnampi ayaṃ yujjatī’ti vutte tikavasena paṭisedhitabbanti apare”ti vuttaṃ. Sāhatthikanissaggiyapayogesu sanniṭṭhāpakacetanāya sattamāya sahuppannakāyaviññattiyā sāhatthikatā veditabbā. Āṇattike pana sattahipi cetanāhi saha vacīviññattisambhavato sattasatta saddā ekato hutvā ekekakkharabhāvaṃ gantvā yattakehi akkharehi attano adhippāyaṃ viññāpeti, tadavasānakkharasamuṭṭhāpikāya sattamacetanāya sahajātavacīviññattiyā āṇattikatā veditabbā. Tathā vijjāmayapayoge. Kāyenāṇattiyaṃ pana sāhatthike vuttanayova. Thāvarapayoge yāvatā parassa maraṇaṃ hoti, tāvatā kammabaddho, āpatti ca. Tato paraṃ atisañcaraṇe kammabaddhātibahuttaṃ veditabbaṃ sati paraṃ maraṇe. Pārājikāpatti panettha ekā. Atthasādhakacetanā yasmā ettha ca dutiyapārājike ca labbhati, na aññattha, tasmā dvinnampi sādhāraṇā imā gāthāyo –

Some, that is, the Mahāsaṅghika teachers, hold as follows. This psychic power. 'Kulumbassa' refers to the fetus. If one should ask, 'How is that psychic power for that person?', when he gazes upon it with a corrupt mind, both that fetus and that psychic power perish together; like the breaking and extinguishing of a pot-fire, it happens in a single moment. It is written: 'Their view does not accord with what is taught in the Suttantas.' It is said by others: 'Having taken their view, when it is said, “This is applicable even to immovable things,” it should be rejected by way of the Tika.' In applications of Nissaggiya offenses by one's own hand, the state of being 'by one's own hand' should be understood by means of the bodily intimation co-arisen with the seventh, decisive intention. In the case of a command, however, because vocal intimation can arise together with all seven intentions, seven sounds, having come together, become single syllables; by as many syllables as one uses to make one's intention known, the state of being a command should be understood by means of the vocal intimation born together with the seventh intention, which originates the final syllable. Likewise in an application by means of knowledge. But in a command by means of the body, the method is the same as that stated for an act by one's own hand. In an application to an immovable thing, insofar as another's death occurs, to that extent one is bound by kamma, and there is an offense. Beyond that, in an excessive arrangement, an excess of being bound by kamma should be understood when a further death occurs. Here, the Pārājika offense is one. Because the purpose-accomplishing intention is found here and in the second Pārājika, and not elsewhere, these verses are common to both:

“Bhūtadhammaniyāmā ye, te dhammā niyatā matā;

Bhāvidhammaniyāmā ye, teva aniyatā idha.

“Those dhammas which are determined by a past phenomenon are considered fixed; those which are determined by a future phenomenon, they are unfixed here.

“Bhūtadhammaniyāmānaṃ, ṭhitāva sā paccayaṭṭhiti;

Bhāvidhammaniyāmānaṃ, sāpekkhā paccayaṭṭhiti.

“For dhammas determined by a past phenomenon, that state of conditionality is established; for dhammas determined by a future phenomenon, the state of conditionality is dependent.”

“Tenaññā hetuyā atthi, sāpi dhammaniyāmatā;

Tassā phalaṃ aniyataṃ, phalāpekkhā niyāmatā.

From that cause, there is another volition; that too is the fixed nature of phenomena. Its fruit is unfixed; the volition that expects a fruit is a fixed nature.

“Evañhi [V 0.0140] sabbadhammānaṃ, ṭhitā dhammaniyāmatā;

Laddhadhammaniyāmā yā, sātthasādhakacetanā.

Thus indeed for all phenomena, the established nature is the fixed nature of phenomena. Whatever volition has obtained this fixed nature of phenomena, that is the purpose-accomplishing volition.

“Cetanāsiddhito pubbe, pacchā tassātthasiddhito;

Avisesena sabbāpi, chabbidhā atthasādhikā.

Because it is accomplished by volition beforehand, and its purpose is accomplished afterwards, generally, all purpose-accomplishing volition is of six kinds.

“Āṇattiyaṃ [M 0.0158] yato sakkā, vibhāvetuṃ vibhāgato;

Tasmā āṇattiyaṃyeva, vuttā sā atthasādhikā.

Because in the case of a command it is possible to explain in detail, therefore, that volition is called 'purpose-accomplishing' only in the context of the effort of a command.

“Micchatte vāpi sammatte, niyatāniyatā matā;

Abhidhamme na sabbatthi, tattha sā niyatā siyā.

In the state of wrongness or in the state of rightness, the fixed and the unfixed are known. In the Abhidhamma, this entire distinction does not exist; therefore, there, that volition would be fixed.

“Yā theyyacetanā sabbā, sahatthāṇattikāpi vā;

Abhidhammanayenāyaṃ, ekantaniyatā siyā.

All volition to steal, whether by one's own hand or by command, according to the Abhidhamma method, would be exclusively fixed.

“Pāṇātipātaṃ nissāya, sahatthāṇattikādikā;

Abhidhammavasenesā, paccekaṃ taṃ dukaṃ bhaje.

Depending on the taking of life, there are efforts such as by one's own hand, by command, and so on. By way of the Abhidhamma, this volition, each one individually, partakes of that dyad.

“Jīvitindriyupacchedo, cetanā ceti taṃ dvayaṃ;

Na sāhatthikakammena, pagevāṇattikāsamaṃ.

The cutting off of the life faculty and the volition—that pair is not the same as an act by one's own hand, how much less the same as an act by command.

“Jīvitindriyupacchedo, cetanā ceti taṃ dvayaṃ;

Na sāhatthikakammena, pagevāṇattikāsamaṃ.

The cutting off of the life faculty and the volition—that pair is not the same as an act by one's own hand, how much less the same as an act by command.

“Jīvitindriyupacchedakkhaṇe vadhakacetanā;

Cirāṭhitāti ko dhammo, niyāmeti āpattikaṃ.

The killer's volition at the moment of cutting off the life faculty has persisted for a long time. Thus, what principle determines the falling into an offense?

“Jīvitindriyupacchedakkhaṇe ce vadhako siyā;

Mato sutto pabuddho vā, kusalo vadhako siyā.

If, at the moment of cutting off the life faculty, the killer were dead, or asleep, or awake, the killer would be blameless.

“Kusalattikabhedo [V 0.0141] ca, vedanāttikabhedopi;

Siyā tathā gato siddho, sahatthā vadhakacetanā”ti.

The breaking of the wholesome triad and also the breaking of the feeling triad would occur. Thus it is established that the killer's volition by his own hand determines the offense.

Yāni pana bījautukammadhammacittaniyāmāni pañca aṭṭhakathāya ānetvā nidassitāni, tesu ayamatthasādhakacetanā yogaṃ gacchatīti maññe “ayaṃ atthasādhakacetanāniyamo natthī”ti cetanānaṃ micchattasammattaniyatānampi natthibhāvappasaṅgato. Bhajāpiyamānā yena, tena sabbepi yathāsambhavaṃ kammacittaniyāme bhajanti gacchantīti veditabbaṃ. Jīvite ādīnavo maraṇavaṇṇadassane na vibhattova, idha pana saṅkappapade atthato “maraṇasaññī maraṇacetano maraṇādhippāyo”ti evaṃ avibhūtattā vibhatto, apākaṭattā, anoḷārikattā vā avibhāgā kāritā [M 0.0159] vā. Nayidaṃ vitakkassa nāmanti na vitakkasseva nāmaṃ, kintu saññācetanānampi nāmanti gahetabbaṃ. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyampi evameva vuttaṃ.

Now, regarding the five fixed orders—seed, season, kamma, dhamma, and mind—which were brought forth and shown in the commentary, some think that this purpose-accomplishing volition is applicable among them; for to hold that 'this fixed order of purpose-accomplishing volition does not exist' would lead to the consequence that even those volitions fixed as wrongness or rightness do not exist. It should be known that, for whatever reason they are included, all of them, as is appropriate, enter into and are comprised within the fixed orders of kamma and mind. The danger in life was not distinguished in the showing of the praise of death; but here, in the term 'resolve' (saṅkappa), it is distinguished in terms of meaning as 'one who is perceptive of death, has the volition for death, and has the resolve for death', because it was thus unmanifest. Or, the non-distinction was made due to it being unclear or not coarse. It should be understood that this is not the name for thought (vitakka) alone, but it is also the name for perception (saññā) and volition (cetanā). In the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī also, it is stated in this very way.

174. Kāyatoti vuttattā “sattiñasū”ti vattabbe vacanasiliṭṭhatthaṃ “ususattiādinā”ti vuttaṃ. Anuddesike kammassārammaṇaṃ so vā hoti, añño vā. Ubhayehīti kiñcāpi paṭhamappahāro na sayameva sakkoti, dutiyaṃ labhitvā pana sakkonto jīvitavināsanahetu ahosi, tadatthameva hi vadhakena so dinno, dutiyo pana aññena cittena dinno, tena suṭṭhu vuttaṃ “paṭhamappahārenevā”ti, “cetanā nāma dāruṇāti garuṃ vatthuṃ ārabbha pavattapubbabhāgacetanā pakatisabhāvavadhakacetanā, no dāruṇā hotī”ti ācariyena likhitaṃ. “Pubbabhāgacetanā parivārā, vadhakacetanāva dāruṇā hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathādhippāyanti ubhopi paṭivijjhati, sāhatthikopi saṅketattā na muccati kira.

174. Because it was said 'by means of the body', although it should have been said 'with a spear and an arrow', for the sake of verbal smoothness, it was said 'by an arrow, a spear, etc.' In the case of an unspecified target, the object of the kamma is either that one or another. Regarding 'by both': although the first blow is not able by itself, upon receiving the second, it becomes a cause for the destruction of life. Indeed, that first blow was given by the killer for that very purpose, but the second was given with a different volition. Therefore, it is well said, 'by the first blow alone'. It was written by the teacher: 'Regarding "volition is indeed cruel": the preliminary volition that arises concerning a grave matter, being a killer-volition of natural disposition, is not cruel.' It is stated: 'The killer-volition, which is the retinue of the preliminary volition, is itself cruel.' Regarding 'according to the intention': he pierces both. Even the one who acts with his own hand is not freed, it is said, due to the prearrangement.

Kiriyāviseso aṭṭhakathāsu anāgato. “Evaṃ vijjha, evaṃ pahara, evaṃ ghāhehī’ti pāḷiyā sametīti ācariyena gahito”ti vadanti. Purato paharitvātiādi vatthuvisaṅketameva kira. Etaṃ gāme ṭhitanti puggalova niyamito. Yo pana liṅgavasena “dīghaṃ…pe… mārehī”ti āṇāpeti aniyametvā. Yadi niyametvā vadati, “etaṃ dīgha”nti vadeyyāti apare. Ācariyā pana “dīghanti vutte niyamitaṃ hoti, evaṃ aniyametvā vadati, na pana āṇāpako dīghādīsu aññataraṃ mārehīti adhippāyo”ti vadanti kira. “Attho pana cittena ekaṃ sandhāyapi aniyametvā āṇāpetī”ti likhitaṃ. “Itaro aññaṃ tādisaṃ māreti, āṇāpako muccatī”ti vuttaṃ yathādhippāyaṃ na gatattā. “Evaṃ dīghādivasenāpi cittena aniyamitassevāti yuttaṃ viya dissatī”ti aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ, suṭṭhu vīmaṃsitvā sabbaṃ [V 0.0142] gahetabbaṃ, okāsassa niyamitattāti ettha okāsaniyamaṃ katvā niddisanto tasmiṃ okāse nisinnaṃ māretukāmova hoti, sayaṃ pana tadā tattha natthi. Tasmā okāsena saha attano jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na hoti, tena attanā mārāpito paro eva mārāpito. Kathaṃ? Sayaṃ rasso ca tanuko ca hutvā pubbabhāge attānaṃ sandhāya āṇattikkhaṇe “dīghaṃ rassaṃ [M 0.0160] thūlaṃ balavantaṃ mārehī”ti āṇāpentassa cittaṃ attani tassākārassa natthitāya aññassa tādisassa jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattati, tena mūlaṭṭhassa kammabaddho. Evaṃsampadamidanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

This specific action is not found in the commentaries. They say, "It is accepted by the teacher as agreeing with the Pāḷi: ‘Thus pierce, thus strike, thus kill.’" The phrase 'having struck in front,' etc., it is said, is merely a discrepancy in the case. By the phrase 'one standing in the village,' the person alone is specified. But whoever commands by way of a characteristic, 'Kill the tall one… etc.,' without specifying. Others say that if he speaks having specified, he should say, 'This is the tall one.' But the teachers, it is said, say: 'When “the tall one” is said, it is specified. Thus he speaks without specifying. It is not, however, the intention of the one who commands to say, “Kill any one among the tall ones, etc.”' It is written: 'But the meaning is that with the mind, even while aiming at one, he commands without specifying.' It is said, 'The other person kills another such person; the one who commands is absolved,' because it did not proceed according to the original intention. In a certain gloss it is written: 'Thus, it appears as if it is proper that it is indeed unspecified by the mind, even by way of “the tall one,” etc.' All this should be understood after thorough investigation. Here, regarding the phrase 'because the place is specified,' one who points out, having specified the place, only desires to kill the one sitting in that place. But he himself is not there at that time. Therefore, his own life faculty, together with the place, does not become the object. Therefore, he causes only another to be killed. How so? At the moment of commanding, 'Kill the tall one, the short one, the stout one, the strong one,' the mind of the commander—who is himself short and thin—proceeds by making the life faculty of another such person its object, due to the absence of that characteristic in himself. Therefore, for the original instigator, it is connected with kamma. It should be understood that this is the accomplishment in this way.

Dūtaparamparāniddese āṇāpeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Itarassa āroceti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti ācariyantevāsīnaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ ārocane, paṭiggaṇhane dukkaṭaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, tassa dukkaṭanti siddhaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana okāsābhāvato na vuttaṃ. Mūlaṭṭhena āpajjitabbāpattiyā hi tassa okāso aparicchinno, tenassa tasmiṃ okāse thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. Vadhako ce paṭiggaṇhāti, mūlaṭṭho ācariyo pubbe āpannadukkaṭena saha thullaccayampi āpajjati. Kasmā? Mahājano hi tena pāpe niyojitoti. Idaṃ pana dukkaṭathullaccayaṃ vadhako ce tamatthaṃ na sāveti āpajjati. Yadi sāveti, pārājikamevāpajjati. Kasmā? Atthasādhakacetanāya abhāvā. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “paṭiggaṇhati, taṃ dukkaṭaṃ hoti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāṭhe na vuttanti ce? Vadhako pana ‘sādhu karomī’ti paṭiggaṇhitvā taṃ na karoti. Evañhi niyame ‘mūlaṭṭhassa kiṃ nāma hoti, kimassa dukkaṭāpattī’ti sañjātakaṅkhānaṃ tadatthadīpanatthaṃ ‘mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti thullaccayassā’”ti vuttaṃ. “Vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti āpatti dukkaṭassa, mūlaṭṭhassa ca āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vuttaṃ na silissati, mūlaṭṭhena āpajjitabbāpattidassanādhikārattā vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassāti vuttaṃ.

In the exposition on the succession of messengers, 'If one gives a command, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If one informs another, there is an offense of wrong-doing'—this is stated with reference to an offense of wrong-doing in informing and accepting, as is appropriate for teachers and pupils. It is established that if the killer does not accept, there is an offense of wrong-doing for him. However, this is not stated due to the absence of an opportunity. For the root-instigator, the opportunity for the offense to be incurred is indeed unlimited; hence for him in that case, a grave offense is stated. If the killer accepts, the root-instigator, the teacher, together with the offense of wrong-doing previously incurred, also incurs a grave offense. Why? Because a great number of people are indeed engaged by him in evil. However, the killer incurs this offense of wrong-doing and grave offense if he does not make known that purpose. If he does make it known, he incurs a pārājika offense itself. Why? Because of the absence of the intention to accomplish the purpose. In the supplementary passage, however, it is said: 'If he accepts, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If so, why is it not stated in the text?' The killer, however, having accepted it, saying, 'Very well, I will do it,' does not do it. Indeed, in such a case of certainty, for those in whom doubt has arisen—'What, then, befalls the root-instigator? Is his offense one of wrong-doing?'—it is stated, 'For the root-instigator, the offense is a grave one,' in order to clarify that meaning. The statement, 'The killer accepts, the offense is one of wrong-doing, and for the root-instigator, the offense is a grave one,' does not cohere, because it is in the section showing the offense to be incurred by the root-instigator that it is stated, 'The killer accepts, the offense is one of wrong-doing.'

Visakkiyadūtapadaniddese “vattukāmatāya ca kicchenettha vatvā payojanaṃ natthīti bhagavatā na vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana “mūlaṭṭhasseva dukkaṭa”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā – ācariyena āṇattena buddharakkhitena tadatthe saṅgharakkhitasseva ārocite kiñcāpi yo “sādhū”ti paṭiggaṇhāti, atha kho ācariyassevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ visaṅketattā, na buddharakkhitassa, kasmā? Atthasādhakacetanāya āpannattā. Teneva “āṇāpakassa ca vadhakassa ca āpatti pārājikassā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana mūlaṭṭhena āpajjitabbadukkaṭaṃ “mūlaṭṭhassa anāpattī”ti iminā aparicchinnokāsattā na vuttaṃ.

In the explanation of the Visakkiyadūta passage, it is stated: “Although there is a desire to speak, since there is no benefit in speaking here with difficulty, it was not said by the Blessed One.” As for what is stated in the commentary, “The dukkaṭa offense is for the original instigator alone,” here is the analysis: When, commanded by the teacher, Buddharakkhita informed Saṅgharakkhita alone of that matter, although the latter accepted it by saying, “Good,” nevertheless, this dukkaṭa offense is for the teacher alone because of the error; it is not for Buddharakkhita. Why? Because of having incurred it with the intention of accomplishing the purpose. For that very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi: “There is an offense of pārājika for both the one who commands and the one who kills.” However, that dukkaṭa offense to be incurred by the original instigator is not stated, because with this statement, 'There is no offense for the original instigator,' the occasion is undefined.

Avisaṅkete [M 0.0161][V 0.0143] “mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vuttattā visaṅkete āpatti dukkaṭassāti siddhanti veditabbaṃ. “Vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti idaṃ pana dukkaṭaṃ vadhakasseva. So hi paṭhamaṃ āṇāpakaṃ buddharakkhitaṃ pārājikāpattiṃ pāpetvā sayaṃ jīvitā voropetvā āpajjissatīti kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ “so taṃ jīvitā voropeti, āṇāpakassa ca vadhakassa ca āpatti pārājikassā”ti na vuttaṃ, tathāpi taṃ atthato vuttameva, “yato pārājikaṃ paññatta”nti pubbe vuttanayattā ca taṃ na vuttaṃ. “So taṃ jīvitā voropeti, āpatti sabbesaṃ pārājikassā”ti hi pubbe vuttaṃ. Ettha pubbe ācariyantevāsikānaṃ vuttadukkaṭathullaccayāpattiyo paṭhamameva anāpannā pārājikāpattiyā āpannattā. Tathāpi vadhakassa pārājikāpattiyā tesaṃ pārājikabhāvo pākaṭo jātoti katvā “āpatti sabbesaṃ pārājikassā”ti ekato vuttaṃ, na tathā “āṇāpakassa, vadhakassa ca āpatti pārājikassā”ti ettha. Kasmā? Vadhakassa dukkaṭāpattiyā āpannattā. So hi paṭhamaṃ dukkaṭāpattiṃ āpajjitvā pacchā pārājikaṃ āpajjati. Yadi pana antevāsikā kevalaṃ ācariyassa garukatāya sāsanaṃ ārocenti sayaṃ amaraṇādhippāyā samānā pārājikena anāpatti. Akappiyasāsanaharaṇapaccayā dukkaṭāpatti hoti eva, imassatthassa sādhanatthaṃ dhammapadavatthūhi migaluddakassa bhariyāya sotāpannāya dhanuususūlādidānaṃ nidassanaṃ vadanti eke. Taṃ tittirajātakena (jā. 1.4.73 ādayo) sameti, tasmā suttañca aṭṭhakathañca anulometīti no takkoti ācariyo. Idha pana dūtaparamparāya ca “itthannāmassa pāvada, itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ pāvadatū”ti ettha avisesetvā vuttattā vācāya vā ārocetu, hatthamuddāya vā, paṇṇena vā, dūtena vā ārocetu, visaṅketo natthi. Sace visesetvā mūlaṭṭho, antarādūto vā vadati, tadatikkame visaṅketoti veditabbaṃ.

When there is no deviation, because it is said, 'For the root-instigator, there is an offense of thullaccaya,' it should be understood that it is established that in case of a deviation, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. However, this statement, 'The killer accepts, there is an offense of dukkaṭa,' refers to a dukkaṭa offense for the killer alone. For he, having first caused the instigator Buddharakkhita to incur a pārājika offense, will himself incur one by depriving of life. Although it is not said in the Pāḷi, 'He deprives that one of life, and for both the instigator and the killer there is an offense of pārājika,' nevertheless, that was indeed said in terms of meaning. And because of the method previously stated, 'from which a pārājika is laid down,' that was not said. For it was previously said, 'He deprives that one of life, and for all there is an offense of pārājika.' Here, the previously mentioned dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses for the teacher and disciples are not incurred right at the beginning, because they have incurred the pārājika offense. Nevertheless, since their state of pārājika became manifest through the killer's pārājika offense, it was said collectively, 'For all there is an offense of pārājika.' It is not so here in the case of, 'For the instigator and the killer there is an offense of pārājika.' Why? Because the killer has incurred a dukkaṭa offense. For he first falls into a dukkaṭa offense, and afterwards falls into pārājika. But if the disciples convey the message merely out of respect for their teacher, they themselves having no intention of killing, there is no offense of pārājika. There is indeed an offense of dukkaṭa because of carrying an improper message. To prove this meaning, some say the giving of a bow, arrows, stakes, etc., by the deer hunter's wife, a stream-enterer, from the stories of the Dhammapada is an example. The teacher says: That agrees with the Tittira Jātaka. Therefore, it conforms to both the Sutta and the Commentary. Such is our reasoning. Here, however, in the case of a succession of messengers, because it is said without specification in the phrase, 'Tell so-and-so, let so-and-so tell so-and-so,' whether one informs by speech, or by hand gesture, or by a leaf letter, or by means of a messenger, there is no deviation. If the root-instigator or an intermediary messenger speaks with specification, it should be known that in transgressing that, there is a deviation.

Idāni imasmiṃyeva adhikāradvaye anugaṇṭhipade vuttanayo vuccati – “vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vadhakasseva āpatti, na āṇāpakassa buddharakkhitassa. Yadi pana so vajjhamaraṇāmaraṇesu avassamaññataraṃ karoti, buddharakkhitassāṇattikkhaṇe eva pārājikadukkaṭesu aññataraṃ [M 0.0162] siyā. “Iti cittamano”ti adhikārato “cittasaṅkappo”ti etthāpi iti-saddo viya “vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti thullaccayassā”ti adhikārato “mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttameva hoti. Kasmā sarūpena na vuttanti ce? Tato cuttari nayadānatthaṃ. “Mūlaṭṭhassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hi vutte mūlaṭṭhasseva vasena niyamitattā “paṭiggaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ hotī”ti na ñāyati. “Vadhako paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti hi aniyametvā vutte sakkā ubhayesaṃ [V 0.0144] vasena dukkaṭe yojetuṃ. Tasmā eva hi aṭṭhakathācariyehi adhikāraṃ gahetvā “saṅgharakkhitena sampaṭicchite mūlaṭṭhasseva dukkaṭanti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhantassa neva anuññātaṃ, na paṭikkhittaṃ, kevalantu buddharakkhitassa aniyamitattā paṭikkhittaṃ, tassa pana pārājikadukkaṭesu aññataraṃ bhaveyyāti ayamattho dīpito, tasmā tampi suvuttaṃ. Yasmā ubhayesaṃ vasena yojetuṃ sakkā, tasmā ācariyehi “paṭiggaṇhantassevetaṃ dukkaṭa”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha mūlaṭṭho neva anuññāto “mūlaṭṭhassā”ti vacanābhāvato, na ca paṭikkhitto “paṭiggaṇhantassa āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti pāḷiyā abhāvato, paṭiggaṇhanapaccayā vadhakassa dukkaṭaṃ siyāti nayaṃ dātuṃ “mūlaṭṭhassā”ti pāḷiyaṃ avuttattā “taṃ paṭiggaṇhantassevetaṃ dukkaṭa”nti yaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi suvuttaṃ. Tatra hi buddharakkhitassa paṭikkhittaṃ, vuttanayena pana tassa āpatti aniyatāti. Kasmā pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuttānaṃ paṭiggaṇhanapaccayā vadhakassa dukkaṭaṃ avatvā mūlaṭṭhasseva vasena dukkaṭaṃ vuttanti ce? Aniṭṭhanivāraṇatthaṃ. “Saṅgharakkhitena sampaṭicchite paṭiggaṇhanapaccayā tassa dukkaṭa”nti hi vutte anantaranayena sarūpena vuttattā idhāpi mūlaṭṭhassa thullaccayaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva hotīti āpajjati. Iti taṃ evaṃ āpannaṃ thullaccayaṃ uttānanti taṃ avatvā paṭiggaṇhantassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Anuttānattā aṭṭhakathāyanti imaṃ aniṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ nivāretuṃ “mūlaṭṭhassevetaṃ dukkaṭa”nti vuttaṃ. Ācariyena hi vuttanayena paṭiggaṇhantassa dukkaṭampi uttānameva. Uttānañca kasmā amhākaṃ khantīti vuttanti ce? Paṭipattidīpanatthaṃ. “Piṭakattayādīsu appaṭihatabuddhiyopi ācariyā sarūpena pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca avuttattā evarūpesu nāma ṭhānesu evaṃ paṭipajjanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana mādisoti suhadayā kulaputtā anāgate vuttanayamanatikkamitvā saṅkaradosaṃ vivajjetvā [M 0.0163] vaṇṇanāvelañca anatikkamma paṭipajjantī”ti ca aparehi vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāya vā avuttattā evarūpesu nāma pāṭho ācariyena pacchā nikkhittattā kesuci potthakesu na dissatīti katvā sabbaṃ likhissāma. Evaṃ sante paṭiggahaṇe āpattiyeva na siyā, sañcarittapaṭiggahaṇamaraṇābhinandanesupi ca āpatti hoti, māraṇapaṭiggahaṇe kathaṃ na siyā, tasmā paṭiggaṇhantassevetaṃ dukkaṭaṃ, tenevettha “mūlaṭṭhassā”ti na vuttaṃ. Purimanayepi cetaṃ paṭiggaṇhantassa veditabbameva, okāsābhāvena pana na vuttaṃ. Tasmā yo yo paṭiggaṇhāti, tassa tassa tappaccayā āpattiyevāti ayamettha amhākaṃ khanti. Yathā cettha, evaṃ adinnādānepīti.

Now, in these two instances, the method stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada is explained: 'The killer accepts; there is an offense of dukkaṭa'—the offense is for the killer only, not for the instigator, Buddharakkhita. However, if that killer certainly brings about for the one to be killed one of two outcomes, death or non-death, then for Buddharakkhita, at the very moment of the command, there would be one of either a pārājika or a dukkaṭa offense. From the context of 'thus, with a pleased mind' (`iti cittamano`), just as the word 'iti' is understood in the phrase 'mental intention' (`cittasaṅkappo`), similarly, from the context of 'the killer accepts; for the root instigator, the offense is a thullaccaya,' it has indeed been stated that 'for the root instigator, the offense is a dukkaṭa.' Why is it not stated explicitly? To provide a further principle. For if it were said, 'For the root instigator, the offense is a dukkaṭa,' because it would be specified by way of the root instigator only, it would not be known that 'for the one who accepts, there is a dukkaṭa.' But by saying, 'The killer accepts; there is an offense of dukkaṭa,' without specifying, it is possible to apply the dukkaṭa to both. Therefore, indeed, the commentary teachers, taking the context, have said: 'When it is accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, it should be known that the dukkaṭa is for the root instigator only.' For the one who accepts, it is neither permitted nor prohibited. For Buddharakkhita, however, it is prohibited because his offense is indeterminate; for him, as this meaning has been explained, there could be one of either a pārājika or a dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, that too is well said. Since it is possible to apply it to both, the teachers said, 'This dukkaṭa is for the one who accepts only.' In that case, the root instigator is neither permitted—due to the absence of the statement 'for the root instigator'—nor prohibited—due to the absence in the Pāḷi of the statement 'for the one who accepts, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.' To give the principle that 'due to the condition of accepting, there would be a dukkaṭa for the killer,' and because 'for the root instigator' is not said in the Pāḷi, what was said, namely 'That dukkaṭa is for the one who accepts only,' that too is well said. For in that Pāḷi, it is prohibited for Buddharakkhita, but according to the method stated, his offense is indeterminate. If one should ask, 'But why in the commentary, without stating the non-obvious dukkaṭa for the killer which is due to the condition of accepting, is the dukkaṭa stated by way of the root instigator only?' To prevent an undesirable meaning. For if it were said, 'When accepted by Saṅgharakkhita, due to the condition of accepting, there is a dukkaṭa for him (the root instigator),' then by the immediately preceding method, it would follow that here too, the thullaccaya for the root instigator has indeed been stated in the commentary. Thus, considering that thullaccaya which has so arisen to be obvious, without stating it, the dukkaṭa for the one who accepts is stated. To prevent this undesirable interpretation that 'it is not obvious in the commentary,' it was said, 'This dukkaṭa is for the root instigator only.' For by the method stated by the teachers, the dukkaṭa for the one who accepts is also obvious. If one should ask, 'And why was the obvious point stated as, "This is our preference"?' To illuminate the practice. 'Even teachers with unimpeded wisdom in the Three Piṭakas and so on, because it is not stated explicitly in the Pāḷi and the commentary, indeed practice in this way in such cases. What then to say of one like me? Thus, good-hearted clansmen in the future, not transgressing the stated method, avoiding the fault of confusion, and not overstepping the boundary of the commentarial explanation, will practice.' This has also been said by others. However, because this commentary passage was inserted later by the teacher, it is not seen in some books; thinking thus, we will write everything. If this were so, there would be no offense at all in accepting. And since there is an offense in acting as a go-between, accepting, and delighting in death, how could there not be an offense in accepting a request to kill? Therefore, this dukkaṭa is for the one who accepts only. For that very reason, it is not said here 'for the root instigator.' And in the previous method too, this should be understood as being for the one who accepts, but it was not stated due to a lack of opportunity. Therefore, whichever monk accepts, for that very monk, due to that condition, there is indeed an offense. This is our preference here. And just as it is here, so too in the case of taking what is not given.

175. Araho rahosaññīniddesādīsu kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyañca dukkaṭameva vuttaṃ, tathāpi tattha paramparāya sutvā maratūti adhippāyena ullapantassa uddese sati uddiṭṭhassa maraṇena āpatti [V 0.0145] pārājikassa, asati yassa kassaci maraṇena āpatti pārājikassa. “Itthannāmo sutvā me vajjhassa ārocetū”ti uddisitvā ullapantassa visaṅketatā dūtaparamparāya vuttattā veditabbā. Sace “yo koci sutvā vadatū”ti ullapati, vajjho sayameva sutvā marati, visaṅketattā na pārājikaṃ. Yo koci sutvā vadati, so ce marati, pārājikaṃ. “Yo koci mama vacanaṃ sutvā taṃ māretū”ti ullapati, yo koci sutvā māreti, pārājikaṃ, sayameva sutvā māreti, visaṅketattā na pārājikanti evaṃ yathāsambhavo veditabbo.

175. Although in the Pāḷi and the Commentary, only a dukkaṭa offense is mentioned regarding matters such as giving an indication while being aware of privacy, nevertheless, in that case, for one who speaks with the intention, 'Let him die after hearing it through a succession of messengers,' if there is a specific designation, a pārājika offense is incurred through the death of the designated person. If there is no designation, a pārājika offense is incurred through the death of anyone whatsoever. For one who speaks, having designated, 'Let so-and-so, having heard my word, inform the one to be killed,' the faulty nature of the communication should be understood as it is stated in the section on the succession of messengers. If one speaks, saying, 'Let whoever hears it, speak,' and the one to be killed hears it himself and dies, it is not a pārājika offense because of the faulty communication. If someone hears and speaks, and as a result he [the one to be killed] dies, it is a pārājika offense. If one speaks, saying, 'Let whoever hears my word kill him,' and someone hears and kills him, it is a pārājika offense. If he [the one to be killed] himself hears and kills himself, it is not a pārājika offense because of the faulty communication. Thus, this should be understood as is appropriate.

176. Mūlaṃ datvā muccatīti ettha bhinditvā, bhañjitvā, cavitvā, cuṇṇetvā, aggimhi pakkhipitvā vā pageva muccatīti atthato vuttameva hoti. Yesaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ gahitanti yesaṃ ñātakaparivāritānaṃ hatthato mūlaṃ tena bhikkhunā gahitaṃ, potthakasāmikahatthato pubbe dinnamūlaṃ puna gahetvā tesaññeva ñātakādīnaṃ datvā muccati, evaṃ potthakasāmikasseva santakaṃ jātaṃ hoti. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “sacepi so vippaṭisārī hutvā sīghaṃ tesaṃ mūlaṃ datvā muccatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yena dhanena potthako kīto, tañca dhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Potthakasāmikahatthato dhane gahite potthake adinnepi muccanato. Sace aññaṃ [M 0.0164] dhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na yuttaṃ potthakassa attaniyabhāvato amocitattā. Sace potthakaṃ sāmikānaṃ datvā mūlaṃ na gaṇhāti, na muccati attaniyabhāvato amocitattā. Sace potthakaṃ mūlaṭṭhena diyyamānaṃ “taveva hotū”ti appeti, muccati attaniyabhāvato mocitattā. Etthāyaṃ vicāraṇā – yathā cetiyaṃ vā paṭimaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ setuṃ vā kiṇitvā gahitampi kārakassevetaṃ puññaṃ, na kiṇitvā gahitassa, tathā pāpampi yena potthako likhito, tasseva yujjati, na itarassāti ce? Na, “satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā”ti vacanato. Parena hi katasatthaṃ labhitvā upanikkhipantassa pārājikanti siddhaṃ. Evaṃ parena likhitampi potthakaṃ labhitvā yathā vajjho taṃ passitvā marati, tathā upanikkhipeyya pārājikanti siddhaṃ hotīti. Cetiyādīti etamanidassanaṃ karaṇapaccayaṃ hi taṃ kammaṃ idaṃmaraṇapaccayanti evaṃ ācariyena vicāritaṃ. Mama pana cetiyādinidassaneneva sopi attho sādhetabbo viya paṭibhāti.

176. Here, regarding 'by giving the price, one is freed,' it is indeed said in terms of meaning that one is freed beforehand by breaking, crushing, destroying, pulverizing, or by putting it into a fire. Regarding 'from whose hand the price was taken': the price was taken by that monk from the hand of those, such as their relatives. By taking again the price previously given from the hand of the book's owner and giving it to those very same relatives and so on, he is freed. In this way, it becomes the property of the book's owner alone. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: 'If he, becoming remorseful, quickly gives them the price, he is freed.' This was said with reference to that very wealth by which the book was bought. Why? Because when the wealth is taken from the hand of the book's owner, one is freed even if the book is not given. If it were said with reference to other wealth, it would not be proper, because the book has not been released from being his own property. If, having given the book to the owners, he does not take the price, he is not freed, because it has not been released from being his own property. If, when the book is being given as the original price, he hands it over, saying, 'Let it be yours,' he is freed, because it has been released from being his own property. Herein is this investigation: If it is said that just as even when a cetiya, an image, a pond, or a bridge is purchased and taken, this merit belongs only to the maker, not to the one who purchased and took it; so too, the evil deed is fitting only for the one by whom the book was written, not for the other? No, because of the teaching, 'Or he should seek a weapon-bearer for him.' For it is established that for one who, having obtained a weapon made by another, places it nearby, it is a pārājika offense. Similarly, it is established that if one, having obtained a book also written by another, were to place it nearby in such a way that the person to be killed sees it and dies, it is a pārājika offense. That 'cetiya, etc.' is not a valid example; for that action (of making) has the act of making as its condition, whereas this (killing) has death as its condition—thus it was investigated by the teacher. But to me, it seems as if that meaning should be established by the very example of the cetiya, etc.

Tattakā pāṇātipātāti “ekāpi cetanā kiccavasena ‘tattakā’ti vuttā satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānānaṃ catukkatā viyā”ti likhitaṃ. Pamāṇe ṭhapetvāti attanā adhippetappamāṇe. “Kataṃ mayā evarūpe āvāṭe khaṇite tasmiṃ patitvā maratū”ti adhippāyena vadhako āvāṭappamāṇaṃ niyametvā sace khaṇi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ āvāṭe”ti. Idāni khaṇitabbaṃ sandhāya ettakappamāṇassa aniyamitattā “ekasmimpi kudālappahāre”tiādi [V 0.0146] vuttaṃ, suttantikattherehi kiñcāpi upaṭhataṃ, tathāpi sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā ubhayattha atthevāti ācariyā. Bahūnaṃ maraṇe ārammaṇaniyame kathanti ce? Vajjhesu ekassa jīvitindriye ālambite sabbesamālambitameva hoti. Ekassa maraṇepi na tassa sakalaṃ jīvitaṃ sakkā ālambituṃ na uppajjamānaṃ, uppannaṃ, nirujjhamānaṃ, atthitāyapāṇātipātacetanāva paccuppannārammaṇā, purejātārammaṇā ca hoti, tasmā tampi yujjati. Pacchimakoṭiyā ekacittakkhaṇe purejātaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ taṃ jīvitamālambaṇaṃ katvā sattamajavanapariyāpannacetanāya opakkame kate atthato tassa sattassa sabbaṃ jīvitindriyamālambitaṃ, voropitañca hoti, ito panaññathā na sakkā; evameva pubbabhāge “bahūpisatte māremī”ti cintetvā sanniṭṭhānakāle visapakkhipanādīsu ekaṃ payogaṃ [M 0.0165] sādhayamānā vuttappakāracetanā tesu ekassa vuttappakāraṃ jīvitindriyaṃ ālambaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati, evaṃ uppannāya panekāya sabbepi te māritā honti tāya eva sabbesaṃ maraṇasiddhito, aññathā na sakkā voropetuṃ, ālambituṃ vā. Tattha ekāya cetanāya bahūnaṃ maraṇe akusalarāsi kathanti ce? Visuṃ visuṃ maraṇe pavattacetanānaṃ kiccakaraṇato. Kathaṃ? Tā pana sabbā upapajjavedanīyāva honti, tasmā tāsu yāya kāyaci dinnāya paṭisandhiyā itarā sabbāpi “tato balavatarakusalapaṭibāhitā ahosikamma”ntiādikoṭṭhāsaṃ bhajanti, punapi vipākaṃ janituṃ na sakkonti. Aparāpariyavedanīyāpi viya taṃ paṭibāhitvā kusalacetanā paṭisandhiṃ deti, tathā ayampi cetanā anantarabhave eva paṭisandhidānādivasena tāsaṃ kiccalesakaraṇato ekāpi samānā “rāsī”ti vuttā. Tāya pana dinnāya paṭisandhiyā atitikkho vipāko hoti. Ayamettha visesotiādi anugaṇṭhipade papañcitaṃ.

Regarding the phrase 'so many acts of killing,' it is written: 'Even a single volition, by way of its function, is called ‘so many,’ like the fourfold nature of the foundations of mindfulness and the right exertions.' 'Having established a measure' means in a measure intended by oneself. With the intention, 'When a pit of such a kind has been dug by me, may one, having fallen into it, die,' if the killer, having determined the measure of the pit, digs it, it is with reference to that that it is said, 'in this pit.' Now, with reference to what is to be dug, because a measure of 'this much' has not been determined, it is said, 'even in a single strike of the spade,' and so on. The teachers state that although this is presented by the Suttantika elders, nevertheless, the determining volition certainly exists in both cases. If one should ask, 'How is the object determined in the death of many?' Among those to be killed, when the life faculty of one is taken as an object, it is indeed taken as an object for all of them. Even in the death of one, it is not possible to take their entire life as an object—not that which is arising, that which has arisen, nor that which is ceasing. Because of its existence, the volition of killing itself has a present object and a pre-nascent object. Therefore, that too is suitable. At the final limit, in one mind-moment, when the effort is made by the volition included in the seventh impulsion moment, having taken as an object that life which stands as pre-nascent, then in effect, the entire life faculty of that being is taken as an object and is cut off. Otherwise, this is not possible. Just so, in the preliminary stage, having thought, 'I will kill many beings,' at the time of determination, while accomplishing a single effort in acts such as administering poison, the volition of the type described arises, having taken as its object the life faculty of the type described of one among them.
