By that one volition which has thus arisen, all those beings are killed, because by that very volition, the death of all is accomplished. Otherwise, it is not possible to cut them off or to take them as an object. If it is asked how a single volition can result in a mass of unwholesomeness due to the death of many, it is because of the performance of the function of the volitions that occurred separately in each death. How? All those volitions are indeed of the type that are experiencable in the next life. Therefore, among them, by whichever one rebirth is given, all the others, being obstructed by wholesome kamma more powerful than that, fall into the category of 'defunct kamma,' and so on, and are unable to produce a result again. Just as a wholesome volition gives rebirth by obstructing that unwholesome kamma, similar to a kamma experiencable in a succession of later lives, so too this volition, although it is single, is called a 'mass' because, in the very next existence, by way of giving rebirth and so on, it performs a fraction of the function of those other volitions. However, when rebirth is given by that volition, the result is extremely severe. This is the distinction here. This and so on is elaborated in the Anugaṇṭhipada.

Amaritukāmā vāti adhippāyattā opapātikamaraṇepi āpatti. “‘Nibbattitvā’ti vuttattā patanaṃ na dissatīti ce? Opapātikattaṃ, patanañca ekamevā”ti likhitaṃ. Atha vā “sabbathāpi anuddissevā”ti vacanato ettha maratūti adhippāyasambhavato “uttarituṃ asakkonto marati pārājikamevā”ti suvuttaṃ. Sace “patitvā maratū”ti niyametvā khaṇito hoti, opapātikamanusso ca nibbattitvā ṭhitaniyameneva “uttarituṃ na sakkā”ti cintetvā maratīti pārājikacchāyā na dissati, tena vuttaṃ “uttarituṃ asakkonto”ti. So hi uttarituṃ asakkonto punappunaṃ patitvā marati, tena pātopi tassa siddho hotīti adhippāyo. Tattha siyā – yo pana “uttarituṃ asakkonto maratī”ti vutto, so opātakhaṇanakkhaṇe arūpaloke jīvati. Vadhakacetanā ca “aniyato dhammo micchattaniyatassa dhammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, rūpajīvitindriyaṃ mātughātikammassa pitughātikammassa arahantaghātikammassa [V 0.0147] ruhiruppādakammassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.15.38 micchattaniyatattika) vacanato rūpajīvitindriyārammaṇaṃ hoti, na ca taṃ arūpāvacarasattassatthi, na ca sā cetanā “aniyato dhammo micchattaniyatassa dhammassa purejātapaccayena paccayo, ārammaṇapurejātaṃ vatthupurejātaṃ ārammaṇapurejātaṃ. Rūpajīvitindriyaṃ [M 0.0166] mātughātikammassa purejātapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.15.48 micchattaniyatattika) vacanato anāgatārammaṇā hoti. Añño idha patitvā maraṇakasatto natthi, evaṃ sante vadhakacetanāya kiṃ ārammaṇanti ce? Yassa kassaci idha jīvanakasattassa paccuppannaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Kiñcāpi so na marati, atha kho pāṇātipāto hoti eva. Yathā kiṃ “yathākkamena ṭhite satta jane ekena kaṇḍena vijjhitvā māremī”ti pubbabhāge cintetvā sanniṭṭhānakāle tesu ekassa jīvitamārammaṇaṃ katvā kaṇḍaṃ vissajjeti, kaṇḍo taṃ virajjhitvā itare cha jane māreti, evaṃ santepi ayaṃ pāṇātipātī eva hoti, evamidhāpi “yo kocī”ti vikappentassa vadhakacetanā yassa kassaci jīvitārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattati, tasmiṃ amatepi itarassa vasena pāṇātipātī. Sace arahā hutvā parinibbāyati, arahantaghātakova hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha evarūpesu. Ayameva hettha ācariyaparamparāgatā yutti vinicchayakathāti vuttaṃ.

Because of the perpetrator's intention, an offense is incurred even in the death of a spontaneously arisen being, as in the case of one not wishing to die. If one should say, 'Because it is said, "having arisen," falling is not seen,' the reply is: 'Spontaneous arising and falling are simultaneous.' Thus it is written. Alternatively, from the statement, 'in every way, even without specifying,' and because the intention 'let him die' is possible here, it is well said: 'being unable to get out, he dies—it is a pārājika offense indeed.' If a pit is dug with the determination, 'Let him die by falling,' and a spontaneously arisen human, having arisen and, by the very nature of his static state, thinks, 'It is not possible to get out,' and dies, the shadow of a pārājika offense is not seen. Therefore it is said, 'being unable to get out.' For he, being unable to get out, dies by falling again and again; by that, the falling is also accomplished according to the digger's wish. This is the meaning. Here, there might be this objection: As for the one who is said to 'die, being unable to get out,' he, at the moment of the digging of the pit, is living in the formless realm. And the murderous volition, according to the statement, 'an undetermined phenomenon is a condition for a wrongly determined phenomenon by way of object condition; the life faculty of form is a condition for the act of killing one’s mother, the act of killing one’s father, the act of killing an arahant, and the act of shedding the Buddha's blood by way of object condition,' has the life faculty of form as its object. But that does not exist for a being of the formless sphere. Nor does that volition, according to the statement, 'an undetermined phenomenon is a condition for a wrongly determined phenomenon by way of prenascence condition... The life faculty of form is a condition for the act of killing one’s mother by way of prenascence condition,' have a future object. There is no other being here who, having fallen, will die. This being so, what is the object of the murderous volition? If this is asked, the answer is: The present life faculty of any living being here is the object. Although that one does not die, nevertheless, the destruction of life does indeed occur. How so? It is like one who, having thought beforehand, 'I will kill seven people standing in sequence by piercing them with a single arrow,' at the time of decision, makes the life of one of them the object and releases the arrow. The arrow, missing that one, kills the other six people. Even so, this person is indeed a killer. So too here, for one who resolves, 'whoever it may be,' the murderous volition proceeds, having made the life of anyone whatsoever its object. Even when that one who was the object does not die, by means of another, he is a killer. If the victim, having become an arahant, attains final Nibbāna, the perpetrator is indeed a killer of an arahant. This is the principle in all such cases. This very thing here is said to be the decisive discourse on what is logical, handed down through the lineage of teachers.

Patanarūpaṃ pamāṇanti ettha yathā mātuyā patitvā parivattaliṅgāya matāya so mātughātako hoti, na kevalaṃ purisaghātako, tasmā patanasseva vasena āpatti. Kasmā? Patanarūpamaraṇarūpānaṃ ekasantānattā, tadeva hissa jīvitindriyaṃ, tassa hi parivattanaṃ natthi, itthipurisindriyāneva pavattiyaṃ nirujjhanuppajjanakāni, itthipurisoti ca tattha vohāramattameva, tasmā mātughātakova, na purisaghātakoti, yathā tassa patanarūpavasenāpatti, tathā idhāpi patanarūpavasena thullaccayaṃ ekasantānattāti ayaṃ paṭhamatheravāde yutti. Dutiye kiñcāpi peto patito, yakkho ca, atha kho ahetukapaṭisandhikattā akusalavipākassa “vāmena sūkaro hotī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.296; mahāni. aṭṭha. 166) ettha vuttayakkhānaṃ paṭisandhi viya sabbarūpānaṃ sādhāraṇattā, amanussajātikattā ca tiracchānarūpena mate maraṇarūpavasena pācittiyaṃ, vatthuvasena lahukāpattiyā parivattanā hoti eva tatthajātakarukkhādichedanapācittiyaparivattanaṃ viya. Ayameva yuttataro, tasmā pacchā vutto. Pārājikassa pana manussajātiko yathā tathā vā patitvā yathā tathā vā maratu, pārājikameva garukattā. Garukāpattiyā hi viparivattanā natthīti vuttaṃ.

Herein, the form at the time of falling is the standard. For example, just as when his mother, having fallen and died after her gender has changed, he becomes a matricide, not merely a killer of a man. Therefore, the offense is incurred by means of the form at the time of falling alone. Why? Because the form at the time of falling and the form at the time of death are of a single continuum. Indeed, that very thing is its life faculty, for there is no transformation of it. Only the female and male faculties cease and arise during the course of existence, and the term 'woman' or 'man' in that case is merely a convention. Therefore, he is only a matricide, not a killer of a man. Just as for that one, the offense is by means of the form at the time of falling, so too here, a grave offense is incurred by means of the form at the time of falling because of the single continuum. This is the reasoning in the view of the first Elder. In the second view, although a peta or a yakkha has fallen, nevertheless, because of having a rootless rebirth-linking, which is the result of unwholesome kamma—like the rebirth-linking of the yakkhas mentioned here in the passage 'on the left, he becomes a pig'—and because of being common to all forms, and because of being of non-human birth, if it dies with the form of an animal, a pācittiya offense is incurred by means of the form at the time of death. There is indeed a change to a lighter offense by means of the object, like the change from a pācittiya offense in the case of cutting a tree, etc., that has grown in that place. This very view is more reasonable; therefore, it was stated last. But in the case of a pārājika, if a being of human birth falls in whatever way and dies in whatever way, it is a pārājika itself because of its gravity. For it is said, 'There is no change for a grave offense.'

Thullaccayaṃ [V 0.0148][M 0.0167] tiracchāne, mate bhedassa kāraṇaṃ;

Sarūpamaraṇaṃ tisso, phusso maññeti aññathā.

A thullaccaya is incurred when an animal dies; the reason for the difference is death in its own form. Tissa thinks thus; Phussa thinks otherwise.

Gaṇṭhipade pana “dutiyavāde puthujjanassa patitvā arahattaṃ patvā marantassa vasena vutto”ti likhitaṃ. “Tiracchāne”ti ettha keci vadanti “devā adhippetā”ti. “Sakasakarūpeneva maraṇaṃ bhavati nāññathā”ti ca vadanti. Yakkhapetarūpena matepi eseva nayoti thullaccayanti attho. “Tiracchānagatamanussaviggahamaraṇe viyā”ti likhitaṃ. Pahāraṃ laddhāti sattānaṃ māraṇatthāya katattā vuttaṃ.

However, in the Gaṇṭhipada, it is written: 'In the second view, it is stated with reference to an ordinary person who, having fallen, attains Arahantship and then dies.' Here, regarding 'tiracchāne' (animals), some say, 'deities are intended.' And they also say: 'Death occurs only in one's own form, not otherwise.' Even if one dies in the form of a yakkha or peta, this same principle applies; therefore, it is a grave offense—this is the meaning. It is written: 'Like in the case of killing a human being in the form of an animal.' The phrase 'having received a blow' is stated because it was done for the purpose of killing beings.

177. Sādhu suṭṭhu maratūti vacībhedaṃ karoti. Visabhāgarogoti sarīraṭṭho gaṇḍapīḷakādi.

177. He makes the verbal expression, 'Good, very good, let him die!' Regarding 'incompatible disease' (visabhāgaroga), this refers to that which is established in the body, such as tumors, boils, and so forth.

178. Kāḷānusārīti ekissā latāya mūlaṃ kira. Mahākacchapena katapupphaṃ vā. Haṃsapupphanti haṃsānaṃ pakkhapattaṃ. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena sāhatthikāṇattikanayañhettha yojetvā kāyavācācittato samuṭṭhānavidhi dassetabbo.

178. 'Kāḷānusārī' is, they say, the root of a certain creeper. Or, it is a flower made with the mahākacchapa flower. 'Haṃsapuppha' refers to the wing feathers of swans and so forth. Here, having applied the principle of acting with one's own hand and of giving a command according to the method stated previously, the method of arising from body, speech, and mind should be explained.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of Words (Padabhājanīya) is concluded.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Vinītavatthu

180. Maraṇatthikāva hutvāti imassa kāyassa bhedena saggapāpanādhippāyattā atthato maraṇatthikāva hutvā evaṃadhippāyino maraṇatthikā nāma hontīti attano maraṇatthikabhāvaṃ ajānantā āpannā pārājikaṃ. Na hi te “attano cittappavattiṃ na jānantī”ti vuccanti. Vohāravasenāti pubbabhāgavohāravasena. Sanniṭṭhāne panetaṃ natthi. Pāse baddhasūkaramocane viya na hoti. Yathānusandhināti antarā amaritvāti attho. Appaṭivekkhitvāti avicāretvā. Heṭṭhimabhāge hi kismiñci vijjamāne vali paññāyati. Dassiteti uddharitvā ṭhapite. Paṭibandhanti tayā paṭibandhaṃ, paribhogantarāyaṃ saṅghassa mā akāsīti attho.

180. Regarding 'having become one who desires death': because their intention is to reach a heavenly realm through the breaking up of this body, in meaning they have become ones who desire death. Those with such an intention are called 'maraṇatthikā' (those who desire death). Because they do not know their own state of desiring death, they fall into a Pārājika offense. For it is not said of them that they 'do not know the process of their own mind'; they indeed know it. Regarding 'by way of convention', it means by way of the convention of the preliminary stage. But in the final determination, this does not exist. It is not like releasing a pig caught in a snare. Regarding 'according to the connection', the meaning is 'without dying in the interim'. Regarding 'without having reflected', it means 'without having considered'. For if something exists in the lower part, a fold appears. Regarding 'shown', it means when it is taken out and placed. Regarding 'hindrance', the meaning is: 'Do not create a hindrance for the Saṅgha that is connected with you, an obstruction to their use'.

181-2. Yasmā [M 0.0168] kiriyaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā “paṭhamaṃ laddha”nti vuttaṃ. Pubbepi attanā laddhapiṇḍapātato paṇītapaṇītaṃ dento tatthapi attakāriyaṃ adāsi. Asañciccāti [V 0.0149] ettha aññaṃ ākaḍḍhantassa aññassa patane sabbena sabbaṃ abhisandhi natthi. Na maraṇādhippāyassāti paṭigho ca payogo ca atthi, vadhakacetanā natthi. Ajānantassāti ettha “vatthuajānanavasena ajānantassa doso natthi, idaṃ kira tesaṃ nānattaṃ. ‘Asañcicco aha’nti pāḷiyaṃ na dissati. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā tathārūpāya pāḷiyā bhavitabba”nti vadanti. No ce, thullaccayanti ettha “dukkhavedanā ce nuppajjati, dukkaṭamevā”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “Muggarā nāma khādanadaṇḍakā. Vemā nāma tesaṃ khādanadaṇḍakānaṃ heṭṭhā ca upari ca tiriyaṃ bandhitabbadaṇḍā”ti likhitaṃ. Heṭṭhāva duvidhāpi paṭhanti. Hatthappatto viya dissati “tassa vikkhepo mā hotū”ti upacchindati. Visesādhigamaṃ byākaritvā tappabhavaṃ sakkāraṃ lajjīyanto āhāraṃ upacchindati sabhāgānaṃ byākatattā. Te hi kappiyakhettaṃ ārocenti.

Because it is not possible to give the action, it is said, 'first obtained.' Even before, a monk giving the most excellent food from the alms-food obtained by himself, even then gave the first portion of the meal which he himself had set aside as choice. Here, in the case of 'unintentionally,' for one who is pulling another, in the falling of that other, there is no intention whatsoever. In the case of 'not having the intention to kill,' there is both aversion and application, but there is no volition to kill. Here, in the case of 'not knowing,' they say: 'For one who does not know by way of not knowing the object, there is no fault; this, it seems, is their difference. The phrase "I am unintentional" is not seen in the Pāḷi. Because it is said in the commentary, there must have been such a Pāḷi text.' Here, in the case of 'if not, a thullaccaya,' they say, 'If a painful feeling does not arise, it is only a dukkaṭa offense'; this should be investigated. It is written: 'Muggarā are mallets with handles fitted into a hole. Vemā are the cross-pieces to be bound crosswise below and above those mallets with handles.' They also recite both kinds as being only below. It appears like something that has come into one's hand. Thinking, 'Let there be no distraction for him,' he cuts it off. Having declared a special attainment, and being ashamed of the honor arising from it, he cuts off the food because it was declared to his peers. For they announce the suitable field.

186. Akataviññattiyāti na viññattiyā. Sā hi anuññātattā katāpi akatā viyāti akataviññatti. “‘Vadeyyātha, bhante yenattho’ti evaṃ akataṭṭhāne viññatti akataviññattī”ti likhitaṃ. Titthiyabhūtānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ sahatthā dātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti. Pitucchā nāma pitubhaginī. Sacepi na yācanti “yācituṃ dukkha”nti, sayaṃ vā evaṃ vattumasakkontā. “Yadā tesaṃ attho bhavissatī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā vā. “‘Vejjakammaṃ vā na hotī’ti vacanato yāva sattamo kulaparivaṭṭo, tāva bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Sabbapadesūti mahāmātuyācūḷamātuyātiādīnaṃ.

186. ‘By an unmade request’ means not by a request. For that, because it is permitted, is as if unmade even when made; therefore, it is an ‘unmade request.’ It is written: ‘A request in an unmade situation, such as, “Venerable sir, you may speak of that which is needed,” is an unmade request.’ It should be known that it is not allowable to give with one's own hand to parents who have become heretics. A ‘pitucchā’ is a father's sister. Even if they do not ask, thinking, ‘It is difficult to ask,’ or if they themselves are unable to say so, or after one has reflected, ‘When they have a need,’ it should be given. Based on the statement ‘or it is not medical practice,’ they say that it is allowable to prepare medicine for relatives up to the seventh generation. ‘In all instances’ refers to the chief maternal aunt, the younger maternal aunt, and so on.

Vuttanayena pariyesitvāti “sāmaṇerehi vā”tiādinā. “Na akataviññattiyā”ti vadanti. “Paccāsīsati sace, dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. Kappiyavasenāti pupphaṃ ānethātiādinā. “Pūjaṃ akāsī’ti vuttattā sayaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti.

Regarding 'having searched in the manner described': this refers to the method beginning with 'by novices,' and so forth. They say, 'Not by an unmade request.' They say, 'If one hopes for it, it is a dukkaṭa offense.' Regarding 'according to what is allowable': this refers to the method beginning with 'bring flowers,' and so forth. They say, 'Because it is said, “he made an offering,” it is not proper to take it oneself.'

“Bhaṇathā”ti vutte pana kātabbaṃ. Dhammañhi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. No ce jānanti, na pādā apanetabbā. Avamaṅgalanti hi gaṇhanti.

However, when told, 'Recite,' it should be done. For indeed, it is fitting to speak the Dhamma. If they do not know, the feet should not be removed. For they consider it inauspicious.

Coranāgassa [M 0.0169] hi āmaṭṭhaṃ dinne kujjhissati, anāmaṭṭhaṃ na vaṭṭatīti aṅgulantare thokaṃ bhattaṃ gahetvā patte bhattaṃ sabbaṃ adāsi, so tena tussi. Varapotthakacittattharaṇanti sibbitvā kātabbattharaṇavikati. Piturājā damiḷassa parājito rohaṇe soḷasavassāni vasitvā mittāmaccaparivuto “rajjaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti āgantvā antarāmagge appamattakassa kāraṇā ekaṃ amaccaṃ [V 0.0150] ghātāpesi. Sesā bhayena palāyantā araññe antarāmagge corehi viluttā hambugallakavihāraṃ gantvā tattha cātunikāyikatissatthero tesaṃ saṅgahaṃ katvā puna ānetvā rañño dassesi, tehi saddhiṃ rajjaṃ gahetvā rājā hambugallakatissattherassa abhayagirivihāraṃ akāsi. Sesāpi ekekavihāraṃ kārāpesuṃ kira.

For if touched food were given to the robber-chief Coranāga, he would be angry, and an untouched first portion of food is not proper; therefore, taking a little food between the fingers, he gave all the food in the bowl, and he (Coranāga) was pleased by that. 'Varapotthakacittattharaṇa' is a special spread that is made by sewing. The father-king, defeated by the Damiḷa king, lived in Rohaṇa for sixteen years. Surrounded by friends and ministers, he came with the intention, 'I will take the kingdom,' but on the way, for a trivial reason, he had one minister killed. The rest, fleeing in fear, were robbed by thieves on the way in the forest. They went to the Hambugallaka monastery, where the elder Tissa, who was versed in the four Nikāyas, gave them support, brought them back, and presented them to the king. Having taken the kingdom together with them, the king built the Abhayagiri monastery for the elder Tissa of Hambugallaka. It is said that the remaining ministers also had one monastery each built.

187. Corasamīpaṃ pesento “vāḷayakkhavihāraṃ pesetī”ti iminā sadiso. Kasmā? Maraṇādhippāyattā. Taḷākādīsu macchādiggahaṇatthaṃ kevaṭṭaṃ aññāpadesena “taḷākatīraṃ gacchā”ti pahiṇantassa pāṇātipātena bhavitabbaṃ, “vāḷayakkhavihāraṃ pāhesī”ti imassa sadiso. Kasmā? “Maraṇādhippāyattā”ti vacanassānulomato, aṭṭhakathāyampi “evaṃ vāḷayakkhampī”ti vuttattā.

187. One who sends someone near a robber is similar to this case: 'He sends him to the monastery of the wild yakkha.' Why? Because of the intention of causing death. For one who, by way of a pretext, sends a fisherman to catch fish and so forth in a reservoir, etc., saying, 'Go to the bank of the reservoir,' it should be considered an offense of destroying life; this should be similar to the case of 'he sent him to the monastery of the wild yakkha.' Why? Because it is in accordance with the statement, 'because of the intention of causing death,' and also because it is stated in the commentary, 'thus also to a wild yakkha.'

189. Taṃ tatraṭṭhitaṃ chindantanti taṃ-saddo ekaccesu natthi. Itaresu pārājikathullaccayaṃ āpannāti attho. “Imaṃ chinditvā sīghaṃ gantvā saṅghassa pattacīvaraṃ dassāmī”ti kusalacittenapi chindituṃ na vaṭṭati ananuññātattā. Aññassa pana bhikkhuno vaṭṭati anuññātattā.

189. Regarding the phrase 'cutting it while it is there,' the word 'taṃ' is absent in some versions. In others, the meaning is that one incurs a pārājika or a thullaccaya offense. Even with a wholesome intention, thinking, 'Having cut this, I will go quickly and give the bowl and robe to the Saṅgha,' it is not allowable to cut it, because it is unpermitted. For another bhikkhu, however, it is allowable, because it is permitted.

190. Kathaṃ? Kuṭirakkhaṇatthañhi bhagavatā paṭaggidānādi anuññātaṃ, kuṭi nāmesā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya. Tasmā “bhikkhurakkhaṇatthaṃ aññassa bhikkhussa vaṭṭatī’ti vattabbamettha natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ acchinnacīvarassa naggabhāvappaṭicchādanatthaṃ bhūtagāmapātabyatā bhagavatā anuññātā, jīvitarakkhaṇatthañca sappadaṭṭhakāle anuññātaṃ, tasmā “api jīvitaṃ pariccajitabbaṃ, na ca rukkho vā chinditabbo”tiādi na vattabbaṃ siyā, tasmā taṃ nidassanaṃ appamāṇaṃ, aṭṭhakathācariyo evettha pamāṇaṃ. Ettha panāyaṃ ācariyassa takko – ariyapuggalesupi sattā naggiyaṃ passitvā appasādaṃ katvā nirayūpagā bhavissanti[M 0.0170], tathā sappā ca ḍaṃsitvā, tesaṃ pāpavimocanatthaṃ bhūtagāmapātabyatā anuññātā. Dānapatīnaṃ cittarakkhaṇatthaṃ paṭaggidānādi. Aññathā lokassa puññantarāyo, saṅghassa ca lābhantarāyo hoti. Vadhakassa pana cittahitakaraṇaṃ natthi, taṃ pana avītikkamaṃ, jīvitapariccajanaṃ passitvā vā “aho dukkaraṃ kata”nti pasādameva labheyyunti attano na vaṭṭati, aññassa vaṭṭati. Aññathā titthiyānaṃ asaddhammasiddhiyāti. Gaṇṭhipade pana “jīvitatthāya rukkhaṃ chindantassa attasinehavasena chindanato akusalattā na vaṭṭati, aññassa vaṭṭatī”ti likhitaṃ. Anekesu rukkhena otthatesu, opāte vā patitesu aññena aññassatthāya rukkhachedanādi [V 0.0151] kātuṃ vaṭṭati, kasmā? Paraparittāṇādhippāyatoti. Parittanti rakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “samantā bhūmitacchana”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

190. How so? For the sake of protecting a hut, the Blessed One permitted the giving of a fire-stick and so forth. This hut is indeed for the benefit of the bhikkhus. Therefore, it is said: 'Since it is permissible for another bhikkhu for the sake of protecting a bhikkhu, there is nothing to be said in this matter.' If this is so, for a bhikkhu robbed of his robe, for the sake of covering his state of nakedness, the destruction of living plants was permitted by the Blessed One. And for the sake of protecting life, it was permitted at the time of a snakebite. Therefore, it should not be said, 'Even life should be given up, but a tree should not be cut,' and so forth. Hence, that illustration is not the standard; the commentary teacher alone is the authority here. Here, however, is the teacher's reasoning: Beings, seeing even noble individuals in a state of nakedness, having generated displeasure, will become those who go to hell. Likewise, when snakes have bitten, for the sake of releasing them from evil, the destruction of living plants was permitted. The giving of a fire-stick and so forth is for the sake of protecting the minds of donors. Otherwise, there would be an obstacle to the world's merit and an obstacle to the Saṅgha's gain. But for a killer, there is no act that benefits his mind; on the contrary, having seen that non-transgression and the giving up of life, they might think, 'Oh, a difficult deed has been done!' and thereby gain faith. Therefore, it is not permissible for oneself, but it is permissible for another. Otherwise, the false doctrines of the heretics would be established. In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is written: 'For a bhikkhu cutting a tree for the sake of his life, because he cuts it through self-love, it is unwholesome and thus not permissible; but for another, it is permissible.' When many are crushed by a tree, or have fallen into a pit, it is permissible for one to do the cutting of a tree and so forth for the sake of another. Why? Because of the intention to protect others. Paritta means protection. To show this, 'clearing the ground all around,' and so forth was said.

191. Tīhi mārite pana visaṅketanti ettha tīsu ekena māritepi “khettameva otiṇṇattā pārājika”nti vuttattā tayopi ekato hutvā mārenti ce, āpajjati, teneva vuttaṃ “paricchedabbhantare vā avisaṅketa”nti. “Paricchedātikkame pana sabbattha visaṅketaṃ hotī”ti vuttattā dvinnaṃ balaṃ gahetvā tatiyo ce māreti āpajjati viya dissati, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “Dve mārentū”ti vutte ekena vā dvīhi vā mārite pārājikanti “dvinnaṃ pahārānaṃ maraṇe sati dve māritā nāma honti, asati ekova hoti, tasmā vijānitabba”nti vadanti.

191. Regarding the phrase 'when killed by three, there is uncertainty,' here, because it is said, 'Even when killed by one of the three, because one has entered the very field of killing, it is a pārājika,' if all three, having come together, kill, an offense is incurred. For that very reason, it is said, 'Within the boundary, there is no uncertainty.' Because it is said, 'But when the boundary is transgressed, there is uncertainty everywhere,' if a third person, having taken the strength of two, kills, it appears as if an offense is incurred; this should be investigated. When it is said, 'Let them kill two,' if one or two are killed by one or two persons, it is a pārājika. Therefore, they say: 'When there is death from two blows, two are said to have been killed; in the absence of death, there is only one. Therefore, it should be known.'

Tatiyapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Pārājika is concluded.

4. Catutthapārājikaṃ

4. The Fourth Pārājika

Vaggumudātīriyabhikkhuvatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Bhikkhus from the Bank of the Vaggumudā River

193. Catutthe vaggu ca sā modayati ca satteti vaggumudā. “Vaggumadā”tipi pāṭho, tassa vaggu ca sā pasannasuddhataraṅgasamiddhattā sukhumā cāti attho jīvitavaggutthanitā jīvitatthanti nīluppalantiādīsu viya. Madassāti ca bahukhajjabhojjapānādisamiddhā nadī chaṇadivasesūti nirutti veditabbā. Vaggu parisuddhāti lokena sammatāti kira attho. Bhāsito bhavissatīti pāṭhaseso.

193. In the Fourth: `Vaggumudā` is so called because that river (`sā`) is both pleasing (`vaggu`) and gladdens (`modayati`) beings (`satte`). There is also the reading `Vaggumadā`. The meaning of this is: that river is pleasing (`vaggu`) and, because it is endowed with clear, pure waves, it is also gentle (`sukhumā`). The term `jīvitavaggutthanitā` (the state of having the quality of causing fullness of life) has the meaning 'for the sake of life' (`jīvitatthaṃ`), just as in the case of `nīluppala`, etc. And regarding `madassā`, the etymology should be known thus: on festival days, the river is endowed with much hard food, soft food, drinks, and so on. The meaning, it seems, is that `vaggu` means pure, and it is esteemed as such by the world. The remainder of the reading is `bhāsito bhavissati`.

194-5. Vaṇṇavā [M 0.0171] vaṇṇavanto vaṇṇavantānītipi sijjhati kira bahuvacanena. Yasmā indriyānaṃ ūnattaṃ, pūrattaṃ vā natthi, tasmā “abhiniviṭṭhokāsassa paripuṇṇattā”ti vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa abhiniviṭṭhokāso hadayavatthu. Catuiriyāpathacakke pākatindriye. Attano dahatīti attanā dahati, attanā paṭividdhaṃ katvā pavedetīti adhippāyo. Santanti vattamānaṃ. Gotrabhunoti gottamattaṃ anubhavattā nāmamattakamevāti attho.

194-5. It is said that `vaṇṇavā`, `vaṇṇavanto`, and `vaṇṇavantāni` are also formed in the plural. Because there is no deficiency or excess of the faculties, it is therefore said, 'due to the completeness of the sphere of application.' The sphere of application of the sixth faculty is the heart-base. In the cycle of the four postures, the faculties are in their natural state. In the phrase `attano dahati`, it means he himself places it or makes it known; the intention is that, having penetrated it himself, he makes it known. `Santaṃ` means the present. Regarding `gotrabhu`, the meaning is that because it experiences only the lineage of the noble ones, it is merely a name.

Savibhaṅgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Training Rule with Its Analysis

197. Padabhājane [V 0.0152] “tisso vijjā”ti vuttattā arūpāvacarajjhānāni paṭikkhittānīti ce? Na, tattheva “yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, taṃ dassanaṃ, yaṃ dassanaṃ, taṃ ñāṇa”nti dassanapadena visesetvā vuttattā, tasmā eva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vijjāsīsena padabhājanaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Dhuraṃ katvāti purimaṃ katvā.

197. If it is said that in the Padabhājaniya, because 'the three knowledges' are stated, the formless-sphere jhānas are rejected? No, because in that very context it is stated, having been specified by the word 'vision', 'what is knowledge, that is vision; what is vision, that is knowledge'. For that very reason, it is said in the commentary, 'The Padabhājaniya is spoken with knowledge as its head'. `Dhuraṃ katvā` means 'having made foremost'.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Padabhājaniya

199. Anāgate uppajjanakarāgādīnaṃ kāraṇattā rāgādayova nimittaṃ nāma. Tissannañca vijjānaṃ aññataraṃ sandhāya “vijjānaṃ lābhīmhī”ti bhaṇati, pārājikaṃ, na vatthuvijjādīnaṃ kilesanahānameva vuttaṃ, taṃkhaṇattā uttarimanussadhammappavatti na hotīti ce? Na, maggakiccadīpanato. Teneva “maggena vinā natthī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cittanti cittassa vigatanīvaraṇatāti attho. “Yāvañca vijjā anāgatā, tāva vipassanāñāṇassa lābhīmhī’ti vadanto yadi lokuttaraṃ sandhāya vadati, sopi ca tathā jānāti, pārājikameva lokuttarassapi taṃnāmattā”ti vadanti. “Avisesenāpi vadato pārājikaṃ vuttanti lokuttaraṃ sandhāya vadato ‘pārājika’nti vattuṃ yujjati. Yathā kiṃ ‘vijjānaṃ lābhīmhī’ti bhaṇantopi pārājikamevā’ti vuttaṭṭhāne vatthuvijjādīnaṃ sambhavepi tāsaṃ anadhippetattā pārājikaṃ hoti, evamidhāpi. Na sakkā aññaṃ pamāṇaṃ kātunti attano guṇamārocetukāmo lokiyena sammissaṃ atthapaṭisambhidaṃ vadato pārājikanti pamāṇaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, itarathā hotī”ti aparehi vuttaṃ, “taṃ pubbāparaviruddhaṃ, tasmā vijjānidassanaṃ idha anidassanaṃ sāsane vatthuvijjādīnaṃ vijjāvidhānābhāvā. Bhagavatā vibhattakhettapade vā tesaṃ pariyāyavacanānaṃ anāmaṭṭhattā na sakkā aññaṃ pamāṇaṃ kātu”nti likhitaṃ. “Paṭisambhidānaṃ lābhīmhī’ti vutte pariyāyena [M 0.0172] vuttattā thullaccayaṃ yutta”nti vadanti, vicāretabbaṃ. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbanti “yo te vihāre vasatī”tiādīhi saṃsandanato pariyāyavacanattā thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ. “Nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjāmī’ti vā ‘lābhīmhāhaṃ tassā’ti vā vadatopī”ti vuttavacanampi “sace panassevaṃ hotī”tiādivacanampi atthato ekameva, sopi hi attano visesaṃ ārocetumeva vadati. “Yo te vihāre vasatī’tiādīsu ahaṃ-vacanābhāvā pariyāyo yujjati, idha pana ‘lābhīmhāhaṃ tassā’ti attānaṃ niddisati, tasmā pārājikaṃ āpajjituṃ yuttaṃ viyā”ti vadanti. “Mahāpaccariyādivacanaṃ uttarimanussadhammesu ekopi na hoti, tasmā pariyāyena vuttattā na hotī”ti [V 0.0153] vadanti, suṭṭhu upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Phalasacchikiriyā-padato paṭṭhāya eva pāṭho gahetabbo, phalasacchikiriyāyapi ekekampi ekekaphalavasena pārājikaṃ veditabbaṃ.

199. Because they are the cause of lust and so forth that are to arise in the future, lust and so forth themselves are called a 'sign' (nimitta). And if, referring to one of the three knowledges, one says, 'I am a possessor of the knowledges,' it is a pārājika offense; it is not a pārājika offense if one says this referring to mundane knowledges (vatthuvijjā), etc. It is said only with reference to the abandoning of defilements. If it is said, 'Because at that moment, the occurrence of a supramundane state does not happen'? No, because it indicates the function of the path. For that very reason, 'Without the path, there is none,' etc., was said. 'Mind' means the state of the mind being free from hindrances—this is the meaning. Some say: 'If one who says, "So long as the knowledges have not been attained, I am a possessor of insight-knowledge," speaks referring to the supramundane, and the listener also understands it as such, it is a pārājika offense indeed, because the supramundane also has that name.' Since a pārājika offense is stated even for one who speaks non-specifically, it is proper to say 'pārājika' for one who speaks referring to the supramundane. Just as in the case where it is said, 'Even one who says, "I am a possessor of the knowledges," commits a pārājika offense,' it is a pārājika offense because, even though mundane knowledges, etc., are possible, they are not intended; so too here. It is not possible to establish another standard. Others have said: 'It is not possible to establish as a standard that for a monk who, wishing to announce his own quality, speaks of the analytical knowledge of meaning mixed with the mundane, it is a pārājika offense; otherwise, it would be different.' That is contradicted by what comes before and after. Therefore, the example of 'knowledge' is not an example here, because in the Teaching, there is no prescription of mundane knowledges, etc., as 'knowledge.' Or, because in the section where the fields are defined by the Blessed One, their synonymous terms are not touched upon, it is not possible to establish another standard,' so it is written. Some say, 'When it is said, "I am a possessor of the analytical knowledges," it is proper for it to be a thullaccaya offense because it is spoken indirectly'—this should be investigated. It should be understood after investigation that by comparison with (phrases such as) 'He who dwells in your monastery,' etc., a thullaccaya offense is stated because it is an indirect expression. The statement about one who says either 'I attain the attainment of cessation' or 'I am a possessor of it,' and the statement 'If it were so for him,' etc., are one and the same in meaning, for he too speaks only to announce his own special quality. Some say: 'In (phrases such as) "He who dwells in your monastery," etc., an indirect expression is proper due to the absence of the word "I." But here, in saying "I am a possessor of it," one indicates oneself; therefore, it seems proper to incur a pārājika offense.' Some say: 'The statement in the Mahāpaccariya, etc., is not even one among the supramundane states; therefore, because it is spoken indirectly, a pārājika offense does not occur'—this should be thoroughly examined. The reading should be taken as starting from the word 'realization of fruition' (phalasacchikiriyā). Even in the case of the realization of fruition, each single one, by way of each single fruition, should be understood as a pārājika offense.

Rāgassa pahānantiādittike kilesappahānameva vuttaṃ, taṃ pana yasmā maggena vinā natthi. Tatiyamaggena hi rāgadosānaṃ pahānaṃ, catutthena mohassa, tasmā “rāgo me pahīno”tiādīni vadatopi pārājikaṃ. Rāgā cittaṃ vinīvaraṇatātiādittike lokuttarameva vuttaṃ, tasmā “rāgā me cittaṃ vinīvaraṇa”ntiādīni vadato pārājikamevāti. Akuppadhammattāti keci uttaravihāravāsino. Kasmā na hotīti ce? “Iti jānāmi, iti passāmī”ti vattamānavacaneneva mātikāyaṃ vuttattā. Yadi evaṃ padabhājane “samāpajjiṃ, samāpanno”tiādinā vuttattā “atītattabhāve sotāpannomhī”ti vadatopi hotūti ce? Na, aññathā atthasambhavato. Kathaṃ? Addhāpaccuppannavasena vattamānatā gahetabbāti ñāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na atītattabhāvaṃ. Atītattabhāvo hi pariyāyena vuttattā “thullaccaya”nti vuttanti ācariyā.

In the triad beginning with 'the abandonment of lust,' the abandonment of defilements alone is spoken of. But since that does not exist without the path—for indeed, by the third path is the abandonment of lust and hatred, and by the fourth, that of delusion—therefore, for one who says, 'My lust is abandoned,' etc., it is a pārājika offense. In the triad beginning with 'the mind is freed from lust,' only the supramundane is spoken of. Therefore, for one who says, 'My mind is freed from lust,' etc., it is a pārājika offense indeed. Regarding [the phrase] 'because of being of an unshakable nature,' some teachers dwelling in the Uttaravihāra [say this]. If one were to ask, 'Why is it not [a pārājika offense]?' Because it is stated in the Mātikā with the present tense verb itself, 'Thus I know, thus I see.' If this is so, then since it is stated in the Padabhājana by way of 'I was attaining, I have attained,' etc., if one were to say, 'Let it also be a pārājika offense for one who says, "In a past existence, I was a stream-enterer."' No, because the meaning is possible in another way. How so? It is stated to make known that the present tense is to be understood in the sense of the actual present, not a past existence. Indeed, because a past existence is spoken of indirectly, the teachers say it is stated to be a thullaccaya offense.

200. “Sacepi na hoti, pārājikamevā”ti aṭṭhānaparikappavasena vuttaṃ kira. “Iti vācā tivaṅgikā”ti vakkhati. Natthetanti purime sati pacchimassābhāvā samāpajjiṃ, samāpannoti imesaṃ kiñcāpi atthato kālaviseso natthi, vacanaviseso pana atthi eva.

200. It is said that [the statement] 'Even if it is not so, it is a pārājika offense indeed' was stated by way of an impossible supposition. He will state [in the verse], 'Thus, the statement has three aspects.' Regarding [the phrase] 'natthetaṃ' (it is not so): because when the former exists, the latter is absent. For these [words] 'samāpajjiṃ' (I was attaining) and 'samāpanno' (I have attained), although there is no distinction in time with respect to meaning, there is indeed a distinction in wording.

207. Ukkheṭitoti uttāsito. Khiṭa utrāsane.

207. Ukkheṭito means 'terrified'. The root 'khiṭa' is in the sense of 'frightening'.

Suddhikavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Suddhikavāra is concluded.

Vattukāmavārakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Vattukāmavāra

Viññattipatheti [M 0.0173] vijānanaṭṭhāne, tena “viññattipathamatikkamitvā ṭhito bhikkhu dibbāya sotadhātuyā sutvā jānāti, na pārājikanti dīpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Jhānaṃ kira samāpajjinti ettha so ce “esa bhikkhu attano guṇadīpanādhippāyena evaṃ vadatī”ti jānāti, pārājikameva. Aññathā jānātīti ce? Pārājikacchāyā na dissatīti ācariyo.

Viññattipathe (in the range of intimation) means 'in a place where one can know'. By that, it is said that it shows this meaning: 'A bhikkhu standing beyond the range of intimation, having heard with the divine ear-element, knows; it is not a pārājika offense.' Regarding [the statement] 'I have, it seems, attained jhāna,' if that [person who hears] knows, 'This bhikkhu speaks thus with the intention of displaying his own quality,' it is a pārājika offense indeed. If he knows otherwise? The teacher says, 'The shadow of a pārājika offense does not appear.'

Vattukāmavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Vattukāmavāra is concluded.

Anāpattibhedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Kinds of Non-Offenses

Anullapanādhippāyoti [V 0.0154] yadi ullapanādhippāyo bhaveyya, dukkaṭamevāti apare. “Taṃ parato ‘nāvuso, sakkā puthujjanena adhivāsetu’nti vatthunā saṃsanditvā gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ.

Regarding [the phrase] 'with no intention to boast': others say that if there were an intention to boast, it would be a dukkaṭa offense indeed. It is said: 'That should be understood by connecting it with the story that follows, “Friend, it is not possible for an ordinary person to endure.”'

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Padabhājanīya is concluded.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Vinītavatthu

225-6. Dukkara āgāra āvaṭakāma abhirativatthūsu “yadi ullapanādhippāyo bhaveyya, pārājika”nti vadanti, kāraṇaṃ pana duddasaṃ, thullaccayaṃ vuttaṃ viya, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Yānena vā iddhiyā vā gacchantopi pārājikaṃ nāpajjatīti padasā gamanavaseneva katikāya katāya yujjati. “Apubbaṃacarimaṃ gacchantoti hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā aññamaññassa hatthaṃ gaṇhanto viya gacchanto”ti vuttaṃ. Uṭṭhetha etha gacchāmāti evaṃ sahagamane pubbāparā gacchantopi nāpajjatīti ācariyassa takko. Vasantassāti tathā vasanto ce upāsakena dissati, pārājiko hoti. “Rattiṃ vasitvā gacchanto na pārājiko”ti vuttaṃ. Nānāverajjakāti nānājanapadavāsino. Saṅghalābhoti yathāvuḍḍhaṃ attano pāpuṇanakoṭṭhāso.

In the cases of the difficult deed, the dwelling, the desire to return, and delight, they say: 'If there were an intention to boast, it is a pārājika offense.' But the reason is difficult to see; it seems to be spoken of as a thullaccaya offense and should be investigated. The statement, 'Even one going by vehicle or by psychic power does not incur a pārājika offense,' is fitting only when the agreement was made on the basis of going on foot. It is said: '“Going neither first nor last” means going without abandoning the distance of a hand’s reach, like one holding another’s hand.' It is the teacher’s reasoning that in going together thus, 'Arise, come, let us go,' even one going before or after does not incur an offense. Regarding 'while dwelling': if, while dwelling thus, he is seen by a lay follower, he is a pārājika offender. It is said: 'One who goes after having stayed for the night is not a pārājika offender.' 'Of various regions' means dwellers of various districts. 'Gain for the Saṅgha' means one's own portion that is received according to seniority.

228. Idhāti “ko nu kho”tiādinā vutte pañhākamme. Dhammadhātu sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ.

228. 'Here' means in the act of questioning spoken of beginning with 'Who now indeed...?'. The element of Dhamma is the knowledge of omniscience.

232. Na [M 0.0174] uppaṭipāṭiyāti na sīhokkantavasena anussari. Tasmā antarābhavabhūtā ekā eva jātīti paṭivijjhatīti attho.

232. 'Not in reverse order' means he did not recollect by means of the lion's leap. Therefore, the meaning is: he penetrates the truth that the immediately preceding existence is only one birth.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

The Concluding Exposition

233. Catuvīsatīti ettha mātughātakapitughātakaarahantaghātakā tatiyapārājikaṃ āpannā. Bhikkhunidūsako, lambiādayo ca cattāro paṭhamapārājikaṃ āpannā evāti katvā kuto catuvīsatīti ce? Na, adhippāyājānanato. Mātughātakādayo hi cattāro idhānupasampannā eva adhippetā, lambiādayo cattāro kiñcāpi paṭhamapārājikena saṅgahitā, yasmā [V 0.0155] ekena pariyāyena methunadhammapaṭisevino na honti, tasmā visuṃ vuttā. “Ekakammaṃ ekuddeso samasikkhatā”ti evaṃ vuttasaṃvāsassa abhabbatāmattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yathā pure tathā pacchā”ti. Aññathā nesaṃ samaññāyapaṭiññāyabhikkhubhāvopi natthīti āpajjati.

233. Regarding 'twenty-four': Here, matricides, patricides, and killers of arahants incur the third pārājika offense. A defiler of a bhikkhunī, and the four such as Lambī, have indeed incurred the first pārājika offense. If, on this account, one should ask, 'How then are there twenty-four?' No, this is due to not understanding the intention. For the four—matricides and the others—are indeed intended here as unordained. Although the four such as Lambī are included under the first pārājika offense, they are stated separately because in one respect they are not partakers of the sexual act. The statement, 'as before, so after,' was said with reference only to the unsuitability for the co-residence that is spoken of as 'one act, one recitation, the same training.' Otherwise, it would follow that their state of being a bhikkhu by designation and by acknowledgement would not exist.

Catutthapārājikavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the fourth pārājika offense is concluded.

Pārājikakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Pārājika section is concluded.

2. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍo

2. The Saṅghādisesa Section

1. Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Training Rule on Emission of Semen

235. “Okkamantāna”nti [V 0.0156][M 0.0175] pāṭho. Etthāha – “yo pana bhikkhū”ti kārako idha kasmā na niddiṭṭhoti? Abhi-niddesena imassa sāpekkhābhāvadassanatthaṃ. Kathaṃ? Kaṇḍuvanādiadhippāyacetanāvasena cetentassa kaṇḍuvanādiupakkamena upakkamantassa, methunarāgavasena ūruādīsu dukkaṭavatthūsu, vaṇādīsu thullaccayavatthūsu ca upakkamantassa sukkavissaṭṭhiyā satipi na saṅghādiseso. Mocanassādasaṅkhātādhippāyāpekkhāva sukkavissaṭṭhi sati upakkame, na aññathā “anāpatti na mocanādhippāyassā”ti vacanato. Tasmā tadatthadassanatthaṃ idha kārako na niddiṭṭho, aññathā “yo pana bhikkhu sañcetanikaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ āpajjeyyā”ti kārake niddiṭṭhe “ceteti na upakkamati muccati, anāpattī”ti vuttavacanavirodho. “Sañcetanikāya sukkavissaṭṭhiyā aññatra supinantā”ti bhumme niddiṭṭhepi sova virodho āpajjati, tasmā tadubhayavacanakkamaṃ avatvā “sañcetanikā sukkavissaṭṭhi aññatra supinantā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nimittatthe bhummavacanābhāvato hetutthaniyamo na kato hoti. Tasmiṃ akate sañcetanikā sukkavissaṭṭhi aññatra supinantā saṅghādisesāpatti, upakkame asati anāpattīti ayamattho dīpitoti veditabbaṃ.

235. “Okkamantāna” is the reading. Here it is asked: Why is the agent, “whatever bhikkhu,” not specified here? In order to show, by way of detailed exposition, the dependent nature of this rule. How so? For one who intends with the volition for the purpose of relieving an itch and so on, and who makes an effort with the exertion of relieving an itch and so on; or for one who, due to sexual lust, makes an effort regarding the thighs and so on (grounds for a dukkaṭa offense), or regarding wounds and so on (grounds for a thullaccaya offense), there is no Saṅghādisesa offense even if there is an emission of semen. An emission of semen, when there is effort, is an offense only when it is dependent on the intention known as 'the pleasure of emission,' not otherwise, in accordance with the text: 'There is no offense for one who does not have the intention of emission.' Therefore, in order to show this meaning, the agent is not specified here. Otherwise, if the agent were specified as “whatever bhikkhu should intentionally cause an emission of semen,” it would contradict the spoken word that says: “He intends, does not make an effort, it is emitted; no offense.” Even if it were stated in the locative case as “with an intentional emission of semen, other than in a dream,” the same contradiction would arise. Therefore, without stating that sequence of two phrases, it is said: “An intentional emission of semen, other than in a dream.” Herein, since there is no locative case in the sense of a condition, a restriction to the meaning of 'cause' is not made. When that restriction is not made, the meaning explained should be understood as follows: an intentional emission of semen—other than in a dream—is a Saṅghādisesa offense when there is effort; when there is no effort, it is not an offense.

236-7. Sañcetanikāti ettha paṭhamaviggahena upasaggassa sātthakatā dassitā, dutiyena ikapaccayassa. Vātapittasemharuhirādiāsayabhedatoti attho. Dhātūti ettha “pathavīdhātuādayo catasso, cakkhudhātuādayo vā aṭṭhārasā”ti gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ. Vatthisīsanti vatthipuṭassa sīsaṃ. “Aṅgajātassa mūlaṃ adhippetaṃ, na aggasīsa”nti vadanti. Tathevāti “nimitte upakkamato”tiādiṃ gaṇhāti. Tato muccitvāti “na sakalakāyato, tasmā pana ṭhānā cutamatte hotū”ti gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ. “Dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte”ti iminā na sametīti ce[V 0.0157]? Tato dakasotorohaṇañcetthātiādi vuccati. Tassattho – nimitte upakkamaṃ katvā sukkaṃ ṭhānā cāvetvā puna vippaṭisāravasena dakasotorohaṇaṃ nivāretuṃ adhivāsemīti. Tato bahi nikkhamante adhivāsetuṃ na sakkā, tathāpi adhivāsanādhippāyena adhivāsetvā antarā dakasotato [M 0.0176] uddhaṃ nivāretuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya “anikkhante vā”ti vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Ṭhānā cutañhi avassaṃ dakasotaṃ otaratīti aṭṭhakathādhippāyo gaṇṭhipadādhippāyena sameti. Tato muccitvāti sakaṭṭhānato. Sakasarīrato hi bahi nikkhantameva hoti, tato “bahi nikkhante vā anikkhante vā”ti vacanaṃ virujjheyya. Yasmā pana tamhā tamhā sarīrapadesā cutaṃ avassaṃ dakasotaṃ otarati, tasmā vuttaṃ “dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte”ti, iminā ca āpattiyā pākaṭakālaṃ dasseti, kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Mocanassādena nimitte upakkamato sukkaṃ bahutarampi sarīrapadesā cutaṃ tattha tattha laggāvasesaṃ yattakaṃ ekā khuddakamakkhikā piveyya, tattake dakasotaṃ otiṇṇamatte saṅghādisesāpatti. Vuttañhi kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) “dakasotaṃ anotiṇṇepi saṅghādiseso”tiādi. Tattakassa bahi nikkhamanaṃ asallakkhento “ceteti upakkamati na muccati, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vacanato thullaccayanti saññāya desentopi na muccati, passāvampi vaṇṇataṃ passitvā vatthikosagatassa picchilatāya vā ñatvā saṅghādisesato vuṭṭhātabbaṃ. Ayamettha tatiyattheravāde yutti. Sabbācariyā ime eva tayo therā, tesampi dakasotorohaṇaṃ nimitte upakkamananti ayaṃ dutiyo vinicchayo sādhāraṇato ettha, evaṃ upatissatthero vadati kira.

236-7. Herein, in the word `sañcetanikā`, by the first etymological analysis, the meaningfulness of the prefix is shown; by the second, that of the 'ika' suffix. The meaning is: by the distinction of the bases, such as wind, bile, phlegm, blood, and so on. Herein, in the word `dhātu`, it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada: 'The four elements beginning with the earth element, or the eighteen elements beginning with the eye element.' `Vatthisīsaṃ` means the base of the bladder-sac. They say: 'The root of the genital organ is intended, not the tip.' By `tatheva` ('just so'), it refers to 'from applying effort to the sign,' and so on. Regarding `tato muccitvā` ('having been released from there'), it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada: 'Not from the whole body, but let it be just upon being dislodged from that place.' If it is said that this does not accord with 'just upon descending into the stream of urine'? Therefore, 'and the descent into the stream of urine here...' and so on is said. Its meaning is: having applied effort to the sign and dislodged the semen from its place, one thinks, 'I will, due to regret, restrain it to prevent its descent into the urinary tract.' It is not possible to restrain it as it is exiting from there. Nevertheless, because of the inability to prevent it in the interim while it is in the upper part of the urinary tract, even though one restrains it with the intention to restrain, it is said, 'or when it has not exited.' Why? For that which is dislodged from its place inevitably descends into the stream of urine. Thus, the intention of the commentary accords with the intention of the Gaṇṭhipada. `Tato muccitvā` means from its own place. For if it were from one's own body, it would indeed be exited outside; therefore, the statement 'whether exited outside or not exited' would be contradicted. But since semen dislodged from this or that part of the body inevitably descends into the stream of urine, it is therefore said, 'just upon descending into the stream of urine.' And by this, it shows the manifest time of the offense. What is meant by this? For a monk who, with enjoyment in emission, makes an effort regarding the sign, even if much semen is dislodged from a part of the body, with a remainder sticking here and there, a Saṅghādisesa offense is incurred just upon an amount as much as a small fly could drink descending into the stream of urine. For it is said in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī: 'Even if it has not descended into the stream of urine, it is a Saṅghādisesa,' and so on. Not noticing the exit of that small amount, even when confessing with the perception that it is a Thullaccaya offense, in accordance with the text, 'He intends, he makes an effort, he is not released; the offense is a Thullaccaya,' he is not absolved. Having seen the appearance of semen in the urine, or having known by the stickiness of that which has gone to the scrotum, he should be rehabilitated from the Saṅghādisesa offense. This here is the reasoning in the view of the third elder. All the teachers are just these three elders. For them too, this second decision concerning the descent into the urinary tract and the effort regarding the sign is common here. Thus, it is said, the Elder Upatissa speaks.

Ṭhānā cutañhi avassaṃ dakasotaṃ otaratīti katvā “ṭhānā cāvanamattenevettha āpatti veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Dakasotaṃ otiṇṇe eva āpatti. Sukkassa hi sakalaṃ sarīraṃ ṭhānaṃ, anotiṇṇe ṭhānā cutaṃ nāma na hotīti vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Ābhidhammikattā therassa “sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma rāgasamuṭṭhānā hotī”ti (kathā. aṭṭha. 307) kathāvatthuṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā sambhavo cittasamuṭṭhāno, “taṃ asuciṃ ekadesaṃ mukhena aggahesi, ekadesaṃ aṅgajāte pakkhipī”ti (pārā. 503) vacanato utusamuṭṭhāno ca dissati, so ca kho avītarāgasseva “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ arahato asuci mucceyyā”ti (mahāva. 353; kathā. 313) vacanato. Parūpāhāraṭṭhakathāyaṃ “atthi tassa āsayoti tassa sukkassa uccārapassāvānaṃ viya patiṭṭhānokāso atthī”ti [M 0.0177] (kathā. aṭṭha. 309) canato tassa āsayoti siddhaṃ. Pākatikacittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ viya asaṃsaṭṭhattā, nikkhamanato ca “vatthisīsaṃ, kaṭi, kāyo”ti tidhā sukkassa ṭhānaṃ pakappenti ācariyā. Sappavisaṃ viya taṃ [V 0.0158] daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ca visassa ṭhānaniyamo, kodhavasena phusantassa hoti, evamassa na ca ṭhānaniyamo, rāgavasena upakkamantassa hotīti takko.

Indeed, semen that has moved from its place inevitably descends to the stream of urine; for this reason, it is said, 'Here, the offense should be known by the mere dislodging from the place.' An offense is incurred only when it has descended to the stream of urine. Indeed, for semen, the entire body is the place; when it has not descended, there is no such thing as 'moved from the place.' This should be investigated. Because the Elder is an Abhidhammika, and because it is said in the Kathāvatthu commentary, 'The emission of semen has lust as its origin,' semen is mind-originated. And from the statement, 'He took a part of that impurity with the mouth; he placed a part in the genital organ,' it is also seen to be season-originated. And that, indeed, is only for one who is not free from lust, because of the statement, 'Monks, it is impossible, it is no occasion that impurity should be emitted from an Arahant.' In the Kathāvatthu commentary, it is said, 'There is a basis for it—just as there is a receptacle for urine and feces, so too there is a resting place for that semen.' Thus, its basis is established. Because it is unmixed like natural mind-originated matter, and because of its exit, the teachers conceive the place of semen in three ways: 'the head of the bladder, the waist, and the body.' It should be regarded like snake venom—there is no fixed place for poison, as it affects one who touches it out of anger. Similarly, for this, there is no fixed place, as it occurs for one who strives through lust. This is our reasoning.

Khobhakaraṇapaccayo nāma bhesajjasenāsanāhārādipaccayo. Saṃsaggabhedatopīti etesu dvīhipi tīhipi. Pahīnavipallāsattāti ettha yaṃ kiñci supinantena sekkhaputhujjanā passanti, taṃ sabbaṃ vipallatthaṃ abhūtamevāti āpajjati. Tato “yaṃ pana pubbanimittato passati. Taṃ ekantasaccameva hotī”ti idaṃ virujjhati, tasmā na visayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi sacco vā hoti, aliko vāti katvā tañce sandhāya vuttaṃ siyā, “asekkhā pahīnavipallāsattā saccameva passanti, nāsacca”nti vattabbaṃ siyā. Kintu dassanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi abhūtaṃ, apassantopi hi passanto viya asuṇantopi suṇanto viya amunantopi munanto viya hoti. Saccampi vipassatīti no takkoti ācariyo. Taṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ na hoti, āgantukapaccuppannaṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kammanimittagatinimittabhūtāni hi rūpanimittādīni bhavaṅgassa ārammaṇāni honti eva. Tattha kammanimittamatītameva, gatinimittaṃ thokaṃ kālaṃ paccuppannaṃ siyā.

The condition called 'khobhakaraṇa' is the condition of medicine, lodging, food, and the like. And also from the distinction of association: among these, by two or by three. In the context of the phrase 'because perversions are abandoned,' it would follow that whatever trainees and ordinary people see in a dream is all distorted and unreal. Therefore, this contradicts the statement, 'But what one sees from a preliminary sign is absolutely true.' Therefore, it was not spoken with reference to the object. For that object may be true or may be false, and if it were spoken with reference to that, it should be said, 'Those beyond training, because they have abandoned perversions, see only the truth, not the untruth.' But in fact, it was spoken with reference to the seeing. For that seeing is unreal; for even though not seeing, one is as if seeing; though not hearing, as if hearing; though not knowing, as if knowing. The teacher says: 'One also discerns the truth. This is our reasoning.' A form-sign and so on is not that object; it was spoken with reference to an adventitious and present object such as a form-sign. For form-signs, etc., which have become kamma-signs and destiny-signs, are indeed the objects of the life-continuum. Among them, the kamma-sign is only past; the destiny-sign may be present for a short time.

Īdisānīti paccakkhato anubhūtapubbaparikappitāgantukapaccuppannarūpanimittādiārammaṇāni, rāgādisampayuttāni cāti attho. Makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti. So hi rukkhasākhato patanabhayā abhikkhaṇaṃ ummīlati ca supati ca. Manussā kiñcāpi punappunaṃ ummīlanti subyattataraṃ paṭibuddhā viya passanti, atha kho paṭibuddhānaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ viya supinakālepi tesaṃ bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ hoti, yena “supatī”ti vuccati. “Bhavaṅgacittena hi supatī”ti vacanato bhavaṅgotaraṇaṃ karajakāyassa nirussāhasantabhāvūpanissayattā “niddā”ti vuccati. Sā karajakāyassa dubbalabhāvena supinadassanakāle bhavaṅgato uttaraṇe satipi nirussāhasantabhāvappattiyā “pavattatī”ti ca vuccati, yato sattā “paṭibuddhā”ti na vuccanti, karajakāyassa nirussāhasantasabhāvappattito ca tannissitaṃ [M 0.0178] hadayavatthu na suppasannaṃ hoti, tato tannissitāpi cittappavatti asuppasannavaṭṭinissitadīpappabhā viya. Teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “svāyaṃ dubbalavatthukattā cetanāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asamattho”tiādi vuttaṃ.

By 'such' is meant: minds that have as their objects visible forms and so on—directly perceived, previously experienced, conceived, adventitious, and present—and are associated with lust and so on. A monkey's sleep is light and frequently interrupted. Due to fear of falling from a tree branch, it repeatedly opens its eyes and sleeps. Although humans open their eyes again and again and see as if more clearly awakened, yet, just as for those who are awake there is a repeated descent into the life-continuum, so too during the time of dreaming, their descent into the life-continuum occurs—by which it is said, 'one sleeps.' Because it is said, 'Indeed, one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness,' the descent into the life-continuum is called 'sleep' due to its being a supporting condition for the physical body's state of effortlessness and tranquility. Due to the physical body's weakness, even when there is an emergence from the life-continuum at the time of seeing a dream, that sleep is also said to 'proceed' on account of having attained a state of effortlessness and tranquility, for which reason beings are not called 'awakened.' And because of the physical body's attainment of a state of effortlessness and tranquility, the heart-base dependent on it is not very clear; therefore, the process of consciousness dependent on it is like the light of a lamp dependent on an unclean wick. For that very reason, it is said in the commentary: 'This volition, due to having a weak physical basis, is unable to draw forth rebirth-linking,' and so on.

Gaṇṭhipade pana “dubbalavatthukattāti supine upaṭṭhitaṃ nimittampi dubbala”nti likhitaṃ. Taṃ anekatthaṃ sabbampi nimittaṃ hoti, na ca dubbalārammaṇavatthukattā cetanā, tāya cittappavatti dubbalā atītānāgatārammaṇāya, paññattārammaṇāya vā adubbalattā, avatthukāya dubbalabhāvo na [V 0.0159] yujjati cetanāya avatthukāya bhāvanāpabhāvāyātirekabalasabbhāvato. Bhāvanābalasamappitañhi cittaṃ arūpampi samānaṃ atibhāriyampi karajakāyaṃ gahetvā ekacittakkhaṇeneva brahmalokaṃ pāpetvā ṭhapeti. Tappaṭibhāgaṃ anappitampi kāmāvacaracittaṃ karajakāyaṃ ākāse laṅghanasamatthaṃ karoti, pagevetaraṃ. Kiṃ panettha taṃ anumānakāraṇaṃ, yena cittasseva ānubhāvoti paññāyeyya cittānubhāvena vā laddhāsevanādikiriyāvisesanibbattidassanato, tasmā dubbalavatthukattāti dubbalahadayavatthukattāti ācariyassa takko. Attano mandatikkhākārena tannissitassa cittassa mandatikkhabhāvanipphādanasamatthañce, hadayavatthu cakkhusotādivatthu viya indriyaṃ bhaveyya, na cetaṃ indriyaṃ. Yato dhammasaṅgahe upādāyarūpapāḷiyaṃ uddesārahaṃ na jātaṃ. Anindriyattā hi taṃ kāyindriyassa anantaraṃ na uddiṭṭhaṃ, vatthurūpattā ca avatthurūpassa jīvitindriyassa anantarampi na uddiṭṭhaṃ, tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ “tassa asuppasannattā tannissitā ca cittappavatti asuppasannā hotī”ti, taṃ na siddhanti ce? Siddhameva anindriyānampi sappāyāsappāyautuāhārādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ samāyogato, cittappavattiyā vikāradassanato, paccakkhattā ca. Yasmā appaṭibuddhopi paṭibuddhaṃ viya attānaṃ maññatīti. Ettāvatā karajakāyassa nirussāhasantabhāvākāraviseso niddā nāma. Sā cittassa bhavaṅgotaraṇākāravisesena hoti, tāya samannāgato satto bhavaṅgato uttiṇṇo supinaṃ passati, so “kapimiddhapareto”ti vuccati, so sutto appaṭibuddho hotīti ayamattho sādhito hoti.

In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is written: 'By "due to having a weak base" is meant that the sign which has appeared in a dream is also weak.' That statement is ambiguous, or it is not certain that every such sign is weak. And the process of consciousness is not weak due to the weakness of the object. Why? Because the process of consciousness with a past or future object, or with a conceptual object, is not weak. For a volition without a physical basis, weakness is not suitable, due to the existence of excessive power originating from mental cultivation. Indeed, a mind endowed with the power of mental cultivation, though it is formless, can take the physical body, though it is very heavy, and in a single mind-moment, cause it to reach the Brahma-world and place it there. Its counterpart, a sense-sphere consciousness, even without absorption, can make the physical body capable of leaping through the air—what then to say of other minds? What, here, is the use of that inferential reasoning by which it might be known that this is the power of the mind alone? For it is from seeing the production of special actions, such as acquired practice, through the power of the mind. Therefore, the teacher's reasoning regarding 'due to having a weak base' is 'due to having a weak heart-base.' If it were capable of producing the dull or sharp nature of the consciousness dependent on it through its own dull or sharp quality, the heart-base, like the eye-base, ear-base, and so on, would be a faculty. But this is not a faculty, for in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the section on derived matter, it is not designated as worthy of enumeration. Indeed, because it is not a faculty, it is not indicated immediately after the body-faculty; and because it is a basis-materiality, it is also not indicated immediately after the life-faculty, which is not a basis-materiality. Therefore, if it is said that the statement, 'Due to its lack of clarity, the process of consciousness dependent on it is also not clear,' is not established, is that so? It is indeed established. This is due to the combination of conditions which are not faculties, such as suitable and unsuitable climate, food, and so on, and from seeing the alteration in the process of consciousness, and because it is directly perceived. For even one who is not awakened considers oneself as if awakened. To this extent, that particular state of the physical body which is the condition of being without exertion and tranquil, is called sleep. It occurs through a particular mode of the mind's descending into the life-continuum. A being endowed with this, having emerged from the life-continuum, sees a dream. Such a one is called 'overcome by monkey-sleep.' That one is asleep, unawakened—this meaning is thus established.

Yasmā [M 0.0179] bhavaṅgavāranirantaratāya accantasutto nāma hoti, tasmā “yadi tāva sutto passati, abhidhammavirodho āpajjatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana niddākkhaṇe na paṭibuddho nāma hoti, tasmā “atha paṭibuddho passati, vinayavirodho”tiādi vuttaṃ, yasmā ca akhīṇaniddo, anotiṇṇabhavaṅgo ca atthi, tasmā “kapimiddhapareto passatī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā ayaṃ neva sutto na paṭibuddho, attanā taṃ niddaṃ anokkanto āpajjeyya. Ettāvatā ca abhidhammo, vinayo, nāgasenattheravacanaṃ yutti cāti sabbaṃ aññamaññasaṃsanditaṃ hoti. Tattha kapimiddhaparetoti bhavaṅgato uttiṇṇaniddāpareto. Sā hi idha kapimiddhaṃ nāma. “Tattha katamaṃ middhaṃ? Yā kāyassa akalyatā akammaññatā…pe… supanaṃ, idaṃ vuccati middha”nti (dha. sa. 1163) evamāgataṃ. Idañhi arūpaṃ, imassa phalabhūto karajakāyassa akalyatā’pacalāyikāsupi niddāviseso kāraṇopacārena “kapimiddha”nti pavuccati. Yañceva “kapimiddhapareto kho, mahārāja, supinaṃ passatī”ti (mi. pa. 5.3.5 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) vuttanti.

Because one is called 'utterly asleep' due to the uninterruptedness of the life-continuum stream, it is therefore said: 'If one sees while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises,' and so on. But because one is not called 'awakened' at the moment of sleep, it is therefore said: 'But if one sees while awakened, a contradiction with the Vinaya arises,' and so on. And because there exists one whose sleep is not exhausted and who has not passed beyond the life-continuum, it is therefore said: 'One sees while overcome by monkey-sleep.' Otherwise, this person would be neither asleep nor awakened, and would fall into a state of not having entered that sleep. By this much, the Abhidhamma, the Vinaya, the statement of the Elder Nāgasena, and reasoning all become mutually consistent. Therein, 'overcome by monkey-sleep' means one who has emerged from the life-continuum and is overcome by sleep. For that sleep is here called 'monkey-sleep.' It is stated thus: 'Therein, what is torpor? Whatever is the body's unwieldiness, unworkability... and so on... drowsiness, this is called torpor' (Dhs 1163). For this torpor is indeed immaterial; its result, a particular kind of sleep which is the unwieldiness, nodding, and drowsiness of the physical body, is called 'monkey-sleep' by way of causal metaphor. And it is for this reason that it was said: 'Indeed, great king, one overcome by monkey-sleep sees a dream' (Mil 5.3.5, slightly different).

Yaṃ [V 0.0160] taṃ āpattivuṭṭhānanti ettha yena vinayakammena tato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ idha āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Avayave samūhavohārena vāti ettha sākhacchedako rukkhacchedakoti vuccatītiādi nidassanaṃ, vedanākkhandhādi ruḷhīsaddassa nidassanaṃ. Na ca mayāti vīmaṃsanapadassa tassa kiriyaṃ sandhāya, mocane ca sanniṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya muccanapakatiyā cāti vuttaṃ.

Herein, regarding the term 'emergence from an offense': that disciplinary act by which there is an emergence from that offense is here called 'emergence from an offense.' Herein, regarding 'or by collective designation for a part,' the example is: 'one who cuts a branch is called a tree-cutter,' and so on; 'the aggregate of feeling, etc.' is an example of a conventional term (ruḷhīsadda). 'And not by me' is said with reference to the action of that investigative term, and in regard to release, with reference to the conclusion and also to the nature of being released.

240. Gehanti pañcakāmaguṇā. Vanabhaṅgiyanti pābhatikaṃ. Sampayuttasukhavedanāmukhena rāgova “assādo”ti vutto. Supantassa cāti idaṃ kapimiddhapareto viya bhavaṅgasantatiṃ avicchinditvā supantaṃ sandhāya vuttanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Jagganatthāyāti sodhanatthāya.

240. In `Gehanti`, the five strands of sensual pleasure are intended. In `Vanabhaṅgiya`, it means a gift. By means of associated pleasant feeling, lust alone is called 'enjoyment.' As for the phrase 'and of one who is asleep,' this should be investigated as being said in reference to one who is asleep without interrupting the continuum of the life-continuum, as if overcome by drowsiness like a monkey. 'For the purpose of awakening' means for the sake of purification.

266. “Dārudhītalikalepacittānaṃ aṅgajātapaṭinijjhānepi dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. “Uppanne pariḷāhe mocanarāgajo”ti likhanti. Vālikāya vā “hatthikāmaṃ nassatī”ti ettha viya “āpatti tva”nti sabbattha pāṭho. “Ehi me tvaṃ, āvuso sāmaṇera, aṅgajātaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āgatattā “vacīkamma”ntipi vattuṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati. Evaṃ sante aññaṃ “evaṃ karohī”ti āṇattiyāpi [M 0.0180] āpatti siyāti saṅkaraṃ hoti. Tasmā na vuttanti gahetabbanti keci.

266. They say: 'There is a `dukkaṭa` offense even in gazing at the genital organ of wooden dolls and painted figures.' They write: 'When distress arises, it is delight born of the lust for emission.' Or, as in the story of Vālikā, in the phrase 'the elephant's lust perishes,' so the reading 'there is an offense for you' exists everywhere. Since the text states, 'Come, friend novice, take my genital organ,' it seems appropriate to say this is also 'verbal action.' If this is so, an offense could also occur through another's command, such as 'Do it this way,' which creates confusion. Therefore, some say it should be taken as not having been said.

267. “Pupphāvaliyaṃ sāsavaḷiya”nti duvidho kira.

267. It seems there are two readings: `Pupphāvaliyaṃ` and `Sāsavaḷiyaṃ`.

Sukkavissaṭṭhisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.

2. Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Physical Contact

270. “Otiṇṇo”ti imināssa sevanādhippāyatā dassitā. “Vipariṇatena cittena mātugāmena saddhi”nti imināssa vāyāmo dassito. “Saddhi”nti hi padaṃ saṃyogaṃ dīpeti, so ca payogo samāgamo allīyanaṃ. Kena cittena? Vipariṇatena cittena, na pattapaṭiggahaṇādhippāyādināti adhippāyo. “Kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā”ti imināssa vāyamato phassapaṭivijānanā dassitā hoti. Vāyamitvā phassaṃ paṭivijānanto hi samāpajjati nāma. Evamassa tivaṅgasampatti dassitā hoti. Atha vā otiṇṇo. Kena? Vipariṇatena cittena yakkhādinā satto viya. Upayogatthe vā etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Otiṇṇo vipariṇataṃ [V 0.0161] cittaṃ kūpādiṃ viya satto. Atha vā “rāgato uttiṇṇo bhavissāmī”ti bhikkhubhāvaṃ upagato, tato uttiṇṇādhippāyato vipariṇatena cittena hetubhūtena tameva rāgaṃ otiṇṇo. Mātugāmena attano samīpaṃ āgatena, attanā upagatena vā. Etena mātugāmassa sārattatā vā hotu virattatā vā, sā idha appamāṇā, na bhikkhunīnaṃ kāyasaṃsagge viya ubhinnaṃ sārattatāya payojanaṃ atthi.

270. By 'Overcome,' his intention to indulge lustfully is shown. 'With a perverted mind, together with a woman'—by this, his effort is shown. For the word 'with' indicates connection, and that connection is coming together and clinging. With what mind? With a perverted mind, not with an intention such as receiving a bowl—this is the meaning. 'He might engage in bodily contact'—by this, his recognition of touch resulting from effort is shown. For one who, having striven, recognizes touch is indeed said to engage. Thus, his accomplishment of the three factors is shown. Alternatively, 'Overcome.' By what? By a perverted mind, like a being possessed by a yakkha or the like. Or, this word in the instrumental case has the sense of the accusative: He has entered the perverted mind, as a being enters a well or the like. Alternatively, having undertaken the state of a monk thinking, 'I will emerge from lust,' he is overcome by that same lust, his cause being a perverted mind arising from that very intention to emerge, with a woman who has come near him, or by himself having approached her. In this case, whether the woman is attached or dispassionate is not a determining factor; unlike the case of bodily contact for bhikkhunīs, there is no requirement for the attachment of both.

Kāyasaṃsagganti ubhinnaṃ kāyānaṃ sampayogaṃ. Padabhājane pana “samāpajjeyyāti ajjhācāro vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ samāpajjanaṃ sandhāya, na kāyasaṃsaggaṃ. Kāyasaṃsaggassa samāpajjanā hi “ajjhācāro”ti vuccati. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yo so kāyasaṃsaggo nāma, so atthato ajjhācāro hotī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ parato pāḷiyaṃ “sevanādhippāyo, na ca kāyena vāyamati, phassaṃ paṭivijānāti, anāpattī”ti (pārā. 279) vuttalakkhaṇena [M 0.0181] virujjhatīti. Phassapaṭivijānanāya hi saṃsaggo dīpito. So ce ajjhācāro hoti, kathaṃ anāpatti hotīti. Suvuttametaṃ, kintu “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā”ti padaṃ uddharitvā “ajjhācāro vuccatī”ti ubhinnampi padānaṃ sāmaññabhājanīyattā, samāpajjitabbābhāve samāpajjanābhāvena “so atthato ajjhācāro hotī”ti vuttaṃ siyā.

‘Physical contact’ is the conjunction of the bodies of the two. However, in the analysis of the term, it is said, ‘He might engage; this is called misconduct.’ That is said referring to the act of engaging, not physical contact. For engaging in physical contact is called ‘misconduct.’ In the Commentary, however, it is said, ‘Whatever is called physical contact, that, in substance, is misconduct.’ This contradicts the characteristic stated further on in the Pāḷi: ‘There is an intention to indulge, but he does not exert himself with the body; he is aware of the touch; there is no offense.’ For by the awareness of touch, contact is indicated. If that contact is misconduct, how could there be no offense? This is well-said. However, it may be that the statement ‘it is, in substance, misconduct’ was made because, after extracting the phrase ‘he might engage in physical contact,’ the words ‘it is called misconduct’ serve as a general analysis for both phrases, and because in the absence of an object to be engaged in, there is an absence of the act of engaging.

“Hatthaggāhaṃ vā”ti ettha hatthena sabbopi upādinnako kāyo saṅgahito, na bhinnasantāno tappaṭibaddho hatthālaṅkārādi. Veṇiggahaṇena anupādinnako abhinnasantāno kesalomanakhadantādiko kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno gahitoti veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “anupādinnakenapi kenaci kesādinā upādinnakaṃ vā anupādinnakaṃ vā phusantopi saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjatiyevā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.274). Tena anupādinnakānampi kesalomādīnaṃ aṅgabhāvo veditabbo. Evaṃ santepi “phassaṃ paṭijānātīti tivaṅgasampattiyā saṅghādiseso. Phassassa appaṭivijānanato duvaṅgasampattiyā dukkaṭa”nti iminā pāḷiaṭṭhakathānayena virujjhatīti ce? Na, tadatthajānanato. Phuṭṭhabhāvañhi paṭivijānantopi phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma, ayameko attho, tasmā mātugāmassa, attano ca kāyapariyāpannānaṃ kesādīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ phuṭṭhabhāvaṃ phusitvā taṃ sādiyanaṃ phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma, na kāyaviññāṇuppattiyā eva. Anekantikañhettha kāyaviññāṇaṃ. Mātugāmassa upādinnakena kāyena, anupādinnakena vā kāyena bhikkhuno upādinnakakāye phuṭṭhe pasannakāyindriyo ce hoti, tassa kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, teneva phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma so hoti. Anupādinnakakāyo, loluppo appasannakāyindriyo vā hoti, timiravātena upahatakāyo [V 0.0162] vā tassa kāyaviññāṇaṃ nuppajjati. Na ca tena phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma, kevalaṃ sevanādhippāyena vāyamitvā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjanto phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma manoviññāṇena, tena vuttaṃ “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyāti imināssa vāyamato phassapaṭivijānanā dassitā”ti. Aparopi bhikkhu mātugāmassa kāyapaṭibaddhena vā nissaggiyena vā phuṭṭho kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppādentena phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma, tasmā vuttaṃ “anekantikañhettha [M 0.0182] kāyaviññāṇa”nti. Aparo vatthaṃ pārupitvā niddāyantaṃ mātugāmaṃ kāyasaṃsaggarāgena vatthassa uparibhāge saṇikaṃ phusanto vatthantarena nikkhantalomasamphassaṃ appaṭivijānantopi sevanādhippāyo kāyena vāyamitvā phassaṃ paṭivijānāti nāma, saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjati. “Nīlaṃ ghaṭṭessāmīti kāyaṃ ghaṭṭeti, saṅghādiseso”ti hi vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ dutiyo attho. Evaṃ anekatthattā, evaṃ duviññeyyādhippāyato ca mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ phassapaṭivijānanaṃ aṅgantveva na vuttaṃ. Tasmiñhi vutte ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ bhikkhu saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjitvāpi nakhena lomena saṃsaggo diṭṭho, na ca me lomaghaṭṭanena kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ, timiravātathaddhagatto cāhaṃ na phassaṃ paṭivijānāmīti anāpannasaññī siyāti na vuttaṃ, apica “phassaṃ paṭivijānāti, na ca phassaṃ paṭivijānātī”ti ca etesaṃ padānaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayaṃ dassetvā so paññāpetabbo. Ettāvatā na tadatthajānanatoti kāraṇaṃ vitthāritaṃ hoti.

‘By “grasping the hand”’: here, by ‘hand,’ the entire appropriated body is included, not a separate continuity connected to it, such as hand ornaments. By ‘grasping the hair,’ it should be understood that what is taken is the unappropriated, with unbroken continuity, consisting of head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, etc., which is produced by kamma as a condition and by temperature. For that reason, it is said in the Commentary: ‘Even by touching an appropriated or unappropriated part with some unappropriated thing like head-hair, etc., one still commits a Saṅghādisesa offense.’ By this, it should be understood that even unappropriated things like head-hair, body-hair, etc., have the nature of being a part of the body. Even so, if it is said that this contradicts the method of the Pāḷi and Commentary which states: ‘“He recognizes contact”: with the fulfillment of three factors, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. Due to not recognizing the contact, with the fulfillment of two factors, it is a Dukkaṭa offense’? No, it does not contradict, because of knowing their meaning. For even one who recognizes the state of being touched is called one who ‘recognizes contact’; this is one meaning. Therefore, when the hair, etc., included in the body of a woman and of oneself touch one another, and one consents to that touch, this is called ‘recognizing contact,’ not only through the arising of body-consciousness. For here, body-consciousness is not absolute. When a woman’s appropriated body or unappropriated body touches a monk’s appropriated body, if he has a clear body-faculty, his body-consciousness arises, and for that very reason, he is called one who ‘recognizes contact.’ If the contact is with an unappropriated body part, or if the monk is greedy, has an unclear body-faculty, or has a body afflicted by a wind that causes stiffness, his body-consciousness does not arise. And by that means, he is not called one who ‘recognizes contact.’ However, one who strives with the intention of indulgence and engages in bodily contact is called one who ‘recognizes contact’ by means of mind-consciousness. For this reason, it is said: ‘“He might engage in bodily contact”: by this striving of his, the recognition of contact is shown.’ Another monk, being touched by something connected to a woman’s body or by a discarded item, is called one who ‘recognizes contact’ by causing body-consciousness to arise. Therefore, it is said: ‘For here, body-consciousness is not absolute.’ Another monk, while slowly touching the upper part of the cloth of a sleeping, clothed woman out of lust for bodily contact, even while not recognizing the contact of body-hair protruding through the cloth, if he has the intention of indulgence and strives with his body, he is called one who ‘recognizes contact’ and commits a Saṅghādisesa offense. For it is said: ‘Thinking, “I will touch the blue thing,” he touches the body; it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.’ This is the second meaning. Thus, because of having multiple meanings and because of having an intention that is difficult to know, ‘recognition of contact’ was not stated as a factor in the Mātikā Commentary. For if it were stated, this situation would exist: a monk, even after having committed a Saṅghādisesa offense, might think, ‘There was contact with a nail or body-hair, but body-consciousness did not arise in me from the brushing of the hair, and I, having a body stiffened by a wind disease, do not recognize the contact,’ and thus perceive himself as not having committed an offense.
