For this reason, it was not stated as a factor. Furthermore, having shown the method stated in the commentary for these phrases, ‘he recognizes contact’ and ‘he does not recognize contact,’ that meaning should be made known. By this much, the reason for the statement ‘No, because of knowing their meaning’ has been elaborated.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis

271. “Rattaṃ cittaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetaṃ vipariṇata”nti kiñcāpi sāmaññena vuttaṃ, vinītavatthūsu “mātuyā mātupemena āmasati…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vuttattā kāyasaṃsaggarāgeneva rattanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā “mātugāmo nāma manussitthī”ti kiñcāpi avisesena vuttaṃ, atha kho avinaṭṭhindriyāva manussitthī idhādhippetā “matitthiyā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajji…pe… āpatti thullaccayassā”ti vuttattā. “Manussitthī”ti ettāvatā siddhe “na yakkhī na petī na tiracchānagatā”ti vacanaṃ avinaṭṭhindriyāpi na sabbā manussaviggahā itthī idha manussitthī nāma. Yakkhiādayo hi attano jātisiddhena iddhivisesena ijjhantiyo manussaviggahāpi hontīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tāsu yakkhī thullaccayavatthu hoti vinītavatthūsu yakkhiyā kāyasaṃsaggena thullaccayassa vuttattā. Tadanulomattā petitthī, devitthī ca thullaccayavatthu. Tiracchānagatitthī dukkaṭavatthu. Tiracchānagatamanussaviggahitthī ca thullaccayavatthumevāti eke. Vibhaṅge pana “manussitthī ca hoti manussitthisaññī”ti pāḷiyā abhāvena [V 0.0163] “itthī ca hoti yakkhisaññī”tiādivacane sati yakkhiādīnaṃ anitthitāpasaṅgato, “itthī [M 0.0183] ca hoti itthisaññī”tiādimhi yakkhiādīnaṃ antokaraṇe sati tāsaṃ saṅghādisesavatthubhāvappasaṅgato ca yakkhiādayo na vuttāti veditabbā. Eke pana “vinītavatthumhi ‘aññataro bhikkhu tiracchānagatitthiyā kāya…pe… dukkaṭassā’ti ettha amanussaviggahā pākatikatiracchānagatitthī adhippetā, tasmā dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. ‘Itthī ca hoti tiracchānagatasaññīti tiracchānagatā ca hoti itthisaññī’tiādivāresupi pākatikatiracchānagatova adhippeto, so ca tiracchānagatapurisova. Teneva duṭṭhullavācāattakaāmapāricariyasikkhāpadesu manussapurisapaṭisaṃyuttavārā viya tiracchānapaṭisaṃyuttavārāpi nāgatā”ti vadanti. Tathā paṇḍakoti idha manussapaṇḍakova, purisoti ca idha manussapurisova āgato, tasmā amanussitthī amanussapaṇḍako amanussapuriso tiracchānagatitthī tiracchānagatapaṇḍako manussāmanussatiracchānagataubhatobyañjanakā cāti aṭṭha janā idha nāgatā, tesaṃ vasena vatthusaññāvimatibhedavasena āpattibhedābhedavinicchayo, anāgatavāragaṇanā ca asammuyhantena veditabbā, tathā tesaṃ dukamissakādivārā, āpattianāpattibhedavinicchayo ca. “Tattha amanussapaṇḍakaamanussapurisatiracchānagatitthitiracchānagatapaṇḍakāti cattāro dukkaṭavatthukā, amanussitthimanussaubhatobyañjanakā thullaccayavatthukā, amanussaubhatobyañjanakā tiracchānagataubhatobyañjanakā dukkaṭavatthukā, pāḷiyaṃ pana amanussitthiyā anāgatattā amanussapaṇḍakā, ubhatobyañjanakā purisā ca nāgatā. Tiracchānagatitthipaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakā tiracchānagatapurisena samānagatikattā nāgatā, manussaubhatobyañjanako manussapaṇḍakena samānagatikattā anāgato”ti vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.281) pana “nāgamāṇavikāyapi supaṇṇamāṇavikāyapi kinnariyāpi gāviyāpi dukkaṭamevā”ti vuttattā tadeva pamāṇato gahetabbaṃ.

271. Although it is generally stated, “An impassioned mind, in this sense, is intended as a perverted one,” it should be known that, because it is said in the decided cases, “He touches his mother with motherly affection… an offense of wrong-doing,” ‘impassioned’ is only by way of lust for physical contact. Similarly, although it is said without distinction, “A woman is a human female,” nevertheless, only a human female with intact faculties is intended here, because it is said, “He engaged in physical contact with a dead woman… an offense of a grave transgression.” When ‘human female’ is established by this much, the statement, “not a female yakkha, not a female peta, not a female animal,” is said to show that not every female with a human form, even with intact faculties, is here called a ‘human female’. For it is said to show that female yakkhas and others, being endowed with their own special power accomplished by birth, can also have human forms. Among them, a female yakkha is an object for a grave transgression, because in the decided cases a grave transgression is stated for physical contact with a female yakkha. Because it follows from that, a female peta and a female deity are also objects for a grave transgression. A female animal is an object for wrong-doing. Some say that a female animal with a human form is also an object for a grave transgression. But in the Vibhaṅga, it should be known that female yakkhas and others are not mentioned for two reasons: due to the absence of the Pāli text, “She is a human female and he is percipient of her as a human female,” if there were a statement like, “She is a female and he is percipient of her as a female yakkha,” it would lead to the consequence that female yakkhas and others are not female; and if female yakkhas and others were included in statements like, “She is a female and he is percipient of her as a female,” it would lead to the consequence of them being objects for a Saṅghādisesa offense. But some say: “Here, in the decided case, ‘A certain monk… with a female animal… an offense of wrong-doing,’ an ordinary female animal without a human form is intended; therefore, an offense of wrong-doing is stated. Also in the clauses like, ‘She is a female and he is percipient of her as an animal,’ and ‘She is an animal and he is percipient of her as a female,’ only an ordinary animal is intended, and that is only a male animal. For that very reason, in the training rules on coarse speech and on attending to one’s own sensual desires, just as the clauses connected with a human male are not included, so too the clauses connected with an animal are not included.” Likewise, here ‘eunuch’ is only a human eunuch, and here ‘male’ is only a human male. Therefore, these eight beings—a non-human female, a non-human eunuch, a non-human male, a female animal, an animal eunuch, and human, non-human, and animal hermaphrodites—are not included here. On account of them, the determination of the distinction and non-distinction of offenses and the enumeration of the unincluded clauses should be known without confusion, by way of the distinctions of object, perception, and doubt; similarly, their clauses of pairs, mixed, etc., and the determination of the distinction between offense and non-offense. “Among them, the four—non-human eunuch, non-human male, female animal, and animal eunuch—are objects for wrong-doing. A non-human female and a human hermaphrodite are objects for a grave transgression. A non-human hermaphrodite and an animal hermaphrodite are objects for wrong-doing. But in the Pāli, because a non-human female is not included, non-human eunuchs, hermaphrodites, and males are not included. Female animals, animal eunuchs, and animal hermaphrodites are not included because they have the same standing as a male animal. A human hermaphrodite is not included because he has the same standing as a human eunuch,” they say. But in the Commentary, because it is said, “Even with a young nāga female, a young supaṇṇa female, a kinnarī, or a cow, it is only an offense of wrong-doing,” that very statement should be taken as the authority.

Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā – “na, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatassa nisinnaparisāya pātimokkhaṃ uddisitabba”nti (mahāva. 183) ettha “tiracchānagatoti yassa upasampadā paṭikkhittā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā tiracchānagatamanussaviggaho pākatikatiracchānagatato visiṭṭho, tathā yakkhapetatiracchānagatamanussaviggahānaṃ “tiracchānagatassa ca dukkhuppattiyaṃ apica dukkaṭamevā”ti ettha [M 0.0184] visesetvā vuttattā ca “patanarūpaṃ pamāṇaṃ, na maraṇarūpa”nti ettha āpattivisesavacanato ca “ubhato avassute yakkhassa vā petassa vā paṇḍakassa vā tiracchānagatamanussaviggahassa vā adhakkhakaṃ ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ kāyena kāyaṃ āmasati, āpatti thullaccayassā”ti (pāci. 661) sāmaññena [V 0.0164] vacanato ca so visiṭṭhoti siddhaṃ. Visiṭṭhattā ca tiracchānagatamanussaviggahitthiyā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjantassāti viseso hoti, tasmā tattha āpattivisesena bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpade tiracchānagatamanussaviggahitthīpi adhippetā, rūpasāmaññena saññāvirāgattāsambhavato duṭṭhullavācāattakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadesupi sā vattabbā bhaveyya, sā cānāgatā. Sarūpena saṃkhittavārattā nāgatāti ce? Itthī ca hoti tiracchānagato ca ubhinnaṃ itthisaññīti idha āgatattā purisaliṅganiddeso na yujjati, tasmā tiracchānagatapuriso ca idha āgato, tiracchānagatamanussaviggahitthiyā pāḷiyaṃ anāgatāyapi dukkaṭameva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattāti imassa vacanassa kāraṇacchāyā pariyesitabbāti adhippāyo. Idaṃ na yujjati. Kasmā? Itthīnaṃ, purisānañca ekato vacane purisaliṅgasabbhāvato. Idha tiracchānagatapurisapaṇḍakitthiyo tissopi ekato sampiṇḍetvā “tiracchānagato”ti vuttaṃ.

Herein is the consideration: Regarding “Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where an animal is present” (Mahāva. 183), since the commentary states “An animal refers to one whose higher ordination is rejected” (Kaṅkhā. Aṭṭha. Nidānavaṇṇanā), a human-shaped animal is distinct from an ordinary animal. Similarly, it is established that yakkhas, petas, and human-shaped animals are distinct because of the specific statement regarding the animal, 'and for an animal, upon the arising of suffering, it is also a dukkaṭa offense,' and because of the statement distinguishing offenses, “the standard is the falling [of the mind], not death,” and because of the general statement “If, with both [parties] aroused, one touches the body of a yakkha, or a peta, or a paṇḍaka, or a human-shaped animal, below the armpit and above the kneecap, with one’s own body, it is an offense of grave misconduct” (Pāci. 661). Because they are distinct, there is a difference when one engages in physical contact with a human-shaped female animal; therefore, a specific offense should be incurred in that case. If a human-shaped female animal were also intended in the training rule on physical contact, then, due to the similarity in form and the impossibility of the perception being altered, she should also be mentioned in the training rules on coarse speech and sexual gratification, but she is not mentioned. If it is said that she is not mentioned because the clauses are condensed in form, then since “she is a female and he is an animal, and he perceives both as a female” is mentioned here, the designation using the masculine gender is not appropriate. Therefore, a male animal is included here, and although a human-shaped female animal is not mentioned in the Pāli, the commentary states that it is merely a wrong-doing. The implication is that the underlying reason for this statement should be sought. This is not appropriate. Why? Because when women and men are spoken of together, the masculine gender is present. Here, male animals, animal paṇḍakas, and female animals—all three—are grouped together and referred to as “animal.”

Tattha ca manussaviggahāmanussaviggahesu itthipaṇḍakapurisasaññitā yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbā. Duṭṭhullavācādisikkhāpadadvaye vārānaṃ saṃkhittattā purisatiracchānagatādayo nāgatā. Yathāvuttesu āpatti, tathā tatthāpi. Aññathā purisaṃ obhāsantassa ca anāpattīti paṇḍakaṃ obhāsantassa ca thullaccayanti mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā te vārā saṃkhittāti paññāyantīti. Viseso ca paṇḍake, purise, tiracchānagate ca itthisaññissa atthi, tathāpi tattha dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva pamāṇanti dvinnametesaṃ vādānaṃ yattha yutti vā kāraṇaṃ vā atirekaṃ dissati, taṃ vicāretvā gahetabbanti āricayo. Evarūpesu ṭhānesu suṭṭhu vicāretvā kathetabbaṃ.

And among those, in the case of animals with a human form and those without, the perceptions of 'female', 'paṇḍaka', and 'male' should be understood as is applicable. Due to the clauses being condensed in the two training rules beginning with coarse speech, cases concerning male animals and the like are not mentioned. There is an offense in the aforementioned cases; similarly, also in those cases. Otherwise, it is stated in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā that for one addressing a man there is no offense, but for one addressing a paṇḍaka there is a grave offense. Therefore, it is understood that those clauses are condensed. And there is a distinction for one who has the perception of 'woman' with regard to a paṇḍaka, a man, or an animal; even so, a dukkaṭa offense is stated in those cases. Therefore, only what is stated in the commentary is the authority. The teacher says that between these two views, whichever appears to have more reason or cause should be examined and adopted. In such instances, one should speak after having deliberated thoroughly.

Tattha pāḷiyaṃ āgatavāragaṇanā tāva evaṃ saṅkhepato veditabbā – itthimūlakā pañca vārā paṇḍakapurisatiracchānagatamūlakā ca pañca pañcāti vīsati vārā ekamūlakā, tathā dumūlakā vīsati, missakamūlakā vīsatīti saṭṭhi [M 0.0185] vārā, tāni tīṇi vīsatikāni honti. Ekekasmiṃ vīsatike ekekamūlavāraṃ gahetvā kāyena kāyapaṭibaddhavārā tayo vuttā. Sesā sattapaññāsa vārā saṃkhittā, tathā kāyapaṭibaddhena kāyavārā tayo vuttā, sesā saṃkhittā, evaṃ kāyapaṭibaddhena kāyapaṭibaddhavārepi nissaggiyena kāyavārepi nissaggiyena kāyapaṭibaddhavārepi nissaggiyena nissaggiyavārepi tayo tayo vārā vuttā, sesā saṃkhittā. Evaṃ channaṃ tikānaṃ vasena aṭṭhārasa vārā āgatāti sarūpato vuttā, sesā dvecattālīsādhikāni tīṇi vārasatāni saṃkhittāni. Tato paraṃ mātugāmassa sārattapakkhe kāyena kāyanti ekamekaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pubbe vuttā aṭṭhārasa vārā āgatāti ekavīsati vārā sarūpena āgatā, navanavutādhikāni tīṇi vārasatāni saṃkhittāni. Tato paraṃ āpattānāpattidīpakā [V 0.0165] cattāro sevanādhippāyamūlakā cattāro mokkhādhippāyamūlakāti dve catukkā āgatā.

Herein, the enumeration of clauses mentioned in the Pāli should first be understood briefly as follows: there are five clauses rooted in a woman, and five each rooted in a paṇḍaka, a man, and an animal—thus twenty single-rooted clauses. Similarly, there are twenty two-rooted clauses and twenty mixed-rooted clauses—thus sixty clauses. These are three sets of twenty. In each set of twenty, taking each single-rooted clause, three clauses concerning 'body-connected by body' are stated. The remaining fifty-seven clauses are condensed. Similarly, three clauses concerning 'body by body-connected' are stated, and the remaining are condensed. In this way, three clauses each are stated for 'body-connected by body-connected,' 'body by relinquished,' 'body-connected by relinquished,' and 'relinquished by relinquished,' while the remaining are condensed. Thus, by way of six triads, eighteen clauses are stated in their specific form; the remaining 342 clauses are condensed. After that, in the case of an impassioned woman, with respect to the 'body by body' permutations, by adding one factor to each, the previously stated eighteen clauses are presented, and thus twenty-one clauses are presented in their specific form; the remaining 399 clauses are condensed. After that, four clauses rooted in the intention to engage and four clauses rooted in the intention of release—which clarify offense and non-offense—are presented as two tetrads.

Tatthāyaṃ viseso – yadidaṃ mātikāya parāmasanapadaṃ, tena yasmā āmasanādīni chupanapariyosānāni dvādasapi padāni gahitāni, tasmā paduddhāraṃ akatvā “āmasanā parāmasanaṃ chupana”nti āha. Parāmasanaṃ nāma āmasanā. “Chupana”nti hi vutte parāmasanampi visuṃ ekattaṃ bhaveyyāti veditabbaṃ. Itthī ca hoti itthisaññī cāti imasmiṃ paṭhamavāre eva dvādasapi āmasanādīni yojetvā dassitāni. Tato paraṃ ādimhi dve padānīti cattāri padāni āgatāni, itarāni saṃkhittānīti veditabbāni. Nissaggiyena kāyavārādīsu pana sabbākārena alābhato āmasanamevekaṃ āgataṃ, netarāni. “Sañcopeti haratī”ti pāṭho, sañcopeti ca. Gaṇṭhipadesu pana “purimanayenevāti rajjuvatthādīhi parikkhipane”ti ca pacchā “purimanayenevāti sammasanā hotī”ti ca “veṇiggāhe āpattiyā paññattattā lomaphusanepi saṅghādiseso”ti ca “taṃ pakāsetuṃ upādinnakena hītiādi vutta”nti ca likhitaṃ.

Herein is this distinction: namely, the term “parāmasana” in the matrix. Because by it the twelve terms beginning with “āmasana” and ending with “chupana” are included, therefore, without extracting the terms, it is stated as “āmasanā, parāmasanaṃ, chupana.” Parāmasana is indeed āmasana. For if “chupana” were stated, it should be understood that parāmasana also would become a separate single term. In this first instance, “itthī ca hoti itthisaññī ca” (she is a woman and he is percipient of her as a woman), all twelve terms beginning with āmasana are applied and shown. After that, two terms at the beginning and two later terms are mentioned, thus four terms are mentioned; it should be understood that the others are abbreviated. However, in the sections on bodily contact, etc., of the Nissaggiya rules, because they are not applicable in every way, only the single term āmasana is mentioned, not the others. The reading is “sañcopeti harati” (he moves, he carries), and also “sañcopeti.” However, in the Gaṇṭhipadas, it is written: “purimanayenevāti” means “by encircling with ropes, cloths, etc.,” and later, “purimanayenevāti” means “it is a touching,” and also, “since an offense is laid down for grasping a braid of hair, even for touching a body-hair there is a Saṅghādisesa,” and further, “to explain that, the passage beginning with ‘upādinnakena hi’ is stated.”

Yathāniddiṭṭhaniddeseti imasmiṃyeva yathāniddiṭṭhe niddese. “Sadisaṃ aggahesī”ti vutte tādisaṃ aggahesīti garukaṃ tattha kārayeti attho, kāyasaṃsaggavibhaṅge vāti attho. Itaropi kāyapaṭibaddhachupanako. Gahaṇe cāti gahaṇaṃ vā. Virāgiteti viraddhe. Sārattanti kāyasaṃsaggarāgena [M 0.0186] rattaṃ, attanā adhippetanti attho. “Mātubhaginiādivirattaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti virattaṃ ñātipemavasena gaṇhi, ettha dukkaṭaṃ yuttaṃ. “Kāyasaṃsaggarāgaṃ vā sārattaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti virattaṃ mātaraṃ gaṇhi, anadhippetaṃ gaṇhi. Ettha mahāsumattheravādena thullaccayaṃ “kāyaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti kāyappaṭibaddhaṃ gaṇhāti, thullaccayanti laddhikattā. “Itthī ca hoti itthisaññī sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā kāyena kāyaṃ āmasati, āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti (pārā. 273) vacanato saṅghādisesopi khāyati. “Virattaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti sārattaṃ gaṇhāti, etthapi saṅghādisesova khāyati “nīlaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti kāyaṃ ghaṭṭeti, saṅghādiseso”ti vacanato. Ettha pana “na pubbabhāge kāyasaṃsaggarāgattā”ti anugaṇṭhipade kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “garukāpattibhayena ‘nīlameva ghaṭṭessāmī’ti vāyāmanto kāyaṃ ghaṭṭeti, pubbabhāge tassa ‘kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ ghaṭṭessāmī’ti pavattattā dukkaṭena bhavitabba”nti vadanti. Dhammasiritthero “evarūpe saṅghādiseso”ti vadati kira. “Itthiubhatobyañjanakaitthiyā purisaubhatobyañjanakapurise vuttanayena āpattibhedo, itthiliṅgassa paṭicchannakālepi itthivaseneva āpattī”ti vadanti.

In this very explanation as it has been detailed. When it is said, 'He grasped what is similar,' it means he grasped an object of that kind; therefore, a grave offense should be decided in that case. This is the meaning. Or, this is also the meaning in the Analysis of Bodily Contact. The other one is also a person who touches something connected to the body. In the phrase `gahaṇe ca`, it means 'or the grasping'. In the phrase `virāgi`, it means 'when it is contrary'. In the word `sārattaṃ`, it means a woman impassioned with lust for bodily contact; this is the meaning: a woman desired by oneself. If, intending, 'I will grasp a dispassionate person such as a mother or sister,' one grasps a dispassionate person through affection for a relative, here a `dukkaṭa` offense is fitting. If, intending, 'I will grasp one with lust for bodily contact or an impassioned one,' one grasps a dispassionate mother, one has grasped what was unintended. Here, according to the view of the Great Elder Sumana, it is a `thullaccaya` offense, because of the established view that if one, intending 'I will grasp the body,' grasps what is connected to the body, it is a `thullaccaya` offense. Because of the statement, 'There is a woman, he is percipient of her as a woman, and he is impassioned; and the monk touches her body with his body—it is an offense of `saṅghādisesa`' (Pārā. 273), a `saṅghādisesa` offense also appears. If, intending, 'I will grasp a dispassionate person,' one grasps an impassioned person, in this case also only a `saṅghādisesa` offense appears, because of the statement, 'Intending to touch the blue, he touches the body; it is a `saṅghādisesa` offense.' Here, however, the reason is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: 'not because of lust for bodily contact in the preliminary stage.' But some say, 'Due to fear of a grave offense, while endeavoring, intending "I will touch only the blue," he touches the body; because in the preliminary stage there was the intention "I will touch what is connected to the body," it should be a `dukkaṭa` offense.' The Elder Dhammasiri is said to have said, 'In such a case, it is a `saṅghādisesa` offense.' They say, 'For a female `ubhatobyañjanaka` and for a male `ubhatobyañjanaka`, the distinction among offenses follows the stated method; even at the time when the female organ is concealed, the offense is determined as for a woman.'

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Decided Cases

281. Tiṇaṇḍupakanti [V 0.0166] hiriverādimūlāni gahetvā kattabbaṃ. Tālapaṇṇamuddikanti tālapaṇṇamayaṃ aṅgulimuddikaṃ, tena tālapaṇṇamayaṃ kaṭaṃ, kaṭisuttakaṃ, kaṇṇapiḷandhanādi sabbaṃ na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Tambapaṇṇivāsino itthirūpaṃ likhitaṃ, kaṭikapaṭañca na chupanti kira. Ākarato muttamatto. Ratanamissoti alaṅkāratthaṃ kato kañcanalatādivinaddho. Suvaṇṇena saddhiṃ yojetvā pacitvāti suvaṇṇarasaṃ pakkhipitvā pacitvā. Bījato dhātupāsāṇato paṭṭhāya. Thero na kappatīti “tumhākaṃ pesita”nti vuttattā. “Cetiyassa pūjaṃ karothā”ti vutte vaṭṭati kira. Bubbuḷakaṃ tārakaṃ. Ārakūṭalohampi jātarūpagatikameva.

281. Regarding tiṇaṇḍupaka: it is an ornament that should be made by taking roots of hirivera and so forth. Regarding tālapaṇṇamuddika: it means a finger-ring made of palm leaves. By this, it is established that all items made of palm leaves—such as anklets, waist strings, ear ornaments, and so forth—are not permissible. The dwellers of Tambapaṇṇi, it is said, do not touch painted female figures or hip cloths. Just a gem freed from its source. Regarding ratanamissa: it means made for decoration, intertwined with golden vines and so forth. Regarding suvaṇṇena saddhiṃ yojetvā pacitvā: it means cooked after adding gold essence. Starting from a seed, from a mineral stone. The Elder does not allow it because it was said, “It was sent for you.” When it was said, “Make an offering to the shrine,” it is said to be permissible. A bubbuḷaka is a star. Even ārakūṭa metal is merely of the nature of gold.

Vuttañhetaṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

As it is said in the Andhaka Commentary:

“Ārakūṭalohaṃ suvaṇṇasadisameva, suvaṇṇaṃ anulometi, anāmāsa”nti.

“Ārakūṭa metal is just like gold, it conforms to gold, it is not to be touched.”

“Bhesajjatthāya [M 0.0187] pana vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayekadesopi anuññāto hotīti tattha tattha adhippāyaṃ ñatvā vibhāvetabbaṃ.

However, by the statement, “It is permissible for medicinal purposes,” even a part of the method stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is permitted. Thus, understanding the intention in each case, it should be explained.

Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Training Rule on Bodily Contact is concluded.

3. Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Training Rule on Gross Speech

283. Tatiye tayo saṅghādisesavārā tayo thullaccayavārā tayo dukkaṭavārā tayo kāyapaṭibaddhavārāti dvādasa vārā sarūpena āgatā. Tattha tayo saṅghādisesavārā dutiyasikkhāpade vuttāti tiṇṇaṃ vīsatikānaṃ ekekamūlā vārāti veditabbā, tasmā idha visesāti paṇṇāsa vārā saṃkhittā honti, aññathā itthī ca hoti vematiko sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā vaccamaggaṃ passāvamaggaṃ ādissa vaṇṇampi bhaṇati…pe… āpatti thullaccayassa. Itthī ca hoti paṇḍakapurisasaññī tiracchānagatasaññī sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā vaccamaggaṃ passāvamaggaṃ ādissa vaṇṇampi bhaṇati akkosatipi, āpatti thullaccayassa. Paṇḍako ca hoti paṇḍakasaññī sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ paṇḍakassa vaccamaggaṃ ādissa vaṇṇampi bhaṇati, āpatti thullaccayassāti evamādīnaṃ āpattiṭṭhānānaṃ anāpattiṭṭhānatā [V 0.0167] āpajjeyya, na cāpajjati, paṇḍake itthisaññissa dukkaṭanti dīpetuṃ “itthī ca paṇḍako ca ubhinnaṃ itthisaññī āpatti saṅghādisesena dukkaṭassā”ti vuttattā “paṇḍake paṇḍakasaññissa thullaccaya”nti vuttameva hoti, tasmā sabbattha saṃkhittavāresu thullaccayaṭṭhāne thullaccayaṃ, dukkaṭaṭṭhāne dukkaṭampi vuttameva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Tathā “itthī ca hoti vematiko sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā vaccamaggaṃ passāvamaggaṃ ṭhapetvā adhakkhakaṃ ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ ādissa vaṇṇampi bhaṇati…pe… thullaccayassā”tiādinā nayena thullaccayakhettepi yathāsambhavaṃ uddharitabbā. Tathā “itthī ca hoti vematiko sāratto ca, bhikkhu ca naṃ itthiyā kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ ādissa vaṇṇampi bhaṇati…pe… dukkaṭassā”tiādinā nayena kāyapaṭibaddhavārāpi yathāsambhavaṃ uddharitabbā. Kāyappaṭibaddhavārattikaṃ viya nissaggiyavārattikaṃ labbhamānampi āpattivisesābhāvato na uddhaṭaṃ. Kāyappaṭibaddhavārattike pana dinnanayattā tampi tadanulomā vārā ca [M 0.0188] uddharitabbā. Sabbattha na-viññū taruṇadārikā, mahallikā ummattikādikā ca anadhippetā, pageva pākatikā tiracchānagatitthīnaṃ, tathā paṇḍakādayopīti veditabbā. Sesaṃ dutiye vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

283. In the third training rule, twelve cases are presented in their own form: three Saṅghādisesa cases, three Thullaccaya cases, three Dukkaṭa cases, and three Kāyapaṭibaddha cases. Among these, the three Saṅghādisesa cases were stated in the second training rule; therefore, they should be understood as the root cases for each of the three groups of twenty. Thus, as there are specifics here, fifty-seven cases are summarized. Otherwise, for grounds of an offense such as: 'A woman is uncertain and lustful, and a monk, referring to the woman's path of excretion or path of urination, speaks in praise… the offense is a Thullaccaya,' it would become a state of no offense. But it does not become so. To show that for one with the perception of a woman towards a eunuch, there is a Dukkaṭa offense, it was said: 'For both a woman and a eunuch, if one has the perception of a woman… the offense is a Saṅghādisesa and a Dukkaṭa.' Thus, it is indeed said: 'For one with the perception of a eunuch towards a eunuch, there is a Thullaccaya.' Therefore, it should be understood that in all the summarized cases, a Thullaccaya is stated in a place for a Thullaccaya, and a Dukkaṭa is also stated in a place for a Dukkaṭa. Similarly, by the method beginning with 'A woman is uncertain and lustful, and a monk, referring to her area below the navel and above the knee-circle, putting aside the path of excretion and the path of urination, speaks in praise… a Thullaccaya offense,' cases should also be extracted in the field of Thullaccaya as is appropriate. Likewise, by the method beginning with 'A woman is uncertain and lustful, and a monk, referring to what is connected to her body, speaks in praise… a Dukkaṭa offense,' the Kāyapaṭibaddha cases should also be extracted as is appropriate. Although the triad of Nissaggiya cases could be obtained, similar to the triad of Kāyapaṭibaddha cases, it was not extracted due to the absence of a specific offense. But in the triad of Kāyapaṭibaddha cases, because the method has been given, those cases and the cases that conform to them should be extracted. In all cases, an undiscerning young girl, an old woman, an insane woman, and so on are not intended—what then to say of ordinary female animals? It should be understood that the same applies to eunuchs and others. The remainder should be understood by the method stated in the second training rule.

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis

285. Vuttanayamevāti “kāyasaṃsagge itthilakkhaṇenā”ti likhitaṃ. “Itthilakkhaṇenā”ti kira mahāaṭṭhakathāpāṭho. Sīsaṃ na etīti akkosanaṃ na hoti, ghaṭite pana hoti. Tatrāyaṃ viseso – imehi tīhi ghaṭite eva saṅghādiseso vaccamaggapassāvamaggānaṃ niyatavacanattā, accoḷārikattā vā, na aññehi animittāsītiādīhi aṭṭhahi. Tattha alohitāsi, dhuvalohitāsi, dhuvacoḷāsi, paggharaṇīsi, itthipaṇḍakāsi, vepurisikāsīti etāni cha maggānaṃ aniyatavacanāni, animittāsi, nimittamattāsīti dve padāni anaccoḷārikāni ca, yato aṭṭhapadāni “saṅghādisesaṃ na janentī”ti vuttāni, tasmā tāni thullaccayavatthūni. Paribbājakavatthumhi viya akkosamattattā dukkaṭavatthūnīti eke. Itthipaṇḍakāsi, vepurisikāsīti etāneva padāni sakalasarīrasaṇṭhānabhedadīpakāni suddhāni saṅghādisesaṃ na janenti sakalasarīrasāmaññattā, itarāni janenti asāmaññattā. Tāni hi passāvamaggameva dīpenti sikharaṇī-padaṃ viya. Ubhatobyañjanāsīti vacanaṃ pana purisanimittena asaṅghādisesavatthunā missavacanaṃ. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa ca itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Yadi tampi janeti, kathaṃ animittāsītiādipadāni na saṅghādisesaṃ janentīti eke, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Purisassapi nimittādhivacanato, “methunupasaṃhitāhi saṅghādiseso”ti mātikāya lakkhaṇassa vuttattā ca methunupasaṃhitāhipi [V 0.0168] obhāsane paṭivijānantiyā saṅghādiseso, appaṭivijānantiyā thullaccayaṃ, itarehi obhāsane paṭivijānantiyā thullaccayaṃ, appaṭivijānantiyā dukkaṭanti eke, sabbaṃ suṭṭhu vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

285. Regarding the phrase 'Vuttanayameva' (Just as stated in the method), it is written: 'in bodily contact, by the characteristic of a woman.' The reading in the Great Commentary is indeed 'by the characteristic of a woman.' When it does not reach the 'head' (i.e., the full extent of the offense), it is not an insult; but when it is connected with the specific terms, it is. Herein lies this distinction: only when connected with these three terms is it a saṅghādisesa offense, because they are specific words for the excretory and urinary passages, or because they are very coarse words; but not when connected with the other eight words beginning with 'you are without a sign.' Among these, the six terms—'you are without blood,' 'you are with continuous blood,' 'you are with a continuous cloth,' 'you are with discharge,' 'you are a female eunuch,' 'you are a hermaphrodite'—are indefinite words for the passages. The two words, 'you are without a sign' and 'you are with just a sign,' are not coarse. Since it is said that these eight words 'do not give rise to a saṅghādisesa,' they are therefore grounds for a thullaccaya offense. Some say they are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense because they are merely insults, as in the case of the wanderer. These very words, 'you are a female eunuch' and 'you are a hermaphrodite,' being indicative of a difference in the entire bodily form, when used by themselves, do not give rise to a saṅghādisesa offense, because they refer to the general state of the entire body. The other words do give rise to it, because they are not general. Indeed, like the word 'sikharaṇī', they indicate only the urinary passage. The statement 'you are one with both signs,' however, is a mixed statement with a case not entailing a saṅghādisesa offense by means of the male organ. And for a male with both signs, the female organ is concealed while the male organ is manifest. Some say, 'If that too gives rise to an offense, how is it that the words beginning with "you are without a sign" do not give rise to a saṅghādisesa?' That is not correct. This is because it is also a designation of the male organ, and because the characteristic is stated in the Mātikā as, 'A saṅghādisesa offense arises from words connected with sexual intercourse.' Some say that even with words connected with sexual intercourse, in making an obscene remark, if she understands, it is a saṅghādisesa offense; if she does not understand, it is a thullaccaya offense. With other words, in making an obscene remark, if she understands, it is a thullaccaya offense; if she does not understand, it is a dukkaṭa offense. All this should be thoroughly investigated and understood.

287. Hasantoti yaṃ uddissa bhaṇati, sā ce paṭivijānāti, saṅghādiseso.

287. Regarding 'hasanto ti' (laughing): If he speaks directed at a certain woman, and if that woman understands, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Settled Cases

289. “Paṭivuttaṃ [M 0.0189] nāmā”ti pāṭho. No-saddo adhiko. “Akkharalikhanenapi hotī”ti vadanti, taṃ āvajjanasamanantaravidhinā sameti ce, gahetabbaṃ.

289. The reading is 'Paṭivuttaṃ nāma.' The word 'no' is superfluous. They say, 'It also occurs by the writing of letters,' and that should be accepted if it accords with the process immediately following adverting.

Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule on lewd speech is concluded.

4. Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Service for One's Own Sensual Pleasure

290. Catutthe tayo saṅghādisesavārā āgatā, sesā sattapaññāsa vārā thullaccayadukkaṭāpattikāya saṃkhittāti veditabbā, tato aññataro asambhavato idha na uddhaṭo. Sesayojanakkamo vuttanayena veditabbo. Nagaraparikkhārehīti pākāraparikhādīhi nagaraparivārehi. Setaparikkhāroti setālaṅkāro, sīlālaṅkāroti attho (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.4). Cakkavīriyoti vīriyacakko. Vasalaṃ duggandhanti nimittaṃ sandhāyāha, tadeva sandhāya “kiṃ me pāpakaṃ, kiṃ me duggandha”nti vuttaṃ.

290. In the fourth, three Saṅghādisesa cases have come; the remaining fifty-seven cases are to be understood as summarized by way of Thullaccaya and Dukkaṭa offenses. From those, another one, being impossible, is not cited here. The remaining order of connection should be understood in the manner stated. Regarding `Nagaraparikkhārehi`: by the city's surroundings such as walls and moats. Regarding `Setaparikkhāro`: the meaning is 'white ornament', that is, 'the ornament of virtue'. Regarding `Cakkavīriyo`: the wheel of effort. Regarding `Vasalaṃ duggandhanti`: this was said referring to the female organ. Referring to that very same thing, it was said, 'What is evil for me? What is foul-smelling for me?'

291. Santiketi yattha ṭhito viññāpeti. “Paṭhamaviggahe sace pāḷivasena yojetīti kāmahetupāricariyāattho. Sesanti ‘adhippāyo’ti padaṃ byañjanaṃ atthābhāvato. Dutiye pāḷivasena kāmahetu-padāni byañjanāni tesaṃ tattha atthābhāvato. Evaṃ cattāri padāni dvinnaṃ viggahānaṃ vasena yojitānīti apare vadantī”ti vuttaṃ.

291. Regarding `Santike`: where one stands and makes something known. It is said: “Others say: 'In the first analysis, if connected according to the Pāḷi text, the meaning is 'service for the sake of sensual pleasure'. Regarding `sesaṃ`, the word `adhippāyo` is a mere verbal expression as it has no meaning. In the second analysis, according to the Pāḷi text, the words `kāmahetu` are verbal expressions as they have no meaning there. Thus, the four words are connected by way of the two analyses.'”

295. Etesu sikkhāpadesu methunarāgena vītikkame sati saṅghādisesena anāpatti. Tasmā “kiṃ bhante aggadānanti. Methunadhamma”nti idaṃ kevalaṃ methunadhammassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na methunadhammādhippāyena tadatthiyā vuttanti veditabbaṃ, parassa bhikkhuno kāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇabhaṇane [V 0.0169] dukkaṭaṃ. “Yo te vihāre vasati, tassa aggadānaṃ dehī”ti pariyāyavacanenapi dukkaṭaṃ. “Attakāmapāricariyāya vaṇṇaṃ bhāseyya. Yā mādisaṃ sīlavanta”nti ca vuttattāti eke. Pañcasu aṅgesu sabbhāvā saṅghādisesovāti eke. Vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade pana “imasmiṃ [M 0.0190] sikkhāpadadvaye kāyasaṃsagge viya yakkhipetīsu duṭṭhullattakāmavacane thullaccaya’nti vadanti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana nāgata”nti likhitaṃ. “Ubhatobyañjanako pana paṇḍakagatikovā”ti vadanti.

295. In these training rules, if there is a transgression with sexual lust, there is no offense by way of Saṅghādisesa. Therefore, it should be known that this statement, 'What, venerable sir, is the foremost gift? Sexual intercourse,' is said merely for the purpose of praising sexual intercourse; it is not said with the intention of sexual intercourse or with the desire for it. In praising the service of sensual pleasure for another monk, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. Even by an indirect statement such as, 'Give the foremost gift to the one who dwells in your monastery,' there is a Dukkaṭa offense. Some say this is so because it is also said: 'One should speak praise of the service of one's own sensual pleasure... who is virtuous like me.' Some say that because of its existence in the five factors, it is indeed a Saṅghādisesa offense. This should be accepted after investigation. But in the Gaṇṭhipada it is written: 'They say that in these two training rules, as in the rule on bodily contact, in the case of yakkhīs and petīs, in speaking a gross word about one's own sensual pleasure, it is a Thullaccaya offense. But this is not found in the commentaries.' They say: 'A hermaphrodite, however, is indeed of the nature of a paṇḍaka.'

Attakāmapāricariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the service of one's own sensual pleasure is concluded.

5. Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Acting as a Go-between

297. Ahamhi duggatāti ahaṃ amhi duggatā. Ahaṃ khvayyoti ettha ayyoti bahuvacanaṃ hoti.

297. `Ahamhi duggatā` means `ahaṃ amhi duggatā` (I am unfortunate). Here, in `Ahaṃ khvayyo`, the word `ayyo` is plural.

298. Oyācantīti nīcaṃ katvā deve yācanti. Āyācantīti uccaṃ katvā ādarena yācanti. Alaṅkārādīhi maṇḍito kesasaṃvidhānādīhi pasādhito. “Maṇḍitakaraṇe dukkaṭa”nti vadanti.

298. `Oyācanti` means they beg the devas, humbling themselves. `Āyācanti` means they beg with reverence, exalting themselves. `Maṇḍito` means adorned with ornaments and so forth; `pasādhito` means beautified with hair arrangements and so forth. They say, 'In the act of adorning, it is a Dukkaṭa offense.'

Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Word-by-word Analysis

303. Saha paridaṇḍena vattamānāti attho. Chandavāsinī nāma “piyā piyaṃ vasetī”ti pāḷi, purisaṃ vāsetīti adhippāyo. “Piyo piyaṃ vāsetī”ti aṭṭhakathā.

303. The meaning is: 'a woman who lives together with control.' The so-called `chandavāsinī` is, according to the Pāḷi, 'the dear one causes the dear one to dwell'; the intention is that she causes a man to dwell. The commentary states: 'The dear one causes the dear one to dwell.'

Taṃ kiriyaṃ sampādessatīti avassaṃ ārocentiyā ce ārocetīti attho. Dvinnaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ce āroceti, saṅghādisesoti vinayavinicchaye “vatthu oloketabba”nti vuttaṃ. Vatthumhi ca “udāyitthero gaṇikāya ārocesī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ “mātādīnampi vadato visaṅketo natthī”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanato nippayojanaṃ. Taṃ panetanti ācariyassa vacanaṃ. Māturakkhitaṃ brūhīti pesitassa gantvā mātāpiturakkhitaṃ vadato tassa tassā māturakkhitabhāvepi sati visaṅketameva, kasmā? “Piturakkhitādīsu aññataraṃ vadantassa visaṅketa”nti vuttattā itarathā ādi-saddo niratthako siyā. Ekaṃ dasakaṃ itarena dasakena yojetvā pubbe sukkavissaṭṭhiyaṃ vuttanayattā māturakkhitāya mātā attano dhītusantikaṃ pahiṇatīti gahetabbaṃ.

The meaning is this: thinking, 'He will accomplish that act,' if he informs a woman who will certainly be informed. If he informs both mother and father, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense; in the Vinayavinicchaya it is said, 'The case should be looked into.' And in the case it is said, 'The Elder Udāyi informed a courtesan.' That is pointless because of the commentary's statement: 'There is no impropriety even when speaking to the mother and others.' This, however, is the teacher’s statement. For a monk who, having been sent with the instruction, 'Speak of one protected by the mother,' goes and speaks of one protected by mother and father, there is indeed an impropriety, even though she is in fact protected by her mother. Why? Because it is said, 'There is an impropriety for one who speaks of any one among those protected by the father, etc.' Otherwise, the word 'ādi' (etc.) would be meaningless. Having combined one group of ten with the other group of ten, because of the method stated previously in the rule on emission of semen, it should be understood that the mother of the woman protected by her mother sends a message to her own daughter.

338. Anabhinanditvāti [V 0.0170] vacanamattameva, yadipi abhinandati, yāva sāsanaṃ nāroceti, tāva “vīmaṃsito”ti na vuccati. Sāsanārocanakāleti āṇāpakassa [M 0.0191] sāsanavacanakkhaṇe. Tatiyapade vuttanayenāti ekaṅgasampattiyā dukkaṭanti attho. Vatthugaṇanāya saṅghādisesoti ubhayavatthugaṇanāya kira.

338. `Anabhinanditvā` (not approving) is merely a statement; even if one approves, as long as one does not announce the message, one is not called 'investigated.' The time of announcing the message refers to the moment when the issuer of the order speaks the message. 'By the method stated in the third clause' means: it is a Dukkaṭa offense due to the fulfillment of one factor. 'It is a Saṅghādisesa offense by counting the bases' means, apparently, by counting both bases.

339. Catutthe anāpattīti ettha pana “paṭiggaṇhāti na vīmaṃsati na paccāharati, anāpattīti ettha viya ‘gacchanto na sampādeti, āgacchanto visaṃvādetī’ti anāpattipāḷiyāpi bhavitabbanti dassanatthaṃ vutta”nti vadanti, ekaccesu potthakesu “atthī”tipi.

339. However, here in the fourth clause, regarding 'no offense,' they say that it was said in order to show that the no-offense text 'going, he does not accomplish; coming, he deceives' should also exist, just as in the case of 'he accepts, does not investigate, does not return it; no offense.' They also say that in some books, it exists.

Vinītavatthuvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Settled Cases

341. Alaṃvacanīyāti na vacanīyā, nivāraṇe alaṃ-saddo. Therapitā vadatīti jiṇṇapitā vadatīti attho. Kiñcāpi ettha “itthī nāma manussitthī na yakkhī na petī na tiracchānagatā, puriso nāma manussapuriso na yakkho”tiādi natthi, tathāpi kāyasaṃsaggādīsu “manussitthī”ti itthīvavatthānassa katattā idhāpi manussitthī evāti paññāyati. Methunapubbabhāgattā manussaubhatobyañjanako ca thullaccayavatthukova hoti, sesā manussapaṇḍakaubhatobyañjanakatiracchānagatapurisādayo dukkaṭavatthukāva micchācārasāsanaṅgasambhavatoti veditabbaṃ. Yathāsambhavaṃ pana vārā uddharitabbā. Paññattiajānane viya alaṃvacanīyabhāvājānanepi acittakatā veditabbā. Duṭṭhullādīsupīti “imasmimpī”ti vuttameva hoti. “Lekhaṃ netvā paṭilekhaṃ ārocitassāpi sañcarittaṃ natthi sañcarittabhāvamajānantassā”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

341. “Alaṃvacanīyā” means 'not to be spoken to'; the word `alaṃ` is in the sense of prevention. “Therapitā vadati” means 'the aged father speaks.' Although the Pāḷi beginning with “A woman means a human woman, not a yakkhī, not a petī, not an animal; a man means a human man, not a yakkha...” is not present here, nevertheless, because the determination of 'woman' as 'human woman' has been made in the training rules such as that on physical contact, it is understood that here also it is only a human woman. Because it is a preliminary part of sexual intercourse, a human with both sexual characteristics is indeed a ground for a grave offense. The remaining cases, such as human paṇḍakas, those with both sexual characteristics, animal males, and so on, are grounds for a dukkaṭa offense, because it can be an element of conveying a message for sexual misconduct; thus it should be understood. However, the sections should be extracted as is possible. Just as in not knowing the regulation, in not knowing the state of being alaṃvacanīya also, it should be understood as unintentional. Regarding coarse speech and so on, it is just what is said by 'in this case as well.' Some say, “For one who, having taken a letter and announced the reply, does not know the nature of sañcaritta, there is no sañcaritta,” but this should be accepted after investigation.

Sañcarittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning acting as a go-between is concluded.

6. Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Building a Hut

342. Yācanāti “detha dethā”ti codanā. Viññattīti iminā no atthoti viññāpanā. “Hatthakammaṃ yācito upakaraṇaṃ, mūlaṃ vā dassatī”ti yācati, na vaṭṭatīti. Vaṭṭati senāsane obhāsaparikathādīnaṃ laddhattāti eke. Anajjhāvutthakanti assāmikaṃ. Na āhaṭaṃ [V 0.0171] paribhuñjitabbanti “sūpodanaviññattidukkaṭaṃ [M 0.0192] hotī”ti vuttaṃ. “Kiñcāpi garubhaṇḍappahonakesūti vuttaṃ, tathāpi yaṃ vatthuvasena appaṃ hutvā agghavasena mahā haritālahiṅgulikādi, taṃ yācituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti.

342. “Yācanā” is urging with “Give, give.” “Viññatti” is making it known with “We have need of this.” If one asks, thinking, “If asked for manual labor, he will give either tools or money,” it is not allowable. To this, some say it is allowable because, in the matter of a lodging, obtaining it through talk of illumination and the like is permitted. “Anajjhāvutthakaṃ” means ownerless. Regarding “What is not brought should not be consumed,” it is said: “Making a hint for soup and rice is a dukkaṭa offense.” Some say: “Although it is said 'in the case of abundant heavy goods,' nevertheless, it is not allowable to ask for that which, being small in substance, is great in value, such as orpiment, cinnabar, and so on.”

344. So kirāti isi. Tadā ajjhagamā tadajjhagamā.

344. He, it is said, was a sage. “Tadajjhagamā” means: at that time (tadā), he went away (ajjhagamā).

348-9. Na hi sakkā yācanāya kātuṃ, tasmā sayaṃ yācitakehi upakaraṇehīti adhippāyo. Byañjanaṃ sameti, na attho. Kasmā? Idha ubhayesaṃ adhippetattā, taṃ dassento “yasmā panā”tiādimāha. Idha vuttanayenāti imasmiṃ sikkhāpadavibhaṅge vuttanayena. “Saññācikāyā”ti vacanato karontenāpi, “parehi pariyosāpetī”ti vacanato kārāpentenāpi paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Ubhopete kārakakārāpakā. Byañjanaṃ vilomitaṃ bhaveyya, “kārayamānenā”ti hi byañjanaṃ “karontenā”ti vutte vilomitaṃ hoti atadatthattā. Na hi kārāpento nāma hoti. “Idha vuttanayenāti desitavatthukapamāṇikanayena. Evaṃ sante ‘karontena vā kārāpentena vā’ti vacanato karontenāpi parehi vippakataṃ vattabbanti ce, tadatthavissajjanatthaṃ ‘yadi panātiādimāhā’”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karonto”ti vacanavasena vuttaṃ. “Āyāmato ca vitthārato cā”ti avatvā vikappatthassa vā-saddassa gahitattā ekatobhāgepi vaḍḍhite āpatti eva. Pamāṇayuttamañco kira navavidatthi. “‘Catuhatthavitthārā’ti vacanena ‘tiriyaṃ tihatthā vā’ti vacanampi sameti ‘yattha pamāṇayutto’tiādisanniṭṭhānavacanāsambhavato”ti vuttaṃ. Pamāṇato ūnatarampīti vitthārato catupañcahatthampi dīghato anatikkamitvā vuttapamāṇameva desitavatthu. Adesitavatthuñhi karoto āpatti. Pamāṇātikkantā kuṭi eva pamāṇātikkantaṃ kuṭiṃ kareyyāti vuttattā. “Thambhatulā”ti pāṭho. Anussāvanānayenāti ettha “damiḷabhāsāyapi vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti.

348-9. For it is not possible to do it by begging; therefore, the intention is 'with materials begged by oneself.' The wording fits, but not the meaning. Why? Because here both are intended, he shows that by saying 'but because,' etc. 'Here, in the manner stated' means in the manner stated in this analysis of the training rule. From the phrase 'by making known one's need,' one should proceed accordingly whether one is doing it oneself, and from the phrase 'gets others to complete it,' whether one is having it done. Both of these are the doer and the one who causes it to be done. The wording would be contrary; for if the wording 'by causing to do' is said as 'by doing,' it would be contrary because it does not have that meaning. Indeed, one who causes something to be done is not called a 'doer.' In the supplementary passage it is said: '“Here, in the manner stated” means by the method of the declared object and the measure. This being so, if one were to say that, on account of the phrase “by doing or by causing to do,” it should be stated that it was left unfinished by others even when one is doing it oneself, then to explain that meaning, he said “but if,” etc.' 'Building a hut by making known one's need'—this is said by way of the wording. Without saying 'in length and in width,' because the word 'or' is taken in the sense of an alternative, there is an offense even if one part is increased. A bed of the proper size, it seems, is of nine spans. It is said, 'By the phrase “four cubits wide,” the phrase “or three cubits across” also fits, because a definitive statement such as “where the proper measure applies” is impossible.' Regarding 'even less than the measure': a hut of even four or five cubits in width, as long as it does not exceed the stated measure in length, is still considered a declared object of the stated measure. For one who makes an undeclared object, there is an offense. A hut that exceeds the measure is itself what causes the offense, because it is said, '...should make a hut exceeding the measure.' The reading is 'post and beam.' By the method of recitation—here, they say, 'it applies even in the Damiḷa language.'

353. Cārabhūmi gocarabhūmi. Na gahitāti na vāritā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kāraṇāya guttibandhanāgāraṃ, akaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ vā dhammagandhikā hatthapādacchindanakā gandhikā”ti likhitaṃ. Dvīhi balibaddehīti heṭṭhimakoṭiyā kira [M 0.0193] vuttato āvijjituṃ na sakkā chinnāvaṭattā, nigamanassāpi atthappakāsanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Pācinanti vatthu adhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tadatthāyāti tacchanatthāya. Paṇṇasālampīti ullittāvalittakuṭimeva paṇṇacchadanaṃ. Teneva “sabhitticchadana”nti vuttaṃ, alittaṃ kira sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Pubbe thokaṃ ṭhapitaṃ puna vaḍḍhetvā. Tasminti dvārabandhane vā vātapāne vā ṭhapite. Paṭhamamevāti ettha pattakāle evāti kira dhammasiritthero. Upatissatthero [V 0.0172] ṭhapitakālevāti kira. Purimena lepassa aghaṭitattā dutiyena vattasīsena katattā ubhinnampi anāpatti. Sace āṇattena kataṃ, “karoti vā kārāpeti vā”ti vacanato āpatti ubhinnaṃ sati attuddesikatāya, asati mūlaṭṭhasseva. Heṭṭhimappamāṇasambhave sati sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭiṃ karoto āpatti dukkaṭena saṅghādisesoti ācariyassa takko.

353. The ground for walking is the ground for roaming. 'Not taken' means 'not forbidden.' In the commentary, it is written: 'For the purpose of inflicting punishment, a guarded prison; or a place where punishment is not inflicted. Things such as executioner's blocks where hands and feet are cut are called dhammagandhikā.' Regarding 'with two bullocks': it is said that from the stated lower limit, it is not possible to turn, because of there being a steep bank. It should be understood that this is said also for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the market-town. 'Pācinan' means site, foundation. 'Tadatthāya' means for the purpose of planing. Regarding 'even a leaf-hut': it is a hut plastered inside and out that has a leaf-roof. For that very reason, it is called 'with walls and roof'. It is said that if, having previously placed a small amount of clay and then increased it, the hut is left unplastered, it is entirely allowable. Regarding 'on that': when it is placed either on the doorframe or on the window. Regarding 'at the very first': the Elder Dhammasiri, it is said, says it means 'at the appropriate time'. The Elder Upatissa, it is said, says it means 'at the very time of placing'. Because the first plastering did not join, and because it was done by the second with a roller-head, there is no offense for both of them. If it is done by one who was commanded, according to the text 'one does it or causes it to be done,' there is an offense for both if there is personal designation; if there is not, there is an offense for the originator only. When the lower measurement is possible, for one who makes a hut entirely of clay, the offense is a Saṅghādisesa together with a Dukkaṭa; this is the teacher's reasoning.

354. Chattiṃsa catukkāni nāma adesitavatthukacatukkaṃ desitavatthukacatukkaṃ pamāṇātikkantacatukkaṃ pamāṇikacatukkaṃ adesitavatthukapamāṇātikkantacatukkaṃ desitavatthukapamāṇikacatukkanti cha catukkāni, evaṃ samādisativārādīsupi pañcasūti chattiṃsa. Āpattibhedadassanatthanti ettha yasmā “sārambhe ce, bhikkhu, vatthusmiṃ aparikkamane…pe… saṅghādiseso”ti mātikāyaṃ avisesena vuttattā sārambhaaparikkamanepi saṅghādisesovāti micchāgāhavivajjanatthaṃ āpattibhedo dassito, tasmā vuttānīti adhippāyo. Vibhaṅge evaṃ avatvā kimatthaṃ mātikāyaṃ dukkaṭavatthu vuttanti ce? Bhikkhū abhinetabbā vatthudesanāya, tehi bhikkhūhi vatthu desetabbaṃ. Kīdisaṃ? Anārambhaṃ saparikkamanaṃ, netaraṃ, itarasmiṃ “sārambhe ce bhikkhu vatthusmiṃ aparikkamane”ti evaṃ ānisaṃsavasena āgatattā vuttaṃ. Yasmā vatthu nāma atthi sārambhaṃ, atthi anārambhaṃ, atthi saparikkamanaṃ, atthi aparikkamanaṃ, atthi sārambhaṃ saparikkamanaṃ, atthi sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ, atthi anārambhaṃ saparikkamanaṃ, atthi anārambhaṃ aparikkamananti bahuvidhattā vatthu desetabbaṃ anārambhaṃ saparikkamanaṃ, netaranti vuttaṃ hoti. Kimatthikā panesā desanāti ce? Garukāpattipaññāpanahetuparivajjanupāyatthā. Vatthudesanāya hi garukāpattipaññāpanahetuttā akataviññatti gihīnaṃ pīḷājananena attadukkhaparadukkhahetubhūto ca sārambhabhāvoti ete vatthudesanāpadesena upāyena parivajjitā honti. Na hi bhikkhu akappiyakuṭikaraṇatthaṃ gihīnaṃ [M 0.0194] vā pīḷānimittaṃ sārambhavatthu. Kuṭikaraṇatthaṃ vā vatthuṃ desentīti paṭhamameva sādhitametaṃ. Vomissakāpattiyoti dukkaṭasaṅghādisesamissakāpattiyo.

354. The thirty-six fourfold categories are: the fourfold category of the unindicated site, the fourfold category of the indicated site, the fourfold category of exceeding the measure, the fourfold category of the proper measure, the fourfold category of the unindicated site exceeding the measure, and the fourfold category of the indicated site of the proper measure—thus, there are six fourfold categories. Similarly, this should be understood in the five sections beginning with the samādhi section; thus, there are thirty-six. Herein, regarding 'for the purpose of showing the distinction of offenses': because it is stated generally in the Mātikā, 'If, O bhikkhu, on a site with hazards, without a surrounding cleared area... it is a Saṅghādisesa,' and in order to abandon the wrong view that a Saṅghādisesa offense occurs even in the case of a site with hazards and without a surrounding cleared area, the distinction of offenses is shown. Therefore, they are stated—this is the intention. If it is asked, 'Why, without stating it thus in the Vibhaṅga, is the basis for a dukkaṭa offense mentioned in the Mātikā?' Bhikkhus are to be brought to indicate the site; by those bhikkhus, the site is to be indicated. What kind? A site without hazards and with a surrounding cleared area, not the other kind. Regarding the other kind, it is stated, 'If, O bhikkhu, on a site with hazards, without a surrounding cleared area...' because this is mentioned by way of its benefit. Because a site is of many kinds—there is one with hazards, one without hazards, one with a surrounding cleared area, one without a surrounding cleared area, one with hazards and with a surrounding cleared area, one with hazards and without a surrounding cleared area, one without hazards and with a surrounding cleared area, and one without hazards and without a surrounding cleared area—due to this multiplicity, it is said that the site to be indicated is one without hazards and with a surrounding cleared area, not the other kind. If it is asked, 'But what is the purpose of this indication?' It is for the purpose of providing a means to avoid the cause for the laying down of a grave offense. Indeed, by the instruction on indicating a site, these things are skillfully avoided: not making a request, which is a cause for the laying down of a grave offense; causing affliction to householders; and the state of having hazards, which is a cause of suffering for oneself and for others. For bhikkhus do not indicate a site for the purpose of making an improper hut, nor do they indicate a hazardous site, which is a cause of affliction for householders, for the purpose of making a hut. This is established from the very beginning. Regarding 'mixed offenses,' these are offenses that are a mixture of dukkaṭa and saṅghādisesa.

355. Tattha “dvīhi saṅghādisesehī”ti vattabbe “dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesenā”ti vibhattibyattayena, vacanabyattayena ca vuttaṃ. “Āpatti dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesāna”ntipi pāṭho.

355. Here, where it should be said ‘dvīhi saṅghādisesehī,’ it is said ‘dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesena’ due to a change of case and of number. There is also the reading, ‘āpatti dvinnaṃ saṅghādisesānaṃ’.

364. Na ghaṭayati chadanalepābhāvato, anāpatti, taṃ parato sādhiyati. Chadanameva sandhāya ullittāvalittatā vuttāti. “Kukkuṭacchikagehaṃ vaṭṭatīti vatvā puna chadanaṃ daṇḍakehītiādinā nayena taṃ dassentehi tiṇapaṇṇacchadanākuṭikāva vuttā. Tattha chadanaṃ daṇḍakehi [V 0.0173] dīghato tiriyañca jālaṃ viya bandhitvā tiṇehi vā paṇṇehi vā chādetuṃ ullittādibhāvo chadanameva sandhāya vuttoti yuttamidaṃ. Tasmā mattikāmayaṃ bhittiṃ vaḍḍhāpetvā upari ullittaṃ vā avalittaṃ vā ubhayaṃ vā bhittiyā ghaṭitaṃ karontassa āpatti eva vināpi bhittilepenā”ti likhitaṃ. “‘So ca chadanameva sandhāyā’ti padhānavasena vuttaṃ, na heṭṭhābhāgaṃ paṭikkhitta”nti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Etthāti tiṇakuṭikāya. Yathāsamādiṭṭhāyāti yathāvuttappakāranti adhippāyo. “Āpatti kārukānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dukkaṭāna”ntiādimhi so suṇātichakkampi labbhati. Ubhayattha samādiṭṭhattā āṇāpakassa anāpatti. Āṇattassa yathā samādiṭṭhaṃ āṇāpakena, tathā akaraṇapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ. Sace “ahampettha vasāmī”ti attuddesampi karoti, saṅghādisesova. “Kuṭiṃ karothā”ti avisesena vuttaṭṭhāne pana āṇāpakassāpi saṅghādiseso acittakattā sikkhāpadassa.

364. It does not apply due to the absence of plastering the roof; there is no offense. This is established by what follows. It is said that the mention of plastering and whitewashing refers only to the thatching. Having said, "A chicken-coop-like dwelling is permissible," and then showing it in the manner of "thatching with sticks," etc., a hut thatched with grass or leaves is described. There, the act of thatching, by binding sticks lengthwise and crosswise like a net and covering them with grass or leaves, and the state of being plastered, etc., are said to refer only to the thatching. Thus, this is appropriate. Therefore, it is written: "For one who, having built up a clay wall, plasters inside, outside, or both on the upper part connected to the wall, there is indeed an offense, even without plastering the wall itself." They say: "'That refers only to the thatching,' which is stated as the main point, not rejecting the lower part." This should be investigated. Here, it refers to a grass hut. "As specified" means in the manner described. In the phrase "An offense of three dukkaṭas for the workers," etc., the reading 'so suṇāti chakkaṃ' is also found. Because it was properly specified for both parties, the one who gives the order incurs no offense. For the one who receives the order, if he does not carry it out as instructed by the order-giver, it is a dukkaṭa. If he also acts with the intention, "I will reside here," it is a saṅghādisesa. However, in a case where the instruction is given generally, such as "Build a hut," the order-giver also incurs a saṅghādisesa because the training rule is one that does not depend on intention.

Ahañca vasissāmīti ettha parassa yassa kassaci uddiṭṭhassa abhāvā āpatti eva “karontassa vā”ti niyamitattā, anāpatti avibhattattā. “Idha paññattijānanamattameva citta”nti ca likhitaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana ahañca vasissāmīti ettha yo “mayhaṃ vāsāgārañca bhavissatī”ti icchati, tassāpatti. Yo pana uposathāgāraṃ icchati, tassa anāpatti, tasmā “ubhayaṃ sametī”ti vatvā ca “vinayavinicchaye āgate garuke ṭhātabba”nti vacanato mahāpaccarivādato itaro pacchā vattabboti ce? Na, balavattā[M 0.0195]. “Vāsāgāraṃ ṭhapetvā sabbattha, anāpattī”ti vacanato, bhojanasālādīnampi atthāya iminā katattā saṅkarā jātā. Yathā – dve tayo “ekato vasissāmā”ti karonti, rakkhati tāvāti ettha viya. “Idaṃ ṭhānaṃ vāsāgāraṃ bhavissati, idaṃ uposathāgāra”nti vibhajitvā katepi āpatti eva. Dvīsu mahāpaccarivādo balavā, tasmā “pacchā vutto”tiādinā atīva papañcitaṃ. Kiṃ tena. “Attanā vippakataṃ attanā ca parehi ca pariyosāpetī”tiādinā nayena aparānipi catukkāni yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā dassetabbāni, leṇādīsu kiñcāpi saṅghādisesena anāpatti, akataviññattiyā sati tappaccayā āpatti eva.

Herein, regarding 'And I will reside,' since there is no other designated person, there is indeed an offense due to the fixed meaning of 'or for the one who is doing it.' There is no offense due to its unassigned nature. And it is written: 'Here, the intention is merely the knowing of the regulation.' However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, regarding 'And I will reside,' for the monk who desires, 'There will also be a dwelling place for me,' for him there is an offense. But for the monk who desires it to be an Uposatha hall, for him there is no offense. Therefore, having said, 'Both are reconciled,' and because of the saying, 'When it comes to a Vinaya decision, one should stand on the weighty opinion,' should it be said that the other tradition, apart from the Mahāpaccarī, should be stated later? No, because of its strength. Due to the saying, 'Except for a dwelling place, there is no offense in all cases,' confusion has arisen because this was also done for the purpose of dining halls and so on. For example, when two or three monks act, saying, 'We will reside together,' it is just as in the case of 'he guards it for now.' Even when it is done after having divided it, saying, 'This place will be a dwelling place, this an Uposatha hall,' there is indeed an offense. Among the two, the Mahāpaccarī tradition is the stronger one. Therefore, it is excessively elaborated with 'it was said later,' and so on. What is the use of that? By the method beginning with, 'A hut left unfinished by oneself, one finishes by oneself and with others,' the other fourfold categories should also be shown, having applied them as is possible. In caves and so on, although there is no Saṅghādisesa offense, if there is an unmade request, due to that cause, there is indeed an offense.

Kuṭikārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the construction of huts is concluded.

7. Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Construction of a Dwelling

366. Sattame [V 0.0174] vā-saddo avadhāraṇatthoti veditabbo.

366. In the seventh, the word 'vā' should be understood as having the meaning of emphasis.

Vihārakārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the construction of a dwelling is concluded.

8. Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Malice

380. Sāvakena pattabbanti pakatisāvakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na aggasāvakaṃ. Yathūpanissayayathāpuggalavasena “tisso vijjā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kenaci sāvakena tisso vijjā, kenaci catasso paṭisambhidā, kenaci cha abhiññā, kenaci kevalo navalokuttaradhammoti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ yathāsambhavaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

380. The statement, “attainable by a disciple,” is said with reference to an ordinary disciple, not a chief disciple. The statement beginning with “the three kinds of knowledge” is said according to the supporting conditions and the individuals. It should be understood that by some disciple, the three kinds of knowledge are to be attained; by some, the four analytical knowledges; by some, the six higher knowledges; and by some, only the nine supramundane states are to be attained. Thus, it is said separately for each, according to what is possible.

382. “Ye te bhikkhū suttantikā”tiādivacanato dharamānepi bhagavati piṭakattayaparicchedo atthīti siddhaṃ. Dhammakathikāti ābhidhammikā ratiyā acchissantītiādi āyasmato dabbassa nesaṃ tiracchānakathāya ratiniyojanaṃ viya dissati, na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Suttantikādisaṃsaggato tesaṃ suttantikādīnaṃ phāsuvihārantarāyaṃ, tesampi tiracchānakathāratiyā abhāvena anabhirativāsaṃ, tato nesaṃ sāmaññā cāvanañca [M 0.0196] parivajjanto evaṃ cintesīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Nimmitānaṃ dhammatāti sāvakehi nimmitānaṃyeva, na buddhehī”ti vadanti. “Sādhakatamaṃ karaṇa”nti evaṃ vutte karaṇattheyeva tatiyāvibhattīti attho.

382. From the statement beginning, “Those monks who are experts in the Suttas,” it is established that the division of the three Piṭakas existed even while the Blessed One was living. Regarding the term ‘Dhamma-speakers,’ the Venerable Dabba's action appears like an encouragement for those monks who are experts in Abhidhamma to delight in animal talk, but it should not be regarded in that way. It should be understood that because of association with the Suttantika teachers and others, it causes an obstacle to their comfortable dwelling, and for those monks as well, due to the absence of delight in animal talk, it causes them to dwell in discontent; therefore, wishing to prevent their falling away from the state of a monk, he thought thus. They say, “The nature of created things” means those created by disciples only, not by Buddhas. When it is said, “The most effective means is the instrument,” the meaning is that the third case ending occurs only in the sense of the instrument.

383-4. Yanti yena. “Kattāti kattā, na kattā”ti likhitaṃ. “Bhariyaṃ viya maṃ ajjhācaratī”ti vadantiyā balavatī codanā. Tena hīti ettha yathā chupanamatte vippaṭisārīvatthusmiṃ kāyasaṃsaggarāgasambhavā apucchitvā eva saṅghādisesaṃ paññāpesi, tatheva pubbevassā dussīlabhāvaṃ ñatvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yadi tāva bhūtāya paṭiññāya nāsitā, thero kārako hoti. Atha abhūtāya, bhagavatā “nāsethā”ti na vattabbaṃ, vuttañca, tasmā vuttaṃ “yadi tāva paṭiññāya nāsitā, thero kārako hotī”ti.

Yanti means yena (by which). It is written: “Kattā means a doer; na kattā means not a doer.” Of the bhikkhunī who says, “He transgresses against me as if I were his wife,” the accusation is strong. In the phrase tena hi, just as in the case of regret over mere touching, because of the possibility of lust arising from physical contact, he laid down the Saṅghādisesa rule without even asking; in that same way, it should be understood that this was said because he knew of her immoral character even beforehand. If, firstly, she is expelled by means of a true confession, the Elder is the doer. Or if by an untrue one, the Blessed One should not have said, “Expel her,” and yet he did say it. Therefore, it was said, “If she is expelled by means of a confession, the Elder is the doer.”

Atha appaṭiññāyāti “ayyenamhi dūsitā”ti imaṃ paṭiññaṃ vinā eva tassā pakatidussīlabhāvaṃ sandhāya nāsitā, thero akārako hoti. Abhayagirivāsinopi attano suttaṃ vatvā “tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako”ti vadanti, kasmā? Dukkaṭaṃ musāvādapaccayā liṅganāsanāya [V 0.0175] anāsetabbattā. Pārājikasseva hi liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbā. “Nāsethā”ti ca vuttattā pārājikāva jātā, sā kiṃ sandhāya, tato thero kārako āpajjati. “Sakāya paṭiññāya nāsethā”ti vutte pana apārājikāpi attano vacanena nāsetabbā jātāti adhippāyo. Mahāvihāravāsinopi attano suttaṃ vatvā “tumhākaṃ vāde thero kārako”ti ca vadanti. Kasmā? “Sakāya paṭiññāya nāsethā”ti hi vutte paṭiññāya bhūtatā āpajjati “nāsethā”ti vacanato. Bhūtāyeva hi paṭiññāya nāsetabbā hoti, nābhūtāyāti adhippāyo. Purimanayeti dukkaṭavāde. Purimo yuttivasena pavatto, pacchimo pāḷivacanavasena pavattoti veditabbo.

Herein, regarding ‘without a confession’: if she is expelled based on her naturally immoral character, without this confession, ‘I have been corrupted by the venerable sir,’ then the elder is not culpable. The Abhayagirivāsins also, citing their own text, say, ‘According to your view, the elder is culpable.’ Why? Because a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to false speech, and because she is unfit to be expelled by the destruction of the characteristic. Indeed, only one who has committed a pārājika should be expelled by the destruction of the characteristic. And because it was said, ‘Expel her,’ she has become a pārājika offender. On what grounds? Therefore, the elder becomes culpable. But when it is said, ‘Expel her based on her own confession,’ then even one who has not committed a pārājika becomes one who should be expelled by her own words—this is the meaning. The Mahāvihāravāsins also, citing their own text, say, ‘According to your view, the elder is culpable.’ Why? For when it is said, ‘Expel her based on her own confession,’ the truthfulness of the confession is established by the command, ‘Expel her.’ For she should be expelled by a truthful confession only, not by a false one—this is the meaning. Regarding the earlier method: this is in the view that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. The earlier view proceeds by way of logic; the later view proceeds by way of a scriptural statement—this should be understood.

385-6. Pītisukhehīti ettha “sukhenā”ti vattabbe pītiggahaṇaṃ tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ, kāyikañca apanetuṃ sampayuttapītiyā vuttaṃ. Sace cuditakavasena kataṃ amūlakaṃ nāma, “anajjhāpannaṃ akata”nti vadeyya, ime karissanti, tasmā “tādisaṃ diṭṭhasaññī hutvā codetī”ti pāṭho[M 0.0197]. “Etena nayena sutamutaparisaṅkitānipi vitthārato veditabbānī”ti pāṭho. “Catunnaṃ aññatarenā”ti pātimokkhuddese eva āgate gahetvā vuttaṃ, itaresaṃ aññatarenāpi anuddhaṃsentassa saṅghādisesovāti no takkoti ācariyo. Bhikkhubhāvā hi cāvanasamatthato. “Samīpe ṭhatvā”ti vacanato parammukhā codentassa, codāpentassa vā sīsaṃ na eti. Diṭṭhañce sutena parisaṅkitena codeti codāpeti, sutaparisaṅkitaṃ vā diṭṭhādīhi codite vā codāpite vā sīsaṃ eti eva amūlakena coditattā. Vuttañhetaṃ “diṭṭhassa hoti pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto, tañce codeti ‘suto mayā…pe… saṅghādisesassā”ti (pārā. 387). “Asuddho hoti puggalo aññataraṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpanno, tañce asuddhadiṭṭhi samāno anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā cāvanādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Okāsaṃ kārāpetvā cāvanādhippāyo vadeti, anāpattī”ti (pārā. 389) iminā na-samentaṃ viya khāyati, kathaṃ? Diṭṭhassa hoti pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjanto nāma asuddho puggalo hoti, “aññatarasmiṃ asuddhadiṭṭhi samāno tañce codeti ‘suto mayā pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosī’ti, āpatti vācāya vācāya saṅghādisesassā”ti vacanato purimanayenāpatti. “Cāvanādhippāyo vadeti, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vacanato pacchimanayena saṅghādisesena āpattīti dve pāḷinayā aññamaññaṃ viruddhā viya dissanti, na ca viruddhaṃ buddhā kathayanti, tasmā ettha yutti pariyesitabbā. Aṭṭhakathācariyā tāvāhu “samūlakena vā saññāsamūlakena vā codentassa anāpatti, amūlakena vā pana saññāamūlakena vā codentassa āpattī”ti. Tassattho – dassanasavanaparisaṅkanamūlena samūlakena vā tadabhāvena amūlakenāpi [V 0.0176] saññāsamūlakena vā codentassa anāpatti, dassanādimūlābhāvena amūlakena vā tabbhāvena samūlakenāpi saññāamūlakena vā codentassa āpatti, tasmā diṭṭhassa hoti.

385-6. In the text “pītisukhehi,” although “sukhena” should have been said, the inclusion of “pīti” is stated by means of associated joy in order to exclude the happiness of the third jhāna and bodily happiness. If, by the power of the accused person, something is made to be baseless, he might say, “It was not fallen into, not done.” Others might then do so. Therefore, there is the text: “Having such a perception of what was seen, he accuses.” There is also the text: “By this method, what is heard, sensed, and suspected should also be known in detail.” “By any one of the four” is stated by taking only those Pārājika offenses that come in the Pātimokkha recitation. The teacher says: It is not our reasoning that for the other offenses, for one who accuses by any one of them, it is a Saṅghādisesa offense. For it is because of the ability to make one fall from the state of a monk. Because of the text “standing nearby,” for one who accuses or causes another to accuse in the person's absence, it does not reach the ‘head’ of the offense. If one accuses or causes another to accuse concerning what was seen by means of what was heard or suspected, or if one accuses or causes another to accuse concerning what was heard and suspected by means of what was seen, etc., it certainly reaches the ‘head’ of the offense, because of accusing baselessly. For this has been said: “He sees someone committing a Pārājika offense, and he accuses that person, saying ‘I have heard… (and so on)... a Saṅghādisesa offense.’” This appears not to reconcile with the following: “An impure person has committed one of the Pārājika offenses. If, being of impure view, he speaks with the intention of expulsion without having an opportunity made, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. If he speaks with the intention of expulsion after having an opportunity made, there is no offense.” How so? “One who sees another committing a Pārājika offense” is an impure person. Because of the text, “Being of impure view regarding someone, if he accuses that person, saying ‘I have heard you have committed a Pārājika offense,’ there is a Saṅghādisesa offense for every single word,” according to the former method, there is an offense. Because of the text, “If he speaks with the intention of expulsion, it is a Dukkaṭa offense,” according to the latter method, there is a Dukkaṭa offense. Thus, the two textual methods appear to contradict each other. But the Buddhas do not speak contradictions. Therefore, the proper reasoning must be sought here. The commentary teachers say: “For one who accuses with a basis or with a perceived basis, there is no offense. But for one who accuses without a basis or with a perceived lack of basis, there is an offense.” Its meaning is this: For one who accuses with a basis rooted in seeing, hearing, or suspicion, or, in the absence of that, even if baseless, with a perceived basis, there is no offense. For one who accuses without a basis rooted in seeing, etc., or, even with such a basis, with a perceived lack of basis, there is an offense. Therefore, “of one who has seen...”

Pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpajjantotiādimhi dassanamūlena samūlakenāpi “suto mayā”ti vacanato saññāamūlakena vā codeti, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Tadatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ “diṭṭhe vematiko”tiādi vārā vuttāti veditabbā.

In the passage beginning with 'one who commits a Pārājika offense,' if one accuses, even with a basis rooted in seeing, yet baselessly by way of perception due to the statement 'I have heard,' there is a Saṅghādisesa offense. To make that meaning clear, it should be understood that the sections beginning with 'one who is doubtful about what was seen,' and so on, are stated.

Asuddho [M 0.0198] hoti puggalobhiādimhi pana samūlakena, saññāsamūlakena vā coditattā anāpattīti. Evamevaṃ pana tadatthadīpanatthaṃ te vārā vuttā. Tattha hi “adiṭṭhassa hotī”tiādivārā amūlakena codentassa āpatti hotīti dassanatthaṃ vuttā. “Diṭṭhe vematiko”tiādinā saññāamūlakena codentassa āpatti hotīti dassanatthaṃ vuttā. Aññathā “diṭṭhassa hoti, diṭṭhe vematiko”tiādivārā nibbisesā bhaveyyuṃ. Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ-yathā asuddhaṃ puggalaṃ anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā codentassa dukkaṭaṃ, akkosādhippāyassa ca omasavādena dukkaṭassa, tathā asuddhadiṭṭhikopi asuddhaṃ asuddhadiṭṭhi amūlakena codeti, āpatti. Samūlakena vā codeti, anāpattīti taṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ yathā “anāpatti suddhe asuddhadiṭṭhissa asuddhe asuddhadiṭṭhissā”ti iminā saṃsandati, tathā gahetabbaṃ. Aññathā yutti pariyesitabbā.

However, in the passage beginning with 'an impure person,' because one accuses with a basis or with a perceived basis, there is no offense. Similarly, those sections were stated to explain that meaning. For therein, the sections beginning with 'for one who has not seen' were stated to show that an offense is incurred by one who accuses without basis. The sections beginning with 'one who is doubtful about what was seen' were stated to show that an offense is incurred by one who accuses baselessly by way of perception. Otherwise, the sections 'for one who has seen, one who is doubtful about what was seen,' and so on, would be without distinction. Herein, this is the conclusion: just as for one who accuses an impure person without having granted an opportunity there is a Dukkaṭa offense, and for one with the intention to insult there is a Dukkaṭa offense from abusive speech, so too, if a monk of impure view, being of impure view, accuses an impure person without basis, there is an offense. But if one accuses with a basis, there is no offense. This conclusion should be understood in such a way that it aligns with the statement, 'There is no offense for one of impure view towards a pure person, nor for one of impure view towards an impure person.' Otherwise, the proper reasoning should be sought.

Sīlasampannoti ettha “dussīlassa vacanaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Bhikkhunī hi bhikkhumhi anissarā, tasmā ukkaṭṭhanaye vidhiṃ sandhāya therena vuttaṃ. Dutiyattherena bhikkhunī ajānitvāpi codeti, sikkhamānādayo vā codenti, tesaṃ sutvā bhikkhū eva vicāretvā tassa paṭiññāya kārenti. Ko ettha dosoti idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatiyena titthiyānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvāpi bhikkhū eva vicārenti, tasmā na koci na labhatīti evaṃ sabbaṃ sametīti apare”ti vuttaṃ. Tiṃsāni tiṃsavantāni. Anuyogoti paṭivacanaṃ. Ehitīti āgamissati. Diṭṭhasantānenāti diṭṭhanayena, diṭṭhavidhānenāti adhippāyo. Patiṭṭhāyāti patiṭṭhaṃ labhitvā. Ṭhāneti lajjiṭṭhāne.

Regarding 'endowed with virtue': here, 'the words of an immoral person are not to be taken as a measure.' For a bhikkhunī is not sovereign over a bhikkhu; therefore, the elder spoke with reference to the procedure in the strict method. By the second elder, it is said with reference to this: 'Even if a bhikkhunī accuses without knowing, or sikkhamānās and others accuse, having heard them, the bhikkhus themselves investigate and make him act according to his acknowledgement. What fault is there in this?' By the third elder, it is said: 'Even upon hearing the words of the sectarians, the bhikkhus themselves investigate. Therefore, no fault whatsoever is found—thus, the whole matter is reconciled,' so others say. Tiṃsāni means 'possessing thirty.' Anuyoga means a reply. Ehiti means 'he will come.' Diṭṭhasantānena means by the seen method, by the seen procedure—this is the meaning. Patiṭṭhāya means having obtained a footing. Ṭhāne means in a place of shame.

Gāhanti “ahaṃ codessāmī”ti attādānaggahaṇaṃ. Cetanāti attādānaggahaṇacetanā. Vohāroti ito, etto ca ñatvā pakāsanaṃ. Paṇṇattīti nāmapaññatti. Yā vacīghosārammaṇassa sotadvārappavattaviññāṇasantānassa anantaraṃ uppannena upaladdhapubbasaṅketena manodvāraviññāṇena [V 0.0177] viññāyati, yassā viññātattā tadattho paramattho vā aparamattho vā tatiyavāraṃ uppannena manoviññāṇena viññāyatīti nāmādīhi chahi byañjanehi pāḷiyā pakāsitā, sā “vijjamānapaññatti avijjamānapaññattī”tiādinā chadhā ācariyehi dassitā. Tabbhāgiyabhāvo atabbhāgiyabhāvo ca nipphannadhammasseva yujjati, na paññattiyā adhikaraṇīyavatthuttā[M 0.0199], adhikaraṇe pavattattā ca adhikaraṇo mañcaṭṭhe mañcopacāro viyāti ca. “Pariyāyenāti amūlakā nāmapaññatti natthi. Pariyāyamattaṃ, sabhāvato natthi. Abhidhānamattameva, abhidheyyaṃ natthī”ti ca likhitaṃ. Idhevāti imasmiṃ eva sikkhāpade. Na sabbatthāti vivādādhikaraṇādīsu. Kasmā? Na hītiādi. Vivādādhikaraṇādīnamatthitā viya amūlakaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ natthīti. Pubbe vuttasamathehīti “yaṃ adhikicca samathā vattantī”ti vuttasamathehīti adhippāyo. Apica sabhāvato natthīti appaṭiladdhasabhāvattā vuttaṃ. Anuppannaṃ viya viññāṇādi. Na hi vivādādīnaṃ paṇṇatti adhikaraṇaṭṭhoti paṇṇattiṃ adhikicca samathā na pavattanti, tasmā na tassā adhikaraṇīyatāti na vivādādīnaṃ paṇṇatti adhikaraṇaṭṭhoti adhippāyo. Hoti cettha –

‘They grasp’ (gāhanti) means the grasping of self-assertion, thinking, ‘I will accuse.’ ‘Intention’ (cetanā) means the intention of grasping with self-assertion. ‘Expression’ (vohāra) refers to knowing and declaring from here and there. ‘Designation’ (paññatti) is name-designation. That which is known by the mind-door consciousness, arising immediately after the continuum of ear-door consciousness that has the sound of speech as its object, and with a previously acquired convention; and because of its being known, its meaning, whether ultimate or non-ultimate, is known by the mind-consciousness arising for the third time—this is expressed in the Pāli by six terms beginning with ‘name,’ and is shown by the teachers in six ways, such as ‘existent designation, non-existent designation,’ and so on.
