Tato paraṃ khettadhaññakaraṇaārāmavihāresu pana parikkhittāparikkhitta-padaṃ puna uddhaṭaṃ satthavibhaṅgena adhikārassa pacchinnattā. “Nānāgabbhā”tiādivacanaṃ pana asambhavato khettadhaññakaraṇaārāmesu na uddhaṭaṃ. Vihāre sambhavantampi tattha pacchinnattā na uddhaṭaṃ. Kulaṃ vuccati sāmiko, tasmā “ekakulassa nānākulassā”ti iminā gāmādīnaṃ cuddasannaṃ cīvaranikkhepaṭṭhānānaṃ sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Ajjhokāsassa pana asambhavato na vuttaṃ. Yasmā panettha ekakulassa, nānākulassa ca aparikkhittesu gāmādīsu parihāraviseso kiñcāpi natthi, parikkhittesu pana atthi, tasmā ekanānākulaggahaṇaṃ, ekanānūpacāraggahaṇañca sātthakanti veditabbaṃ. Tatthapi ayaṃ viseso – satthe, rukkhamūle ca kulabhedatova bhedo, nopacārabhedato. Ajjhokāse upacārabhedato ca, so pana pāḷiyaṃ na dassitoti. “Taṃ pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvāti vacanato ākāsepi aḍḍhateyyaratanappamāṇe doso natthī”ti vadanti.

477-8. Here, in the phrase 'for the purpose of establishing the characteristic of non-separation,' the characteristic of non-separation is established by the statement beginning with 'Having placed the robe within the village, one should dwell within the village.' The characteristic of separation should be understood by the opposite method. However, in the text beginning with 'A village is a single common-ground,' setting aside a caravan, the root of a tree, and an open space, in the remaining cases, the state of being a single common-ground or different common-grounds should be understood by way of being enclosed or unenclosed. Because a caravan is of two kinds, encamped and unencamped. Among these, an unencamped caravan, whether of one family or of different families, is only unenclosed. An encamped one may be enclosed or may be unenclosed. Therefore, in that case, without indicating it by way of enclosure and so on, it is stated by way of the internal measure. Likewise in an open space. At the root of a tree, it is by way of the shade. Otherwise, the statement beginning with 'A caravan is a single common-ground, a different common-ground' would be a contradiction to the summary statement, because it is not shown in the Analysis. Therefore, for a caravan, seven abbhantaras in front and behind, and one abbhantara on the sides—this is the single common-ground. Beyond that is a different common-ground. Similarly, for the root of a tree, where the shade spreads at midday, this is the single common-ground. The other is a different common-ground. Why? Because there, the enclosure is without measure; the shade itself is the measure. For an open space, it is as stated in the Pāḷi. It is written: 'For a caravan and so on, the state of being a single common-ground is by way of being the property of a single family.' Therefore, thinking that in a dwelling and in a residence the aforementioned delimitation is as in the commentaries and so on, it is summarized. After that, however, in the cases of a field, a threshing floor, a park, and a monastery, the terms 'enclosed' and 'unenclosed' are brought up again. Since the topic was concluded with the analysis of the caravan, the statement beginning with 'different rooms,' however, is not brought up in the cases of a field, a threshing floor, and a park, as it is impossible. In a monastery, although it is possible, it is not brought up because it has already been determined in that context. The owner is called 'family.' Therefore, by this phrase 'of one family, of different families,' it indicates the state of being common or not common for the fourteen robe-placing locations beginning with a village. For an open space, however, it is not stated because it is impossible. Because here, although in unenclosed villages and so on belonging to one family or different families there is no special allowance, in enclosed ones there is. Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of 'one family' and 'different families,' and the inclusion of 'single common-ground' and 'different common-grounds' is meaningful. Even there, this is the distinction: in a caravan and at the root of a tree, the distinction is only from the difference of family, not from the difference of common-ground. In an open space, it is also from the difference of common-ground, but that distinction is not shown in the Pāḷi. Because of the statement 'having exceeded that measure,' they say that even in the space above, at a measure of two and a half ratanas, there is no fault.

479. “Sabhā”ti itthiliṅgaṃ. “Sabhāya”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, tena vuttaṃ “liṅgabyattanayenā”ti. Napuṃsakaliṅgadassanatthaṃ kira “sabhāya”nti paccattavasena niddiṭṭhaṃ, tassa anupayogattā [V 0.0207] “dvāramūla”ntipi. Attano nikkhittaṭṭhāne anikkhittattā vīthihatthapāso na rakkhati, yasmiṃ ghare cīvaraṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ ghare vatthabbaṃ. “Sabhāye vā vatthabbaṃ dvāramūle vā, hatthapāsā [M 0.0232] vā na vijahitabba”nti hi vuttaṃ. “Hatthapāseyeva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapetabba”nti niyamitattā jānituṃ na sakkāti ce? Antoghare na sakkā, tathā tathā vuttattā, tasmā “yutti pamāṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Ayamattho aṭṭhakathāyampi pakāsito, punapi khuddakagāme sabbasādhāraṇagāmadvāravasena. Sace tassa dvāradvayaṃ hoti, majjhe ca gharasabhāyaṃ, yatthicchati, tattha vasitabba”nti.

479. The word “sabhā” is feminine. The word “sabhāyaṃ” is neuter; therefore, it is said, “by way of distinction in gender.” To show the neuter gender, “sabhāyaṃ” is indeed pointed out by way of the nominative case. As that is not applicable, “at the foot of the gate” is also mentioned. Because it is not placed in its own designated place, the hand's reach of the street does not afford protection. In whichever house the robe is placed, in that house one should reside. For it has been said: “One should reside either in the assembly hall or at the foot of the gate, or the hand's reach should not be abandoned.” If one were to say, “Is it not possible to know, because it is determined that ‘dawn should be made to arise only within hand's reach’?” It is not possible inside a house, because it has been stated for various reasons. Therefore, it is said, “Reason is the standard.” This meaning is also explained in the commentary. And again: “In a small village, by way of a village gate common to all, if it has two gates, and in the middle of the house and in the middle of the assembly hall, one may reside wherever one wishes.”

480-1. Yāni nivesanādīni gāmasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchanti, tāni nivesanādīnīti adhippetāni. Ajjhokāse aparisaṅkitampi cīvaraṃ atirekasattabbhantare nikkhittaṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti, ettha antosīmatā na rakkhati, satthe pana rakkhati. “Nadīparihāro ca labbhatī”ti vacanato udakukkhepasīmāyaṃ parihāro labbhatīti siddhaṃ. Sāmantavihāro ce ekasīmo, cīvaraṃ na nissaggiyaṃ.

480-1. Those dwellings and the like that do not come under the designation of 'village' are intended by 'dwellings, etc.' In an open space, even if the place is not considered dangerous, a robe placed beyond seven abbhantaras becomes subject to forfeiture. Here, being inside the boundary does not afford protection, but in a caravan, it does. From the statement, “And a river allowance is obtained,” it is established that in a water-throwing boundary, an allowance is obtained. If a nearby monastery has a single boundary, the robe is not subject to forfeiture.

Idāni –

Now –

“Chinnaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ sāsaṅka-sammato santaruttaraṃ;

Acīvarassānāpatti, paccuddhārādisiddhito”ti. –

The matter of a cut robe, the ascetic practice, a place designated as dangerous, the under-robe and upper-robe, and that there is no offense for one without a robe because of its accomplishment through rescission, etc.—this miscellaneous section should be known.

Idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ, tatthāyaṃ codanāpubbaṅgamo vinicchayo – keci “diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti (mahāva. 348) vacanato “ekaccikā saṅghāṭipi nādhiṭṭhātabbā. Sace adhiṭṭhāti na ruhatī”ti vatvā upasampadāpekkhānampi diguṇameva saṅghāṭiṃ datvā upasampādenti, te iminā suttalesena saññāpetabbā. Bhagavatā hi “chinnakaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ chinnakaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ chinnakaṃ antaravāsaka”nti paṭhamaṃ anuññātaṃ. Tato “aññatarassa bhikkhuno ticīvare kariyamāne sabbaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahoti. Dve chinnakāni ekaṃ acchinnakaṃ nappahoti. Dve acchinnakāni ekaṃ chinnakaṃ nappahotī”ti imasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, anvādhikampi āropetu”nti (mahāva. 360) anuññātaṃ, tasmā ekaccikāpi saṅghāṭi vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Yā chijjamānā nappahoti, tassā kuto diguṇatāti. Aṭṭhakathāyampissa vuttaṃ “anvādhikampi āropetunti āgantukapattampi dātuṃ. Idaṃ pana appahonake āropetabbaṃ. Sace pahoti, āgantukapattaṃ na vaṭṭati, chinditabbamevā”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 360). Kathinaṃ pana chinnakameva vaṭṭati āveṇikalakkhaṇattā[V 0.0208], “chinnakaṃ diguṇaṃ nappahotī”ti vacanābhāvato cāti sanniṭṭhānamettha gantabbaṃ.

This is the miscellaneous section. Herein, this is the decision preceded by an objection: some, based on the statement “a double-layered outer robe,” having said, “Even a single-layered outer robe should not be determined. If one determines it, it is not valid,” give only a double-layered outer robe even to those expecting ordination and then ordain them. They should be made to understand by this brief scriptural passage. Indeed, by the Blessed One it was first allowed, “a cut outer robe, a cut upper robe, a cut inner robe.” Then, in the case where, for a certain monk making the three robes, a robe made entirely of cut pieces was not sufficient, or two cut pieces and one uncut piece were not sufficient, or two uncut pieces and one cut piece were not sufficient, it was allowed: “I allow, monks, to apply even an additional piece.” Therefore, it is established that even a single-layered outer robe is allowable. For a robe that is insufficient when being cut, how can it be double-layered? In its commentary, it is also said: “‘To apply even an additional piece’ means to give an extra patch. But this should be applied in a case of insufficiency. If it is sufficient, an extra patch is not allowable; it must be a cut robe.” However, for the Kathina, only a cut robe is allowable, because of its special characteristic and because of the absence of a statement saying, “a cut, double-layered one is not sufficient.” Thus, this conclusion should be reached here.

Dhutaṅganti [M 0.0233] anupasampannānaṃ tecīvarikadhutaṅgābhāvato ticīvareneva tecīvarikoti. Tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānābhāvato “adhiṭṭhitenevā”ti vattabbaṃ hotūti ce? Na, dhutaṅgabhedena virodhappasaṅgato. Catutthacīvarasādiyanena hi dhutaṅgabhedo, na ticīvaravippavāsena, nāpi atirekacīvarasādiyanena, nāpi atirekacīvaradhāraṇena. Yasmā pana bhikkhūnaṃyeva bhagavatā adhiṭṭhānavasena nava cīvarāni anuññātāni, jātivasena ca vuttāni, na evaṃ anupasampannānaṃ. Tasmā tesaṃ cīvaraniyamābhāvā na taṃ dhutaṅgaṃ anuññātaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ viya, tasmā tassa samādānavidhāne avacanato ca sanniṭṭhānamettha gantabbaṃ.

Regarding the ascetic practice: for the unordained, since they do not have the three-robe ascetic practice, one is a 'three-robe-wearer' simply on account of the three robes. If it were said that for them, due to the absence of determination, it should be stated 'only by what is determined,' this should not be said. Why? Because it would lead to a contradiction with the breaking of the ascetic practice. For the breaking of the ascetic practice occurs by consenting to a fourth robe, not by being separated from the three robes, nor by consenting to an extra robe, nor by wearing an extra robe. Because it was for monks alone that the Blessed One allowed nine robes by way of determination, and they were spoken of by way of type, it was not so for the unordained. Therefore, for them, due to the absence of a regulation on robes, that ascetic practice is not allowed, just as for householders. Therefore, and also because it is not mentioned in the procedure for undertaking it, a conclusion should be reached in this matter.

Sāsaṅkasammatoti kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ sāsaṅkasikkhāpade visuṃ aṅgāni na vuttāni, “sesamettha cīvaravaggassa dutiyasikkhāpade vuttanayena veditabba”nti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, na ca panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha rattivippavāso catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ, idha chārattavippavāso, ayamettha visesoti, tasmā aṅgasāmaññato, sammutisāmaññato ca sāsaṅkasikkhāpadameva vadanti. Idaṃ nippadesaṃ, taṃ sappadesaṃ māsaparamattā. Tattha bahigāmepi gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvā vasitvā pakkamantassa anāpatti, idha na tathā, idha anantare anantare aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ, tattha sattameti ayaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ viseso. Aṅgāni pana cīvaranikkhepaṅgasampattito vipariyāyena, idha vuttanayena ca siddhattā na vuttāni. Tāni kāmaṃ na vuttāni, tathāpi catutthamaṅgaṃ visesitabbaṃ, na pana visesitaṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Idha vuttanissajjanakkamena nissajjetvā āpattidesanato, tatthāpannāpattivimokkhadīpanatthaṃ. Saṃvaccharavippavutthampi rattivippavutthameva, pageva chārattaṃ vippavutthaṃ. Evaṃ santepi tattha yathāvuttaaṅgasampattiyā sati tattha vuttanayeneva nissajjitabbaṃ. Hemante vā gimhe vā nissajjati ce? Idha vuttanayenāpi nissajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti ñāpanatthaṃ catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ na visesitanti no takkoti ācariyo. Māsātikkantampi cīvaraṃ “dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā nissaṭṭhameva. Dvayena ūnamāsaṃ hutvā “dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā māsātikkantanti eke. Tathāpi sace paccāsācīvaraṃ hoti, nissaggiyaṃ “dasāhātikkanta”nti vatvā, mūlacīvaraṃ pana “māsātikkanta”nti vatvā nissajjitabbaṃ.

Regarding `Sāsaṅkasammata`: In the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, in the Sāsaṅka training rule, the factors are not stated separately. It is said, “Herein, the remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the second training rule of the Cīvaravagga,” but this is not actually stated. There, absence for one night is the fourth factor; here, it is an absence for six nights. This is the difference herein. Therefore, due to the similarity of the factors and the similarity of the designation, they call it the Sāsaṅka training rule itself. This one is without specification, while that one has a specification, on account of its limit of one month. There, for one who, even from outside the village, enters the village boundary, dwells, and then departs, there is no offense; here, it is not so. Here, at the very next dawn, it becomes subject to forfeiture; there, on the seventh. This is the difference between these two. As for the factors, they are not stated because they are established in reverse order from the completion of the factors for laying aside the robe, and also by the method stated here. Although those factors are not stated, nevertheless, the fourth factor should be specified, but it is not specified. For what reason? Here, it is because of confessing the offense after forfeiting according to the stated sequence of forfeiture; there, it is for the purpose of showing the release from an offense that has been incurred. Even an absence for a year is just an absence for one night; how much more so an absence for six nights. Even so, when there is the completion of the factors as stated there, it should be forfeited only by the method stated there. The teacher says: It is our reasoning that the fourth factor is not specified in order to make it known that it is allowable to forfeit in the winter or in the summer also by the method stated here. A robe that is over a month old is indeed forfeited by saying, “It is over ten days.” Some say that when it is less than a month, one forfeits by saying, “It is over ten days,” and when it is over a month, by saying, “It is over a month.” Nevertheless, if it is an expected robe, it is to be forfeited by saying, “It is over ten days.” The original robe, however, is to be forfeited by saying, “It is over a month.”

“Santaruttara”nti [M 0.0234] vā “saṅghāṭi”nti vā “cīvara”nti vā kiṃ ticīvaraṃ, udāhu aññampīti[V 0.0209]. Kiñcettha – yadi ticīvarameva paṭisiddhaṃ, pariyāpannavasena acchinnacīvaracchindanadhovāpanaviññattiādivirodho. Atha aññampi, “niṭṭhitacīvarasmi”nti evamādinā virodhoti? Vuccate – na niyamato veditabbaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ gahetabbato. Tathā hi “cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā santaruttarena janapadacārikaṃ pakkamantī”ti (pārā. 471) evamādīsu ticīvarameva. “Na, bhikkhave, santaruttarena gāmo pavisitabbo, santaruttaraparamaṃ tato cīvaraṃ sādhitabba”nti evamādīsu yaṃkiñci, tathā saguṇaṃ katvā saṅghāṭiyo dātabbā, nivāsanaṃ dātabbaṃ, saṅghāṭi dātabbā, handa te, āvuso, saṅghāṭi, dehi me paṭantiādīsu. Vuttañhetaṃ “sabbañhi cīvaraṃ saṅghaṭitaṭṭhena ‘saṅghāṭī’ti vuccatī”ti. Tathā “niṭṭhitacīvarasmi”nti etthāpīti eke. Antosamaye hi yāvadatthaṃ cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ kariyamānaṃ kadā niṭṭhānaṃ gacchissati, tasmā ticīvaramevāti eke. Acīvarassānāpatti paccuddhārādisiddhitoti kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Udositasikkhāpadassa nippayojanabhāvappasaṅgato ticīvaravippavāse tecīvarassa āpattīti eke. Tatthetaṃ vuccati na hoti āpatti paccuddhārādisiddhito. “Anāpatti antoaruṇe paccuddharati, vissajjetī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Aññathā paccuddharantassa, antoaruṇe vissajjentassa ca yāva añño nādhiṭṭhāti, tāva āpattiṃ āpajjati yathāvuttanayena. Aññathā sattabbhantarena vippavāsassāti vippavāsato yathārutaṃyeva sati vippavāse vippavāsato avippavāse sati avippavāsatoti.

When it is said 'santaruttara' or 'saṅghāṭi' or 'cīvara', does this mean the three robes, or also another robe? Herein, if only the three robes are prohibited, then by way of inclusion, there is a contradiction with the training rules concerning robes being snatched away, cutting, having them washed, requesting, and so on. And if it is also another robe, there is a contradiction with such passages as 'when the robe is finished'.

It is said in reply: This is not to be understood as a fixed rule, since it should be taken according to what is possible. For indeed, in such passages as 'having put down the robe, they set out on a journey through the country with an undergarment and an upper robe', it is only the three robes. In such passages as 'Monks, a village is not to be entered with an undergarment and an upper robe; at most an undergarment and an upper robe, from that a robe should be procured', it is any robe. Likewise, in such passages as 'having folded them well, the outer robes should be given', 'the lower robe should be given', 'the outer robe should be given', 'Come, friend, your outer robe', and 'give me the cloth'. For this was said: 'Indeed, any robe, because of being folded together, is called a "saṅghāṭī"'.

Likewise, also in the case of 'when the robe is finished', so say some. For during the robe-period, robes are allowed as much as is needed. If all of that were being made, when would it reach completion? Therefore, it is only the three robes, so say some.

What is meant by 'There is no offense for one without a robe due to the validity of cancellation of determination and so on'? Because it would lead to the Udosita training rule being useless, there is an offense for one who possesses the three robes when separated from them, so say some.

Herein, this is said: there is no offense, because of the validity of cancellation of determination and so on. For it is said: 'There is no offense if one cancels the determination or relinquishes it before dawn'. Otherwise, for one cancelling the determination and for one relinquishing it before dawn, as long as another robe is not determined, one falls into an offense, according to the method stated. Otherwise, regarding 'of separation within seven days', the term vippavāsato (from separation) is to be understood just as it is stated: when there is separation, it is on account of separation; when there is no separation, it is on account of no separation.

Udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.

3. Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Third Kathina Training Rule

497. Nappahotīti lāmakaparicchedaṃ na pāpuṇāti, teneva ticīvarassa muṭṭhipañcakādilāmakaparicchedova tāva vutto. Cīvare paccāsā cīvarapaccāsā. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – taṃ cīvaraṃ pacchā labbhatu vā mā vā, yāva sā paccāsā chijjati, tāva idaṃ mūlacīvaraṃ ṭhapetuṃ anujānāmīti. “Cīvarapaccāsā”ti mariyādatthe nissakkavacanaṃ, bhummatthe vā paccattavacanaṃ kataṃ.

497. `Nappahoti` means 'it does not reach the inferior limit.' For that very reason, the inferior limit of the three robes, such as the five handfuls, was stated first. `Cīvarapaccāsā` is expectation (`paccāsā`) for a robe (`cīvare`). By this, it is explained: 'Whether that robe is obtained later or not, I allow this original robe to be kept for as long as that expectation is not severed.' The word `cīvarapaccāsā` is an ablative expression in the sense of a limit, or it is a nominative expression used in the sense of the locative.

499-500. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ [M 0.0235] …pe… cīvarāsā vā upacchinnātiādimhi tīsu cīvaresu aññataraṃ kataṃ hoti, sesā atthi, rakkhati. Cīvarapalibodhassa upacchede, ubbhatasmiñca kathine samaye vā hemantassa samaye vā akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya, khippameva kāretabbaṃ[V 0.0210]. Sati pāripūriyā paccāsā na rakkhati, asati natthi ce paccāsā, na rakkhati. “Anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppanna”nti vacanato aparakattikā atthate vā anatthate vā samayova. Hemanto siyā samayo atthate, siyā asamayo anatthate. Tato paraṃ ekaṃsato asamayo vāti. “Ādissa dinna”nti idaṃ idha alabbhamānampi atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ dutiyanissaggiye (pāci. 738 ādayo) sesaṃ akālacīvaraṃ viya. Tattha hi bhikkhunisaṅghassa “sampattā bhājentū”ti evaṃ ādissa dinnameva “akālacīvaraṃ kālacīvara”nti adhiṭṭhahitvā bhājentiyā nissaggiyaṃ. Tathā hi tattha yathā “akālacīvaraṃ nāma anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppannaṃ, atthate kathine sattamāse uppanna”nti idaṃ atthuddhāravasena vuttaṃ, evaṃsampadamidaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “ekapuggalassa idaṃ tuyhaṃ damhīti dinna”nti idaṃ kimatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na hi taṃ bhājanīyanti ce? Abhājanīyasāmaññato vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā saṅghassa ādissa dinnaṃ atthatakathinehi eva bhikkhūhi abhājanīyattā akālacīvaraṃ nāma jātaṃ, evaṃ puggalikampi itarehīti attho. Evaṃ santepi kassaci siyā “ādissa dinnampi dasāhameva parihāraṃ labhatī”ti. Tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ. Paṭhamakathine “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine”ti idañhi niratthakanti. Anubbhatasmimpi hi kathine dasāhaparamameva dhāretabbanti viññātattā anādissa dinnameva sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ siyāti ce? Evaṃ santepi anādissa dinnampi anatthatakathinānaṃ aparakattikāya dasāhameva parihāraṃ labhati “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine”ti vuttattā. Āmantāti ce? “Anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppanna”nti vacanena virujjhati, tasmā yathāvuttanayenevettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ gantabbaṃ.

499-500. 'When the robe-making is finished... (and so on)... or when the hope for a robe is cut off': when, of the three robes, one has been made, the others exist, and he protects them. When the robe-impediment is cut off, and when the Kathina is withdrawn, or at the proper time, or in the winter season, should an out-of-season robe arise, it should be made very quickly. When there is sufficiency, he does not maintain the expectation; when there is no sufficiency, if there is no expectation, he does not maintain it. Because of the statement 'arisen in the eleven months when the Kathina is not spread,' the later Kattika month is indeed the proper time, whether the Kathina is spread or not spread. When the Kathina is spread, the winter season may be the proper time; when it is not spread, it may be the improper time. After that, it is definitely the improper time. The phrase 'given with designation,' although not applicable here, is stated by way of extracting the meaning, as in the second Nissaggiya offense for nuns, where the remainder is like an out-of-season robe. For there, when something is given to the Sangha of nuns with the designation 'Let those who have arrived distribute it,' for the nun who distributes it after having determined an 'out-of-season robe' as a 'season-robe,' it is a Nissaggiya offense. For just as it is stated there, 'An out-of-season robe is one that arises in the eleven months when the Kathina is not spread, or in the seven months when the Kathina is spread,' by way of extracting the meaning, so too is this case. If so, one might ask: 'For what reason was it stated, "Given to a single individual, saying, ‘We give this to you,’" since that is not to be distributed?' It is stated because of the commonality of being non-distributable. Just as what is given to the Sangha with designation becomes what is called an out-of-season robe because it is non-distributable by the monks who have spread the Kathina, so too, that which is a personal gift becomes an out-of-season robe for the others because it is non-distributable by them; this is the meaning. Even so, someone might think, 'Even what is given with designation obtains a period of keeping of only ten days.' This thought of his is merely a conjecture. For then, in the first Kathina section, this statement 'when the robe-making is finished for the monk, when the Kathina is withdrawn' would be meaningless. If one were to say: 'For even when the Kathina is not withdrawn, it is understood that a robe should be kept for ten days at most; therefore, this statement might have been said referring only to what is given without designation.' Even so, even what is given without designation obtains a period of keeping of only ten days in the later Kattika month for those who have not spread the Kathina, because it is stated, 'when the robe-making is finished for the monk, when the Kathina is withdrawn.' If one were to say, 'Yes'? It contradicts the statement 'arisen in the eleven months when the Kathina is not spread.' Therefore, the conclusion here should be reached according to the method already stated.

Anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ “paṭhamasikkhāpade sabbacīvarānaṃ yāvadatthacīvaravasena kathinamāsabbhantare dasāhātikkamepi anāpatti parihārassa dinnattā. Yathā [M 0.0236] kathinamāsabbhantare ādissa dinnamakālacīvaraṃ kālacīvaraparihārameva labhati, tathā itaramāsepi labhatīti veditabbaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ ‘niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine bhikkhuno paneva cīvaraṃ uppajjeyyā’tiādinā sikkhāpade siddhepi anatthatakathinānaṃ pacchimakattikamāsaṃ anujānantena ‘akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyyā’ti vuttaṃ. Evañhi avutte akālacīvaraṃ nāma ‘anatthate kathine ekādasamāse uppanna’nti na sakkā vattuṃ. Evañhi vacanato anatthatakathinānaṃ atthatakathinānaṃ viya sabbacīvarānaṃ pacchimakattikamāse dasāhātikkame nissaggiyaṃ na hotī”tiādi.

In the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'In the first training rule, for all robes, by way of robes as needed, even when the ten days are exceeded within the Kathina month, there is no offense, because an allowance has been given. Just as an out-of-season robe given with a specific person in mind within the Kathina month receives the very allowance of a seasonal robe, so too, it is received in other months; thus it should be understood. Therefore, even though it is established in the training rule by the text beginning, ‘When a monk has finished his robe, and the Kathina is withdrawn, should another robe arise for the monk…’, by permitting the last Kattika month for those for whom the Kathina is not spread, it is said, ‘an out-of-season robe may arise’. Indeed, if this were not said, it would not be possible to say that what is called an out-of-season robe is ‘one that has arisen in the eleven months when the Kathina is not spread’. Indeed, because it is so, for those for whom the Kathina is not spread, like for those for whom the Kathina is spread, for all robes, in the last Kattika month, exceeding the ten-day limit does not become an item for forfeiture, and so on.'

Bhiyyopi evaṃ vuttaṃ – yaṃ pana mayā “paṭhamakathine dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti [V 0.0211] anuññātaṃ, tampi kathinamāsato bahi uppannameva, na antoti ayamattho dīpito hoti. Kathaṃ? Atirekacīvarassa dasāhaparihārato uddhaṃ āpajjitabbāpattiṃ “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine”ti anupaññattiyā kathinabbhantare vāretvā tato uddhaṃ uppannesu dasāhātikkame āpajjitabbāpattiṃ iminā sikkhāpadena vāretuṃ “akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena “kālepi ādissa dinnaṃ, etaṃ akālacīvaraṃ nāmā”ti vacanato kathinubbhārato uddhaṃ dasāhaparihāraṃ na labhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti, tehi saddhiṃ puna kathinubbhārato uddhaṃ pañca divasāni labhatīti pasaṅgopi “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine bhikkhuno paneva akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya…pe… khippameva kāretabba”nti akālacīvarassa uppattikālaṃ niyametvā vuttattā nivārito hoti, tadubhayena kathinabbhantare uppannacīvaraṃ kathinubbhārato uddhaṃ ekadivasampi parihāraṃ na labhatīti siddhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ apare vadantīti.

Furthermore, it is said thus: That which was permitted by me—'In the first Kathina, an extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days'—that too applies only to a robe that has arisen outside the Kathina month, not within it. This meaning is clarified. How so? The offense to be incurred after the ten-day allowance for an extra robe is prevented within the Kathina period by the supplementary regulation, 'When the Kathina has been withdrawn by a bhikkhu whose robe-making is finished.' Then, in order to prevent the offense to be incurred by exceeding ten days with regard to robes that have arisen after that period, this training rule states, 'should an untimely robe arise,' etc. Therefore, because of the statement, 'Even if given specifically in season, this is called an untimely robe,' it is clarified that after the withdrawal of the Kathina, the ten-day allowance is not obtained. Also, the implication that one again obtains five days after the withdrawal of the Kathina is prevented, because it was said, having defined the time of arising for an untimely robe: 'When the Kathina has been withdrawn by a bhikkhu whose robe-making is finished, should an untimely robe arise for a bhikkhu... it should be made quickly.' By both of these, it is established that a robe that has arisen within the Kathina period does not obtain an allowance of even one day after the withdrawal of the Kathina. Thus others say.

Punapi vuttaṃ – ācariyā pana evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine bhikkhuno paneva akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyyā”ti ettha “niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ kathine”ti vadanto evaṃ viññāpeti “etthantare tiṇṇannampi akālacīvarānaṃ uppatti abhāva”nti. Kasmā pana padabhājane vitthāritānīti? Vuccate – idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, kintu paṭhame dasāhaṃ anujānitvā tasmiṃ appahonte sace paccāsā atthi, tameva vaḍḍhetvā māsaṃ anujānanto imampi atthavisesaṃ dīpeti akālacīvaraṃ nāma [M 0.0237] sammukhībhūtena bhājetabbantipi dīpeti. Taṃ pana “ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabba”nti iminā sikkhāpadena vaḍḍhetvā vuttanti, tasmā tīṇipi padabhājane vitthāritānīti.

Again, it is said: The teachers, however, might say thus: Herein, in the passage “When the robe-making is finished by a monk and the kathina has been withdrawn, an untimely robe might arise for that very monk,” the Blessed One, by saying, “When the robe-making is finished... and the kathina has been withdrawn,” makes it known that “within this interval, there is the non-arising of the three kinds of untimely robes.” Why then are they elaborated in the word-analysis? It is said: This training rule is stated with reference to the determination. But indeed, in the first rule, having allowed ten days, if that is insufficient and there is an expectation, He, while extending that very period to a month, also reveals this special meaning: that what is called an untimely robe is to be distributed by one who is present. That, however, is stated by extending it with this training rule: “It should be accepted by a monk who is waiting for it.” Therefore, all three are elaborated in the word-analysis.

“Khippameva kāretabbanti dasāhā kāretabba”nti idaṃ pana pahonakabhāve purimasikkhāpadalakkhaṇenāti dīpetuṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā “evaṃ sīghanti vā lahunti vā”tiādinā avatvā “dasāhā”ti vuttaṃ. Atthatakathinassa evaṃ hotu, anatthate pana kathine kathanti vutte anatthatassa paṭikkhepataṃ dassetīti vutto apassanto vighātaṃ āpajjatīti. Ekatiṃse aruṇuggamane nissaggiyanti mahantenapi paccāsācīvarena saha ghaṭitampi tabbhāvaṃ anupatitvā nissaggiyaṃ hoti sati pacchimappamāṇasambhave, asati na hoti, puna ghaṭite hoti, aññena ghaṭite na hoti. Chinnaṃ aññavatthu hoti. Pubbaparicchedaṃ atikkantaṃ ghaṭitaṃ puna aññaparicchedaṃ labhatīti eke, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade pana “saṅghassa vā idaṃ akālacīvaranti uddissa dinna’nti ettha saṅghassa dinne āpatti nāma natthi, ‘sotassa [V 0.0212] raho’tiādīsu viya paduddhārena vuttaṃ, tassa lābhaṃ sandhāyāti ce? Saṅghato vā uppajjeyyāti anena siddhattā adhikamevā”ti ca “saṅgho cīvarāni labhissati gaṇo vā’tiādināpi pāṭho atthī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Gaṇṭhipade kosallatthaṃ pana mayā sabbaṃ likhitaṃ, suṭṭhu vicāretvā kathetabbaṃ.

This statement, ‘It should be made quickly; it should be made within ten days,’ was said to show the characteristic of the previous training rule in a case of sufficiency. Therefore, instead of saying ‘so swiftly’ or ‘so lightly,’ and so on, it was said ‘within ten days.’ For one for whom the kathina has been spread, let it be so. But for one for whom the kathina is not spread, when it is asked, ‘How is it?’, the answer shows the rejection for the one for whom it is not spread. The one who was told this, not understanding, falls into trouble. At the dawn of the thirty-first day, it becomes forfeitable. Even when joined with a large hoped-for robe, having attained that state, it becomes forfeitable if there is the possibility of the final measurement; if there is not, it does not. When joined again, it does; when joined with another, it does not. A cut piece becomes another object. Some say that what has exceeded the previous boundary, when recombined, gains another boundary; this should be examined and taken up. But in a certain Ganthipada it is said: ‘Here, in the phrase “This was given, having been designated for the Sangha or as an untimely robe,” when it is given to the Sangha, there is no offense. It is said by way of “extraction of a word,” as in “the ear in private,” etc.’ If it is said that this refers to its gain, the reply is: because it is already established by ‘or it might arise from the Sangha,’ it is simply redundant. And it is also said that there is a reading, ‘The Sangha will receive robes, or a group,’ etc. But for the sake of skill in the Ganthipada, everything was written by me; it should be discussed after careful consideration.

Tatiyakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third Kathina training rule is completed.

4. Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes

503-505. Bhattavissagganti bhattakiccādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Bhattakiccādhiṭṭhānavibhāganti porāṇā. Tattha nāma tvanti tattha tayā katakamme evaṃ akattabbe sati dhovāpissasi nāma. Atha vā so nāma tvanti attho. Ubhatosaṅghe upasampannāti bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampadāya paṭikkhittattā tadanupasaṅgabhayā evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Purāṇacīvara”nti ettha purāṇabhāvadīpanatthameva “sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā “cīvaraṃ nāma channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ vikappanupagaṃ pacchima”nti vacanassa okāso na [M 0.0238] jātoti eke. Yasmā vikappanupagapacchimaṃ idha nādhippetaṃ, nivāsanapārupanupagamevādhippetaṃ, teneva nisīdanapaccattharaṇe dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā na vuttanti eke. Jātippamāṇāvacanato yaṃ kiñci purāṇavatthaṃ dhovāpentassa nissaggiyameva, teneva “anāpatti cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ dhovāpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Thavikampi hi asucimakkhitaṃ paribhuttaṃ dhovāpeti, nissaggiyameva oḷārikattā, appatirūpattā ca. Teneva kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne cīvaraparicchedo na vuttoti eke, vicāretvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ. “Rajitvā kappaṃ katvāti kappiyaṃ katameva nivāsetuṃ, pārupituṃ vā vaṭṭati, netara”nti vuttaṃ. Iminā ca majjhimattheravādo upatthambhito hoti, nopatthambhito. Rajitvātiādi pana vinayavidhidassanatthaṃ vuttanti mama takko. Yathā aññātikāya aññātikasaññīvāre tīṇi catukkāni, evaṃ vematikañātikavāresu cāti nava catukkāni honti. Etthāha – ekavāraṃ dhovitvā dhovanesu dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā puna “duddhota”nti maññamānā dhovati, anāpattiyā bhavitabbaṃ, dutiyavāraṃ avuttā dhovati nāma hotīti? Vuccate – sace bhikkhu “alaṃ ettāvatā dhotenā”ti paṭikkhipati, puna dhovantī avuttā dhovati nāmāti yujjati. No ce, vuttāva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Bhikkhussa liṅgaparivattane ekatoupasampannāya vasena āpatti sākiyānīnaṃ viya.

503-505. Herein, `bhattavissagga` means the arrangement of the meal duty. The ancient teachers say it means the arrangement and division of the meal duty. Herein, `tattha nāma tvaṃ` means: when there is an action done by you that should not have been done, will you indeed have it washed? Alternatively, the meaning is: you, being such a one. Regarding `ubhatosaṅghe upasampannā` (ordained in both Saṅghas), it should be understood that this is said because, her higher ordination having been rejected in the presence of the bhikkhus, there is fear of the transgression that would follow that. Herein, regarding `purāṇacīvara` (an old robe), it is said, 'even if worn once as an under-robe or once as an outer-robe,' only to indicate its state of being old. Therefore, some say there is no occasion for the statement, 'A robe is any one of the six robes, the smallest being suitable for `vikappana`.' Because the smallest robe suitable for `vikappana` is not intended here; only that which is suitable for wearing as an under-robe or an outer-robe is intended. For that very reason, a `dukkaṭa` offense is stated for a sitting-cloth or a ground-covering. Therefore, some say, it is not stated. Because the type and measure are not specified, for one who has any old cloth whatsoever washed, it is indeed a `nissaggiya` offense. For that very reason, it is said, 'There is no offense if, having set aside a robe, one has another requisite washed.' Indeed, if one has even a used bag smeared with impurity washed, it is a `nissaggiya` offense, because of its coarseness and unsuitability. For that very reason, some say that the delimitation of a robe is not stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī in this context; having investigated, what is more suitable should be adopted. It is stated: 'Having dyed it and made the `kappa` mark,' it is allowable to wear as an under-robe or an outer-robe only what has been made allowable, not what is other than that. And by this, the view of the middle elders is supported. Or rather, it is not supported. Instead, `rajitvā`, and so on, is said to show the Vinaya procedure; this is my reasoning. Just as in the section on a non-relative perceived as a non-relative there are three tetrads, so too in the sections on doubt and on her being a relative, there are thus nine tetrads. Herein, one asks: If, having washed once and set aside the responsibility for washing, she washes again thinking, 'It was badly washed,' should there be no offense? Is washing a second time called 'washing without being told'? The reply is given: If the bhikkhu rejects it, saying, 'Enough with this much washing,' then her washing again is properly called 'washing without being told.' If he does not reject it, it should be understood that she has been told. In the case of a bhikkhu's sex change, an offense is incurred by way of one ordained on one side, similar to the offense for the Sākyan women.

506. Ekena [V 0.0213] vatthunāti yena kenaci paṭhamena. “Tiṇṇaṃ catukkānaṃ vasenā”ti pāṭho. Bhikkhūnaṃ santike aṭṭhavācikāya upasampannāya pākaṭattā taṃ avatvā sākiyāniyova vuttā apākaṭattā.

506. ‘By one basis’ means by any first one. There is the reading: “by way of the three tetrads.” Because her higher ordination with the eight pronouncements in the presence of the bhikkhus was well-known, that was not mentioned; only the Sākyanī was mentioned, because she was not well-known.

Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes is concluded.

5. Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes

508-510. Apaññatte sikkhāpadeti ettha “gaṇamhā ohīyanasikkhāpade”ti likhitaṃ. Araññavāsīnisedhanasikkhāpade apaññatteti eke, “taṃ na sundara”nti vadanti. Vihatthatāyāti āyāsena.

508-510. Regarding the phrase 'When the training rule was unpromulgated,' it is written as 'in the training rule concerning leaving the group.' Some say this refers to when the training rule prohibiting dwelling in the forest was unpromulgated; others say, 'That is not suitable.' `Vihatthatā` means 'with difficulty.'

512. Upacāroti dvādasahattho. Mahāpaccariyaṃ, kurundiyañca vuttanti ettha rattibhāge dhammakathikassa bhikkhuno bahūsu cīvaresu mahājanena pasādadānavasena [M 0.0239] paṭikkhittesu punadivase “upāsakānaṃ pasādadānāni etānī”ti suddhacittena gaṇhantassa doso natthi, “bhikkhunīhipi dinnāni idha santī”ti ñatvā gaṇhato doso. Taṃ acittakabhāvenāti bhikkhunīhi dinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā bahūsu tassā cīvarassa ajānanenāti attho. Paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvāti “bhikkhunīhi nu kho dinnaṃ siyā”ti avikappetvā “paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhāmī”ti gaṇhantassa vaṭṭati. Kurundiādīsu vuttopi attho ayameva, ekaṃ, “acittakabhāvenā”ti vacanena “yathā tathā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti uppathova paṭisedhitoti apare. Evaṃ dhammasiritthero na vadati, ujukameva vadatīti papañcitaṃ. Tasseva visayo, tassāyaṃ adhippāyo – yathā “paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhissatīti ṭhapitaṃ kāmaṃ bhikkhunisantakampi avikappetvā paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, tathā dhammakathikassa bhikkhuniyā dinnampi apaññāyamānaṃ vaṭṭatīti, tasmā taṃ vuttaṃ mahāpaccariyaṃ, kurundiyañca acittakabhāvena na sametīti. Paṭikkhepo pana vikappaggahaṇe eva ruhati. Aññathā pubbāparaṃ virujjhatīti. Taṃ na yuttaṃ paṃsukūlena asamānattā. Paṃsukūlabhāvena saṅkārakūṭādīsu ṭhapitaṃ bhikkhunīhi, na taṃ tassā santakaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ hoti. Assāmikañhi paṃsukūlaṃ sabbasādhāraṇañca, aññopi gahetuṃ labhati. Idaṃ pubbeva “bhikkhunīnaṃ cīvara”nti jānitvāpi paṃsukūliko gahetuṃ labhati tadā tassā asantakattā. “Paṃsukūlaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā”ti sallekhakkamanidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Maṃsaṃ dadantena tathāgatena sallekhato kappiyampi bhuttaṃ nissaggiyaṃ cīvaramāha yo maṃsaṃ kathanti sayamādiseyyāti.

512. An `upacāra` is an area of twelve cubits. In the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundiya it is said: In the night, when many robes have been presented by the great populace by way of a gift of faith to a Dhamma-preaching bhikkhu, on the next day, for one who takes them with a pure mind, thinking, 'These are gifts of faith from the lay devotees,' there is no fault. For one who takes them knowing, 'There are also robes given by bhikkhunīs here,' there is a fault. 'Due to the state of being unintentional' means: knowing the fact that they were given by bhikkhunīs, but not knowing her specific robe among the many. Regarding 'having determined it as a rag-robe': for one who takes it thinking, 'I am taking a rag-robe,' without specifically considering, 'Could this have been given by bhikkhunīs?', it is allowable. The meaning stated in the Kurundī and other commentaries is this very one. However, others say that by the statement 'due to the state of being unintentional,' the wrong path, 'it is allowable to take it in any way whatsoever,' is rejected. The Elder Dhammasiri does not speak thus; he speaks only straightforwardly. This has been elaborated. This is his sphere, this is his intention: just as it is said, 'It is allowable to take even what belongs to a bhikkhunī, which was placed with the thought, "He will take it as a rag-robe," by determining it as a rag-robe without specific consideration,' so too for a Dhamma-preacher, what is given by a bhikkhunī, being unrecognizable, is allowable. Therefore, it is said that what is stated in the Mahāpaccariya and the Kurundiya does not accord with 'due to the state of being unintentional.' The rejection, however, applies only in the case of taking with specific consideration. Otherwise, the former and latter statements would be contradictory. That is not proper, because of the dissimilarity with a rag-robe. What is placed by bhikkhunīs on refuse heaps and so on, as a rag-robe, does not remain as her property. For a rag-robe is ownerless and common to all; another person may also take it. This, even having known beforehand, 'This is a bhikkhunī's robe,' a rag-robe-dweller may take, because at that time it is not her property. The phrase 'having determined it as a rag-robe' is stated to show the method of austere practice. The Tathāgata, while permitting meat, partook of what is allowable from the standpoint of austere practice and spoke of a robe entailing forfeiture. How could one who eats meat himself point this out?

Acittakattā [V 0.0214] kathaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ vaṭṭatīti ce? Tāya tassa adinnattā, bhikkhunāpi tato bhikkhunito aggahitattā ca. Assāmikampi hi paṃsukūlaṃ aññissā hatthato gaṇhāti, na vaṭṭati “aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti vuttalakkhaṇasambhavato. Aññātikāya santakaṃ ñātikāya hatthato gaṇhāti, vaṭṭatīti eke. Yathā sikkhamānasāmaṇerādīnaṃ hatthato paṭiggaṇhantassa anāpatti, tathā kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyañca “aññātikāya hatthato gahaṇa”nti (kaṅakhā. aṭṭha. cīvarappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) aṅgaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā ñātikāya [M 0.0240] santakaṃ sikkhamānāya, sāmaṇeriyā, upāsakassa, upāsikāya, bhikkhussa, sāmaṇerassa santakaṃ aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā hatthato gaṇhantassa ca anāpatti evaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇāsambhavatoti eke, teneva “ekatoupasampannāya cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhātī’ti avatvā ‘hatthato paṭiggaṇhāti aññatra pārivattakā, āpatti dukkaṭassā’ti (pārā. 513) vuttaṃ, tasmā aññātikāya santakampi ekatoupasampannāya hatthato paṭiggaṇhantassa dukkaṭa”nti vadanti, ubhopete na sārato daṭṭhabbā, kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

If it is asked, 'Given that it is without intention, how is the rag-robe permissible?' It is because she has not given it to that bhikkhu, and because the bhikkhu has not taken it from that bhikkhunī. Indeed, even if one takes an ownerless rag-robe from the hand of another bhikkhunī, it is not permissible, because of the occurrence of the characteristic stated thus: '...should receive a robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī.' Some say it is permissible if one takes what belongs to an unrelated bhikkhunī from the hand of a related bhikkhunī. Just as there is no offense for one who receives from the hands of a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, and so on, so too in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, 'taking from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī' is stated as a factor. Similarly, some say there is indeed no offense for one who takes from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī the property of a related bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇerī, a male lay follower, a female lay follower, a bhikkhu, or a sāmaṇera, because of the non-occurrence of the aforesaid characteristic. For that very reason, instead of saying, 'He receives a robe from one ordained in both Saṅghas,' it is said, 'He receives it from her hand, except in exchange—there is an offense of wrong-doing.' Therefore, they say that for one who receives even the property of an unrelated bhikkhunī from the hand of one ordained in both Saṅghas, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Both these views should not be taken as definitive; the reason must be sought.

514. Ko pana vādo pattatthavikādīsūti anadhiṭṭhātabbesu bahūsu paṭalesu. Tenevāha mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pattatthavikādimhi anadhiṭṭhātabbaparikkhāre”ti. Adhiṭṭhānupagesu vā tesaṃ parikkhārattā bhisichaviyā viya anāpatti. Kiṃ paṭaparissāvanaṃ parikkhāraṃ na hotīti? Hoti, kintu taṃ kira nivāsanādicīvarasaṇṭhānattā na vaṭṭati. Tasmā idha nivāsanādicīvarasādhanaṃ vikappanupagapacchimaṃ cīvaraṃ nāma. Anantarātīte nivāsanapārupanupagamevāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ sante kaṅkhāvitaraṇiyaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. cīvarappaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) kappanupagapacchimatā, pārivattakābhāvo, aññātikāya hatthato gahaṇanti tīṇeva aṅgāni avatvā aparikkhāratāti catutthamaṅgaṃ vattabbanti ce? Na vattabbaṃ, imasmiṃ sikkhāpade pattatthavikādiparikkhārassa acīvarasaṅkhyattā. Paṭhamakathinādīsu vikappanupagatā pamāṇaṃ, idha kāyaparibhogupagatāti. “Aññaṃ parikkhāra”nti uddharitvā “pattatthavikādiṃ yaṃkiñcī”ti vuttattā vikappanupagampi pattatthavikādiṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, “paṭaparissāvanampī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne ca “cīvaraṃ nāma vikappanupagapacchima”nti vacanato paṭaparissāvanaṃ cīvarameva, na parikkhāraṃ. “Ko pana vādoti nigamanavacanampi sādhaka”nti keci vadanti, paṇṇattiṃ ajānanato acittakaṃ, na vatthuṃ, “aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā santakabhāvājānanato, cīvarabhāvājānanato ca acittaka”nti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

514. What is to be said of bowl-bags and so forth, among the many pieces of cloth that are not to be determined? Therefore, it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: 'Regarding bowl-bags and other requisites not to be determined.' Or, in the case of those items suitable for determination, because they are requisites, like a mat or hide covering, there is no offense. Is a cloth water-strainer not a requisite? It is, but it is said that because its shape is like that of a robe such as a lower garment, it is not allowable. Therefore, here, that which serves as a robe such as a lower garment, the smallest one suitable for shared ownership, is called a 'robe'. In the immediately preceding training rule, the conclusion was made that it is only that which is suitable for a lower garment or an upper garment. This being so, if it is asked whether in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, instead of stating only the three factors—(1) being the smallest suitable for shared ownership, (2) the absence of exchange, and (3) receiving it from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī—a fourth factor, 'not being a requisite,' should be stated? It should not be stated, because in this training rule, requisites such as bowl-bags are not counted as robes. In the first kaṭhina, and so forth, suitability for shared ownership is the measure; here, it is suitability for bodily use. By extracting the phrase 'another requisite' and because it is said 'whatever bowl-bag, etc.,' it is allowable to receive even a bowl-bag, etc., that is suitable for shared ownership. And in the place where it is said 'even a cloth water-strainer,' because of the statement 'a robe is the smallest one suitable for shared ownership,' the cloth water-strainer is indeed a robe, not a requisite. Some say, 'The concluding statement, "What is to be said?" is also evidence,' but this is unintentional due to not knowing the regulation, not due to the object. It is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: 'It is unintentional due to not knowing it was the property of an unrelated bhikkhunī, and due to not knowing it was a robe.'

Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on receiving robes is concluded.

6. Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Soliciting from an Unacquainted Person

515. Parikkhārānanti [M 0.0241][V 0.0215] upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Ekasāṭakanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, “aññātako moghapurisā”ti vacanena pavāritopi adātukāmo aññātako appavāritaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti dīpitaṃ hoti. Aññathā “anāpatti pavāritāna”nti iminā virujjhati.

515. The word 'parikkhārānaṃ' is a genitive case in the sense of utility. The word 'ekasāṭakaṃ' is a verbal noun in the neuter gender. By the statement, “O worthless person, a non-relative!” it is shown that even if invited, a non-relative who does not wish to give stands in the position of one not invited. Otherwise, this would contradict the statement, “There is no offense for those who have been invited.”

517. Neva tāva viññāpetabbaṃ, na bhañjitabbanti anacchinnānaṃ cīvarānaṃ attano santakānaṃ atthitāya, tattha paccāsāsabbhāvato ca. Paccāsā kittakaṃ kālaṃ rakkhatīti? Yāva gāmantarā, yāva addhayojanāti eke. Yāva dassanasavanūpacārāti eke. Yāva aññe na passantīti eke. Yāva paccāsā chijjatīti eke. Yāva sākhāpalāsapariyesanabhañjanasajjanakālaparicchedāti eke. Idaṃ sabbaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yujjati. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? “Sace pana etesaṃ vuttappakārānaṃ gihivatthādīnaṃ bhisichavipariyantānaṃ kiñci na labbhati, tena tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā paṭicchādetvā āgantabba”nti aṭṭhakathāvacanato.

517. One should neither solicit nor break off [branches]; this is on account of one's own robes not having been stolen, and because there is an expectation regarding them. How long does this expectation last? Some say as far as the next village, or as far as half a yojana. Some say as far as the range of sight and hearing. Some say as long as others do not see. Some say as long as the expectation is cut off. Some say as long as the time-limits for searching for, breaking, and preparing branches and leaves. All this is suitable according to the circumstances. If it is asked, 'How is this known?' It is known from the commentary statement: 'But if for these aforementioned things, from householder's cloth up to mats and hides, nothing is obtained, one should cover oneself with grass or leaves and then come.'

Na tāva therānaṃ dātabbānīti na tāva attano ruciyā dātabbāni, yadā therā “dethāvuso”ti vadanti, tadā dātabbāni. “Evaṃ sati daharāpi acchinnacīvaraṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti, sākhāpalāsaṃ bhañjituṃ vaṭṭati, na aññathā. ‘Yehi kehici vā acchinnaṃ hotī’ti hi vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Ācariyo pana evaṃ vadati “attano ruciyāpi dātuṃ labhantī”ti. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “paribhogajiṇṇaṃ vā’ti ettha ca ‘acchinnacīvarānaṃ ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ attanā tiṇapaṇṇehi paṭicchādetvā dinnacīvarampi saṅgahaṃ gacchatī’ti vattuṃ yujjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Athāpi siyā ācariyādīhi “āharāvuso”ti vutteyeva, nāvutteti, na, “kehici vā acchinna”nti ettha vuttalesato dutiyalesassa avisesabhāvappasaṅgatoti. Atha kimatthaṃ “na tāva therānaṃ dātabbānī”ti vuttanti ce? Yāva therānaṃ atthāya sākhāpalāsāni bhañjati, tāva na dātabbāni, tato tāni theruddissakāni sākhāpalāsāni sayaṃ paridahitvā vināpi therāṇattiyā attano ruciyā dātabbāni, bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiyaṃ na hoti satthunāpi anuññātattā. “Tiṇena vā paṇṇena vā”ti hi vuttaṃ, taṃ kappiyameva sandhāya vuttanti ce? Na, “tadalābhe na tveva…pe… dukkaṭassā”ti [M 0.0242] vacanavirodhato. Etthāha – dukkaṭabhayā pācittiyavatthu ce atikkamitabbaṃ, tadalābhe thullaccayavatthu saṅghikaṃ, tadalābhe pārājikavatthupi atikkamitabbaṃ siyāti? Na, pārājikassa lokavajjattā. Apica na sabbaṃ bhūtagāmaṃ pācittiyavatthumeva, tato dukkaṭādivatthupi atthi, anāpattivatthupi kālodisakaṃ, tasmā idaṃ tadā [V 0.0216] anāpattivatthukanti veditabbaṃ. Kittāvatā bhikkhu acchinnacīvaro naṭṭhacīvaro hotīti? Ettāvatā naggo hotīti eke. Vikappanupagapacchimabhāvena, vikappanupagapacchimamādiṃ katvā viññāpentassa āpattīti eke. Nivāsanapārupanupagābhāvenāti eke. Ticīvarābhāvenāti eke. Santaruttaraparamābhāvenāti eke. Ayaṃ ekevādo yutto “santaruttaraparamaṃ tato cīvaraṃ sāditabba”nti hi vacanato, tasmā santaruttare sati vikappanupagapacchimaṃ viññāpentassa paṭilābhena nissaggiyaṃ. Yadi evaṃ “viññāpetvā paṭilabheyya nissaggiya”nti sikkhāpadena bhavitabbanti ce? Tanna, tadatthasiddhito nānatthattā dhātūnaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā hi “tikkhattuṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ abhiviññāpesī”ti (pārā. 36) vutte pavattesīti attho, tathā idhāpi “cīvaraṃ viññāpeyyā”ti viññattiyā pavatteyya uppādeyyāti attho.

“They should not yet be given to the elders” means they should not yet be given by one's own wish; when the elders say, “Give, friend,” then they should be given. “If this is so, even young monks stand in the position of one whose robe has been stolen, and it is allowable to break off branches and leaves, but not otherwise. For it is said, ‘It has been stolen by someone or other.’” The teacher, however, says: “They are able to give even by their own wish.” For thus it is said in the commentary: “And here, regarding ‘or worn out by use,’ it is proper to say that ‘even a robe given by oneself after covering oneself with grass and leaves to teachers, preceptors, and others whose robes have been stolen, is included.’” It might be argued that this is proper only when teachers and others say, “Bring it, friend,” and not when it is unsaid. This is not so, because of the consequence that the second reason would have no distinction from the reason stated in ‘stolen by someone or other.’ Then, if it is asked for what reason it was said, “They should not yet be given to the elders,” the answer is: As long as one breaks branches and leaves for the sake of the elders, they should not be given. After that, having worn those branches and leaves intended for the elders oneself, they should be given by one's own wish, even without the elders' command. There is no pācittiya offense for destroying plant life, because it has been permitted even by the Teacher. For it is said, “With grass or with leaves.” If one were to say that this was said referring only to what is allowable, that is not so, because of the contradiction with the statement, “If that is not obtained, one should not… out of fear of a dukkaṭa.” Here one says: If an object of a pācittiya offense is to be transgressed out of fear of a dukkaṭa, then if that is not obtained, would an object of a thullaccaya offense belonging to the Sangha be transgressed, and if that is not obtained, might even an object of a pārājika offense be transgressed? No, because a pārājika is condemned by the world. Moreover, not all plant life is solely an object of a pācittiya offense; from that, there are also objects of dukkaṭa and others, and there is also an object of no offense specified by time. Therefore, this should be understood as an object of no offense at that time. To what extent is a bhikkhu considered ‘one whose robe has been stolen’ or ‘one whose robe is lost’? Some say: To the extent that he is naked. Some say: By the state of having only the last robe fit for determination; there is an offense for one who requests, having made the last robe fit for determination the starting point. Some say: By the absence of a robe fit for wearing as a lower or upper garment. Some say: By the absence of the three robes. Some say: By the absence of an inner and outer robe as the limit. This last view is correct, for it is said, “A robe should be accepted up to the limit of an inner and outer robe.” Therefore, when an inner and outer robe are present, for one who requests the last robe fit for determination, it is to be forfeited upon acquisition. If one were to say that if this is so, the training rule should be, “Having requested, should he receive it, it is to be forfeited,” that is not so, because that meaning is established and because verbal roots have various meanings. What is meant? Just as when it is said, “He solicited sexual intercourse three times,” the meaning is “he engaged in it,” so also here, in “he should request a robe,” the meaning is “by requesting, he should cause it to arise, he should produce it.”

Tena nivatthoti taṃnivattho. Aññassa alābhena tameva paribhuñjato jirati, na lesena. Attanāti sayameva vattuṃ yujjati, tasmā ayuttaparibhogena aparibhuñjitvā yuttaparibhogavasena paribhuñjato jiṇṇaṃ paribhogajiṇṇaṃ nāma. Tassa sabhāgānaṃ acchinnakāle dānampi yuttaparibhoge eva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti adhippāyo. “Ime kira dve lesā aṭṭhakathāyo, vācentānaṃ ācariyānaṃ matanti dhammasiritthero āhā”ti vuttaṃ.

Herein, `tena nivattho` means one who has worn that. It wears out from using that very robe due to not obtaining another, not from contrived use. Herein, `attanā` means it is fitting to say 'by oneself'; therefore, what has become worn out from being used in a proper manner, not having been used improperly, is called 'worn out by use'. The intention is that even a robe given to monks of the same group at a time when robes are not stolen is included only in proper use. It is said: 'The Elder Dhammasiri said: “These two points, it is said, are the view of the teachers who teach the commentaries.”'

521. Nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā na labhatīti yathāsukhaṃ na labhatīti adhippāyo. “Aññassatthāyā”ti etthāpi “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti anuvattati eva. Atthāya kassa? Tasseva aññassa. Yathā aññātake tikapācittiyaṃ, tathā appavāritepīti dassanatthaṃ “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti vuttaṃ. Aññathā “ñātake ñātakasaññī”ti iminā siddhattā na niccaṃ sesaṃ āpajjati. Apicettha aññātakaggahaṇena appavāritaggahaṇaṃ hoti[M 0.0243], appavāritaggahaṇena aññātakaggahaṇaṃ, aññātakā hi appavāritā honti. Tathā ñātakaggahaṇena pavāritaggahaṇaṃ hoti, katthaci na hoti. Na pavāritaggahaṇena ñātakaggahaṇaṃ hotīti imassa atthavisesassa dassanatthaṃ “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā appavāritāya ca cīvaraṃ aññatra pārivattakā paṭiggaṇhantassa āpatti. Ñātikāya pana pavāritāya ca vissāsaṃ gaṇhāti, anāpatti. Tathā purāṇacīvaraṃ ñātikāya anāpatti, pavāritāya pana tikapācittiyameva. Ñātakānañca ekaccānaṃ purāṇacīvaraṃ nāma dātuṃ vaṭṭati, na pavāritānaṃ. Tikacchedo ca mātikāpadeneva hoti, na aññena. Tatthāpi ekeneva, na dutiyādīhīti ayaṃ vinaye dhammatā veditabbā.

521. ‘Is not able to sit or lie down’ means one is not able to do so as one wishes; this is the intention. Herein, in ‘for the sake of another,’ the phrase ‘of relatives who have been invited (to request)’ also follows on. For whose sake? For that very other. To show that just as in the case of a non-relative there is a tikapācittiya offense, so too for one who is not invited, the phrase ‘of relatives who have been invited (to request)’ is stated. Otherwise, since it is established by the phrase ‘perceiving a relative as a relative,’ one does not always fall into the remaining offense. Moreover, here, by the mention of ‘non-relative,’ the mention of ‘uninvited’ is implied; by the mention of ‘uninvited,’ the mention of ‘non-relative’ is implied, for non-relatives are indeed uninvited. Similarly, by the mention of ‘relative,’ the mention of ‘invited’ is implied, but in some cases it is not. To show this specific meaning that by the mention of ‘invited,’ the mention of ‘relative’ is not implied, the phrase ‘of relatives who have been invited (to request)’ is stated. For instance, for a bhikkhu who accepts a robe from a bhikkhunī who is a non-relative and uninvited, except in an exchange, there is an offense. But if he takes it from a bhikkhunī who is a relative and has been invited (to request), out of familiarity, there is no offense. Similarly, regarding an old robe, from a relative there is no offense, but from one who has been invited (to request), it is indeed a tikapācittiya offense. And for some relatives, it is allowable to give what is called an old robe, but not to those who have been invited (to request). The threefold classification is made only by the mātikā-phrase, not by another. And there too, only by one, not by the second and so on—this should be understood as the nature of things in the Vinaya.

Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Soliciting from a Non-Relative is concluded.

7. Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning (Requesting) Beyond That

522-4. Paggāhikasālaṃ [V 0.0217] vāti dussapasāraṃ vā. Hatthena paggahetvā ṭhatvā sālāyaṃ pasāretabbadussaṃ pasārentīti codanā. Ticīvarikenevāti vinayaticīvarikena. So hi adhiṭṭhahitvā ṭhapitaparikkhāracoḷādīsu santesupi ticīvare acchinne santaruttaraparamaṃ viññāpetvā gahetuṃ labhati. Aññathāpīti “pamāṇikaṃ ticīvaraṃ parikkhāracoḷavasena adhiṭṭhahitvā paribhuñjato tasmiṃ naṭṭhe bahūnipi gahetuṃ labhati, na santaruttaraparama”nti ca, tasmā taṃ vibhāganti “ticīvarikassa taṃ vibhāganti attho, na parikkhāracoḷikassā”ti ca keci vadanti. Ācariyo pana “aññenāti aticīvarikena, aññathāti ito vuttaggahaṇaparicchedato aññenā”ti ettakameva vadati. Aññathāti pana sace tīṇipi naṭṭhāni, santaruttaraparamaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, sace dve vā ekaṃ vā naṭṭhaṃ, tena “aññathāpī”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttanti eke. Gaṇṭhipadesu vicāraṇā eva natthi, tasmā upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Pakatiyā santaruttarena carati, sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavasena vā taṃsammutivasena vā tatiyassa alābhena vā.

522-4. Regarding `Paggāhikasālaṃ vā` (or a hall for holding up) or `dussapasāraṃ vā` (or a place for spreading out cloth): The accusation is that they spread out cloth to be displayed in a hall, standing and holding it up with their hands. `Ticīvarikena` refers to one who observes the three-robe practice according to the Vinaya. Indeed, such a person, even when there are other requisites like determined spare cloths available, is allowed to solicit and receive at most an under-robe and an upper-robe if the three robes have been stolen. Regarding `Aññathāpi`: 'For a monk who uses a requisite cloth after having determined the standard three robes, if that requisite cloth is lost, he is allowed to receive many robes, not limited to just an under-robe and an upper-robe.' Therefore, some say, 'This allowance is for one who observes the three-robe practice, not for one who uses a requisite cloth.' The Teacher, however, says only this much: '`Aññena` means by one who does not observe the three-robe practice; `aññathā` means in a way other than the limit for receiving stated here.' As for `aññathā`, some say: if all three robes are lost, at most an under-robe and an upper-robe should be taken; if two or one are lost, the phrase `aññathāpi` is said in order to show this alternative procedure. There is no investigation of this in the knotty passages; therefore, one should understand it after careful examination. By nature, one goes about with an under-robe and an upper-robe; or one does so on account of the training rule involving suspicion, or by an agreement to that effect, or from not obtaining a third robe.

526. “Pamāṇameva [M 0.0244] vaṭṭatī”ti sallekhadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ micchā gahetvā ñātakādiṭṭhāne taduttari gaṇhantassa āpattīti ce? Taṃ pāḷiyā na sameti, “anāpatti ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti hi pāḷi. Ettha ca pavāritā nāma acchinnakālato pubbe eva pavāritā, na acchinnakāle. “Abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā”ti hi vuttaṃ, tasmā yo acchinnakālassatthāya pavāreti, ubhopi appavāritā evāti veditabbā. Te hi acchinnakāraṇā naṭṭhakāraṇāva denti nāma. Apica yathā piṭṭhisamaye satuppādaṃ katvā ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānato vassikasāṭikaṃ nipphādentassa tena sikkhāpadena nissaggiyaṃ, tathā idhāpi ñātakapavāritaṭṭhānepi acchinnanaṭṭhakāraṇā na vaṭṭati, tasmā “aṭṭhakathāsu pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī’ti vuttavacanameva pamāṇa”nti dhammasiritthero āha, taṃ ayuttaṃ, kasmā? Yasmā idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ taduttari viññāpentassa paññattaṃ, tasmiñca “aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā”ti mātikāya pāḷi, vibhaṅge ca “aññātako nāma mātito vā…pe… asambaddho”ti pāḷi, anāpattivāre ca “ñātakānaṃ pavāritāna”nti pāḷi, tasmā tividhāyapi pāḷiyā na sametīti ayuttameva, tasmā kevalaṃ sallekhameva sandhāya vuttanti apare. Upari kāṇamātāsikkhāpade aṭṭhakathāsu pana “tesampi pātheyyapaheṇakatthāya paṭiyattato pamāṇameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, na pana “pāḷiyā na sametī”ti vuttaṃ, na tattha ca idha ca nānākaraṇaṃ paññāyati[V 0.0218], tasmā therassa laddhi sundarā viya mama khāyati, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Yasmā panidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ aññassatthāya viññāpanavatthusmiṃyeva paññattaṃ, tasmā idha “aññassatthāyā”ti na vuttaṃ. “Sesaṃ uttānatthamevā”ti pāṭho. “Aññassatthāyā”ti nidānavirodhato na vuttaṃ. Tathāpi anantare vuttanayena labbhatīti ācariyo. Evarūpesu gahapatipaṭisaṃyuttasikkhāpadesu kiñcāpi “gahapati nāma yo koci agāraṃ ajjhāvasatī”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi pañca sahadhammike ṭhapetvā avasesā ca sikkhāpaccakkhātako ca titthiyo ca veditabbo.

526. “‘Only the measure is allowable’ is said for the purpose of showing austerity. If one argues that, taking that wrongly, there is an offense for one who accepts something beyond that from relatives and such, that does not accord with the Pāḷi, for the Pāḷi states, ‘There is no offense for relatives who have been invited.’ And here, ‘invited’ refers to those who were invited before the time of having the robe stolen, not at the time of having the robe stolen. For it is said, ‘One should invite for bringing.’ Therefore, it should be understood that if one invites for the sake of a monk at the time of having his robe stolen, both are considered uninvited. Indeed, they give on account of the robe being stolen or on account of it being lost. Moreover, just as for a monk who, in the period following, having made an effort, has a rains-bathing cloth completed from the place of a relative's invitation, it becomes an item for forfeiture under that training rule, so too here, even at the place of a relative's invitation, it is not allowable if given on account of the robe being stolen or lost. Therefore, the Elder Dhammasiri said, ‘The statement made in the commentaries, “Only the measure is allowable,” is the authority.’ That is incorrect. Why? Because this training rule was laid down for one who requests beyond that measure, and in its matrix, the Pāḷi states, ‘an unrelated householder or householder's wife’; and in the analysis, the Pāḷi states, ‘“Unrelated” means not related from the mother's side… etc. … not connected’; and in the no-offense section, the Pāḷi states, ‘for relatives who have been invited.’ Thus, as it does not accord with the Pāḷi in these three ways, it is incorrect. Therefore, others say it was spoken referring only to austerity. Above, in the training rule concerning Kāṇā's mother, the commentaries, however, say, ‘For them too, since it is prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey and as a gift, only the measure is allowable,’ but it is not said, ‘it does not accord with the Pāḷi.’ No difference is discernible between that case and this one, so the Elder's view seems reasonable to me, but it should be investigated. However, since this training rule was laid down specifically in a case of requesting for another, ‘for another’ is not stated here. The reading is, ‘The rest is of plain meaning.’ ‘For another’ is not stated due to contradicting the origin story. Still, it is obtained by the method stated in the immediately preceding rule, says the teacher. In such training rules connected with householders, although it is said, ‘A “householder” is anyone who dwells in a home,’ nevertheless, it should be understood that this excludes the five co-religionists but includes the rest, such as one who has renounced the training and an adherent of another sect.

Tatuttarisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning 'Beyond That' is concluded.

8. Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What is Prepared

527-8. Api [M 0.0245] hoti cittanti attho. Meyyāti pāṭhassa mayhanti attho. Na ime sukarā, “na imesaṃ sukarā”ti vā pāṭho. “Tassa na imesaṃ sukarā acchādetunti attho”ti likhitaṃ. “Pubbe appavārito”ti vacanato tasmiṃ khaṇe pavāritopi appavāritova hotīti.

527-8. The meaning is 'indeed, there is a thought'. For the reading `meyyāti`, the meaning is 'mine'. The reading is `Na ime sukarā` (It is not easy for these), or alternatively, `na imesaṃ sukarā` (It is not easy for them). It is written: 'Of that reading, the meaning is: "It is not easy for these monks to cover."' Because of the statement, 'previously uninvited,' it should be understood that at that moment, even if invited, one is indeed as one uninvited.

Paṭhamaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What is Prepared is concluded.

9. Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning What is Prepared

532. Dutiyaupakkhaṭena kiṃpayojananti? Natthi, kevalaṃ aṭṭhuppattivasena paññattaṃ bhikkhuniyā rahonisajjasikkhāpadaṃ viya. Evaṃ sante tanti anāropetabbaṃ bhaveyya vināpi tena tadatthasiddhito, anissarattā, anāropetuṃ anuññātattā ca. Vuttañhetaṃ “ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, saṅgho…pe… samūhaneyyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216). Idaṃ sabbamakāraṇaṃ. Na hi buddhā appayojanaṃ vācaṃ nicchārenti, pageva sikkhāpadaṃ, tenevāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tañhi imassa anupaññattisadisa”ntiādi. Anupaññatti ca nippayojanā natthi, taṃsadisañcetaṃ, na nippayojananti dassitaṃ hoti, evaṃ sante ko panettha visesoti? Tato āha “paṭhamasikkhāpade ekassa pīḷā katā, dutiye dvinnaṃ, ayamettha viseso”ti. Iminā atthavisesena ko panañño atirekattho dassitoti? Porāṇagaṇṭhipade tāva vuttaṃ “ekasmimpi vatthusmiṃ [V 0.0219] ubhinnaṃ pīḷā kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti ayamatirekattho dassito”ti. Tenetaṃ dīpeti “na kevalaṃ paṭiladdhacīvaragaṇanāyeva āpattigaṇanā, pīḷitapuggalasaṅkhātavatthugaṇanāyapī”ti.

532. What is the purpose of the second rule concerning what is prepared? There is none; it was laid down merely on account of an occasion arising, like the training rule for a bhikkhunī on sitting in a secluded place. If this is so, it might be argued that it should not have been included in the canon, since its purpose is achieved even without it. However, because one is not master to alter the canon and because its inclusion was permitted, it should be included. For it has been said: 'If it wishes, Ānanda, the Saṅgha... may abolish...' All this is not the reason. Indeed, Buddhas do not utter a useless word, how much more so a training rule. For that very reason, it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: 'For this is like a supplementary regulation,' etc. And a supplementary regulation is not without purpose, and this is similar to that; thus it is shown that it is not without purpose. This being so, what is the distinction here? Therefore, it is said: 'In the first training rule, harm is done to one; in the second, to two. This is the distinction here.' By this distinction in meaning, what other additional meaning is shown? In the ancient glossary, it is first said: 'Even in a single case, it is possible to cause harm to two. This additional meaning is shown.' By that, this is clarified: 'The counting of offenses is not merely by the count of robes received, but also by the count of cases, which are reckoned as the individuals harmed.'

Honti cettha –

And herein are these verses:

“Vatthuto gaṇanāyāpi, siyā āpatti nekatā;

Iti sandassanatthañca, dutiyūpakkhaṭaṃ idha.

By counting the cases as well, an offense might be manifold; and for the purpose of demonstrating this, the second rule concerning what is prepared was stated here.

“Kāyasaṃsaggasikkhāya, vibhaṅge viya kintetaṃ;

Ekitthiyāpi nekatā, āpattīnaṃ payogato”ti.

It is as in the Vibhaṅga of the training rule on physical contact. What is this? Even with a single woman, there is a multiplicity of offenses due to the various applications.

Apicetaṃ [M 0.0246] sikkhāpadaṃ taṃjātikesu sikkhāpadesu sabbesupi gahetabbavinicchayassa nayadassanappayojananti veditabbaṃ. Āha ca –

Moreover, this training rule is to be understood as serving the purpose of showing the method for the determination to be made in all training rules of that kind. And it is said:

“Aññātikāya bahutāya vimissatāya,

Āpattiyāpi bahutā ca vimissatā ca;

Iccevamādividhisambhavadassanatthaṃ,

Satthā upakkhaṭamidaṃ dutiyaṃ avocā”ti.

“Because of the multiplicity and mixture of non-relatives, there is also a multiplicity and mixture of offenses; in order to show the possibility of such methods and so forth, the Teacher spoke this second training rule concerning what is prepared.”

Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepato adhippāyapubbaṅgamā vicāraṇā – purāṇacīvaraṃ ekameva bhikkhu bhikkhunīhi dvīhi, bahūhi vā dhovāpeti, bhikkhunigaṇanāya pācittiyagaṇanā, tathā dvinnaṃ, bahūnaṃ vā sādhāraṇaṃ ekameva cīvaraṃ aññatra pārivattakā paṭiggaṇhāti, idhāpi tathā dvinnaṃ, bahūnaṃ vā sādhāraṇamekaṃ viññāpeti, viññattapuggalagaṇanāya āpattigaṇanā. Tathā aññesupi evarūpesu sikkhāpadesu nayo netabbo. Ayaṃ tāva bahutāya nayo. Missatāya pana ñātikāya, aññātikāya ca ekaṃ dhovāpeti, ekato niṭṭhāpane ekaṃ pācittiyaṃ. Atha ñātikā paṭhamaṃ thokaṃ dhovitvā ṭhitā, puna aññātikā sudhotaṃ karoti, nissaggiyaṃ. Atha aññātikā paṭhamaṃ dhovati, pacchā ñātikā sudhotaṃ karoti, aññātikāya payogavasena bhikkhuno dukkaṭameva. Aññātikāya ca ñātikāya ca aññātikasaññī, vematiko, ñātikasaññī vā dhovāpeti, yathāvuttanayena nissaggiyadukkaṭādiāpattibhedagaṇanā veditabbā. Tathā aññātikāya ca ñātikāya ca santakaṃ cīvaraṃ ubhohi ekato diyyamānaṃ paṭiggaṇhantassa[V 0.0220], aññātikāya eva hatthato paṭiggaṇhantassa ca nissaggiyameva. Atha ñātikāya anāpatti. Atha ubhosu aññātikādisaññī vuttanayeneva nissaggiyadukkaṭādiāpattibhedagaṇanā veditabbā. Tathā aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadesupi yathāsambhavaṃ nayo netabbo. Ayaṃ missatāya nayo. Ādi-saddena pana aneke aññātikā viññattāviññattapuggalagaṇanāya dukkaṭaṃ. Eko deti, eko na deti, nissaggiyaṃ. Atha aviññatto deti, na nissaggiyaṃ. Atha viññattāviññattānaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ viññatto deti, nissaggiyameva. Ubho denti, nissaggiyameva. Aviññatto deti, nissaggiyena anāpatti. Viññattassa vacanena aviññatto deti, anāpatti eva. Tathā upakkhaṭādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ nayo netabbo.

Here is a concise analysis, with its intention as a preamble: A monk has a single old robe washed by two or by many nuns; the counting of pācittiya offenses is according to the number of nuns. Similarly, when he receives a single robe common to two or many, except for an exchange; and here also, similarly, when he requests a single robe common to two or many, the counting of offenses is according to the number of persons requested. This method should be applied to other such training rules. This is the method concerning multiplicity. Now, concerning mixed cases: he has a robe washed by a related and an unrelated nun; upon its completion together, it is one pācittiya offense. Furthermore, if a related nun first washes it a little and stops, and then an unrelated nun completes the washing, it is a nissaggiya offense. Furthermore, if an unrelated nun washes it first, and afterwards a related nun completes the washing, for the monk, due to the action of the unrelated nun, it is only a dukkaṭa offense. If he has it washed by a related and an unrelated nun while perceiving her as unrelated, being uncertain, or perceiving her as related, the counting of the various offenses—nissaggiya, dukkaṭa, etc.—should be understood according to the method as stated. Similarly, for a monk who receives a robe belonging to both an unrelated and a related nun when it is being given by both together, and for one who receives it from the hand of the unrelated nun only, it is a nissaggiya offense. Furthermore, if he receives it from the related nun, there is no offense. Furthermore, in the case of both, if he perceives them as non-relatives, etc., the counting of the various offenses—nissaggiya, dukkaṭa, etc.—should be understood by the method already stated. Similarly, this method should be applied as is suitable in the training rules concerning requesting from an unrelated person. This is the method concerning mixed cases. Now, by the word “ādi” (etc.): in the case of many unrelated persons, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred according to the number of persons requested and not requested. If one gives and one does not give, it is a nissaggiya offense. Furthermore, if an unrequested person gives, it is not a nissaggiya offense. Furthermore, if the requested one gives what is common to the requested and the unrequested, it is a nissaggiya offense. If both give, it is a nissaggiya offense. If an unrequested person gives, there is no offense by way of nissaggiya. If an unrequested person gives by the word of the requested one, there is no offense at all. Similarly, in the training rules concerning prepared items (upakkhaṭa), etc., this method should be applied as is suitable.

Dutiyaupakkhaṭasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second training rule concerning prepared items is concluded.

10. Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a King

537. “Na [M 0.0247] kho mayaṃ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma…pe… kālena kappiya”nti ito pubbe eva rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadassa paññattattā vuttaṃ. Aññathā āyasmā upanando maṃsassa cetāpannaṃ ekampi kahāpaṇaṃ hatthena paṭiggaṇhanto tato mahantataraṃ cīvaracetāpannaṃ kathaṃ na paṭiggaṇhissati, evaṃ santepi cīvarapaṭisaṃyuttattā cīvaravagge saṅgāyiṃsūti.

537. This statement, "Indeed, friends, we do not accept a price for robes... at the proper time, it is allowable," was said because the training rule on accepting money had already been laid down just before this. Otherwise, the venerable Upananda, while accepting with his hand even a single kahāpaṇa as a price for meat, how would he not accept a much larger price for robes than that?
