Even so, because of its connection with robes, they included it in the Robes Chapter.

538-9. “Āgatakāraṇaṃ bhañjatī”ti vuttattā nanu puna codetuṃ na labhatīti eke. Āgamanassa sātthakaṃ na hoti, cīvaraṃ na labhissati paṭisanthārassa katattāti eke. Codanālakkhaṇaṃ na hotīti katvā vuttanti eke. “Ṭhatvā codemī”ti āgato taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhañjati, karoti cekaṃ, tīṇipi ce karoti, ekameva, ekavacanattāti eke. Tīṇi ṭhānāni bhañjatīti eke. Upatissatthero “na codanādiṃ bhañjati, codetukāmo akattabbaṃ akāsi, tena vattabhede dukkaṭa”nti vadati. Dhammasiritthero pana “āsane ce nisīdati, ekāya nisajjāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Āmisaṃ ce paṭiggaṇhāti, ekena paṭiggahena dve ṭhānāni bhañjati. Dhammaṃ ce bhāsati, dhammadesanasikkhāpade vuttaparicchedāya ekāya vācāya dve ṭhānāni bhañjati, taṃ sandhāya vutta”nti vadati. “Yatthā”ti vutte attano eva santikaṃ gantabbanti vuttaṃ viya hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “byañjanaṃ pana na sametī”ti. Upāsakehi āṇattā taṃ. Mūlaṃ asādiyantenāti mūlassa akappiyabhāve sati asādiyantena. Tañca kho cittena[V 0.0221], na mukhena. Sace evaṃ vutte akappiyaṃ dassetīti katvā cittena akappiyaṃ icchantova mukhena kappiyaṃ niddisati “cīvaraṃ me dethā”ti, na vaṭṭati. Paṭilābhe rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpadena āpatti.

538-9. Because it is said, 'He breaks the reason for coming,' some say, 'Is it not that one does not get to request again?' Some say, 'The coming is not fruitful; he will not get the robe because hospitality was performed.' Some say, 'It is not the characteristic of a request; it was said with this in mind.' The one who came thinking, 'Having stood, I will request,' breaks that standing. If he does one of these actions, or if he does all three, he breaks only one, because it is a similar statement; thus some say. He breaks the three grounds; thus some say. The Elder Upatissa says, 'He does not break the request and so on. One who wishes to request did what should not be done; thereby, due to the breach of duty, there is a dukkaṭa offense.' But the Elder Dhammasiri says, 'If he sits on a seat, with one sitting he breaks two grounds. If he accepts a material thing, with one acceptance he breaks two grounds. If he speaks the Dhamma, with one utterance of the stated limitation in the training rule on teaching the Dhamma, he breaks two grounds. It was said referring to that.' When 'yatthā' is said, it is as if it were said, 'One should go to one's own presence.' Therefore, it is said, 'But the wording does not fit.' He was instructed by the lay supporters. By 'not consenting to the price' is meant: by not consenting when there is the unsuitability of the price. And that is with the mind, not with the mouth. If, when this has been said, he—while desiring with his mind what is unsuitable—indicates with his mouth what is suitable, saying, 'Give me a robe,' it is not allowable. Upon receiving it, there is an offense under the training rule on accepting money.

Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā – cittena sādiyantopi mukhena kappiyavohārena ce voharati “kahāpaṇārahena, pādārahena vā kappiyabhaṇḍena idañcidañca āharā”ti. Kiñcāpi rūpiyaṃ sandhāya vadati, vaṭṭati eva. Kasmā? Kañci sassuṭṭhānakaṃ bhūmipadesaṃ sandhāya “sīmaṃ demāti vadanti, vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato, “vihārassa demā”ti vutte “paṭikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato ca. Anugaṇṭhipade pana vuttaṃ “saṅghaṃ sandhāya ‘vihārassa demā’ti dinnaṃ garubhaṇḍaṃ na hoti, dakkhiṇodakaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ, ‘sādhū’ti ca vattuṃ, anumodetuñca [M 0.0248] vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Saṅghassa ‘vihāro’ti nāmābhāvato, khettasseva ‘sīmā’ti nāmabhāvato ca, cittena ārammaṇaṃ kataṃ appamāṇaṃ, kappiyavohārova pamāṇaṃ. Kappiyamevācikkhitattā ‘na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kenaci pariyāyena jātarūparajataṃ sāditabbaṃ pariyesitabbanti vadāmī’ti (mahāva. 299) vacanenapi na virujjhati. Kappiyavacanapaccayā dāyako sayameva kattabbayuttakaṃ jānissatīti adhippāyato dāyakena etassa adhippāyaṃ ñatvā kappiyakārakassa hatthe ṭhapitaṃ bhikkhussa santakameva hotī”ti. Idaṃ sabbamayuttaṃ, kasmā? Sīmāvihāravacanassa dāyakavacanattā. Idha ca bhikkhuno vacanaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Tenevāha “athāpi ‘mama taḷākaṃ vā pokkharaṇiṃ vā saṅghassa dammī’ti vutte ‘sādhu, upāsaka, saṅgho pānīyaṃ pivissatī’tiādīni vatvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati evā”ti. Aññathā khettaṃ sandhāya bhikkhuno khettapaṭibaddhavacanāni sīmāvacanena kappantīti āpajjati. Avihārassa ca bhikkhussa rūpiyaṃ dassetvā “idaṃ vihārassa dammī”ti vutte attano atthāya diyyamānaṃ jānantenāpi taṃ appaṭikkhipitabbaṃ. Tathā kahāpaṇārahādino akappiyabhaṇḍabhāvaṃ, kahāpaṇādibhāvameva vā jānantameva sandhāya tathāvoharantassa ca anāpattīti āpajjati. “Na tvevāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kenaci pariyāyenā”ti nippadesato vuttattā na sakkā lesaṃ oḍḍetunti no takko, vicāretvā pana gahetabbaṃ. “No ce icchati, na kathetabba”nti vacanato yathāvuttasāmiciyā akaraṇe anāpatti dukkaṭassāti dasseti.

Herein is this consideration: Even while consenting in the mind, if one speaks with the mouth using an allowable expression, such as, 'Bring this and that allowable article worth a kahāpaṇa or worth a pāda,' then even though one speaks referring to money, it is indeed permissible. Why? Because of the statement, 'Referring to a certain plot of land for cultivation, they say, "We give the boundary," and it is permissible,' and because of the statement, 'When it is said, "We give to the monastery," it is not allowable to refuse.' Moreover, in the Anugaṇṭhipada it is said: 'When, referring to the Saṅgha, something is given with the words, "We give to the monastery," it does not become a heavy article. It is permissible to receive the water of dedication, to say "Sādhu," and to express appreciation. Why? Because the Saṅgha does not have the name 'monastery,' whereas a field does have the name 'boundary.' The object intended by the mind is not the measure; only the allowable expression is the measure. Because only what is allowable was stated, it does not conflict with the statement: "Monks, I do not say that in any way gold and silver should be consented to or sought." With the intention that, "Because of the allowable expression, the donor himself will know what ought to be done," what is placed in the hand of the kappiyakāraka by the donor, who has understood his [the monk's] intention, becomes the monk's own possession.' All this is incorrect. Why? Because the words 'boundary' and 'monastery' are the donor's speech. And here, the monk's speech is the measure. Therefore, he said: 'If it is said, "I give my tank or my lotus pond to the Saṅgha," it is indeed permissible to use it after saying such things as, "Good, lay supporter, the Saṅgha will drink the water."' Otherwise, it would follow that a monk's words connected with a field, when referring to a field, would become allowable by the word 'boundary.' And for a monk without a monastery, when shown money and told, 'I give this for the monastery,' it would have to not be refused by him, even while knowing it is being given for his own benefit. Similarly, for one who speaks in such a way, referring to one who knows the state of being unallowable goods for things worth a kahāpaṇa, etc., or their very nature as kahāpaṇas, etc., it would follow that there is no offense. Because the statement, 'Monks, I do not in any way...' was spoken unconditionally, it is not possible to insert a pretext—this is our reasoning. But it should be accepted after investigation. Because of the statement, 'If he does not wish, it should not be spoken,' it shows that for not performing the proper conduct as stated, there is no offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

“Aññātakaappavāritesu viya paṭipajjitabba”nti vacanato yathāvuttasāmicimpi na katvā ce nipphādeti, aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadena kāretabboti dasseti. Kappiyakārakā sayameva codetvā denti, vaṭṭati. “Sayaṃ karaṇameva paṭikkhitta”nti ca vadanti. Piṇḍapātādīnaṃ [V 0.0222] …pe… eseva nayoti ettha “dukkaṭa”nti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ, dadantesupīti api-saddena saṅgahitattā nissaggiyapācittiyameva. Jātarūparajataṃ “saṅghe sādite dukkaṭa”nti ca vikappenti. Taṃ visesetvā navuttattā pācittiyamevāti dasseti. “Nissaggiyamevāti yevāpanakasikkhāpadesu siyā”ti vadanti, upaparikkhitabbaṃ. “Yassa kassaci hi aññassa…pe… mahāpaccariyaṃ vutta”nti vacanato apabbajitānaṃ antamaso mātāpitūnampi atthāya sampaṭicchantassa dukkaṭamevāti dasseti.

Because of the statement, 'One should act as if among strangers and those who have not given an invitation,' it shows that if one accomplishes this without acting according to the stated propriety, the matter should be decided by the training rule on requesting from an unrelated person. If the suitable-makers request it themselves and give, it is allowable. And they say, 'Only doing it oneself is prohibited.' … Herein, some say it is an offense of wrongdoing, but that is not proper. Because it is included by the particle `api` in `dadantesupi`, it is indeed an offense entailing relinquishment and confession. They also opine regarding gold and silver, 'If the Saṅgha consents to it, it is an offense of wrongdoing.' It shows that because that case was not stated with a special distinction, it is indeed a pācittiya offense. Some say, 'It would be an offense entailing relinquishment only, as in the training rules concerning `yevāpanaka`.' This should be examined. Because of the statement in the Mahāpaccarī, 'For any other person whatsoever…,' it shows that for a monk who accepts something for the sake of non-monastics, even for the sake of his mother and father, it is indeed an offense of wrongdoing.

Sabbattha [M 0.0249] sampaṭicchanaṃ nāma “uggaṇheyya vā uggaṇhāpeyyavā upanikkhittaṃ vā sādiyeyyā”ti evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇameva. Evaṃ santepi katthaci paṭikkhipitabbaṃ, katthaci na paṭikkhipitabbaṃ, katthaci paṭikkhittaṃ sādituṃ vaṭṭati, evaṃ appaṭikkhittaṃ kiñci vaṭṭati, idaṃ sabbampi dassetuṃ “sace panā”ti vitthāro āraddho. Tattha “cetiyassa…pe… na vaṭṭatī”ti vacanato appaṭikkhittaṃ vihārassa dinnaṃ sādituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Tathā therassa “mātuyā demā”tiādinā vuttepi paṭiggahaṇe āpatti pācittiyameva. Sāpattiko hotīti ettha kāya āpattiyā sāpattiko hotīti? Dukkaṭāpattiyāti eke. Na yāya kāyaci, kevalaṃ aṭṭhāne codetīti katvā “sāpattiko”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā kathanti? “Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato saddhivihāriko paṇāmetabbo…pe… paṇāmento anatisāro”ti (mahāva. 68) ettha na sammāvattantaṃyeva apaṇāmentassa dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha – “na ca, bhikkhave, asammāvattanto na paṇāmetabbo, yo na paṇāmeyya, āpattidukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 68), tasmā adhimattapemādiabhāvepi apaṇāmentassa anāpatti dissati. Apica “sātisāro hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāya “sātisāro hotīti sadoso hoti, āpattiṃ āpajjatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 68) vuttattā na yuttanti ce? Na, tadanantarameva taṃmicchāgāhanivattanatthaṃ, tasmā “na sammāvattanto paṇāmetabbo”ti vuttattā anāpattikā katāti. Dukkaṭāpatti hotīti ācariyo, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. “Kappiyabhaṇḍampi akappiyamevāti taḷākato nipphannadhaññena parivattetvā laddhaṃ gorasampi na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

In all cases, what is called 'acceptance' is precisely of the characteristic thus stated: 'one should receive, or cause to be received, or consent to what is placed nearby.' Even so, in some cases it should be rejected, in some cases it should not be rejected; in some cases, it is allowable to consent to what has been rejected, and thus, something not rejected is allowable. To show all this, the detailed exposition beginning with 'But if...' has been undertaken. Therein, from the statement 'for a shrine... it is not allowable,' it is established that it is allowable to consent to what is given to a monastery without being rejected. Similarly, even when it is said to the elder, 'Let us give to the mother,' etc., on account of receiving, the offense is a pācittiya indeed. In the phrase 'He becomes an offender,' by what offense does he become an offender? Some say it is by a dukkaṭa offense. It is not by just any offense; it is said, 'he becomes an offender,' simply because he reproaches in an inappropriate place. How so? In the passage, 'Monks, a co-resident endowed with five factors should be dismissed... one who dismisses is not at fault,' it is stated that for one who does not dismiss a person who is not behaving properly, there is a dukkaṭa offense. As it is said: 'And, monks, one who is not behaving properly should be dismissed; whoever should not dismiss him, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.' Therefore, even in the absence of excessive affection, etc., no offense is seen for one who does not dismiss. Moreover, it is said, 'He is at fault.' This should be seen as an example of this. If one should say that this is not proper because in the commentary it is said, '"He is at fault" means he is with fault, he incurs an offense,' this is not so. Immediately after that, it is for the purpose of dispelling that wrong grasp; therefore, because it is said, 'one who is not behaving properly should be dismissed,' it is made to be a non-offense. The teacher says that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred; this should be investigated. It is said: 'Even an allowable requisite becomes unallowable,' thus even milk products obtained by exchanging them for grain produced from a reservoir are not allowable.

Kappiyavohārepi vidhānaṃ vakkhāma, seyyathidaṃ – “udakavasenā”tiādi. Dubbinibbhogaṃ hotīti idaṃ parato “tasseva akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Dhaññassa vicāritattā”ti iminā asadisaṃ, tasmā suvuttaṃ. Idañhi bhikkhussa payogavasena ādito paṭṭhāya uppannena missanti. Akatapubbaṃ navasassaṃ nāma. Khale vā ṭhatvā rakkhatīti “idaṃ vā ettakaṃ vā mā gaṇha, idaṃ gahetuṃ labbhatī”ti vā “ito apanehi, idha puñjaṃ karohī”ti evamādinā vā payogena [V 0.0223] ce rakkhati, taṃ akappiyaṃ. “Sace ‘mayiṭhite rakkhitaṃ hotī’ti rakkhati, gaṇhante vā passitvā ‘kiṃ karothā’ti, bhaṇati vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Rūpiyapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpade “dvāraṃ pidahitvā rakkhantena vasitabba”nti hi [M 0.0250] vuttaṃ. Tasseva taṃ akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Apubbassa anuppāditattā. Heṭṭhā “sassaṃ katvā āharathā”ti vattuṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti. Paṇṇepi eseva nayo. “Pakatiyā sayameva karontānaṃ ussāhajananato”ti vuttaṃ. Kasmā? “Kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattā”ti vacanato, pageva uṭṭhāpitattāti siddhaṃ hoti. Sace dāyakā vā saṅghassa gāmakhettārāmādiṃ keṇiyā gahitamanussā vā tattha kuṭumbino “ime saṅghassa kahāpaṇā āhaṭā”ti vadanti, “na kappatī”ti ettakameva vattabbaṃ. Kappiyakārakāva ce vadanti, “saṅghassa kahāpaṇā na kappanti, sappiādīni vaṭṭantī”ti vattabbaṃ, tasmā “saṅghassa kappiyakārake vā guttaṭṭhānaṃ vā ācikkhathā”ti vatvā tehi sampāditaṃ kenaci akattabbatāya “iminā sappiṃ āharāhī”ti vicāreti niṭṭhāpetvā itaresaṃ kappiyaṃ parato pattacatukke catutthapatto viya. Vuttañhi tattha “ime kahāpaṇe gahetvā imaṃ dehī’ti kahāpaṇe dāpetvā gahito, ayaṃ patto etasseva bhikkhuno na vaṭṭati, dubbicāritattā, aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭati, mūlassa asampaṭicchitattā”tiādi. Yadi evaṃ sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ. Kasmā? Kahāpaṇānaṃ vicāritattāti. Idaṃ duvuttanti ce? Na, mūlassa sampaṭicchitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya imassa vuttattā pattacatukke dutiyatatiyapattā viya, teneva vuttaṃ sayaṃkārivāre “na kappatī”ti ettakameva vattabba’nti. Tato paraṃ mūlaṃ sampaṭicchati nāma.

We will explain the procedure regarding permissible transactions, namely, that beginning with 'by means of water.' This statement, 'it is difficult to separate,' is not similar to the later statement, 'it is impermissible for him alone. Why? Because the grain was managed'; therefore, it is well-said. Indeed, this is mixed from the very beginning with the grain that has arisen through the monk's effort. What has not been previously done is called new grain. If, standing on the threshing floor, he guards it with such efforts as saying, 'Do not take this or that much,' or 'This is allowed to be taken,' or 'Remove it from here, make a pile here,' then that is impermissible. It is said, 'If he guards it thinking, "While I am present, it is guarded," or if, seeing those who are taking it, he says, "What are you doing?" it is allowable,' and that is proper. For indeed, in the training rule on accepting money, it is said, 'One should dwell, having closed the door and guarding.' For that very one, it is impermissible. Why? Because what was new was not produced by him. However, it should be known that it is not allowable to say below, 'Having prepared the grain, bring it.' In the case of leaves also, this is the same principle. It is said, 'Because of generating effort in those who are doing it naturally by themselves.' Why? Because of the statement, 'due to the kahāpaṇas having been managed,' it is established that it was prompted from the very beginning. If donors, or people who have taken a village, field, monastery grounds, etc., of the Saṅgha on rent, or householders there, say, 'These kahāpaṇas for the Saṅgha have been brought,' only this much should be said: 'It is not permissible.' If the stewards themselves say, it should be said: 'Kahāpaṇas are not permissible for the Saṅgha; ghee and so forth are allowable.' Therefore, having said, 'Inform us of the Saṅgha's steward or a safe place,' some monk manages what has been procured by them—because it is not fit to be done otherwise—by settling the matter, saying, 'With this, bring ghee.' For the other monks, it is permissible, like the fourth bowl in the section on the four bowls later on. For it has been said there: 'A bowl taken after having caused kahāpaṇas to be given with the words, "Having taken these kahāpaṇas, give this," is not allowable for that very monk, due to being improperly managed. But for others it is allowable, because the price was not accepted by them,' and so on. If so, it would be impermissible for all. Why? Because the kahāpaṇas were managed. If it is said, 'This is poorly stated'? No, because this was said with reference to the place where the price is accepted, it is like the second and third bowls in the section on the four bowls. For that very reason, it was said in the section on acting by oneself: 'Only this much should be said: "It is not permissible."' Beyond that, it is called 'accepting the price'.

Mahāvisayasikkhattā, rājasikkhāpadaṃ idaṃ;

Rañño viya duviññeyyaṃ, cittādhippāyatopi vā.

This training rule concerning the king is difficult to understand, just as the mind of a king is, either because of its great scope of training or because of its profound intention.

Rājasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning rulers is concluded.

Niṭṭhito cīvaravaggo paṭhamo.

The first division, the section on robes, is concluded.

2. Kosiyavaggo

2. The Division on Silk

1. Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Silk

542. Kosiyakārakoti [V 0.0224] ettha kosaṃ karontīti “kosakārā”ti laddhavohārānaṃ pāṇakānaṃ kosato nibbattaṃ kosiyaṃ nāma. Attanā kataṃ ce? Nissajjanakāle “sayaṃ kataṃ nissaggiya”nti vattabbaṃ. Ubhohi [M 0.0251] ce kataṃ, yathāpāṭhameva vattabbaṃ. Attanā ca parehi ca vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpetītiādicatukkampi sambhavantaṃ na dassitaṃ. Vinayadhammatā hesā, yadidaṃ ekasmiṃ tike vā catukke vā dassite itaraṃ sambhavantampi na vuccatīti.

542. Here, in the section on the silk-maker: that which is produced from the cocoon of creatures who have received the designation 'cocoon-makers' (kosakārā) because 'they make a cocoon' (kosaṃ karonti), is called silk (kosiya). If it is made by oneself? At the time of relinquishment, it should be stated, 'Made by myself, it is to be forfeited.' If it is made by both, it should be stated just as in the text. The tetrad beginning with 'what was left unfinished by oneself and others, one finishes oneself,' although possible, is not shown. For this is the nature of the Vinaya: that when one triad or tetrad is shown, another, although possible, is not stated.

Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning silk is concluded.

2. Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Pure Black

547. Suddhakāḷakānanti ettha yathā paṭhame “ekenapi kosiyaṃsunā”ti vuttaṃ, tathā idha “ekenapi aññena amissetvā”ti vacanābhāvato aññehi missabhāve satipi apaññāyamānarūpakaṃ “suddhakāḷaka”micceva vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

547. Here, regarding 'pure black': just as it was said in the first training rule, 'even with one silk thread,' so here, due to the absence of the statement 'without mixing with even one other,' even if there is a state of being mixed with other wools, if its appearance is not discernible, it should be understood that it is called simply 'pure black'.

Suddhakāḷakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning pure black is concluded.

3. Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Two Parts

552. “Dhārayitvā dve tulā ādātabbā”ti vacanato yathā tulādhāraṇāya kāḷakā adhikā na honti, tathā kāḷakānaṃ dve bhāvā gahetabbā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti? Suddhakāḷakapaṭisedhananidānena. Tatiyaṃ odātānaṃ catutthaṃ gocariyānanti heṭṭhimaparicchedo. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ekassapi kāḷakalomassa atirekabhāve nissaggiya”nti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ, taṃ tulādhāraṇāya kiñcāpi na sameti, acittakattā pana sikkhāpadassa pubbe tulāya dhārayitvā ṭhapitesu ekampi lomaṃ tattha [V 0.0225] pateyya nissaggiyanti adhippāyoti no takko. Aññathā dve tulā nādātabbā, ūnakatarā ādātabbā siyuṃ. Na hi lomaṃ gaṇetvā tulādhāraṇā karīyati. Atha gaṇetvāva kātabbaṃ. Kiṃ tulādhāraṇāya payojananti keci. “Gocariyaodātesu ekameva diguṇaṃ katvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ avicāritattā vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

552. In accordance with the statement, 'Having weighed them, two measures should be taken,' two parts of the black wool should be taken as the maximum limit, so that by weighing, the black wool is not in excess. How is this known? By the reason for the prohibition of purely black wool. The phrase 'a third part of white, a fourth part of tawny' is the minimum limit. However, in the Mātikā Commentary, it is said: 'If even one black wool fiber is in excess, it is to be forfeited.' Although this does not accord with weighing, our reasoning is this: because the training rule is unintentional, the meaning is that even if one were to weigh it beforehand and set it aside, if even a single fiber were to fall there, it is to be forfeited. Otherwise, two measures should not be taken; a lesser amount should be taken. Indeed, weighing is not done by counting the fibers. Then must it be done only by counting? What, then, would be the use of weighing? Some say: 'Among the tawny and white wools, it is permissible to take one of them, having made it double.' Because this is not examined in the Commentary, it should be investigated.

Dvebhāgasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning two parts is concluded.

4. Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Six Years

562. Navaṃ [M 0.0252] nāma karaṇaṃ upādāyāti idaṃ ādikaraṇato paṭṭhāya vassagaṇanaṃ dīpeti. Karitvā vāti vacanaṃ niṭṭhānadivasato paṭṭhāyāti dīpeti. Dhāretabbanti vacanaṃ pana paribhogato paṭṭhāyāti dīpeti, yasmā laddhasammutikassa gatagataṭṭhāne channaṃ channaṃ vassānaṃ oratova katāni bahūnipi honti, tasmā aññaṃ navanti kiṃ katato aññaṃ, udāhu dhāritato aññanti? Kiñcettha yadi katato aññaṃ, tesu aññataraṃ dukkataṃ vā paribhogajiṇṇaṃ vā puna kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tañca kho vināpi purāṇasanthatassa sugatavidatthiṃ appaṭisiddhapariyāpannattā. Katato hi aññaṃ paṭisiddhaṃ, idañca pubbakatanti tato anantarasikkhāpadavirodho hoti. Atha dhāritato aññaṃ nāma, sammuti niratthikā āpajjati, paṭhamakataṃ ce aparibhuttaṃ, satiyāpi sammutiyā aññaṃ navaṃ na vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo? Tatridaṃ sanniṭṭhānanidassanaṃ – niṭṭhānadivasato paṭṭhāya channaṃ channaṃ vassānaṃ paricchedo veditabbo. Tattha ca sattame vasse sampatte chabbassāni paripuṇṇāni honti. Tañca kho māsaparicchedavasena, na vassaparicchedavasena. Sattame paripuṇṇañca ūnakañca vassaṃ nāma, tasmā vippakatasseva sace chabbassāni pūrenti, puna niṭṭhānadivasato paṭṭhāya chabbassāni labhanti. Tañca kho paribhuttaṃ vā hotu aparibhuttaṃ vā, dhāritameva nāma. Yasmā “navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā channaṃ vassānaṃ parato tameva pubbakataṃ dukkatabhāvena, paribhogajiṇṇatāya vā vijaṭetvā puna karoti, niṭṭhānadivasato paṭṭhāya chabbassaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ, atirekaṃ vā. Anto ce karoti, tadeva aññaṃ navaṃ nāma hoti karaṇaṃ upādāya, tasmā nissaggiyaṃ. Aññathā “navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāyā”ti iminā na koci viseso atthi. Evaṃ sante kiṃ hoti? Aṭṭhuppattīti. “Yācanabahulā viññattibahulā viharantī”ti hi tattha vuttaṃ, tañca aññassa karaṇaṃ dīpeti. Yadi evaṃ taṃ nibbisesameva āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati. Ayaṃ panassa viseso, yasmā “aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjati, anāpattī”ti vuttattho visesoti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti[V 0.0226]? “Navaṃ nāma karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccatī”ti vutte atirekacīvarassa uppatti viya paṭilābhenassa uppatti navatā āpajjati. Tato paṭiladdhadivasato paṭṭhāya [M 0.0253] chabbassaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ. Orena ce channaṃ vassānaṃ…pe… kārāpeyya, nissaggiyanti āpajjati, tasmā navaṃ nāma karaṇameva upādāya vuccati, na paṭilābhaṃ. Orena channaṃ vassānaṃ attano anuppannattā “nava”nti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ, appaṭiladdhaṃ ce kārāpeyya, yathā lābho, tathā kareyya vā kārāpeyya vāti ca na hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjati, anāpattīti visesoti.

562. 'New' is said with reference to the making; this indicates the counting of years from the initial making. The statement 'or having made' indicates counting from the day of completion. But the statement 'should be used' indicates counting from the time of use. Since for one who has received permission, many rugs may be made in various places even within six years, therefore, what is 'another new one'? Is it other than what is made, or other than what is used? Moreover, if it is 'other than what is made', then it is permissible to remake any one of them, whether it was badly made or worn out from use, and that too without the Sugata's span of the old rug, because it is included in what is not forbidden. For 'another than what was made' is forbidden, and this was made before; therefore, there is a contradiction with the immediately subsequent training rule. But if it is 'another than what is used', the permission becomes meaningless. Is the intention that if the first-made rug is unused, even with permission, another new one is not allowable? Here is the decisive explanation: The period of six years should be understood as counted from the day of completion. And there, when the seventh year arrives, six years are completed. And that is by way of reckoning by months, not by way of reckoning by years. In the seventh year, a year is called both complete and incomplete. Therefore, if six years are completed for an unfinished rug, they obtain another six years from the day of completion. And that, whether it has been used or not used, is indeed called 'used'. Since it is said, "'New' is said with reference to the making," therefore, after six years, if one unravels that same previously made rug—due to its being badly made or worn out from use—and remakes it, it should be used for a maximum of six years from the day of completion, or more. If one remakes it within that period, that very rug is called 'another new one' with reference to the making; therefore, it is to be forfeited. Otherwise, by this phrase "'New' is said with reference to the making," there is no distinction. If this is so, what is the result? The distinction is the origin story. For it is said there, "They dwell asking much, requesting much," and that indicates the making of another. If so, does it become without distinction? It does not. But this is its distinction: the stated meaning, "If one obtains what is made by another and uses it, there is no offense," is the distinction. What is meant by this? If, when it is said, "'New' is said with reference to the making," its arising through acquisition were to constitute 'newness'—just like the arising of an extra robe—then it would follow that from the day of acquisition, it should be used for a maximum of six years. If one had it made within six years... it would have to be forfeited. Therefore, 'new' is said with reference only to the making, not to acquisition. Within six years, because it has not arisen for oneself, it is reckoned as 'new'. And it is not the case that if one has it made without having acquired it, one may make it or have it made in whatever way one might acquire it. Why? Because the distinction is: "If one obtains what is made by another and uses it, there is no offense."

Chabbassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Six Years is concluded.

5. Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Sitting-Rug

565. Nāssudha kocīti ettha assudha-iti avadhāraṇatthe nipāto. Tattha kiñcāpi “evaṃ bhanteti kho te bhikkhū”ti bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi te bhikkhū bhagavato paṭissuṇitvā idha tesu bhikkhūsu koci bhagavantaṃ nāssudha upasaṅkamati aññatra ekenāti attho gahetabbo. Taṃ suggāhaṃ ekāhaṃ bhante bhagavantaṃ varantiādīsu (mahāva. 337) viya, anujānāmi…pe… yathāsukhaṃ maṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamantūti dassanatthāya upasaṅkamantu.

565. Herein, in 'nāssudha koci', the word 'assudha' is a particle in the sense of emphasis. Therein, although the plural is stated in 'evaṃ bhante ti kho te bhikkhū', nevertheless, the meaning to be understood is this: after those bhikkhus had assented to the Blessed One, here among those bhikkhus, not even one approached the Blessed One, except for one. This is a good understanding, just as in cases such as 'For one day, venerable sir, they attend on the Blessed One' and so on. In 'I allow... let them approach me for a sight as they please', this means 'let them approach for the purpose of seeing'.

566-7. “Mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ upasena”nti tassa gaṇapāmokkhattā vuttaṃ. Āraññikapiṇḍapātikapaṃsukūlikavasena sabbāni vuttāni. Tenevāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “santhate catutthacīvarasaññitāyā”ti. Kiṃ sabbepi te cīvaraṃ na bujjhantīti ce? Yathā hotu. Katamaṃ cīvaraṃ nāmāti? Channaṃ aññataraṃ vikappanupagaṃ pacchimanti. Kiñca vāyimaṃ avāyimanti? Vāyimamevāti. Katarasuttenāti? Addhā so suttameva na passati, siveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ, iddhimayikañca devadattiyañca acīvaraṃ karoti. Yadi evaṃ avāyimampīti vadāmīti. Evaṃ sante siddhā santhate cīvarasaññitā kambalasīsena uṇṇāmayasāmaññato. Kiṃ pana te santhataṃ adhiṭṭhahiṃsūti? Duṭṭhu adhiṭṭhahiṃsu acīvarattā, na adhiṭṭhānupagattā ca santhatassa. Atha nādhiṭṭhahiṃsu, pubbeva tattha acīvarasaññino eteti katvā tattha cīvarasaññitāya tadubhayaṃ na yujjatīti. Kiṃ panetaṃ adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ natthīti? Tatthevāgataṃ[M 0.0254], apicetaṃ avikappanupagaṃ ce, cīvaraṃ na hoti, aññathā “cīvaraṃ nāma channaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññatara”nti ettāvatā siddhaṃ “vikappanupagaṃ pacchima”nti na vattabbaṃ. Atha na vikappanupagampi cīvarameva siddhaṃ, anadhiṭṭhānupagaṃ[V 0.0227], avikappanupagañca ekajjhaṃ “cīvara”nti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tenevāha “tecīvarikassa catutthacīvaraṃ vattamānaṃ aṃsakāsāvameva vaṭṭatī”ti.

566-7. 'We [go to] the venerable Upasena' was said because he was the leader of that group. All the ascetic practices were stated by way of forest-dwelling, alms-gathering, and rag-robe wearing. For that reason, the commentary says, 'because of the perception of a fourth robe in a felt rug.' If it is asked, 'Do all of them not understand what a robe is?'—let it be so. What is called a robe? The last one among the six that is suitable for `vikappana`. And is it woven or un-woven? It is indeed woven. By which Sutta? Surely, that person does not see the Sutta itself; he makes the pair of cloths from the Sivi country, the one created by psychic power, and the one given by a deva not a robe. If so, one should say that even an un-woven item is a robe. This being so, the perception of a robe in a felt rug is established, due to the commonality of being made of wool, with the woolen blanket as the primary example. But did they determine the felt rug? They determined it wrongly, because it was not a robe and because the felt rug is not suitable for determination. Or, if they did not determine it, it is because they already had the perception of it not being a robe; having considered thus, because of the perception of it not being a robe there, neither of the two [woven or un-woven] is applicable. But is there then no felt rug that is suitable for determination? It is stated right there. Moreover, if that which is unsuitable for `vikappana` is not a robe, then otherwise, it would be established by just this much: 'A robe is any one of the six robes,' and it would not be necessary to say, 'the last one, suitable for `vikappana`.' Or, if it is not established, then that which is unsuitable for determination and that which is unsuitable for `vikappana` are taken together and are counted as a 'robe.' Therefore, it is said, 'For one who practices with three robes, when a fourth robe is present, only the shoulder-cloth is allowable.'

Apica santhate cīvarasaññitā na kevalaṃ tesaṃyeva, aññesampi anubandhati eva “purāṇasanthataṃ nāma sakiṃ nivatthampi sakiṃ pārutampī”ti vacanato. Aṭṭhakathācariyo panassa acīvarataṃ sandhāyabhāsitatthadīpanena dīpeti. Nivatthapārutanti etesaṃ nisinnañceva nipannañcāti attho. Apica evaṃ santepi santhate cīvarasaññitā anubandhati eva. Khandhake (mahāva. 358) hi “nisīdanaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ na vikappetu”nti ca, parivāre (pari. 329) “nava cīvarāni adhiṭṭhātabbānī”ti ca nisīdanasikkhāpade “dasā vidatthī”ti ca idha “nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccatī”ti ca vuttaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyañcassa “santhatasadisaṃ santharitvā ekasmiṃ ante sugatavidatthiyā vidatthimattapadese dvīsu ṭhānesu phāletvā tisso dasā karīyanti, tāhi dasāhi sadasaṃ nāma vuccatī”ti ca “nisīdanaṃ vuttanayena adhiṭṭhātabbameva, tañca kho pamāṇayuttaṃ ekameva, dve na vaṭṭantī”ti ca vuttaṃ, tasmā nisīdanaṃ nāma navannaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, tañca santhatasadisaṃ eḷakalomamayasanthatavisesanti siddhaṃ, tathā nisīdanameva nisīdanasanthatañca siddhaṃ. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade ca “ekamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ siddhe siddhā santhate cīvarasaññitāti attho. Kasmā? Santhatasāmaññato.

Moreover, the perception of a robe in a felt rug applies not only to those monks, but it certainly follows for others as well, because of the saying: 'An old felt rug is that which has been worn once or put on once.' The commentary teacher, however, with reference to its state of not being a robe, elucidates it by explaining the meaning of what was said. The meaning of 'worn' and 'put on' is 'having been sat upon and having been lain upon.' Furthermore, even so, the perception of a robe in a felt rug certainly follows. Indeed, in the Khandhaka it is said, 'One should determine a sitting-cloth, not make it a shared item'; and in the Parivāra, 'Nine robes are to be determined'; and in the training rule on the sitting-cloth, 'The border is a span'; and here, 'A sitting-cloth is called "that which has a border".' And in its commentary it is said: 'Having spread something similar to a felt rug, at one end, in a place the measure of a Sugata's span, having split it in two places, three borders are made; by means of those borders it is called "that which has a border".' And it is said: 'A sitting-cloth should indeed be determined in the manner stated; and that, endowed with the proper measure, should be only one; two are not allowable.' Therefore, what is called a sitting-cloth is a certain robe among the nine robes to be determined. And that, being similar to a felt rug, is established as a special felt rug made of sheep's wool. Likewise, the sitting-cloth itself and the sitting-cloth-felt-rug are established. And in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada, it is said, 'Only one.' When that is established, the meaning is that the perception of a robe in a felt rug is established. Why? Because of the commonality of being a felt rug.

Etthāha – kathaṃ adasameva santhataṃ cīvarasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Anekampi anadhiṭṭhitampi mahantampi vaṭṭati, yato sadasameva santhataṃ cīvarasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, tato adhiṭṭhānañca upagacchatīti. Asanthatapariyāpannattā orena ca channaṃ vassānaṃ vināpi sammutiṃ, tañca porāṇaṃ vissajjetvā eva, na avissajjetvā “tañca kho pamāṇayuttaṃ ekameva, dve na vaṭṭantī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.469) vacanatoti. Athāpi siyā santhataṃ sayanatthameva karīyati, nisīdanaṃ asanthatamevāti. Tañca na niyamato “purāṇasanthataṃ nāma sakiṃ nivatthaṃ sakiṃ pārutampī”ti vuttattāti. Ettha vuccati, na ettha kāraṇaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ vinayapaññattiyā anaññavisayattā.

Here, a questioner says: How is it that a felt mat without a border does not attain the designation of 'robe'? A borderless felt mat is allowable even if there are many, even if they are not determined, and even if they are large. Since only a felt mat with a border attains the designation of 'robe', determination is therefore suitable for it. [The answer is:] Because it is not included in the category of a felt mat, [a sitting-cloth] is counted as a robe. And [a new one may be made] within six years even without authorization, but that is only after having relinquished the old one, not without having relinquished it, according to the statement: 'And that very one should be of the proper measure; only one is allowable, two are not allowable.' Or, it might be the view of some that a felt mat is made only for the purpose of a bed, and a sitting-cloth is indeed not a felt mat. But that view should not be held as a fixed rule, because it has been said: 'An old felt mat is one that has been worn once or wrapped around once.' Here, it is said: A reason should not be sought in this matter, because a Vinaya regulation is not the domain of anyone other than the Buddha.

Santhatassa [M 0.0255] pana acīvarabhāve ayaṃ yutti – ādito “tīṇi santhatāni pana vinayakammaṃ katvā paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭantī”ti aṭṭhakathāvacanato tāni akappiyānīti siddhaṃ, bhagavatā ca khomādīni cha anuññātānīti koseyyaṃ kappiyanti siddhaṃ. Evaṃ sante suddhakoseyyampi cīvaraṃ kappiyaṃ jātaṃ, pageva kosiyamissakasanthatacīvaranti [V 0.0228] āpajjati. Tathā kambalañca anuññātaṃ, tañca suddhikampi hoti jātikāḷakabhāvena, pageva odātagocariyamissakasanthatacīvaranti āpajjati. Tato ca aññamaññavirodho, tasmā na santhataṃ cīvaraṃ nāma hoti, nisīdanaṃ pana hoti tassa pamāṇasaṇṭhānaparicchedasambhavato. Etthāhu keci ācariyā “duvidhaṃ nisīdanaṃ santhataṃ, asanthatañca. Tattha santhataṃ santhatameva. Asanthataṃ khomādichabbidhaṃ, tadanulomaṃ vā hoti, ayametesaṃ viseso”ti.

But regarding the felt mat's state of not being a robe, this reasoning should be known: From the beginning, because of the statement in the commentary, 'Three kinds of felt mats, even if obtained after performing a Vinaya act, are not allowable to be used,' it is established that they are unallowable. And since the Blessed One permitted six kinds of material for robes, such as linen, it is established that silk is allowable. This being so, a robe of even pure silk becomes allowable; what then needs to be said of a felt-mat-robe mixed with silk? This conclusion would arise. Similarly, woolen cloth was also permitted, and that woolen cloth, even when pure, is allowable by its nature of being naturally black; what then needs to be said of a felt-mat-robe mixed with the wool of white and dappled sheep? This conclusion would arise. And from that, a mutual contradiction arises. Therefore, a felt mat is not called a 'robe.' A sitting-cloth, however, is a robe, because of the possibility of determining its measure, shape, and boundary. Here, some teachers say: 'A sitting-cloth is of two kinds: felted and non-felted. Among them, the felted one is just a felt mat. The non-felted one is of the six kinds, such as linen, or is in conformity with them. This is the distinction between them.'

Etthāha – kasmā panettha “santhataṃ pana bhikkhunā”ti sikkhāpadaṃ apaññāpetvā “nisīdanasanthata”nti paññattanti? Cīvarasaññitāya santhatānaṃ ujjhitattā tesaṃ acīvarabhāvadassanatthaṃ tathā paññattanti vuttaṃ hoti, tasmā te bhikkhū dhutaṅgabhedabhayā tāni ujjhitvā terasāpi dhutaṅgāni samādiyiṃsu, sīsadassanavasena tīṇeva vuttāni, bhagavā ca tesaṃ santhataṃ anujāni, tato nesaṃ evaṃ hoti “nisīdanacīvarasaṇṭhānampetaṃ nisīdanasanthataṃ no anuññātaṃ, catutthacīvarabhāvena pageva katasanthataṃ vā”ti. Tato santhate nesaṃ cīvarasaññitā na bhavissatīti tadatthaṃ bhagavatā nisīdanasanthatanti paññattanti adhippāyo. “Pacchimāni dve vaṭṭantī”ti kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? “Anāpatti aññena kataṃ paṭilabhitvā paribhuñjatī”ti vacanatoti.

Here it is said: Why, in this case, was the training rule not laid down as, 'A felt mat, however, by a bhikkhu,' but was instead laid down as, 'a sitting-felt-mat'? It is said that it was laid down in that way because the felt mats were discarded due to the perception of them as robes, and to show that they were not robes. Therefore, those bhikkhus, fearing the breach of the ascetic practices, discarded them and undertook all thirteen ascetic practices. Only three were mentioned as principal examples. And the Blessed One permitted them a felt mat. Then this thought occurred to them: 'Even this sitting-felt-mat, which has the appearance of a sitting-robe, is not permitted; how much more so a felt mat made as a fourth robe!' Therefore, so that their perception of the felt mat as a robe would not arise, the Blessed One laid it down as 'a sitting-felt-mat.' This is the intention. If it is asked, 'How is it known that "the latter two are allowable"?', it is known from the statement, 'There is no offense in obtaining and using one made by another.'

Nisīdanasanthatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting-felt-mat is concluded.

6. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Sheep's Wool

572-3. Addhānamaggappaṭipannassāti iminā pakatiyā dīghamaggappaṭipannassa uppannānipi tiyojanaparamameva haritabbāni, pageva appaṭipannassāti dasseti. Addhānamaggappaṭipannassa nissaggiyanti vā sambandho. Teneva vāsādhippāyassa paṭippassaddhagamanussāhattā “appaṭipanno”ti saṅkhyaṃ gatassa [M 0.0256] anāpattīti siddhā. Imasmiṃ atthavikappe hi bhikkhuno paneva eḷakalomāni uppajjeyyuṃ…pe… asantepi hārake addhānaṃ maggappaṭipannassa nissaggiyaṃ pācittiyanti yojanā veditabbā. Ākaṅkhamānena bhikkhunā paṭiggahetabbānīti attano santakānaṃyeva tiyojanātikkame āpattiṃ dasseti. Tena anākaṅkhamānena parasantakāni paṭiggahitāni atirekatiyojanaṃ harantassa anāpatti siddhā. Ayamattho “bhikkhuno uppajjeyyu”nti iminā, “acchinnaṃ paṭilabhitvā”ti iminā ca dīpitova hotīti. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade [V 0.0229] ca “aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ harāpento gacchati ce, dvinnaṃ anāpattīti vuttaṃ, tasmā dve bhikkhū tiyojanaparamaṃ patvā aññamaññassa bhaṇḍaṃ parivattetvā ce haranti, anāpattīti siddhaṃ, teneva anāpattivāre “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiṃ harāpeti? Jānantaṃ ajānantaṃ. Kiñcettha yadi jānantaṃ, “añño harissatīti ṭhapeti, tena haritepi āpattiyevā”ti ekaṃsato na vattabbaṃ. Jānantopi hi ekacco haratīti. Tato aṭṭhakathāya virujjhati. Atha ajānantaṃ, “aññassa yāne vā bhaṇḍe vā ajānantassa pakkhipitvā tiyojanaṃ atikkāmeti, nissaggiyānī”ti pāḷiyā virujjhati, atha ubhopi ekato ekaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ harāpenti, tampi nissaggiyaṃ siyā. Anissaggiyanti yuttiyā virujjhati “tiyojanaparamaṃ sahatthā haritabbāni asante hārake”ti avisesena ca pāḷi vuttā. Hārakopi sacetano acetanoti duvidho. Sacetanopi eḷakalomabhāvaṃ vā “ahamidaṃ harāmī”ti vā “maṃ esa idaṃ harāpetī”ti vā jānanājānanavasena duvidho hoti. Tattha acetano nāma hārako nadīsoto vā nāvā vā assāmikayānaṃ vā hoti. Sacetano pākaṭova. Tattha “maṃ esa idaṃ harāpetī”ti ettakaṃ jānantaṃ manussaṃ vā tiracchānagataṃ vā aññaṃ harāpeti, anāpattīti anugaṇṭhipadanayo. Ayaṃ pāḷiyā, aṭṭhakathāya ca ekaraso vinicchayo, “asante hārake”ti kiñcāpi idaṃ avisesato vuttaṃ, “aññassa yāne vā bhaṇḍe vā ajānantassā”ti vacanato pana sacetanova hārako tattha adhippetoti paññāyati, so ca eḷakalomabhāvañca “idaṃ harāmī”ti ca jānanto nādhippeto. Tena vuttaṃ “añño harissatīti ṭhapeti, tena haritepi āpattiyevā”tiādi. Tattha hetukattuno abhāvatova. Pāḷiyañhi “aññaṃ harāpetī”ti hetukattuvasena vuttā[M 0.0257]. Itare dve jānantā idha sambhavanti. “Ajānantassa pakkhipitvā”ti pāḷiyaṃ “esa harāpetī”ti vā “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamāpetī”ti vā jānantassa yāne vā bhaṇḍe vā pakkhipitvā tiyojanaṃ atikkamāpeti, na nissaggiyā hontīti dīpeti.

By “for one who has undertaken a long journey,” it is shown that for a monk who is naturally traveling a long road, even sheep's wool that has arisen should be carried for a maximum of three yojanas; how much more so for one who is not traveling. Or, the connection is: “For one who has undertaken a long journey, it is subject to forfeiture.” For that very reason, for one whose intention is to reside and whose effort in traveling has ceased, and who is thus counted as “not traveling,” it is established that there is no offense. Indeed, in this alternative meaning, the connection should be understood as: “If sheep's wool should arise for a monk... etc... even without a carrier, for one who has undertaken a long journey, it is a pācittiya offense involving forfeiture.” By the phrase “They are to be accepted by a monk who desires them,” it is shown that an offense occurs only in the exceeding of three yojanas with regard to his own property. Therefore, it is established that there is no offense for one who, not desiring them, carries another's property, which he has accepted, beyond three yojanas. This meaning is indeed clarified by “if they should arise for a monk” and by “having received them uncut.” And in the Ancient Gloss, it is said: “If, while causing another monk to carry it, he goes, there is no offense for the two of them.” Therefore, if two monks, having reached the limit of three yojanas, exchange each other's goods and carry them, it is established that there is no offense. For that very reason, in the section on non-offenses, it is said, “he causes another to carry.” Whom does he cause to carry? One who knows or one who does not know. And here, if it is one who knows, it should not be said definitively: “He puts it down thinking, ‘Another will carry it’; even when it is carried by that person, there is still an offense.” For a certain person might carry it even while knowing. Then it contradicts the Commentary. Now, if it is one who does not know, it contradicts the Pāli text: “Having placed it in another's vehicle or goods without their knowledge and causing it to exceed three yojanas, they are to be forfeited.” Or, if both together cause one item to be carried, that too would be subject to forfeiture. It contradicts the reasoning that it should not be subject to forfeiture, and the Pāli is stated without distinction: “They are to be carried by one's own hand for a maximum of three yojanas when there is no carrier.” A carrier, too, is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. The animate carrier is also of two kinds, depending on whether he knows or does not know: either the fact that it is sheep's wool, or “I am carrying this,” or “This person is causing me to carry this.” Therein, an inanimate carrier is a river current, a boat, or an ownerless vehicle. The animate one is obvious. Therein, if one causes another—be it a human or an animal—who knows only this much, “This person is causing me to carry this,” to carry it, there is no offense. This is the method of the sub-glosses. This is a consistent decision in both the Pāli and the Commentary. Although “when there is no carrier” is stated without distinction, from the phrase “in another's vehicle or goods without their knowledge,” it is understood that an animate carrier is indeed intended there. And that person is not intended to be one who knows that it is sheep's wool and “I am carrying this.” Therefore it is said: “He puts it down thinking, ‘Another will carry it’; even when it is carried by that person, there is still an offense,” and so on. Therein, it is precisely because of the absence of a causer. For in the Pāli, “he causes another to carry” is stated in the causative sense. The other two cases of knowing are possible here. The Pāli phrase “having placed it for one who does not know” clarifies that if one places it in the vehicle or goods of someone who knows either “this person is causing me to carry” or “he is causing me to go beyond this place,” and causes it to exceed three yojanas, the items do not become subject to forfeiture.

“Harāpetī”ti idaṃ hetukattuvacanataṃ sādheti, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sāmikassa ajānantassevā”ti idaṃ “maṃ esa harāpetī”ti evaṃ ajānantaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Sāreti codeti anubandhāpetī”ti idaṃ “maṃ esa idaṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamāpetī”ti evaṃ jānantaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ajānantopi sāraṇādīhi ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ nātikkamati, na vā anubandhati. Atha sāraṇādīhi anatikkamitvā attano ruciyā atikkamati āpatti eva bhikkhuno hetukattubhāvāsambhavato.

The word 'harāpeti' establishes the sense of a causative agent. Therefore, in the Commentary, the phrase 'even without the owner knowing' is said with reference to one who is unaware, thus: 'He is causing me to carry.' The phrase 'He reminds, incites, or causes to follow' is said with reference to one who is aware, thus: 'He is causing me to go beyond this place.' Even one who is unaware does not go beyond the place where he is through reminding and so on, nor does he follow. But if, without going beyond through reminding and so on, one goes beyond of one's own accord, it is an offense indeed for the bhikkhu, because the state of being a causative agent is impossible for him.

Idāni yathāṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya vakkhāma, “asantepi hārake”ti hārakālābhapaccayāpi sayaṃ [V 0.0230] haraṇato nissaggiyameva, pageva sati hāraketi ayameko attho. Avadhāraṇatthaṃ api-saddaṃ gahetvā asante eva hārake nissaggiyaṃ, sati pana hārake na tena harāpentassa nissaggiyanti ayaṃ dutiyo attho. “Saṅghato vā…pe… attano vā dhanenā”ti iminā kiñcāpi acittakamidaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ, saṅghādito pana attanā ākaṅkhamānena paṭiggahitasseva eḷakalomassa tiyojanātikkame āpatti, na ajānato appaṭiggahitassa cīvarādīsu kutoci laggassa atikkamaneti dīpeti. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “kambalassa upari nipajjitvā gacchantassa sace ekampi lomaṃ cīvare laggaṃ hoti, āpatti eva kambalato vijaṭitattā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ kambalassa paṭiggahitattā attano icchāya paṭiggahitameva hotīti yuttaṃ. Yasmā “anāpatti katabhaṇḍe”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā taṃ anekampi katabhaṇḍaṭṭhāniyameva hoti. Tañhi anena paṭiggahitaṃ, na lomaṃ. Atha lomampi aggahitameva hoti, katabhaṇḍaṃ dupparihāriyalomavinibbhogakatabhaṇḍo niyamo. Evaṃ sante akatabhaṇḍe tikapācittiyaṃ, katabhaṇḍe tikadukkaṭañca nayato dassetabbaṃ bhaveyya, aññathā tikassa dassitattā. Saussāhattāti appaṭippassaddhagamanattā. Acittakattā cāti bhikkhuno ussāhānurūpaṃ lomānaṃ tiyojanātikkamanato vināpi payogacittena haraṇacittena āpajjati evāti adhippāyo. Sā anāpatti pāḷiyā na sametīti [M 0.0258] anto pana payogena tiyojanaparamaṃ atikkamitattā anāpatti. “Tiyojanaṃ haratī”ti iminā tiyojanaṃ padasā netukāmopi antotiyojane pade pade dukkaṭaṃ nāpajjatīti dasseti, taṃ yuttaṃ “tiyojanaṃ vāsādhippāyo gantvā tato paraṃ haratī’ti vacanassatthitāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Punapi vuttaṃ “aññaṃ harāpetīti ‘idaṃ harissāmī’ti saussāhameva aññaṃ harāpetīti attho. Itarathā gacchantassa sīse ṭhapesi, tasmiṃ ajānantepi anāpatti siyā”ti. Sace pana “agacchante yāne vā”tiādinā nayena vuttattā haraṇādīhi janitaussāhānaṃ hatthiādīnaṃ ‘idaṃ karissāmā’ti vā ‘harissāmā’ti vā ābhoge janite eva anāpatti, na ajaniteti upatissatthero āhā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Parivattetvā ṭhapiteti dvinnampi bahi nikkhipitattāti upatissatthero. Bahisīmāya ṭhapitaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ anto antosīmāyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ bahi karoto anāpattīti keci, na sundaraṃ viya.

Now, starting from the established position, we shall explain. “Even when there is no carrier”: this means that if one carries it oneself due to the lack of a carrier, it is an offense requiring forfeiture; how much more so when there is a carrier. This is one meaning. Taking the word “api” for emphasis: it is an offense requiring forfeiture only when there is no carrier; but when there is a carrier, there is no offense for one who has it carried by him. This is the second meaning. By the phrase “From the Sangha or… with one’s own wealth,” it is shown that although this training rule is unintentional, an offense is incurred in exceeding three leagues only for sheep’s wool that has been received from the Sangha and so on by one desiring it for oneself; there is no offense for exceeding the limit with wool that has attached from somewhere to robes, etc., which has not been received by one who is unaware. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: “If one is traveling, having lain down upon a blanket, and if even a single hair becomes attached to the robe, it is indeed an offense, because it has been detached from the blanket.” This is appropriate, for since the blanket has been received, it is considered as having been received by one's own wish. Because it is said, “There is no offense for a finished article,” therefore even many such items are only in the category of a finished article. For it is the finished article that is received by him, not the loose wool. Then the wool is also indeed unreceived. The rule concerning a finished article is that it is an article made by the separation of difficult-to-manage wool. This being so, for an unfinished article a triple pācittiya, and for a finished article a triple dukkaṭa, should be indicated according to the method, because otherwise the triple offense has been shown. “With effort” means due to the movement not being calmed. “And because of being unintentional” means that a monk indeed incurs an offense when the wool exceeds three leagues in accordance with his effort, even without the intention of using it or the intention of carrying it; this is the meaning. That non-offense does not align with the Pāḷi. However, within the limit, because of traversing at most three leagues with effort, there is no offense. By “carries it three leagues,” it is shown that even one who intends to carry it step by step within three leagues does not incur a dukkaṭa offense at every step. This is appropriate, because of the existence of the statement, “Having gone three leagues with the intention of residing, one carries it further than that.” Again it is said: “‘Has another carry it’ means one has another carry it with effort, thinking ‘I will have this carried.’ Otherwise, if one placed it on the head of someone who is going, even if that person is unaware, there would be no offense.” And it is also said: “But if, as stated in the method beginning ‘or in a vehicle that is not going,’ for elephants, etc., whose effort is generated by carrying, etc., there is no offense only when the cognition ‘we will do this’ or ‘we will carry this’ is generated—not when it is not generated; thus said the Elder Upatissa.” “Having exchanged and placed” means because of having placed both outside, according to the Elder Upatissa. Some say there is no offense for one who brings a bundle placed outside the boundary inside, or takes what was placed inside the boundary outside; but this does not seem proper.

575. Paṭilabhitvā haratīti paṭhamatiyojanato paraṃ harati, na dutiyāditoti attho. Katabhaṇḍe uppannokāsābhāvā anāpatti.

575. “Having obtained, one carries it” means one carries it beyond the first three leagues, not from the second and so on; this is the meaning. There is no offense regarding a finished article because there is no occasion for it to arise.

Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning sheep’s wool is concluded.

7. Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having Sheep's Wool Washed

581. Kiñcāpi [V 0.0231] purāṇacīvaradhovanasikkhāpade cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā “aññaṃ parikkhāraṃ dhovāpetī”ti (pārā. 507) anāpattivāre vuttaṃ. Imassa pana sikkhāpadassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya eḷakalomadhovāpanādinā āpattīti eke. Sā vā anāpatti mūlāpattito eva, na imamhāti eke. Eḷakalomānaṃ aparikkhārattā bhaṭṭhaṃ aggahaṇamevāti eke. Imassa antimanayassa atthappakāsanatthaṃ idaṃ pañhākammaṃ – “dhovāpetī”ti idaṃ rajāpanavijaṭāpanaggahaṇena nippadesavācipadaṃ, udāhu aggahaṇena sappadesavācipadaṃ. Kiñcettha yadi nippadesavācipadaṃ, sabbattha idameva vattabbaṃ, na itarāni. Atha sappadesavācipadaṃ, “avuttā dhovati, aparibhuttaṃ dhovāpetī”ti ettha virodho. “Avuttā rajati vijaṭeti, nissaggiya”nti aniṭṭhappasaṅgatoti? Desanāvilāsamattaṃ [M 0.0259] bhagavato vacanaṃ, katthaci tikapadavacanaṃ, katthaci ekapadavacanaṃ, nippadesapadameva te vadantīti. Sace “katabhaṇḍaṃ dhovāpetī”ti ettha paṭivirodho, “katabhaṇḍaṃ vijaṭāpeti, anāpattī”ti aniṭṭhappasaṅgato anāpatti evāti ce? Na, akatabhaṇḍassa suddhalomassa vijaṭāpanaṃ ito vā dātabbaṃ. Udakādidhovanavasena piṇḍetvā ṭhitānaṃ vijaṭāpanaṃ labbhatīti ce? Purāṇasanthatassa vijaṭāpane anāpattiyā bhavitabbaṃ, na ca taṃ yuttaṃ “aparibhuttaṃ dhovāpetī”ti vacanato. Tena paribhuttaṃ dhovāpeti rajāpeti vijaṭāpeti, nissaggiyamevāti siddhaṃ hoti, tañca paribhuttaṃ nāma katabhaṇḍameva hoti. Na hi sakkā eḷakalomāni paribhuñjituṃ, aññathā “paribhuttaṃ dhovāpetī”ti vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ hoti. Na hi ettha “purāṇāni eḷakalomāni dhovāpeyya vā”ti vacanaṃ atthi purāṇacīvarasikkhāpade viya. Tattha ādinnakappavasena, idha taṃ likhitaṃ. Lekhadosoti ce? Na, visesahetuno abhāvā, purāṇacīvarasikkhāpade aparibhuttaṃ katabhaṇḍaṃ nāma, “kambalakojavasanthatādi”nti vacanato ca. Kiñcāpi iminā saddena ayamattho siddho, “dhovāpetī”ti idaṃ pana siyā nippadesaṃ. Siyā sappadesaṃ. Tañhi “avuttā dhovatī”tiādīsu nippadesaṃ. “Katabhaṇḍaṃ dhovāpetī”ti ettha sappadesaṃ. “Akatabhaṇḍaṃ dhovāpeti rajāpeti, anāpattī”ti “vijaṭāpeti, anāpattī”ti vacanappamāṇato anāpatti evāti ce? Na, vacanappamāṇato eva āpattīti āpajjanato. “Aparibhuttaṃ dhovāpetī”ti vacanameva hi taṃ aparibhuttaṃ santhataṃ vijaṭāpentassa anāpattīti dīpeti ce? Siddhaṃ paribhuttaṃ vijaṭāpentassa āpatti evāti.

581. Although in the training rule concerning the washing of old robes, it is stated in the section on no-offense that, setting aside a robe, there is no offense for having another requisite washed, some say that from the time this training rule was established, an offense is incurred by having sheep’s wool, etc., washed. Others say that that non-offense applies only to the root offense, not to this one. Some argue that since sheep’s wool is not a requisite, it is merely a case of not accepting what is spoiled. To clarify the meaning of this last opinion, this question is raised: Is the term ‘have it washed’ (dhovāpeti) an all-inclusive term, encompassing dyeing and carding, or a specific term, not encompassing them? And if it is an all-inclusive term, then this alone should be stated everywhere, not the others. But if it is a specific term, there is a contradiction in statements like ‘one washes without being asked’ or ‘one has an unused item washed.’ Is this due to the undesired consequence that ‘one dyes or cards without being asked, it is to be forfeited’? The Blessed One’s word is merely a matter of teaching style; sometimes it is a three-word expression, sometimes a one-word expression, but they express an all-inclusive meaning. If there is a contradiction regarding 'having a finished article washed', if it is said that there is indeed no offense due to the undesirable consequence 'having a finished article carded is no offense'? No, for the carding of an unfinished article, of pure wool, must be understood from this rule or elsewhere. If it is said that carding is possible for wool that has been balled up after washing it with water, etc.? There should be no offense for carding an old felt rug, but that is not correct because of the statement ‘one has an unused item washed.’ Therefore, it is established that having a used item washed, dyed, or carded is indeed to be forfeited, and that which is called ‘used’ is a finished article. For it is not possible to ‘use’ sheep’s wool; otherwise, the statement ‘one has a used item washed’ would be meaningless. Indeed, here there is no statement like ‘one may have old sheep’s wool washed’ as in the training rule concerning old robes. There, it is by way of the Ādinnakappa allowance; here, that has been written. Is this a scribal error? No, because there is no special reason, and because in the training rule concerning old robes, an ‘unused finished article’ refers to ‘a blanket, felt rug, mat, etc.’ Although this meaning is established by this word, the term ‘have it washed’ could be either all-inclusive or specific. For in phrases like ‘one washes without being asked,’ it is all-inclusive. But in ‘having a finished article washed,’ it is specific. If it is said that based on the authority of the statements ‘having an unfinished article washed or dyed is no offense’ and ‘having it carded is no offense,’ it is indeed no offense? No, precisely by the authority of the statement, it follows that an offense is incurred. If the very statement ‘one has an unused item washed’ indicates that there is no offense for one who has an unused felt rug carded? It is established that for one who has a used item carded, there is indeed an offense.

Eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule concerning having sheep's wool washed is concluded.

8. Rūpiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Training Rule concerning Money

583-4. Sabbampīti [V 0.0232] tividhampi. “Muttā maṇi veḷuriyo saṅkho’tiādi pana kiñcāpi rājasikkhāpade ‘na vaṭṭatī’ti pasaṅgato vuttaṃ, sarūpato pana āpattidassanavasena sakaṭṭhānepi vattumāraddha”nti vuttaṃ. Kathametaṃ? Muttādīnaṃ sakaṭṭhānaṃ jātaṃ, na hi tāni idha pāḷiyaṃ dissantīti imassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttāni, rājasikkhāpadassapi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttānīti. Na kevalaṃ [M 0.0260] hiraññasuvaṇṇameva, aññampi khettavatthādikaṃ “akappiyaṃ na sampaṭicchitabba”nti sāmaññena, na sarūpato. Pāḷiyaṃ pana sarūpato “cīvaracetāpannaṃ nāma hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā muttā vā maṇi vā”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, tasmā rājasikkhāpadamevassa sakaṭṭhānaṃ. Muttāmaṇiggahaṇena cettha tajjātiyaggahaṇaṃ siddhamevāti nāgato imassa paṭhamameva paññattattā. Yadi evaṃ idha anāgatattā kataraṃ nesaṃ sakaṭṭhānanti? Idameva atthato, no sarūpato.

All three kinds are included. However, although 'pearls, gems, beryl, conch,' and so on, were stated in the Rāja Sikkhāpada by way of implication as 'not allowable,' it has been said that 'it has begun to be spoken of in its own form, even in its proper place, by way of showing the offense.' How is this? The proper place for pearls and so on has been established. For, since they are not seen here in the Pāḷi text, they are mentioned in the commentary on this rule, and they are also mentioned in the commentary on the Rāja Sikkhāpada. Not only gold and silver, but also other things like fields and land are covered by the general statement, 'what is improper should not be accepted,' but not in their specific form. In the Pāḷi text, however, only this much is stated specifically: '“Money for robes” means gold or silver or pearls or gems.' Therefore, the Rāja Sikkhāpada itself is their proper place. And here, by the inclusion of pearls and gems, the inclusion of items of that kind is indeed established; it was not included because this was not laid down from the very beginning. If so, since it is not included here, which is their proper place? This very rule is their context in meaning, but not in specific form.

Kathaṃ? Etāni hi ratanasikkhāpade nissaggiyavatthūni, dukkaṭavatthūni ca ekato “ratana”nti āgatāni, “ratanasammata”nti kappiyavatthu āgataṃ. Tesu ca dasasu ratanesu rajatajātarūpadvayaṃ idha nissaggiyavatthu, avasesaṃ dukkaṭavatthūti siddhaṃ. Idha ca siddhattā eva ratanasikkhāpadassa anāpattivāre “ratanasammataṃ vissāsaṃ gaṇhāti, tāvakālikaṃ gaṇhāti, paṃsukūlasaññissā”ti vuttaṃ, na ratanaṃ vuttaṃ. Sattavidhadhaññadāsidāsakhettādi pana brahmajālādisuttavasena (dī. ni. 1.1 ādayo) akappiyanti siddhaṃ, tasmā idha dukkaṭavatthūti siddhaṃ, teneva anuyogavatte “dhammaṃ jānāti, dhammānulomaṃ, vinayaṃ, vinayānulomaṃ jānātī”ti (pari. 442) vuttaṃ. Tathā āmakamaṃsampi dukkaṭavatthuṃ āpajjatīti? Na, idha vinaye anuññātattā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, amanussikābādhe āmakamaṃsa”ntiādinā (mahāva. 264), tasmā na āmakamaṃsaṃ sutte āgatampi dukkaṭavatthu hoti, tathāpi attano paribhogatthāya paṭiggahaṇe dukkaṭamevāti no takkoti ācariyo. “Idha nikkhipāhī’ti vutte upanikkhittasādiyanameva hotī”ti vadanti. “Akappiyavicāraṇā eva na vaṭṭatīti ce? Kappiyañca akappiyañca nissāya ṭhitanti ettha taṃ sayaṃ aparibhogārahaṃ hutvā tadagghanakaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ paribhogārahaṃ hutvā ṭhitanti attho”ti likhitaṃ, “paṃsukūlabhāvena ṭhitattā, guttaṭṭhānācikkhanassa kappiyattā ca kappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. ‘Idaṃ gaṇhā’tiādinā vadantassa akappiyattā akappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhita”nti ca. Evampi kappiyañca akappiyañcāti “imasmiṃ okāse ṭhapitaṃ, kiṃ na passasīti chekatare imeva kahāpaṇe”tiādivacanassa kappiyattā kappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. “Idaṃ gaṇhā”ti vutte dubbicāritattā attano akappiyattā tato āgataṃ [V 0.0233] akappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitameva hoti. “Idaṃ gaṇhā’ti vutte tena gahite ‘uggaṇhāpeyya [M 0.0261] vā’ti vuttavidhiṃ na pāpuṇāti, kevalaṃ dubbicāritattā tasseva taṃ akappiyaṃ hoti, mūlapaṭiggahaṇassa suddhattā parato pattacatukke tatiyapatto viyāti ca evaṃ upatissatthero vadatī”ti anugaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Kiṃ bahunā, visuddhāgamattā kappiyaṃ. Dubbicāraṇāya sati akappiyaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ hotīti no takkoti ācariyo. “Evaṃ saṅghagaṇādīnampi atthāya pariccattepi tena samānagatikattā ṭhapetvā āpattivisesa”nti vuttaṃ.

How so? For in the training rule on valuables, these objects requiring forfeiture and objects involving a `dukkaṭa` offense have come together under the term 'valuable'. In the phrase 'regarded as valuable', a permissible object is mentioned. Among these ten valuables, the pair—silver and gold—are here objects requiring forfeiture, while the remainder are objects involving a `dukkaṭa` offense; thus it is established. And because this is established, in the non-offense section of the training rule on valuables, it is said: "He accepts what is regarded as valuable on trust, accepts it temporarily, for one who perceives it as refuse-rag cloth"—'valuable' is not said. However, the seven kinds of grain, female and male slaves, fields, and so on, are established as impermissible by way of the Brahmajāla Sutta and others; therefore, here they are established as objects involving a `dukkaṭa` offense. For that very reason, in the procedure of inquiry, it is said: "He knows the Dhamma, what is in conformity with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, what is in conformity with the Vinaya." Furthermore, does raw meat also become an object involving a `dukkaṭa` offense? No, because here in the Vinaya it is permitted by the text beginning, "I allow, monks, raw meat in case of an illness caused by non-humans." Therefore, even though raw meat is mentioned in a sutta, it is not an object involving a `dukkaṭa` offense. Nevertheless, in accepting it for one's own consumption, it is indeed a `dukkaṭa` offense; this is our reasoning, thus says the teacher. They say: "When it is said, 'Place it here,' it is only a matter of consenting to what is placed nearby." If one were to say, "Is not the very handling of an impermissible item disallowed?" In the phrase 'it stands depending on the permissible and the impermissible,' it is written that this is the meaning: that item, being itself unsuitable for use, stands as a permissible requisite of that value which has become suitable for use. And also: "Because it stands in the state of being refuse-cloth, and because of the permissibility of indicating a safe place, it stands depending on the permissible. Because of the impermissibility for one who says, 'Take this,' etc., it stands depending on the impermissible." Thus also, regarding 'the permissible and the impermissible': because of the permissibility of speech such as, "It is placed in this spot. Do you not see, O very clever one, these very coins?", it stands depending on the permissible. When it is said, "Take this," because of improper handling and because of its being impermissible for oneself, what has come from that indeed stands depending on the impermissible. It is said in the Anugaṇṭhipada: "When it is said, 'Take this,' and it is taken by him, it does not meet the procedure described as 'or he may cause it to be taken up.' Merely because of improper handling, it becomes impermissible for that very person. Because of the purity of the original acceptance, it is like the third bowl in the set of four bowls from another. Thus says the Elder Upatissa." What is the use of saying more? Because of its pure origin, it is permissible. When there is improper handling, it comes to stand depending on the impermissible; this is our reasoning, thus says the teacher. It is said: "Likewise, even when it is relinquished for the sake of the Sangha, a group, etc., because it has the same nature, it is treated similarly, setting aside the specific offense."

Na kiñci kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ cetāpitanti cetāpitañce, upāyābhāvaṃ dasseti. “Upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvāti sace so upāsako ‘atibahuṃ etaṃ hiraññaṃ, idaṃ bhante ajjeva na vināsetabba’nti vatvā sayaṃ upanikkhepadese ṭhapeti, aññena vā ṭhapāpeti, etaṃ upanikkhepaṃ ṭhapetvā tato laddhaṃ udayaṃ paribhuñjanto saṅgho paccaye paribhuñjati nāmā”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding the phrase 'No permissible requisite has been procured': if one has been procured, this shows the absence of a proper means. It is said: 'Regarding 'having set aside a deposit': if that lay supporter says, "Venerable Sir, this gold and silver is too much; it should not be wasted this very day," and either sets it aside himself in a place for deposits or has someone else set it aside, then, having set aside that deposit, the Sangha, by consuming the profit obtained therefrom, is said to be enjoying the requisites.'

585. Ayaṃ kira itthaṃlakkhaṇasampanno ukkaṃsato. Evaṃ aṅgasampannopi aparabhāge lobhavasena vā aññena vā kāraṇena sace nimittaṃ katvā pāteti, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhogeti pavese pavese. So hi kāraṇantarena rukkhamūlikassa, abbhokāsikassapi vaṭṭati eva, ṭhānanisajjādivasena nivāsādhippāye sati paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Bhesajjassa satipaccayatā sabbakālampīti eke. Asannihitassa pacchābhattameva, sannihitassa purebhattampīti no takkoti ācariyo. “Yāmakālikaṃ sattāhakālikaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ āhāratthāya…pe… paṭiggaṇhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Ajjhohāre ajjhohāre āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pāci. 244) hi vuttaṃ. Dukkaṭañhi vikālabhojanasikkhāpade āgataṃ vikāle āpajjati, no kāle āhārakālattā, sannidhisikkhāpade āgataṃ pana kālepi sannidhijātattā, teneva tattha sattāhakālikayāvajīvikadvayameva vuttanti. “Sati paccaye”ti vacanato nāyaṃ viseso labbhatīti ce? Na, aniṭṭhappasaṅgato, vacanāniyamato ca. Sannidhisikkhāpade hi “anāpatti yāvakālikaṃ yāvakālaṃ nidahitvā bhuñjati. Yāmakālikaṃ yāme nidahitvā bhuñjatī”ti (pāci. 256) ettha vacanappamāṇato yāmakālikaṃ na purebhatte, na pacchābhatte, na divase, na rattiyaṃ yāmameva nidahitvā bhuñjantassa anāpattīti [M 0.0262] aniṭṭhappasaṅgo. Tathā tattheva “yāmakālikaṃ yāmaṃ nidahitvā bhuñjati, sattāhakālikaṃ sattāhaṃ nidahitvā bhuñjatī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “sati paccaye”ti, tasmā satipaccaya-vacanaṃ katthaci hoti, katthaci na hotīti vacanāniyamato āpattiyāpi aniyamo siyā. Evaṃ santepi yathāvuttadukkaṭaṃ āpajjati [V 0.0234] eva. Na anāhārappayojanattā yāmakālikādīnanti ce? Na, sappiādimissabhojanassa paṇītabhojanabhāvappattito. Apica sabbakālikesu yāvakālikaṃ oḷārikaṃ, taṃ āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhantassa kāle anāpatti, pageva anoḷārikaṃ yāmakālikādiṃ, āhāratthāya eva anuññātattā. Yāvakālike eva anāpattīti ce? Na, anāhāratthāya gaṇhantassa āpattisambhavato itaraṃ āhāratthāya gaṇhantassa viya, tasmā yathāvuttamevettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ pāḷiṃ, yuttiñca anulometīti.

585. It is said that this monk is, in the highest degree, endowed with such characteristics. Even a monk so endowed with qualities, if in a later part, either through the power of greed or through another reason, having made a sign, he should cause it to be placed, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Regarding 'uses the lodging again and again,' this means at each and every entry. Indeed, that reflection, for a different reason, is allowable also for a monk dwelling at the foot of a tree and for a monk dwelling in the open air. When there is the intention of dwelling, it should be reflected upon at each and every use, by way of standing, sitting, and so on. Some say that when there is the requisite of medicine, it should be reflected upon at all times. The teacher said: 'For what is not stored, it should be reflected upon only in the after-meal period; for what is stored, it should be reflected upon also in the fore-meal period. Thus is our reasoning.' For indeed it is said: 'If one receives yāmakālika, sattāhakālika, or yāvajīvika for the purpose of food… there is an offense of wrong-doing. At each swallowing, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' Indeed, the wrong-doing that comes in the training rule on eating at the wrong time is incurred at the wrong time; it is not incurred at the proper time, because it is the time for food. But the wrong-doing that comes in the training rule on storing is incurred even at the proper time because it has become stored. For that very reason, only the two—the seven-day and the lifetime—are mentioned therein. If one should say: 'This distinction is not obtained on account of the words, "when there is a cause"?' It is not so, because of the consequence of an undesirable meaning and because of the non-fixedness of the wording. For in the training rule on storing, in the text 'There is no offense if one stores and consumes yāvakālika for its proper time; or yāmakālika for a watch,' if one takes this wording as the sole authority, an undesirable consequence would follow: that for yāmakālika, there would be no offense only for one who stores and consumes it for a watch, but not in the fore-meal period, not in the after-meal period, not during the day, and not at night. Similarly, in that very place, only this much is said: 'one consumes yāmakālika having stored it for a watch; one consumes sattāhakālika having stored it for seven days.' The words 'when there is a cause' are not said. Therefore, because the words 'when there is a cause' are present in some texts and not present in others, due to this non-fixedness of the wording, a non-fixedness of the offense would also arise. Even this being so, the aforementioned wrong-doing is indeed incurred. If one should say this is because yāmakālika and so on are not for the purpose of nourishment, it is not so, because food mixed with ghee and so on attains the state of fine food. Furthermore, among all kālikas, yāvakālika is coarse. For a monk who receives it at the proper time for the purpose of food, there is no offense. What then needs to be said of the not-coarse yāmakālika and so on? Because they are permitted for the very purpose of food. If one should say: 'Is there no offense only in the case of yāvakālika?' It is not so, because an offense is possible for one who takes it for a non-food purpose, just as for one who takes another kālika for the purpose of food. Therefore, the conclusion herein, just as it has been stated, conforms to both the Pāḷi and to reason.

Desanāsuddhīti ettha desanā nāma vinayakammaṃ, tena vuṭṭhānampi desanā eva nāma hotīti. “Paṭiggaṇhātī”ti avatvā “paṭisevatī”ti vuttattā paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpatti. Khīṇāsavā katakiccattā vibhattadāyādā viya honti, tena tesaṃ sāmiparibhogā honti. Aññathā yāvakālikabhāvaṃ anatikkantattā virujjhati. Iṇaparibhogo na vaṭṭati, bhesajje āpattito, itarasmiṃ ayuttaparibhogato, iṇaṃ viya ananuññātabhuttattā ca. “Ādito paṭṭhāya hi alajjī nāma natthi, tasmā na koci saṅkitabbo”ti likhitaṃ. Bhārabhūtā saddhivihārikādayo. Yathādānameva gahitattāti ettha “attano hatthena ce deti, na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ, “atirekabhāgaṃ gahetvā punadivase attano atthāya uddhaṭabhāgaṃ tattheva dāpeti, vaṭṭatī”ti ca. Parivattakaṃ deti, dhammiyañce, vaṭṭati. No adhammiyaṃ. “Taṃ dhammānuggahena uggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kena lesenāti ce? “Alabbhamānāya sāmaggiyā anāpatti sambhoge saṃvāse”ti (mahāva. 130) iminā upasampadakkhandhakavacanalesena.

In 'Purity by Confession,' 'confession' (desanā) means a Vinaya act. Therefore, even the rising (from an offense) is indeed called 'confession.' Since it is said 'he makes use of' (paṭisevati) instead of 'he receives' (paṭiggaṇhāti), there is no offense for one who makes use of something without having applied mindfulness at the time of receiving. Those whose taints are destroyed, having done their task, are like heirs who have had their inheritance divided. Therefore, their use is that of an owner. Otherwise, because the state of being for a limited time has not been overcome, it is contradictory. Use as a debt is not allowable: in the case of medicine, because of an offense; in the case of other things, because it is improper use and because, like a debt, it is used without permission. It is written: 'Indeed, from the beginning, there is no one called ‘shameless’; therefore, no one should be suspected.' Co-resident disciples and others who are burdensome. In the context of 'because it was taken just as it was given,' here it is said: 'If one gives with one's own hand, it is not allowable.' And also: 'Having taken an extra portion, if on the next day one has the portion set aside given there for one's own benefit, it is allowable.' If one gives in exchange, and it is in accordance with the Dhamma, it is allowable; not if it is unrighteous. It is said: 'It is allowable to learn it for the benefit of the Dhamma.' If it is asked, 'By what pretext?' By the pretext of this passage from the Chapter on Ordination: 'When harmony is unobtainable, there is no offense in communion and co-residence.'

586. Assatiyā dinnanti ettha “assatiyā dinnaṃ nāma apariccattaṃ hoti, tasmā dussante baddhakahāpaṇādīni satiṃ paṭilabhitvā dāyakā ce [M 0.0263] puna gaṇhanti, nissaggiyameva desetabbaṃ. Tena akappiyabhaṇḍena te ce dāyakā sappiādīni kiṇitvā saṅghassa denti, tassapi bhikkhuno kappati dāyakānaṃyeva santakattā. Bhikkhunā hi ‘vatthaṃ gaṇhāmī’ti vatthasaññāya eva gahitaṃ, na rūpiyasaññāya. Idañca sikkhāpadaṃ attano atthāya uggahaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na ca tena taṃ attano atthāya paresaṃ vā atthāya gahitaṃ. Atha te dāyakā no ce āgantvā gaṇhanti, dāyake pucchitvā attano atthāya ce pariccattaṃ, saṅghe nissajjitvā āpatti desetabbā. No ce, āpatti eva desetabbā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pubbāparaviruddhaṃ. Āpattidesanāya hi sati rūpiyaṃ paṭiggahitanti siddhaṃ, tasmiṃ siddhe “tato uppannaṃ tassapi kappatī”ti idaṃ na yujjatīti. Kappati evāti ce? Na, vatthuṃ anissajjitvā [V 0.0235] āpatti desetabbāti na yujjati. Acittakattā sikkhāpadassa yujjatīti ce? Na, sabbattha “rūpiyaṃ paṭiggaṇhātī”ti vacanato. “Rūpiyaṃ paṭiggaṇhātī”ti hi vuttaṃ, aññathā sabbattha “rūpiya”nti padaṃ niratthakaṃ hoti vināpi tena tadatthasiddhito. Anena ca vatthaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ, dāyakena ca vatthameva dinnaṃ, vatthagatampi rūpiyaṃ theyyacittena gaṇhanto padavārena kāretabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyañca “rūpiye arūpiyasaññīti suvaṇṇādīsu kharapattādisaññī”ti vuttaṃ “rūpiyaṃ paṭiggaṇhātī”ti vacanavasena.

586. Herein, regarding 'given without mindfulness': What is given without mindfulness is not truly relinquished. Therefore, if donors, having regained mindfulness, take back again coins and so on that were tied in the hem of a cloth, the offense entailing forfeiture must be confessed. If those donors, with that unallowable article, buy ghee and so on and give them to the Saṅgha, it is allowable for that bhikkhu also, because it is the property of the donors themselves. For it was taken by the bhikkhu with the perception of it being an article, thinking, 'I am receiving an article,' and not with the perception of it being money. And this training rule was stated in reference to receiving for one's own benefit, and it was not taken by him for his own benefit or for the benefit of others.
