Likewise, a robe given in the third or fourth year from now with instructions such as, 'Take it at Pavāraṇā,' should also be stored and taken only as it was given. This meaning is manifest in the commentary. If it is said, 'Are those robes not subject to forfeiture if the robe-time and season is passed?' No, because they were given with a specific designation. Because this 'samaya' appears as 'kāla' in the phrase 'given with a designation even at the proper time,' and it appears only as 'samaya' in the training rules on group meals and so on, therefore, it should be understood that here, to show their single meaning, it is stated together as 'cīvarakālasamaya' (robe-time-season). Here in the Mātikā, however, such a robe is spoken of with reference to a personal robe that has come into one's own possession. For that very reason, it says, 'If an emergency robe should arise for a monk...' Indeed, being unable to give to a monk who has completed the rains-residence in his own dwelling, a donor completes the act of giving within the rains-residence itself and departs; likewise for the Sangha. Therefore, there is this emergency robe which, starting from the time it arose, comes into the possession of the Sangha or an individual, and which was not given as a rains-residence robe. There is the case where, not coming into possession from the time it arose, it comes into the possession of an individual or the Sangha only at the time of having completed the rains-residence, which, having arisen as a rains-residence robe, was given at the proper time. There is also the case where, even though given at the proper time, it does not come into an individual's possession, but comes into the possession of the Sangha or the possession of the donor. With reference to this kind of robe, it is said, 'It should be stored after making a mark.' This robe may be stored even for more than a year because it has not come into one's own possession. Therefore, it is established that the phrase 'not having reached ten days' is stated with reference to something other than this. Having received it earlier than ten days, it is not permissible to store it until Pavāraṇā. Therefore, only that which has come into one's own possession should be determined. With reference to that very thing, 'not having reached ten days' is stated, since in the section on no offense it is stated, 'If he determines or assigns it within the season...' But that which is to be stored after making a mark has not come into one's own possession because it is to be given to another. Indeed, with reference to that, it is not possible to say, 'he determines or assigns it,' and it is not subject to forfeiture in this sense, because there is no forfeiture procedure for the Sangha. In the commentary also, this meaning is indeed very manifest. If it is asked, 'What is to be stored after making a mark?' A robe that is the property of another is indeed Sangha property. Then, by this phrase, 'having marked it, it will be easy to give,' the ownership by another is indeed shown.

“Tato paraṃ ekadivasampi parihāro natthīti dasāhaparamato uddhaṃ anupagatattā”ti likhitaṃ, ito samayato uddhameva dasāhassa anupagatattā samayato paraṃ dasāhaṃ na labhatīti kirassa [V 0.0250] adhippāyo. “Etaṃ parihāraṃ labhatiyevā”ti ettha “ekādasamaṃ aruṇaṃ cīvaramāse uṭṭhetī”ti kāraṇaṃ likhitaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “anadhiṭṭhahitvā ekādasadivase nikkhipituṃ labhatī’ti vadanto bhagavā itarampi anaccekacīvarādiṃ anujānāti, accekacīvaramukhenāti apare”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha kataraṃ subhāsitaṃ? Ubhayampīti eke. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ “accekacīvarassa anatthate kathine dasadivasādhiko māso, atthate kathine dasadivasādhikā pañcamāsā”ti iminā sameti, anugaṇṭhipadaladdhiyā hi ettha “ekādasadivasādhiko”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, dutiyaṃ “dasāhānāgatanti…pe… dasāhena asampattāti attho”ti iminā sameti. Imassa nayassa vasena “pañcamito paṭṭhāya uppannassa cīvarassa nidhānakālo dassito hotī”ti pāṭho yujjati. Tathā gaṇṭhipadaladdhiyā “navāhānāgataṃ kattikatemāsikapuṇṇama”nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, tassa vasena “kāmañcesa dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbanti imināva siddho, aṭṭhuppattivasena pana apubbaṃ viya atthaṃ dassetvā sikkhāpadaṃ ṭhapita”nti ayaṃ pāṭho yujjati. Ko panettha sāroti? Yo pacchā vutto, sova sāro. Teneva aṭṭhakathācariyena “pañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Porāṇagaṇṭhipadehi aṭṭhakathāya ca saddhiṃ saṃsandanato, “dasāhānāgata”nti pāḷiyā saṃsandanato ca ettha gaṇṭhipadaladdhipi pāḷiyā sameti.

It is written, “Beyond that, there is no dispensation even for a single day, because it has not gone beyond the ten-day limit.” The meaning, it is said, is that because the ten-day period is not obtained beyond this robe-season, one does not obtain the ten days beyond the season. In the context of “This dispensation is indeed obtained,” the reason is written: “The eleventh dawn arises in the robe-month.” However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is said: “Others say that the Blessed One, in stating, ‘One may keep it for eleven days without determining it,’ also permits other non-emergency robes, etc., by means of the emergency robe.” Here, which is the well-spoken statement? Some say both. How so? The first statement agrees with this: “For an emergency robe, when the Kathina is not spread, there is a month exceeding by ten days; when the Kathina is spread, there are five months exceeding by ten days.” For, according to the tradition of the Anugaṇṭhipada, here it should be said, “exceeding by eleven days.” The second statement agrees with this: “‘The ten days have not arrived’… that is… the meaning is ‘not reached within ten days.’” According to this method, the passage, “From the fifth onwards, the time for storing a robe that has arisen is shown,” is appropriate. Likewise, according to the Gaṇṭhipada tradition, it should be said, “The Kattika full-moon of the three-month season, not having reached nine days.” By this reasoning, this passage is appropriate: “Although it is established by this very statement that an extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days, yet by way of the occasion of its arising, the training rule was established by showing a meaning as if it were unprecedented.” What, then, is the essence here? That which was said later is the essence. For that very reason, the commentary teacher said, “From the fifth onwards.” Because of its collation with the ancient Gaṇṭhipadas and the commentary, and because of its agreement with the Pāḷi phrase “not having reached ten days,” here the Gaṇṭhipada tradition also agrees with the Pāḷi.

Kathaṃ? Yasmā pavāraṇādivase aruṇuggamane bhikkhu vassaṃvuttho hoti, tasmā iminā dasamena ahena saddhiṃ chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya navadivasā dasa ahānīti dasāhaṃ, tena dasāhena, sahayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamā cīvarasamayaṃ asampattāti katvā “anāgatā”ti vuccati. Yathā aparakattikapuṇṇamāya vassikasāṭikaṃ paccuddharitvā vikappento “cātumāsaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti vuccati[M 0.0281], evaṃsampadamidanti. Ettha vuccatīti ce? Na, imassa nippayojanabhāvappasaṅgato. Accekacīvarapaṭiggahaṇakālaṃ niyamitanti ce? Na, “chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya uppannacīvaraṃ accekameva na hoti. Paṭhamakathinena siddhattā”ti porāṇaṭṭhakathāgaṇṭhipadesu vuttattā tato upari “accekacīvara”nti vuccati, paṭiggaṇhantassa āpattisaṅgaho ca. Na ca sā āpatti pāḷiyā, aṭṭhakathāya, yuttito vā sambhavati. Aṭṭhuppattimattavasena vuttanti ce? Na, dasāhādhiccakārikā aṭṭhuppattipāyaṃ na dissati. “Bhikkhū accekacīvaraṃ paṭiggahetvā cīvarakālasamayaṃ atikkāmentī”ti ettha ettikā eva hi aṭṭhuppatti. Tathā hi parivāre (pari. 47-53) “kismiṃ vatthusmi”nti ārabhitvā ettakameva vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Accekacīvaraṃ cīvarakālaṃ nātikkāmetabbaṃ, itaraṃ atikkāmetabbanti dassanatthaṃ idaṃ paññattanti ce? Na, accekacīvarasseva aparādhadassanato, visesakāraṇābhāvā[V 0.0251], “kāmañcesa dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbanti imināva siddho”tiādivacanavirodhato ca yathāvuttavacanāsambhavato ca.

How so? Because on the day of Pavāraṇā, at dawn, a monk has completed the rains-residence. Therefore, from the sixth day onwards, together with this tenth day, nine days become ten days—thus, 'ten days' (dasāhaṃ). By that ten-day period, the instrumental case is used in the sense of association. Since the Kattika full moon marking the three-month period has not arrived as the robe season, it is called 'not yet come.' Just as it is said regarding one who makes the rainy-season robe shared property after taking it back on the following Kattika full moon, 'He should determine it for four months, and after that, make it shared property,' so too is this case complete. If it is said so? No, because this would lead to this training rule being purposeless. If it is asked, 'Is the time for receiving an emergency robe fixed?' No, because it is stated in the ancient commentaries and glosses, 'A robe that has arisen starting from the sixth day is not exclusively an emergency robe, because it is accomplished by the first kaṭhina.' Therefore, beyond that, it is called an 'emergency robe,' and because it would entail an offense for the one who receives it. But that offense is not found in the Pāḷi, the commentaries, or by logical reasoning. If it is asked, 'Is it mentioned merely based on its occasion of arising?' No, the occasion of arising for the ten-day extra allowance is not seen in the Pāḷi. Here, in the phrase, 'Monks, having received an emergency robe, they let the robe-season-time pass,' only this much is the occasion of arising. Indeed, in the Parivāra, starting with 'In what case?' only this much is said; it should be understood thus. If it is asked, 'Is this rule established to show that an emergency robe should not be allowed to pass the robe season, but another robe may?' No, because it shows the fault of the emergency robe only, because there is no special reason, and because of the contradiction with statements such as, 'If one wishes, one may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days; by this itself it is accomplished,' and because the aforementioned statement is untenable.

Kathaṃ? Dasāhena saha kattikapuṇṇamā “anāgatā”ti hi vutte dasāhato aññā sā puṇṇamāti āpajjati. Anaññā ce, saha-saddo na sambhavati, na hi attanāva attano yogo sambhavati, anāgata-saddo ca na sambhavati. Āgatā sampattā eva hi sā puṇṇamā. Cīvarasamayassa anantarattā ekībhāvaṃ anāgatattā anāgatāyevāti ce? Na, tathāpi anāgata-saddassa sambhavato, āgamanasambhave satiyeva hi anāgata-saddo sambhavati, na hi nibbānaṃ, paññatti vā “anāgatā”ti vuccati. Nibbānaṃ viya khaṇattayaṃ, sā ca puṇṇamā na kadāci samayabhāvaṃ pāpuṇātīti ayuttameva. “Tato paraṃ vikappetu”nti pana vacanaṃ piṭṭhisamayaṃ gahetvā ṭhitattā sambhavati. Apica pavāraṇāyaṃ aruṇe ca uṭṭhite sā puṇṇamā cīvarasamayaṃ ekāhānāgatā evāpajjati pubbe sahayogapattattā. Evaṃ sante ekībhāvagatāpi sā cīvarasamayaṃ anāgatā eva jātāti sabbadā na tathāviggahakaraṇavacanatthaṃ kocideva vacanato dīpetīti veditabbaṃ.

How so? If it is said that the Kattika full moon is 'not yet come' together with the ten days, it follows that that full moon is other than the ten days. If it were not other, the word 'together with' would not be possible, for indeed, a thing cannot be associated with itself, and the word 'not yet come' would also not be possible. For indeed, that full moon has already come, has already been reached. If it is said: 'Because it is immediately after the robe-season, and because it has not reached a state of oneness, it is indeed "not yet come"'? No, because even so, the word 'not yet come' is not possible, for indeed, the word 'not yet come' is only possible when there is the possibility of arrival. Indeed, neither Nibbāna nor a concept is called 'not yet come'. Like Nibbāna, the three moments are not spoken of as 'not yet come'. And that full moon never attains the state of being the season; therefore, that argument is indeed unsuitable. However, the statement 'He may make it shared property after that' is possible because it stands having taken the post-season. Furthermore, on the Pavāraṇā day, when the dawn has arisen, that full moon becomes 'not yet come' to the robe-season by one day, because it had previously attained association with the ten days. This being so, even having reached a state of oneness, it becomes indeed 'not yet come' to the robe-season. Therefore, it should be understood that a particular word does not always illuminate the meaning of the analytical statement in such a way.

Kimatthaṃ [M 0.0282] panettha “dasadivasādhiko māso”tiādi vuttanti? Taṃ pāripūrisambhavato. Pañcamiyañhi pure aruṇaṃ uppannaaccekacīvarassa dasadivasādhiko māsoyeva paripūroti katvā tathā vuttaṃ. Apica tassā pañcamiyā divasabhāgopi sampattāya rattiyā “hiyyo”ti vuccati, pageva pure aruṇaṃ, tenevāha “hiyyo kho, āvuso, amhāka”ntiādi. “Evaṃ sante ‘chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāyā’ti vuttapaṭhamapāṭhassa vasena ‘anaccekacīvarampi paccuddharitvā ṭhapitaṃ ticīvarampi etaṃ parihāraṃ labhatiyevā’”ti ca “dasadivasādhiko māso”tiādi ca yaṃ likhitaṃ. Taṃ na, “pañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti pāṭhe sajjiteva etena pariyāyena yathāvuttaatthasambhavato, na tāni ṭhānāni puna sajjitāni. Yathāṭhitavaseneva ajjhupekkhitabbānīti no takkoti ācariyo. Idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ puṇṇamāyaṃ anissaggiyatthamevāti upatissatthero. “Pavāraṇāmāsassa juṇhapakkhapañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti pāṭhe sajjite etena pariyāyena yathāvutto uppannassa cīvarassa nidhānakālo dassito hoti, “accekacīvaranti accāyikacīvaraṃ vuccatī”tiādi pāṭho. “Chaṭṭhito paṭṭhāyā”ti ca “kāmañcesa dasāhaparama”ntiādi ca yaṃ likhitaṃ, taṃ na pāṭho, tasmā ekādasadivasaṃ parihāraṃ labhatīti katvā ācariyena “pañcamito paṭṭhāyā”ti likhāpito kira. “Pavāraṇāmāsassa juṇhapakkhachaṭṭhito paṭṭhāya pana uppannaṃ anaccekacīvarampi paccuddharitvā ṭhapitaṃ [V 0.0252] ticīvarampi etaṃ parihāraṃ labhatiyevāti pāṭho”ti ca “accekacīvarassa anatthate kathine ekādasadivasādhiko māso, atthate kathine ekādasadivasādhikā pañcamāsāti pāṭho”ti ca ettha papañcenti, tasmā suṭṭhu sallakkhetvā kathetabbaṃ, tuṇhībhūtena vā bhavitabbaṃ.

Why is it said here, 'a month with an additional ten days,' etc.? That is said because of the possibility of completion. Indeed, for an emergency robe that has arisen on the fifth day before dawn, a month with an additional ten days is indeed complete; for this reason, it is said thus. Moreover, when the night has arrived, even a portion of the day of that fifth day is called 'yesterday'—how much more so before dawn. For that very reason, he said, 'Yesterday, friend, for us,' etc. Even though this is so, what is written based on the first reading which states 'starting from the sixth day'—namely, 'even a non-emergency robe and a set of three robes that have been withdrawn and set aside obtain this allowance,' and also 'a month with an additional ten days,' etc.—that is not so, because when the reading 'starting from the fifth day' is established, the meaning as stated arises through this method. Those points are not established again. They should be disregarded just as they stand. This is our reasoning," says the teacher. "This training rule is solely for the purpose of non-forfeiture on the full-moon day," says the Elder Upatissa. When the reading 'starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the Pavāraṇā month' is established, by this method the period for keeping a robe that has arisen, as stated, is shown. There is a reading such as: 'An emergency robe is called an urgent robe.' And what is written as 'starting from the sixth day,' and 'if he wishes, for a maximum of ten days,' etc., that is not the authoritative reading. Therefore, thinking that one obtains an allowance of eleven days, the teacher supposedly had it written as 'starting from the fifth day.' Here some elaborate, saying: 'There is a reading: "But starting from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the Pavāraṇā month, even a non-emergency robe and a set of three robes that have been withdrawn and set aside obtain this allowance,"' and also, 'There is a reading: "For an emergency robe, when the Kathina is not spread, it is a month with an additional eleven days; when the Kathina is spread, it is five months with an additional eleven days."' Therefore, one should speak after having considered it well, or one should remain silent.

Accekacīvarasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule on the emergency robe is finished.

9. Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Apprehension

652. “Tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññataraṃ cīvaranti idaṃ ticīvare eva ayaṃ vidhi, itarasmiṃ yathāsukhanti dassanatthaṃ vutta”nti vadanti. “Atirekachārattaṃ vippavasantī”ti tasmiṃyeva senāsane vāso na vippavāsoti katvā vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Cīvarappavattijānanato. Ettha kiñcāpi “āraññakaṃ nāma [M 0.0283] senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti vacanato atirekatopi vuttaṃ, āraññakameva pana senāsanaṃ hoti, dhutaṅgaṃ rakkhati cīvarappavattijānanapalibodhasambhavato.

652. They say: 'The phrase "any one robe among the three robes" — this rule applies only to the triple robe; it was said to show that regarding other requisites, it is "as one pleases."' Regarding 'dwelling apart for more than six nights', this was said having considered that dwelling in that very same lodging is not 'dwelling apart'. Why? Because of knowing of the arising of robes. Here, although it is said according to the statement, 'A lodging called "forest-dwelling" is at a minimum five hundred bow-lengths away,' even if it is beyond that, it is still a forest-dwelling lodging. One protects the ascetic practice because of the possibility of the obstruction that comes from knowing about the arising of robes.

653. “Gāvutato atirekappamāṇena labhatī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? “Siyā ca tassa bhikkhuno kocideva paccayo tena cīvarena vippavāsāyā”ti vacanato. Yojanappamāṇepi siyāti ce? Na, “puna gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvā vasitvā pakkamatī”ti anāpattivāre anuññātattā. Yadi evaṃ “yojanappamāṇe na labhatī”ti idaṃ kinti? Idaṃ nibaddhāvāsavaseneva vuttaṃ. Tattha dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjatīti? Na bhijjati, kintu na idha dhutaṅgādhikāro atthīti. Atha kasmā “ayaṃ dhutaṅgacoroti veditabbo”ti vuttanti? Asambhavato. Kathaṃ paññāyatīti? Aṅgesu abhāvato. Dhutaṅgadharassa patirūpasenāsanadīpanato dhutaṅgadharatā tassa siddhā. Vacanappamāṇatoti ce? Na, vacanappamāṇato ca pāḷiyeva pamāṇaṃ. “Anāpatti puna gāmasīmaṃ okkamitvā vasitvā pakkamatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Gāmasīmā nikkhamitvā kittakaṃ kālaṃ vasitvā pakkamitabbanti ce? Punadivaseyeva, tasmā aṭṭhamo aruṇo nibaddhāvāse vā gantabbaṭṭhāne vā uṭṭhetabboti eke. Antochārattanti eke. Yāva nibaddhāvāsaṃ na kappetīti eke. Yāva maggaparissamavinodanāti eke. Sati antarāye antochārattaṃ vasati, anāpatti. Nibaddhāvāsakappane sati aruṇuggamane āpatti. Sace taṃsattamo divaso, tadaheva nikkhittacīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ, paccuddharitabbaṃ vāti eke. Sace antarā [V 0.0253] navamaggapātubhāvena vā navagāmasannivesena vā, taṃ senāsanaṃ aṅgasampattito parihāyati. Tadaheva cīvaraṃ gahetabbaṃ vā paccuddharitabbaṃ vā. Chārattaṃ vippavasantassa ce parihāyati, anāpatti anuññātadivasattāti eke. Āpatti eva anaṅgasampattitoti eke. Yuttataraṃ panettha vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ. Sace dhutaṅgadharo hoti, gāmasīmāyaṃ avasitvā pacchimappamāṇayutte ṭhāne vasitvā pakkamitabbaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ baddhaavippavāsasīmo ce gāmo hoti, aññasmimpi māse antosīmāya vasato anāpatti. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade “yathāvuttasenāsane vasantenāpi chārattameva cīvaraṃ gāme nikkhipitabbanti adhippāyena aññaṃ antochārattampi aññampi vasato āpattiyevā”ti vuttaṃ.

653. If it is said, 'One obtains it by a measure exceeding a gāvuta,' how is this to be understood? It is understood from the statement: 'There might be for that bhikkhu some reason for being separated from that robe.' If it is said, 'Might it be even for the measure of a yojana?' No, because in the section on no-offense it is permitted, stating: 'having re-entered the village boundary, having stayed, one departs.' If so, what is this statement, 'At the measure of a yojana, one does not obtain it'? This was said only with reference to residing in a fixed dwelling. Is the ascetic practice broken there? It is not broken, but here there is no section concerning the ascetic practices. Then why was it said, 'This one should be known as a thief of the ascetic practices'? Because of the impossibility. How is this to be understood? Due to the absence of the factors. For one who upholds the ascetic practices, his status as an upholder of the ascetic practices is established by the pointing out of a suitable lodging. If it is said, 'Is it from the authority of the statement?' No, for the Pāḷi itself is the authority, more so than the authority of the statement. For indeed, it is said: 'There is no offense for one who, having re-entered the village boundary and stayed, then departs.' If it is asked, 'Having gone out from the village boundary, for how long a time should one stay before departing?' Some say: 'On the very next day; therefore, the eighth dawn should arise either at the fixed dwelling or at the destination.' Some say: 'Within six nights.' Some say: 'Until one does not arrange a fixed dwelling.' Some say: 'Until the fatigue of the journey is relieved.' If there is an obstacle, one may stay within six nights; there is no offense. If a fixed dwelling has been arranged, there is an offense at the rising of the dawn. Some say: 'If that is the seventh day, on that very day the robe that was laid aside should be taken or reclaimed.' If in the meantime, due to the appearance of a new road or the establishment of a new village, that lodging becomes deficient in the completeness of its factors, on that very day the robe should be taken or reclaimed. Some say: 'If it becomes deficient for one who is away for six nights, there is no offense because of the permitted days.' Others say: 'There is an offense indeed, due to the incompleteness of the factors.' Here, what is more suitable should be adopted after investigation. If one is an upholder of the ascetic practices, one should not stay within the village boundary, but having stayed in a place at the final limit of the measure, one should depart. If a village was originally one with a formally established boundary of non-separation, there is no offense for one staying within the boundary, even in another month. In the ancient Ganthipada it is said: 'With the intention that even one staying in the aforesaid lodging should deposit the robe in the village for six nights only, for one staying otherwise, even within the six nights, there is an offense indeed.'

Sāsaṅkasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning apprehension is finished.

10. Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. 10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Designated Property

657. Dethāvuso [M 0.0284] amhākanti ettha akataviññatti hoti na hotīti? Hoti, yadi evaṃ aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadassa ca imassa ca kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Taṃ aññātakaappavāriteyeva viññāpentassa, idaṃ ñātakapavāritepi, taṃ anacchinnacīvarasseva, idaṃ tassapi, taṃ cīvaraṃyeva viññāpentassa, idaṃ acīvarampi. Evaṃ sante idaṃ taṃ antokatvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, tasmā dvinnampi aṅgasampattiyā sati kena bhavitabbanti? Iminā bhavitabbaṃ imassa nippadesatoti eke. Dvīhipi bhavitabbaṃ ubhinnampi aṅgasiddhitoti eke. Imāni tassa aṅgāni vikappanupagacīvaratā, samayābhāvo, aññātakaviññatti, tāya ca paṭilābhoti cattāri. Imassa pana saṅghe pariṇatabhāvo, ñatvā attano pariṇāmanaṃ, paṭilābhoti tīṇi. Ettha paṭhamo vādo ayutto katvāpi okāsaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, parivāre ca avicāritattā. Yadi evaṃ tattha aṅgesu “anaññapariṇatatā”ti vattabbanti ce? Na vattabbaṃ, atthato siddhattā. Pariṇatasikkhāpadadvayasiddhito, pariṇatasaññito, āpattisambhavato ca “mayhampi dethā”ti vadati, “vaṭṭatī”ti anuddiṭṭhaṃ, “amhākampi atthī”ti vuttattā vaṭṭati. “Saṅghassa pariṇataṃ…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti ettha “puggalassā”ti na vuttaṃ, yato suddhapācittiyavasena āgatattā. “Aññacetiyassā”ti na vuttaṃ saṅghassa acetiyattā, tasmāyeva “cetiyassa pariṇataṃ…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti etthāpi “aññasaṅghassa aññapuggalassā”ti na vuttaṃ. “Yato tathā idha ca ‘puggalassa pariṇataṃ…pe… āpatti dukkaṭassā’ti ettha ca ‘attanopī’ti kiñcāpi na vuttaṃ, tathāpi sambhavatī”ti vadanti. Taṃ [V 0.0254] pana idha attano pariṇāmanādhikārattā imassa sikkhāpadassa na vuttanti eke. Tatuttarisikkhāpade “aññassatthāyā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.526) padaṃ viyāti eke. Taṃ na, ettha puggalapariṇāmanasikkhāpade avuttattā. Dhammasiritthero panāha –

657. Here, regarding the phrase 'Friend, give to us,' does this constitute an uninvited request or not? It does. If so, what is the difference between the training rule on requesting from non-relatives and this one? That one is laid down for a monk who requests from a non-relative who has not invited them, while this one is laid down even for a monk who requests from a relative who has invited them. That one is laid down only for a monk whose robe-cloth has not been taken away; this one is laid down for him also. That one is for requesting only robe-cloth; this one is for non-robe-cloth also. This being so, this rule stands by encompassing that one. Therefore, when the factors of both are fulfilled, by which training rule should it be judged? Some say it should be judged by this rule, because it is a ruling without exception. Others say it should be judged by both, because the factors of both are accomplished. These are the four factors of that rule: the state of being robe-cloth suitable for `vikappana`, the absence of the proper time, requesting from a non-relative, and receiving it through that request. The factors of this rule, however, are three: the state of being designated for the Saṅgha, knowing this and having it designated to oneself, and receiving it. Here, the first opinion is unsuitable, because although the opportunity is made in the Commentary and in the Parivāra, it is not investigated. If so, should it not be stated among the factors that it is 'not designated for another'? It should not be stated, because it is established by the meaning. And because the two training rules on designated things are accomplished, because of the perception of it being designated, and because an offense is possible, one says, 'Give to me too'. Although it is not indicated that 'it is allowable', because it was said, 'There is for us too', it is allowable. In the phrase, 'What is designated for the Saṅgha… an offense of wrong-doing,' 'for an individual' is not stated, because it comes by way of a pure and a mixed offense. 'For another shrine' is not stated because the Saṅgha is not a shrine. For that very reason, 'for a shrine, for another individual' is not stated. They say: 'Because just so here also, in the phrase "what was designated for an individual... an offense of wrong-doing", although "for oneself also" is not stated, it is nevertheless possible.' But some say that this is not stated here because this training rule is in the section on causing it to be designated to oneself. Some say it is like the phrase 'for the sake of another' in the subsequent training rule. That should not be accepted. Why? Because it is not stated here in the training rule on causing designation for an individual. The Elder Dhammasiri, however, said—

“Attano aññato lābhaṃ, saṅghassaññassa vā nataṃ;

Pariṇāmeyya nissaggi, pācittiyampi dukkaṭa”nti.

Should one divert a gain received from another, which was designated for the Saṅgha or for someone else, to oneself or to another, it entails a Nissaggiya offense, a Pācittiya offense, and also a Dukkaṭa offense.

Tassattho – saṅghassa pariṇataṃ attano pariṇāmeyya nissaggiyaṃ. Tadeva aññato pariṇāmeyya pācittiyaṃ. Aññassa pariṇataṃ attano vā [M 0.0285] parassa vā pariṇāmeyya dukkaṭanti, tasmā aññātakaviññattiādīsu vuttāpattisambhavato idha pariṇatadvaye “attano”ti padaṃ na vuttaṃ. Tasmiñhi vutte dukkaṭamattappasaṅgo siyā, avutte panetesu vuttāpattīnaṃ yathāgamamaññatarā ca idha avuttasiddhi dukkaṭañcāti dve āpattiyo ekato hontīti vinayadharānaṃ anavasesañāṇassa okāso kato hotīti.

Its meaning is: if one were to divert to oneself what was designated for the Saṅgha, it is a Nissaggiya offense. If one were to divert that very gain to another, it is a Pācittiya offense. If one were to divert what was designated for another person to oneself or to another, it is a Dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, because of the possibility of the offenses mentioned in the rules on requesting from an unrelated family and so on, here in the two training rules on designated things, the word 'attano' (for oneself) is not stated. For if it were stated, there would only be the occasion for a Dukkaṭa offense. But since it is not stated, in these cases, in accordance with the texts, one of the stated offenses arises, and here also a Dukkaṭa offense is established by the principle of the unstated. Thus, two offenses occur together. In this way, an opportunity is made for the complete knowledge of the experts in Vinaya.

Iti tiṃsakakaṇḍaṃ sāramaṇḍaṃ,

Alametaṃ vinayassa sāramaṇḍe;

Idha niṭṭhitasabbasāramaṇḍaṃ,

Vinayavasena punāti sāramaṇḍanti.

Thus, this thirty-part section is an excellent ornament, fit to adorn, by the power of the Vinaya, the sons of good family who are themselves excellent ornaments. Here, the entire collection of excellent ornaments is completed; by means of the Vinaya, it purifies the son of good family who is an excellent ornament.

Pariṇatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning designated property is finished.

Niṭṭhito pattavaggo tatiyo.

The third section, the Bowl Chapter, is completed.

Nissaggiyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nissaggiya rules is finished.

Pācittiyavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Pācittiya Rules

5. Pācittiyakaṇḍo

5. The Pācittiya Section

1. Musāvādavaggo

1. The Chapter on False Speech

1. Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on False Speech

1. Vādakkhittoti [V 0.0255][M 0.0286] ettha avisesena vādajappavitaṇḍasaṅkhāto tividhopi kathāmaggo “vādo” icceva vuttoti veditabbo. Tesu “titthiyehi saddhi”nti vacanato ṭhapetvā vādaṃ “sesā”ti vadanti. Chalajātiniggahaṭṭhānakusalatāya kadāci katthaci avajānitvā paṭijānāti, tathā pubbe kiñci vacanaṃ paṭijānitvā pacchā avajānāti. Evaṃ vā aññathā vā aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati. Evaṃ pavatto sampajānamusā bhāsaṃ paṭissuṇitvā asaccāyanto saṅketaṃ katvā visaṃvādento evaṃ so vādakkhitto samāno pācittiyavatthuñca paripūrento vicaratīti evamadhippāyo veditabbo. Attano vādeti ettha “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti (dha. pa. 279; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 7; netti. 5; mahāni. 27) paṭhamamāraddhe attano vāde. “Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) no samayo. “Sabbe dhammā”ti vutte nibbānampi saṅgahaṃ gacchati. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (dha. pa. 203-204; ma. ni. 2.215) vuttattā pana taṃ na dukkhaṃ. No ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Ayaṃ paravādī “yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti suttaṃ dassetvā siddhantaṃ sambhametvā “virodhi viruddho”ti vuttaṃ dosaṃ āropessatīti tasmiṃ paṭhamavāde kañci dosaṃ sallakkhento āropite vā dose anāropite vā “nāyaṃ mama vādo”ti taṃ avajānitvā “nibbānantveva sassata”nti, “anattā iti nicchayā”ti [V 0.0256] ca suttaṃ disvā tassa paṭhamavādassa niddosataṃ sallakkhetvā “mameva ayaṃ vādo”ti tameva pacchā paṭijānāti. Evaṃ tattha yathāvuttamānisaṃsaṃ sallakkhento taṃ paṭijānitvā yadi anattā sabbe dhammā, dhammā eva na te bhavanti. Sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti hi “dhammā”ti vuccanti.

1. In this context, regarding `vādakkhitta`, it should be known that the threefold path of speech—designated as debate (`vāda`), chattering (`jappa`), and wrangling (`vitaṇḍa`)—is, without distinction, referred to simply as 'debate' (`vāda`). Among these, some say that on account of the phrase 'with the adherents of other sects,' debate (`vāda`) is excluded, and only the remaining two are intended. Due to skill in the six kinds of grounds for censure, one might at some time or place deny something and later accept it; similarly, having first accepted some statement, one later denies it. In this way or otherwise, one prevaricates. One who is engaged thus, having agreed to speak a deliberate falsehood, not being truthful, having made an appointment and then deceiving—such a person, being one confounded in debate (`vādakkhitta`), goes about fulfilling the basis for a Pācittiya offense. This is the intention that should be understood. Regarding 'in one's own doctrine,' this refers to one's own doctrine as first undertaken, namely, 'all phenomena are non-self.' The context is not 'whatever is suffering, that is non-self.' When 'all phenomena' is said, Nibbāna is also included. But because it is said, 'Nibbāna is the supreme bliss,' it is not suffering. This situation does not exist. This opponent, by presenting the sutta 'whatever is suffering, that is non-self' to confuse the established doctrine, will impute the fault called 'contradictory and conflicting.' Thus, perceiving some fault in that first doctrine—whether a fault is imputed or not—one denies it, saying, 'This is not my doctrine.' But having seen the suttas 'Nibbāna indeed is permanent' and 'it is certain that it is non-self,' and having perceived the faultlessness of that first doctrine, one later accepts that very same thing, saying, 'This is indeed my doctrine.' Thus, perceiving the aforementioned benefit in that case and accepting that doctrine, if all phenomena are non-self, then they are not phenomena at all. For they are called 'phenomena' (`dhammā`) because they bear their own-nature.

Ayañca atta-saddo sabhāvavācīti evaṃ āropite vā dose anāropite vā dosoti sallakkhetvā “nāyaṃ mama vādo”ti tameva paṭhamavādaṃ pacchā avajānāti. Atha so paravādī sapakkhaṃ paṭisedhe paṭijānanattāpanayanaṃ[M 0.0287]. Paṭijānāti patyāssa iti vacanato “paṭiññā aññā so nāma te niggaho”ti vutto. Sabhāvātirittaṃ atthaṃ paṭisedhādhippāyato sabhāvato atirittaṃ bālaparikappitamattānaṃ sandhāya “anattā sabbe dhammā”ti me paṭiññātakathā, sā ca tadavatthāyevāti na me taṃ paṭiññātattāpanayanaṃ atthi, “nāyaṃ mama vādo”ti avajānanaṃ pana sabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ attānaṃ sandhāya “anattā sabbe dhammā”ti na vadāmīti adhippāyena katanti iminā aññena kāraṇena taṃ pubbe paṭiññātattāpanayanaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicchādeti. “Anattā sabbeva dhammā”ti na vattabbaṃ “atta-saddassa sabhāvavācittā”ti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca tena pubbe paṭiññātattāpanayanaṃ kataṃ. Tamaññakāraṇaṃ pacchā dassitena aññena kāraṇena paṭicchādetīti adhippāyo.

And this word 'self' denotes intrinsic nature. Thus, having discerned it as a fault whether a fault is imputed or not, he later rejects that very first statement, thinking, 'This is not my view.' Then, for that opponent, when his own position is refuted, there is the retraction of what was acknowledged. Because of the statement, 'He acknowledges in return,' it is said, 'Your acknowledgement is another; that is a point of defeat for you.' (He argues:) 'My acknowledged statement, “All phenomena are non-self,” was made with the intention of refuting a meaning that transcends intrinsic nature, referring to a self imagined by the foolish that transcends intrinsic nature, and it stands only in that context. Therefore, for me, there is no retraction of what was acknowledged. The rejection, “This is not my view,” however, was made with the intention, referring to the self designated as intrinsic nature, “I do not say, ‘All phenomena are non-self’.”' By this other reason, he conceals the reason for that earlier retraction of what was acknowledged. He had previously made the retraction of what was acknowledged on account of this reason: 'One should not say, “All phenomena are indeed non-self,” because the word “self” denotes intrinsic nature.' The meaning is that he conceals that other reason with another reason shown later.

Yasmā na kevalaṃ yathādassitanayena so atthameva avajānāti, paṭijānāti ca, kintu vacanampi, tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 1) “jānitabbato”ti paṭhamaṃ kāraṇaṃ vatvā paravādinā “yadi jānitabbato aniccaṃ, nibbānaṃ te aniccaṃ siyā”ti vutte “na mayā ‘jānitabbato’ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, ‘jātidhammato’ti mayā vuttaṃ, taṃ tayā badhiratāya aññena sallakkhitantiādīni vadatīti adhippāyo. ‘Jānitabbato’ti vatvā puna ‘jātidhammato’tiādīni vadatī”ti vuttaṃ. “Avajānitvā puna paṭijānanto taṃ avajānanaṃ iminā paṭicchādeti nāmā”ti likhitaṃ.

Because, in the manner shown, he does not only reject and acknowledge the meaning, but also the wording itself. Therefore, in the commentary (Pāc. Aṭṭha. 1), the meaning is that having first stated the reason as 'from knowability,' when the opponent says, 'If it is impermanent from knowability, your Nibbāna would be impermanent,' he replies, 'The reason “from knowability” was not stated by me; “from having the nature of arising” was stated by me. Due to your deafness, you perceived it as something else,' and so on. It is said: 'Having said “from knowability,” he then says “from having the nature of arising,” and so on.' It is written: 'Having rejected and then acknowledging again, he indeed conceals that rejection by this means.'

2. Jānitvā jānantassa cāti jānitvā vā jānantassa vāti atthadvayaṃ dīpetīti.

2. ‘Jānitvā jānantassa ca ti’: This phrase illuminates two meanings – ‘having known’ or ‘to one who knows’.

3. Apica micchāvācāpariyāpannāti catubbidhamicchāvācāpariyāpannā. Sīhaḷādināmabhedagatāti keci, tasmā evaṃ vadato vacanaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanāti ubhayaṃ vuttanti mātikāyaṃ ubhinnaṃ saṅgahitattā. Vibhaṅge taṃ vacanaṃ yasmā vinā viññattiyā natthi, tasmā [V 0.0257] “vācasikā viññattī”ti viññatti ca dassitā. “Evaṃ vadato vacana”nti lokavohārena vatvā paramatthato dassento “taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā vā cetanāti vutta”nti ca vadati. Oḷārikenevāti cetanāsamuṭṭhānavācānaṃ sukhumattā visayavaseneva katāti.

3. Furthermore, ‘micchāvācāpariyāpannā’ means encompassed by the fourfold wrong speech. Some say it falls under classifications of names like 'Sīhaḷa,' etc. Therefore, because both the speech of one who speaks thus and the volition that gives rise to it are included in the mātikā, both are mentioned. In the Vibhaṅga, since that speech does not exist without intimation, 'verbal intimation' is also shown. Having stated 'the speech of one who speaks thus' according to worldly convention, while showing it in the ultimate sense, he also says, 'or the volition that gives rise to it is said.' The phrase ‘oḷārikeneva’ means: because of the subtlety of speech arisen from volition, its classification is made only by way of its object.

9. Diṭṭhassa [M 0.0288] hotīti diṭṭho assa, anena vā upacārajjhānavasena na mayā abyāvaṭo mato, “na mayā pavanto paṭo diṭṭho”tiādiṃ bhaṇantassa ca paramatthasuññataṃ upādāya eva “itthiṃ na passāmi, na ca purisa”nti bhaṇantassa ca na musāvādo.

9. ‘Diṭṭhassa hoti’ means 'it is seen by him.' Or, for one who, due to access concentration, says, 'He did not die while I was inattentive,' and for one who says, 'A cloth being woven was not seen by me,' etc., and for one who says, 'I do not see a woman, nor a man,' based on ultimate emptiness—it is not false speech.

11. Āpattiṃ āpajjatiyevāti ettha “dubbhāsitāpattī”ti vadanti. Kasmā? “Keḷiṃ kurumāno”ti vuttattā. “Vācā girā…pe… vācasikā viññattī”ti ujukaṃ sandhāya, kāyo na ujuko.

11. ‘Āpattiṃ āpajjatiyeva ti’: Here, they say it is an “offense of wrong speech.” Why? Because it is said, “while making a jest.” “Speech, utterance... pe... verbal intimation” is directly intended, but the body is not directly involved.

Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on False Speech is Concluded.

2. Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Offensive Speech

13. “Puna are patteti puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ parivaṭṭetvā āgate aññasmiṃ are”ti likhitaṃ. Patiṭṭhitārappadesanti bhūmiṃ. Puna areti puna tasmiṃyeva are bhūmiṃ patteti atthoti keci, taṃ na sundaraṃ viya. Jāpitoti parājito, “parājito”ti vā pāṭho. Pāpesīti abhibhavasi. Manāpaṃ bhāsamānassa brāhmaṇassa garuṃ bhāraṃ. Udabbahīti ākaḍḍhīti attho, anādaratthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. Dhanañca naṃ alābhesīti yathā so dhanaṃ alabhi, tathā akāsīti adhippāyo.

13. It is written that 'puna are patte' means: 'having turned from that place, it comes to another spoke.' 'Patiṭṭhitārappadesaṃ' means the ground. Some say 'puna are' means 'it lands on the ground at that very same spoke again,' but that does not seem right. 'Jāpito' means 'defeated'; or the reading is 'parājito.' 'Pāpesi' means 'you overpower.' 'For a brahmin who speaks pleasingly, a heavy burden.' 'Udabbahi' means 'he dragged' or 'he pulled'; or it is the genitive case in the sense of disrespect. 'Dhanañca naṃ alābhesi' means: 'he acted in such a way that the other did not obtain the wealth'—this is the intention.

15. Pubbeti nidāne. Avakaṇṇakanti chinnakaṇṇakanāmaṃ. Javakaṇṇakanti vaṅkakaṇṇakanāmaṃ. Dhaniṭṭhakaṃ dhanavaḍḍhakanāmaṃ, sirivaḍḍhakanāmaṃ kulavaḍḍhakasseva nāmaṃ. Tacchakakammanti khaṇanakammakārā koṭṭhakā, pāsāṇakammakārāti keci. “Muddāti pabbagaṇanā. Gaṇanāti mahāgaṇanā”ti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Madhumehaṃ omeha”nti likhitaṃ. Thūlakāyassa maṃsūpacayoti eke. Yabha methune. Vītarāgatādīhi akkosantopi kileseheva kira akkosati nāma, tathā “sotāpanno”ti akkosanto āpattiyā akkosati nāmāti eke. Liṅgāyattattā accodātādipi liṅgameva jātaṃ.

15. 'Pubbe' means in the origin story. 'Avakaṇṇaka' means the name 'one with cut ears.' 'Javakaṇṇaka' means the name 'one with crooked ears.' 'Dhaniṭṭhaka' is the name 'wealth-increaser'; 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' is a name just like 'Kulavaḍḍhaka' (lineage-increaser). 'Carpenter’s work' means diggers and builders; some say stoneworkers. 'Muddā is counting on the finger joints. Gaṇanā is a large calculation,' is said in the ancient glossary. 'Madhumehaṃ omeha' is what is written. Some say it is the accumulation of flesh of a stout body. The root ‘yabh’ is in the sense of sexual intercourse. Even if one insults with words such as “one devoid of lust,” it is said that one indeed insults through defilements. Similarly, some say that one who insults by calling another a “stream-enterer” insults by way of an offense. Due to dependence on gender, even “very white” and similar terms have become gender-specific.

16. Sabbattha [V 0.0258] vadetīti uddeso. Bhaṇatīti vitthāro. Vadetīti vā iminā paraviññāpanaṃ dīpeti.

16. 'He speaks everywhere' is the summary. 'He speaks' is the detailed explanation. Or, by 'he speaks,' it indicates making something known to others.

26. Aññāpadesavāresu [M 0.0289] pana “evaṃ vadetī”ti vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Pubbe dassitauddesakkamanidassanatthaṃ. Pubbepi “hīnena hīnaṃ, hīnena ukkaṭṭhaṃ, ukkaṭṭhena hīnaṃ, ukkaṭṭhena ukkaṭṭha”nti jātyādīsu ekekasmiṃ catudhā catudhā dassitauddesakkamassa nidassanaṃ “eva”nti iminā karoti. “Hīnena hīnaṃ vadetī”ti vuttaṭṭhāneyeva hi “evaṃ vadetī”ti vutte so ākāro nidassito hotīti adhippāyo. Aññathā aññāpadesena so ākāro na sambhavatīti āpajjati. Na sambhavati evāti ce? Na, visesakāraṇābhāvā, tattha anāpattippasaṅgato, aniyamaniddesena aniyamatthasambhavato ca. “Santi idhekacce caṇḍālā”tiādinā hi aniyamaniddesena caṇḍālaṃ vā acaṇḍālaṃ vā sandhāya bhaṇantassa āpattīti aniyamattho sambhavatīti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ ettakameva vattabbaṃ tāvatā pubbe dassitauddesakkamanidassanasiddhitoti? Na, “vadetī”ti iminā ayojite “eva”nti pade imaṃ nāma ākāraṃ dassetīti anavabodhato. Aññāpadesanayepi paraviññāpaneyeva dukkaṭapācittiyaṃ viyāti niyamanapayojanaṃ vā “vadetī”ti padanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā attano samīpe ṭhatvā aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpento hīnena hīnaṃ vadeti bhaṇati, āpatti pācittiyassa. Sace sayaṃ hīno hīnena hīnaṃ caṇḍālaṃ…pe… pukkusaṃ “pukkuso”ti bhaṇati āpatti vācāya vācāya pācittiyassa, esa nayo aññāpadesavāresupīti yojanā veditabbā. Ayamattho duṭṭhadosesu pariyesitabbo. Aññathā “vadeti bhaṇatī”ti etesaṃ aññataraṃ ubhayattha anaññāpadesavāraaññāpadesavāresu, visesena vā aññāpadesavāresu niratthakaṃ āpajjati vināyeva tena vacanasiliṭṭhatāsambhavato. Attato pāḷiyaṃ avuttattā panettha “sāṇattika”nti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ padasandhi vadetīti vada itīti. Asammukhā vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ “sammukhā pana sattahipi āpattikkhandhehi vadantassa dukkaṭa”nti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā. Davakamyatā nāma keḷi, taṃ dassetuṃ “hasādhippāyatā”ti vuttaṃ. “Asammukhāpi davakamyatāya vadantassa dubbhāsitamevā”ti ācariyā vadanti. Pāpagarahitāya kujjhitvāpi vadantassa dukkaṭaṃ, asammukhā anāpattīti.

26. However, in the sections on indirect reference, it is stated, “He speaks thus.” Why? For the purpose of illustrating the order of exposition shown previously. By this word 'thus', he illustrates the order of exposition shown previously, fourfold in each of the categories such as birth, as: 'low with low, low with high, high with low, high with high'. Indeed, the intention is that when “he speaks thus” is said in the very place where “he speaks of the low with a low term” is stated, that manner is illustrated. Otherwise, it would follow that that manner is not possible through indirect reference. If it is said, “Is it not possible indeed?” No, due to the absence of a special reason, due to the implication of no offense there, and due to the possibility of an indefinite meaning through an indefinite statement. Indeed, the intention is that by an indefinite statement such as “There are some outcastes here,” an indefinite meaning is possible, implying an offense for one who speaks referring to either an outcaste or a non-outcaste. If this is so, should only this much be said, since by that much the establishment of the illustration of the order of exposition shown previously is accomplished? No, because when the word 'thus' is not connected with this word 'speaks', it is not understood that it indicates this particular manner. Or, it should be understood that the word 'speaks' has the purpose of defining, just as in the method of indirect reference, a dukkaṭa or pācittiya offense arises only when conveying it to another. Alternatively, one who, standing near, commands another bhikkhu, speaks of the low with a low term; there is an offense of pācittiya. If he himself, being low, speaks of a low person—an outcaste... a scavenger—with a low term, saying, “You are a scavenger,” there is an offense of pācittiya for each and every word. This method should be understood as applicable also in the sections on indirect reference. This meaning should be sought in the sections on corrupted malice. Otherwise, one of these words, 'speaks' or 'says', would become meaningless in both places—the sections on non-indirect reference and indirect reference, or especially in the sections on indirect reference—because even without it, the coherence of the statement is possible. It should be understood that here the term 'by command' is stated because it is not stated in the Pāḷi itself. Therein, this is the word-juncture: vadetīti is vada iti. For one who speaks not in the person's presence, there is a dukkaṭa offense, because in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā it is stated, “But for one who speaks in the person's presence using the seven groups of offenses, there is a dukkaṭa.” Davakamyatā means playfulness; to show this, “having the intention of laughter” is stated. The teachers say, “Even when not in the person's presence, for one who speaks playfully, it is indeed wrong speech.” For one who speaks out of anger due to being reproached for evil, there is a dukkaṭa offense; if not in the person's presence, there is no offense.

Omasavādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on offensive speech is completed.

3. Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Tale-bearing

36-7. “Imassa [M 0.0290][V 0.0259] sutvā amussā”ti pāṭho. “Imesaṃ sutvā”ti na sundaraṃ. Bhedāyapīti bhedāya. Tiṇṇampi bhikkhubhāvatoyeva nipajjanato “bhikkhūnaṃ pesuññe”ti bahuvacanaṃ kataṃ.

36-7. “Imassa sutvā amussā” is the reading. “Imesaṃ sutvā” is not good. “Bhedāyapīti” means ‘for division’. Because all three are established in the state of being a bhikkhu, the plural “bhikkhūnaṃ pesuññe” is used.

38-9. “Itthannāmo āyasmā caṇḍālo…pe… pukkusoti bhaṇatī”ti vatvā pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatīti yojanā. Aññathā “pukkusoti bhaṇatī”ti vattabbatā āpajjati. Ettha anupasampannavāro labbhamānopi na uddhaṭo omasavāde dassitanayattā, saṅkhepato ante dassetukāmatāya vā. Tathā hi ante tīṇi dukkaṭāni dassitāni. Tāni pana dassento bhagavā yasmā “upasampannassa sutvā upasampannassa pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatī”ti vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ aññataravipallāsavasena vā ubhayavipallāsavasena vā pācittiyanti katvā dvepi tāni ekato vuttānīti dassetukāmo, tasmā sabbapaṭhamaṃyeva “upasampanno upasampannassa sutvā upasampannassa pesuññaṃ upasaṃharati, āpatti pācittiyassā”ti āha. “Dvīsu panetesu yasmā pārājikaṃ ajjhāpannopi upasampanno tādisaṃyeva upasampannaṃ khuṃsetukāmo omasati, tādisassa sutvā tādisassa pesuññaṃ upasaṃharati, āpatti pācittiyassa, tasmā ‘upasampanno’ti idaṃ ādipadaṃ sabbattha vutta”nti keci vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ, anavasesaāpattiṃ āpannassa puna āpattiyā asambhavato, tasmā kevalaṃ mātikāyaṃ bhikkhupadābhāvatoyeva “bhaṇati upasaṃharatī”ti padānaṃ kārakaniddesābhāve asambhavato eva taṃ ādipadaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ pāḷilesābhāvato anāṇattikameva. “Na piyakamyassa, na bhedādhippāyassā”ti upasaṃharaṇāpekkhaṃ sāmivacanaṃ tuṇhībhūtassa vacanappayojanābhāvato, tena vuttaṃ “pāpagarahitāya bhaṇantassa anāpattī”ti.

38-9. Having said, 'The venerable so-and-so says that he is a caṇḍāla... a pukkusa,' he engages in tale-bearing—this is the connection. Otherwise, it would become necessary to say, 'he says he is a pukkusa.' Here, although the section concerning the unordained is obtainable, it is not extracted because the method has been shown in the case of abusive speech, or because of the desire to show it briefly at the end. Indeed, at the end, three dukkaṭa offenses are shown. Furthermore, while showing these, the Blessed One wished to show that a pācittiya offense arises from the reversal of one or both of the two terms in the statement, 'having heard from an ordained one, he engages in tale-bearing to an ordained one,' and that both these cases are stated together. Therefore, first of all, he said: 'An ordained one, having heard from an ordained one, engages in tale-bearing to an ordained one—there is an offense of pācittiya.' Some say: 'In these two cases, because even an ordained one who has committed a pārājika, wishing to scold a similar ordained one, abuses him, and having heard from such a one, engages in tale-bearing to such a one, there is an offense of pācittiya; therefore, this initial word 'ordained' is stated everywhere.' That is not correct, because it is impossible for one who has committed an offense without remainder to commit another offense. Therefore, it should be understood that this initial word is stated simply because, due to the absence of the word 'bhikkhu' in the mātikā, the specification of the agent for the verbs 'says' and 'engages in tale-bearing' would be impossible. Due to the absence of any subtle hint in the Pali, this is indeed not by command. 'Not for one desiring affection, not for one with the intention of causing dissension'—this genitive statement refers to the act of engaging in tale-bearing, for there is no purpose in speaking for one who is silent. Therefore, it is said: 'There is no offense for one who speaks for the sake of censuring evil.'

Pesuññasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Tale-bearing is concluded.

4. Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma Syllable by Syllable

45-6. Sabbametaṃ [M 0.0291] padaso dhammo nāmāti ettha dhammo nāma buddhabhāsitoti evaṃ sambandho. Akkharasamūhoti asamattapade. Paccekabuddhabhāsitaṃ buddhabhāsite eva. Anupāsakagahaṭṭhehi bhāsito isibhāsitādisaṅgahaṃ gacchatīti veditabbaṃ. Katthaci potthake “devatābhāsito”ti [V 0.0260] padaṃ natthi, yattha atthi, sā pāḷi. Gāthābandhepi ca esa nayoti ekameva akkharaṃ vatvā ṭhānaṃ labbhati eva. “Evaṃ me suta”ntiādisuttaṃ bhaṇāpiyamāno ekāraṃ vatvā tiṭṭhati ce, anvakkharena pācittiyaṃ, aparipuṇṇapadaṃ vatvā ṭhite anubyañjanena. Padesu ekaṃ paṭhamapadaṃ virujjhati ce, anupadena pācittiyaṃ. Aṭṭhakathānissitoti aṭṭhakathānissitavasena ṭhito. Pubbe pakatibhāsāya vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ sandhāya. Pāḷinissitoti pāḷiyaṃ evāgato. Maggakathādīnipi pakaraṇāni.

45-6. All this, word by word, is called Dhamma. Here, the connection is thus: Dhamma means what is spoken by the Buddha. Akkharasamūho refers to an incomplete word. What is spoken by Paccekabuddhas is indeed included in what is spoken by a Buddha. It should be understood that what is spoken by householders who are not lay disciples falls into the category of sayings of sages, and so on. In some books, the word “spoken by deities” is not found; where it is found, that is the Pāḷi. And even in verse composition, this is the method: a basis [for an offense] is indeed established by uttering just one syllable. If, while causing a sutta beginning with “Evaṃ me sutaṃ” to be recited, one stops after uttering the syllable ‘e’, there is a pācittiya offense for each subsequent syllable; if stopping after uttering an incomplete word, [there is an offense] for each subsequent consonant. If, among the words, the first word is disrupted, there is a pācittiya offense for each subsequent word. Aṭṭhakathānissito means established based on the commentary, referring to the commentary previously stated in common language. Pāḷinissito means that which comes from the Pāḷi itself. Discussions on the path and so on are also treatises.

48. Upacāranti dvādasahatthaṃ. “Opātetīti ekato bhaṇati samāgacchatī”ti likhitaṃ. Kiñcāpi apalāladamanampi sīlupadesopi bhagavato kāle uppanno, atha kho tesu yaṃ yaṃ buddhavacanato āharitvā vuttaṃ, taṃ tadeva āpattivatthu hotīti viññāpanatthaṃ mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vadantī”ti vacanehi sithilaṃ kataṃ. Buddhavacanato āharitvā vuttassa bahulatāya tabbahulanayena tesu āpatti vuttā, tasmā mahāpaccariyaṃ tassādhippāyo pakāsitoti attho. “Sabbesameva vacananti apare”ti vuttaṃ. Sace ācariyo ṭhito nisinnānaṃ pāṭhaṃ deti, “na ṭhito nisinnassa dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti vuttāpattiṃ nāpajjatīti eke. Tesampi pāṭhadānaṃ dhammadesanato na aññanti taṃ na yuttaṃ, chattapāṇikādīnaṃ pāṭhadānena anāpattippasaṅgato, āpattibhāvo ca siddho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

48. Upacāra means twelve cubits. It is written: “Opāteti means one speaks together, one comes together.” Although the taming of the nāga-king Apalāla and the instruction on virtue also arose in the time of the Blessed One, nevertheless, to make it known that among those, only what was spoken having been brought from the word of the Buddha constitutes a basis for an offense, the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā made it flexible with the word “vadantī” (they say). Because of the abundance of what was spoken having been brought forth from the Buddha’s word, an offense was stated in those cases according to that principle of abundance; therefore, the meaning is that in the Mahāpaccarī that intention was revealed. It is said: “'It is the word of all indeed,' say others.” If a teacher, while standing, gives a lesson to those who are seated, some say he does not incur the offense stated as, “I will not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated while I am standing.” But that is not correct, as giving a lesson is not different from teaching the Dhamma; otherwise, it would lead to the consequence of there being no offense for giving a lesson to one holding an umbrella, etc., yet the state of being an offense is established. For it was said:

“Ubho atthaṃ na jānanti, ubho dhammaṃ na passare;

Yo cāyaṃ mantaṃ vāceti, yo cādhammenadhīyatī”ti. (pāci. 647);

“Both do not know the meaning, both do not see the Dhamma—the one who teaches the mantra and the one who learns it improperly.” (Pāc. 647)

Ettha adhīyatīti attho, tasmā pāṭhadānampi dhammadesanāva. Sekhiyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pāci. aṭṭha. 634) “dhammaparicchedo panettha padasodhamme vuttanayena veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0292], tasmā ayameva dhammo sabbattha dhammapaṭisaṃyuttasikkhāpadesu veditabbo. Yadi evaṃ saṅkhārabhāsādivasena cittadhammaṃ desentassa sekhiyavasena anāpatti siyā, tato chapakajātakavirodho. Tattha mantānaṃ bāhiraganthattāti ce? Na, tadadhippāyājānanato. Ayañhi tattha adhippāyo “bāhirakaganthasaṅkhātampi mantaṃ ucce āsane nisinnassa vācetuṃ me bhikkhave amanāpaṃ, pageva dhammaṃ desetu”nti. “Tadāpi me, bhikkhave, amanāpaṃ nīce āsane nisīditvā ucce āsane nisinnassa mantaṃ vācetuṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana etarahi…pe… dhammaṃ desetu”nti (pāci. 647) hi ayaṃ pāḷi yathāvuttameva adhippāyaṃ dīpeti, na aññaṃ. Teneva “mantaṃ vācetuṃ dhammaṃ desetu”nti vacanabhedo kato. Aññathā ubhayattha “dhammaṃ desetu”micceva vattabbanti.

Here, the meaning is ‘one studies’; hence, even teaching by recitation is a Dhamma discourse. In the commentary on the Sekhiya rules (Pācittiya Aṭṭhakathā 634), it is stated: “The definition of Dhamma here should be understood in the manner explained in the section on 'Dhamma word by word'.” Therefore, this very Dhamma should be understood universally in all training rules connected with the Dhamma. If, in this way, there were no offense under the Sekhiya rules for one who teaches the Dhamma of the mind through explanations like formations and speech, then it would contradict the Chapaka Jātaka. Is it because there the mantras are considered external texts? No, it is due to not understanding that intention. For the intention there is this: “Monks, it is displeasing to me to teach even a mantra, which is considered an external text, to one seated on a high seat; how much more so to teach the Dhamma!” Indeed, this Pali passage, “Even then, monks, it was displeasing to me to teach a mantra while seated on a low seat to one seated on a high seat; what then to say now… to teach the Dhamma?” (Pācittiya 647), reveals the intention just as stated, and not another. For that very reason, the distinction in wording was made: “to teach a mantra” and “to teach the Dhamma.” Otherwise, in both cases, it should have been said only as “to teach the Dhamma.”

Mayā [V 0.0261] saddhiṃ mā vadātiādimhi pana anugaṇṭhipade evaṃ vutto “sace bhikkhu sāmaṇerena saddhiṃ vattukāmo, tathā sāmaṇeropi bhikkhunā saddhiṃ vattukāmo sahasā opāteti, ‘yebhuyyena paguṇaṃ ganthaṃ bhaṇantaṃ opātetī”tiādīsu viya anāpatti, na hi ettāvatā bhikkhu sāmaṇerassa uddisati nāma hoti. Yasmā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi, tasmāpi yuttamevetaṃ. Sace tattha vicāretvā paṭikkhittaṃ siyā āpatti, kiriyākiriyañca nāpajjati. Kasmā? Yasmā cittena ekato vattukāmo, atha kho naṃ ‘ekato mā vadā’ti paṭikkhipitvāpi ekato vadanto āpajjati. Avattukāmassa sahasā virajjhitvā ekato vadantassa anāpatti, tena vuttaṃ ‘mayā saddhiṃ mā vadāti vutto yadi vadati, anāpattī’ti. Tathāpi ācariyānaṃ matimanuvattantena evarūpesu ṭhānesu yathāvuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi, natthibhāvatoyeva āpatti. Sace tattha anāpattiavacanaṃ na sambhavati ayamaṭṭhānattā”ti.

However, in the supplementary passage beginning with “Do not speak with me,” it is stated thus: “If a bhikkhu wishes to speak with a sāmaṇera, and likewise the sāmaṇera wishes to speak with the bhikkhu, and one suddenly interrupts—like in the cases beginning with ‘one interrupts another who is reciting a mostly familiar text’—there is no offense. For by this much, it is not that the bhikkhu is instructing the sāmaṇera. Because this is not in the Great Commentary, this is also reasonable. If, having investigated there, it were rejected, there would be an offense, but one does not incur an offense of action and non-action. Why? Because one who wishes to speak together with intention, even after being forbidden with ‘Do not speak together,’ incurs an offense by speaking together. For one who does not wish to speak, who, having been suddenly disrupted, speaks together, there is no offense. Therefore it is said: ‘If one who has been told, “Do not speak with me,” speaks, there is no offense.’ Nevertheless, by one following the opinion of the teachers, in such cases, one should practice only according to the method as stated. Why? Because it is not in the Great Commentary, and precisely because of its absence, there is an offense. If the statement of ‘no offense’ is not possible there, it is because this is an inappropriate case.”

Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā – “mayā saddhiṃ mā vadā”ti vutto yadi vadati, bhikkhuno anāpattīti yuttametaṃ bhikkhuno vattukāmatāyābhāvato, bhāvepi sajjhāyakaraṇādīsu tīsu anāpattito ca. Atha sāmaṇerena byattatāya “mayā saddhiṃ mā vadā”ti vutto bhikkhu abyattatāya vadati, āpatti eva vattukāmatāsabbhāvato. Sahasā ce vadati, anāpatti tadabhāvato. Sace bhikkhu evaṃ “mayā saddhiṃ mā vadā”ti [M 0.0293] vatvā tena saddhiṃ sayaṃ vadati, āpatti eva. Na hi etaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ kiriyākiriyaṃ. Yadi etaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ kiriyākiriyaṃ bhaveyya, yuttaṃ. Tattha anāpattīti adhippāyo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ imināva adhippāyena “mayā saddhiṃ mā vadā”ti vuttaṃ siyā. Na hi sāmaṇerassa kiriyā idha pamāṇanti, imasmiṃ pana adhippāye vutte atiyuttaṃvāti attho. Akkharattho byañjanattho. Kiñcāpi “yañca padaṃ yañca anupadaṃ yañca anvakkharaṃ yañca anubyañjanaṃ, sabbametaṃ padasodhammo nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, tathāpi “padena vāceti, pade pade āpatti pācittiyassa, akkharāya vāceti, akkharakkharāya āpatti pācittiyassā”ti idameva dvayaṃ yojitaṃ, taṃ kasmāti ce? Padena anupadaanubyañjanānaṃ saṅgahitattā. Vuttañhetaṃ “anupadanti dutiyapādo. Anubyañjananti purimabyañjanena sadisaṃ pacchābyañjana”nti (pāci. aṭṭha. 45), tasmā anupadekadesamattameva anubyañjananti siddhaṃ. “Akkharānubyañjanasamūho pada”nti ca vuttattā padamattameva vattabbaṃ tena anupadādittayaggahaṇatoti ce? Na vattabbaṃ vacanavisesato. Padena vācento hi pade vā anupade vā anubyañjane vā āpattiṃ āpajjati. Na akkharena. Akkharena vācento pana padādīsu aññatarasmiṃ āpajjati. Na hi “varo varaññū varado varāharo”tiādimhi [V 0.0262] paṭhamaṃ va-kāraṃ vācento dutiyādiva-kāre opāteti, paṭhamaṃ ro-kāraṃ vācento dutiyaro-kāre opāteti, paṭhamaṃ ra-kāraṃ vācento dutiyara-kāre opāteti, āpatti pācittiyassāti sambhavati. Anubyañjanānulomato sambhavati evāti ce? Na, “pade pade āpatti pācittiyassā”ti iminā viruddhattā. Idañhi vacanaṃ ekasmiṃ pade ekā āpattīti dīpeti. “Rūpaṃ aniccanti vuccamāno rūti opātetī”ti vacanato sakalaṃ pādaṃ vācentassa paṭhamaakkharamatte ekato vutte āpattīti siddhanti ce? Na, “akkharakkharāya āpatti pācittiyassā”ti iminā viruddhattā, tasmā rūti opātetīti vattuṃ asambhavato rū-kārassa yathāvuttadhammapariyāpannabhāvasiddhito taṃ avatvā kevalaṃ akkharāya vācentassa yathāvuttadhammapariyāpannaakkharabhāvadassanatthaṃ “rūpaṃ aniccanti vuccamāno”ti vuttaṃ, vacanasiliṭṭhatāvasena vā anubyañjane vedanāvacanaṃ viyāti veditabbaṃ.

Herein is the deliberation: If a monk is told, “Do not speak with me,” and he speaks, it is proper that there is no offense for the monk, because of the monk's lack of desire to speak; and even if there is such a desire, there is no offense in the three cases such as making a recitation. But if a monk, having been told by a competent novice, “Do not speak with me,” speaks due to incompetence, there is indeed an offense because of the presence of the desire to speak. If he speaks thoughtlessly, there is no offense due to the absence of that desire. If a monk, having himself said, “Do not speak with me,” then speaks with that person, there is indeed an offense. For this training rule is not a matter of action and non-action. If this training rule were a matter of action and non-action, it would be proper; in that case, the intention is “no offense.” In the Mahāpaccarī, it might have been said with this very intention, “Do not speak with me.” For the novice's action is not the standard here; but when this meaning is stated, the meaning is that it is very fitting. The meaning of the letter is the meaning of the expression. Although it is said, “Whatever is a word, and whatever is a subsequent phrase, and whatever is a subsequent letter, and whatever is a secondary characteristic, all this is called the principle of purifying words,” nevertheless, only these two are applied: “If one teaches by the word, for every word there is an offense of pācittiya; if one teaches by the letter, for every letter there is an offense of pācittiya.” If one asks, “Why is that?” Because the subsequent phrase and the secondary characteristic are included by the word. For this has been said: “`Anupada` means the second foot of a verse. `Anubyañjana` means a later consonant similar to a former consonant.” Therefore, it is established that `anubyañjana` is merely a part of the `anupada`. If one were to argue: “And because it is said, ‘A word is a collection of letters and secondary characteristics,’ only the word should be mentioned, because by that the three beginning with `anupada` are included”? (The reply is:) This should not be said, due to the specific statement. For one who teaches by the word incurs an offense in a word, or a subsequent phrase, or a secondary characteristic. Not by the letter. But one who teaches by the letter incurs an offense in any one of the categories beginning with 'word'. For it is not possible that in a phrase such as “varo varaññū varado varāharo,” one who teaches the first 'va'-syllable thereby omits the second and subsequent 'va'-syllables; or that one who teaches the first 'ro'-syllable omits the second 'ro'-syllable; or that one who teaches the first 'ra'-syllable omits the second 'ra'-syllable, and that for this there is an offense of pācittiya. If one were to say, “It is indeed possible, in accordance with the secondary characteristic”? No, because it contradicts this statement: “For every word, there is an offense of pācittiya.” For this statement indicates one offense in one word. If one were to argue that, based on the statement “Being taught ‘Form is impermanent,’ he omits ‘rū’”, it is established that for one teaching the entire phrase, there is an offense when just the first letter is uttered? No, because it contradicts this statement: “For every letter, there is an offense of pācittiya.” Therefore, since it is impossible to say “he omits ‘rū’”, and since it is established that the syllable ‘rū’ is included in the aforementioned teaching, the phrase “being taught ‘Form is impermanent’” was stated not to say that, but for the purpose of showing—for one who teaches merely by the letter—that the letter is included in the aforementioned teaching. Or, it should be understood by way of verbal fluency, like the term ‘feeling’ in the context of secondary characteristics.

Padasodhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Padasodhamma training rule is concluded.

5. Paṭhamasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Shared Lodging

50. “Na [M 0.0294] sahaseyyaṃ kappetabba”nti bhāvavasena vuttaṃ, kesuci “na sahaseyyā kappetabbā”ti pāṭho, na kappetabbā bhikkhunāti paññattanti adhippāyo. “Apassenaṃ vāti vāyimamañcakameva hotī”ti likhitaṃ. Yaṃ etesaṃ na kappati, taṃ tesampīti upajjhāyādīnaṃ santikaṃ agantvā sahaseyyaṃ kappeyyāti pāṭhaseso.

50. The phrase 'Shared lodging should not be undertaken' is stated in the abstract sense of the action. In some textual versions, the reading is 'Shared lodgings should not be undertaken'; the intended meaning is that it is laid down that it should not be undertaken by a bhikkhu. It is written: 'Or without a support' means it is simply a woven couch. The remainder of the text should be supplied as follows: 'Whatever is not allowable for these (monks), is also not allowable for those (novices). Thinking thus, one might undertake shared lodging without first going to one's preceptors and so on.'

52. “Anupasampanno nāma bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā avaseso’ti vuttattā mātugāmo anupasampannoti catuttharattiyaṃ mātugāmo dvepi sahaseyyāpattiyo janetīti apare”ti vuttaṃ, “bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā…pe… pannoti pārājikavatthubhūto tiracchānapuriso adhippeto”ti ca, ubhayampi vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Dutiyasikkhāpade mātugāmo nāmāti manussitthiṃyeva gahetvā yakkhī petī tiracchānagatā pārājikavatthubhūtā na gahitā tesu dukkaṭattā. “Sace pana attanopi sikkhāpade dukkaṭaṃ bhaveyya, atha kasmā paṭhamasikkhāpade pācittiya”nti ca vuttaṃ. “Aparikkhitte pamukhe anāpattī”ti sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ, tassatthaṃ dīpetuṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “bhūmiyaṃ vinā jagatiyā pamukhaṃ sandhāya kathita”nti vuttaṃ. Puna vasatīti catutthadivase vasati. Bhikkhunipanneti bhikkhumhi nipanne. Sannipatitamaṇḍapaṃ nāma mahāvihāre sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ. “Tīṇi [V 0.0263] ca divasāni dukkaṭakhette vasitvā catutthe divase sahaseyyāpattipahonake sayati, pācittiyevā”ti ekacce vadanti kira, taṃ na yuttaṃ.

52. Because it is said, 'An unordained person means anyone remaining, having excluded a bhikkhu,' some say, 'Therefore, on the fourth night, a woman is an unordained person and causes both offenses of shared lodging to arise.' And it is said: 'Here, in the phrase "having excluded a bhikkhu... unordained person," a male animal, which is the basis for a Pārājika offense, is intended.' Both of these statements should be investigated. In the second training rule, in the phrase 'a woman means,' only a human female is taken, while female yakkhas, petīs, and animals, which are the basis for a Pārājika offense, are not taken, because in those cases it is a dukkaṭa offense. It is also said: 'But if in one's own training rule it were a dukkaṭa offense, then why in the first training rule is it a pācittiya?' There is this statement from the Sinhalese commentary: 'There is no offense in an unenclosed porch.' To explain its meaning, in the Andhaka commentary it is said: 'This was said in reference to a porch on a terrace, not on the ground.' Here, 'dwells again' means dwells on the fourth day. 'When a bhikkhu is lying down' means when a bhikkhu is lying down. The 'assembly hall' is the meeting place in the Mahāvihāra. Some are said to claim: 'Having dwelt for three days in a domain of a dukkaṭa offense, if on the fourth day one dwells in a place sufficient to incur an offense of shared lodging, it is a pācittiya offense indeed.' That is not correct.

Paṭhamasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Shared Lodging is concluded.

6. Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Shared Lodging

55. “Atha kho te manussā”ti ca “te addhikā”ti ca pāṭho. “Ekaratta”ntipi atthi, so na sundaro. Paṇḍake pāḷiyaṃ dukkaṭassa vuttattā “ubhatobyañjanehi mūlāpattīti dissatī”ti, “animittādayo itthiyovā”ti ca vadanti ubhatobyañjanake vuttaṃ viya. Kiñcāpi matitthī pārājikavatthu hoti, anupādinnapakkhe ṭhitattā pana idha āpattiṃ na karoti. Pārājikāpattiṭṭhānañcettha na oloketabbaṃ.

55. “Then those people” and “those travelers” are variant readings. The reading “one night” also exists, but it is not good. Because it is stated in the Pāḷi that for a paṇḍaka there is a dukkaṭa offense, and because it appears that for a hermaphrodite there is a root offense, some say, “Those without distinguishing features and so on are indeed women,” as was said regarding the hermaphrodite. Although a dead woman is an object for a pārājika offense, nevertheless, because she is in the category of the un-grasped, she does not create an offense here. And the basis for a pārājika offense should not be considered here.

Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lying Down Together is finished.

7. Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma

66. “Viññū [M 0.0295] paṭibalā”ti vacanato aviññū itthiyāpi desentassa anāpatti. Idha yakkhīādayo manussitthī viya anoḷārikattā dukkaṭavatthukā jātā. Tiracchānagatamanussaviggahitthiyā paṭibalatāya vuttattā itarāpi dukkaṭavatthuyevāti eke. “Mātugāmāyā”ti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ. “Aṭṭhakathādipāṭhaṃ ṭhapetvā damiḷādinā yathāruci kathetuṃ labhati kirā”ti likhitaṃ, yathā yakkhīādayo dukkaṭavatthukā jātā, tathā purisaviggahaṃ gahetvā ṭhitena yakkhādinā saddhiṃ ṭhitassa mātugāmassa dhammaṃ desento dukkaṭaṃ anāpajjitvā kasmā pācittiyamāpajjatīti ce? Īsakampi dutiyapakkhaṃ abhajanato. Manussamātugāmopi na dutiyo, pageva yakkhādayoti. Na dutiyāniyate tassa dutiyattāti ce? Na tattha duṭṭhullavācāpekkhā dutiyatā, kintu nisajjāpekkhā, idha ca na nisajjamattaṃ, kintu desanā idhādhippetā. Sā ca nipajjanato oḷārikā, tasmā asamatthanidassanaṃ.

66. Because of the statement, “An intelligent person is able,” there is no offense for one who teaches even an unintelligent woman. Here, female yakkhas and so on, because of not being coarse like a human woman, have become objects for a dukkaṭa offense. Because the capability of a female animal with a human form is stated, some say that others too are indeed objects for a dukkaṭa offense. “Of a woman” is stated with a change of gender. It is written: “It is said that, having set aside the text of the commentary and so on, one may speak as one wishes in Tamil and so on.” If one were to ask: “Just as female yakkhas and so on have become objects for a dukkaṭa offense, why does one who teaches the Dhamma to a woman standing together with a yakkha or the like who has taken a male form not incur a dukkaṭa, but instead incur a pācittiya?” Because of not entering into the second party, even a little. A human woman is not a second party, how much more so yakkhas and so on. If one were to say: “One does not incur an offense because of her being a second party in the second Aniyata rule,” it should be said: There, being a second party is not with reference to lewd speech, but with reference to sitting. And here, it is not mere sitting, but teaching that is intended here. And that teaching is coarser than sitting. Therefore, that is an unfitting example.

Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma is finished.

8. Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Announcing a True Attainment

67. “Catutthapārājikavatthu [V 0.0264] ca idañca ekamevā”ti vuttaṃ, na yuttaṃ. Kasmā? Tattha “moghapurisā”ti vuttattā. Te ariyamissakā na hontīti dvepi ekasadisānīti mama takko. “Ariyāpi paṭijāniṃsu, tesampi abbhantare vijjamānattā uttarimanussadhammassā”ti likhitaṃ. “Sabbepi bhūtaṃ bhagavāti puthujjanaariyānaṃ uttarimanussadhammassa ārocitattā ‘bhūta’nti vuttaṃ, na attano uttarimanussadhammaṃ sandhāyāti apare”ti vuttaṃ.

67. It was said: 'The matter of the fourth pārājika and this are one and the same,' but that is not suitable. Why? Because there it is said, 'worthless men.' They are not mixed with the noble ones; thus, my reasoning is that both are similar. It is written: 'Noble ones also confessed, because the superior human state exists within them.' It was said: 'All informed the Blessed One, saying, "It is true." Thus, others say that "true" was said because the superior human state of ordinary persons and noble ones was announced, not referring to one's own superior human state.'

77. Pubbe avuttehīti catutthapārājike avuttehīti.

77. “By those not spoken of before” means by those not spoken of in the fourth pārājika.

Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Announcing a Truthful Attainment is concluded.

9. Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Announcing a Grave Offense

78-80. “Teneva [M 0.0296] hatthena upakkamitvā asuciṃ mocesī”ti pāṭho sampatipāṭho sundaro. Apaloketvāva kātabbā. No ce, pāḷiyaṃyeva vuttaṃ siyā. “Ottappenā”ti vattabbe ruḷhīvasena paresu “hirottappenā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ uttānattā na vuttaṃ, pācittiyāsambhavadassaneneva hi dukkaṭanti siddhaṃ.

The reading, “With that very hand, having approached, he released impurity,” is a good one. It should be done only after asking permission. If not, it would have been stated in the Pāḷi itself. When “with moral dread” should be said, by way of convention among others, “with moral shame and moral dread” is said. In the Great Commentary, it is not stated because it is obvious; for indeed, it is established that it is a dukkaṭa offense simply by seeing the impossibility of a pācittiya offense.

83. Tattha “kamma”nti vuttaajjhācārepi pariyāpannattā taṃ tassa daṇḍakammavatthu. “Tattha kammaṃ āpanno”ti pubbepi likhitaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “attakāmaṃ āpanno”ti pāṭho, “ayameva gahetabbo”ti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

83. There, because it is included even in the misconduct spoken of as an 'act' (kamma), that misconduct is the basis for his disciplinary action. “There he has committed an act” has also been written previously. In the Great Commentary, there is the reading “he has fulfilled his desire,” and they say, “This very reading should be taken.” It should be investigated.

Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Announcing a Grave Offense is concluded.

10. Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Earth

86. Kaṭasakkharā setamattikā viya mudukā sakkharajāti. “Akatapabbhāreti avalañjitabbaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ vutta”nti likhitaṃ. “Anovassakaṭṭhānadassanattha”nti vattabbaṃ. Mūsikukkuranti mūsikāhi uddhaṭapaṃsu. Suddhacittāti kiñcāpi “evaṃ pavaṭṭite pathavī bhijjissatī”ti [V 0.0265] jānanti, no pana ce pathavībhedatthikā, suddhacittā nāma honti. Paṃsuādayo dve koṭṭhāsā āpattikarā. Keci “sabbacchannādīsu upaḍḍhe dukkaṭassa vuttattā sace dukkaṭaṃ, yutta”nti vadanti. Tattha yuttaṃ tādisassa vatthuno sambhavā, idha pana jātapathavī ca ajātapathavī cāti dveyeva vatthūni, tasmā dvinnaṃ ekena bhavitabbanti na yuttaṃ. Etthāpi dukkaṭavacanaṃ atthīti ce? Taṃ pana saññāvasena, na vatthuvasenāti na yuttameva.

86. A type of gravel that has been worked on is soft like white clay. It is written: '“Unprepared ground” is stated for the purpose of showing a place that should not be used.' It should also be said: 'for the purpose of showing a place not soaked by rain.' In 'mūsikukkura,' it refers to earth dug up by rats. Regarding 'with a pure mind': although they know, 'If it is disturbed in this way, the earth will break,' if they do not desire the destruction of the earth, they are called 'of pure mind.' Earth and so forth, the two portions, are what cause an offense. Some say, 'Because a dukkaṭa offense is mentioned for a half portion in cases such as fully-roofed dwellings, if it is a dukkaṭa offense here, it is appropriate.' There, it is appropriate because of the possibility of such a case. But here, there are only two grounds: 'earth that has come into being' and 'earth that has not come into being.' Therefore, it must be one of the two, and for that reason, it is not appropriate. If one were to say, 'Here too there is the statement of a dukkaṭa offense,' the reply is: that, however, is stated by way of perception, not by way of the object; therefore, it is indeed not appropriate.

87. Aggiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti ettha ettāvatā usumaṃ gaṇhāti, tasmā vaṭṭatīti keci. Evaṃ sati pathaviyā aggimhi kate dūratopi bhūmi uṇhā hoti, tattakaṃ kopetabbaṃ siyā, na ca kappati, tasmā yasmiṃ ṭhāne patati, taṃ so aggi ḍahati, tasmā vaṭṭatīti eke. Aḍahitepi “adaḍḍhāya [M 0.0297] pathaviyā aggiṃ ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā attanā pātanāyeva doso patite upadāheti veditabbaṃ.

87. Herein, regarding 'It is allowable to make a fire': some say that by this much it takes on heat; therefore, it is allowable. This being so, when a fire is made on the earth, the ground becomes hot even from a distance, and that much of the area would have to be disturbed, which is not allowable. Therefore, some say that in whatever place it falls, that fire does not burn that place; therefore, it is allowable. Even if it is not burnt, because it is said, 'It is not allowable to place a fire on unburnt earth,' it should be understood that by one's own act of causing it to fall, if there is scorching where it has fallen, there is an offense.

Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth is concluded.

Samatto vaṇṇanākkamena musāvādavaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter, the one on false speech, is concluded in accordance with the order of the commentary.

2. Bhūtagāmavaggo

2. The Chapter on Plants

1. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
