Because of having a tongue, by which they drink water, all are called ‘pādapā’ (foot-drinkers). Because of having body sensitivity, asoka trees blossom by the touch of women." "Saṅghātaṃ" means destruction.

970. Idha [M 0.0380] ca vassacchedena dukkaṭaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ āvasitvā pacchā cārikā caraṇapaccayā pācittiyaṃ āpajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Atha vassaṃ avasitvā carati, avassupagamanapaccayā [V 0.0348] dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade pana “antosattāhe antovasse cārikaṃ carantiyā pācittiyaṃ. Sattāhakaraṇīyena pana vaṭṭati, bhikkhuno dukkaṭaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

970. And here, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for breaking the rains-residence. It should be known that if one first dwells and afterwards goes on tour, one incurs a pācittiya offense on account of going on tour. If one goes on tour without having dwelt for the rains, one incurs a dukkaṭa offense on account of not undertaking the rains-residence. But in the ancient glosses it is said: “For a bhikkhunī who goes on tour within the rains-residence, there is a pācittiya. For a seven-day duty, however, it is allowable; for a bhikkhu, there is a dukkaṭa.”

972. Kenaci ubbāḷhāti vassacchedakāraṇenāti no takkoti ācariyo. Kittāvatā cārikā hotīti? Idaṃ na sabbattha vicāritaṃ. Anantarasikkhāpade “antamaso chappañcayojanānipī”ti vuttattā so ca maññe heṭṭhimaparicchedoti.

972. Regarding "harassed by someone": the teacher states that one should not infer this to mean "by a reason for breaking the rains-residence." The question of to what extent it is considered wandering has not been investigated in all glossaries. Because it is said in the following training rule, "at least five or six yojanas," I think that this is the lower limit.

Navamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ninth Training Rule is concluded.

10. Dasamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Tenth Training Rule

973. Dasame “āhundarikā”ti paṭhanti kira.

973. In the tenth, it is said that they read ‘āhundarikā’.

Dasamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tenth Training Rule is concluded.

Tuvaṭṭavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tuvaṭṭa Vagga is concluded.

5. Cittāgāravaggavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Cittāgāra Vagga

1. Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Training Rule

978. Kīḷanaupavanaṃ nāma kañcinagarassa nagarupavanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uyyānaṃ nāma tattheva nandavanauyyānaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Tattheva ṭhatvā taṃ taṃ disābhāgaṃ viloketvā passantiyā pana pāṭekkā āpattiyo”ti pāṭho. Evaṃ vutte yaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ padaṃ “anuddharamānā”ti, taṃ ekasmiṃyeva disābhāgeti siddhanti eke. Upacāro dve leḍḍupātoti ca.

978. A ‘recreational grove’ should be understood as like a city grove of a certain city. A ‘park’ should be understood as like the Nandavana pleasure garden there. The reading is: “But for her, standing right there, looking around and seeing in each different direction, there are separate offenses.” When this is said, some conclude that the previously mentioned phrase “not withdrawing” refers to just one direction. And the ‘approach’ is two clod-throws.

Paṭhamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first training rule is concluded.

2. Dutiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Training Rule

984. “Āharimehi [M 0.0381][V 0.0349] vāḷehī”ti “asaṃhārimenā”ti ca duvidho pāṭho. “Visuṃ katvā pacchā saddhiṃ tehi vāḷehī”ti likhitaṃ. Yathā tathā vāḷarūpe uṭṭhapetvā katapādaṃ “pallaṅka”nti vuccati anāpattivāre “asaṃhārimehi vāḷehi kataṃ paribhuñjatī”ti vacanābhāvato.

984. There are two readings: “with removable borders” and “with a non-removable one.” It is written: “Having first separated them, afterwards joining those borders together.” In any case, what is made by raising up border-like forms and making legs is called a ‘couch’ (pallaṅka), because in the section on non-offenses there is no statement, “one may use one made with non-removable borders.”

Dutiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule is concluded.

3. Tatiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Third Training Rule

988. “Ujjavujjaveti hatthappasāraṇe”ti likhitaṃ, taṃ na yuttaṃ “yattakaṃ hatthena añchitaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ takkamhi veṭhite ekāpattī”ti vacanato.

988. It is written: “‘Ujjavujjaveti’ means stretching out the hand,” but that is not appropriate, because of the statement: “For whatever amount is drawn out by the hand, there is one offense for each winding on the spindle.”

Tatiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the third training rule is concluded.

4. Catutthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule

993. “Yāgupāneti yāgudāne”ti likhitaṃ. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade “mātāpitūnaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

993. It is written: “‘Yāgupāne’ means in the giving of rice-gruel.” In the ancient glossary, it is stated: “It is allowable to give to one’s parents.”

Catutthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the fourth training rule is concluded.

994. Pañcamasikkhāpadaṃ uttānatthameva.

994. The fifth training rule is clear in meaning.

6. Chaṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Sixth Training Rule

1001. Chaṭṭhe bhikkhuvibhaṅge acelakasikkhāpadena ekaparicchedaṃ. Idha agāriko viseso, tasmā “asādhāraṇa”nti vadanti.

1001. The sixth rule is treated as a single section along with the training rule concerning the naked ascetic in the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga. Here, the householder is the special case; therefore, they call it “uncommon.”

Chaṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the sixth training rule is concluded.

1003-8. Sattamaṭṭhamesu [V 0.0350] vattabbaṃ natthi.

There is nothing that needs to be said regarding the seventh and eighth.

9. Navamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule

1015. “Khīlanamantaṃ [M 0.0382] dārusārakhīlaṃ mantetvā pathaviyaṃ pavesetvā māraṇamantaṃ. Nāgamaṇḍalaṃnāma nāgarodhamantaṃ, piṭṭhādīhi vā parikkhepaṃ katvā tattha manusse pavesenti guttatthāyā”ti likhitaṃ.

1015. It is written: “The peg incantation is to recite a mantra over a hardwood peg and drive it into the ground; the death incantation. The ‘serpent-circle’ is the incantation for confining snakes, or, having made a boundary with flour and the like, they cause people to enter there for protection.”

Navamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the ninth training rule is concluded.

1017. Dasamasikkhāpadaṃ uttānatthameva.

1017. The tenth training rule is of clear meaning.

Cittāgāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Cittāgāra Vagga is concluded.

6. Ārāmavaggavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Ārāma Vagga

1021. Paṭhamasikkhāpadaṃ uttānatthameva.

1021. The first training rule is of clear meaning.

2. Dutiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Training Rule

1030. Bhikkhunī ce bhikkhuṃ akkosati, iminā sikkhāpadena pācittiyaṃ. Bhikkhuniṃ ce akkosati, omasavādena āpajjati. Omasavāde sammukhāva ruhati, idha pana parammukhāpi.

1030. If a bhikkhunī reviles a bhikkhu, there is a pācittiya offense by this training rule. If she reviles a bhikkhunī, she incurs an offense through disparaging speech. In the case of disparaging speech, the offense is incurred only when face-to-face, but here, it is also incurred in absence.

Tatrāyaṃ vicāraṇā – bhikkhuvibhaṅge osamavādasikkhāpade bhikkhunī anupasampannaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti katvā bhikkhunivibhaṅgepi omasavādasikkhāpade bhikkhu bhikkhuniyā anupasampannaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti siddhaṃ. Idha ca anupasampannassa akkosane dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, bhikkhussa upasampannassa akkosane pācittiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā imāni dve sikkhāpadāni bhikkhumhi [V 0.0351] saṃsandiyamānāni aññamaññaṃ na samenti. Yathā samenti, tathā jānitabbaṃ. Tattha porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttanayena bhikkhunīnaṃ omasavādasikkhāpade anupasampannoti na gahetabbo, idamettha yuttaṃ. Paribhāseyyāti aññatra akkosavatthūhi. Tesu hi aññatarasmiṃ sati omasavādapācittiyamevāti eke, taṃ na yuttaṃ[M 0.0383]. Omasavāde pāḷimuttakaakkose hi dukkaṭaṃ hotīti. Dukkaṭokāse idaṃ pācittiyaṃ tehi niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti, tasmā “bālā etā”ti pāḷiyaṃ idha āgatapadānaṃyeva vasena paribhāsanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein is the investigation: In the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, concerning the training rule on disparaging speech, a bhikkhunī stands in the place of an unordained person. Therefore, in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga as well, concerning the training rule on disparaging speech, it is established that a bhikkhu stands in the place of an unordained person in relation to a bhikkhunī. And here, a dukkaṭa offense is stated for reviling an unordained person, while a pācittiya offense is stated for reviling an ordained bhikkhu. Therefore, these two training rules, when compared with respect to a bhikkhu, do not agree with each other. How they agree should be understood. Therein, according to the method stated in the ancient glosses, in the bhikkhunīs’ training rule on disparaging speech, the term ‘unordained’ should not be taken; this is proper here. The term `paribhāseyya` (‘one should revile’) is to be understood as something other than the grounds for insult. For if any of those grounds are present, some say it is solely a pācittiya offense for disparaging speech, but that is not correct. For in the case of disparaging speech, a dukkaṭa offense occurs for insults that are not found in the Pāḷi. This pācittiya offense would thus be designated by them in an instance that is properly a dukkaṭa. Therefore, the reviling should be understood as being based only on the terms that appear here in the Pāḷi, such as, ‘these are foolish’.

Dutiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the second training rule is concluded.

1033. Tatiyasikkhāpadaṃ uttānatthameva.

1033. The third training rule is of clear meaning.

4. Catutthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule

1038. Nimantitā vā pavāritā vāti ettha porāṇagaṇṭhipade tāva evaṃ vuttaṃ “pavāritāpi yāguṃ pātuṃ labhati, bhojjayāguṃ na labhati. Yāgu panettha khādanīyabhojanīyasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Nimantitā bhikkhunī piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjitukāmā sāmike apaloketvāva bhuñjituṃ labhati. Paramparabhojanāpatti bhikkhunīnaṃ natthi. Nimantitā taṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vā abhuñjitvā vā pavāritā kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā bhuñjituṃ na labhati, akappiyanimantanena nimantiyamānā dve nimantanāni sampaṭicchituñca na labhatī”ti. Tattha “pavāritāpi yāguṃ pātuṃ labhatī”ti vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyañca anuññātattā. “Nimantitā appavāritā yāguṃ pivatī”ti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatridaṃ sikkhāpadavaṇṇanāpubbaṅgamasanniṭṭhānaṃ – nimantitā vā pavāritā vāti ettha vāsaddena akappiyanimantanena nimantitā appavāritā ṭhapetvā yāguṃ aññaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā khādeyya vā bhuñjeyya vā, pācittiyaṃ aññatra sāmikānaṃ apalokanā. Paramparabhojanābhāvena bhikkhunīnaṃ ko guṇo jātoti? Na etāsaṃ guṇalābho, kevalaṃ pākaṭataraṃ jātaṃ. Bhikkhūpi vikappetvā missetvāva bhuñjituṃ labhanti. Samaye yathāsukhaṃ labhanti. Iminā apalokanena kinti? Pavāritā vā animantitā vā na kiñci kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā gilānātirittampi labhanti, nimantitā ca pavāritā ca yāgumpi na labhanti, apaloketvāpi na labhantīti.

1038. In the phrase 'invited or refused', it is stated thus in the ancient glosses: 'Even one who has refused is allowed to drink gruel; she is not allowed to eat gruel that is a meal. Herein, gruel does not fall into the category of staple or non-staple food. An invited bhikkhunī, having gone for alms-food, if she wishes to eat, is allowed to eat only after informing the donors. There is no offense of consecutive eating for bhikkhunīs. An invited one, whether she has eaten that meal or not, if she has refused, is not allowed to eat after having it made allowable. A bhikkhunī being invited with an improper invitation is not allowed to accept two invitations.' Therein, the statement 'Even one who has refused is allowed to drink gruel' is made because it is permitted in the Pāḷi and in the Commentary. Indeed, in the Pāḷi it is said, 'An invited one who has not refused drinks gruel.' Therein, this is the conclusion preceded by the explanation of the training rule: In the phrase 'invited or refused', by the word 'or' it is understood that if a bhikkhunī who was invited with an improper invitation and has not refused should eat or consume any other staple or non-staple food, setting aside gruel, it is a Pācittiya offense, unless she informs the donors. If it is asked, 'Due to the absence of consecutive eating, what benefit has arisen for the bhikkhunīs?' For them, no gain of benefit has arisen; it has merely become more evident. Bhikkhus too are allowed to eat only after making a formal disposal and mixing it. At the proper time, they receive it as they wish. What is gained by this informing? Those who have refused or are uninvited do not receive anything, not even the remainder for the sick, after having it made allowable. And those who are invited and have refused do not receive even gruel; they do not receive it even after informing. Thus it should be understood.

Catutthasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the fourth training rule is concluded.

Ārāmavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ārāma Vagga is concluded.

7. Gabbhinivaggavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Gabbhinī Vagga

1. Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First and Subsequent Training Rules

1067. “Gabbhini”nti [M 0.0384][V 0.0352] dassanādīhipi gabbhasambhavato vuttaṃ. Padabhājanepi pavāritabhāvo na dissati.

1067. The term "pregnant" (`gabbhinī`) is used because of the arising of conception through seeing and so forth. And in the analysis of words, the state of having refused is not found.

1074. Dhāti vāti ettha dārakaṃ sāmikānaṃ datvā āhaṭe vaḍḍheti, tathā mātāpīti keci.

1074. Herein, regarding 'nurse' (`dhāti`), some say it is one who, having given the child to its owners, raises it when it is brought back; and that the mother also does so similarly.

1080. “Sikkhamāna”nti pāṭhaṃ dīpavāsino rocenti kiriyākiriyattā, jambudīpavāsino “sikkhamānā”ti. Tassattho sikkhādhammamānanato sikkhamānāti. Idha kiriyā na hoti, saññāva adhippetā. Na etāsu asikkhitā upasampādetabbā upajjhāyinīādīnaṃ āpattibhāvā. “Tassā upasampadā hoti evā”ti vadanti.

1080. The reading 'sikkhamānaṃ' is favored by the island-dwellers because of it being both action and non-action; the dwellers of Jambudīpa favor 'sikkhamānā'. Its meaning is: she is called a 'sikkhamānā' because she honors the rules of training. Here, it is not an action; only a designation is intended. One who has not trained in these rules should not be given higher ordination, because of the occurrence of an offense for the preceptor nun and others. They say, 'Her higher ordination indeed occurs.'

1082. Dhammakammeti upasampadakammaṃ adhippetaṃ.

1082. By 'a formal act in accordance with the Dhamma' (`dhammakamma`), the act of higher ordination (`upasampadakamma`) is intended.

1112. Vuṭṭhāpitanti sāmaṇeribhūmito yāya theriyā upasampadāpekkhā vuṭṭhapitā, sā therī vuṭṭhāpitā nāma, teneva puna visesanatthaṃ “pavattini”nti āha.

1112. Regarding 'one who has raised up' (`vuṭṭhāpitā`): that female elder by whom a candidate for higher ordination has been raised from the state of a female novice is called `vuṭṭhāpitā`. For that very reason, for the purpose of further specification, it is said 'preceptor' (`pavattinī`).

Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the first and subsequent training rules is concluded.

Gabbhinivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Gabbhinī Vagga is concluded.

8. Kumāribhūtavaggavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Kumāribhūta Vagga

2. Dutiyādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second and Subsequent Training Rules

1124. “Anujānāmi[V 0.0353], bhikkhave, aṭṭhārasavassāya kumāribhūtāya…pe… sikkhāsammutiṃ dātu”nti idha vuttaṃ viya “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, dasavassāya gihigatāya…pe… sikkhāsammutiṃ dātu”nti na vuttaṃ, tasmā “paripuṇṇadvādasavassāya eva gihigatāya sikkhāsammuti dātabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Gihigatāya sikkhāsammuti dātabbāti eketi katvā dasavassāyapi vaṭṭati[M 0.0385]. Kasmā? “Anāpatti paripuṇṇadvādasavassaṃ paripuṇṇasaññā vuṭṭhāpetī’ti (pāci. 1093-1095) ca ‘anāpatti paripuṇṇadvādasavassaṃ gihigataṃ…pe… sikkhitasikkhaṃ vuṭṭhāpetī’ti (pāci. 1097-1101) ca vuttattā”ti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Kiṃ iminā parihārena. “Dasavassāya gihigatāya sikkhāsammuti dātabbā”ti hi vuttaṃ. “Gihigatātipi vattuṃ na vaṭṭatī’ti sace vadanti, kammaṃ kuppatī”ti likhitaṃ.

1124. Just as it is stated here, 'I allow, Bhikkhus, to give the consent for training to a maiden (`kumāribhūtā`) of eighteen years... (etc.)', it is not stated, 'I allow, Bhikkhus, to give the consent for training to one who has gone to a household life (`gihigatā`) at ten years... (etc.)'. Therefore, it is said, 'The consent for training should be given only to a `gihigatā` who has completed twelve years.' Some say, 'The consent for training should be given to a `gihigatā`.' For this reason, it is also allowable for a ten-year-old. Why? Because it is stated in the ancient glosses (`porāṇagaṇṭhipada`): 'There is no offense for one who gives higher ordination to one who has completed twelve years, perceiving her to be complete,' and 'There is no offense for one who gives higher ordination to a `gihigatā` who has completed twelve years... (etc.) ... and has trained in the training rules.' What is the use of this explanation? For it is said, 'The consent for training should be given to a `gihigatā` of ten years.' In this matter, if they say, 'It is not allowable even to say `gihigatā`,' it is written, 'the formal act is invalid.'

1146. Ahameva nūna…pe… alajjinī, yā saṅghoti ettha yā ahameva nūna bālāti attho. “Yaṃ saṅgho”tipi atthi, tattha yaṃ yasmā deti, tasmā ahameva nūna bālāti attho.

1146. Regarding 'Ahameva nūna… alajjinī, yā saṅgho': Herein, the meaning is: 'Am I not indeed the foolish one?' There is also the reading 'yaṃ saṅgho'. Therein, 'yaṃ' means 'yasmā' (because); therefore, the meaning is, 'Am I not indeed the foolish one?'

1159. Purisasaṃsaṭṭhā kumārakasaṃsaṭṭhā caṇḍī sokāvāsāvakathaṃ sikkhamānāti vuccati, padabhājane eva cāyaṃ sikkhamānā “chasu dhammesu sikkhitasikkhā”ti kasmā vuttanti? Pubbe gahitasikkhattā, pubbe paripuṇṇasikkhattā ca evaṃ vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

1159. How is one who associates with men, associates with youths, is irascible, and dwells in sorrow called a probationer? And in the Padabhājanī itself, why is this probationer said to be 'one trained in the six rules'? It should be understood that she is so called because she has previously undertaken the training and because she has previously perfected the training.

1166-7. Pahūtaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ passitvāti ettha “sikkhamānāya ñātakā kira sampādayiṃsu, taṃ passitvā there bhikkhū uyyojesi. Uyyojetvā tesaṃ chandaṃ gahetvā pubbe chandadāyake gaṇaṃ katvā sesānaṃ chandaṃ chandameva katvā kammaṃ kārāpesī”ti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Chandaṃ vissajjetvāti ettha anugaṇṭhipade evaṃ vuttaṃ “idaṃ kammaṃ ajja na kattabbaṃ. ‘Yathāsukha’nti vatvā vissajjitaṃ hoti, tasmā yo koci mukharo, bālo vā kiñcāpi ‘yathāsukha’nti vadati, therāyattattā pana therassa anumatiyā satiyā vissajjito hoti, asatiyā [V 0.0354] na hoti, tathāpi puna chandaṃ gahetvāva kammaṃ karonti, ayaṃ payogo. Gahaṇe payojanaṃ pana natthi. Saṅghatthero ce vissajjeti, chandaṃ gahetvāva kātabbaṃ. Chandaṃ vissajjetvā kāyena vuṭṭhitāyāti ettha idha sambādho, ‘amukamhi ṭhāne karissāmā’ti hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvāpi gacchanti ce, natthi doso. Kiñcāpi natthi, tā pana hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvāva gacchanti, ayaṃ payogo”ti. “Rattipārivāsiye uposathapavāraṇāva na vaṭṭati, aññakammaṃ pana vaṭṭati. Uposathapavāraṇāpi anuposathapavāraṇadivase na vaṭṭanti, itaraṃ sabbakālaṃ vaṭṭati. Parisapārivāsiye [M 0.0386] hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā catūsu gatesu catuvaggakaraṇīye aññasmiṃ pañcasu dasasu vīsatīsu gatesu sesehi visuṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ gantvāpi puna sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Ajjhāsayapārivāsiye hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā yathānisinnāva nisinnā ce, puna kātuṃ vaṭṭati hatthapāsassa avijahitattā”ti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ porāṇānaṃ matena chandapārivāsiyamevekaṃ na vaṭṭatīti āpannaṅgañca dassitaṃ, idhāpi taṃ visuṃ na dassitaṃ asambhavatoti eke. Chandadāyake parisaṃ patvā gate tassa pubbachandadānaṃ chandapārivāsiyanti no takkoti ācariyo.

Regarding 'having seen abundant hard and soft food,' it is said in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: 'It is said that the relatives of the probationer provided it. Seeing that, she dismissed the elder bhikkhus. Having dismissed them, having taken their consent, having first formed a group with the consent-giver, and having treated the consent of the remaining ones as just consent, she had the formal act performed.' Regarding 'having dismissed the consent,' it is thus stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: 'This formal act should not be performed today. Having said, "As you please," it is considered dismissed. Therefore, although any talkative or foolish person might say, "As you please," it is nevertheless dependent on the elder. It is dismissed when there is the elder's approval, but not when there is not. Nevertheless, they perform the formal act only after taking consent again; this is the procedure. But there is no benefit in taking it. If the elder of the Saṅgha dismisses it, it must be done only after taking consent.' Regarding 'having dismissed the consent and having risen up with the body,' here there is a confined space. Even if they go, having left the hand's reach, thinking, 'We will do it in such-and-such a place,' there is no fault. Although there is no fault, they go only without leaving the hand's reach; this is the procedure.' 'In the case of an overnight stay invalidating the quorum, only the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are not allowable; another formal act, however, is allowable. The Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are also not allowable on a non-Uposatha, non-Pavāraṇā day; the other is allowable at all times. In the case of the assembly's quorum being invalidated, without leaving the hand's reach, when four have gone for another act requiring a quorum of four, or when five, ten, or twenty have gone, it is allowable for the remaining ones, having gone separately here and there, to perform it after returning again to the meeting place. In the case of the intention invalidating the quorum, if they remain seated just as they were, without leaving the hand's reach, it is allowable to perform it again because of not having left the hand's reach.' This is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada. According to the opinion of those ancients, only the one case of consent invalidating the quorum is not allowable, and thus the factor of falling into an offense is shown. Here too, that is not shown separately because of its impossibility, say some. The teacher says: When the consent-giver, having reached the assembly, has gone, his prior giving of consent is not a case of consent invalidating the quorum; this is our reasoning.

Tatridaṃ sanniṭṭhānaṃ – parisapārivāsiye aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “aññatra gacchāmāti chandaṃ avissajjetvāva uṭṭhahanti…pe… kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttavacane hatthapāsā vijahanaṃ na paññāyati. Ettha pana kammappattānaṃ hatthapāsassa avijahanameva icchitabbanti katvā porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi na paññāyati, appaṭikkhittattā pana vaṭṭatīti ce? Na, paṭikkhittattā. Kathaṃ? Chando nāma kammappattesu bhikkhūsu ekasīmāya sannipatitesu āgacchati, nāsannipatitesu. Idha hi “chandaṃ avissajjetvā”ti ca “chandassa pana avissaṭṭhattā”ti ca vuttaṃ. “Ajjhāsayaṃ avissajjetvā”ti ca “ajjhāsayassa avissaṭṭhattā”ti ca na vuttaṃ, tasmā chandassa avissajjanaṃ kammappattānaṃ hatthapāsāvijahaneneva hoti, na vijahaneti siddhaṃ.

Herein, this is the conclusion: In the commentary on the Parisapārivāsiya, in the statement, “Without having relinquished their consent, saying ‘Let us go elsewhere,’ they rise… it is permissible to perform the formal act,” the abandonment of the hand’s reach is not apparent. Here, however, because it is said in the ancient gloss that only the non-abandonment of the hand’s reach of those eligible for the formal act should be intended, if one were to say, “Although it is not apparent, is it permissible because it is not rejected?”—it should not be said, because it is rejected. How so? Consent, it is said, arises among monks eligible for the formal act when they have assembled within a single boundary, not when they are not assembled. For here it is said, “without having relinquished consent,” and “because consent has not been relinquished.” It is not said, “without having relinquished intention,” nor “because intention has not been relinquished.” Therefore, it is established that the non-relinquishing of consent by those eligible for the formal act occurs only through the non-abandonment of the hand’s reach, not through its abandonment.

Hoti cettha –

And on this matter, there is this summary verse:

“Yato āgamanaṃ yassa, tadabhāvassa niggahe;

Tasmā sannipatitesu, bhikkhūsu tassa bhedato”ti.

From which cause the arrival of which consent occurs, for the sake of controlling its absence; therefore, among the assembled monks, it is determined by the specific nature of that consent.

Rattipārivāsiyachando viya rattipārivāsiyapārisuddhipīti tadanulomena vaṭṭati svātanāya chando [V 0.0355] vā pārisuddhi vā pavāraṇā vā, tāya kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Uposathapavāraṇā pana anuposathadivase na vaṭṭati, itaraṃ vaṭṭati. Pannarasiuposathaṃ cātuddasiyaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati khettattā. Na cātuddasiuposathaṃ pannarasiyaṃ akhettattā anuposathadivasattā pāṭipadadivasattāti ekacce ācariyā, tasmā tesaṃ [M 0.0387] matena cātuddasiuposathaṃ tatiyaṃ, sattamaṃ vā pannarasiyaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ panettha vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sace cātuddasikaṃ uposathaṃ karissāmāti nisinnā, pannarasoti kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato “pannarasiyameva ‘cātuddasikaṃ uposathaṃ karissāmā’ti nisinnā punadivase attano taṃ uposathaṃ ‘pannaraso’ti kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti attho”ti evaṃ pariharanti, taṃ tesaṃ mataṃ “tathārūpapaccaye sati aññasmimpi cātuddase uposathaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) iminā mātikāṭṭhakathāvacanena na sameti. Na hi tattha “aññasmimpi pannarase cātuddasikaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepi “sakiṃ pakkhassa cātuddase vā pannarase vā”ti anuññātadivase pariyāpannattā channaṃ cātuddasikānaṃ pacchimā pannarasī anuposathadivaso na hotīti siddhaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi siddhaṃ, iminā pana “āvāsikānaṃ pannaraso, āgantukānaṃ cātuddaso, āgantukehi āvāsikānaṃ samasamehi vā appatarehi vā anuvattitabba”nti vacanamettha niratthakaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Just as the consent for a night's probation and the purity for a night's probation are allowable, so too, in accordance with that, consent, purity, or invitation for the morrow is allowable; it is allowable to perform a formal act based on that. However, the Uposatha-Pavāraṇā is not allowable on a non-Uposatha day, whereas another formal act is allowable. It is allowable to perform the fifteenth-day Uposatha on the fourteenth day, as it is a proper occasion. It is not allowable to perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha on the fifteenth day, as it is not a proper occasion, is a non-Uposatha day, and is the first day of the next fortnight—thus say some teachers. Therefore, according to their view, it is not allowable to perform the third or the seventh fourteenth-day Uposatha on the fifteenth day. As for what is stated in the commentary—'If, having sat down intending, "We will perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha," it is allowable to perform it as the fifteenth'—they resolve this thus: 'The meaning is that having sat down on the fifteenth day itself intending, "We will perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha," it is allowable on the next day to perform that Uposatha as "the fifteenth."' This view of theirs does not agree with the statement from the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: 'When such a condition exists, it is allowable to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day.' For it is not stated there: 'It is allowable to perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha on another fifteenth day.' Even so, since it is included among the permitted days—'once in a fortnight, on the fourteenth or on the fifteenth'—it is established that the fifteenth day following the last of the six fourteenth-day Uposathas is not a non-Uposatha day. Although this is established, it should be understood that in this context the statement, 'For residents, the fifteenth; for visitors, the fourteenth; the residents should follow the visitors if they are equal or fewer in number,' becomes meaningless.

Dutiyādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second and Subsequent Training Rules is finished.

Kumāribhūtavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Young Women is finished.

9. Chattupāhanavaggavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Sandals

11. Ekādasamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Eleventh and Subsequent Training Rules

1214. Upacāraṃ sandhāya kathitanti “dvādasahatthaṃ upacāro”ti likhitaṃ.

1214. This is said with reference to the vicinity: 'The vicinity is twelve cubits,' so it is written.

1221. Suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā vinayaṃ vā abhidhammaṃ vā pucchatīti ettha ca tīṇi piṭakāni attano attano nāmena vuttānīti katvā abhidhammo buddhena bhāsito evāti dīpitaṃ hoti.

1221. Here also, in the passage, “Having created an opportunity in the Suttanta, one asks about the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma,” because the three Piṭakas are spoken of by their own respective names, it is thereby shown that the Abhidhamma was indeed spoken by the Buddha.

1224-5. Thano [V 0.0356] ca udaro ca thanudarā. “Saṃkaccikāya pamāṇaṃ tiriyaṃ diyaḍḍhahatthā”ti porāṇagaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ. “Aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ [M 0.0388] okkamantiyā”ti bahūsu potthakesu, saṅghādisesakaṇḍe viya “upacāraṃ atikkamantiyā”ti pāṭho appakesu, sova pāṭho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “parikkhepaṃ atikkamantiyāti ekena pādena atikkante dukkaṭaṃ, dutiyena pācittiyaṃ. Upacārepi eseva nayo”ti vacanampi “upacāraṃ atikkamantiyā”ti pāṭhoti dīpetīti no takkoti ācariyo.

The breast and the belly are thanudarā. In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is said: “The measurement of the saṃkaccikā across is one and a half cubits.” In many books, the reading is “entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village”; in a few, like in the Saṅghādisesa section, the reading is “crossing the vicinity”; that very reading is found. The teacher said: “It is our inference that the statement in the commentary—‘When crossing the boundary, there is a dukkaṭa for crossing with one foot, and a pācittiya for the second; this same method applies also to the vicinity’—also shows that the reading is ‘crossing the vicinity.’”

Ekādasamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Eleventh and Subsequent Training Rules is concluded.

Chattupāhanavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear is concluded.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Conclusion

Giraggasamajjādīni “acittakāni lokavajjānī”ti vuttattā “nacca”nti vā “gandho”ti vā ajānitvāpi dassanena, vilimpanena vā āpajjanato vatthuajānanacittena acittakāni. “Nacca”nti vā “gandho”ti vā jānitvā passantiyā, vilimpantiyā ca akusalattā eva lokavajjāni. Corivuṭṭhāpanādīni “corī”tiādinā vatthuṃ jānitvā karaṇe eva āpattisabbhāvato sacittakāni. Upasampadādīnaṃ ekantena akusalacitteneva akattabbattā paṇṇattivajjāni. “Idha sacittakācittakatā paṇṇattijānanājānanatāya aggahetvā vatthujānanājānanatāya gahetabbā”ti likhitaṃ. Anugaṇṭhipade pana “giraggasamajjādīni ‘acittakāni lokavajjānī’ti vuttattā ‘nacca’nti vā ‘saṅghāṇī’ti vā ‘gandho’ti vā tassa nāmavasena ajānitvā māyākārassa māyāni sīsaṭṭhiādīni paṭisaṅkhāya passantiyā, akkhamālādiatthāya saṅghāṇiṃ kaṭiyā bandhantiyā, ‘sedagandhaṃ apanetvā buddhapūjaṃ karissāmī’ti uppannena cittena gandhaṃ vilimpetvā nahāyantiyā ca āpattisabbhāvato nāmena saddhiṃ nāmavasena vā vatthussa ajānanacittena acittakāni nāma. Na andhakāre ‘kaṭisuttamida’nti saññāya saṅghāṇiṃ gahetvā kaṭiyaṃ dhāraṇakāle, mattikāsaññāya ca gandhaṃ gahetvā vilimpanakāle āpattisabbhāvato ‘acittakānī’ti vattabbāni. Tasmiṃ kāle anāpatti, teneva saṅghāṇiyā asaṅghāṇisaññāvārepi ‘āpatti pācittiyassā’ti pāḷi na vuttā. Yathā ‘khettaābādhapaccayā, kaṭisuttakaṃ dhāretī’ti vacanato vināpi akusalena saṅghāṇiādīni sakkā dhāretunti siddhaṃ, evaṃ [V 0.0357] ābādhapaccayā vināpi akusalena na sakkā suraṃ [M 0.0389] pātunti siddhaṃ ‘anāpatti ābādhapaccayā majjaṃ pivatī’ti pāḷiyā abhāvato. Akusalena vinā madhupuṇṇamuṭṭhiyaṃ pakkhittamajjassa ajjhoharaṇakālādīsu surāpānāpattiṃ āpajjatīti ca siddhaṃ ‘majje amajjasaññī pivati, āpatti pācittiyassā’ti (pāci. 328) vuttattā. Kiṃbahunā, kāmabhogasaññāya saddhiṃ ‘saṅghāṇī’ti ca ‘gandho’ti ca jānitvā vinā anāpattikāraṇena dhārentiyā ekantākusalattā lokavajjāni nāma vuccanti. Iminā upāyena sesesupi nayo netabbo. Ettha surāpānādhikāre upatissattheravādo”ti vuttaṃ. Asaṃkaccikasikkhāpade “aparikkhittassa gāmassa upacāraṃ okkamantiyāti pāṭho”ti ca “paṇītabhojanaviññatti, acelakasikkhāpadaṃ, nimantitassa cārittāpajjanaṃ, duṭṭhullappaṭicchādanaṃ, ūnavīsativassupasampadaṃ, mātugāmena saddhiṃ saṃvidhāya addhānagamanaṃ, rājantepurappavesanaṃ, santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā vikāle gāmappavesanaṃ, nisīdanaṃ, vassikasāṭikanti pāṭho”ti ca vuttaṃ.

Because the Giragga festival and others are called 'mindless worldly faults,' they are mindless because an offense is incurred by seeing or anointing even without knowing it as 'dancing' or 'perfume,' with a mind that does not know the object. For a bhikkhunī who sees or anoints knowing it as 'dancing' or 'perfume,' they are worldly faults precisely because of unwholesomeness. Reinstating a female thief and other such acts are mindful offenses because an offense occurs precisely when the act is done with knowledge of the object, such as 'this is a female thief.' Higher ordination and similar acts are faults of designation because they must not be done with an entirely unwholesome mind. It is written: 'Here, the state of being mindful or mindless should be understood based on knowing or not knowing the object, not on knowing or not knowing the designation.' However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is said: 'Because the Giragga festival and others are called “mindless worldly faults,” they are called mindless when, with a mind that does not know the object either together with its name or by way of its name, an offense occurs for a bhikkhunī who, having reflected, sees the illusions of a magician, such as a skull, without knowing it by name as “dancing,” “a girdle,” or “perfume”; or for one who ties a girdle on her waist for the sake of a rosary, etc.; or for one who bathes after anointing with perfume with the thought that has arisen, “Having removed the smell of sweat, I will make an offering to the Buddha.” They should not be called 'mindless' on the grounds that an offense occurs when, in the dark, one takes a girdle with the perception 'this is a waistband' and wears it on the waist, or when one takes perfume with the perception of clay and anoints with it, for at that time, there is no offense. For that very reason, even in the section on perceiving a girdle as not a girdle, the Pāḷi does not state, “There is a pācittiya offense.” Just as it is established from the text, “On account of an illness of the ‘field,’ one may wear a waistband,” that girdles and so on can be worn even without unwholesomeness, so too, it is established that one cannot drink liquor on account of illness even without unwholesomeness, because of the absence of a Pāḷi text stating, “There is no offense if one drinks intoxicants on account of illness.” And it is also established that one incurs the offense of drinking liquor when swallowing liquor that has been put into a handful of honey, etc., without unwholesomeness, because it is stated, “If one drinks an intoxicant, perceiving it as a non-intoxicant, there is a pācittiya offense” (Pāc. 328). What more is there to say? For a bhikkhunī who knowingly wears a girdle or applies perfume together with the perception of enjoying sensual pleasures, without a reason for no offense, these are called “worldly faults” because of being entirely unwholesome. By this method, the principle should be applied in the remaining cases as well. Herein, in the section on drinking liquor, this is the view of the Elder Upatissa,” it is said. In the Asaṃkaccika training rule, it is also said: “The reading is ‘entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village.’” And also: “The reading is ‘requesting fine food,’ ‘the training rule concerning a naked ascetic,’ ‘incurring a transgression after being invited,’ ‘concealing a grave offense,’ ‘ordaining one under twenty years of age,’ ‘going on a journey by arrangement with a woman,’ ‘entering the royal inner quarters,’ ‘entering a village at the wrong time without asking leave of a monk who is present,’ ‘a sitting cloth,’ and ‘a rains-cloth.’”

Nigamanavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Conclusion is concluded.

Pācittiyakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pācittiya Section is concluded.

Ubhatovibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Subcommentary on the Ubhatovibhaṅga is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Great Chapter

1. Mahākhandhakavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Great Khandhaka

Bodhikathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Bodhi Story

Yaṃ [M 0.0391][V 0.0358] khandhake līnapadādibheda-pakāsanaṃ dāni supattakālaṃ;

Tasmā apubbaṃ vinayatthameva, vakkhāmi saṅkhepagahaṇatthaṃ.

Now is the suitable time for the exposition of the distinctions of obscure terms and so forth in the Khandhaka; therefore, I will explain only the meaning of the Vinaya, which has not been explained before, for the sake of concise comprehension.

Tattha kenaṭṭhenāyaṃ khandhakoti? Khandhānaṃ samūhattā vibhaṅgo viya. Te pana kathanti? Khandhānaṃ pakāsanato dīpanato. Khandhāti cettha pabbajjādivinayakammasaṅkhātā, cārittavārittasikkhāpadasaṅkhātā ca paññattiyo adhippetā. Pabbajjādīni hi bhagavatā paññattattā “paññattiyo”ti vuccanti. Paññattiyañca khandha-saddo dissati “dārukkhandho aggikkhandho udakakkhandho”tiādīsu viya. Tesaṃ paññattisaṅkhātānaṃ khandhānaṃ pakāsanato vaṇṇanato pabbajjakkhandhakādayo vīsati “khandhakā”ti vuttā, avasāne dve taṃsadisattā velāya sadisattā sīlassa velāti vacanaṃ viya. Apica bhāgarāsatthatāpettha yujjate tesaṃ paññattīnaṃ bhāgato ca rāsito ca vibhattattā. Kiṃ panetesaṃ khandhakānaṃ anupubbakāraṇanti? Nāyaṃ pucchā sambhavati, aññathā vuttesupi tappasaṅgānatikkamanato. Atha vā pabbajjupasampadāpubbaṅgamattā sāsanappavesanassa tadatthasaṅgahako mahākhandhako paṭhamaṃ vutto. Kenāti [V 0.0359] ce? Dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi. Bhagavatā pana tattha tattha uppannavatthuṃ paṭicca tathā tathā vuttāni, na iminā anukkamena. Therā pana taṃ taṃ payojanaṃ paṭicca samānajātike ekajjhaṃ katvā anukkamena sajjhāyiṃsu. Sesānaṃ payojanaṃ tattha tattheva āvi bhavissati.

Herein, for what reason is this called 'Khandhaka'? It is so called because it is a collection of sections, like the Vibhaṅga. Alternatively, it is so called because it proclaims and clarifies the sections. Here, by 'khandha' are meant the regulations designated as the disciplinary acts beginning with the going forth, as well as the training rules concerning conduct to be followed and conduct to be avoided. For the acts beginning with the going forth were laid down by the Blessed One; hence, they are called 'regulations'. And the word 'khandha' is seen in the sense of a regulation, as in 'a log of wood,' 'a mass of fire,' 'a body of water,' and so forth. Because it proclaims and explains these sections, which are designated as regulations, the twenty sections beginning with the 'Going-Forth Khandhaka' are called 'Khandhakas'; at the end, the two are also called so because of their similarity to those, just as the phrase 'the boundary of morality' (sīlassa velā) is used because of its similarity to a boundary (velā). Moreover, the sense of 'portion' and 'collection' is also fitting here, because these regulations are divided into portions and collections. But what is the sequential reason for these Khandhakas? This question is not fitting, for even if they were stated otherwise, the pertinent connection would not be avoided. Alternatively, because the going forth and higher ordination are the precursors for entry into the Dispensation, the Mahākhandhaka, which collects those matters, is stated first. By whom? By the Elders who compiled the Dhamma. The Blessed One, however, spoke in various ways in those respective places, depending on the circumstances that arose; they were not spoken in this sequence. But the Elders, depending on the various purposes, grouped similar matters together and rehearsed them in sequence. The purpose of the remaining sections will become clear in their respective places.

Khandhakovidāti paññattibhāgarāsaṭṭhena nesaṃ khandhatthakovidā, niruttipaṭisambhidāpārappattāti attho. Tesaṃ anuttānatthānaṃ padānaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā. Kasmā panevaṃ visesitanti? Tato sesabhāgā yuttā. Mātikāṭṭhuppattiggahaṇampettha [M 0.0392] padabhājaniyaggahaṇeneva veditabbaṃ. Yehi atthā yesaṃ padavisesānaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pakāsitā, tesaṃ te padavisese puna idha vadeyyāma, vaṇṇanāya pariyosānaṃ kadā bhave te te attheti vuttaṃ, taṃ tassa niddesena yujjati. Uttānā ceva yā pāḷi, tassā saṃvaṇṇanāya kinti vattabbaṃ? Na hi atthā uttānāti sambhavati. Adhippāyānusandhīhītiādivacanehipi taṃ vacanaṃ sambhavatīti ce? Na, atthaggahaṇena cettha padavisesānaṃ gahitattā. Te hi atthato anapetatthena, abhidhānatthena vā atthopacārena vā atthāti veditabbā. Saṃvaṇṇanānayoti saṃvaṇṇanā nāma avuttesu uhāpohakkamanidassanato “nayo”ti vutto.

‘Skilled in the Khandhakas’ means skilled in the meaning of ‘khandha’ by way of the meaning of ‘concept,’ ‘division,’ and ‘collection’; it means those who have reached the further shore of the analytical knowledge of language. This is the meaning. An explanation of those words whose meanings are not clear. But why is it thus specified? From that, the remaining portions are connected. Herein, the grasping of the origin of the mātikā’s meaning should also be known through the grasping of the Padabhājanī itself. For if we were to speak again here of those specific words whose meanings have been explained in the commentary, saying ‘those various meanings,’ when would the explanation ever end? That is fitting with its exposition. What is to be said by way of explanation for the Pāḷi that is already clear? For the interpretation ‘the meanings are not clear’ is possible. If one should say, ‘That statement is also possible through such words as “by intention and connection”?’ No, because here the specific words are also grasped by the grasping of the meaning. For they should be known as ‘meanings’ either by their nature of being inseparable from the meaning, by their expressed meaning, or by metaphorical usage in relation to the meaning. Regarding ‘the method of explanation,’ an explanation is called a ‘method’ because it indicates the procedure of addition and subtraction concerning matters that are unstated.

1. Uruvelāti yathāvuttavālikarāsivasena laddhanāmako gāmo, tasmā samīpatthe etaṃ bhummaṃ. Tathābhāvadassanatthaṃ “najjā nerañjarāya tīre”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aññathā tasmiṃ vālikarāsimhi viharatīti āpajjati, “uruvelaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisīti yena uruvelasenānigamo”tiādivacanavirodho ca. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mūlakāraṇameva dassitaṃ. Tattha taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ…pe… daṭṭhabboti nigamanavacanaṃ. Taṃ kimatthanti ce? Gāmaṃ sandhāya yathāvuttapadatthasambhavadassanatthaṃ. “So pana gāmo tadupacārena evaṃ nāmaṃ labhatī”ti vacanaṃ pana avuttasiddhanti katvā na vuttanti veditabbaṃ, atha vā yassa “uruvelā”ti yathāvuttavālikarāsissa, tassa samīpagāmassapi nāmaṃ. Tattha āyasmā upālitthero na idha gāmaṃ sandhāya “uruvelāyaṃ viharatī”ti āha gocaragāmapayojanābhāvato. Na hi bhagavā taṃ gāmaṃ gocaraṃ katvā tadā tattha vihāsi, tasmā ettha vālikarāsissa samīpe bodhirukkhamūle vihāraṃ sandhāya so evamāhāti dassetukāmo aṭṭhakathācariyo evamāhāti veditabbaṃ, tasmā bhagavato gāmato dūratare araññe abhisambodhidīpanena dutiyuppattiṭṭhānaniyamaṃ tīhi padehi akāsi theroti veditabbaṃ, aññathā padattayavacanapayojanābhāvato. Tattha nadantā gacchatīti nadī. Nelañjalāyāti vattabbe la-kārassa ra-kāraṃ katvā “nerañjarāyā”ti vuttaṃ, kaddamasevālavirahitattā niddosajalāyāti attho, nīlajalāyāti tassā nāmameva vā etaṃ.

1. Uruvelā is a village that has obtained its name by means of the aforementioned heap of sand; therefore, this locative case is in the sense of proximity. To show that it is so, it is said, 'on the bank of the river Nerañjarā,' and so on. Otherwise, it would be implied that he dwelled on that heap of sand, and there would be a contradiction with statements such as, 'he entered Uruvelā for alms,' and 'where the market town of Uruvelā was.' In the commentary, however, only the root cause itself is shown. There, with reference to that, the concluding statement '...should be understood' is said. If one should ask, 'For what purpose is that?' It is for the purpose of showing, with reference to the village, the possibility of the meaning of the aforementioned word. However, the statement, 'That village obtains such a name by metaphorical extension from that,' should be understood as not having been stated, because it is established without being said. Alternatively, 'Uruvelā' is the name of the aforementioned heap of sand, and it is also the name of the village near it. In this context, the Venerable Upāli Thera did not say 'he dwelled in Uruvelā' with reference to the village, because there was no purpose for an alms-resort village. Indeed, the Blessed One did not dwell there at that time, having made that village his alms-resort. Therefore, it should be understood that the commentary teacher, wishing to show that he [Upāli] spoke with reference to the dwelling near the heap of sand, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, said this. Therefore, it should be understood that the Elder, by indicating the full enlightenment of the Blessed One in the wilderness farther from the village, established with three phrases the determination of the place of the second birth (i.e., the enlightenment). Otherwise, there would be no purpose for the utterance of the three phrases. Therein, it is called a 'river' (nadī) because it goes along making a sound. When 'Nelañjalāya' should have been said, the 'la' character was made into an 'ra' character, and 'Nerañjarāya' was said. The meaning is 'having faultless water' because it is free from mud and algae. Alternatively, 'Nīlajalā' is simply its name.

Bodhirukkhamūleti [M 0.0393][V 0.0360] ettha ca bodhi vuccati abhisambodho. So ca atthato bhagavato catutthamaggañāṇaṃ hoti “vimokkhantikametaṃ nāma”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.162) paṭisambhidāvacanato. Kiñcāpi taṃ nāmakaraṇabhūtaṃ catutthaphalañāṇampi vattuṃ sambhavati, kattabbakiccānaṃ pana karaṇato taṃ catutthamaggañāṇameva ettha bodhīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “tatiyavijjāya āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyā”ti tadeva dassitaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “bojjhaṅgā”ti, “bodhipakkhiyā dhammā”ti ca. Tattha yasmā catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ “bodhī”ti vuccati, tasmā sāmaññato vattukāmatādhippāyavasena “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) vuttaṃ idhādhippetañāṇassapi tadantogadhattā. Atha vā pāḷiyaṃ bhagavato ādimaggattayavacanassa vuttaṭṭhānābhāvā catutthamaggañāṇameva bhagavato uppannaṃ, na bhagavā sotāpannādibhāvaṃ patvā buddho jātoti samayantarappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ “catūsū”ti vuttaṃ ādittayassa catutthaupanissayasambhavena bodhipariyāyasiddhito. “Puggalopi senāsanampi upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.9 paccayaniddesa) vacanato phalahetuko phalajanako rukkho phalarukkhoti viya bodhiheturukkho bodhirukkhoti veditabbo. Ettha “yasmā kevalaṃ bodhīti rukkhassapi nāmaṃ, tasmā bodhī”ti parato vuttaṃ. Nigrodhādirukkhato assa visesanavacanaṃ pana tadaññabodhimūlappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ. Maggañāṇañhi kusalamūlattā bodhi ca taṃ mūlañcāti saṅkhyaṃ labheyya. Paṭhamābhisambuddho nisīdatīti sambandho. Tena abhisambuddhadivasena saddhiṃ aṭṭhāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinnabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ettha eka-saddo tassa nisajjāsaṅkhātassa pabbajjānuyogānurūpassa pallaṅkassa aññena iriyāpathena anantariyabhāvaṃ athassa akopitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Vimuttisukhanti ettha vimuttiyaṃ vā sukhanti na sambhavati. Pañcamajjhānikattā bhagavato phalasamāpattisaṅkhātā vimutti eva anujaṅghanaṭṭhena nibbānasukhanti vimuttisukhaṃ, taṃ samāpajjanena paṭisaṃvedī anubhavanto nisīdi. Veneyyakālānatikkamanato taṃ apekkhamāno nisīdi, na vimuttisukhasaṅgena.

At the foot of the Bodhi tree—here, 'bodhi' refers to full awakening. In essence, this is the Blessed One’s knowledge of the fourth path, as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'This is called the culmination of liberation' (Paṭi. Ma. 1.162). Although it is possible to refer also to the knowledge of the fourth fruition, which is the basis for this name, yet because it performs the tasks that must be done, here 'bodhi' should be understood as the knowledge of the fourth path itself. For this very reason, in the Pāḷi it is shown as, 'for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints through the third knowledge,' indicating just that. In the commentary, however, it is shown as 'the enlightenment factors' and 'states conducive to enlightenment'. Therein, because knowledge in the four paths is called 'bodhi', therefore, with the intention of speaking generally, it is said, 'Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths' (Cūḷani. Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121), since the knowledge intended here is also included within them. Alternatively, because there is no place in the Pāḷi where the Blessed One's first three paths are spoken of, only the knowledge of the fourth path arose for the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not become a Buddha after attaining the state of a stream-enterer and so on. Thus, to prevent the arising of a different doctrine, 'in the four' was said, because the first three paths are established as a synonym for 'bodhi' by being the proximate cause for the fourth. According to the statement, 'A person and a dwelling are also conditions by way of proximate condition' (Paṭṭhā. 1.1.9, Paccayaniddesa), just as a tree that is for the sake of fruit and produces fruit is called a 'fruit tree', so too a tree that is the cause of enlightenment should be known as the 'Bodhi tree'. Here, it is stated subsequently, 'Because "bodhi" is also simply the name of a tree, therefore "bodhi"'. The distinguishing term, however, is used to differentiate it from other trees like the banyan and to prevent the implication of any other 'bodhi-root'. Indeed, path-knowledge, because it has wholesome roots, may be designated as both 'bodhi' (awakening) and 'mūla' (its root). The connection is: 'Having first become fully awakened, he sat'. By this, it shows that He remained seated in a single cross-legged posture for eight days, including the day of His full awakening. Here, the word 'eka' (one) shows that His cross-legged posture—which is called a 'seat' and is suitable for an ascetic's practice—was uninterrupted by any other posture and was undisturbed. Regarding 'the bliss of liberation', here 'bliss in liberation' is not a possible meaning. Because the Blessed One possesses the fifth jhāna, liberation itself, which is designated as the attainment of fruition, is the bliss of Nibbāna in the sense of the cessation of defilements; thus it is 'the bliss of liberation'. He sat experiencing and feeling that bliss by entering into that attainment. He sat awaiting the proper time, so as not to let the occasion for training those who could be trained pass, not out of attachment to the bliss of liberation.

Atha khoti adhikārantarārambhe nipātadvayaṃ. Tena vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedayamāno na paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasākāsi, kintu tato vuṭṭhāyāti dasseti[M 0.0394]. Paṭivedhavaseneva sumanasikatassa paṭiccasamuppādassa punappunaṃ manasikaraṇaṃ gambhīrattā assādajananato, na apubbanayadassanādhippāyato. Paccakkhabhūtasabbadhammattā bhagavato asammohato, paṭividdhassa visayato vā manasikaraṇaṃ pana vijitadesapaccavekkhaṇaṃ viya rañño apubbaṃ pītiṃ janeti. Vuttañhi “amānusī ratī hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato”ti (dha. pa. 373). Rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmanti accantasaṃyogavasena upayogavacanaṃ, tena tassa vikappanānattataṃ dasseti. Kiñcāpi [V 0.0361] “anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasākāsī”ti ekatova vuttaṃ, tathāpi iminā anukkamenāti dassanatthaṃ “avijjāpaccayā”tiādi. Tattha ca kiñcāpi pavattimattapaccavekkhaṇā adhippetā kathaṃ paññāyatīti? Paṭhamabhāvāya, paṭilomamanasikaraṇaṃ pana anulome paccayānaṃ, paccayuppannānañca tathābhāvasādhanatthaṃ. Yasmā avijjāya eva nirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, na aññathā, tasmā saṅkhārānaṃ avijjā paccayo, tassā ca saṅkhārā phalanti dīpanato. Tathā nibbānapaccavekkhaṇāya anulomamanasikaraṇaṃ kāraṇanirodhā phalanirodhasādhanatthaṃ. Ettha ca anubhāvato nibbānaṃ dassitaṃ. Na hi taṃ avijjādinirodhamattanti. Tattha “yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedī”ti vacanena anulomo nādhippetoti siddhaṃ. Maggapaccavekkhaṇāya vattabbaṃ natthi, ubhayatthapi kiccato, ārammaṇato ca tassa maggassa visayato ca tattha maggo dassito.

Now then, these two particles indicate the commencement of another topic. By this, it is shown that while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he did not attend to dependent origination, but rather, having arisen from that, he did attend to it. The repeated mental attention to dependent origination, which had been well attended to by the power of penetration, was due to its profundity and its production of relish, not due to the intention of seeing a new method. Because all phenomena are directly realized by the Blessed One, who is free from delusion, the mental attention to the object that has been penetrated—like a king surveying his conquered territory—produces unprecedented joy. For it is said: “For one who rightly sees the Dhamma, there is a non-human delight” (Dhammapada 373). The phrase “during the first watch of the night” is an accusative usage in the sense of continuous connection; by this, it shows the diversity of its specific aspects. Although it was stated as one phrase, “he attended to it in forward and reverse order,” nevertheless, to show that he attended to it with this sequence, the text beginning “With ignorance as condition…” was stated. And here, although only the contemplation of the mere process of existence is intended, how is this known? Because it comes first. The reverse mental attention, however, is for the purpose of establishing the true nature of the conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena within the forward order. Because it is only from the cessation of ignorance that there is the cessation of formations, and not otherwise, it is therefore illuminated that ignorance is the condition for formations, and formations are its result. Similarly, for the contemplation of Nibbāna, the forward mental attention is for the purpose of establishing the cessation of the effect through the cessation of the cause. And here, Nibbāna is shown by its power, for it is not merely the cessation of ignorance and so on. There, by the statement “when he understood the destruction of the conditions,” it is established that the forward order is not intended. Regarding the contemplation of the path, there is nothing to be said, for in both cases the path is shown there in terms of its function, its object, and the scope of that path.

Tatthāha – “paṭiccasamuppādaṃ paṭilomaṃ manasākāsī”ti na yujjati, na hi paṭilomāpadesena niddiṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo bhavitumarahatīti? Vuccate – na, tadatthajānanato. Anulomapaṭilomanti hi bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ. Anulomato, paṭilomato ca taṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasākāsīti hi tattha attho. Aññathā nirodhassa paṭilomappasaṅgāpattiyevāpajjati. Paṭilome ca panetasmiṃ anukkamaniyamo anulome anukkamaniyamato siddhoti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sati paṭiccasamuppādassa paṭilomo nāma apaṭiccasamuppādoti siddhaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “nirodho hotīti anuppādo hotī”tiādi. Evaṃ sante pubbāparavirodho hoti. Kathaṃ? Paṭiccāti hi iminā phalassa paccayapariggahena, paccayānañca paccayāyattupagamanena tassa uppādābhimukhabhāvadīpanato [M 0.0395] asamuppādo na sambhavati, tasmā apaṭiccasamuppādoti evaṃ ubhayapaṭikkhepena panassa paṭilomatā veditabbāti eke. Taṃ ayuttaṃ tassa anulomabhāvaniyamanato, atthātisayābhāvato, tasmā appaṭiccasamuppādo tassa paṭilomoti veditabbaṃ. Teneva bhagavatā pāḷiyaṃ paccayapaccayuppannanirodho vutto. Tattha hi “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā”ti evaṃ paccayassa samucchinnapaccayabhāvavasena paccayanirodhaṃ, phalassa paccayapaṭiggahābhāvavasena paccayuppannanirodhañca dīpeti. Duvidho pāḷiyaṃ nirodho atthato anuppādo nāma hotīti katvā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “nirodho hotīti anuppādo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sante nibbānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannānaṃ nirodhamattanti āpajjatīti ce? Na, tassānubhāvadīpanādhippāyato. Viditavelāyanti manasikatavelāyanti attho, aññathā tato pubbe aviditappasaṅgato.

Herein, a questioner said: The statement, ‘He reflected on dependent origination in reverse,’ is not suitable. Why? Because Nibbāna, which is indicated by way of the reverse order, is not fit to be dependent origination. The reply is: It is not so, because its meaning is known. For ‘forward and reverse’ is a neuter verbal noun. The meaning there is that he reflected on that dependent origination both in the forward order and in the reverse order. Otherwise, it would indeed lead to the consequence of Nibbāna being the reverse order. And in this reverse order, it should be understood that the rule of sequence is established from the rule of sequence in the forward order. This being so, it is established that what is called the reverse of dependent origination is non-dependent origination. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: ‘Cessation is non-arising,’ and so on. This being so, there is a contradiction between the former and the latter. How so? By this word ‘dependent,’ because it indicates the state of facing towards arising for the result through the grasping of conditions, and through the conditions’ proceeding by dependence on other conditions, non-arising is not possible. Therefore, some say that its reverse nature is to be understood by the rejection of both, and thus it would be non-dependent origination. That is unsuitable, because it is determined by the nature of the forward order and because there is no excess of meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that non-dependent origination is its reverse. For that very reason, the Blessed One stated in the Pāḷi the cessation of conditions and conditioned phenomena. Therein, with the words, ‘through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance itself,’ he thus shows the cessation of the condition by way of the state of its cause being utterly cut off, and the cessation of the conditioned phenomenon by way of the result’s state of not grasping a condition. Having considered that cessation in the Pāḷi is twofold and is, in meaning, called non-arising, it is said in the commentary: ‘Cessation is non-arising.’ If this is so, does it follow that Nibbāna is the mere cessation of conditions and conditioned phenomena? No, because of the intention to show its power. ‘At the time of knowing’ means at the time of attending with the mind; otherwise, there would be the consequence of it being unknown before that.

Jhāyatoti [V 0.0362] ettha kāmaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena jhāyato bodhipakkhiyadhammā pātubhavanti, catuariyasaccadhammā vā pakāsanti, tathāpi pubbabhāge samathādiyānikavibhāgadassanatthaṃ ārammaṇūpanijjhānaggahaṇaṃ. Catusaccadhammaggahaṇaṃ kāmaṃ anulomapaṭiccasamuppādadassanādhikārena virujjhati, tathāpi “yo dukkhaṃ parijānāti, so samudayaṃ pajahatī”ti laddhivasena katanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, in the phrase 'one contemplates': indeed, for one who contemplates by means of the close examination of characteristics, the factors of enlightenment become manifest, or the four noble truths become clear. Nevertheless, in the preliminary stage, the taking up of the close examination of an object is for the purpose of showing the division of the vehicles beginning with serenity. Although this indeed conflicts with the section on showing dependent origination in forward order, it should be understood as done according to the received principle: 'Whoever fully understands suffering, they abandon its origin.'

2. “Paccayakkhayassā”ti kiccapariyāyavasena vuttaṃ. Tena paccayanibbānaṃ, tadupanissayanibbānañcāti duvidhaṃ nibbānaṃ dassitaṃ hotīti. Kāmañca taṃ na kevalaṃ paccayakkhayamattaṃ karoti, atha kho paccayuppannakkhayampi karoti. Yato ubhinnampi nirodho dassito, tathāpi hetunirodhā phalanirodhoti katvā “paccayakkhayassā”ti vuttaṃ. Vuttappakārā dhammāti ettha catusaccaggahaṇaṃ paṭhamagāthāyaṃ vuttanayavipallāsena katanti veditabbaṃ.

2. ‘Of the destruction of conditions’ is stated by way of the function-aspect. By this, two kinds of Nibbāna are shown, namely: Nibbāna as the condition, and Nibbāna as the causally arisen which is dependent on that. And indeed, that does not bring about only the mere destruction of the condition, but rather it also brings about the destruction of what is causally arisen. Although the cessation of both is shown, it is stated as ‘of the destruction of conditions’ because ‘through the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of the result.’ Herein, in the phrase ‘the dhammas of the kind spoken of,’ the taking up of the four truths should be understood as done by way of reversing the method spoken of in the first verse.

3. Samudayanirodhasaṅkhāto atthoti ettha samudayo kiccavasena, nirodho ārammaṇakiriyāya. Etena dvippakārā nirodhā dassitā honti tassa anubhāvassa vasenāti attho. Yasmā pallaṅkābhujitaṭṭhānañca “pallaṅko”ti vuccati, tasmā phalādhigamaṭṭhānaṃ “pallaṅka”nti vuttaṃ.

3. Herein, in the phrase ‘the meaning designated as origin-cessation’: ‘origin’ is by way of function, and ‘cessation’ is by the activity of the object. By this, two kinds of cessation are shown by way of its power. Because the place of sitting cross-legged is also called a ‘pallaṅka’ (seat), therefore the place of attaining the fruit is called ‘pallaṅka’.

Ajapālakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Ajapāla Story

4. Sammodīti [M 0.0396] hitakāmatāya bhagavā tena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ sammodi. Vedehi antanti ettha nibbānaṃ anto nāma. Vedānaṃ vā antaṃ gatattāti ettha arahattaṃ. Tattha paṭhamena vedantagū yasmā, tasmā eva vusitabrahmacariyo. Dutiyena vedantagū yasmā, tasmā vusitabrahmacariyoti evaṃ yojanā kātabbā. Kiñcāpi brāhmaṇassa catusaccayuttaṃ atthato vuttaṃ, udānagāthāyaṃ vuttapaṭivedhābhāvaṃ sandhāya “dhammacakkappavattana”nti vuccatīti parihāro.

4. Regarding ‘sammodi’ (He rejoiced): The Blessed One spoke joyfully with that brahmin out of a desire for his welfare. Herein, regarding ‘vedehi antaṃ’ (the end with the Vedas): Nibbāna is called the end. Or, regarding ‘vedānaṃ...antaṃ gatattā’ (having gone to the end of the Vedas): Arahantship is the end. In that regard, by the first interpretation, because he is a ‘vedantagū’ (one who has gone to the end of knowledge), therefore he has lived the holy life. By the second, because he is a ‘vedantagū’, therefore he has lived the holy life—thus the connection should be made. Although for the brahmin a discourse connected with the Four Truths was spoken in terms of its meaning, with reference to the absence of the penetrative knowledge of what was spoken in the Udāna verse, it is called ‘the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma’—this is the resolution.

Ajapālakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ajapāla story is finished.

Mucalindakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Mucalinda Story

5. Mucalindavatthumhi etamatthanti idāni vattabbamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Taṃ vivekanti upadhivivekaṃ[V 0.0363]. “Abyāpajjaṃ sukhaṃ loke”ti iminā paṭhamamaggaṃ dasseti tena sattesu māraṇavasena uppajjanakabyāpādappahānasiddhito. “Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo”ti iminā dutiyamaggaṃ dasseti. Maggī hi puggalo avasiṭṭhabyāpādatanuttavasena pāṇabhūtesu saṃyato hoti vihiṃsādhippāyābhāvato. Evaṃ cattāro hi maggā anukkamenāpi gahitā honti.

5. The phrase ‘etam atthaṃ’ (this meaning) in the Mucalinda story was said with reference to the meaning that is now to be spoken. Regarding ‘taṃ vivekaṃ’ (that seclusion), it means seclusion from the substrata of existence. By the phrase ‘abyāpajjaṃ sukhaṃ loke’ (Harmlessness is happiness in the world), he teaches the first path, because by that path the accomplishment of abandoning the ill-will that arises by way of the desire to kill beings is achieved. By the phrase ‘pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo’ (restraint towards living beings), he teaches the second path. Indeed, a person possessing the path is restrained towards living beings by way of the attenuation of the remaining ill-will, due to the absence of an intention to harm. Thus, the four paths are also taken in sequence.

Mucalindakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mucalinda story is finished.

Rājāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Rājāyatana Story

6. Rājāyatanaṃ pātali. “Catuddisā āgantvā”ti pāṭhaseso. Mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ kirassa dinnānaṃ catunnampi lekhāparicchedo atthi, te vāṇijā devatāya gāravadassanena bhagavato rūpakāyadassanena pasannattā saraṇaṃ aggahesuṃ. Devatāya “bhagavā rājāyatanamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti vacanaṃ sutvā sāvakasaṅghābhāvaṃ, abhisambuddhadhammasabbhāvañca jāniṃsūti veditabbaṃ. Jānantīti buddhāti sambandho.

6. The Rājāyatana is the Pāṭali tree. ‘Catuddisā āgantvā’ (Having come from the four directions) is the remainder of the text to be understood. It is said that on the rim of the four bowls that were offered to him, there was a line of demarcation. Those merchants, because they were pleased by the deity's showing of reverence and by seeing the physical body of the Blessed One, took refuge. Upon hearing the deity’s words, ‘The Blessed One first became fully enlightened at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree,’ it should be understood that they knew of the non-existence of a community of disciples and the actual existence of the Dhamma of the Fully Enlightened One. The connection of ‘jānanti’ (they know) is with ‘buddha’.

Rājāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Rājāyatana story is finished.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of Brahmā’s Request

7. Adhigato [M 0.0397] kho myāyantiādimhi dhammoti catusaccadhammo, gambhīrattā duddaso. Duddasattā duranubodho. Santoti nibbuto. Paṇītoti atappako. Idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atakkāvacaroti takkena ākāraparivitakkena ogāhitabbo na hoti, ñāṇeneva avacaritabboti attho. Paṇḍitavedanīyoti sammāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipannehi paṇḍitehi vedanīyo. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbaṃ nibbānameva. Tañhi phalūpacārena ekampi samānaṃ tathā tathā vuccati. Rāmāti pajā. Anu anu acchariyā anacchariyā. Tesaṃ bhagavato pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ sutapubbānaṃ, dhammassa vā gambhīrabhāvaṃ adhigatapubbānaṃ. Kiñcāpi bhagavato cattāropi maggā sukhappaṭipadā, tathāpi bodhisattapaṭipadaṃ sandhāya “kicchena me”ti vuttaṃ. “Pakāsitaṃ pakāsitu”nti ubhayathāpi pāṭho. Paretehi yuttehi. Rāgarattāti kāmarāgadiṭṭhirāgehi rattā. Attaniccādigāhakā na dakkhanti na passissanti.

7. In the phrase beginning with 'Adhigato kho myāyaṃ,' 'Dhamma' refers to the Four Noble Truths. Because of its profundity, it is difficult to see. Because it is difficult to see, it is difficult to awaken to. 'Peaceful' (santo) means extinguished. 'Sublime' (paṇīto) means insatiable. These two terms are said referring solely to the supramundane. 'Beyond the sphere of logic' (atakkāvacaro) means it is not to be grasped by mere reasoning about its characteristics; the meaning is that it is to be traversed by wisdom alone. 'To be experienced by the wise' (paṇḍitavedanīyo) means it is to be experienced by the wise who have undertaken the right practice. 'The stilling of all formations' (sabbasaṅkhārasamatho) and so on all refer to Nibbāna itself. For, though it is one, it is spoken of in various ways by a figurative use of 'fruit'. `Rāmā` means beings. `Anu anu acchariyā anacchariyā`: For those who had previously heard of the Blessed One’s practice in a former time, or who had previously understood the profundity of the Dhamma, these wonders are not wonders. Although the Blessed One’s four paths are of easy practice, it is said, 'with difficulty by me' (kicchena me), referring to the Bodhisatta’s practice. There are two readings: 'declared' (pakāsitaṃ) and 'to declare' (pakāsituṃ). `Paretehi` means yoked with. `Rāgarattā` means dyed with the lust of sensual desire and the lust of views. Those who grasp at self, permanence, and so on will not see (`na dakkhanti`), that is, they will not perceive (`na passissanti`).

8. Sahaṃpati [V 0.0364] kira “nassati vata bho loko”ti imaṃ saddaṃ tathā nicchāreti, yathā dasasahassilokadhātubrahmāno sutvā sannipatiṃsu. Paññāmaye akkhimhi santānānusayitavasena appaṃ parittaṃ rāgādirajaṃ etesaṃ, evaṃsabhāvāti apparajakkhajātikā. Assavanatāti assavanatāya.

8. Brahmā Sahampati, it is said, uttered this cry, “Alas, the world is perishing!” (nassati vata bho loko) in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system heard it and gathered. In the eye of wisdom, due to the power of what lies latent in the continuity, there is little, slight dust of lust and so on in them; having such a nature, they are therefore of a species with little dust in their eyes (apparajakkhajātikā). `Assavanatā` means because of not hearing (`assavanatāya`).

Samalehi satthārehi. Apāpuretanti vivara etaṃ. Amatassa dvāranti ariyamaggaṃ, catusaccadhammaṃ vā. Vijjattayacatumaggañāṇehi punappunaṃ buddhaṃ paṭividdhaṃ. Seleti silāmaye. Vigatarajattā sukhadassanayogge ito ca etto ca āgantvā yathā ṭhito cakkhumā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya. Tvampi sumedha sundarapañña sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamāya samantacakkhu. Sabbakilesasaṅgāmānaṃ vijitattā vijitasaṅgāma. Jātikantārādinittharaṇatthaṃ veneyyajanasatthavāhanasamatthatāya satthavāha. Kāmacchandaiṇassa abhāvato aṇaṇa.

By the six teachers who have stains. `Apāpurantūti`: `vivara etaṃ`, meaning 'open this'. `Amatassa dvāraṃ` means the Noble Path, or the Four Noble Truths. The Dhamma, penetrated and known again and again by means of the three kinds of knowledge and the four path-knowledges. On a rock (`sele`) means on one made of stone (`silāmaye`). Just as a man with sight, standing on a mountain peak free from dust and suitable for pleasant seeing, without going from here or there, would see the multitude of people all around. You too, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, having attained the knowledge of omniscience, are the All-seeing Eye. Because you have conquered all the battles which are the defilements, you are the Conqueror of the battle (`vijitasaṅgāma`). For the purpose of crossing over the wilderness of birth and so on, due to your capability to lead forth the multitude of trainable beings, you are the Caravan Leader (`satthavāha`). Because of the absence of the debt which is sensual desire, you are the Unindebted One (`aṇaṇa`).

9. Buddhacakkhunā indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ. Uppaliniyanti uppalavane. Evaṃ sesesupi[M 0.0398]. Anto nimuggaposīnīti yāni anto nimuggāneva posiyanti, tattha yāni udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni, tāni sūriyaraṃsisamphassaṃ āgamayamānāni ṭhitāni ajja pupphanakāni. Yāni samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, tāni sve pupphanakāni. Yāni udakānuggatāni, tāni tatiyadivase pupphanakāni. Udakā pana anuggatāni aññānipi sarogauppalādīni nāma honti. Yāni neva pupphissanti macchakacchapabhakkhāneva bhavissanti, tāni pāḷināruḷhāni, āharitvā pana dīpetabbāni. Etehi ugghaṭitaññū vipañcitaññū neyyo padaparamoti cattāro puggalā yojetabbā. Paccabhāsīti pati abhāsi.

9. By the Buddha-eye, that is, by the knowledge of the disposition of faculties of beings and by the knowledge of their inclinations and underlying tendencies. For the name of these two knowledges is 'Buddha-eye.' In `uppaliniyaṃ`: it means 'in the lotus grove.' It should be understood likewise in the remaining phrases. In `anto nimuggaposinīti`: those lotuses that will grow while being submerged inside. Among them, those that stand having risen above the water, awaiting the touch of the sun's rays, will bloom today. Those that stand level with the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that are submerged in the water will bloom on the third day. However, other lotuses that have not risen from the water are called diseased lotuses and so on. Those that will never bloom and will just become food for fish and turtles are not included in the Pāḷi text, but they should be brought up and explained. With these, these four persons should be connected: the one who understands with a brief instruction (`ugghaṭitaññū`), the one who understands with a detailed explanation (`vipañcitaññū`), the one who is to be led (`neyyo`), and the one for whom the words are the highest attainment (`padaparamo`). In `paccabhāsīti`: `pati abhāsi` means 'he spoke in return.'

Apārutāti vivaṭā. Pacchimassa padadvayassa ayamattho. Ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattampi imaṃ paṇītaṃ uttamaṃ dhammaṃ kāyavācākilamathasaññī hutvā nābhāsi.

`Apārutāti` means `vivaṭā`, 'are opened.' This is the meaning of the last two words. For I, perceiving that it would be wearisome for body and speech, did not speak this sublime, supreme Dhamma of mine, even though it was well-practiced and well-mastered.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of Brahmā’s Request is concluded.

Pañcavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse to the Group of Five.

10. Idāni pana sabbo jano saddhābhājanaṃ upanetu, pūressāmi nesaṃ saṅkappanti. Apparajakkhajātikoti [V 0.0365] samāpattiyā vikkhambhitakilesattā nikkilesajātiko. Ājānissatīti ce na niṭṭhānamakaṃsu dhammasaṅgāhakā te vinayakkamaññā, ahaṃ deseyyaṃ paṭivijjhissatīti adhippāyo, “muddhāpi tassa vipateyyā”ti (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 2) ettha viya abhūtaparikappo kireso. Loke tassa adhimuttabhāvadīpanatthañhi idaṃ vacanaṃ attano tadupadesena aviditabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Tassa anantevāsikabhāvadīpanatthanti evamādīni panettha payojanāni. Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇanti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ tassa maraṇārammaṇaṃ uppajji. Tena tato pubbe tassa sati dhammadesanāya khippaṃ jānanabhāvārammaṇanti dīpeti. Paropadesato ajānitvā paccakkhato maraṇasacchikiriyampi dasseti. Buddhānampi anekañāṇasamodhānābhāvato suvuttametaṃ. Cittapubbikā hi cittappavatti, aññathā navasattapātubhāvappasaṅgo. Sabbadhammānaṃ ekato gahaṇe viruddhakālānaṃ ekato [M 0.0399] jānanappasaṅgo. Tato ekañāṇassa vitathabhāvappattidoso, tasmā sabbassa vinānekañāṇasamodhānaṃ āpajjitadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇavantattā pana sabbaññū eva bhagavāti veditabbaṃ, na sabbakālaṃ ekato. Āḷārādīnaṃ maraṇājānanatoti ce? Na, tassa jānanena puthujjanassāpi sabbaññutāpattippasaṅgato. Yadābhāvena yadābhāvo tabbhāvena tassābhāvappasaṅgo loke siddhoti. “Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti vacanato tassa maraṇajānanaṃ siddhanti katvā bhavaṃ mateneva bhagavā sabbaññūti siddhaṃ na devatārocanato pubbe ajānanatoti ce? Na, visesaṃ pariggahetvā antarā pajānanato, devatāya sabbaññubhāvappattidosato ca. Na hi so kassaci vacanena aññāsīti.

10. Now, however, may all people bring forth the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspiration. Regarding 'of little dust': because the defilements were suppressed by attainment, he was of a nature free from defilements. Regarding 'Would he understand?': If those Elders, the compilers of the Dhamma who know the order of the Vinaya, had not made a decision, the intention is: 'I would teach, and he would penetrate the truth.' This is like in the passage 'his head would surely split.' This is indeed an unreal supposition. Indeed, in the world, this statement is for the purpose of showing that person's state of high resolve, for the purpose of showing His own state of not having known through that indication of his, and for the purpose of showing that he was not His disciple. Such as these are the purposes here. Regarding 'Even for the Blessed One, knowledge arose': the knowledge of omniscience, with his death as its object, arose. Therefore, it shows that before that, while he was alive, the teaching of the Dhamma had as its object the state of being quickly known. It also shows the direct realization of death, not having known it from another's instruction. This is well-said because even for the Buddhas, there is no simultaneous arising of multiple knowledges. Indeed, the occurrence of thought is preceded by thought; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the appearance of a new being. If all phenomena were grasped at once, there would be the consequence of knowing things of contradictory times at once. From that, there would be the fault of a single knowledge becoming false. Therefore, because the Blessed One possesses unimpeded knowledge regarding phenomena to be adverted to, without the simultaneous arising of multiple knowledges, he should be known as truly omniscient—but not knowing all things at all times at once. If it is asked, 'Is it because of not knowing the death of Āḷāra and others?' No, for by knowing that, there would be the consequence of even an ordinary person attaining omniscience. It is established in the world that when the existence of one thing entails the non-existence of another, the existence of the latter entails the non-existence of the former. If it is said: 'Because of the statement, "Knowledge arose for the Blessed One," it is established that He knew of the death. Having established this, it is proven by your own view that the Blessed One is omniscient, and not that He did not know before the devas' announcement'? No, because He knew in the interim, having grasped a distinction, and because there would be the fault of the deva attaining the state of omniscience. For indeed, He did not know through the word of anyone.

Apica kimidaṃ tattha jānanaṃ nāma tadārammaṇañāṇuppattīti ce? Na, loke sabbaññuno accantābhāvappasaṅgato. Sādhikā hi mayā ekañāṇakkhaṇe sabbaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tadaññesañca tadaññāṇānuppatti. Apica sabbaññuno sabbadhammavisaye ñāṇapaccupaṭṭhānasiddhi tassa ñāṇassa attanāva attano avisayoti ce? Na, hetunidassanānuppattito. Apica “bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti ettha visesavacanaṃ atthi. Yena devatārocanuttarakālameva bhagavato ñāṇaṃ udapādīti paññāyati. Na hi vacanapubbāpariyabhāvamattena tadatthapubbāpariyatā hoti, tasmā ayuttametaṃ. Abhidosakālaṃkatoti paṭhamayāme kālaṃkato. “Majjhimayāme”tipi vadanti. Ubhayatthapi mahājāniyo. Sattadivasabbhantare, ekadivasabbhantare ca pattabbamaggaphalato parihīnattā mahatī jāni assāti mahājāni. Tesu hi dvīsu āḷāro ākiñcaññāyatanabhave nibbatto, udako bhavagge, tasmā nesaṃ dhammadesanāya akkhaṇe nibbattabhāvaṃ sandhāya bhagavā evaṃ cintesi, na ito manussalokato cutibhāvaṃ sandhāyāti veditabbaṃ. Abuddhaveneyyatañca sandhāyāti no takko, aññathā aniṭṭhappasaṅgoti ācariyo.

Furthermore, what is this so-called knowing there? Is it the arising of knowledge having that as its object? No, because it would logically follow that there is the absolute non-existence of an omniscient one in the world. For it has been established by me that all is known in a single moment of knowledge, and also the non-arising of non-knowledge concerning other things. Furthermore, if one should say that for an omniscient one, the establishment of the manifestation of knowledge in the sphere of all phenomena means that this knowledge, by itself, is not its own object? No, because of the unsuitability of showing a reason. Furthermore, in the statement, 'Indeed, knowledge arose for the Blessed One,' there is a distinguishing word, by which it is understood that the Blessed One's knowledge arose only at the time after the announcement by the devas. Indeed, the sequence of the meaning does not occur merely by the sequence of the words; therefore, this is inappropriate. 'He passed away recently' means he passed away in the first watch. Some also say, 'in the middle watch.' In both cases, it was a great loss. Because he was deprived of the attainable path and fruit within seven days or one day, his loss was great; hence, it is called a 'great loss'.
