Indeed, among those two, Āḷāra was reborn in the sphere of nothingness, and Uddaka at the peak of existence. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One thought thus considering their having been reborn at an inopportune time for the teaching of the Dhamma, not considering their having passed away from this human world. And our reasoning is not that He thought thus with reference to their being untrainable by a Buddha; otherwise, says the teacher, an undesirable consequence would follow.

Bodhisattassa [V 0.0366] jātakāle supinapaṭiggāhakā ceva lakkhaṇapariggāhakā ca aṭṭha brāhmaṇā. Tesu tayo dvidhā byākariṃsu “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto rājā hoti cakkavatti, pabbajanto buddho”ti. Pañca brāhmaṇā “agāre na tiṭṭhati, buddhova hotī”ti ekaṃsabyākaraṇāva ahesuṃ. Tesu purimā tayo yathāmantapāraṃ [M 0.0400] gatā. Ime pana mantapāraṃ atikkamantā attanā laddhaṃ puññamahattaṃ vissajjetvā bodhisattaṃ uddissa puretarameva pabbajiṃsu. Ime sandhāya vuttaṃ “pañcavaggiyā”ti. “Tesaṃ puttā”tipi vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Kasmā panettha bhagavā “bahūpakārā kho me”ti cintesi. Kiṃ upakārakānaṃ eva esa dhammaṃ deseti, itaresaṃ na desetīti? No na deseti. Upakārānussaraṇamattakeneva vuttanti aṭṭhakathānayo. Attano kataññukatavedibhāvappakāsanatthaṃ, kataññutādipasaṃsanatthaṃ, paresañca kataññubhāvādiniyojanatthaṃ, khippajānanappasaṅganivāraṇatthaṃ.

At the time of the Bodhisatta's birth, there were eight brahmins who were receivers of dreams and interpreters of marks. Among them, three made a two-fold declaration: 'One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, becomes a wheel-turning monarch; if he goes forth, he becomes a Buddha.' Five brahmins made a one-sided declaration: 'He will not remain in the household; he will surely become a Buddha.' Among them, the first three prophesied according to the lore of the sacred texts. These others, however, surpassing the lore of the sacred texts and relinquishing the great merit they had acquired, went forth even earlier for the sake of the Bodhisatta. It is with reference to these that it is said, 'the group of five.' Some also say they were their sons, but that is refuted in the commentary. Why, in this context, did the Blessed One think, 'They have been very helpful to me'? Does he teach the Dhamma only to those who have been helpful and not to others? It is not that he does not teach others. This was said merely out of recollection of their help; this is the method of the commentary. It was said for the purpose of revealing his own state of being grateful and acknowledging what has been done, for praising gratitude and so on, for encouraging others in the state of gratitude and so on, and for preventing the implication of knowing quickly.

11. Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhinti gayāya ca bodhiyā ca majjhe tigāvutantare ṭhāne. Bodhimaṇḍato hi gayā tīṇi gāvutāni. Bārāṇasinagaraṃ aṭṭhārasa yojanāni. Upako pana bodhimaṇḍassa ca gayāya ca antare bhagavantaṃ addasa. Antarā-saddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kataṃ. Īdisesu ca ṭhānesu akkharacintakā ekameva antarāsaddaṃ payujjanti, so dutiyapadepi yojetabbo. Ayojiyamāne pana upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Idha pana yojetvāva vuttoti.

11. The phrase 'Between Gayā and the Bodhi tree' refers to a place in the middle of Gayā and the Bodhi tree, within a distance of three gāvutas. Indeed, Gayā is three gāvutas from the Bodhi seat. The city of Bārāṇasī is eighteen yojanas away. Upaka, however, saw the Blessed One between the Bodhi seat and Gayā. Because of the connection with the word 'antarā', the accusative case is used. And in such instances, grammarians use the word 'antarā' only once, and it should be connected to the second term as well. If it is not connected, however, the accusative case is not obtained. Here, however, it is stated as having been connected.

Sabbābhibhūti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Taṇhakkhayeti nibbāne. Vimuttoti ārammaṇato vimutto. Natthi me paṭipuggaloti mayhaṃ paṭipuggalo nāma natthi, asadisoti attho, mama sabbaññubhāve dosaṃ dassetvā loke ṭhātuṃ asamatthatāya mama paccatthikapuggalo vā natthīti attho. Āhañchaṃ amatadundubhinti dhammacakkhupaṭilābhāya amatabheriṃ paharissāmīti gacchāmi.

"All-conquering"—having subdued all phenomena of the three realms, one is established. "In the destruction of craving"—in Nibbāna. "Liberated"—freed from the object. "There is no counterpart for me"—for me, there is no person who is a counterpart; the meaning is 'unequalled'. Or alternatively, because of the inability to stand in the world having pointed out a fault in my omniscience, there is no rival person for me. "I shall beat the drum of the Deathless"—I go, having thought thus: "I will strike the great drum called the Deathless for the sake of attaining the Dhamma-eye."

Arahasi anantajino bhavituṃ yutto tvanti attho. Idampi attano satthunāmaṃ. Hupeyyāsīti āvuso evampi nāma bhaveyya. Pakkāmīti vaṅkahārajanapadaṃ nāma agamāsi. Bhagavāpi “tattha tassa migaluddakassa dhītuyā cāpāya ukkaṇṭhitvā puna āgantvā anāgāmī ayaṃ bhavissatī”ti upanissayasampattiṃ disvā tena saddhiṃ ālapi. So ca tathevāgantvā pabbajitvā anāgāmī hutvā anukkamena kālaṃ katvā avihesu uppajjitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

"You are worthy to become the Infinite Conqueror; it is fitting for you to become the Infinite Conqueror—this is the meaning. This name, Anantajina, is also his own name as a Teacher. "May it be so, friend"—meaning, "Friend, even such a name may be." "He departed"—he went to the country named Vaṅkahāra. The Blessed One also, seeing the supportive condition that "There, on account of Cāpā, the daughter of a deer hunter, he will become dissatisfied, return again, and this one will become a non-returner," spoke with him. And he, having returned to that very place, gone forth, and become a non-returner, in due course passed away, was reborn in the Avihā realm, and attained Arahantship.

12. Saṇṭhapesunti [M 0.0401][V 0.0367] katikaṃ akaṃsu. Padhānavibbhantoti padhānato bhaṭṭho parihīno. “Abhijānātha nu bhāsitameta”nti, “vācaṃ bhāsitameva”nti ca evarūpaṃ kañci vacanabhedaṃ akāsīti adhippāyo. Bhagavantaṃ sussūsiṃsūti bhagavato vacanaṃ sotukāmā ahesuṃ. Aññāti aññāya, jānitunti attho.

12. "They established"—they made an agreement. "Strayed from striving"—fallen from striving, diminished. "'Do you remember this being said?' and 'Do you remember such a word being spoken?'"—the intention is to ask whether he made any such alteration in his words. "They wished to hear the Blessed One"—they were desirous of hearing the Blessed One's word. "He understood"—the meaning is 'having understood', 'to know'.

13. Atha kimatthaṃ āmantesīti? Tatopi suṭṭhutaraṃ paṭijānanatthaṃ, dhammassa abhibhāriyadullabhabhāvadīpanatthaṃ, akkharavikkhepanivāraṇatthañca. Tattha dvemeti antadvayavacanaṃ aññesampi tadantogadhabhāvato. Apica yojanāvasena. Taṇhāavijjāti hi saṃsārappavattiyā sīsabhūtā dve kilesā. Te ca samathavipassanānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtattā antā nāma. Tesu taṇhāvasena kāmasukhallikānuyogaṃ bhajanto samathaṃ parihāpeti bālo, tathā avijjāvasena attakilamathānuyogaṃ bhajanto gacchanto vipassananti na sakkā ubho dve ante appahāya amataṃ adhigantunti evaṃ vuttā. Apica līnuddhaccapahānadassanametaṃ. Līno hi nikkhittavīriyārambho kāmasukhañca bhajati, itaro accāraddhavīriyo attakilamathaṃ. Ubhopi te vīriyasamatāya paṭipakkhattā antā nāma. Apica tisso sāsane paṭipadā vuttā āgāḷhā, nijjhāmā, majjhimā ca. Tattha āgāḷhā “pāṇātipātī hoti, natthi kāmesu doso”ti evamādikā. Nijjhāmā “acelako hoti, muttācāro”ti evamādikā, majjhimā “ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti evamādikā. Tattha kāmasukhallikānuyogo āgāḷhā nāma paṭipadā hoti sabbākusalamūlattā. Attakilamathānuyogo nijjhāmā nāma attajjhāpanato. Ubhopete majjhimāya paṭipadāya paṭipakkhabhūtattā antā nāma, tasmā imeva sandhāya dvemeti. Kimatthaṃ bhagavā “pabbajitena na sevitabbā”ti pabbajite eva adhikaroti, na gahaṭṭheti? Pabbajitānaṃ tadadhimuttattā, sukhaparivajjanasamatthatāya, tadadhikatattā ca pabbajitā ettha adhikatā, na gahaṭṭhā. Yadi evaṃ kimatthaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogamāha, nanu te pakatiyāpi kāmapariccāgaṃ katvā taṃ nissaraṇatthaṃ pabbajitāti? Na, tesaṃ antadvayanissitattā. Te hi idha loke kāmena visuddhimicchanti attakilamathānuyogamanuyuttā tasseva tapassa phalena pecca dibbe kāme āsīsamānā daḷhataraṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogamanuyuttāti veditabbā[M 0.0402]. Antattho pana idha kucchitaṭṭhena veditabbo “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ, yadidaṃ piṇḍolya”ntiādīsu (itivu. 91; saṃ. ni. 3.80) viya.

13. Then, for what purpose did he address them? For the purpose of a more ready acceptance, for showing the exceedingly weighty and difficult-to-obtain nature of the Dhamma, and for preventing the mind from wandering in the interim. Herein, the word 'these two' refers to the two extremes because others are also included within them. Furthermore, this is by way of connection. For craving and ignorance are the two defilements that are the chief causes for the continuation of saṃsāra. And because they are opposed to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), they are called extremes. Among them, the fool who, through craving, indulges in the devotion to sensual pleasures causes serenity to decline. Likewise, the fool who, through ignorance, indulges in the devotion to self-mortification causes insight to decline. Therefore, it is said thus: it is not possible to attain the Deathless without having abandoned both these two extremes. Furthermore, this is a teaching on the abandoning of sloth (līna) and agitation (uddhacca). For the slothful one, who has given up the undertaking of effort, indulges in sensual pleasure; while the other, who is overly energetic, indulges in self-mortification. Both are called extremes because they are opposed to the balance of energy. Furthermore, three practices are spoken of in the Dispensation: the excessive (āgāḷhā), the scorching (nijjhāmā), and the middle (majjhimā). Herein, the excessive is such as: 'He is a killer of living beings; there is no fault in sensual pleasures,' and so on. The scorching is such as: 'He is a naked ascetic, of unrestrained conduct,' and so on. The middle is such as: 'This is the Noble Eightfold Path,' and so on. Herein, the devotion to sensual pleasures is the practice called excessive because it is the root of all unwholesome states. The devotion to self-mortification is the practice called scorching because it scorches the self. Both of these are called extremes because they are opposed to the middle practice. Therefore, it is with reference to these that 'these two' is said. For what reason does the Blessed One, in saying 'They should not be pursued by one gone forth,' make it apply only to those gone forth, and not to householders? Because those gone forth are inclined towards these, are capable of avoiding pleasure, and because their state is one of attainment through such renunciation, those gone forth are the subject here, not householders. If so, for what reason did he speak of the devotion to sensual pleasures? Have they not gone forth for the sake of liberation from that, having renounced sensual pleasures by their very nature? No, because of their reliance on the two extremes. For they do not desire purity in this world by means of sensual pleasure; rather, being devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and hoping for divine sensual pleasures in the next life as the fruit of that very austerity, they are to be understood as being even more firmly devoted to the devotion to sensual pleasures. The meaning of 'extreme,' however, should be understood here in the sense of 'contemptible,' as in such passages as: 'This, bhikkhus, is an extreme livelihood, that is, collecting alms-food'.

Yo cāyaṃ kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogoti ettha kāmesūti vatthukāmo adhippeto, dutiyo kilesakāmo[V 0.0368]. Taṃsampayuttasukhamettha kāmasukhaṃ nāma. Tena vipākasukhassa niravajjabhāvaṃ dīpetīti. Allīyanaṃ nāma tadabhinandanā. Anuyogo nāma bhavantare tadanuyogapatthanā. Hānabhāgiyakarattā kusalapakkhassa, hīnapuggalabhāvitattā, hīnadhātupabhavattā ca lāmakaṭṭhena hīno. Gāmanivāsisattadhammattā gammo. Puthujjanasādhāraṇattā pothujjaniko. Anariyoti ariyānaṃ anadhippetattā, ariyadhammapaṭipakkhattā, anariyakarattā, anariyadhammattā, anariyāciṇṇattā ca veditabbo. Anatthasaṅkhātasaṃsārabhayāvahattā, anatthaphalanibbattakattā ca anatthasaṃhito. Attano kevalaṃ khedūpagamo attakilamatho nāma. So diṭṭhigatapubbakattatapānukkamakiriyāvisesaṃ nissāya pavattati, tassa diṭṭhivasena anuyogo attakilamathānuyogo nāma. Attaviyogavittāparissamattā, anupāyapavattattā sampajjamāno migayonigoyonikukkurayonisūkarayonīsu pātāyati. Vipaccamāno narakaṃ netīti anatthasaṃhito. Ete tvāti ete tu. Tathāgatenāti attānaṃ avitathāgamanaṃ āvi karoti, tenetaṃ dasseti “na mayā parivitakkitamattena vitakkitā, kintu mayā tathāgateneva satā abhisambodhiñāṇena abhisambuddho”ti. Cakkhukaraṇītiādīhi pana tameva paṭipadaṃ thometi. Bhesajjaṃ āturassa viya “cakkhukaraṇī”ti iminā ñāṇacakkhuvisodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ñāṇakaraṇīti iminā andhakāravidhamanaṃ vuttaṃ. Upasamāyāti kilesapariḷāhapaṭippassaddhi vuttā. Abhiññāyāti saccapaṭivedhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Sambodhāyāti saccapaṭivijjhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Nibbānāyāti sopādisesanibbānadhātuyā anupādisesanibbānadhātuyāti evaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetvā kathetabbaṃ.

And concerning this 'indulgence in sensual pleasures' (kāmasukhallikānuyoga): here, in 'kāmesu,' first sensual objects (vatthukāma) are intended, and second, sensual defilements (kilesakāma). The pleasure associated with these is here called 'sensual pleasure' (kāmasukha). By this, the blamelessness of resultant pleasure is shown. 'Allīyanaṃ' (indulgence) means delighting in that. 'Anuyogo' (pursuit) means the aspiration for association with it in another existence. Because it leads to decline on the wholesome side, because it is cultivated by inferior individuals, and because it arises from inferior elements, it is 'low' (hīna) in the sense of being base. Because it is the nature of village-dwelling beings, it is 'vulgar' (gamma). Because it is common to ordinary people, it is 'of ordinary people' (pothujjanika). 'Ignoble' (anariya) should be understood as such because it is not desired by the noble ones, is opposed to the noble Dhamma, is of an ignoble nature, and is practiced by the ignoble. Because it brings the danger of saṃsāra, which is designated as unbeneficial, and because it produces an unbeneficial result, it is 'connected with what is unbeneficial' (anatthasaṃhita). 'Self-mortification' (attakilamatha) is merely the undertaking of one's own exhaustion. It proceeds depending on a specific kind of action, which is a sequence of asceticism preceded by wrong view; and its pursuit by way of wrong view is called 'the pursuit of self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyoga). Because of being unendowed with the wealth of wisdom that is separate from a self, and because it proceeds without proper method, when undertaken, it causes one to fall into the wombs of deer, cattle, dogs, and pigs. When it ripens, it leads to hell; therefore, it is 'connected with what is unbeneficial'. 'Ete tva' means 'ete tu' (but these). 'By the Tathāgata' (Tathāgatena)—he reveals his own unerring arrival, thus showing: 'It was not thought out by me merely by way of conjecture, but rather, by me, being a Tathāgata, it was fully awakened to with the knowledge of full awakening.' By phrases like 'eye-making' (cakkhukaraṇī), he praises that very path. 'Eye-making' refers to the purification of the eye of wisdom. 'Knowledge-making' (ñāṇakaraṇī) refers to the dispelling of darkness. 'For peace' (upasamāya) means the pacification of the fever of defilements. 'For direct knowledge' (abhiññāya) means the penetration of the truths. 'For full enlightenment' (sambodhāya) means the piercing of the truths. 'For Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) refers to the Nibbāna-element with residue and the Nibbāna-element without residue—thus, it should be explained by connecting them as appropriate.

14. Kasmā panettha bhagavā aññattha viya anupubbiṃ kathaṃ akathetvā paṭhamameva asevitabbamantadvayaṃ vatvā majjhimapaṭipadaṃ desesīti? Attādimicchābhimānanivāraṇatthaṃ, kummaggapaṭipattinivāraṇatthañca antadvayavajjanaṃ vatvā attano [M 0.0403] visesādhigamadīpananayena abāhullikādibhāvadassanatthaṃ, tesañca majjhimapaṭipadādīpanena tattha anuyojanatthaṃ pacchā sammāpaṭipadaṃ desesi, tato tassa majjhimapaṭipadāsaṅkhātassa ariyamaggassa visayadassanatthaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ saṅkhepavitthāravasena desetukāmo “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkha”ntiādimāha, ayamettha anusandhi. “Idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti me, bhikkhave”tiādi suttānusandhipakaāsanatthaṃ ayamanukkamo veditabbo. Yathāvuttaṃ paṭipadaṃ sutvā kira koṇḍañño āha “kathaṃ bhagavatā vuttapaṭipadāya uppatti siyā. Ayañhi paṭipadā kilesānaṃ anuppattiyā sati sambhavati, na aññathā. Kilesānañca yadi lobhato uppatti khuppipāsānaṃ viya, tadāsevanāya anuppatti siyā, tadavatthussa vā tesaṃ uppatti. Tadavatthuviparītakāyakilamathāsevanāya anuppatti siyā. Ubhopetā bhagavatā ‘antā’ti vuttā, tasmā kathaṃ panetissāya [V 0.0369] sammāpaṭipadāya uppatti sambhaveyyā”ti. Bhagavā āha anupāyāsevanato. Kathanti ce? –

14. Why here did the Blessed One, unlike in other suttas, not give a gradual discourse, but instead, at the very beginning, having spoken of the two extremes that should not be followed, teach the Middle Path? He taught thus for the purpose of preventing wrong conception regarding self and so on, and for the purpose of preventing the practice of a wrong path. Having spoken of the avoidance of the two extremes, by the method of showing the attainment of His own special state, for the purpose of showing the state of non-indulgence and so on, and by showing the Middle Path to them, for the purpose of their engagement in it, He afterwards taught the right practice. After that, desiring to teach the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of brief and detailed explanation, for the purpose of showing the domain of that Noble Path called the Middle Path, He said, 'This, indeed, O bhikkhus, is suffering,' and so on. This is the connection here. This sequence, starting with 'This, O bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering,' etc., should be understood for the purpose of showing the connection of the sutta. It is said that having heard the practice as it was spoken, Koṇḍañña said: 'How could there be the arising of the practice spoken of by the Blessed One? For this practice is possible when there is the non-arising of defilements, not otherwise. And if the arising of defilements is from greed, like hunger and thirst, then by indulging in that, there would be the non-arising of the practice. Or, for the state which is its basis, there is the arising of them. By indulging in bodily mortification, which is the opposite of that which is its basis, there would be the non-arising of the practice. Both of these have been called 'extremes' by the Blessed One. Therefore, how could the arising of this right practice be possible?' The Blessed One said: 'From not indulging in what is not the means.' And if asked how? –

“Saṃsāramūlato ñāṇaṃ, tañca ñāṇā pahiyyati;

Jīvite sati taṃ hoti, tañca jīvitasādhane.

From the root of saṃsāra, there is ignorance, and that ignorance is destroyed by knowledge. When there is life, that knowledge exists, and that knowledge is dependent on what accomplishes life.

“Tasmā ñāṇāya medhāvī, rakkhe jīvitamattano;

Ñāṇasādhanabhūtañca, sīlañca paripālaye.

Therefore, for the sake of knowledge, a wise person should protect their own life; and should perfectly maintain virtue, which is the means for accomplishing knowledge.

“Jīvitañca yathā loke, bhinne kāye na vijjati;

Tatheva bhinnasīlassa, natthi ñāṇassa sambhavo.

Just as in the world, when the body is broken, life does not exist, in the very same way, for one with broken virtue, there is no possibility for the arising of knowledge.

“Tasmā āyuñca sīlañca, ñāṇatthaṃ rakkhatā satā;

Sevitabbā na kāmāpi, nāpi kāyavināsanā.

Therefore, by a mindful person protecting life and virtue for the sake of knowledge, sensual pleasures should not be indulged in, nor should bodily destruction be indulged in.

“Kāmesu gedhamupagamma hino gammañca,

Accuddhano kilamathaṃ gamupeti mūḷho;

Yo majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ paramaṃ upeti,

So khippameva labhate paramaṃ vimokkha”nti.

Having fallen into greed for sensual pleasures, one is base and adopts the conduct of villagers; the deluded one, for a very long time, comes to weariness. Whoever attains the supreme Middle Path, that one quickly obtains the supreme liberation.

Sutvā [M 0.0404] tadetaṃ sugatassa vākyaṃ,

Paññaṃ munī so sutajaṃ labhitvā;

Cintāmayaṃ ñāṇa pavesamāno,

Ucchindayaṃ pañhamimaṃ apucchi.

Having heard that utterance of the Sugata, that sage, having obtained wisdom born of learning and applying knowledge born of reflection, asked this question, wishing to sever it.

“Nibbedhapadaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya ghoraṃ,

Tapaṃ kathamivāti so tvaṃ;

Brūhi tadeva hoti bhikkhu cara,

Virāgamupayāti ca dukkhasaccassa;

Dassaneneva [V 0.0370] dukkhānubhavanā,

Tamhi dosassa paccayo”ti.

‘Having abandoned the severe ascetic practice, the basis for penetration, how then should one practice?’ Thus he asked. ‘You, sir, please explain that.’ The Blessed One said: ‘O bhikkhu, it is just that. Practice that very thing. One reaches dispassion.’ And ‘one reaches dispassion’ occurs only by seeing the truth of suffering. Therein, the experiencing of suffering is the condition for aversion.

Sutvāva koṇḍañño munivacanaṃ,

Vuṭṭhāya haṭṭho sahasā avoca;

“Udāhara tvaṃ bhagavā mametaṃ,

Bhikkhu yathā passati dukkhasacca”nti.

Just upon hearing the Sage's word, Koṇḍañña, joyful, rose up hastily and spoke: 'O Blessed One, please declare this to me—how a bhikkhu sees the truth of suffering.'

Cintāmayissa paññāparipuṇṇā bhāvanāmayipaññāsampatti jānitabbā imehi iti bhagavā suttamidamāhāti kira. Kasmā bhagavā koṇḍaññassa purimameva saccadesanaṃ avaḍḍhetvā attano adhigatakkamamāhāti? Nāhaṃ kassaci āgamaṃ desemi, apica kho sayameva evamadhigatomhīti dassanatthaṃ. Tattha “pubbe ananussutesu dhammesū”ti iminā idaṃ atthadvayaṃ dasseti, na mayā āḷārato, udakato vā ayaṃ dhammo suto, kintu pubbe ananussutesveva ñāṇaṃ me udapādīti majjhimāya paṭipadāya ānubhāvaṃ pakāseti. Apica yasmā evaṃ paṭipanno vināpi paropadesena ariyasaccāni passati, tasmā kathaṃ tumheva mamāpadesena na passathāti.

The accomplishment of wisdom born of cultivation, which perfects the wisdom of one with wisdom born of reflection, is to be known by these monks. Thus, it is said, the Blessed One spoke this discourse. Why, without elaborating on the first teaching of the truths to Koṇḍañña, did the Blessed One speak of the sequence of his own attainment? It was to show, 'I do not teach a tradition from anyone, but rather, I myself have attained it thus.' Therein, by the phrase 'in things not formerly heard,' he shows this twofold meaning: 'This Dhamma was not heard by me from Āḷāra or from Udaka, but rather, knowledge arose in me only in regard to things not formerly heard'—thus he reveals the power of the Middle Path. Furthermore, since one who has practiced thus sees the Noble Truths even without instruction from another, how then could you not see them with my instruction?

15. Cakkhuntiādīni pañca padāni ñāṇavevacanāneva. Ñāṇañhi saccānaṃ ālocanato cakkhubhūtatthajānanato ñāṇaṃ. Pakārehi jānanato paññā. Kilesavidāraṇato, vijjanato ca vijjā. Saccacchādakatamavināsanato, tesaṃ gatikoṭipakāsanato ālokoti veditabbaṃ. Tattha paṭhamena parivaṭṭena saccānaṃ aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato ṭhapanapaññaṃ [M 0.0405] dasseti, dutiyena tesaṃ kattabbākāraparicchindanapaññaṃ, tatiyena saccesu ñāṇakiccasanniṭṭhānaṃ dasseti.

15. The five terms beginning with 'eye' (cakkhu) are merely synonyms for knowledge. For knowledge (ñāṇa) is so called because it illuminates the truths and because it knows the meaning that has become manifest to the eye. Because it knows by way of modes, it is wisdom (paññā). Because it tears apart the defilements and because it penetrates, it is true knowledge (vijjā). Because it destroys the darkness that covers the truths and reveals their sphere and limit, it is to be understood as light (āloko). Therein, by the first round, it shows the wisdom that establishes the truths without mixing them with one another; by the second, the wisdom that determines the aspect of what is to be done regarding them; by the third, it shows the completion of the task of knowledge regarding the truths.

16. Yāvakīvañcāti dvīhi padehi yāvaicceva vuttaṃ hoti “iti cittamano”tiādi viya. Rāgādīhi akuppatāya akuppā vimutti. Veyyākaraṇanti dhammadesanā. Sā hi dhammānaṃ byākaraṇato pakāsanato “veyyākaraṇa”nti vuccati. Virajaṃ vītamalanti ettha virajaṃ visamahetuvādavigamato. Vītamalaṃ ahetukavādavigamato. Virajaṃ sassatadiṭṭhippahānato. Vītamalaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhippahānato. Virajaṃ pariyuṭṭhānappahānato. Vītamalaṃ anusayappahānato. Dhammacakkhunti dhammamattadassanaṃ, na tattha satto vā jīvo vā kārako vā vedako vāti, tenevāha “yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbantaṃ nirodhadhamma”nti. Idañhi tassa dhammacakkhussa uppattiākāradassanatthaṃ [V 0.0371] vuttaṃ. Tañhi nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccavasena eva saṅkhataṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati.

16. By the two terms in `yāvakīvañca`, only `yāva` is meant, like in `iti cittamano`, etc. Unshakeable liberation (akuppā vimutti) is so called because it is unshaken by lust and the like. 'Explanation' (veyyākaraṇa) refers to the teaching of the Dhamma, for it is called 'explanation' because it clarifies and expounds the Dhamma. Regarding 'stainless, immaculate' (virajaṃ vītamala): herein, 'stainless' is from the removal of the view of an inconsistent cause, and 'immaculate' is from the removal of the view of causelessness. 'Stainless' is from the abandoning of the eternalist view; 'immaculate' is from the abandoning of the annihilationist view. 'Stainless' is from the abandoning of active defilements; 'immaculate' is from the abandoning of latent tendencies. The 'Dhamma-eye' (dhammacakkhu) is the vision of mere phenomena—not of a being, a soul, an agent, or an experiencer. Therefore it is said, 'Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease.' This was stated to show the manner of the arising of that Dhamma-eye. For it arises by taking cessation as its object and, by way of its function alone, penetrating the conditioned.

17. Dhammacakkanti ettha desanāñāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, paṭivedhañāṇañca labbhateva. Ettha kimatthaṃ devā saddamanussāvesunti? Nānādiṭṭhigatandhakāravidhamanato laddhālokattā, apāyabhayasamatikkamanato assāsaṃ pattattā, devakāyavimānadassanato pītipāmojjacalitattā cāti evamādīnettha kāraṇāni vadanti. Pathavikampanamahāsaddapātubhāvo ca dhammatāvaseneva hotīti eke. Devatānaṃ kīḷitukāmatāya pathavikampo. Bahuno devasaṅghassa sannipātato, bhagavato sarīrappabhājālavisajjanato cāti ekacce.

17. Here, by 'Dhammacakka,' the knowledge of teaching is intended, and the knowledge of penetration is certainly obtained. Here, why did the devas cause the sound to be heard? Because, with the darkness of diverse wrong views dispelled, they had obtained light; because, having overcome the fear of the lower realms, they had attained relief; and because they were moved by joy and gladness upon seeing the celestial mansions of the hosts of devas—such reasons and others are given here. Some say that the appearance of the earthquake and the great sound occurred merely according to the nature of things. Others say that the earthquake was due to the deities' desire to sport, and that the great light appeared due to the assembly of a great multitude of deities and to the release of the net of the Blessed One's bodily radiance.

18. Pabbajjupasampadāvisesanti attho. Tattha iti-saddo tassa ehibhikkhūpasampadāpaṭilābhanimittavacanapariyosānadassano. Tadavasāno hi tassa bhikkhubhāvo. Svākkhātotiādi “ehī”ti āmantanāya payojanadassanavacanaṃ. “Ehibhikkhū”ti bhagavā avoca “svākkhāto dhammo cara…pe… kiriyāyā”ti ca avocāti padasambandho. Tattha cara brahmacariyanti avasiṭṭhaṃ maggattayabrahmacariyaṃ samadhigaccha. Kimatthaṃ? Sammādukkhassantakiriyāyāti attho. “Ehibhikkhū”ti iminā bhagavato vacanena nipphannattā kāraṇūpacārena “ehibhikkhūpasampadā”ti vuttā. Sāva tassāyasmato yāvajīvaṃ upasampadā ahosīti attho. Tena tassā upasampadāya [M 0.0406] sikkhāpaccakkhātādinā vicchedā vā tadaññāya upasampadāya kiccaṃ vā natthīti idamatthadvayaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dasseti. Aṭṭhannampi upasampadānaṃ ehibhikkhuovādapaṭiggahaṇapañhabyākaraṇagarudhammapaṭiggahaṇūpasampadānaṃ catunnaṃ aññatarāya upasampannassa antarā vicchedo vā tadaññūpasampadāya kiccaṃ vā natthi, itarassatthīti. Nikāyantarikā panāhu “buddhapaccekabuddhānaṃ niyāmokkantisaṅkhātāya upasampadāya ñatticatutthakammupasampadañca dasavaggapañcavaggakaraṇīyavasena dvidhā bhinditvā dasavidhopasampadā”ti. Kā panettha atthato upasampadā nāmāti? Tadadhigatakiriyāvasena nibbattiyā asekkhā tadadhivāsanacetanāya paribhāvitapañcakkhandhikā ajjhattasantati. Kā panettha paribhāvanā nāma? Tabbipakkhadhammajjhācāraviruddhabhāvo, tassa pattiyā tāya paribhāvanāya vasena katthaci “samannāgato”ti vuccati. Yathāha “lobhena samannāgato, bhikkhave, abhabbo cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni bhāvetu”ntiādi. Etthāhu nikāyantarikā “yathāvuttāya upasampadāya pattisaṅkhāto cittavippayutto saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno dhammo atthi, tassa santativasena pubbāpariyaṃ uppajjamānassa yāva avicchedo, tāva upasampannoti, aññathā tato dhammantaruppattikkhaṇe [V 0.0372] tassa upasampannassa anupasampannabhāvappasaṅgo āpajjatī”ti. Te vattabbā “suttaṃ āharathā”ti. Te ce vadeyyuṃ “yo tesaṃ dasannaṃ asekkhānaṃ dhammānaṃ upādāya paṭilābhasamannāgamo ariyo hoti vippahīnoti evamādīni no suttānī”ti. Evaṃ sati asantadhammehi, parasattehi ca samannāgamadosappasaṅgo nesaṃ pāpuṇāti. Kiṃkāraṇaṃ? Suttasambhavato. Yathāha – “rājā, bhikkhave, cakkavattī sattahi ratanehi samannāgato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 3.199-200 atthato samānaṃ) vitthāro. Vasibhāvo tattha samannāgatasaddena vutto. Tassahitesu ratanesu vasibhāvo kāmacāro atthīti ce? Ettha vasibhāvo samannāgamasaddena vutto, aññattha pattisaṅkhāto, taṃ dhammantaranti. Kimettha visesakāraṇaṃ? Natthi ca, tasmā yathāvuttalakkhaṇāva upasampadā. Ayameva nayo pabbajjādīsupi netabbo.

18. The meaning is the distinction of going forth and higher ordination. Therein, the word 'iti' indicates the conclusion of the statement that is the cause for attaining the 'ehi bhikkhu' higher ordination. For his status as a bhikkhu has its conclusion in that. The passage beginning with 'Svākkhāto' is a statement showing the purpose of the address 'Come.' The Blessed One said, 'Come, bhikkhu,' and he also said, 'The Dhamma is well-expounded; practice... for the ending of suffering.' This is how the connection of the words should be made. Therein, by 'practice the holy life' is meant: attain the holy life of the remaining three paths. For what purpose? For the sake of making a complete end of suffering; this is the meaning. Because it is accomplished by this utterance of the Blessed One, 'Come, bhikkhu,' it is called the 'ehi bhikkhu higher ordination' by a figurative use of the cause. That very ordination was the higher ordination for that venerable one for as long as he lived; this is the meaning. By this, the commentary shows this twofold meaning: that for that higher ordination, there is neither an interruption by means of renouncing the training and so on, nor is there a need for another higher ordination. Of the eight kinds of higher ordination, for one who has been ordained by any one of the four—the 'ehi bhikkhu' higher ordination, the higher ordination by acceptance of an exhortation, the higher ordination by answering a question, and the higher ordination by acceptance of the weighty rules—there is neither an interruption in the interim nor a need for another higher ordination. For the other types, there is. However, those of other schools say: 'Including the higher ordination of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, known as 'entry into the fixed course,' and dividing the higher ordination by a motion and three announcements into two—according to whether it is to be performed by a chapter of ten or a chapter of five—there are ten kinds of higher ordination.' Herein, what, by meaning, is called higher ordination? It is the internal continuity of the five aggregates of one beyond training, accomplished by means of the action of attaining that, and imbued by the volition that resolves upon it. Herein, what is called 'imbuing'? It is the state of being contrary to the practice of transgressing those things which are its opposite. By means of that imbuing, through having attained that state, one is in some cases called 'endowed.' As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, one endowed with greed is incapable of developing the four establishments of mindfulness,' and so on. Herein, those of other schools say: 'In the aforementioned higher ordination, there exists a phenomenon, dissociated from mind and included in the aggregate of formations, called 'attainment'. By the power of its continuity, arising before and after, as long as there is no interruption, one is called 'ordained'. Otherwise, at the moment of the arising of a different phenomenon from that, the consequence of the ordained one becoming unordained would occur.' They should be told: 'Bring forth a sutta.' And if they should say: 'Such suttas as "The noble one is endowed with the acquisition and attainment on account of those ten qualities of one beyond training, having abandoned..." are our suttas.' This being so, the fault of being endowed with non-existent things and with other beings would follow for them. What is the reason? Because of what is found in the suttas. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with seven treasures.' The details should be understood. Therein, mastery is expressed by the word 'endowed.' If it is said that regarding those treasures, he has mastery and freedom of action? Here, mastery is expressed by the word 'endowment'; elsewhere, what is called 'attainment' is expressed. That is a different phenomenon. What is the distinguishing reason here? There is none. Therefore, higher ordination is just as defined above. This same method should be applied to going forth and so on as well.

19. Kiñcāpi vappattherassa pāṭipadadivase…pe… assajittherassa catutthiyanti evaṃ nānādivasesu pāṭekkaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi, tathāpi ovādasāmaññena [M 0.0407] vappabhaddiyānaṃ, mahānāmaassajīnañcettha ekato vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

19. Although the eye of the Dhamma arose separately on different days—such as on the first day for the elder Vappa… and on the fourth day for the elder Assaji—nevertheless, it should be understood that by virtue of the common instruction, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji are stated together here.

20. “Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā”ti kimatthaṃ āditova anattalakkhaṇaṃ dīpetīti? Tesaṃ puthujjanakālepi itaralakkhaṇadvayassa pākaṭattā. Te hi manāpānaṃ kāmānaṃ aniccatādassanena saṃviggā pabbajiṃsūti aniccalakkhaṇaṃ tāva nesaṃ ekadesena pākaṭaṃ, pabbajitānañca attakilamathānuyogato kāyikadukkhaṃ, tañca mānasassa paccayoti mānasikadukkhañca pākaṭaṃ, tasmā tadubhayaṃ vajjitvā anattalakkhaṇameva dīpetuṃ ārabhi. Tañca dīpento dukkhalakkhaṇeneva dīpetuṃ “rūpañca hidaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissā”tiādimāha. Kimatthanti? Aniccalakkhaṇatopi tesaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇassa suṭṭhutaraṃ pākaṭattā. Tesañhi attakilamathānuyogamanuyuttattā, tapparāyaṇabhāvato ca dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ suṭṭhu pākaṭaṃ, tasmā tena tāva suṭṭhu pākaṭena anattalakkhaṇaṃ dīpetvā puna tadeva tadubhayenāpi dīpetuṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti vakkhati. Kallaṃ nūti yuttaṃ nu. Etaṃ mamāti taṇhāggāho. Esohamasmīti mānaggāho. Eso me attāti diṭṭhiggāho. Taṇhāggāho cettha aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritavasena, mānaggāho navavidhamānavasena, diṭṭhiggāho dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhivasena veditabbo.

20. “Form, monks, is not-self”—why does he begin by revealing the characteristic of not-self from the outset? Because, even in their time as worldlings, the other two characteristics were apparent to them. For they had gone forth, stirred by seeing the impermanence of desirable sensual pleasures, so the characteristic of impermanence was, to some extent, already apparent to them. And after going forth, due to their engagement in self-mortification, physical suffering arose, which was a condition for mental suffering—thus, mental suffering was also apparent. Therefore, setting aside both of those, he began to reveal only the characteristic of not-self. And while revealing it, he revealed it by means of the characteristic of suffering, saying, “For if, monks, this form were self…” and so on. Why? Because the characteristic of suffering was more clearly apparent to them than the characteristic of impermanence. For since they were engaged in the practice of self-mortification and had it as their resort, the characteristic of suffering was exceedingly apparent. Therefore, having first revealed the characteristic of not-self by means of that which was exceedingly apparent, he will then say, “What do you think, monks—is form permanent or impermanent?” in order to reveal that very characteristic by means of both. The phrase ‘Is it proper?’ means ‘Is it suitable?’. ‘This is mine’ is the grasping of craving. ‘I am this’ is the grasping of conceit. ‘This is my self’ is the grasping of view. Herein, the grasping of craving should be understood by way of the 108 modes of craving’s activity, the grasping of conceit by way of the nine kinds of conceit, and the grasping of view by way of the 62 kinds of views.

Pañcavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Group of Five is concluded.

Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Going Forth

25. Yena [V 0.0373] samayena bhagavā pañcavaggiye pañcamiyaṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā sattamiyaṃ nāḷakattherassa nāḷakapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhitvā bhaddapadapuṇṇamāyaṃ yasassa indriyānaṃ paripakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ udikkhanto bārāṇasiyaṃ vihāsi, tena samayena yaso nāmāti sambandho. Tassa kira uppattito paṭṭhāya tassa kulassa kittisaddasaṅkhāto, parijanasaṅkhāto vā yaso visesato pavaḍḍhati. Tena tassa mātāpitaro evaṃ nāmamakaṃsu. “Sukhumālo”tiādi kimatthaṃ āyasmatā upālittherena vuttanti? Pacchimajanassa nekkhamme samussāhanajananatthaṃ. Evaṃ uttamabhogasamappitānampi uttamesu bhogesu appamattakenāpi [M 0.0408] asubhanimittena vitajjetvā kālākālaṃ agaṇetvā vivekābhiratiyā mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ tiṇaṃ viya pahāya gehato nikkhamanā ahosi, kassa panaññassa na siyāti adhippāyo. Samaṅgībhūtassāti tehi ekattaṃ upagatassa, avivittassāti attho. Niddā okkamīti manāpesupi visayesu pavattiṃ nivāretvā tassa cittaṃ atikkamitvā abhibhavitvā attano vasaṃ upanesīti attho. Sabbarattiyo cāti tayopi yāme. Tena parijanassa vikāradassane kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Ratti-saddo panettha kāle sūriyābhāve, yāme ca pavattatīti viññeyyo. Yāmevidha viññeyyo ticīvaravippavāse ca. Kaccheti kacchapasse. Kaṇṭheti kaṇṭhassa heṭṭhā. Mudiṅgassa hi upari kaṇṭhaṃ ṭhapetvā sayantiyā kaṇṭhe mudiṅgaṃ addasāti attho. Āḷambaranti paṇavaṃ. Ubhatomukhassa tanukā dīghā. Vitthinnasamatalassa vāditassa etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vippalapantiyoti supinadassanādivasena asambandhapalāpaṃ vippalapantiyo. Susānaṃ maññeti susānaṃ viya addasa sakaṃ parijananti sambandho. Ādīnavoti asubhabhāvo. Nibbidāya cittaṃ saṇṭhātīti vimuccitukāmatāsaṅkhātāya ukkaṇṭhāya cittaṃ namīti attho. Udānaṃ udānesīti “ito paṭṭhāya imāhi itthīhi saha nāhaṃ bhavissāmī”ti attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi. Dve kira ākārā tassa pamādasuttaparijanadassane pākaṭā jātā kilesānaṃ balavabhāvo, asubhākārassa atioḷārikabhāvo ca. Evaṃ sati oḷārikatare ca asubhākāre kilesavasenāyaṃ sabbopi loko ettha pīḷito mucchito. Aho kilesā balavatarāti hi passato passato tassa dvepi te ākārā pākaṭā jātā, yenevamavocāti.

25. At the time when the Blessed One dwelt in Bārāṇasī—having established the monks of the group of five in Arahantship on the fifth day, having explained the Nāḷaka practice to the Elder Nāḷaka on the seventh day, and having known on the full moon day of Bhaddapada the mature state of the faculties of the young nobleman Yasa, he waited for him—at that time, the connection to be made is: 'a wealthy merchant's son named Yasa...' It is said that from his birth, the fame of his family, known as reputation, or the esteem of his retinue, grew especially. Therefore, his parents gave him this name. Why did the Venerable Upāli Thera say “delicate” and so forth? It was for the purpose of generating encouragement in renunciation for later generations. Thus, even for those endowed with supreme enjoyments, having been startled by even a slight unattractive sign amidst supreme enjoyments, not considering whether it was the right time or the wrong time, delighting in seclusion, there was a going forth from the home, having abandoned a great mass of wealth like grass. For what other person, then, would there not be a going forth? This is the intention. ‘Being united’ means having attained a state of oneness with them, meaning not secluded. This is the meaning. ‘Sleep overcame’ means: having prevented the occurrence of consciousness even in delightful objects, having surpassed and overwhelmed his mind, it brought it under its own power. This is the meaning. ‘And all night’ means throughout all three watches. By this, it shows the reason for seeing the distorted state of his retinue. Here, it should be understood that the word ‘ratti’ (night) occurs in the sense of time, the absence of the sun, and a watch. Here, it should be understood in the sense of a watch, and also in the training rule on the separation from the three robes. ‘In the armpit’ means at the side of the armpit. ‘At the neck’ means below the neck. The meaning is that he saw a mudiṅga drum at the neck of a sleeping woman who was lying with her neck placed on the upper part of the mudiṅga drum. ‘Āḷambara’ means a paṇava drum. It has two faces and is small and long. This is a designation for an instrument that is played and has a wide, even surface. ‘Rambling’ means talking incoherently due to dreams and so forth. ‘He thought it was a charnel ground’ means the connection to be made is: he saw his own retinue as a charnel ground. ‘Danger’ means the unattractive nature became manifest. ‘His mind settled on disenchantment’ means his mind inclined towards weariness, which is designated as the desire for liberation. This is the meaning. ‘He uttered an inspired utterance’ means he sent forth a joyful utterance: “From now on, I shall not be with these women.” It is said that two aspects became manifest in his seeing the retinue sleeping in heedlessness: the powerful nature of the defilements, and the extremely coarse nature of the unattractive aspect. This being so, in this fathom-long body with its even more coarse unattractive aspect, this entire world is oppressed and deluded by the power of the defilements. Indeed, as he saw again and again, 'Ah, the defilements are so powerful!', those two aspects became manifest to him, for which reason he spoke thus.

“Suvaṇṇapādukāyo ārohitvā”ti etenassa nissaṅgatāya vissaṭṭhagamanaṃ dīpeti. So hi balavasaṃvegābhitunnahadayattā parijanassa pabodhe satipi attano gamananivāraṇasamatthabhāvaṃ asahamāno attānaṃ takkento vissaṭṭho agamāsi. Amanussāti devatā. Tā hi manussehi sugatipaṭivedhañāṇasaṇṭhānādiguṇasāmaññena [V 0.0374] “amanussā”ti vuccanti. Na hi asamānajātikā tiracchānādayo “abrāhmaṇā”ti vā “avasalā”ti vā vuccanti, kintu jātisabhāgatāya eva vasalādayo “abrāhmaṇā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ manussehi kenaci ākārena sabhāgatāya [M 0.0409] devatā “amanussā”ti vuttā. Aññathā manussā na hontīti tiracchānagatāpi “amanussā”ti vattabbā bhaveyyuṃ.

“Having mounted the golden sandals”—this indicates his unhindered departure due to non-attachment. For he, his heart pierced by strong spiritual urgency, unable to endure the possibility of his attendants preventing his departure even if they were to awaken, urged himself on and departed freely. “Non-humans”—these are deities. For they are called “non-humans” because of a commonality of qualities with humans, such as the attainment of a good destination, penetrative knowledge, and similarity in form. For animals and other beings of different species are not called “non-brahmins” or “non-outcastes”; rather, outcastes and others are called “non-brahmins” precisely because of sharing the same species. Similarly, deities are called “non-humans” because of a shared nature with humans in some respect. Otherwise, if the criterion were simply that they are not human, even animals would have to be called “non-humans.”

26. Vanagahanaṃ disvā “sumuttohaṃ nagarato”ti pamuditattā bhagavato avidūre udānesi. Idaṃ kho yasāti bhagavā nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi taṇhādikilesehi anupaddutaṃ, anupasaṭṭhatañca dassanamattenāpi assādajananato. Dhammaṃ desessāmīti yena taṃ nibbānaṃ idha nisinnamattova tvaṃ adhigamissasīti adhippāyo. Kirāti assaddheyyaabyattiparihāsesu nipāto, idha abyattiyaṃ. Suvaṇṇapādukāyo orohitvāti ca suvaṇṇapādukāhi otaritvā. Nissakkatthe hi idaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Tassa nisinnamattasseva aññaṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ akatvā anāmantetvā anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Suparipakkindriyattā, paṭivedhakkhaṇānatikkamanatthaṃ anupaddutānupasaṭṭhatānaṃ pāpakadhammadesanābhimukhacittattā, seṭṭhissa gahapatino acirāgamanadassanato ca. Kimatthaṃ bhagavā tassa suṭṭhutaraṃ saṃviggahadayassa bhavato muccitukāmassa bhavābhavūpāyānisaṃsakathaṃ paṭhamameva kathesīti? Sabbabhavādīnavadassanatthaṃ. So hi manussalokasseva upaddutaupasaṭṭhabhāvaṃ addasa, na saggānanti kadāci saggalokaṃ sukhato maññeyya. Tattha sukhasaññena nibbānābhimukhaṃ cittaṃ peseyyāti saggānampi ādīnavaṃ dassetukāmatāya anupubbiṃ kathaṃ ārabhi. Ettha dānaṃ, dānānisaṃsaṃ, sīlānisaṃsañca kathento dānasīlakathaṃ katheti nāma. Saggavaṇṇaṃ kathento saggakathaṃ katheti nāma. Tattha vatthukāmakilesakāmānaṃ aniccataṃ, apasādataṃ, mahādīnavatañca kathento kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ, okāraṃ, saṃkilesañca pakāseti. Nekkhamme tadabhāvato ca taṃnissaraṇato ca tabbiparītaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ kathento nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāseti nāma. Tattha okāranti avakāraṃ lāmakabhāvaṃ. Saṃkilesanti saṃkilissanaṃ bādhanaṃ upatāpanaṃ vāti attho. Kallacittaṃ paññindriyassa ānubhāvena, diṭṭhiyogavicikicchāyogānaṃ paññindriyena vihatattā. Muducittaṃ satindriyasamāyogena, vihiṃsāsārambhādikilesapavesaṃ nivāretvā cittamudutādikusaladhammappavesanaṃ karontaṃ sahajātaṃ cittaṃ muduṃ karoti. Samādhindriyassa ānubhāvena vinīvaraṇacittaṃ. Tañhi visesato nīvaraṇavipakkhabhūtanti. Vīriyindriyavasena udaggacittaṃ. Tañhi thinamiddhasaṅkhātalīnabhāvavipakkhanti. Saddhindriyassa ānubhāvena [M 0.0410] pasannacittaṃ tassa pasādalakkhaṇattā. Sāmukkaṃsikāti etaṃ visayavasena desanaṃ upālitthero pakāseti. Saccāni hi sāmukkaṃsikadesanāya [V 0.0375] visayāni. Aññathā dukkhādīni sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanāti āpajjati tassa vibhāvane saccānaṃ niddiṭṭhattā.

26. Seeing the dense forest, due to his joy he uttered an inspired utterance near the Blessed One: "I am well freed from the city!" The Blessed One said this referring to Nibbāna. For it is unafflicted by defilements such as craving, and unassailed, because it generates delight even by merely being seen with wisdom. In "I will teach the Dhamma," the intention is: I will teach that Dhamma by which you, while merely sitting here, will attain that Nibbāna. The word 'kirā' is a particle used in the sense of disbelief, lack of clarity, or contempt; here, it is used in the sense of lack of clarity. And "descending from the golden sandals" means having stepped down from the golden sandals. For this is the nominative case used in the sense of the ablative (separation). To him, who was merely sitting there, without making any other pleasant conversation or greeting him, He taught a gradual discourse. This was because his faculties were well-matured; in order not to let the moment of penetration pass; because his mind was inclined towards the Dhamma teaching for those who are unafflicted and unassailed; and because of seeing the imminent arrival of the householder, the millionaire. For what reason did the Blessed One first teach a discourse on the cause and benefit of various existences to him, whose heart was greatly agitated and who desired to be freed from existence? In order to show the danger in all existences. For he had seen the afflicted and assailed nature of the human world only, not of the heavenly worlds; thus, he might at some time consider the heavenly world to be happiness. Thinking that with a perception of happiness there, he might not direct his mind towards Nibbāna, with the desire to show the danger of the heavenly worlds also, He began the gradual discourse. Here, when speaking of generosity, the benefits of generosity, virtue, and the benefits of virtue, it is called 'teaching the discourse on generosity and virtue.' When speaking of the excellence of heaven, it is called 'teaching the discourse on heaven.' There, when speaking of the impermanence, the unloveliness, and the great danger of sensual pleasures—both as objects and as defilements—He is said to 'reveal the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures.' When speaking of the benefit of renunciation, which is the opposite of those things, due to their absence in it and because it is the escape from them, this is called 'revealing the benefit in renunciation.' Therein, 'degradation' (okāra) means baseness, the state of being low. 'Defilement' (saṃkilesa) means pollution, or affliction, or torment. His mind became competent through the power of the faculty of wisdom, because the yokes of wrong view and doubt were destroyed by the faculty of wisdom. His mind became soft through connection with the faculty of mindfulness; for it prevents the entry of defilements such as violence and stubbornness, and by causing the entry of wholesome states such as mental softness, it makes the co-arisen mind soft. Through the power of the faculty of concentration, his mind became free from hindrances. For it is especially the opponent of the hindrances. By means of the faculty of energy, his mind became uplifted. For it is the opponent of the state of sluggishness known as sloth and torpor. Through the power of the faculty of faith, his mind became serene, because its characteristic is clarity. Regarding 'sāmukkaṃsikā,' the Elder Upāli explains this teaching by way of its subject matter. For the Truths are the subject matter of the sāmukkaṃsikā teaching. Otherwise, it would follow that suffering and so on are the sāmukkaṃsikā Dhamma teaching; because in its explanation, the Truths are specified.

27. Catuddisāti catūsu disāsu. Abhisaṅkharesīti abhisaṅkhari. Kimatthanti ce? Ubhinnaṃ paṭilabhitabbavisesantarāyanisedhanatthaṃ. Yadi so puttaṃ passeyya, puttassapi dhammacakkhupaṭilābho arahattuppatti, seṭṭhissapi dhammacakkhupaṭilābho na siyā. Diṭṭhasaccopi “dehi te mātuyā jīvita”nti vadanto kimaññaṃ na kareyya. Yasopi taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā arahāpi samāno sayaṃ appaṭikkhipitvā bhagavantaṃ ullokento kimaññāya saṇṭhaheyya.

27. “In the four directions” means in the four directions. “He fashioned” means He fashioned. If it be asked, “For what purpose?” For the purpose of preventing the danger to the special attainment to be obtained by both. If that setthi were to see his son, for the son also the attainment of the Dhamma-eye and the arising of Arahantship would not occur, and for the setthi also the attainment of the Dhamma-eye would not occur. Even one who has seen the truth, while saying, “Give your mother her life,” what other thing would he not do? And Yasa, having heard those words, even though he was an Arahant, not rejecting them himself and looking up at the Blessed One, how could he be established in the final knowledge?

28. Ubhohipi pattabbavisesakoṭiyā pattattā bhagavā puna taṃ paṭippassambhesi. Pubbe agārikabhūtoti tassa sotāpannakālaṃ sandhāyāha. Sotāpanno hi agāramajjhe vasanārahattā agāriyabhūto nāma hoti apabbajito. Sampati pabbajito samāno agāramajjhavasanassa abhabbattā “agāriko”ti na vuccati, tasmā evamāha. Yassa diṭṭhoti sambandho, yena diṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Seyyathāpi pubbe agārikabhūto”ti vacanena laddhanayattā pacchā gahapati gihivesadhārimeva yasaṃ sandhāyāha “yasena kulaputtena pacchāsamaṇenā”ti. Tattha cara brahmacariyanti ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ brahmacariyaṃ cara paripūrehi tāva, yāva sammādukkhassantakiriyā, yāva cuticittāti adhippāyo. Liṅgabrahmacariyaṃ sandhāyāti porāṇā, tañca yuttaṃ. Liṅgamattañhi sandhāya so āyasmā “labheyyāhaṃ, bhante, pabbajjaṃ upasampada”nti āha.

28. Because both had reached the pinnacle of the special attainment to be reached, the Blessed One then withdrew it. When it says, “formerly a householder,” He said this referring to the time he was a stream-enterer. For a stream-enterer, because he is worthy of living in the midst of a household, is called a 'householder', not having gone forth. Now, being one who has gone forth, because it is unfitting to live in the midst of a household, he is not called a 'householder'; therefore He spoke thus. The connection is to be made as 'of whom it is seen'; what is meant is 'by whom it was seen.' Because the method was obtained through the words, “just as formerly he was a householder,” the householder (father) afterwards, referring to Yasa who was still wearing the guise of a layman, said, “by Yasa the clansman, afterwards a recluse.” Therein, 'practice the holy life' means: 'Practice the holy life, which is the morality of proper conduct; fulfill it completely for as long as there is the making of a complete end to suffering, up to the death-consciousness'—this is the intended meaning. The ancients say that He said this referring to the holy life as the outward sign, and that is fitting. For indeed, referring merely to the outward sign, that venerable one said, “Venerable sir, may I receive the going forth, the higher ordination.”

Kimatthaṃ bhagavā yasassa mātu, pajāpatiyā ca bhattakiccaṃ akatvāva dhammaṃ desesīti? Yasassa pabbajjāya sokasallasamappitattā dānañca somanassikacittena na dadeyyuṃ, satthari ca domanassappattā hutvā maggapaṭivedhampi na labheyyunti bhagavā paṭhamaṃ tāva tā vigatasokasallahadayāyo katvā puna bhattakiccaṃ akāsi.

For what reason did the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to Yasa’s mother and wife without first performing the duty of the meal? This is the question. Because, being pierced by the dart of sorrow due to Yasa’s going forth, they would not give alms with a joyful mind, and having become afflicted with grief towards the Teacher, they would not attain the penetration of the path. Therefore, the Blessed One first made them have hearts freed from the dart of sorrow and then performed the duty of the meal.

30. Seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnanti anukkamaseṭṭhīnanti porāṇā. “Seṭṭhino cānuseṭṭhino ca yāni kulāni, tāni seṭṭhānuseṭṭhāni kulāni, tesaṃ [M 0.0411] seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnaṃ kulāna”nti likhitaṃ. Dhammavinayoti sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ pāvacananti idha atthato ekaṃ. Atha vā dhammena vinayo, na daṇḍasatthehīti dhammavinayo, dhammāya vinayo, na hiṃsatthanti vā dhammato vinayo, nādhammatoti vā dhammo vinayo, nādhammoti vā dhammānaṃ vinayo, na aññesanti vā dhammakāyattā, dhammasāmittā [V 0.0376] vā dhammo bhagavā, tassa dhammassa vinayo, na takkikānanti vā dhammavinayo. Samānādhikaraṇavasena vā dhammavinayo nīluppalaṃ viya, dhammo ca vinayo cāti dhammavinayo phalāphalaṃ viya napuṃsakamiti pulliṅgāpadesato assa liṅgabhāvo siddho, yassa vā dhammo vinayo, so dhammavinayo setapaṭo puriso viya, dhammena yutto vā vinayo dhammavinayo assaratho viyāti evamādinā nayena yojanā veditabbā.

30. Regarding 'Seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnaṃ', the ancients say it means 'of treasurers in succession'. It is written: 'Those families that are of treasurers and successive treasurers are seṭṭhānuseṭṭhāni families; of those families of treasurers and successive treasurers.' Regarding 'Dhammavinayo', here it is one in meaning with 'the holy life of the teaching' and 'the word of the Buddha'. Alternatively, it is 'Dhammavinayo' because it is discipline by means of Dhamma, not by rod and weapons; or, discipline for the sake of Dhamma, not for the sake of harming; or, discipline from Dhamma, not from non-Dhamma; or, the discipline which is Dhamma, not that which is non-Dhamma; or, the discipline of the Dhammas, not of others. Or, because of being the Dhamma-body or because of being the Lord of the Dhamma, the Blessed One is 'Dhamma'; it is the discipline of that 'Dhamma' (the Blessed One), not of the sophists. Or, by way of having a common referent, 'Dhammavinayo' is like 'nīluppalaṃ' (blue water-lily). Or, 'Dhamma and Vinaya', therefore 'Dhammavinayo', like 'phalāphalaṃ' (fruit and non-fruit); it is neuter, and its gender is established by not indicating the masculine. Or, he for whom the Dhamma is the discipline, he is 'Dhammavinayo', like a man with a white cloth. Or, the discipline connected with the Dhamma is 'Dhammavinayo', like a horse-chariot. The application should be understood by this method and so on.

34. “Khaṇḍasīmaṃ netvā”ti bhaṇḍukammārocanapaṭiharaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena “sabhikkhuke vihāre aññampi etassa kese chindā”ti vattuṃ na vaṭṭatīti. Pabbājetvāti imassa adhippāyapakāsanatthaṃ “kāsāyāni acchādetvā ehī”ti vuttaṃ. Upajjhāyo ce kesamassuoropanādīni akatvā pabbajatthaṃ saraṇāni deti, na ruhati pabbajjā. Kammavācaṃ sāvetvā upasampādeti, ruhati upasampadā. Appattacīvarānaṃ upasampadāsiddhidassanato, kammavipattiyā abhāvato cetaṃ yujjatevāti eke. Hoti cettha –

34. The phrase “Having led him to the broken boundary” was said for the purpose of preventing the announcement of the act of tonsure. By this, it is shown that it is not proper to say, “In a monastery where monks reside, let others also cut this person’s hair.” To clarify the intention of the word ‘pabbājetvā’ (having given the going-forth), it was said, “Come, having been clothed in ochre robes.” If a preceptor, without performing the shaving of the hair and beard and so on, gives the refuges for the purpose of the going-forth, the going-forth is not valid. If he confers the higher ordination after having the formal act announced, the higher ordination is valid. Some say that this is indeed proper because it is seen that the higher ordination is accomplished for those without a bowl and robes, and because there is no defect in the formal act. And here there is a summary verse:

“Saliṅgasseva pabbajjā, viliṅgassāpi cetarā;

Apetapubbavesassa, taṃ dvayaṃ iti cāpare”ti.

“The going-forth is valid only for one with the proper appearance; the other (higher ordination) is also valid for one without the proper appearance. For one who has abandoned the former appearance, both are valid. So say others.”

Bhikkhunā hi sahatthena vā āṇattiyā vā dinnameva kāsāvaṃ vaṭṭati, adinnaṃ na vaṭṭatīti pana santesveva kāsāvesu, nāsantesu asambhavatoti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Evañca pana, bhikkhave, pabbājetabbo upasampādetabbo. Paṭhamaṃ…pe…anujānāmi, bhikkhave, imehi tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajjaṃ upasampadanti ettha iminā anukkamena dinnehi tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajjaṃ upasampadaṃ anujānāmi kevalehīti adhippāyadassanato –

Indeed, an ochre robe given by a bhikkhu with his own hand or by his command is valid; one not so given is not valid. However, this applies only when ochre robes are available; when they are not, it does not apply, because it is impossible. This is their intention. And in the passage, “And in this way, monks, one should be given the going-forth, one should be given the higher ordination. First… I allow, monks, the going-forth and the higher ordination by these three goings for refuge,” because the intention is seen as: “I allow the going-forth and the higher ordination by means of only these three goings for refuge given in this sequence…”

Ādinnapubbaliṅgassa, naggassāpi dvayaṃ bhave;

Netarassāti no khanti, sabbapāṭhānulomatoti. –

“For one habituated to the former appearance, even if naked, both would be valid. That it would not be so for the other is our view, because of its conformity with all the texts.” Thus said the Teacher.

Ācariyo[M 0.0412]. Ācariyena adinnaṃ na vaṭṭatīti ettha “pabbajjā na ruhatīti vadantī”ti likhitaṃ. Porāṇagaṇṭhipadepi tatheva likhitaṃ. Urādīni ṭhānāni nāma. Saṃvutādīni karaṇāni nāma. “Anunāsikantaṃ katvā ekasambandhaṃ katvā dānakāle antarā aṭṭhatvā vattabbaṃ. Vicchinditvā dānepi yathāvuttaṭṭhāne eva vicchedo, aññatra na vaṭṭatī”ti likhitaṃ. Anunāsikante diyyamāne khalitvā “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti makārena missībhūte khette otiṇṇattā [V 0.0377] vaṭṭatīti upatissatthero. Missaṃ katvā vattuṃ vaṭṭati, vacanakāle pana anunāsikaṭṭhāne vicchedaṃ akatvā vattabbanti dhammasiritthero. “Evaṃ kammavācāyampī”ti vuttaṃ. Ubhatosuddhiyāva vaṭṭatīti ettha mahāthero patitadantādikāraṇatāya acaturassaṃ katvā vadati, byattasāmaṇero samīpe ṭhito pabbajjāpekkhaṃ byattaṃ vadāpeti. Mahātherena avuttaṃ vadāpetīti na vaṭṭati. Kammavācāya itaro bhikkhu ce vadati, vaṭṭatīti. Saṅgho hi kammaṃ karoti, na puggaloti. Na nānāsīmapavattakammavācāsāmaññanayena paṭikkhipitabbattā. Atha therena caturassaṃ vuttaṃ pabbajjāpekkhaṃ vattuṃ asakkontaṃ sāmaṇero sayaṃ vatvā vadāpeti, ubhatosuddhi eva hoti therena vuttasseva vuttattā. Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchanto asādhāraṇe buddhaguṇe, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchanto nibbānaṃ, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchanto sekkhadhammaṃ, asekkhadhammañca saraṇaṃ gacchatīti aggahitaggahaṇavasena yojanā kātabbā. Aññathā saraṇattayasaṅkaradoso. Sabbamassa kappiyākappiyanti dasasikkhāpadavinimuttaṃ parāmāsāparāmāsādi. “Ābhisamācārikesu vinetabbo”ti vacanato sekhiyaupajjhāyavattādiābhisamācārikasīlamanena pūretabbaṃ. Tattha cārittassa akaraṇe vārittassa karaṇe daṇḍakammāraho hotīti dīpeti.

The Teacher. Regarding 'what is not given by the teacher is not valid,' here it is written, 'They say the going-forth does not take root.' In the ancient glosses also, it is written in the same way. The chest and so on are called the places of articulation. The constricted organs and so on are called the instruments of articulation. 'Having made it end with a nasal, having made it a single connection, it should be spoken at the time of giving without stopping in between. Even when giving with an interruption, the break is only at the place as stated; elsewhere, it is not allowable,' it is written. When giving the words ending with a nasal, if one stumbles and it becomes mixed with the letter 'm' as in 'buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi,' it is allowable because it has fallen within the field of acceptable pronunciation, so says the Elder Upatissa. It is allowable to speak having mixed it, but at the time of recitation, it should be recited without making a break at the place of the nasal, so says the Elder Dhammasiri. 'Thus it is also in the Kammavācā,' it is said. Regarding 'it is allowable only with purity on both sides,' here the great elder speaks unclearly due to reasons such as having fallen teeth, while a competent novice standing nearby causes the ordination candidate to speak competently. That he, the novice, causes the candidate to say what was not said by the great elder is not allowable. If another monk speaks during the Kammavācā, it is allowable. For the Saṅgha performs the act, not an individual. No, it is not allowable, because it is to be rejected by the principle of the commonality of a Kammavācā occurring in different boundaries. Alternatively, if the ordination candidate is unable to say what was spoken clearly by the elder, and the novice, having said it himself, causes him to say it, there is indeed purity on both sides, because what was said by the elder is precisely what was said. One going for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to the unique qualities of the Buddha; one going for refuge to the Dhamma goes for refuge to Nibbāna; and one going for refuge to the Saṅgha goes for refuge to the qualities of the trainees and the adepts. The connection should be made by way of grasping what has not been grasped. Otherwise, there would be the fault of confusing the three refuges. 'All that is allowable and unallowable for him' refers to that which is apart from the ten training rules, such as what is to be touched and not to be touched. In accordance with the saying, 'He should be trained in the rules of good behavior,' the virtue of good behavior—such as the sekhiya rules, the duties towards a preceptor, and so on—should be fulfilled by this novice. Therein, in the non-performance of what should be done and in the performance of what is prohibited, he becomes liable to punishment—this is explained.

Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Account of the Going-Forth is concluded.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Account of Māra

35. “Tena hetunā”ti vacanato pāḷiyaṃ “yonisomanasikārāsammappadhānā”ti hetvatthe nissakkavacananti veditabbaṃ.

35. Regarding 'For that reason' (tena hetunā): it should be understood that in the Pāli text, the word 'yonisomanasikārāsammappadhānā' is an ablative expression in the sense of cause.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Account of Māra is concluded.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of the Miracles at Uruvelā

37-8. Vaseyyāmāti [M 0.0413] “tvañca ahañca vaseyyāmā”ti piyavacanena tassa saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ kira. Tejasā tejanti ānubhāvena ānubhāvaṃ. Tejodhātuyā vā tejodhātuṃ. Ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānanti anādaratthe sāmivacanaṃ, bhāvasattamīatthe vā. Agyāgārameva ādittaṃ, na tattha vasanako sattajātiko. Acinteyyo hi iddhivisayo. Kasmā pana bhagavā agyāgārampi anādittaṃ nādhiṭṭhāsīti? Attano dukkhuppādābhāvassa anativimhādibhāvappasaṅgato. Kimatthaṃ parasantakaṃ [V 0.0378] mahāsambhārapavattaṃ taṃ vināsetīti? Puna yathāporāṇaṃ iddhānubhāvena kattukāmatādhippāyato. Pariyādinnoti khayaṃ nīto. Tejasā tejanti ānubhāvena ānubhāvaṃ. Agyāgārassa parittattā itaro attho na sambhavati. Ayamattho “makkhaṃ asahamāno”ti iminā ativiya sameti. Iddhānubhāvamakkhanañhi tattha makkho nāma. Pattenāti padumapattenātipi porāṇā. Paduminisaṇḍe ṭhito hi bhagavā tattha ahosīti tesaṃ mati.

37-8. "Let us dwell": it is said that this was spoken with affectionate words, "You and I, let us dwell," for the purpose of winning him over. "By fire, fire" means by power, power; or by the fire element, the fire element. "Of the two, having become radiant": this is a genitive case in the sense of disregard, or in the sense of the locative absolute. The fire-house alone was ablaze; no living being dwelling there was set ablaze. For the sphere of psychic power is inconceivable. But why then did the Blessed One not resolve that the fire-house also not be set ablaze? Because of the consequence of the non-arising of his (the ascetic's) own suffering and the state of it not being excessively astonishing. Why did he destroy that greatly furnished structure, which was another's property? Because of the intention to remake it as it was before through the power of psychic ability. "Consumed" means brought to destruction. "By fire, fire" means by power, power. Because of the smallness of the fire-house, the other meaning is not possible. This meaning agrees very well with "not tolerating contempt." For in that context, the disparagement of psychic power is called 'contempt.' "With a leaf": the ancients also say, "with a lotus leaf." For the Blessed One stood in a lotus grove; 'he was there'—such is their opinion.

39. Dinnanti anumatinti attho. Abhīto nibbhayo. Kasmā? Yato so maggena bhayamatīto. “Sumanamanasoti sundaracittasaṅkhātamano. Sumano eva vā”ti likhitaṃ. Tejovāti aggi viya. Dhātukusaloti tejodhātumhi kusalo. “Byavahitā ce”ti saddalakkhaṇattā ca upasaggo. Tejodhātusamāpattīsu kusalo iccevattho. Udicchareti ullokesuṃ. “Saṃparivāresu”nti ca likhitaṃ. Iti evaṃ bhaṇantīti attho. Hatāti samāti attho, kāḷakāva hontīti kirettha adhippāyo. Īsakampi byāpāraṃ akatvā upasamānurūpaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Ye ca anekavaṇṇā acciyo hontīti taṃ dassetuṃ “nīlā atha lohitikā”tiādimāha.

39. "Given" means consented. Fearless, without fear. Why? Because he has gone beyond fear by the path. "Of joyful mind" means a mind reckoned as beautiful. Or simply "joyful," as it is written. "Fiery" means like fire. "Skilled in the element" means skilled in the fire element. "Byavahitā ce" — and because of its grammatical characteristic, it is a prefix. The meaning is simply skilled in the attainments of the fire element. "They looked up" means they gazed upward. "They surrounded" is also written. The meaning is that they speak thus. "Destroyed" means extinguished; the intent here, it is said, is that they become just black. They stand without making even the slightest effort, in accordance with peace. And to show that those flames are of many colors, he says, "blue, then red," and so on.

40. Catuddisāti catūsu disāsu.

40. "In the four directions" means in the four quarters.

44. Paṃsukūlaṃ uppannanti pariyesamānassa paṭilābhavasena uppannaṃ hoti. Cittavicittapāṭihīradassanatthāya ca sā pariyesanā. Sā ayaṃ sāyaṃ[M 0.0414]. Tā imā tayimā. Dve ekato gahetvā vadati. Āyāmi ahaṃ āyamahaṃ. Etanti etassa. Yathā mayanti yasmā mayaṃ.

44. "A rag-robe has arisen" means it has arisen by way of acquisition for one who is seeking. And that seeking is for the purpose of showing the wonder of varied miracles. Sāyaṃ is sā and ayaṃ. Tayimā is tā and imā. He speaks taking two together. Āyamahaṃ is āyāmi and ahaṃ. The word etaṃ has the meaning of etassa. The phrase yathā mayaṃ means yasmā mayaṃ.

50-51. Udakavāhakoti udakogho. Udakasototi porāṇā. “Yāya tva”nti pubbabhāgavipassanāpaṭipadaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cirapaṭikāti cirapabhuti, nāgadamanato paṭṭhāya cirapaṭikā. “Cirapaṭisaṅkhā”tipi vadanti. Kesamissantiādimhi abbokiṇṇaṃ visuṃ visuṃ bandhitvā pakkhittattā kesādayova kesamissāti porāṇā. Khārikājamissanti ettha khārī vuccati tāpasaparikkhāro. Jaṭile pāhesīti dve tayo tāpase pāhesi. “Soḷasātirekaaḍḍhauḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassānī”ti vuttaṃ.

50-51. "Udakavāhako" means a flood of water. The ancients say it means "udakasoto" (a current of water). "Yāya tvaṃ" is said with reference to the preliminary practice of insight. "Cirapaṭikā" means from a long time ago; from the taming of the Nāga onwards, it has been a long time. They also say "cirapaṭisaṅkhā." In the phrase beginning with "kesamissa," the ancients say that because hair and other things are tied separately and put in unmixed, they are themselves called "kesamissa." In "Khārikājamissa," the ascetic's equipment is called "khārī." "He sent the matted-hair ascetics" means he sent two or three ascetics. It is said, "three and a half thousand miracles plus sixteen."

54. Aggihutte kataparicayattā bhagavā tesaṃ ādittapariyāya-mabhāsi (saṃ. ni. 4.28). Tattha ekaccaṃ ārammaṇavasena ādittaṃ cakkhādi rāgagginā, ekaccaṃ sampayogavasena cakkhusamphassapaccayā vedayitādikeneva, ekaccaṃ abhibhūtatthena cakkhādi eva jātiādinā[V 0.0379], ekaccaṃ paccayatthena, tadeva sokādināti yathāsambhavamettha ādittatā veditabbā. Ettha kiñcāpi dukkhalakkhaṇamevekaṃ pākaṭaṃ, tadanusārena pana itaraṃ lakkhaṇadvayampi tehi diṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ dukkhākārassa itarākāradīpanato. Santasukhataṇhābhiniviṭṭhattā panesaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇapubbaṅgamā desanā katāti veditabbā.

54. Because they were practiced in the fire-offering, the Blessed One delivered the Ādittapariyāya discourse to them (Saṃ. Ni. 4.28). Therein, some—the eye and so on—is burning by way of the object with the fire of lust; some, by way of association, through feeling and so on arising from the condition of eye-contact; some—the eye itself—by the nature of being overwhelmed by birth and so on; and some, by way of condition, that very thing by sorrow and so on. Thus, the state of being ablaze should be understood here according to what is possible. Here, although only the one characteristic of suffering is manifest, it should be understood that, following that, the other two characteristics were also seen by them, because the aspect of suffering reveals the other aspects. It should be understood that for them, because of their devotion to the craving for existing happiness, the teaching was given with the characteristic of suffering as its forerunner.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of the Miracles at Uruvelā is concluded.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Account of the Meeting with Bimbisāra

55-7. Vatthukāmabhūtā itthiyo kāmitthiyo. Dutiyādayo assāsakā. Yasmā anuppanne eva bhagavati buddhakolāhalaṃ loke paṭhamameva vassasahassaṃ uppajjati. Brahmāno ca brāhmaṇavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā vedesu sahassattayamattaṃ buddhapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ pariyattiṃ pakkhipitvā vācenti, bhagavato jātito paṭṭhāya ca buddhakathā lakkhaṇaññūhi brāhmaṇehi uppāditā, patthaṭā loke, tasmā yujjanti, na aññathā. “Tamaddasa [M 0.0415] bimbisāro, pāsādasmiṃ patiṭṭhito”tiādigāthāhi bodhisattakāle eva abhisittatā bimbisārassa siddhā.

55-7. Women who are objects of sensual pleasure are called kāmitthiyo. The second and others are comforters. Because even before the Blessed One’s arising, a 'Buddha-uproar' first arises in the world for a thousand years. And Brahmās, having created the appearance of brahmins, insert into the Vedas a body of teaching amounting to three thousand connected with the Buddha and have it recited. Moreover, from the Blessed One’s birth onwards, talk of the Buddha has been produced and spread in the world by brahmins who know the marks; therefore, they are fitting, not otherwise. The verses beginning with “Tamaddasa bimbisāro, pāsādasmiṃ patiṭṭhito” establish that Bimbisāra was already consecrated in the Bodhisatta’s time.

58. Idhāvuso khīṇāsavo bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti chaḷaṅgasamannāgato ekārakkho caturāpasseno paṇunnapaccekasacco samavayasaṭṭhesano anāvilasaṅkappo passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro suvimuttacitto suvimuttapaññoti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360; a. ni. 10.19) dasa ariyavāsā nāma. Rūpārūpasamāpattiyo aṭṭha nirodhasamāpatti mahākaruṇāsamāpattītipi porāṇā. Tattha nīvaraṇā pañcaṅgā ca. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā chaḷaṅgā. Satārakkhena ekārakkhā. Saṅkhāya ekaṃ paṭisevati, adhivāseti, parivajjeti, saṅkhāya ekaṃ vinodetīti ayaṃ caturāpasseno. Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ puthupaccekasaccāni cattāri pahīnāni, evaṃ paṇunnapaccekasacco. Kāmesanā bhavesanā pahīnā hoti, brahmacariyesanā paṭippassaddhā, evaṃ samavayasaṭṭhesano. Kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāsaṅkappo pahīno hoti, evaṃ anāvilasaṅkappo, sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati evaṃ suvimuttacitto hoti. Rāgo pahīno ucchinnamūlo…pe… anuppādadhammoti pajānāti, doso, moho anuppādadhammoti pajānāti, evaṃ suvimuttapaññoti.

58. Here, friends, a monk whose taints are destroyed has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has the one guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has quests relinquished, has untroubled intentions, has bodily formations calmed, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated by wisdom—these are called the ten noble abodes. The ancients also speak of the eight attainments of form and formlessness, the attainment of cessation, and the attainment of great compassion. Herein, the five hindrances are the five factors. Six-limbed equanimity is the six factors. Guarded by mindfulness is the one guard. 'One makes use of something after reflection, endures, avoids, and removes after reflection'—this is the four supports. The various individual truths of various ascetics and brahmins are abandoned—thus, one has dispelled individual truths. The quest for sensual pleasures and the quest for existence are abandoned, and the quest for the holy life is pacified—thus, one has quests relinquished. Intentions of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty are abandoned—thus, one has untroubled intentions. 'Having abandoned pleasure... one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna'—thus, one is well-liberated in mind. One understands that greed is abandoned, its root cut off... that it will not arise again; one understands that hatred and delusion will not arise again—thus, one is well-liberated by wisdom.

“Ṭhānāṭhānaṃ [V 0.0380] vipākañca, ñāṇaṃ sabbatthagāminiṃ;

Anekadhātuyo lokaṃ, adhimuttiñca pāṇinaṃ.

The knowledge of what is possible and impossible, and the knowledge of the results of kamma; the knowledge of the path leading to all destinations; the knowledge of the world with its many elements; and the knowledge of the dispositions of beings.

“Jānāti indriyānañca, paropariyataṃ muni;

Jhānādisaṃkilesādi-ñāṇaṃ vijjattayaṃ tathā”ti. –

The sage knows the higher and lower states of the faculties of beings; the knowledge of the jhānas, defilements, and so forth, and likewise the threefold true knowledge.

Imāni dasa balāni. Asekkhaṅgāni nāma asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi…pe… asekkhavimutti asekkhavimuttiñāṇadassananti. Tattha dasamaṃ asekkhaṃ. Etehi dasahi cupeto pāramīhīti porāṇā.

These are the ten powers. The factors of one beyond training are: the Right View of one beyond training… up to… the liberation of one beyond training, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. Therein, the tenth is that of the one beyond training. The ancients say that he is endowed with these ten factors and also with the perfections.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of the Meeting with Bimbisāra is concluded.

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Story of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna

60. Kiṃ kāhasīti kiṃ kāhati. “Kiṃ karoti, kiṃ karosī”ti vā byañjanaṃ bahuṃ vatvāti attho. Paṭipādentoti nigamento. “Paccabyathā[M 0.0416], paccabyatha”ntipi paṭhanti. Kappanahutehīti ettha dasakānaṃ sataṃ sahassaṃ, sahassānaṃ sataṃ satasahassaṃ, satasahassānaṃ sataṃ koṭi, koṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ pakoṭi, pakoṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ koṭipakoṭi, koṭipakoṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ nahutanti veditabbaṃ. Kappanahutehīti evamanusārato abbhatītaṃ nāmāti khandhakabhāṇakānaṃ pāṭhoti.

60. In `Kiṃ kāhasi`, it means `kiṃ kāhati` (What will he do?). Or, having stated the expression at length, the meaning is 'What does he do? What do you do?'. In `Paṭipādento`, it is the conclusion. They also recite `Paccabyathā, paccabyatha`. Here, regarding `kappanahutehi`, it should be understood that a hundred tens is a thousand; a hundred thousands is a hundred-thousand; a hundred hundred-thousands is a koṭi; a hundred hundred-thousand-koṭis is a pakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousand-pakoṭis is a koṭipakoṭi; and a hundred hundred-thousand-koṭipakoṭis is a nahuta. Regarding `kappanahutehi`, [the meaning is that] according to this sequence, it is called 'that which has passed beyond'—this is the reading of the Khandhaka reciters.

63. “Kulacchedāyā”ti pāṭho, kulupacchedāyāti attho. Manussā “dhammena kira samaṇā sakyaputtiyā nayanti, nādhammenā”ti na puna codesunti evaṃ pāṭhasesena sambandho kātabbo.

63. The reading is `kulacchedāya`; the meaning is `kulupacchedāya` (for the cutting off of the family). 'It is said the Sakyan ascetics lead by the Dhamma, not by non-Dhamma,' [and so] people did not admonish them again—thus the connection should be made with the remaining part of the reading.

Ettāvatā thero nidānaṃ niṭṭhapesīti veditabbaṃ. Honti cettha –

By this much, it should be understood that the Elder concluded the introduction. And here there are:

“Yaṃ dhammasenāpati ettha mūla-

Ganthassa siddhikkamadassanena;

Nidānaniṭṭhānamakaṃsu [V 0.0381] dhamma-

Saṅgāhakā te vinayakkamaññū.

That conclusion of the introduction which the General of the Dhamma made here by showing the successful sequence of the root text, those compilers of the Dhamma, skilled in the sequence of the Vinaya, also made.

“Nidānalīnatthapadānameva,

Nidāniṭṭhānamidaṃ viditvā;

Ito paraṃ ce vinayatthayutta-

Padāni vīmaṃsanameva ñeyya”nti.

Having understood this conclusion of the introduction, which is only of terms whose meaning is hidden in the introduction, from here onward, only the investigation of terms connected with the meaning of the Vinaya should be understood.

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Story of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is concluded.

Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā
