By those who are causing others to rise from the Rains-residence in a place other than the monastery, it should be done only after having assembled right there and announced: 'For this and that reason, having brought them to this monastery in this so-named place, we will cause them to rise from the Rains-residence.'

Vajādīsuvassūpagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Undertaking the Rains-residence in a Cattle-pen and So Forth

203. Vajena saddhiṃ gatassa vassacchede anāpattīti vassacchedo na hotīti kira adhippāyo. Satthassa avihārattā “imasmiṃ vihāre”ti avatvā “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti ettakaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Satthe pana vassaṃ upagantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti ‘imasmiṃ vihāre imaṃ temāsa’nti vā ‘idha vassaṃ upemī’ti vā na vaṭṭati, ālayakaraṇamatteneva vaṭṭatīti adhippāyo”ti likhitaṃ. Taṃ pana aṭṭhakathāya virujjhati. “Idha vassaṃ upemīti tikkhattuṃ vattabba”nti hi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāvacanampi pubbāparaṃ virujjhatīti ce? Na, adhippāyājānanato. Sattho duvidho ṭhito, sañcāroti. Tattha ṭhite kuṭikāya “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti vatvā vasitabbaṃ. Idañhi sandhāya “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, satthe vassaṃ upagantu”nti vuttaṃ, sañcārimhi pana satthe kuṭikāya abhāvato vassaṃ upagantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sati sivikāya vā sakaṭakuṭikāya vā vaṭṭati, tathā vajepi. Tīsu ṭhānesu bhikkhuno natthi vassacchede āpatti.

203. Regarding the statement, 'There is no offense in the breaking of the rains-residence for one who has gone with a cattle-pen,' the intention, it is said, is that the breaking of the rains-residence does not occur. Because a caravan is not a monastery, without saying, 'in this monastery,' just this much, 'I undertake the rains-residence here,' should be said. It is written: 'Regarding, "However, it is not proper to undertake the rains-residence in a caravan," the intention is that it is not proper to undertake it by saying either, "in this monastery for these three months," or, "I undertake the rains-residence here"; it is proper merely by making it a dwelling place.' But that contradicts the commentary. For it is said, '“I undertake the rains-residence here” should be said three times.' If one were to say, 'The statement of the commentary also contradicts what comes before and after,' it is not so; this is due to not knowing the intention. A caravan is of two kinds: stationary and traveling. Therein, in a stationary caravan, one should reside after saying in a hut, 'I undertake the rains-residence here.' Indeed, it was with reference to this that it was said, 'I allow, bhikkhus, to undertake the rains-residence in a caravan.' But in a traveling caravan, due to the absence of a hut, it is not proper to undertake the rains-residence. If there is a palanquin or a cart-hut, it is proper; likewise also in a cattle-pen. In these three situations, there is no offense of breaking the rains-residence for a bhikkhu.

Pavāretuñca labhatīti etthāyaṃ vicāraṇā – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yena vajo, tena gantu”nti idaṃ kiṃ vassarakkhaṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ, udāhu vassacchedāpattirakkhaṇatthanti? Kiñcettha yadi vassarakkhaṇatthaṃ, “na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti idaṃ virujjhati. Atha vassacchedāpattirakkhaṇatthaṃ vuttanti siddhaṃ na so pavāretuṃ labhatīti, kā panettha yutti? Yato ayameva tividho pavāretuṃ labhati, netaro. Vāḷehi ubbāḷhādiko hi upagataṭṭhānāpariccāgā labhati. Pariccāgā na labhatīti ayamettha yutti. Yena gāmo, tattha gatopi pavāretuṃ labhatīti ekenāti ācariyo. Yo hi pubbe “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti na upagato, “imasmiṃ vihāre”ti upagato, so [M 0.0470] ca pariccatto. Aññathā vinā vihārena kevalaṃ gāmaṃ sandhāya “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti upagantuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Āpajjatūti ce? Na, “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vaje satthe nāvāya vassaṃ upagantu”nti vacanaṃ viya “gāme upagantu”nti vacanābhāvato. Yasmā [V 0.0429] “tīsu ṭhānesu bhikkhuno natthi vassacchede āpattī”ti vacanaṃ tattha vassūpagamanaṃ atthīti dīpeti tadabhāve chedābhāvā, tasmā “satthe pana vassaṃ upagantuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti kuṭiyā abhāvakālaṃ sandhāya vuttanti siddhaṃ. Tīsu ṭhānesu bhikkhuno natthi vassacchede āpattīti “tehi saddhiṃ gacchantasseva natthi, virujjhitvā gamane āpatti ca, pavāretuñca na labhatī”ti likhitaṃ, tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “atha sattho antovasseyeva bhikkhunā patthitaṭṭhānaṃ patvā atikkamati…pe… antarā ekasmiṃ gāme tiṭṭhati vā vippakirati vā”tiādi, taṃ ettāvatā virujjhitvā gatānampi virujjhitvā gamanaṃ na hoti, tasmā pavāretabbanti dassanatthanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding the statement, 'And he is allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā,' this is the investigation: Was this statement, 'Bhikkhus, I allow you to go where the cattle-pen is,' spoken for the sake of protecting the Rains-residence, or for the sake of protecting against the offense of breaking the Rains-residence? And here, if it was said for the sake of protecting the Rains-residence, then this statement, 'Bhikkhus, the Rains-residence should not be undertaken by one without a dwelling,' is contradicted. But if it is established that it was said for the sake of protecting against the offense of breaking the Rains-residence, then he is not allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā. What is the reasoning here? Because only this one of three kinds is allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā, not another. A teacher states that, according to one opinion, 'Even one who has gone to a village is allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā.' For there is the case of one who previously did not undertake the Rains saying, 'I undertake the Rains-residence here,' but undertook it saying, 'in this monastery,' and that monastery was abandoned. Otherwise, it would follow that without a monastery, it is permissible to undertake the Rains merely with reference to a village, saying, 'I undertake the Rains-residence here.' If one should say, 'Let it be so,' the reply is: No, because there is no statement 'to undertake the Rains in a village' like the statement, 'Bhikkhus, I allow you to undertake the Rains-residence in a cattle-pen, in a caravan, or in a boat.' Because the statement, 'In three situations, there is no offense of breaking the Rains-residence for a bhikkhu,' indicates that undertaking the Rains-residence is valid there, for in the absence of that undertaking, there is no breaking. Therefore, it is established that the statement, 'But it is not permissible to undertake the Rains-residence in a caravan,' was said with reference to a time when there is no hut. Regarding, 'In three situations, there is no offense of breaking the Rains-residence for a bhikkhu,' it is written: 'There is no offense only for one who goes together with them; in going after separating from them, there is an offense, and he is not allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā.' Therefore, what was said in the commentary—'Then a caravan, while the bhikkhu is still within the Rains-residence, having reached the desired destination, passes beyond… or on the way stops in a certain village or disperses,' and so on—was said for the purpose of showing that, by this much, even for those who have gone after separating, their going does not constitute a separation that breaks the Rains. Therefore, the Pavāraṇā should be performed. Thus it should be understood.

Tattha “padaracchadanaṃ kuṭiṃ katvā upagantabba”nti vacanato senāsanatthāya rukkhaṃ āruhituṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ hoti, na pāḷivirodhatoti ce? Na, tappaṭikkhepeneva siddhattā, imassa idha punapi paṭikkhepanato. “Na, bhikkhave, asenāsanikena vassaṃ upagantabba”nti iminā paṭikkhepena siddhe “na, bhikkhave, ajjhokāse vassaṃ upagantabba”nti paṭikkhepo viya siyāti ce? Na, ajjhokāsassa asenāsanabhāvānumatippasaṅgato. Ajjhokāso hi “ajjhokāse palālapuñje”ti vacanato senāsananti siddhaṃ. Catusālaajjhokāse vasantopi “catusālāya vasatī”ti vuccati, tasmā tattha vaṭṭatīti āpajjati, tasmā idha asenāsaniko nāma attanā vā parena vā attano nibaddhavāsatthaṃ apāpitasenāsanikoti veditabbaṃ. Aññathā dvinnaṃ paṭikkhepānaṃ aññatarātirekatā ca rukkhamūlepi nibbakosepi vassaṃ upagantuṃ vaṭṭatīti ca, apāpitasenāsanikenāpi gabbhe vasituṃ vaṭṭatīti ca āpajjati, sadvārabandhameva senāsanaṃ idha adhippetanti kathaṃ paññāyatīti ce? Nidānato. Ayañhi asenāsanikavassūpagamanāpatti “tena kho pana samayena bhikkhū asenāsanikā vassaṃ upagacchanti, sītenapi uṇhenapi kilamantī”ti imasmiṃ nidāne paññattā, tasmā [M 0.0471] sītādipaṭikkhepameva idha senāsananti adhippetabbanti siddhaṃ. Evaṃ sante siddhaṃ pubbapakkhanidassananti ce? Na, pubbe aparatthapavattisūcanato. Dutiyajjhānaniddese “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti (dī. ni. 1.228; ma. ni. 1.271) vacanāni nidassanaṃ. Ajjhokāsapaṭikkhepanidānena bahiajjhokāsova paṭikkhitto, na catusālādimajjhagato ajjhokāsoti āpajjati, tasmā na nidānaṃ pamāṇanti ce? Na, niyamato. Kiñci hi sikkhāpadaṃ nidānāpekkhaṃ hotīti sādhitametaṃ. Idaṃ sāpekkhaṃ, idaṃ anapekkhanti kathaṃ paññāyati, na hi ettha ubhatovibhaṅge viya sikkhāpadānaṃ padabhājanaṃ, anāpattivāro vā atthīti? Idhāpi desanāvidhānato paññāyati. “Deve vassante rukkhamūlampi [V 0.0430] nibbakosampi upadhāvantī”ti hi imehi dvīhi nidānavacanehi bahi vā anto vā sabbaṃ ovassakaṭṭhānaṃ idha ajjhokāso nāma. Anovassakaṭṭhānampi anibbakosameva idha icchitabbanti siddhaṃ hoti. Tena na upagantabbanti na ālayakaraṇapaṭikkhepo, “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti vacanapaṭikkhepo. Chavasarīraṃ dahitvā chārikāya, aṭṭhikānañca atthāya kuṭikā karīyatīti andhakaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ. “Ṭaṅkitamañcoti kasikuṭikāpāsāṇaghara”nti likhitaṃ. “Akavāṭabaddhasenāsane attano pāpite sabhāgaṭṭhāne sakavāṭabaddhe vasati ce, vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Payogopi atthi, “asenāsanikena vassaṃ na upagantabba”nti pāḷi ca aṭṭhakathā ca, tasmā upaparikkhitabbaṃ.

Here, by the statement, “Having made a hut with a roof of planks, one should undertake the Rains Retreat,” it is established that it is permissible to climb a tree for the purpose of a lodging. If it is said, “This is not established because it contradicts the Pāli,” this is not so, for it is established by that very prohibition, and because of the prohibition for this one here again. If it is said that when it is established by the prohibition, “Monks, one who is without lodging should not undertake the Rains Retreat,” it would be like the prohibition, “Monks, one should not undertake the Rains Retreat in the open air,” this is not so, because it would lead to the implication that the open air is not a lodging. For the open air is established as a lodging by the statement, “in the open air, on a heap of straw.” Even one dwelling in a four-gabled open space is said to be “dwelling in a four-gabled hall”; therefore, it would follow that it is permissible there. Therefore, here, “one without lodging” should be understood as one for whom a lodging has not been secured for one's fixed dwelling, either by oneself or by another. Otherwise, one of the two prohibitions would be redundant, and it would also follow that it would be permissible to undertake the Rains Retreat even at the foot of a tree or in a place where water drips, and that one for whom a lodging has not been secured could dwell in a room. If it is said, “How then is it understood that only a lodging with a door-fastening is intended here?” From the origin story. For this offense of undertaking the Rains Retreat without lodging was laid down in this origin story: “At that time, monks without lodgings undertook the Rains Retreat and suffered from cold and heat.” Therefore, it is established that here, a lodging is intended as a shelter from cold and the like. This being so, if it is said that the presentation of the initial view is established, this is not so, because it indicates what follows later elsewhere. In the description of the second jhāna, the words, “with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought…” (Dīgha Nikāya 1.228; Majjhima Nikāya 1.271) serve as an example. By the origin story of the prohibition against the open air, only the external open air is prohibited, and it would follow that the open air within a four-gabled hall or the like is not prohibited. Therefore, if it is said that the origin story is not the standard, this is not so, because it is definitive. For it is established that some training rules depend on the origin story. How is it discerned whether “This one is dependent” or “This one is not dependent”? For here, unlike in the two Vibhaṅgas, there is no word-analysis of the training rules, nor is there a section on non-offenses. Here too, it is discerned from the method of teaching. For by these two statements from the origin story—“When it rains, they run to the foot of a tree or to a place where water drips”—every place exposed to rain, whether outside or inside, is here called “open air.” It is established that here, a place not exposed to rain is intended to be only a place where water does not drip. Therefore, “one should not undertake” is not a prohibition against making a dwelling, but a prohibition against the statement, “I will undertake the Rains Retreat here.” The Andhakaṭṭhakathā states: “Having burned a corpse, a small building is made for the ashes and for the bones.” It is written: “A ṭaṅkitamañca means a grass hut or a stone house.” It is said: “When a lodging without a door-fastening has been secured for oneself, if one dwells in a shared place that is secured with a door-fastening, it is permissible.” There is also a practical application: “One without a lodging should not undertake the Rains Retreat”—both the Pāli and the commentary state this, so it should be examined.

Adhammikakatikādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Unrighteous Rules, and so forth.

205. Mahāvibhaṅge vuttanti ettha ayaṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ ūnapannarasavassena sāmaṇerena idha vihāre na vatthabbā, na paṃsukūlaṃ āhiṇḍitabbaṃ, na coḷabhikkhā gahetabbā, na aññavihāre bhuñjitabbaṃ, na aññassa bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā santakaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ, aññamaññaṃ neva ālapeyyāma na sallapeyyāma, na sajjhāyitabbaṃ, mattikāpattena vaṭṭati, na aparipuṇṇaparikkhārassa vāsoti.

205. As for “stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga,” herein this is a saying from the Andhakaṭṭhakathā: A novice under fifteen years of age should not stay in this monastery; should not wander about for rag-robes; should not accept cloth for robes; should not eat in another monastery; should not make use of what belongs to another monk or nun; they should not address one another nor converse with one another; should not recite. An earthen bowl is allowable. There is no dwelling for one with incomplete requisites.

206. Musāvādoti visaṃvādo adhippeto. Keci “visaṃvādanavasena paṭissuṇitvāti vutta”nti ca, “rañño vuttavacanānurūpato musāvādoti gahaṭṭhā gaṇhantīti vutta”nti ca vadanti.

206. By musāvāda, deception is intended. Some say that it is stated, “Having promised with the intention to deceive,” and also that it is stated, “Householders understand it as musāvāda in accordance with the word spoken by the king.”

207. “Purimikā [M 0.0472] ca na paññāyati. Kasmā? ‘Dutiye vasāmī’ti citte uppanne paṭhamasenāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati. Puna ‘paṭhame eva vasāmī’ti citte uppanne dutiyo paṭippassambhati. Ubhayāvāse vidhānaṃ natthī”ti likhitaṃ. Porāṇagaṇṭhipade pana “paṭhamaṃ gahitaṭṭhāne avasitvā aññasmiṃ vihāre senāsanaṃ gahetvā dvīhatīhaṃ vasati, tato paṭhamaggāho paṭippassambhatīti purimikā ca na paññāyati. Pacchimaggāho na paṭippassambhati. Idañhi divasavasena paṭippassambhanaṃ nāma hoti. Atha pacchimaṃ temāsaṃ aññasmiṃ vasati, purimikā ca na paññāyati, idaṃ senāsanaggāhānaṃ vasena paṭippassambhanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Ubhopete atthavikappā idha nādhippetā. Yatthāyaṃ paṭissuto, tattha purimikā ca na paññāyati, paṭissave ca āpatti dukkaṭassa. Kattha pana purimikā paññāyatīti? Antarāmagge dvīsu āvāsesu yattha [V 0.0431] tadaheva pacchimaggāho, tattha paṭhamaṃ gahitaṭṭhāne sattāhakaraṇīyena gacchato na vassacchedo, so tadaheva akaraṇīyo pakkamatītiādimhi “karaṇīyaṃ nāma sattāhakaraṇīya”nti likhitaṃ.

207. “And the former is not apparent. Why? When the thought, ‘I will reside in the second,’ arises, the first taking of a lodging is pacified. Again, when the thought, ‘I will reside in the first itself,’ arises, the second is pacified. ‘There is no provision for both residences,’ thus it is written. However, in the ancient textual gloss it is said: ‘Having not resided in the place first taken, and having taken a lodging in another monastery, one resides for two or three days; because of that, the first taking is pacified, and the former is not apparent. The later taking is not pacified. For this is called pacification by way of days. Or, if one resides in another for the latter three-month period, the former is not apparent; this is called pacification by way of the takings of lodgings,’ thus it is stated. Both these alternative meanings are not intended here. Wherein this has been promised, there the former is not apparent, and for the promise, there is an offense of wrong-doing. But where is the former apparent? On the road between two residences, wherein the later taking is on that very day, there is no break in the rains-residence for one going to the first taken place for a seven-day business. In the text beginning, ‘if one departs on that very day without business,’ it is written: ‘Business means a seven-day business.’”

Pāḷimuttakaratticchedavinicchaye “dhammassavanādī”ti vuttaṃ. Ādimhi catūsu vāresu nirapekkhapakkamanassādhippetattā “sattāhakaraṇīyenā”ti na vuttaṃ tasmiṃ sati nirapekkhagamanābhāvato. Tattha purimā dve vārā vassaṃ anupagatassa vasena vuttā, tasmā upagatassa tadaheva sattāhakaraṇīyena gantvā antosattāhaṃ āgacchato na vassacchedoti siddhaṃ. Pacchimā dve vārā upagatassa nirapekkhagamanavasena vuttā, “sattāhaṃ anāgatāya pavāraṇāya sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti tato bahiddhā sattāhaṃ vītināmentassa vassacchedoti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha “akaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti vacanābhāvā vinā ratticchedakāraṇena gantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ. Pavāretvā pana gantuṃ vaṭṭati pavāraṇāya taṃdivasasannissitattā. Tattha na vā āgaccheyyāti antarāyena. Ācariyo pana “na puna idhāgacchāmī’ti nirapekkhopi sakaraṇīyova gantuṃ labhatīti dassanatthaṃ akaraṇīyo’ti na vutta”nti vadati. “Sīhaḷadīpe kira cūḷapavāraṇā nāma atthi, taṃ pavāraṇaṃ katvā yathāsukhaṃ sakaraṇīyā gacchanti, payogañca dassentī”ti vuttaṃ. “Tattha cha aruṇā antovasse honti[M 0.0473], eko bahi, tasmā so temāsaṃ vuttho hotīti apare”ti ca, “ācariyo evaṃ na vadatī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Sabbattha vihāraṃ upetīti attano vassaggena pattagabbhaṃ upetīti porāṇā. Asatiyā pana vassaṃ na upetīti ettha “imasmiṃ vihāre imaṃ temāsa”nti avacanena. “Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaratticchedakāraṇaṃ vinā tirovihāre vasitvā āgacchissāmīti gacchatopi vassaccheda”nti likhitaṃ.

In the determination of the breaking of the night outside the Pāḷi, it is said, “through hearing the Dhamma, etc.” In the beginning, in the four cases, because a departure without attachment is intended, it is not said, “with a seven-day duty,” since when that is present, there is no departure without attachment. Therein, the first two cases are stated for one who has not entered the Rains-residence; therefore, for one who has entered, who goes on that very day with a seven-day duty and returns within seven days, it is established that there is no breaking of the Rains-residence. The latter two cases are stated for one who has entered, with reference to a departure without attachment; it is said, “he departs with a duty when the Pavāraṇā is less than seven days away,” in order to show that for one who spends seven days outside of that, there is a breaking of the Rains-residence. Therein, because there is no statement, “he departs without a duty,” it is established that it is not proper to go without a reason for breaking the night. However, it is proper to go after having performed the Pavāraṇā, because of its dependence on that day of the Pavāraṇā. Therein, “or he might not return” means due to an obstacle. The teacher, however, says: “In order to show that even one who is without attachment, thinking, ‘I will not come here again,’ is indeed permitted to go with a duty, it was not said, ‘without a duty.’” It is said: “In the island of Sri Lanka, it seems, there is what is called the Lesser Pavāraṇā. Having performed that Pavāraṇā, those with a duty go as they please, and they show the procedure.” And it is said: “Therein, six dawns are within the Rains-residence, one is outside; therefore, he has resided for three months,” say others. And it is said: “The teacher does not speak thus.” In all cases, “he approaches the monastery” means he approaches the cell obtained according to his seniority in the Rains, say the ancients. However, regarding “in the absence of mindfulness, he does not enter the Rains-residence,” this is by not saying, “in this monastery for this three-month period.” It is written: “Even for one who goes intending, ‘I will stay in another monastery and return,’ without a reason for breaking the night as stated in the commentary, there is a breaking of the Rains-residence.”

208. Paṭissuto hoti pacchimikāyāti antarā pabbajitabhikkhunā, chinnavassena vā paṭissuto, aññena pana purimaṃ anupagantvā pacchimikāyaṃ paṭissavo na kātabbo. Ratticchede sabbattha vassacchedoti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā vadanti. Keci pana na icchanti. Taṃ sādhetuṃ anekadhā papañcenti. Kiṃ tena.

208. In the phrase, “He is promised for the later rains-residence,” this means having been promised by a monk ordained in the interim, or by one whose rains-residence has been broken. However, for some other reason, without having entered the earlier rains-residence, a promise for the later rains-residence should not be made. When there is a breaking of the night, in all cases, they make the conclusion and say, “It is a breaking of the rains-residence.” But some do not accept this. To prove that, they elaborate in many ways. What is the use of that?

Vassūpanāyikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Taking up the Rains-residence is finished.

4. Pavāraṇākkhandhakavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Chapter

Aphāsukavihārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on Uncomfortable Dwellings

210. “Saṅghaṃ [V 0.0432][M 0.0474] āvuso pavāremī”ti vuttattā pacchāpi “vadatu maṃ saṅgho”ti vattabbaṃ viya dissati. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yasmā ahaṃ saṅghaṃ pavāremi, tasmā tattha pariyāpannā therā, majjhimā, navā vā avisesenāyasmanto sabbepi maṃ vadantūti.

210. Because it is said, “Friends, I invite the Saṅgha,” it appears as if “Let the Saṅgha speak to me” should also be said afterwards. This is the intention here: Because I invite the Saṅgha, therefore, let all the venerable ones included therein—whether elders, of middle standing, or new—without distinction, speak to me.

Pavāraṇābhedavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Divisions of Pavāraṇā

212. Dvemā, bhikkhave, pavāraṇāti ettha tādise kicce sati yattha katthaci pavāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Teneva mahāvihāre bhikkhū cātuddasiyaṃ pavāretvā pannarasiyaṃ kāyasāmaggiṃ idānipi denti. Cetiyagiri mahādassanatthampi aṭṭhamiyaṃ gacchanti, tampi cātuddasiyaṃ pavāretukāmānaṃyeva hoti. “Sattāhaṃ anāgatāya pavāraṇāya sakaraṇīyo pakkamati, anāpattīti vacanato idaṃ āciṇṇa”nti likhitaṃ. “No ce adhiṭṭhaheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti ekassa vuttadukkaṭaṃ, tasseva vuttaṃ pubbakiccañca saṅghagaṇānampi netabbaṃ.

212. In the phrase, “Monks, there are these two Pavāraṇās,” when such a duty exists, it is proper to perform Pavāraṇā in any place whatsoever. For this very reason, even now, the monks at the Mahāvihāra, having performed Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day, establish bodily concord on the fifteenth day. They also go to Cetiyagiri on the eighth day for the purpose of the great sight. That too is only for those who wish to perform Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day. It is written: “Because of the saying, ‘If one with business to attend to departs when the Pavāraṇā is seven days away, there is no offense,’ this has become customary.” In the phrase, “If one should not determine, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” the wrong-doing spoken of is for a single individual; and the prior duty spoken of for that same one should also be applied to the Saṅgha and to groups.

Pavāraṇādānānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Authorization of Giving the Pavāraṇā

213. Tena ca bhikkhunāti pavāraṇādāyakena.

213. “And by that monk” means by the one who gives the Pavāraṇā.

Anāpattipannarasakādikathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Fifteen Grounds for No Offense and Others

“Tassā [V 0.0433] ca pavāraṇāya ārocitāya saṅghena ca pavārite sabbesaṃ suppavāritaṃ hotīti vacanato kevalaṃ pavāraṇāya pavāraṇādāyakopi pavāritova hotī”ti vadantīti.

They say: “Because of the statement, ‘When that Pavāraṇā has been announced and the Saṅgha has performed Pavāraṇā, it is well-performed for all,’ merely by the Pavāraṇā, even the one who gives the Pavāraṇā is indeed one who has performed it.”

222. Avuṭṭhitāya parisāyāti pavāretvā pacchā aññamaññaṃ kathentiyā. Ekaccāya vuṭṭhitāyāti ekaccesu yathānisinnesu ekaccesu sakasakaṭṭhānaṃ gatesu. Puna pavāretabbanti punapi sabbehi samāgantvā [M 0.0475] pavāretabbaṃ. Āgacchanti samasamā, tesaṃ santike pavāretabbanti “gate anānetvā nisinnānaṃyeva santike pavāretabbaṃ, uposathakkhandhakepi eseva nayo”ti likhitaṃ. Sabbāya vuṭṭhitāya parisāya āgacchanti samasamā, tesaṃ santike pavāretabbanti “yadi sabbe vuṭṭhahitvā gatā, sannipātetuñca na sakkā, ekacce sannipātāpetvā pavāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Kasmā? Ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā kattabbasaṅghakammābhāvā vaggaṃ na hoti kira. Ettha pana ekaccesu gatesupi sabbesu gatesupi sabbe sannipātāpetvā ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvā kevalaṃ pavāretabbaṃ. Ekacce sannipātāpetvā pavāretuṃ na vaṭṭati “saṅghaṃ, bhante, pavāremī”ti vacanato. Sabbepi hi sannipatitā pacchā diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā parisaṅkitaṃ vā vattāro honti. Anāgatānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ ñatvāpi ekaccānaṃ santike pavāraṇāvacanaṃ viya hoti. Sammukhībhūte cattāro sannipātāpetvā nissaggiyaṃ āpannacīvarādinissajjanaṃ viya pavāraṇā na hoti sabbāyattattā. “Samaggānaṃ pavāraṇā paññattā”ti vacanañcettha sādhakaṃ. “Ito aññathā na vaṭṭati aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ananuññātattā”ti upatissatthero vadati. “Thokatarehi tesaṃ santike pavāretabbaṃ ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvāvā”ti vuttaṃ. Āgantukā nāma navamito paṭṭhāyāgatā vā vajasatthanāvāsu vutthavassā vā honti.

222. “In an assembly that has not risen” means an assembly conversing with one another after having performed the Pavāraṇā. “In an assembly where some have risen” means while some monks remain seated as they were, others have gone to their respective places. “They should perform the Pavāraṇā again” means that all should gather together again and perform the Pavāraṇā. Regarding “They come together equally, and the Pavāraṇā should be performed in their presence,” it is written: “Without bringing back those who have left, the Pavāraṇā should be performed only in the presence of those who are seated; this is the same principle in the Uposathakkhandhaka as well.” Regarding “If the entire assembly has risen and they come together equally, the Pavāraṇā should be performed in their presence,” they say: “If all have risen and left, and it is not possible to gather them, it is permissible to have some gather and perform the Pavāraṇā.” Why? Because there is no formal act of the Saṅgha to be done by presenting a motion, it is said that an incomplete group does not occur. Here, however, whether some have left or all have left, all should be made to gather, and without presenting a motion, merely the Pavāraṇā should be performed. It is not permissible to have some gather and perform the Pavāraṇā, because of the statement, “Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha.” For, when all are gathered, they are afterwards able to speak of what has been seen, or heard, or suspected. Even knowing of the existence of those who have not come, it would be like the word of Pavāraṇā in the presence of only some. The Pavāraṇā is not like the relinquishment of a robe, etc., that has become subject to forfeiture, which is done by having four monks who are present gather, because it is dependent on all. And the statement, “The Pavāraṇā is prescribed for those in harmony,” is the proof here. The Elder Upatissa says, “Otherwise than this is not permissible, because it is not allowed in the commentary.” It is said: “The Pavāraṇā should be performed in their presence by a smaller number, or without presenting a motion.” “Newcomers” are those who have arrived from the ninth day onwards, or those who have spent the rains-residence in cattle-pens, caravans, or boats.

237. “Dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi hoti tathāgatotiādī”ti likhitaṃ. “Natthi dinnantiādī”ti vuttaṃ.

237. It is written: “The ten-fold wrong view is that which begins with ‘Tathāgata,’ and so on.” It is said: “There is nothing given, and so on.”

239. “Upaparikkhitvā jānissāmāti tena saha pavāretabba”nti likhitaṃ.

239. It is written: “Having investigated, we will know”; therefore, one should perform Pavāraṇā with him.

Pavāraṇākkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Section is concluded.

5. Cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Leather Section

Soṇakoḷivisavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story Concerning Soṇa Koḷivisa

242. Asītiyā [M 0.0476][V 0.0434] …pe… kāretīti “asīti gāmikasahassāni sannipātāpetvā”ti imassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tattha “gāmānaṃ asītiyā sahassesū”ti vattabbe “asītiyā gāmasahassesū”ti vuttaṃ. Gāmappamukhā gāmikā, tesaṃ sahassāni. “Kammacittīkatānī”ti upacārena vuttaṃ. Kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāne hi tesaṃ añjanavaṇṇabhāvo. “Kenacideva karaṇīyenā”ti vattabbe “kenacidevā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha evaṃ-saddo opamme pavattati. Evamupamānopadesapucchāvadhāraṇapaṭiññātaopamme. Purato pekkhamānānanti anādaratthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tato pana bhagavato gandhakuṭiyā kavāṭaṃ subaddhaṃ passitvā icchitākārakusalatāya iddhiyā gantvā kuṭiṃ pavisitvā ārocesi. Vihārapacchāyāyanti vihārassa vaḍḍhamānacchāyāyaṃ. “Aho nūnāti aho mahanto”ti likhitaṃ. Bhagavato sambahulehi saddhiṃ āhiṇḍanaṃ āyasmato soṇassa vīriyārambhanidassanena anāraddhavīriyānaṃ uttejanatthaṃ, evaṃ sukhumālānaṃ pādarakkhaṇatthaṃ upāhanā anuññātāti dassanatthañca.

242. The phrase ‘Asītiyā…pe… kāretī’ is a statement of reason for the text ‘asīti gāmikasahassāni sannipātāpetvā’ (having caused eighty thousand village headmen to assemble). Therein, when it should have been said ‘gāmānaṃ asītiyā sahassesū’ (among eighty thousand villages), it was said ‘asītiyā gāmasahassesū’ (among eighty village-thousands). The village headmen are the village chiefs; their thousands are meant. The phrase ‘Kammacittīkatāni’ (made variegated by kamma) is spoken figuratively. For their color like dark collyrium arises in a place conditioned by kamma and season. When it should have been said ‘kenacideva karaṇīyena’ (for some reason or other), it was said ‘kenacideva’. Here, the word ‘evaṃ’ occurs in the sense of a simile. ‘Evaṃ’ occurs in the senses of simile, instruction, questioning, restriction, agreement, and comparison. The phrase ‘Purato pekkhamānānaṃ’ (of those looking ahead) is a genitive case in the sense of disrespect. Then, seeing the door-leaf of the Blessed One’s fragrant hut well-secured, due to his skill in the desired manner, he went by psychic power, entered the hut, and informed him. ‘Vihārapacchāyāyaṃ’ (in the shade of the monastery) means in the growing shade of the monastery. It is written: ‘Aho nūna’ means ‘aho mahanto’ (oh, great!). The Blessed One’s wandering together with many monks was for the purpose of inciting those who had not undertaken energy by showing the Venerable Soṇa’s undertaking of energy, and also for the purpose of showing that footwear was permitted for protecting the feet of the delicate.

Soṇassapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Soṇa's Going Forth

243. Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti tesaṃ indriyānaṃ ākāraṃ upalakkhehi.

243. And there, 'take the sign' means to mark the characteristic of their faculties.

244. Adhimutto hotīti paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā ṭhito hoti. Nekkhammādhimuttotiādīhi nibbānaṃ, arahattañca vuttaṃ. “Tañhi sabbakilesehi nikkhantattā ‘nekkhamma’nti ca gehato pavivittattā ‘paviveko’ti ca byāpajjābhāvato ‘abyāpajja’nti ca arahattaṃ upādānassa khayante uppannattā ‘upādānakkhayo’ti ca taṇhāya khayante uppannattā ‘taṇhakkhayo’ti [V 0.0435] ca sammohābhāvato ‘asammoho’ti ca vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbehi arahattaṃ vuttanti keci. Siyā kho evamassāti kadāci evamassa, assa vā āyasmato evaṃ siyā. Paccāgacchanto jānanto. Karaṇīyamattānanti attano. So eva vā [M 0.0477] pāṭho. Nekkhammādhimuttoti imasmiṃyeva arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Sesesu nibbānanti keci. Asammohādhimuttoti ettheva nibbānaṃ. Sesesu arahattanti keci. “Sabbesvevetesu ubhayampī”ti vadanti. Pavivekañca cetaso, adhimuttassa, upādānakkhayassa cāti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ uppādañca vayañca disvā.

244. “He is resolute” means he stands having penetrated and directly experienced. By “resolute in renunciation” and so on, Nibbāna and Arahantship are spoken of. For it is said: “It is called 'renunciation' because it has departed from all defilements; 'seclusion' because it is secluded from the household; 'non-ill will' because of the absence of malice. And Arahantship is called 'the destruction of clinging' because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging; 'the destruction of craving' because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving; and 'non-delusion' because of the absence of delusion.” Some say that Arahantship is spoken of by all these terms. “Perhaps it might be so” means sometimes it might be so, or it might be so for that venerable one. “Returning, knowing.” “Karaṇīyamattānaṃ” means “of oneself.” Or that itself is the reading. Some say that in this very term “resolute in renunciation,” Arahantship is spoken of, and in the remaining terms, Nibbāna is spoken of. Some say that right here in “resolute in non-delusion,” Nibbāna is spoken of, and in the remaining terms, Arahantship is spoken of. Others say, “In all these very terms, both are spoken of.” Regarding “pavivekañca cetaso, adhimuttassa, upādānakkhayassa ca,” the genitive case is in the sense of application. “Having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases.”

Sabbanīlikādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Rejection of All Things Blue, etc.

246. “Rañjanacoḷakena puñchitvā”ti pāṭho. “Khallakādīni apanetvā’ti vuttattā dve tīṇi chiddāni katvā vaḷañjetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadantānaṃ vādo na gahetabbo.

246. “Having wiped with a dyed cloth” is a reading. Because it is said, “Having removed the khallaka and other things,” the argument of those who say, “It is allowable to use it after making two or three holes,” should not be accepted.

Yānādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Rejection of Vehicles, etc.

254. “Caturaṅgulādhikānī”ti vuttattā caturaṅgulato heṭṭhā vaṭṭatīti eke. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānanti ettha “kāsāvaṃ pana vaṭṭati, kusumbhādirattameva na vaṭṭatī”ti likhitaṃ.

254. Because it was said, “more than four finger-breadths,” some say it is allowable if it is less than four finger-breadths. In the context of “a pillow red on both sides,” it is written: “But an ochre-colored one is allowable; only that which is dyed with safflower and so on is not allowable.”

Sabbacammapaṭikkhepādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Rejection of All Leather, etc.

255. Kissa tyāyanti kissa te ayaṃ.

255. For the phrase “kissa tyāyanti,” the word division should be made as “kissa te ayaṃ.”

256. Gihivikatanti gihīnaṃ atthāya kataṃ. “Yattha katthaci nisīdituṃ anujānāmīti attho”ti likhitaṃ. Kiñcāpi dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ, atha kho vinayapariyāyaṃ patvā garuke ṭhātabbato idha vuttanayenevettha attho gahetabbo. “Tattha pana suttantikadesanāya gahaṭṭhādīnampi vasena vuttattā tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ ṭhapetvā ‘tūlikaṃ…pe… vaṭṭantī’ti vuttaṃ viya khāyatīti apare”ti vuttaṃ.

256. Regarding 'gihivikata': it means made for the benefit of householders. It is written, "It means 'I allow sitting anywhere.'" Although in the commentary to the Dīghanikāya it is said, "Except for a cotton-filled mattress, all items such as gonaka cloths adorned with jewels are permissible," nevertheless, having come to the Vinaya discourse, because it must be established in a weighty matter, the meaning here should be taken only in accordance with the method stated here. It is also said: "However, some say it appears as if it was said there in the Suttanta teaching by way of householders and so on in order to include them, thus: 'Except for a cotton-filled mattress... are permissible.'"

259. Migamātukoti tassa nāmaṃ. Vātamigoti ca tassa nāmaṃ. “Kāḷasīho kāḷamukho [V 0.0436] kapī”ti likhitaṃ. Cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti yena pariyāyena cammaṃ vaṭṭissati, so parato āvi bhavissati. “Attano puggalikavasena [M 0.0478] parihāro paṭikkhitto”ti vuttaṃ. “Na, bhikkhave, kiñci cammaṃ dhāretabba”nti ettāvatā siddhe “na, bhikkhave, gocamma”nti idaṃ parato “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbapaccantimesu janapadesu cammāni attharaṇānī”ti ettha anumatippasaṅgabhayā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

259. "Migamātuka" is its name. "Vātamiga" is also its name. It is written: "A kāḷasīha is a black-faced monkey." As for the statement "Leather is not allowed," the way in which leather will become allowable will become evident later. It is said: "Use as a personal possession is prohibited." Since it was already established by "No leather whatsoever should be used, bhikkhus," it should be understood that this statement, "No, bhikkhus, cowhide," was said out of fear of implying permission in the later statement, "I allow, bhikkhus, in all border regions, leather coverings."

Cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Leather Khandhaka is concluded.

6. Bhesajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Khandhaka on Medicines

Pañcabhesajjādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Five Medicines, etc.

260. “Yaṃ [M 0.0479][V 0.0437] bhesajjañceva assā”ti parato “tadubhayena bhiyyoso mattāya kissā hontī”tiādinā virodhadassanato nidānānapekkhaṃ yathālābhavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yathānidānaṃ kasmā na vuttanti ce? Tadaññāpekkhādhippāyato. Sabbabuddhakālepi hi sappiādīnaṃ sattāhakālikabhāvāpekkhāti tathā vacanena bhagavato adhippāyo, teneva “āhāratthañca phareyya, na ca oḷāriko āhāro paññāyeyyā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjitunti ettha ca kālaparicchedo na kato. Kutoyeva pana labbhā tadaññāpekkhādhippāyo bhagavato mūlabhesajjādīni tāni paṭiggahetvā yāvajīvanti kālaparicchedo. Yaṃ pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tāni pañca bhesajjāni kāle paṭiggahetvā kāle paribhuñjitu”nti vacanaṃ, taṃ “sannidhiṃ katvā aparāparasmiṃ divase kāle eva paribhuñjituṃ anujānāmī”ti adhippāyato vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aññathā atisayattābhāvato “yaṃ bhesajjañceva assā”tiādi vitakkuppādo na sambhavati. Paṇītabhojanānumatiyā pasiddhattā ābādhānurūpasappāyāpekkhāya vuttānīti ce? Tañca na, bhiyyoso mattāya kisādibhāvāpattidassanato. Yathā “ucchurasaṃ upādāya phāṇita”nti vuttaṃ, tathā “navanītaṃ upādāya sappi”nti vattabbato navanītaṃ visuṃ na vattabbanti ce? Na, visesadassanādhippāyato. Yathā phāṇitaggahaṇena siddhepi parato ucchuraso visuṃ anuññāto ucchusāmaññato guḷodakaṭṭhāne ṭhapanādhippāyato. Tathā navanīte visesavidhidassanādhippāyato navanītaṃ visuṃ anuññātanti veditabbaṃ. Visesavidhi panassa bhesajjasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāvasena veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha “pacitvā sappiṃ katvā paribhuñjitukāmena adhotampi pacituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.622). Tattha sappi pakkāva hoti, nāpakkā. Tathā phāṇitampi. Navanītaṃ apakkameva.

260. It should be known that the statement was made without regard to a specific occasion, but according to what is available, because of the contradiction seen later in the words, 'By both of these, why are they excessively thin beyond measure?' If one asks, 'Why was it not stated according to the specific occasion?' It is because the intention was to consider other factors. For indeed, even in the time of all Buddhas, the nature of ghee and other such items as being allowable for seven days is considered; such is the Blessed One's intention in that statement. For that very reason, it was said, 'It should suffice for nourishment, and coarse food should not be apparent.' Indeed, in the phrase 'having accepted at the proper time, one may consume at the proper time,' no time-limit was specified. Given that the Blessed One's intention was to consider other factors, from where could the time-limit 'for as long as life lasts' possibly be obtained for those root-medicines and so on, once they have been accepted? As for the statement, 'I allow, monks, these five medicines to be accepted at the proper time and consumed at the proper time,' it should be known that this was said with the intention, 'Having stored them, I allow them to be consumed on subsequent days only at the proper time.' Otherwise, due to the absence of any special meaning, the arising of the thought, 'That which would be medicine...' would not be possible. If one were to say, 'They were stated in accordance with what is suitable for an illness, since this is established by the allowance for fine food'? That is not so, because it indicates the possibility of attaining a state of emaciation and so on from an excessive amount. If one were to say: 'Just as it was said, "Molasses, being derived from sugarcane juice," so too, because it should be said, "Ghee, being derived from fresh butter," fresh butter should not be stated separately'? This is not so, because of the intention to show a distinction. Just as sugarcane juice, though its inclusion is accomplished by the mention of molasses, was later permitted separately with the intention of placing it in the category of sugar-water in a general sense, so too, it should be known that fresh butter was permitted separately with the intention of showing a special procedure for it.

Etthāha [V 0.0438] – navanītaṃ viya ucchurasopi sattāhakālikapāḷiyaṃ eva vattabboti? Na vattabbo. Kasmā? Sattāhakālikapāḷiyaṃ vutte [M 0.0480] ucchuraso guḷāpadesena yathā agilānassa phāṇitaṃ paṭisiddhaṃ, tathā ucchurasopīti āpajjati, avutte pana guḷaṃ viya so phāṇitasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Idha avatvā pacchā vacanena guḷodakaṭṭhāneva ṭhapito hoti. Tadatthameva pacchābhattaṃ vaṭṭanakapānakādhikāre vutto, tasmā eva yāmakālikoti ce? Na, aṭṭhakathāvirodhato. Na upādāyatthassa nissayatthattāti ce? Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ucchurasaṃ upādāya ucchuvikati phāṇitanti veditabbā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) yadetaṃ nissaggiyaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ, tattha “upādāyā”ti imassa nissāya paccayaṃ katvāti atthoti. Na, parato aparakiriyāya adassanato. Yathā “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.204, 400; 3.421, 425; saṃ. ni. 2.43) “paṭiccā”ti imassa ussukkavacanassa “uppajjatī”ti aparakiriyā dissati, na tathā “ucchurasaṃ upādāyā”ti ettha aparakiriyā dissatīti. Ayuttametaṃ tattha tadabhāvepi siddhattā. Yathā “cattāro ca mahābhūtā catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya rūpa”nti (dha. sa. 584) ettha aparakiriyāya abhāvepi ussukkavacanaṃ siddhaṃ, tathā etthāpi siyāti? Na, tattha pāṭhasesāpekkhattā. Yathā cattāro mahābhūtā upādāya vuttaṃ, pavattakaṃ vā rūpanti imaṃ pāṭhasesaṃ sā pāḷi apekkhati, na tathā idaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ kañci pāṭhaṃ apekkhati. Paripuṇṇavādino hi aṭṭhakathācariyā. Saññākaraṇamattaṃ vā tassa rūpassa. “Atthi rūpaṃ upādāyā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 584) hi saññākaraṇamattaṃ, evamidhāpīti veditabbaṃ. Idha pana “ucchurasaṃ upādāyā”ti ucchurasaṃ ādiṃ katvā, tato paṭṭhāyāti attho, tasmā “ucchurasena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ agilāno bhikkhu viññāpetvā bhuñjanto paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadena kāretabbo, bhikkhunī pāṭidesaniyenā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ ayuttanti eke. Te visesahetuno abhāvaṃ dassetvā paññāpetabbā.

Here it is said: 'Like fresh butter, should sugarcane juice also be mentioned only in the text on seven-day allowances?' It should not be so stated. Why? If it were mentioned in the text on seven-day allowances, it would follow that, by implication of jaggery, just as molasses is prohibited for a monk who is not ill, so too would sugarcane juice be prohibited. But if it is not mentioned, like jaggery, it does not attain the designation of 'molasses'. Here, not having been mentioned, it is later, by a subsequent statement, placed in the category of jaggery-water. If it is said: 'For that very reason, it is mentioned in the section on allowable drinks after the meal; therefore, it is a yāmakālika item,' the reply is: No, because it contradicts the Commentary. If it is said: 'Is it not because the meaning of 'upādāya' is that of dependence?' What is meant? In this statement from the Nissaggiya Commentary, '“Having taken sugarcane juice as the basis, it should be known as phāṇita, a product of sugarcane,”' the meaning of this word 'upādāya' is 'having made it a condition, a dependence'. The reply is: No, because a subsequent action is not seen afterwards. Just as in 'dependent on the eye and forms,' etc., for this active term 'paṭicca', the subsequent action 'arises' is seen, it is not so here in 'based on sugarcane juice' that a subsequent action is seen. This is unsuitable, because there it is established even in the absence of that. If one were to ask: 'Just as here in “the four great elements, and form derived from the four great elements,” the active term is established even in the absence of a subsequent action, could it be so here as well?' The reply is: No, because there it is dependent on the remainder of the text. Just as that Pāḷi text depends on this remainder of the text—namely, 'form that is spoken of in dependence on the four great elements, or that proceeds from them'—this Commentary statement does not similarly depend on any text. For the Commentary masters are speakers of what is complete. Or, it is merely the making of a name for that form. For in 'There is form derived from…,' etc., it is merely the making of a name; so it should be understood here also. But here, in 'based on sugarcane juice,' the meaning is 'having made sugarcane juice the beginning, starting from that.' Therefore, it is said: 'A monk who is not ill, having requested and while eating food mixed with sugarcane juice, is to be dealt with according to the training rule on fine foods; a nun, according to the Pāṭidesaniya.' Some say this is unsuitable. They should be made to understand by showing the absence of a special reason.

Ettāvatā “ucchurasaṃ upādāyāti ucchurasaṃ ādiṃ katvā”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ micchā gahetvā yadi “ucchurasaṃ upādāyā”ti vacanena ucchuraso phāṇitaṃ siyā, “apakkā vā”ti vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ apakkavacanena ucchurasassa gahitattā. Atha “pakkā vā”ti vacanena ucchuraso phāṇitanti siddhaṃ, “ucchurasaṃ upādāyā”ti vacanaṃ niratthakanti uttaraṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ anuttaranti sādhitaṃ hoti. So cetehi apakkā vāti sāmaṃ bhikkhunā apakkā [M 0.0481] vā. Avatthukapakkā vāti bhikkhunāva sāmaṃ vinā vatthunā pakkā vāti attho. Tasmā aññathā “savatthukapakkā vā”ti ca vattabbanti attho dassito, so duṭṭhu dassito. Kasmā? Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “jhāmaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā koṭṭitaucchuphāṇitaṃ vā purebhattameva vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā, “savatthukapakkā vā”ti vacanassa ca laddhivirodhato avuttattā. “Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana ‘etaṃ savatthukapakkaṃ vaṭṭati no vaṭṭatī’ti [V 0.0439] pucchaṃ katvā ‘ucchuphāṇitaṃ pacchābhattaṃ no vaṭṭanakaṃ nāma natthī’ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yutta”nti (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.623) vuttattā ca savatthukapakkā vāti attho ca vuttoyeva hoti, tasmā duddassitoti siddhaṃ. Āhāratthanti āhārapayojanaṃ. Āhārakiccaṃ yāpananti atthoti ca.

By this much, the following is established: if one, having wrongly taken the meaning of phrases such as 'ucchurasaṃ upādāya' to be 'starting with sugarcane juice,' were to hold that by the statement 'ucchurasaṃ upādāya' sugarcane juice is molasses, then the statement 'or unboiled' would be meaningless, because sugarcane juice is included by the word 'unboiled.' Now, if by the statement 'or boiled' it is established that sugarcane juice is molasses, then the statement 'ucchurasaṃ upādāya' would be meaningless—this reply was given, but it is untenable. And this 'or unboiled' means unboiled by the bhikkhu himself. 'Or boiled without a substance' means boiled by the bhikkhu himself without a substance; this is the meaning. Therefore, the meaning that it should also be stated as 'or boiled with a substance' is shown, but it is poorly shown. Why? Because in the Mahāaṭṭhakathā it is stated, 'Molasses from burnt sugarcane or molasses from pounded sugarcane is allowable only before the meal,' and because the statement 'or boiled with a substance' is not stated, being contrary to the established view. And because in the Mahāpaccarī it is stated, 'Having posed the question, “Is this boiled with a substance allowable or not allowable?” it was said, “There is no such thing as sugarcane molasses that is not an allowable item after the meal,” and that is proper,' the meaning of 'or boiled with a substance' is indeed stated; therefore, it is established that this is poorly shown. 'Āhāratthaṃ' means for the purpose of food. And the meaning is that the function of food is sustenance.

262. Telaparibhogenāti sattāhakālikaparibhogena.

262. `Telaparibhogena` means by the use of a seven-day allowance.

263. Sati paccayeti ettha satipaccayatā gilānāgilānavasena dvidhā veditabbā. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadassa hi anāpattivāre yāmakālikādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi avisesena satipaccayatā vuttā. Imasmiṃ khandhake “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷaṃ, agilānassa guḷodakaṃ, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa loṇasovīrakaṃ, agilānassa udakasambhinna”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmā siddhaṃ satipaccayatā gilānāgilānavasena duvidhāti. Aññathā asati paccaye guḷodakādīsu āpajjati. Tato ca pāḷivirodho.

263. Here, in `sati paccaye` ('when there is a reason'), the state of having a reason should be understood as twofold, by way of being sick or not sick. For in the non-offense section of the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time, the state of having a reason is stated without distinction for all three kālikas, such as yāmakālika. In this Khandhaka, it is stated: 'I allow, Bhikkhus, molasses for the sick, and molasses-water for the not-sick; I allow, Bhikkhus, salt-sour gruel for the sick, and that mixed with water for the not-sick.' Therefore, it is established that the state of having a reason is twofold, by way of being sick or not sick. Otherwise, if there were no reason, one would incur an offense with regard to molasses-water and so forth. And from that, there would be a contradiction with the Pāḷi.

Piṭṭhehīti pisitatelehi. Koṭṭhaphalanti koṭṭharukkhassa phalaṃ. “Madanaphalaṃ vā”ti ca likhitaṃ. Hiṅgujatu nāma hiṅgurukkhassa daṇḍapallavapavāḷapākanipphannā. Hiṅgusipāṭikā nāma tassa mūlasākhapākanipphannā. Takaṃ nāma tassa rukkhassa tacapākodakaṃ. Takapattīti tassa pattapākodakaṃ. Takapaṇṇīti tassa phalapākodakaṃ. Atha vā “takaṃ nāma lākhā. Takapattīti kittimalomalākhā. Takapaṇṇīti pakkalākhā”ti likhitaṃ. Ubbhidaṃ nāma ūsapaṃsumayaṃ.

`Piṭṭhehi` means with pressed sesame oils. `Koṭṭhaphalaṃ` means the fruit of the koṭṭha tree. And it is also written: 'or madana fruit.' `Hiṅgujatu` is that which is produced from cooking the stems, young leaves, and shoots of the hiṅgu tree. `Hiṅgusipāṭikā` is that which is produced from cooking its roots and branches. `Takaṃ` is the decoction of that tree's bark. `Takapattī` is the decoction of its leaves. `Takapaṇṇī` is the decoction of its fruit. Alternatively, it is written: '`Takaṃ` is lac. `Takapattī` is kittimaloma-lac. `Takapaṇṇī` is cooked lac.' `Ubbhidaṃ` salt is that which is made from saline soil.

264. Chakaṇaṃ gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ nāma apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ, tena “ṭhapetvā gandhacuṇṇaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Cālitehīti parissāvitehi.

264. `Chakaṇaṃ` is salt made from cow dung. `Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ` means uncooked astringent powder; therefore, they say, 'Setting aside scented powder, all is allowable.' `Cālitehi` means with that which has been strained.

265. Nānāsambhārehi katanti nānosadhehi.

265. 'Made with various ingredients' means 'with various medicines'.

Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Allowance for Molasses and So Forth

274. Sāmaṃ [M 0.0482] pakkaṃ samapakkanti duvidhaṃ viya dīpeti, tasmā khīrādīsu uṇhamattameva pāko. Tena uttaṇḍulādisamānā honti.

274. `Sāmaṃ pakkaṃ` and `samapakkaṃ`—this indicates it as if twofold. Therefore, in the case of milk and so forth, mere heat itself is 'cooking'. For that reason, they become similar to rice with uncooked grains and so forth.

276-8. “Buddhappamukha’nti [V 0.0440] āgataṭṭhāne ‘bhikkhusaṅgho’ti avatvā ‘saṅgho’ti vuccati bhagavantampi saṅgahetu”nti vadanti. Nāgoti hatthī.

They say: 'In the place where `buddhappamukha` ("with the Buddha at its head") occurs, instead of saying `bhikkhusaṅgha` ("the community of bhikkhus"), the word `saṅgha` is used in order to include the Blessed One as well.' By `nāgo` is meant 'an elephant.'

279. Sambādheti vaccamagge bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā ca passāvamaggepi anulomato. Dahanaṃ paṭikkhepābhāvā vaṭṭati. Satthavattikammānulomato na vaṭṭatīti ce? Na, paṭikkhittapaṭikkhepā, paṭikkhipitabbassa tapparamatādīpanato, kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Pubbe paṭikkhittampi satthakammaṃ sampiṇḍetvā pacchā “na, bhikkhave…pe… thullaccayassā”ti dvikkhattuṃ satthakammassa paṭikkhepo kato. Tena sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulaṃ paṭikkhipitabbaṃ nāma. Satthavattikammato uddhaṃ natthīti dīpeti. Kiñca bhiyyo pubbe sambādheyeva satthakammaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ, pacchā sambādhassa sāmantā dvaṅgulampi paṭikkhittaṃ, tasmā tasseva paṭikkhepo, netarassāti siddhaṃ. Ettha “satthaṃ nāma satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā”tiādīsu viya yena chindati, taṃ sabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “kaṇṭakena vā”tiādi. Khāradānaṃ panettha bhikkhunivibhaṅge pasākhe lepamukhena anuññātanti veditabbaṃ. Eke pana “satthakammaṃ vā”ti pāṭhaṃ vikappetvā vatthikammaṃ karonti. “Vatthī”ti kira agghikā vuccati. Tāya chindanaṃ vatthikammaṃ nāmāti ca atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti, te “satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā”ti imassa padabhājanīyaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Aṇḍavuḍḍhīti vātaṇḍako. Ādānavattīti ānahavatti.

279. `Sambādheti` means 'it obstructs': in the passage for defecation of a monk and of a nun, and also, accordingly, in the passage for urination. Cauterization (`dahanaṃ`) is allowable due to the absence of a prohibition. If it is asked, 'Is a surgical operation not allowable accordingly?' That is not so; it is indeed allowable. Why? Because it prohibits only what should be prohibited, and because it indicates that what is to be prohibited has that as its limit. What is meant? Previously, having combined even the surgical operation that was prohibited, later the prohibition of surgical operation was made twice, saying, 'Monks... it entails a grave offense.' By that, what is called 'to be prohibited' is two finger-widths around the afflicted area. It indicates that there is nothing beyond the surgical operation. Furthermore, previously, the surgical operation was prohibited only in the afflicted area itself; later, two finger-widths around the afflicted area were also prohibited. Therefore, the prohibition is only for that area; there is no prohibition for what is beyond it. Thus, the meaning is established. Here, as in passages such as 'one should seek a knife-carrier for him,' 'knife' (`satthaṃ`) is any object with which one cuts. Therefore, it is said, 'or with a thorn,' etc. Here, however, the giving of caustic substances should be understood as being permitted in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga for a side-branch (`pasākhe`) by means of a paste. Some, however, having altered the reading 'or surgical operation,' perform an act of binding with cloth (`vatthikamma`). `Vatthī`, it is said, is called a coarse cloth (`agghikā`). And they explain the meaning that cutting with that coarse cloth is called `vatthikamma`. They are to be refuted by showing the word-analysis of the phrase 'one should seek a knife-carrier for him.' `Aṇḍavuḍḍhi` is hydrocele (`vātaṇḍako`). `Ādānavattī` is a suppository (`ānahavatti`).

Manussamaṃsapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Prohibition of Human Flesh

280. “Na, bhikkhave, manussamaṃsaṃ…pe… thullaccayassā”ti vuttattā, “na ca, bhikkhave, appaṭi…pe… dukkaṭassā”ti ca vuttattā appaṭivekkhaṇadukkaṭañca thullaccayañcāti dve āpajjati, tasmā kappiyamaṃsepi appaṭivekkhaṇapaccayā dukkaṭameva. Keci “maṃsabhāvaṃ jānantova āpajjati. Pūvādīsu ajānantassa kā paccavekkhaṇā”ti vadanti. Ajānantopi āpajjati sāmaññena vuttattāti keci.

280. Because it is said, 'Monks, human flesh... entails a grave offense,' and also because it is said, 'And monks, without reflecting... entails an offense of wrong-doing,' one incurs two offenses: an offense of wrong-doing for not reflecting and a grave offense. Therefore, even with permissible meat, due to the cause of not reflecting, an offense of wrong-doing is indeed incurred. Some say, 'One incurs an offense only when knowing it to be meat. In the case of cakes and so forth, what reflection is there for one who does not know?' Some say that even one who does not know incurs an offense, because it is stated generally.

Hatthimaṃsādipaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Prohibition of Elephant Flesh and So Forth

281. Imesaṃ [M 0.0483] …pe… sabbaṃ na vaṭṭatīti idaṃ dasannampi manussamaṃsādīnaṃ akappiyabhāvamattaparidīpanavacanaṃ, nāpattivibhāgadassanavacanaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci ñatvā vā añatvā vā khādantassa āpattiyevāti idampi aniyamitavacanameva “ayaṃ nāma āpattī”ti avuttattā[V 0.0441]. Tadubhayampi heṭṭhā manussādīnaṃ maṃsādīsu thullaccayadukkaṭāpattiyo hontīti gahitanayehi adhippāyo jānituṃ sakkāti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yasmā etesaṃ manussādīnaṃ maṃsādīni akappiyāni, tasmā manussānaṃ maṃsādīsu thullaccayāpatti. Sesānaṃ sabbattha dukkaṭāpattīti. Pāṭheyeva hi lohitādiṃ maṃsagatikaṃ katvā “na, bhikkhave, manussamaṃsaṃ…pe… thullaccayassā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattheva hatthādīnaṃ maṃsādīsupi dukkaṭāpatti paññattā. Tena vuttaṃ sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “manussamaṃse vā kese vā nakhe vā aṭṭhimhi vā lohite vā thullaccayamevā”ti vuttaṃ. Iminā eva –

281. This statement, 'Among these... all are not permissible,' is a statement that merely clarifies the state of being impermissible for the ten kinds of human flesh and so forth; it is not a statement that shows the classification of offenses. This statement also, 'For one who eats anything, whether knowing or not knowing, there is indeed an offense,' is merely an indefinite statement, because it is not said, 'This is such-and-such an offense.' The meaning of both these can be known by the principles established below, namely that for the flesh, etc., of humans, etc., there are grave offenses and offenses of wrong-doing; therefore, it is said thus. Therein, this is the meaning: because the flesh, etc., of these humans, etc., are impermissible, therefore, for the flesh, etc., of humans, there is a grave offense. For the rest, in all cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Indeed, in the text itself, having treated blood, etc., as being of the same nature as flesh, it is said, 'Monks, human flesh... entails a grave offense.' In that very text, an offense of wrong-doing is also prescribed for the flesh, etc., of elephants, etc. Therefore, it is said in the Sinhalese commentary: 'For human flesh, or hair, or nails, or bone, or blood, there is indeed a grave offense.' By this very...

“Aṭṭhipi lohitaṃ cammaṃ, lomamesaṃ na kappatī”ti. –

'Of these beings, bone also, blood, skin, and hair are not permissible.'

Khuddasikkhāgāthāpadassa attho ca adhippāyo ca suviññeyyoti. Paṭiggahaṇeti ettha anādariyadukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ. “Udakamanussādimaṃsampi na vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Nāgarājena vuttādīnave satipi ujjhāyanādhikārameva gahetvā “paṭikūlatāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

...the meaning and the intention of the verse of the Khuddasikkhā are easily understood. Here, regarding 'acceptance,' an offense of wrong-doing due to disrespect is stated. Some say, 'The flesh of water-humans and so forth is also not permissible.' Although there is the danger spoken of by the Nāga king, having taken only the grounds for complaint, it is stated, 'due to repulsiveness.'

Yāgumadhugoḷakādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse concerning Gruel, Honey Balls, and So Forth

283. Yathādhammo kāretabboti idaṃ saṅgītikārakavacanaṃ. Na hi bhagavā tameva sikkhāpadaṃ dvikkhattuṃ paññapesi, evaṃ evarūpesūti eke. Paṭhamapaññattameva sandhāya vuttaṃ, tathāpi na ca te bhikkhū sāpattikā jātā. Kathaṃ? Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadassa aṭṭhuppattiyā. “Apica mayaṃ kālasseva piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjimhā”ti vuttaṃ. Mātikāvibhaṅge (pāci. 227) ca “paramparabhojanaṃ nāma pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena bhojanena nimantito, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, etaṃ paramparabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā aññaṃ bhojanaṃ nāma nimantanato laddhaṃ yaṃ kiñcīti siddhaṃ. Yasmā na bhojjayāgunimantanato laddhabhojanaṃ, tasmā [M 0.0484] “ettha anāpattī”ti te bhikkhū paribhuñjiṃsūti. Ettha “yathādhammo kāretabbo”ti vuttattā pana aññanimantanato laddhabhojanameva bhuñjantassa āpatti, netaranti anuññātaṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya tassa anāpattivāre “niccabhatte salākabhatte pakkhike uposathike pāṭipadike”ti vuttaṃ. Pubbe vesāliyā paññattakāle natthi, yadi atthi, aṭṭhuppattimātikāvibhaṅgavirodho, tasmā “apica mayaṃ kālasseva piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjimhā”ti aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ vuttattā, padabhājanepi “aññaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññataraṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjatī”ti avisesena vuttattā ca paṭhamaṃ vā pacchā vā nimantitaṃ bhojanaṃ ṭhapetvā animantitameva [V 0.0442] bhuñjantassa āpatti, netaranti kiñcāpi āpannaṃ, “na, bhikkhave, aññatra nimantitena aññassa bhojjayāgu paribhuñjitabbā”ti vuttattā pana paṭhamanimantitabhojanato aññaṃ pacchā laddhaṃ nimantitabhojanaṃ, niccabhattādīni ca bhuñjantassa āpattīti āpajjamānaṃ viya jātanti anupaññattippasaṅganivāraṇaṃ, animantanabhojane āpattippasaṅganivāraṇañca karonto, paṭhamapaññattisikkhāpadameva iminā atthena pariṇāmento ca “yathādhammo kāretabbo”ti bhagavā āha, tasmā tato paṭṭhāya pacchā nimantanabhojanaṃ bhuñjantasseva āpatti. Tesu na niccabhattādīnīti āpannaṃ. Tenevāyasmā upālitthero tassa anāpattivāre “niccabhatte”tiādīni pañca padāni pakkhipitvā saṅgāyi. Adhippāyaññū hi te mahānāgā, tasmā paṭhamameva yaṃ bhagavatā vuttaṃ “pañca bhojanāni ṭhapetvā sabbattha anāpattī”ti vacanaṃ, pacchāpi taṃ anurakkhantena abhojanaṃ madhugoḷakaṃ aparāmasitvā bhojjayāgu eva vuttāti evaṃ ācariyo.

283. “It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma”—this is the statement of the compilers. Indeed, the Blessed One did not lay down the same training rule twice. Thus it should be understood in such cases, say some. It was stated with reference to the first promulgation, yet those monks did not become guilty of an offense. How so? Because of the origin story of the training rule on successive meals. It is said, “Moreover, we ate after going for alms early.” And in the Mātikāvibhaṅga it is said: “What is called ‘successive meals’? Having been invited with one of the five kinds of meals, and then, setting that aside, eating another of the five kinds of meals—this is called ‘successive meals.’” Therefore, it is established that ‘another meal’ means any food whatsoever obtained from an invitation. Because it was not food obtained from an invitation for food-gruel, those monks partook, thinking, “There is no offense in this.” Here, however, because it is said, “It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma,” it was permitted that an offense is incurred only for one who eats food obtained from another invitation, and not for the other case. From then on, in the exemption clause for that rule, it is stated: “In the case of a regular meal, a ticket meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha meal, or a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal.” Previously, at the time of the promulgation in Vesālī, these did not exist. If they had, it would contradict the origin story and the Mātikāvibhaṅga. Therefore, because it was said in the origin story, “Moreover, we ate after going for alms early,” and also because in the Padabhājanī it was said without specification, “eating another of the five kinds of meals,” although it would follow that an offense is incurred for one who, setting aside an invited meal (whether invited first or later), eats only an uninvited meal, and not for the other case; however, because it was said, “Monks, apart from what is invited, another food-gruel should not be consumed,” it became as if an offense was incurred for one who eats invited food obtained later after the first invited food, and also regular meals and so on. And so, while preventing the occasion for a supplementary rule and preventing the occasion for an offense regarding uninvited food, and while adapting the first-promulgated training rule with this meaning, the Blessed One said, “It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma.” Therefore, from then on, an offense is incurred only for one who eats food from a later invitation. In those cases, it follows that there is no offense for regular meals and so on. For that very reason, the venerable Elder Upāli, in the exemption clause for that rule, inserted the five terms beginning with “in the case of a regular meal” and recited it at the council. Indeed, those great Nāgas are knowers of the intention. Therefore, the teacher says thus: The Blessed One later upheld the statement he had made at the very beginning—“Setting aside the five kinds of meals, there is no offense in all cases”—by not touching upon non-food like honey-balls and speaking only of food-gruel.

Etthāha – yathā pacchāladdhalesena therena niccabhattādipakkhepo kato, evaṃ kathinakkhandhake paramparabhojanaṃ pakkhipitvā “atthatakathinānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, cha kappissantī”ti kimatthaṃ na vuccanti? Vuccate – yathāvuttalesanidassanatthaṃ. Aññathā idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vesāliyaṃ, andhakavinde cāti ubhayattha upaḍḍhupaḍḍhena paññattaṃ siyā. No ce, sāpattikā bhikkhū siyuṃ, na ca te sāpattikā appaṭikkhittepi tesaṃ kukkuccadassanato. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhūnaṃ dehīti. Bhikkhū kukkuccāyantā na paṭiggaṇhantī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tesañhi “paribhuñjathā”ti bhagavato āṇattiyā paribhuttānampi “odissakaṃ nu kho idaṃ amhāka”nti vimatippattānaṃ vimativinodanatthaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāguñca madhugoḷakañcā”ti [M 0.0485] vuttaṃ. Evamidhāpete paññattaṃ paramparabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ omadditvā paramparabhojanaṃ kathaṃ bhuñjissantīti. Etthāhu keci ācariyā paramparabhojanasikkhāpadeneva “aññassa bhojanaṃ na kappatī”ti jānantāpi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāguñcā”ti visuṃ anuññātattā “paṭaggidānamahāvikaṭādi viya kappatī”ti saññāya bhuñjiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “apica mayaṃ kālasseva bhojjayāguyā dhātā”tiādi, taṃ ayuttaṃ tattha aṭṭhuppattimātikāvibhaṅgavirodhena anāpattivāre niccabhattādīnaṃ asambhavappasaṅgato, bhikkhūnaṃ sāpattikabhāvānatikkamanato, micchāgāhahetuppasaṅgena bhagavatā anuññātappasaṅgato ca. Te hi bhikkhū yasmā bhagavā katthaci vinayavasena kappiyampi “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.194; su. ni. 81; mi. pa. 4.5.9) paṭikkhipati, tasmā bhagavato adhippāyaṃ pati “kukkuccāyantā na paṭiggaṇhantī”ti vuttaṃ, sikkhāpadaṃ pati bhagavāpi attano adhippāyappakāsanatthameva [V 0.0443] “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yāguñcā”ti āha. Duravaggāho hi bhagavato adhippāyo. Tathā hi bhāradvājassa pāyāsaṃ abhojaneyyanti akataviññattippasaṅgato paṭikkhipi. Ānandattherena viññāpetvā sajjitaṃ tekaṭulayāguṃ pana “yadapi, ānanda, viññattaṃ, tadapi akappiya”nti avatvā “yadapi, ānanda, antovuttha”ntiādimevāha. Tena no ce taṃ antovutthaṃ kappatīti adhippāyadassanena paṇītabhojanasūpodanaviññattisikkhāpadāni upatthambheti bhagavatopi kappati, pageva amhākanti.

Here it is said: Just as the inclusion of regular meals, etc., was made by the Elder who later obtained a hint, similarly, in the Kathinakkhandhaka, after including successive meals, why was it not said, “For you, O monks, who have spread the kathina, six things will be allowable”? It is said: For the purpose of illustrating the aforementioned point. Otherwise, this training rule would have been laid down half in Vesālī and half in Andhakavinda. If it were not so, the monks would be guilty of an offense. And they were not guilty of an offense, even though it was not prohibited, because their scruple was seen. For it was said: “Well then, brahmin, give to the monks.” The monks, being scrupulous, did not accept. For, to dispel the doubt of those monks who, even after having consumed by the Blessed One's command, “Consume!”, had fallen into doubt, thinking, “Is this indeed specifically for us?”, it was said, “I allow, O monks, gruel and honey-balls.” Similarly here also, how would these monks, having transgressed the laid-down training rule on successive meals, consume successive meals? Here, some teachers said that even while knowing through the training rule on successive meals itself that “food from another is not allowable,” they consumed it with the perception that “it is allowable, like the case of the offering at the forefront of the fire, great delicacies, etc.,” because it was separately allowed by the words, “I allow, O monks, gruel…” Therefore, it was said, “Moreover, we were satisfied in the morning with food and gruel,” etc. That is incorrect because of the contradiction with the origin story, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga in that training rule; and because of the consequence that regular meals, etc., would be impossible in the section on non-offenses; and because the monks would not have overcome the state of being guilty of an offense; and because of the consequence that the Blessed One would have allowed it due to a reason that would lead to wrong view. For, since the Blessed One in some cases, by way of discipline, rejects even what is allowable—as when he said, “What is sung with verses is not to be eaten by me”—it was therefore said with regard to the Blessed One's intention that “being scrupulous, they did not accept.” With regard to the training rule, the Blessed One also said, “I allow, O monks, gruel…” for the very purpose of clarifying His own intention. For the Blessed One's intention is difficult to fathom. For so it is: He rejected Bhāradvāja's milk-rice, saying it was “not to be eaten,” because of the implication of it being an item obtained by a hint without a formal request. But as for the three-spiced gruel prepared after being requested by the Elder Ānanda, without saying, “Ānanda, even what is requested is also unallowable,” He only said, “Ānanda, that which is stored indoors,” etc. Therefore, by showing the intention that if it was not stored indoors, it is allowable, He supports the training rules on requesting fine foods, curries, and rice. He supports the view that it is allowable even for the Blessed One, how much more so for us.

284. Gilānasseva bhagavatā guḷo anuññātoti “yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisāyanīyānī”ti (pārā. 622) vacanavasena vuttaṃ, teneva te idha paṭiggahaṇe kukkuccāyiṃsu. Idha pana “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gilānassa guḷodaka”nti vattabbe guḷādhikārattā pubbe anuññātañca vatvā agilānassa guḷodakaṃ anuññātaṃ, tena gilānena sati paccaye guḷo paribhuñjitabbo, guḷodakaṃ asati paccayepi vaṭṭatīti imaṃ visesaṃ dīpeti. Tattha “guḷodakaṃ kālikesu sattāhakālikaṃ, bhagavatā odissānuññātattā sattāhātikkamena dukkaṭa”nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ, udakasambhinnattā sattāhakālikabhāvaṃ jahati. “Yathā ambādi udakasambhinnaṃ yāmakālikaṃ jātaṃ, tathā sattāhakālikaṃ jahitvā tadanantare [M 0.0486] yāvajīvike ṭhita”nti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ, tañca bhagavatā odissānuññātattā paccavekkhaṇābhāve doso natthi. “Guḷodaka’nti vuttattā udakagatika”nti vadanti. Yadi udakamissaṃ udakagatikaṃ hoti, madhupi siyā taṃ tathā anuññātattā. Mā hotu, appaṭiggahetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ siyā udakagatikattā, tañca na hoti, “sabbatthāpi upaparikkhitvā gahetabba”nti aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade vuttaṃ.

284. That jaggery was allowed by the Blessed One only for the sick was stated by way of the phrase, 'Whatever is suitable for sick monks' (Pārā. 622); for that very reason, they felt scrupulous about accepting it here. Here, however, although it should have been said, 'I allow, monks, jaggery-water for the sick,' because jaggery is the main topic, having stated what was previously allowed, jaggery-water was allowed for the non-sick. By this, he clarifies the following distinction: a sick monk, when there is a reason, may consume jaggery; jaggery-water is allowable even when there is no reason. Therein, some say, 'Among time-limited items, jaggery-water is a seven-day allowable; because it was specifically allowed by the Blessed One, after the passing of seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' That is not correct; because it is mixed with water, it abandons its nature as a seven-day allowable. Some say, 'Just as mango, etc., when mixed with water, becomes allowable for a watch of the night, so too, having abandoned its nature as a seven-day allowable, it becomes established immediately after as a lifetime allowable.' That is correct. And since it was specifically allowed by the Blessed One, there is no fault in the absence of reflection. Some say, 'Because it is called "jaggery-water," it has the same status as water.' If something mixed with water has the same status as water, then honey would also be so, because it was allowed in the same way. Let it not be so. It would be consumable without being formally received because it has the same status as water, and that is not the case, for it is said in a certain gloss: 'In all cases, it should be accepted after examining.'

285. Suññāgāranti catutthajjhānaṃ.

285. An empty dwelling is the fourth jhāna.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Allowance of Permissible Ground

295. Oravasaddanti mahāsaddaṃ. Bahūhi samparivāretvāti ettha ekenāpi vaṭṭati. “Bahūsu ekassapi vacanena saha siyāti vutta”nti vadanti. “Āmasitvā”ti vuttattā anāmasite na vaṭṭati. “Doso natthī”ti vacanena sesāpi anuññātā. “Bhittiñce upasante pacchā taṃ pūrenti, tattha kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, pakatibhūmiyaṃyeva kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Taṃ upari aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “iṭṭhakādīhi katācayassā”tiādinā virujjhati viya. Mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vāti ettha “asatiyā [V 0.0444] anadhiṭṭhitāya saritaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya ce upari adhiṭṭhitā, heṭṭhā ṭhitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ akappiyaṃ, upariṭṭhitameva kappiyaṃ, ayamettha viseso”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha kappiyakuṭi laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti evaṃvidhe puna kātabbāti attho. Kappiyakuṭiṃ kātuṃ demāti ettha kappiyakuṭikiccaṃ kātunti adhippāyo. Bhojanasālā pana senāsanameva, tasmā tattha kātabbanti apare. “Akatepi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ.

295. ‘Oravasaddaṃ’ means a great sound. Regarding ‘surrounded by many,’ even one is allowable. They say, ‘It is said, “Among many, it may be [valid] with the word of even one.”’ Because it is said, ‘Having touched,’ it is not allowable if not touched. By the statement, ‘There is no fault,’ the remaining commentaries are also permitted. They say, ‘If they fill a wall after it is finished, it is not allowable to do so there; it is allowable to do so only on the natural ground.’ This seems to contradict what is said above in the commentary, beginning with ‘of a structure made with bricks, etc.’ Regarding ‘or a lump of clay,’ it is said here: ‘If, through a lapse of mindfulness, it was not determined, and if it is then determined for the upper part, starting from the place one remembers, the item placed below is not allowable; only that which is placed above is allowable. This is the distinction here.’ Here, it is allowable to obtain a suitable hut; the meaning is that in such a case, it should be done again. Regarding ‘We give [permission] to make a suitable hut,’ the intention is ‘to do the work of a suitable hut.’ A dining hall, however, is indeed a lodging; therefore, others say it should be done there. It is said, ‘Even if not done, it is allowable.’

“Mukhasannidhi nāma bhojanakāle sannidhī”ti likhitaṃ. Mukhasannidhīti tassa nāmaṃ. “Yadi sannidhi hoti, pācittiyaṃ bhaveyya, mukhasannidhi pana dukkaṭaṃ, tasmā sannidhi anadhippetā”ti vuttaṃ. “Tassa santakaṃ katvā”ti vuttattā anapekkhavissajjanaṃ nādhippetaṃ. Cīvaravikappane viya kappiyamattaṃ ñātabbanti keci.

It is written: 'What is called mukhasannidhi is storing at mealtime.' Mukhasannidhi is the name for that. It is said: 'If it were storing (sannidhi), it would be a pācittiya offense; mukhasannidhi, however, is a dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, storing (sannidhi) is not intended.' Because it is said, 'Having made it the property of that novice,' an unconcerned relinquishing is not intended. Some say that, as in the case of the formal determination (vikappana) of a robe, it should be understood as merely making it allowable.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Ascetic Keṇiya

300. “Attanā paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattameva pariccajitvā sāmaṇerādīhi pānakaṃ katvā dinne purebhattameva vaṭṭati, na pacchābhattaṃ savatthukapaṭiggahitattā”ti vadanti, tattha puna paṭiggahaṇe niddosattā, purebhattameva paṭiggahaṇassa [M 0.0487] nissaṭṭhattā, attanā ca aggahitattā doso na dissati, upaparikkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Sālūkā nāma kandā, “ito kiñcitaka”nti voharanti. “Phārusakanti goḷavisaye eko rukkho”ti ca likhitaṃ. “Pakkaḍākarasa”nti visesitattā “apakkaṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kurundivacanenapi siddhameva. Taṇḍuladhovanodakampi dhaññaraso eva. “Nikkasaṭo ucchuraso sattāhakāliko”ti likhitaṃ. Sāvittīti gāyatti. Chandasoti vedassa. “Na, bhikkhave, pabbajitena akappiye samādapetabba’nti vuttattā anupasampannassāpi na kevalaṃ dasasu eva sikkhāpadesu, atha kho yaṃ bhikkhussa na kappati, tasmimpīti adhippāyo”ti vuttaṃ.

300. They say: 'Having relinquished an item received by oneself only in the forenoon, when juice is prepared and given by novices and others, it is allowable only in the forenoon, not after midday, because it was received together with its basis.' In that case, because there is no fault in receiving it again, because the item received only in the forenoon has been relinquished, and because it was not held by oneself, no fault is seen; it should be taken after examination. 'Sālūkā' are tubers; they are called 'a little from this.' And it is written: 'Phārusaka is a certain tree in the Goḷa region.' Because it is specified as 'juice of ripe pakkaḍāka,' it is said: 'The unripe is allowable.' This is established also by the word of the Kurundī. Even rice-washing water is indeed grain juice. It is written: 'Sugarcane juice without dregs is a seven-day allowable.' 'Sāvittī' is the Gāyatrī meter. 'Chandaso' refers to the Veda. Because it was said, 'Monks, one who has gone forth should not be made to undertake what is unallowable,' it is said that the meaning is this: for one not yet fully ordained also, it is not only in regard to the ten training rules, but also in regard to whatever is not allowable for a monk, that he should not be made to undertake it.

305. Dve paṭā desanāmenevāti cīnapaṭṭasomārapaṭṭāni. Tīṇīti pattuṇṇena saha tīṇi. Iddhimayikaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ nibbattaṃ. Devadattiyaṃ anuruddhattherena laddhaṃ. “Yāmātikkame sannidhivasena sattāhātikkame bhesajjasikkhāpadavasenā”ti likhitaṃ.

305. Regarding 'two cloths by the name of their country': they are Chinese cloth and Somāra cloth. Regarding 'three': it means three together with Pattuṇṇa cloth. The robe made by psychic power is the one that arose for the 'ehi-bhikkhu' monks. The Devadattiya robe was obtained by the Elder Anuruddha. It is written: 'In exceeding the watch, it should be decided by way of storing; in exceeding seven days, by way of the training rule on medicines.'

Bhesajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is finished.

7. Kathinakkhandhakavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Kathina Chapter

Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Allowance of the Kathina

306. “Kathinanti [M 0.0488][V 0.0445] pañcānisaṃse antokaraṇasamatthatāya thiranti attho”ti likhitaṃ. “Pañca kappantī”ti avatvā “kappissantī”ti anāgatavacanaṃ “vo”ti imassa sāmivacanapakkhe yujjati tesaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe anatthatakathinattā. Dvīsu panetesu atthavikappesu pacchimo yutto sabbesampi tesaṃ pāveyyakānaṃ sabbadhutaṅgadharattā. Nimantanaṃ sādiyantasseva hi anāmantacāro paññatto, tathā gaṇabhojanaṃ.
