Tattha kusalacittehi karaṇakāle kusalo, arahantānaṃ karaṇakāle abyākato, etesaṃ akusalapaṭipakkhattā akusalassa sambhavo natthi, tasmā ‘natthi sammukhāvinayo akusalo’ti vutta”nti likhitaṃ. “Yebhuyyasikā adhammavādīhi vūpasamanakāle salākaggāhāpake dhammavādimhi kusalā, dhammavādīnampi adhammavādimhi salākaggāhāpake jāte akusalā, sabbattha arahato vaseneva abyākatatā, anarahato sañcicca sativinayadāne sativinayo akusalo, amūḷhavinayo anummattakassa dāne, paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ mūḷhassa ajānanato paṭiññāyakaraṇe, tassapāpiyasikā suddhassa karaṇe, tiṇavatthārakaṃ mahākalahe, sañcicca karaṇe ca akusala”nti likhitaṃ.

303. When there is a confession in the presence of the Sangha, that confession is called 'presence of the Sangha.' Therefore, they say: 'With reference to that person's mind of confession, it is said, “The procedure in the presence is wholesome,” and so on.' Regarding 'The procedure in the presence is not unwholesome,' it is written: 'The procedure in the presence has three factors: the presence of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person; without these, it does not exist. Therein, at the time of its performance with wholesome minds, it is wholesome; at the time of its performance by Arahants, it is indeterminate. Because these are the opposite of the unwholesome, there is no possibility of the unwholesome. Therefore, it is said, “The procedure in the presence is not unwholesome.”' It is also written: 'The procedure of the majority, at the time of pacifying those who speak against the Dhamma, is wholesome when the one who makes them take the voting-tickets is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma. When those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma have one who speaks against the Dhamma as the one who makes them take the voting-tickets, it is unwholesome. In all cases, for an Arahant, it is indeterminate by their very nature. For a non-Arahant, the procedure of mindfulness is unwholesome when given with intention; the procedure for one who is no longer deluded is unwholesome when given to one who is not insane; the procedure of acknowledgement is unwholesome when carried out for one who is confused and unknowing; the procedure for further misconduct is unwholesome when carried out for one who is pure; and the covering over with grass is unwholesome in a great quarrel and when done with intention.'

Yatthavārapucchāvāravaṇṇanā

The Section on 'Where': Explanation of the Section on Questions

304. Labbhatīti pucchā.

304. The question is: “Is it obtained?”

Samathavāravissajjanāvāravaṇṇanā

The Section on Settlements: Explanation of the Section on Answers

305. Yasmiṃ samaye sammukhāvinayena cātiādi tassā vissajjanaṃ. Yasmiṃ samaye sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasammati, tasmiṃ samaye yattha yebhuyyasikā labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatīti evaṃ sabbattha sambandho. Yattha paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatīti ettha ekaṃ vā dve vā bahū vā āpattiyo āpanno [M 0.0550] bhikkhu “imaṃ nāma āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti pucchito “āmā”ti āpattiṃ [V 0.0503] paṭijānāti, dvepi labbhanti. Tattha saṅghasammukhatā dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatāti evaṃ vuttasammukhāvinaye saṅghassa purato paṭiññātaṃ kataṃ ce, saṅghasammukhatā. Tattheva desitaṃ ce, dhammavinayasammukhatāyopi laddhā honti. Avivadantā aññamaññaṃ paṭijānanti ce, puggalasammukhatā. Tasseva santike desitaṃ ce, dhammavinayasammukhatāyopi laddhā honti. Ekasseva vā ekassa santike āpattidesanakāle “passasi, passāmī”ti vutte tattha dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatāsaññito sammukhāvinayo ca paṭiññātakaraṇañca laddhaṃ hoti.

305. This is the answer to that question: ‘At the time when by the procedure in the presence,’ etc. At the time when a legal issue is settled by the procedure in the presence and by the procedure of the majority, at that time, wherever the procedure of the majority is obtained, there the procedure in the presence is also obtained—thus the connection should be made in all cases. Where the procedure of acknowledgment is obtained, there the procedure in the presence is also obtained. Here, when a monk who has committed one, two, or many offenses is asked, “Monk, have you committed such-and-such an offense?” and he acknowledges the offense by saying, “Yes, I have committed it,” then both are obtained. In this regard, in the procedure in the presence thus stated as the presence of the Sangha, the presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and the presence of individuals: if an acknowledgment is made before the Sangha, it is the presence of the Sangha. If it is confessed right there, the presences of the Dhamma and Vinaya are also obtained. If they acknowledge among themselves without disputing, it is the presence of individuals. If it is confessed in the presence of that very individual, the presences of the Dhamma and Vinaya are also obtained. Or, in the case of just one person, at the time of confessing an offense in the presence of one person, when “Do you see?” “I see” is said, then the procedure in the presence—designated as the presence of the Dhamma, Vinaya, and individuals—and the procedure of acknowledgment are obtained.

Saṃsaṭṭhavārādivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Associated Matters and So Forth

306. Adhikaraṇānaṃ vūpasamova samatho nāma, so adhikaraṇaṃ vinā natthi, tasmā na ca labbhā vinibhujjitvā nānākaraṇaṃ kātuṃ.

306. The settling of legal issues is itself called a settlement. It does not exist without a legal issue. Therefore, it is not possible to separate them and make a distinction.

309-310. Samathā samathehi sammantīti ettha sammantīti sampajjanti. Adhikaraṇā vā pana sammanti vūpasammantīti attho, tasmā “yebhuyyasikā sammukhāvinayena sammatī”ti imāya sammukhāvinayena saddhiṃ sampajjati, na sativinayādīhi tesaṃ tassā anupakārattāti attho. Samathā adhikaraṇehi sammantīti ettha samathā abhāvaṃ gacchantīti attho.

Here, in ‘settlements are settled by settlements,’ ‘are settled’ means they are accomplished. Or, the meaning is that legal issues are settled, are pacified. Therefore, the meaning is: ‘the procedure of the majority is settled by the procedure in the presence’ means it is accomplished in conjunction with the procedure in the presence, not with the procedure of mindfulness and so forth, because they are not helpful to it. Here, in ‘settlements are settled by legal issues,’ the meaning is that settlements cease to exist.

311. “Sammukhāvinayo vivādādhikaraṇena na sammatī”ti pāṭho. Yebhuyyasikāya samānabhāvato ca avasāne “sammukhāvinayo na kenaci sammatī”ti (pari. 313) vuttattā ca sammukhāvinayo sayaṃ samathena vā adhikaraṇena vā sametabbo na hotīti katvā vutto. Sativinayo kiccādhikaraṇena sammati. Amūḷhavinayatassapāpiyasikatiṇavatthārakāpi kiccādhikaraṇena sammanti.

311. The reading is: 'The procedure in the presence is not settled by a dispute-issue.' And because it is equivalent to the procedure of the majority, and because at the end it is stated (Pari. 313), 'The procedure in the presence is not settled by any settlement,' it is said, having considered that the procedure in the presence is not to be settled by a settlement itself or by an issue. The procedure of mindfulness is settled by a duty-issue. The procedures for one who is no longer deluded, for further misconduct, and of covering over with grass are also settled by a duty-issue.

313. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇena sammatīti “suṇātu me, bhante…pe… paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ nikkhipāmī”ti evaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇena sammati. Anuvādādhikaraṇaāpattādhikaraṇāpi kiccādhikaraṇena sammanti. “‘Akataṃ kammaṃ dukkaṭaṃ kamma’nti evaṃ kiccādhikaraṇampi kiccādhikaraṇena sammatīti [M 0.0551] evaṃ pāṭho veditabbo”ti likhitaṃ. Aññatarasmiṃ pana gaṇṭhipade “‘samathā adhikaraṇehi sammantī’ti ettha yasmā sabbe samathā kiccādhikaraṇena sammanti, tasmā ‘samathā kiccādhikaraṇena sammantī’ti pāṭho gahetabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

313. A dispute-issue is settled by a procedural-issue—as in, 'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me… I cast the first voting slip.' Thus, a dispute-issue is settled by a procedural-issue. Accusation-issues and offense-issues are also settled by a procedural-issue. It is written: 'The reading should be understood thus: Regarding the statement, “The act was not done; the act was wrongly done,” thus even a procedural-issue is settled by a procedural-issue.' However, in a certain sub-commentary, it is said: 'Herein, regarding the text “settlements are settled by issues,” because all settlements are settled by a procedural-issue, therefore the reading should be taken as “settlements are settled by a procedural-issue.”'

314. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ [V 0.0504] katamaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti “nāyaṃ dhammo”ti vuttamattena kiñci adhikaraṇaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti.

314. What issue does a dispute-issue give rise to? By the mere saying, 'This is not the Dhamma,' it does not give rise to any issue.

318-9. “Katamādhikaraṇapariyāpanna”nti pāṭho. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ bhajatīti paṭhamuppannavivādaṃ pacchā uppanno bhajati. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dve samathe bhajatīti “imaṃ vūpasametuṃ samatthā tumhe”ti vadantaṃ viya bhajati “mayaṃ taṃ vūpasamessāmā”ti vadantehi viya dvīhi samathehi saṅgahitaṃ.

The reading is: 'In which issue is it included?' A dispute-issue resorts to a dispute-issue—meaning, a later arisen dispute resorts to a first arisen dispute. A dispute-issue resorts to two settlements—it resorts as if to one saying, 'You are capable of settling this issue,' and it is encompassed by two settlements as if by those saying, 'We will settle that dispute-issue.'

Samathabhedavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Analysis of Settlements is concluded.

Khandhakapucchāvāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Questions about the Khandhakas

Pucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on Questions and Answers

320. Nidānaṃ nāma kālañca nagarañca deso ca bhagavā ca. Vatthupuggalādi niddeso. Yāni tattha upasampadakkhandhake “na, bhikkhave, ūnavīsativasso puggalo upasampādetabbo”tiādinā nayena uttamāni padāni vuttānīti sambandho. Sā sā tassa tassa padassa āpattīti vuccatīti yā “na, bhikkhave, ūnavīsativasso puggalo upasampādetabbo”ti padena paññattā āpatti, sā tassa padassāti adhippāyo. Cammasaṃyutteti cammakkhandhake.

320. The introduction is called the time, the city, the region, and the Blessed One. The exposition is of the subject matter, individuals, and so on. The connection is thus: supreme terms were spoken there in the Ordination Chapter by the method beginning with, 'Monks, a person under twenty years of age should not be ordained.' Regarding the statement, 'That is the offense for that particular term,' the intention is this: the offense established by the term, 'Monks, a person under twenty years of age should not be ordained,' is the offense of that term. 'Connected with hides' means in the Chapter on Hides.

Ekuttarikanayavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Method of Increasing by One

Ekakavāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Single Section

321. Ekuttarikanaye [V 0.0505][M 0.0552] āpatti jānitabbāti ettha āpatti nāma kiṃ paramatthasabhāvā, udāhu na vattabbasabhāvāti? Na vattabbasabhāvā. Vuttañhi parivāre “vatthu jānitabbaṃ, gottaṃ jānitabbaṃ, nāmaṃ jānitabbaṃ, āpatti jānitabbā”ti etesaṃ padānaṃ vibhaṅge “methunadhammoti vatthu ca gottañca. Pārājikanti nāmañceva āpatti cā”ti. Nāmañca gottañca “nāmagottaṃ na jīratī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.76) vacanato sammutimattaṃ, tasmā “kusalattikavinimuttā na vattabbadhammabhūtā ekaccā sammuti evā”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ samathakkhandhake “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākata”nti (cūḷava. 222), taṃ “vivādādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusalaṃ, siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākata”nti (cūḷava. 220) ettha viya pariyāyato vuttaṃ. Atthato hi vivādo nāma ekacco sammutiviseso. Yo cittasamaṅgino, so “taṃ cittapariyāyena pana siyā kusala”ntiādi vohāraladdho, tathā āpattādhikaraṇampīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āpattiṃ āpajjamāno hi akusalacitto vā āpajjati kusalābyākatacitto vā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā). Aññathā samathehi adhikaraṇīyatā na sambhavati. Na hi samathā kusalādiṃ akusalādiṃ vā adhikiccapavattanti, samathavasena vā kusalādi sammati. Na ca kusalassa vivādassa, anuvādassa vā kusalādisamathehi vūpasametabbatā āpajjatīti tesaṃ adhikaraṇamattameva na sambhaveyya, tasmā adhikaraṇānaṃ, samathānañca kusalādibhāvo pariyāyadesanāya labbhati, no aññathā, teneva sammukhāvinaye viya āpattādhikaraṇe tikaṃ na pūritaṃ. Sañcicca āpattiṃ āpajjamānassa yasmā sañcetanā ekantato akusalāva hoti. Itarassa sacittakassa vā acittakassa vā tadābhāvamattaṃ upādāya “abyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Yathā hi “tikkhattuṃ codayamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṃ kusala”ntiādīsu (pārā. 538) na kusalasaddo sukhavipāko, “samparāyikānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭighātāyā”tiādīsu (pari. 498) na akusalā vā hoti. Itarassa sacittakassa [M 0.0553] vā acittakassa vā tadābhāvamattaṃ upādāya “abyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Yathā hi dvikkhattuṃ codayamāno taṃ cīvaraṃ abhinipphādeyya, yaṃ panettha “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ akusala”nti vuttaṃ, tassa [V 0.0506] vasena tadakusalato satta vinītavatthūni veditabbāni, tato cīvaranti sambhavato acīvarakā, antarāpattikā ca. Anantarikalakkhaṇappattassa vasena niyatā ca nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Sammutiniddese garukalahukaniddesopi sambhavati. Aññathā “anantarāyikā paṇṇattivajjā, anavajjāpaṇṇattī”ti ca vuttā. Kuṭikāramahallakāpatti antarāyikā lokavajjasāvajjapaṇṇattito. Sampajānamusāvādo omasavādādito garukādi na sambhaveyya, tato vā ayaṃ lahukādīti idaṃ sabbaṃ ekaccānaṃ ācariyānaṃ mataṃ, “sabbaṃ ayutta”nti vadanti. Kasmā? Yasmā “pārājikanti nāmañceva āpatticā”ti vacanena ce āpatti na vattabbadhammo siyā, vatthu ca na vattabbadhammo siyā gottena samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vuttattā, tasmā “methunadhammo”ti padaṃ ajjhācārasaṅkhātaṃ vatthuñca dīpeti. Ajjhācāravaseneva āpattiyā laddhanāmaṃ asādhāraṇanāmattā “gotta”nti ca vuccatīti ayaṃ tattha attho.

321. In the method of counting by ones, regarding the statement 'an offense should be known,' is what is called 'offense' of an ultimate nature, or is it of a nature that cannot be spoken of? It is of a nature that cannot be spoken of. For it is stated in the Parivāra, in the analysis of these terms—'The object should be known, the family should be known, the name should be known, the offense should be known'—that 'sexual intercourse is the object and the family, and pārājika is the name and the offense.' The name and the family are merely conventional, according to the saying 'name and family do not decay' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.76). Therefore, it is said: 'Some conventions, being free from the wholesome triad, are indeed phenomena that cannot be spoken of.' However, what is stated in the Samathakkhandhaka—'An offense-issue may be unwholesome or indeterminate' (Cūḷavagga 222)—is said figuratively, just as it is said there: 'A dispute-issue may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate' (Cūḷavagga 220). For in essence, a dispute is a particular kind of convention. In the case of one endowed with a mind, that particular convention is designated by common usage through the way of the mind, as in 'it may be wholesome,' etc. Similarly, it should be understood that an offense-issue is also designated thus. Thus, it is stated in the commentary: 'Indeed, one who commits an offense does so either with an unwholesome mind or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind' (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Aṭṭhakathā, First Pārājika Explanation). Otherwise, the state of being an issue to be settled by settlements would not be possible. For settlements do not proceed by focusing on the wholesome, etc., or the unwholesome, etc., nor does the wholesome, etc., become settled by way of settlements. Moreover, since the state of being settled by wholesome, etc., settlements does not apply to a wholesome dispute or accusation, their mere status as issues would not be possible. Therefore, the nature of issues and settlements as wholesome, etc., is obtained through figurative teaching, not otherwise. For this reason, the triad is not fully applied to offense-issues, as it is in the face-to-face procedure. Because for one who intentionally commits an offense, the volition is entirely unwholesome. For another case, whether it be a precept involving consciousness (sacittaka) or one without consciousness (acittaka), it is called 'indeterminate' merely by virtue of the absence of that unwholesome volition. Just as in statements like 'If one urges three times and produces that robe, this is wholesome' (Pārā. 538), the term 'wholesome' does not mean a pleasant result; and just as in 'for the destruction of unwholesome states leading to the hereafter' (Pari. 498), unwholesome states do not arise. For another case, whether it be a precept involving consciousness or one without consciousness, it is called 'indeterminate' merely by virtue of the absence of that wholesome or unwholesome state. Just as if one urges twice and produces that robe. Regarding what is stated here, 'An offense-issue is unwholesome,' based on that, from that unwholesomeness, seven settled cases should be understood. From that, because the existence of a robe is possible, those without robes are subject to intermediate offenses. And it should be understood that they are fixed in name by virtue of having the characteristic of immediacy. In the exposition of conventions, the exposition of grave and minor also applies. Otherwise, it would be said: 'Non-obstructive offenses are transgressions by convention,' and 'Blameless offenses are mere conventions.' The offense of constructing a large hut is obstructive due to being a worldly fault and a blameworthy convention. Intentional false speech would not be heavier, etc., than abusive speech, etc., nor would this offense be lighter, etc., than that one. All this is the opinion of some teachers, but they say, 'All this is incorrect.' Why? Because if, by the statement 'pārājika is the name and the offense,' the offense were a phenomenon that cannot be spoken of, then the object would also be a phenomenon that cannot be spoken of, since it is stated to be co-referential with the family. Therefore, the term 'sexual intercourse' clarifies the object, which is called transgression. The name obtained for the offense through the transgression itself, because it is a unique name, is also called 'family' (gotta). This is the meaning there.

“Āpattādhikaraṇassa kiṃ pubbaṅgamanti? Lobho pubbaṅgamo, doso, moho, alobho, adoso, amoho pubbaṅgamo”ti “kati hetūti? Cha hetū tayo akusalahetū, tayo abyākatahetū”ti ca vuttattā nippariyāyeneva “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Samathakkhandhake pana sandhāyabhāsitavasena tathā eva vuttaṃ. Tasmā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ sabhāvato nippariyāyeneva akusalā cattāro khandhā, rūpaabyākatā ca honti. “Natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti (cūḷava. 222) vuttattā kusalameva paṭikkhittaṃ, khīṇāsavānaṃ kiriyābyākataṃ nāma hotīti kusale paṭikkhitte kiriyābyākatampi paṭikkhittameva hoti. Tasmiṃ paṭikkhitte sabbathā avāvaṭaṃ vipākābyākataṃ paṭikkhittameva hoti. Nibbānābyākate vattabbameva natthīti eke, taṃ ayuttaṃ “cha hetuyo”ti vuttattā. Kiñcāpi vuttaṃ sāmaññena, tathāpi vipākahetuyeva tattha adhippeto, na kiriyāhetu, te hi kusalasabhāvā ca, tasmā rūpaṃ, vipākābyākatañcāpatti. Tattha akusalāpattito vinītavatthūni. Itarassāpi ādito chādanā kusalacittatoti vuttaṃ [M 0.0554] hoti. Antarāyikaniyatasāvajjapaññattibhāvopi cassā vevacanavasena veditabbo paṇṇattivajjāya, sañcicca āpannāya ca, tasmā “jīvitindriyaṃ siyā sārammaṇaṃ siyā anārammaṇa”nti vacanaṃ viya ekantākusalaṃ anekantākusalañca lokavajjaṃ, ekantābyākataṃ bhūtārocanaṃ anekantābyākatañca sesaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ ekato sampiṇḍetvā “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyābyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Samathakkhandhake pana paṇṇattivajjameva sandhāya tathā vuttaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, gaṇṭhipade ca “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākataṃ, natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala’nti ettha sandhāyabhāsitavasena attho veditabbo. Yasmiñhi pathavikhaṇanādike [V 0.0507] āpattādhikaraṇe apakataññuno sandhāya appaharitakaraṇādikāle kusalacittaṃ aṅgaṃ hoti, khaṇanādipayogasaṅkhātaṃ rūpābyākataṃ āpattisamuṭṭhāpentaṃ hotīti adhippāyo”ti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atthāpatti kusalacitto āpajjati, kusalacitto vuṭṭhātī”tiādi. Tasmiñhi sati na sakkā vattuṃ “natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti. Yasmā āpattisamuṭṭhāpakaṃ cittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ na hoti, tasmā na yidaṃ aṅgappahonakacittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yadi taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, “siyā kusala”nti ca vattabbaṃ bhaveyya, na ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā idaṃ pana sandhāya vuttaṃ – yaṃ tāva āpattādhikaraṇaṃ lokavajjaṃ, taṃ ekantato akusalameva, tattha “siyā akusala”nti vikappo natthi. Yaṃ pana paṇṇattivajjaṃ, taṃ yasmā sañcicca “imaṃ āpattiṃ vītikkamāmī”ti vītikkamantasseva akusalaṃ hoti, asañcicca pana kiñci ajānantassa sahaseyyādivasena āpajjato rūpavipākaṃ abyākataṃ hoti anuṭṭhānato. Tasmā tassa paṇṇattivajjassa sañciccāsañciccavasena imaṃ vikappabhāvaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ, siyā abyākataṃ, natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti.

“What is the forerunner of a legal matter concerning an offense? Greed is the forerunner, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion are the forerunners.” And, “How many roots are there? There are six roots: three unwholesome roots and three indeterminate roots.” Because this has been stated, it is said without qualification that “a legal matter concerning an offense may be unwholesome or may be indeterminate.” However, in the Chapter on Settlement, it is stated in the same way by way of an implicit statement. Therefore, a legal matter concerning an offense, by its intrinsic nature and without qualification, consists of the four unwholesome aggregates and indeterminate form. Because it is stated, “There is no wholesome legal matter concerning an offense,” only the wholesome is rejected. For the Arahants, there is what is called functional indeterminate consciousness; thus, when the wholesome is rejected, the functional indeterminate is also rejected. When that is rejected, the resultant indeterminate, which is in no way prohibited, is also rejected. Regarding indeterminate Nibbāna, there is nothing to be said. So say some. That is incorrect, because it is stated, “six roots.” Although it is stated in a general sense, nevertheless, only the resultant roots are intended there, not the functional roots, for they are not of a wholesome nature. Therefore, form and resultant indeterminate consciousness constitute the offense. In that regard, the settled cases are to be known from the unwholesome offense. For the other type as well, it is said to be from the outset from a concealing unwholesome consciousness. And its nature as an obstructive, fixed, and blameworthy-by-prescription offense should be understood by way of its synonyms for a blameworthy-by-rule offense and for one committed intentionally. Therefore, just like the statement, “The life faculty may be with an object or may be without an object,” having combined into one the worldly offense, which is both exclusively and not exclusively unwholesome, and the blameworthy-by-rule offense—which is exclusively indeterminate (such as confessing a fault) and not exclusively indeterminate (in other cases)—it is said, “A legal matter concerning an offense may be unwholesome or may be indeterminate.” In the Chapter on Settlement, however, it is stated thus with reference only to the blameworthy-by-rule offense. And this is stated in the commentary and in the sub-commentary: “In the passage, ‘A legal matter concerning an offense may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate; there is no wholesome legal matter concerning an offense,’ the meaning should be understood by way of an implicit statement. For in a legal matter concerning an offense such as digging the earth, with reference to those unskilled in the Vinaya, at the time of clearing green plants, etc., wholesome consciousness is a factor, and the indeterminate form, known as the effort of digging, etc., originates the offense—this is the intention.” That with reference to which it is said, “There is an offense which one commits with a wholesome mind and from which one emerges with a wholesome mind,” etc. For if that were the case, it could not be said, “There is no wholesome legal matter concerning an offense.” Because it is not said with reference to the consciousness that originates the offense, therefore this is not said with reference to the consciousness that is a mere component. If it were said with reference to that, it would have to be said, “it may be wholesome,” but it was not said. Therefore, this is said with reference to the following: whatever legal matter concerning an offense is a worldly offense, that is exclusively unwholesome; in that case, there is no alternative of “may be unwholesome.” But as for what is a blameworthy-by-rule offense, since it is unwholesome only for one who transgresses intentionally, thinking, “I will transgress this offense,” whereas for one who is unaware and transgresses unintentionally by way of co-sleeping, etc., it is indeterminate form and resultant indeterminate consciousness, due to not having arisen from sleep. Therefore, with reference to this state of being an alternative for that blameworthy-by-rule offense, based on whether it is intentional or unintentional, this is said: “A legal matter concerning an offense may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate; there is no wholesome legal matter concerning an offense.”

Sace pana koci vinaye apakataññū “yaṃ kusalacitto āpajjati, idaṃ vuccati āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti vadeyya, tassevaṃvādino acittakānaṃ eḷakalomādisamuṭṭhānānampi kusalacittasamaṅgikāle tāsaṃ āpattīnaṃ kusalacitto āpajjeyya, na vā āpajjati[M 0.0555]. Kiṃkāraṇaṃ? Na ca tattha vijjamānampi kusalacittaṃ āpattiyā aṅgaṃ. Attabhāvo sabhāvo pakatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kataraṃ pana tassā āpattiyā tadā aṅgasabhāvoti? Vuccate – kāyavacīviññattivasena pana calitassa kāyassa, pavattāya vācāya cāti etesaṃ dvinnaṃ calitappavattānaṃ kāyavācānaṃ aññatarameva aṅgasabhāvo, tañca rūpakkhandhapariyāpannattā abyākatanti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Kāyo, vācā ca tadā āpattādhikaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yā panettha akusalāpattikkhaṇe kāyavācāyo abyākatabhāvo, tā abbohārikā honti kāyavacīkammakāle manokammaṃ viya. Tadā hi kāyavācāyo āpattikarādiṭṭhāne tiṭṭhanti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āpattikarā dhammā jānitabbā. Kati mūlānīti cha āpattisamuṭṭhānāni mūlānī”tiādi. Yadā pana kāyavācāyo āpattiyā aṅgameva honti, tadā “cittaṃ cittādhipateyya”nti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusalavaṇṇanā) vacanaṃ viya pubbapayogānaṃ aparapayogassa paccayabhāvato āpattikarādipaññattiṃ na vijahanti. Yathā tabbhāvepi “āpattādhikaraṇassa kati vatthūnīti? Satta āpattikkhandhā vatthūni. Kati bhūmiyoti? Satta āpattikkhandhā bhūmiyo”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā tabbhāvepi āpattikarā “āpattisamuṭṭhānā”icceva vuccantīti veditabbā. Ettāvatā āpatti nāma cattāro akusalakkhandhā sañcicca vītikkamakāle [V 0.0508] bhūtārocanaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbāpi avisesato, visesato pana sabbāpi ekantākusalā akusalā, anekantākusalā pana giraggasamajjacittāgārasaṅghāniitthālaṅkāragandhavaṇṇakavāsitapiññākappabhedā, bhikkhuniādīnaṃ ummaddanaparimaddanappabhedā cāti dasappabhedā sakanāmehi paricchinditvā vatthujānanasacittakakāle eva akusalā, tadabhāvato acittakakāle vinā anāpattādhikaraṇena kammaṭṭhānādisīsena kusalacittena taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ vītikkamantassa āpatti kevalaṃ rūpaabyākatameva.

But if some monk, unskilled in the Vinaya, were to say, “The offense which one commits with a wholesome mind, this offense-matter is called wholesome,” then in the view of one who speaks thus, even for offenses that are unintentional, such as those originating from goat's wool and so on, at the time of being endowed with a wholesome mind, one would commit those offenses with a wholesome mind, yet one does not actually commit them. What is the reason? For even though a wholesome mind is present there, it is not a factor of the offense. It is said: “Personal existence is its intrinsic nature, its natural state.” But what, then, is the characteristic nature of the constituent of that offense at that time? It is said: By means of bodily and verbal intimation, of the moved body and the uttered speech—of these two, the moved and the uttered, that is, the body and speech—one or the other is the very characteristic nature of the constituent, and since it is included in the form aggregate, it is indeterminate. What is said? It is said that the body and speech at that time are the offense-matter. Herein, the indeterminate nature of the body and speech at the moment of an unwholesome offense is not subject to designation, like mental action at the time of bodily and verbal action. For then, the body and speech stand in the position of being offense-causing, and so on. With reference to which it was said: “Offense-causing phenomena should be known. How many roots? Six origins of offenses are the roots,” and so on. But when body and speech are the very factors of an offense, then, like the saying, “Mind has mind as its dominant condition,” because of prior effort being a condition for subsequent effort, they do not abandon the designation of “offense-causing,” and so on. Just as, although this is the case, it is said: “How many objects are there for an offense-matter? The seven offense-aggregates are the objects. How many grounds? The seven offense-aggregates are the grounds.” Similarly, although this is the case, the offense-causers are called just “origins of offenses”; this should be known. To this extent, an offense, by name, is the four unwholesome aggregates. At the time of an intentional transgression, excluding the rule about reporting a fact, all offenses are so without distinction. But specifically, all such offenses are exclusively unwholesome. The not-exclusively unwholesome ones, however, are of ten types: those related to festivals on mountain-tops, picture galleries, the saṅghāṇī robe, women's ornaments, scents and colors, and scented sesamum paste; and those related to massaging and rubbing bhikkhunīs and others. These, having been delimited by their own names, are unwholesome only at the time of being conscious and knowing the object. Due to the absence of that, at a time of non-consciousness, for one transgressing that particular object with a wholesome mind headed by a meditation subject, etc., without it being a non-offense matter, the offense is merely material and indeterminate.

Keci panettha “appakāse ṭhāne kaṭisuttakasaññāya saṅghāṇiṃ, mattikāsaññāya gandhavaṇṇakādiṃ vā dhārentiyāpi āpatti, tasmā acittakāyevā”ti vaṇṇayanti. Te “saṅghāṇiyā asaṅghāṇisaññāya dhāreti, āpatti pācittiyassā”ti pāṭhābhāvaṃ dassetvā paṭikkhipitabbā. Surāpānāpatti pana acittakāpi ekantākusalāva. Teneva [M 0.0556] “majje amajjasaññī pivati, āpatti pācittiyassā”ti (pāci. 328) vuttaṃ. Yasmā panettha ābādhapaccayāpi na sakkā vinā akusalena surāpānaṃ pātuṃ, tasmā yathāvuttesu anekantākusalesu viya lokavajjesu idha “surāpānesu anāpatti ābādhapaccayā”ti na vuttaṃ. Sūpasaṃpākādi pana amajjameva. Tattha kukkuccavinodanatthaṃ “anāpattī”ti vuttaṃ udakadantapoṇe viya. Bhūtārocanāpatti rūpābyākatameva, acittakakāle sahaseyyādi rūpavipākābyākatameva, tattha supinanto vijjamānampi akusalaṃ anaṅgattā abbohārikaṃ hoti. Kusale kathāva natthi anāpatti sabhāvattā kusalassa. Tathā kiriyāti iminā nayena sabbattha yathāsambhavaṃ akusalaṃ vā suddharūpaṃ vā savipākaṃ vāti tidhā bhijjatīti ayamattho dassito hoti.

Some explain here: “For a bhikkhunī who, in an unapparent place, wears a saṅghāṇī with the perception of it being a waist-string, or scented powder and the like with the perception of it being clay, there is also an offense. Therefore, it is only unintentional.” They should be refuted by showing the absence of a passage such as: “For one who wears a saṅghāṇī with the perception of it not being a saṅghāṇī, there is a pācittiya offense.” The offense of drinking intoxicants, however, is exclusively unwholesome, even if unintentional. For that very reason, it is said: “If one, perceiving an intoxicant as a non-intoxicant, drinks it, there is a pācittiya offense.” Because here, even on account of illness, it is not possible to drink an intoxicant without unwholesomeness, therefore, unlike in the case of the aforementioned worldly faults which are not exclusively unwholesome, it is not said here: “In the case of drinking intoxicants, there is no offense on account of illness.” But soup-seasoning and the like are indeed not intoxicants. There, for the sake of dispelling scrupulousness, it is said, “There is no offense,” just as in the case of water for a tooth-stick. The offense of reporting a fact is merely indeterminate form. At an unintentional time, lying down together and so on is merely indeterminate form and indeterminate resultant. In that case, even an unwholesome state existing in a dream, because of not being a factor, is not reckonable. In the case of the wholesome, there is no question, because the nature of the wholesome is to be without offense. Likewise for the functional. By this method, it is shown that this meaning, everywhere, as is possible, is divided in three ways: as unwholesome, or pure form, or form with resultant.

Tattha ṭhapetvā surāpānaṃ ekaccañca paṇṇattivajjaṃ, ekantākusalañca sacittakameva, bhūtārocanaṃ acittakameva, sesaṃ saha surāpānena anekantākusalaṃ lokavajjañca anekantābyākataṃ paṇṇattivajjañca yebhuyyena sacittakācittakanti sabbasikkhāpadaṃ tippabhedaṃ hoti. Yaṃ panettha sacittakameva, taṃ methunādivatthujānanacitteneva sacittakaṃ, sabbaṃ sekhiyaṃ paṇṇattijānanacitteneva sacittakaṃ “anādariyaṃ paṭiccā”ti vacanatoti sacittakaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti. Ekantācittakaṃ paṇṇattijānanacittābhāvena, na vatthujānanacittābhāvena. Tadabhāvato ekantākusalaṃ surāpānaṃ, ekantābyākataṃ sañcarittaṃ, vatthujānanacittassa vā paṇṇattijānanacittassa vā ubhinnaṃ abhāvena acittakabhāvena acittakaṃ hoti. Surāpānaṃ pana sacittakaṃ hoti vatthujānanacitteneva. Ariyapuggalānaṃ itaresaṃ ubhinnaṃ vā aññatarassa bhāvena sesaṃ cittakācittakaṃ[V 0.0509]. Visesato ca vatthujānanacittābhāvena, apakataññuno paṇṇattijānanacittābhāvena vā acittakabhāvena acittakaṃ hoti. Tattha ekantācittakañca sacittakañca “acittaka”micceva vuccati. Ayaṃ tāva “āpatti jānitabbā”ti ettha vinicchayo.

Herein, all training rules are of three kinds. Setting aside the drinking of intoxicants, some offenses by prescription are exclusively unwholesome and only intentional. Reporting a fact is only unintentional. The remaining rules, together with the drinking of intoxicants—which are not-exclusively unwholesome, worldly faults, not-exclusively indeterminate, and offenses by prescription—are for the most part both intentional and unintentional. As to what herein is only intentional, it is intentional only through the mind that knows the object, such as in the case of sexual intercourse. All the Sekhiya rules are intentional only because of the mind that knows the prescription, due to the statement, 'on account of disrespect.' Thus, 'intentional' is of two kinds. An offense is exclusively unintentional due to the absence of the mind that knows the prescription, not due to the absence of the mind that knows the object. Due to the absence of that, the drinking of intoxicants, which is exclusively unwholesome, and acting as a go-between, which is exclusively indeterminate, become unintentional; this state of being unintentional is due to the absence of either the mind that knows the object or the mind that knows the prescription, or both. However, the drinking of intoxicants is intentional only through the mind that knows the object. For noble individuals and others, the remaining rules are both intentional and unintentional due to the presence of one or the other of these two types of mind. And specifically, an offense becomes unintentional due to the absence of the mind that knows the object; or, for one who is unskilled, it becomes unintentional due to the absence of the mind that knows the prescription. Herein, both what is exclusively unintentional and what is intentional are also called 'unintentional.' This, for now, is the determination herein regarding 'an offense should be known.'

Mūlavisuddhiyā antarāpattīti antarāpattiṃ āpajjitvā mūlāyapaṭikassanaṃ katvā ṭhitena āpannāpatti. Ayaṃ agghavisuddhiyā antarāpattīti [M 0.0557] sambahulā āpattiyo āpajjitvā tāsu sabbacirapaṭicchannavasena agghasamodhānaṃ gahetvā vasantena āpannāpatti. “Punapi āpajjissāmī”ti saussāheneva cittena. “Ayaṃ bhikkhuniyā evā”ti likhitaṃ. “Pārājikamevā”ti idañca bhūtavasena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. “Evaṃ desite pana yā kāci āpatti na vuṭṭhātīti apare, taṃ na gahetabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Dhammikassa paṭissavassa asaccāpane”ti vuttattā adhammikapaṭissave dukkaṭaṃ na hoti. “Pubbe suddhacittassa ‘tumhe vibbhamathā’ti vutte ‘sādhū’ti paṭissuṇitvā sace na vibbhamati anāpatti, evaṃ sabbatthā”ti ca vuttaṃ. “Āvikaro jānitabbo”tipi pāḷi. Kālena vakkhāmi, no akālenā”tiādīsu pañcadasasu dhammesu. Bhabbāpattikā nāma āpattiṃ āpajjituṃ bhabbā.

An intermediate offense in terms of root-purity is an offense committed by one who, having fallen into an intermediate offense and having performed the restoration to the root, is now established. An intermediate offense in terms of value-purity is an offense committed by one who, having committed numerous offenses, undertakes the agghasamodhāna probation by way of the longest-concealed offense among them all, and is undergoing it. It is written: “A confession made with a mind that is indeed eager, thinking, ‘I will commit it again,’ is for a bhikkhunī only.” And this, “It is only a pārājika,” is said in order to show what is real. It is said: “Some say that when a confession is made in this way, one is not lifted from any offense whatsoever; that view should not be accepted.” Because it is said, “for failing to fulfill a lawful promise,” there is no offense of wrong-doing in the case of an unlawful promise. And it is also said: “Previously, for one with a pure mind, when it is said, ‘You should disrobe,’ if, having replied, ‘Very well,’ he does not disrobe, there is no offense; it is thus in all cases.” There is also the Pāli text: “One who reveals should be known.” In the fifteen factors, such as, “I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time.” One called ‘capable of an offense’ is one who is capable of committing an offense.

Dukavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section of Dyads

322. Nidahane ātape. “Ekarattampi ce bhikkhu ticīvarena vippavaseyya (pārā. 472). Chārattaparamaṃ tenā”tiādinā (pārā. 653) vuttāpattiko gaṇapūrako hutvāpi kammaṃ kopeti nānāsaṃvāsakattā. Kammena vā salākaggāhena vāti ettha uddeso ceva kammañca ekanti ettha pātimokkhuddesoti vā kammanti vā atthato ekameva, tesu yaṃ kiñci kate saṅghabhedo hotīti attho. Pubbabhāgāti saṅghabhedato pubbabhāgā. “Pamāṇa”nti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ aññatarena bhedo hoti, na itarehīti vuttaṃ. Vinaye siddhā vinayasiddhā, romajanapade jātaṃ romakaṃ, anuññātaloṇattā dukesu vuttāti.

322. In the burning heat of the sun. A bhikkhu who has committed the aforesaid offense, such as in, “If a bhikkhu were to be separated from his three robes even for one night... the limit is six nights for him,” even if he is a quorum-filler, invalidates the formal act because he is of a different communion. Regarding “by a formal act or by the taking of voting-tickets”: here, the recitation and the formal act are one. That is, the recitation of the Pātimokkha or the formal act are indeed one in meaning. The meaning is that when any one of these two is done, there is a schism in the Saṅgha. “Preliminary parts” means the preliminary parts of a schism of the Saṅgha. Regarding “standard”: it is said that schism occurs by one of these two, not by the others. Established in the Vinaya is vinayasiddha; born in the Roman country is romaka; because it is a permitted salt, it is mentioned in the dyads.

Tikavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section of Triads

323. Vo tumhehi na samudācaritabbaṃ. Vacīsampayuttaṃ kāyakiriyaṃ katvāti kāyena nipaccakāraṃ katvāti attho. Upaghāteti vināseti. Omadditvāti abhibhavitvā. Vadatoti vadantassa. “Bālassa nissayo dātabbo”ti duke āgataṃ, idha pana “na dātabbo”ti vuttaṃ, āpattibāhullaṃ [V 0.0510] sandhāya nādātabbaṃ, “imasmā vihārā paraṃ mā nikkhamāhi, vinayadharānaṃ vā santikaṃ āgaccha vinicchayaṃ dātu”nti vutte tassa vacanaṃ na gahetabbanti attho. Tikabhojanaṃ nāma sace tayo hutvā bhuñjanti, gaṇabhojanena [M 0.0558] anāpatti, idaṃ sandhāya tikaṃ. “Pasutto”ti bāhullato vuttaṃ. Atha vā nipajjitvāti attho. “Idaṃ ṭhapetvā gacchāmi, tāvakālikaṃ bhante dethāti vutte ‘navakammādiatthaṃ vinā dātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti likhitaṃ. Vikappetvā ṭhapitaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ pacchime pāṭipadadivase nivāsento dukkaṭaṃ āpajjatīti attho. Apaccuddharitvāti paccuddharaṇaṃ akatvāti attho. “Vikappetu”nti vacanato avikappanapaccayā āpatti hemante āpajjati, vikappanā pana kattikapuṇṇamadivase kātabbāti dassanatthaṃ vuttanti ñātabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo avikappanaṃ sandhāya, purimo vikappitaparibhogapaccayāpattiṃ sandhāya. Vatthapaṭicchādi sabbakappiyatāyāti vatthapaṭicchādi sabbattha kappiyattāti attho. Keci imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā “vatthapaṭicchādi sabbakappiyatā tāya paṭicchannenā”ti likhanti. “Vatthameva paṭicchādi vatthapaṭicchādī”ti viggahattā “tāyā”ti na yujjati. “Tenā”ti bhavitabbattāti idaṃ sabbaṃ aññatarasmiṃ gaṇṭhipade likhitaṃ, vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

323. You should not speak. `A bodily action connected with speech` means having performed a bodily act of reverence. `To destroy` means to ruin. `Having crushed` means having overpowered. `Speaking` refers to one who is speaking. “The support of a fool should be given” is stated in the Duka (Book of Twos), but here it is said “should not be given”; with reference to an abundance of offenses, it should not be given. When it is said, “Do not go out from this monastery to another, or come to the presence of the Vinaya experts to give a decision,” his words should not be heeded—this is the meaning. A `tikabhojana` (meal for three) is so called because if three eat together, there is no offense under the rule of group meals; this is with reference to a group of three. `Asleep` is said due to its prevalence. Alternatively, it means having lain down. When it is said, “Having set this aside, I will go; venerable sir, give me temporary permission,” it is written, “It is not allowable to give it without a purpose such as new construction.” Having designated and set aside a rainy-season robe, one who wears it on the day after the prescribed period incurs a dukkaṭa offense—this is the meaning. `Not having revoked` means not having performed the revocation—this is the meaning. Because of the text “One should designate,” an offense is incurred in winter due to not designating. This is said, however, to show that the designation should be made on the full-moon day of Kattika; this should be understood. This method is with reference to non-designation; the former, with reference to the offense incurred through using what was designated. `The allowability of covering with a cloth everywhere` means that covering with a cloth is allowable everywhere—this is the meaning. Some, not discerning this meaning, write, “The allowability of covering with a cloth everywhere is by that covering.” Because of the analysis, “the cloth itself is the covering, hence ‘cloth-covering’,” `tāyā` (‘by that’ [fem.]) is not suitable. It should be `tenā` (‘by that’ [neu.])—all this is written in a certain sub-commentary and should be accepted after careful consideration.

Catukkavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section of Fours

324. Catūhākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjati…pe… kammavācāya āpajjatīti ettha yañhi āpattiṃ kammavācāya āpajjati, na tattha kāyādayoti āpannaṃ, tato kammavācāya saddhiṃ āpattikarā dhammā sattāti āpajjati, evaṃ sati “cha āpattisamuṭṭhānānī”ti vacanavirodho, tāni eva āpattikarā dhammā nāma. Atha tatthāpi kāyādayo ekato vā nānāto vā labbhanti, catūhākārehīti na yujjatīti “chahākārehi āpattiṃ āpajjatī”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti evaṃ etāni suttapadāni virodhitāni honti. Kathaṃ avirodhitāni? Saviññattikāviññattikabhedabhinnattā. Kāyādīnaṃ yā kiriyā āpatti, naṃ ekaccaṃ kāyena saviññattikena āpajjati, ekaccaṃ saviññattikāya vācāya, ekaccaṃ saviññattikāhi kāyavācāhi āpajjati, yā pana akiriyā āpatti, taṃ ekaccaṃ kammavācāya āpajjati, tañca kho avasiṭṭhāhi aviññattikāhi kāyavācāhiyeva, na vinā “no ce kāyena vācāya paṭinissajjati, kammavācāpariyosāne āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti (pārā. 414) vacanato, avisesena vā ekaccaṃ āpattiṃ kāyena āpajjati, ekaccaṃ vācāya[M 0.0559], ekaccaṃ kāyavācāhi[V 0.0511]. Yaṃ panettha kāyavācāhi, taṃ ekaccaṃ kevalāhi kāyavācāhi āpajjati, ekaccaṃ kammavācāya āpajjatīti ayamattho veditabboti evaṃ avirodhitāni honti.

324. One commits an offense by four modes… (etc.) …one commits an offense by a formal act. Herein, for the offense that one commits by a formal act, body and so forth are not present; this is the meaning that is reached. Therefore, it follows that, together with the formal act, the factors that cause an offense are seven. This being so, there would be a contradiction with the statement, “There are six origins of an offense,” for those very things are called the factors that cause an offense. Furthermore, if even in that case body and so forth are found either together or separately, then “by four modes” is not suitable, and it should be said, “one commits an offense by six modes.” Thus, these text passages are contradictory. How are they not contradictory? Because of the distinction between actions with intimation and without intimation. Of an offense that is an action of the body and so forth, one commits a certain one by the body with intimation, a certain one by speech with intimation, and a certain one by body and speech with intimation. But as for an offense that is not an action, one commits a certain one by a formal act, and that indeed is only by the remaining body and speech without intimation—not without them—because of the statement: “If one does not renounce by body or speech, at the conclusion of the formal act, there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa.” Or, without distinction, one commits a certain offense by the body, a certain one by speech, and a certain one by body and speech. Herein, of that which is committed by body and speech, one commits a certain one by mere body and speech, and a certain one by a formal act. This is the meaning that should be understood. In this way, they are not contradictory.

Tatrāyaṃ samāsato atthavibhāvanā – kāyena āpajjatīti kāyena saviññattikena akattabbaṃ katvā ekaccaṃ āpajjati, aviññattikena kattabbaṃ akatvā āpajjati, tadubhayampi kāyakammaṃ nāma. Akatampi hi loke “kata”nti vuccati “dukkaṭaṃ mayā, yaṃ mayā puññaṃ na kata”nti evamādīsu, sāsane ca “idaṃ te, āvuso ānanda, dukkaṭaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ na pucchī”ti (cūḷava. 443) evamādīsu, evamidha vinayapariyāyena kāyena akaraṇampi “kāyakamma”nti vuccati. Ayameva nayo “vācāya āpajjatī”tiādīsu. Puratīti puriso, pura aggagamane. Puratīti purato gacchati sabbakammesu pubbaṅgamo hoti. Paṭhamuppannavasenāti paṭhamakappiyesu hi paṭhamaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ uppajjati, “purima”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ purisaliṅgaṃ jāyatīti attho. Sataṃ tiṃsa cāti ettha asādhāraṇāpi pārājikā no antogadhāyeva jātā pārājikāpannānaṃ bhikkhubhāvāya abhabbattā. “Asādhāraṇavacanena pana sāmaññena uddhaṭānī”ti vadanti. “Satañceva tiṃsañca sikkhāpadānīti pāṭho”ti ca vadanti. Bhikkhussa ca bhikkhuniyā ca catūsu pārājikesūti sādhāraṇesu eva. Atthi vatthunānattatā no āpattinānattatāti paṭhamapañho idha dutiyo nāma. Atthi āpattisabhāgatā no vatthusabhāgatāti etena viseso natthi. Mantābhāsāti matiyā bhāsā. “Abhivādanārahāti yathānisinnāva sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā vandanti. Navamabhikkhunito paṭṭhāya anuṭṭhitabbato āsanā na paccuṭṭhenti. Avisesenāti upajjhāyassa, itarassa vā vippakatabhojanassa, samīpagato yo koci vuḍḍhataroti attho. Vippakatabhojanenāpi hi uṭṭhahitvā āsanaṃ dātabbaṃ. Idha na kappantīti vadantopīti paccantimajanapadesu ṭhatvā “idha na kappantī”ti vadanto vinayātisāradukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Kappiyañhi “na kappatī”ti vadanto paññattaṃ samucchindati nāma. Tathā idha kappantītiādīsupi ṭhatvā “idha kappantī”ti vadanto vinayāgatabhikkhu vinayo pucchitabboti attho.

Herein, this is the concise explanation of the meaning. Regarding 'one falls into an offense by means of the body': one falls into a certain offense by doing with the body possessing intimation what ought not to be done, or by not doing with the body possessing non-intimation what ought to be done; both of these are called 'bodily action'. For even what is not done is called 'done' in the world, as in such cases as, “A wrong deed was done by me, in that merit was not done by me,” and in the Teaching, as in such cases as, “Friend Ānanda, this was a wrong deed for you, in that you did not ask the Blessed One” (Cūḷava. 443). Thus, according to the Vinaya method, even not doing by means of the body is called 'bodily action'. This very same method applies in cases such as 'one falls into an offense by means of speech'. Because he goes before (purati), he is called a person (purisa); the word 'pura' is in the sense of going foremost. 'Purati' means: he goes before, he is a forerunner in all actions. By way of being first arisen: for among the beings of the first aeon, the male characteristic arises first. The meaning is: the male characteristic, which has come to be designated as 'first' (purima), is born. Regarding 'one hundred and thirty': here, even the uncommon Pārājika offenses are not included, because those who have fallen into a Pārājika offense are unfit for the state of a bhikkhu. Some say, “But by the term ‘uncommon,’ they are excluded in a general sense.” And some say, “The reading is ‘one hundred and thirty training rules’.” Regarding 'in the four Pārājikas for a bhikkhu and for a bhikkhunī': this refers only to the common ones. The first question, 'Is there a variety of bases but not a variety of offenses?', is here called the second. By this phrase, 'Is there a commonality of offense but not a commonality of basis?', there is no distinction. 'Mantābhāsā' is speech with wisdom. Regarding 'worthy of salutation': they pay homage just as they are seated by raising their heads. Starting from the ninth bhikkhunī, because one should not stand up, they do not rise from their seats. Regarding 'without distinction': the meaning is any elder whatsoever who has approached a preceptor or another who has an unfinished meal. For even one with an unfinished meal should stand up and offer a seat. Regarding 'one who says, “Here it is not allowable”': one who, while staying in the border districts, says, “Here it is not allowable,” falls into a dukkaṭa offense of transgressing the Vinaya. For one who says of what is allowable, “It is not allowable,” is called one who cuts off the regulation. Similarly, one who, while staying there, says, “Here it is allowable,” and so on, [also cuts off the regulation]. The meaning is that a bhikkhu versed in the Vinaya should be asked about the Vinaya.

Pañcakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section of Fives

325. Na [M 0.0560] upeti puggalo. “Nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā”ti (pāci. 299) vacanato nimantanābhāvā piṇḍapātikassa anāmantacāro vaṭṭati. “Gilānasamayo”tiādinā ābhogaṃ katvā bhojanaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā bhojanaṃ nāma. “Mayhaṃ [V 0.0512] bhattapaccāsaṃ itthannāmassa dammī”ti evaṃ avikappanā. Parammukhe aguṇavacanaṃ ayaso. Sammukhā garahā. Sīladiṭṭhibyasanānaṃ vinayapariyāpannattā tehi saddhiṃ itare pañcakaṃ pūretuṃ vuttā. “Vinayadharapañcamena gaṇenā”ti (mahāva. 259) vuttattā pañcakaṃ jātaṃ. Aññatarasmiṃ vihāre eko theroti attho. “Yonakavisayatoti cīnaṭṭhānā”ti likhitaṃ. Aṭṭha kappe anussarīti pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ nibbattesīti attho. Anantare ṭhāne ṭhatvāti attho. Ñattiyā kammappatto hutvāti ñattiṭṭhapitakāle kammappatto hoti. Puna kammavācāya kammasiddhi. Ñattikhettanti ñattiyāva kātabbaṭṭhānaṃ tassā khettaṃ, ñattidutiyādikamme paṭhamaṭṭhapanaṃ tassā okāso nāma. Āraññake idañcidañcānisaṃsanti evaṃ idamatthitanti attho.

325. A person is not liable. Because of the text, “Having been invited to a meal, without asking permission from a present monk” (Pāc. 299), and due to the absence of an invitation, wandering without being invited is allowable for one who lives on alms. By means of the phrase “The time of illness,” etc., having made a mental note and having determined the food, it is called eating. The statement “I give my share of the meal to so-and-so” is thus a case of non-disposal. Speaking of faults in one's absence is disgrace; in one's presence, it is censure. Because the misfortunes of conduct and view are included in the Vinaya, the others are mentioned together with them in order to complete the pentad. Because it is said, “by a chapter with a Vinaya expert as the fifth” (Mahāva. 259), a pentad is formed. The meaning is: one elder in a certain monastery. It is written: ‘Regarding “from the country of the Yonakas,” it means “from the region of China.”’ Regarding “He recollected eight eons,” the meaning is: he produced the knowledge of previous existences. The meaning is: having stood in the adjacent place. Regarding “having become subject to the formal act by the motion,” at the time the motion is established, he becomes subject to the formal act. Then, by the proclamation of the formal act, the completion of the formal act occurs. The field of the motion means the place where something is to be done by the motion itself; that is its field. In a formal act with a motion as the second, etc., the first placement is called its occasion. Regarding a forest-dweller, the phrase “there is this and that benefit” means thus: this is desired.

Chakkavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section of Sixes

326. “Chabbassaparamatā dhāretabba”nti vibhaṅge pāṭhattā evaṃ vuttaṃ. Cuddasaparamāni nava chakkāni honti. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ ekaṃ chakkaṃ, sesesu aṭṭhasu ekekena saddhiṃ ekekanti evaṃ tīṇi chakkāni antarapeyyāle vuttāni. Kathaṃ? “Catutthena āpattisamuṭṭhānena cha āpattiyo āpajjatī”tiādinā nayena pañcamena, chaṭṭhena ca tīṇi chakkāni. Lobhādayo cha vivādamūlāni, tathā anuvādassa. Dīghaso cha vidatthiyo vassikasāṭikāya. Tiriyaṃ cha vidatthiyo sugatacīvarassa. Vippakatacīvaraṃ ādāya pakkamane niṭṭhānantiko, sanniṭṭhānanāsana savana sīmātikkantikasahubbhārāti cha, samādāya vārepi chāti chakkadvayaṃ. Sattake pakkamanantikena saha satta.

326. “A maximum of six years should be kept”—because this text is found in the Vibhaṅga, it is thus stated. The fourteen maxima consist of nine sets of six. How so? The first is one set of six; with each of the remaining eight, there is one each. Thus, three sets of six are stated in the intermediate abbreviation section (antarapeyyāla). How so? By the method beginning with, “Through the fourth origin of an offense, one commits six offenses,” and similarly with the fifth and the sixth, there are three sets of six. Greed and so forth are the six roots of dispute; likewise for accusation. The rains-bathing cloth is six spans in length. The Sugata's robe is six spans in width. In the case of departing with an unfinished robe, there are six types of withdrawal of the kathina privilege: ending with completion (niṭṭhānantika), ending with determination (sanniṭṭhāna), ending with loss (nāsana), ending with hearing (savana), ending with crossing the boundary (sīmātikkantika), and ending with the Sangha's withdrawal (sahubbhāra). In the section on undertaking, there are also six. Thus, there are two sets of six. In the section of sevens, together with ending with departure (pakkamanantika), there are seven.

Sattakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section of Sevens

327. Chakke [M 0.0561] vuttāniyeva sattakavasena yojetabbānīti chakke vuttacuddasaparamāni sattakavasena yojetabbāni. Sattame aruṇuggamane nissaggiyanti “chārattaparamaṃ tena bhikkhunā tena cīvarena vippavasitabbaṃ, tato ce uttari vippavaseyyā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Campeyyakkhandhake sugatacīvarabhāṇavārassa parato “idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa na hoti āpatti daṭṭhabbā, tamenaṃ codeti saṅgho vā sambahulā vā ekapuggalo vā”tiādinā nayena vuttasattakāti.

327. The phrase 'What was stated in the section of sixes is to be applied in the manner of the section of sevens' means that the fourteen maxima stated in the section of sixes are to be applied in the manner of the section of sevens. As for the phrase, 'At the seventh sunrise, it is to be relinquished': the robe spoken of thus, 'For a maximum of six nights, that monk may be separated from that robe; if he should be separated beyond that,' becomes subject to relinquishment. In the Campeyyakkhandhaka, after the recitation section on the Sugata's robe, the sets of seven are stated by the method beginning with, 'Herein, O monks, it should be understood that there is no offense for the monk. The Saṅgha, or a group, or an individual may accuse him.'

Aṭṭhakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section of Eights

328. Tena [V 0.0513] saddhiṃ uposathādikaraṇaṃ ānisaṃso, akaraṇaṃ ādīnavo, tasmā ete aṭṭhānisaṃse sampassamānenāti attho. “Ayaso akkoso”ti vuttaṃ. Pubbevassa hoti “musā bhaṇissa”nti, bhaṇantassa hoti “musā bhaṇāmī”ti, bhaṇitassa hoti “musā mayā bhaṇita”nti, vinidhāya diṭṭhiṃ khantiṃ ruciṃ bhāvaṃ saññanti evaṃ akappiyakataṃ hoti appaṭiggahitakatantiādayo aṭṭha anatirittā. Sappiādi aṭṭhame aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhavācikā bhikkhunīnaṃ upasampadā ubhatoñatticatutthattā. Vassikasāṭikadānādīni aṭṭha varāni.

328. With that monk, performing the Uposatha and other duties is a benefit, and not performing them is a drawback. Therefore, the meaning is 'by one who is clearly seeing these eight benefits.' It is said, 'Abuse is disrepute.' Before speaking, one thinks, 'I will speak falsely'; while speaking, one thinks, 'I am speaking falsely'; after speaking, one thinks, 'I have spoken falsely'; having laid aside view, tolerance, preference, disposition, and perception; thus what is done improperly is what is not received—these and others are the eight, no more. Ghee and so on becomes subject to forfeiture at the eighth sunrise. The ordination of nuns has eight verbal announcements because it is a motion-as-fourth-act by both Sanghas. The giving of the rains-cloth and so on are eight boons.

Navakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Chapter of Nines

329. Navahi bhikkhūhi bhijjati. Manussamaṃsavajjehi nava maṃsehi vinicchayo. Sundaraṃ na sundaranti saṅghāṭiādīni nava cīvarāni. Tāneva adhiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya na vikappetabbāni, adhiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya apaccuddharitvā na vikappetabbānīti adhippāyo. Nava vidatthiyo sugatacīvarassa. “Vaggaṃ bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ vaggasaññī ovadatī”tiādinā nayena adhammakamme dve navakāni pācittiyavasena vuttāni.

329. A schism is created by nine monks. A decision is made concerning nine kinds of meat, excluding human flesh. There are nine robes, such as the Saṅghāṭi, etc., whether beautiful or not. The meaning is that those same robes, from the time of determination onwards, should not be placed under joint ownership; from the time of determination onwards, without having withdrawn the determination, they should not be placed under joint ownership. The Sugata’s robe is nine spans. By the method beginning with, 'Perceiving a faction of the nuns' Sangha as a faction, one admonishes them,' in the case of an unlawful act, two sets of nine are stated by way of a Pācittiya offense.

Dasakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Chapter of Tens

330. “Oramattakañca adhikaraṇaṃ hoti, na ca gatigata”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 204) dasa adhammikā salākaggāhā. Viparītā dhammikā. Samathakkhandhake vuttehi [M 0.0562] samannāgato hotīti sambandho. “Saṃkaccikaṃ vā pakkhipitvā dasā”ti vuttaṃ kappiyattā etesaṃ. Māturakkhitādayo dasa itthiyo. Dhanakkītādayo dasa bhariyā. “Sikkhāsammutiṃ datvā dasavassāya tassā dvādasavassakāle sayampi dvādasavassā bhavissatī”ti vuṭṭhāpanasammuti sāditabbā. “Vinayadharasseva ‘āpattānāpattiṃ na jānātī’ti ārabbha yāva ‘ubhayāni kho panassa…pe… anubyañjanaso’ti pañcaṅgāni vatvā punapi ‘āpattānāpattiṃ na jānāti’cceva ārabbha yāva ‘adhikaraṇe ca na vinicchayakusalo hotī’ti pañca vuttā, te tathā tathā pañca pañca katvā dasa hontī”ti likhitaṃ. “Dasavassāya bhikkhuniyā nissayo dātabbo”ti ekaccesu potthakesu natthi, kiñcāpi natthi, pāṭho eva pana hoti.

330. By the text beginning with, “A dispute that is minor and not recurring,” there are ten unlawful takings of voting tickets. The opposite are the lawful ones. The connection should be understood as: he is endowed with what is stated in the Samathakkhandhaka. It is said, “Having inserted a shoulder-strap or the fringes,” because of the allowability of these. Ten women, such as those protected by their mother. The agreement for ordination should be sought with the understanding that “having given the training permission to a ten-year-old, when she is twelve years old, she (the preceptor) herself will also be twelve years ordained.” It is written: “Regarding one who upholds the Vinaya, beginning with ‘he does not know offenses and non-offenses,’ up to ‘both…and so on…in detail,’ five factors are stated; and again, beginning with the very text ‘he does not know offenses and non-offenses,’ up to ‘and he is not skilled in settling a dispute,’ five are stated. Those, having been made five and five in that respective way, become ten.” The text, “Support should be given to a bhikkhunī of ten years' standing,” is not found in some books; although it is not found, it is indeed the root text.

Ekādasakavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Chapter of Elevens

331. Na [V 0.0514] vodāyanti na pakāsenti. Rogameva rogātaṅkaṃ. Rogantarāyaṃ vā.

331. `Na vodāyanti` means they do not reveal. Illness itself is the affliction of illness, or the danger from illness.

Ekuttarikanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the numerical sequence is complete.

Uposathādipucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Questions and Answers Concerning the Uposatha and So On

332. “Saṅghaṃ, bhante, pavāremī”tiādi pavāraṇakathā nāma vinītagāthāsu viya.

332. “Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha,” and so on, is called the Pavāraṇā Talk, as in the Vinīta Gāthās.

Atthavasapakaraṇavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on the Reasons of Purpose

334. Dasa atthavase paṭiccāti ettha tassa tassa sikkhāpadassa paññāpane guṇavisesadīpanato, apaññāpane ādīnavadassanato ca saṅghasuṭṭhutā hoti. Tattha yathāsambhavaṃ lokavajjassa apaṇṇattisambhavassa paññāpane payogavisuddhi guṇo. Paṇṇattisambhavassa pana sekhiyassa lokavajjassa paññāpane [M 0.0563] paṭipattivisuddhi guṇo, paṇṇattivajjassa āsayavisuddhi guṇo appicchādiguṇāvahanato, tenevāha “subharatāya suposatāya appicchatāya appicchassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitvā”ti. Samaṇācāravisuddhi cassa guṇoti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā lokavajjassa paññāpane saṅghasuṭṭhutā hoti pākaṭādīnavato, paṇṇattivajjassa paññāpane saṅghaphāsutā hoti pākaṭānisaṃsattā. Tathā paṭhamena dummaṅkūnaṃ niggaho, dutiyena pesalānaṃ phāsuvihāro, paṭhamena samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighāto, dutiyena diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ, tathā paṭhamena appasannānaṃ pasādo, dutiyena pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvo, tathā paṭhamena saddhammaṭṭhiti, dutiyena vinayānuggaho hotīti veditabbo. Parivāranayena vā paṭhamena pāpicchānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pakkhupacchedo, dutiyena gihīnaṃ anukampā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “dve atthavase paṭicca tathāgatena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ gihīnaṃ anukampāya pāpicchānaṃ pakkhupacchedāyā”ti (pari. 498). Tathā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ verānaṃ vajjānaṃ akusalānaṃ vasenapi yojanā kātabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “dve atthavase…pe… paññattaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ verānaṃ samparāyikānaṃ verānaṃ paṭighātāyā”tiādi (pari. 498). Apicettha sabbampi akataviññattipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ, gihīnaṃ pīḷāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ, tesaṃ pasādabhogakkhayarakkhāpaṭisaṃyuttañca gihīnaṃ anukampāya paññattaṃ nāma, kuladūsakagaṇabhojanāni pāpicchānaṃ pakkhupacchedāya paññattaṃ. Sabbaṃ lokavajjaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaverādipaṭighātāya[V 0.0515], mātugāmena saṃvidhānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaverādisaṃvarāya paññattanti veditabbaṃ. Apicettha ādito paṭṭhāya dasaatthavasapakaraṇameva nissāya vinicchayo veditabbo.

334. “For ten reasons” — here, the establishment of each training rule, by demonstrating special qualities and by seeing the dangers if not established, results in the Saṅgha’s well-being. In this regard, as appropriate: for the establishment of what is blameworthy in the world, which is unsuitable for prescription, the benefit is the purification of effort. But for the establishment of what is suitable for prescription, namely the Sekhiya rules which are blameworthy in the world, the benefit is the purification of practice. For what is an offense by prescription, the benefit is the purification of intention, as it brings about qualities such as fewness of wishes; for that reason he said, “for ease of support, for ease of sustenance, for fewness of wishes, having spoken in praise of one with few wishes.” Alternatively, the establishment of what is blameworthy in the world ensures the Saṅgha’s well-being because of its obvious drawbacks, while the establishment of what is an offense by prescription ensures the Saṅgha’s comfort due to its obvious benefits. Thus, by the first, the restraint of the ill-behaved; by the second, the comfortable living of the virtuous. By the first, the prevention of future influxes; by the second, of present ones. Similarly, by the first, the inspiring of faith in the unfaithful; by the second, the increase of faith in the faithful. Similarly, by the first, the stability of the True Dhamma; by the second, the support of the Discipline—this should be understood. Or, according to the method of the Parivāra, by the first, the cutting off of the faction of wicked bhikkhus; by the second, compassion for householders. As it is said: “For two reasons the Tathāgata has laid down a training rule for his disciples: out of compassion for householders and for the cutting off of the faction of wicked bhikkhus.” Similarly, the connection should be made with reference to present and future enmities, faults, and unwholesome things. As it is said: “For two reasons… it has been laid down for the prevention of present enmities and future enmities,” and so on. Moreover, here, every rule connected with improper asking, connected with oppressing householders, and connected with protecting their faith and wealth from destruction is laid down out of compassion for householders. The rules on corrupting families and group meals are laid down for the cutting off of the faction of wicked bhikkhus. Everything blameworthy in the world is laid down for the prevention of present and future enmities, and so on. Making arrangements with a woman is laid down for the restraint of present enmities, and so on—this should be understood. Moreover, here, from the beginning, the judgment should be understood based solely on the section on the ten reasons.

Vatthuvītikkamena yaṃ, ekantākusalaṃ bhave;

Taṃ saṅghasuṭṭhubhāvāya, paññattaṃ lokavajjato.

Whatever training rule is entirely unwholesome by transgressing its object, that is laid down for the well-being of the Saṅgha because it is blameworthy in the world.

Pārājikādiṃ,

The Pārājika and so on,

Paññattijānaneneva, yatthāpatti na aññathā;

Taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiyā vāpi, pasāduppādabuddhiyā.

Wherein an offense is incurred only by knowing the prescription, and not otherwise, that is laid down for the stability of the Dhamma, or for the purpose of giving rise to confidence.

Dhammadesanāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ itarañca sekhiyaṃ, idaṃ paṇṇattisambhavaṃ lokavajjaṃ nāma. Vatthuno, paññattiyā vā vītikkamacetanāyābhāvepi paṭikkhittassa karaṇe, kattabbassa akaraṇe vā sati yattha āpatti pahoti, taṃ sabbaṃ ṭhapetvā surāpānaṃ paṇṇattivajjanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha ukkoṭanake pācittiyaṃ, “yo pana bhikkhu dhammikānaṃ kammānaṃ chandaṃ datvā pacchā khīyanadhammaṃ āpajjeyya, pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 475), yo pana bhikkhu saṅghe vinicchayakathāya vattamānāya [M 0.0564] chandaṃ adatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkameyya, pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 480), yo pana bhikkhu samaggena saṅghena cīvaraṃ datvā pacchā khīyanadhammaṃ āpajjeyya…pe… pācittiya”nti (pāci. 485) evamādi saṅghaphāsutāya paññattaṃ. “Aññavādake vihesake pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 101), pārājikādīhi anuddhaṃsane saṅghādisesādi ca dummaṅkūnaṃ niggahāya, anupakhajjanikkaḍḍhanaupassūtisikkhāpadādi pesalānaṃ phāsuvihārāya, sabbaṃ lokavajjaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, sabbaṃ paṇṇattivajjaṃ diṭṭhadhammikānameva saṃvarāya. Sabbaṃ gihipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ appasannānaṃ vā pasādāya pasannānaṃ vā bhiyyobhāvāya ca. Visesena ariṭṭhasamaṇuddesasikkhāpadaṃ, sāmaññena paccayesu mariyādapaṭisaṃyuttañca saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, “appicchassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo mahicchassā”ti (dī. ni. 3.358; a. ni. 8.30) ādisuttamettha sādhakaṃ. “Sikkhāpadavivaṇṇake (pāci. 439) mohanake pācittiya”ntiādi (pāci. 444) vinayānuggahāya paññattanti veditabbaṃ. “Bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pācittiya”nti (pāci. 90) idaṃ kimatthanti ce? Appasannānaṃ pasādāya, pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya ca. Kathaṃ?

The training rule connected with teaching the Dhamma and the other Sekhiya training rule, this is called a worldly offense arising from a prescription. Regarding the object or the rule, even in the absence of an intention to transgress, when there is the doing of what is prohibited or the not-doing of what should be done, wherever an offense arises, all that—except for the drinking of alcohol—is to be known as an offense by prescription. For overturning a formal act, it is a pācittiya offense: 'If a bhikkhu, having given consent to lawful formal acts, afterwards speaks disparagingly, it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 475); 'If a bhikkhu, while a legal discussion is being conducted in the Saṅgha, rises from his seat and departs without having given consent, it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 480); 'If a bhikkhu, having given a robe with a united Saṅgha, afterwards speaks disparagingly… it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 485), and so on—these were prescribed for the comfort of the Saṅgha. 'For speaking evasively or for being vexatious, it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 101); and the saṅghādisesa and so on for not censuring with pārājika and so on were prescribed for the restraint of the ill-behaved. The training rules concerning encroaching, dragging out, and eavesdropping, and so on, were prescribed for the comfortable living of the virtuous. All worldly offenses are for the warding off of cankers in the present life and in future lives. All offenses by prescription are for restraint only in the present life. All rules connected with householders are for inspiring faith in the unfaithful and for the increase of it in the faithful. Specifically, the training rule concerning the novice Ariṭṭha, and generally the one connected with the limit on requisites, were prescribed for the stability of the good Dhamma. 'This Dhamma is for the contented, not for the greedy' (Dī. Ni. 3.358; A. Ni. 8.30)—this sutta and so on is the authority here. 'For disparaging the training rules, it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 439), 'for causing confusion, it is a pācittiya' (Pāc. 444), and so on—it should be known that these were prescribed to uphold the Vinaya. If it is asked, 'For what purpose was this rule, "It is a pācittiya for destroying plant life" (Pāc. 90), prescribed?' For inspiring faith in the unfaithful and for the increase of it in the faithful. How so?

“Bhūtagāmo [V 0.0516] sajīvoti, avipallattadiṭṭhino;

Tassa kopanasaññāya, pasādo buddhasāvake.

'The plant world is alive,' thus is the view of those of unperverted view. Because of the perception of destroying it, faith arises in the Buddha's disciple who refrains from doing so.

“Nijjīvasaññitaṃpetaṃ, akopento kathaṃ muni;

Jīvaṃ kopeyya niddoso, macchamaṃsānujānane.

The sage, not destroying even this which is perceived as lifeless, how could he destroy a living being? Therefore, he is faultless in allowing fish and meat.

Evampi –

Even so—

“Tassa kopanasaññāya, pasādo buddhasāvake;

Yato titthakarāvime, viratā bhūtagāmato;

Lokassa cittarakkhatthaṃ, tatopi virato munī”ti. –

Because of the perception of destroying it, faith arises in the Buddha's disciple. Since these sectarians abstain from destroying the plant world, for that reason, to protect the minds of the world, the sage also abstains from that.

Pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvo hoti.

There is an increase of faith for the faithful.

Vivittasenāsanabhogataṇhāvasenanijjīvamitārakkhaṃ;

Buddhobhininnañca vivajjayanto;

Sikkhāpadaṃ tattha ca paññapesi.

And wishing to avoid excessive blame—[people saying,] 'By the power of craving for enjoying various lodgings, he destroys this lifeless thing that has a guardian'—the Buddha laid down the training rule in that matter.

Nijjīvassāpi [M 0.0565] maṃsassa, khādanakaṃ yatiṃ pati;

Nindamānaṃ janaṃ disvā, bhūtagāmaṃ pariccaji.

Seeing the people criticizing the ascetic who eats meat, even though it is lifeless, He proscribed [the destruction of] the plant world.

Tikoṭiparisuddhattā, macchamaṃsānujānane;

Paṭicca maṃsānujānanaṃ, kamme diṭṭhippasaṅgabhayā.

The allowance of fish and meat is due to its purity in three aspects; it should be known that the allowance of meat is on account of fear of the occasion of wrong view concerning kamma.

Aparikkhakassa lokassa, parānuddayatāya ca;

Bhūtagāmapātabyatāya, pāṇātipātappasaṅgabhayā.

For the uninvestigating world, and out of compassion for others, the rule regarding the destruction of the plant world was laid down out of fear of the occasion of destroying life.

Tattha pariyāyavacanaṃ anujāni bhagavā, uddissa kataṃ paṭikkhipi parassa vā pāpappasaṅgabhayena. Idha pana bhūtagāmapātabyatāya pāpābhāvañāpanatthaṃ attuddesikaṃ vihāraṃ, kuṭiñca [V 0.0517] anujānīti veditabbaṃ. Pakiriyanti ettha te te payojanavisesasaṅkhātā atthavasāti atthavasapakaraṇanti.

In that case [of meat], the Blessed One permitted indirect speech; he rejected what was prepared specifically for him, out of fear of the occasion of evil for another. But here, in the matter of destroying the plant world, it should be known that he allowed a monastery and a hut intended for oneself for the purpose of making known the absence of evil. Herein, those various grounds of benefit, known as specific purposes, are set forth. Therefore, this is the Section on the Grounds of Benefit.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mahāvagga is concluded.

Paṭhamagāthāsaṅgaṇikavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the First Collection of Verses

Sattanagaresu paññattasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Training Rules Promulgated in the Seven Towns

335. Vacanasampaṭicchanatthe [M 0.0566] vā nipātoti attho. Aḍḍhuḍḍhasatānīti tīṇi satāni, paññāsāni ca. Viggahanti manussaviggahaṃ. Atirekaṃ vāti dasāhaparamaṃ atirekacīvaraṃ. Kāḷakanti “suddhakāḷakāna”nti (pārā. 552-554) vuttakāḷakaṃ. Bhūtanti bhūtārocanaṃ. Paramparabhattanti paramparabhojanaṃ. Bhikkhunīsu ca akkosoti yā pana bhikkhunī bhikkhuṃ akkoseyya vā paribhāseyya vā (pāci. 1029). Antaravāsakanti aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā cīvarapaṭiggahaṇaṃ. Rūpiyanti rūpiyasabbohāraṃ. Suttanti sāmaṃ suttaṃ viññāpetvā tantavāyehi. Ujjhāpanaketi ujjhāpanake khīyanake. Pācitapiṇḍanti bhikkhunīpaapācitapiṇḍapātaṃ. Cārittanti nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ. Cīvaraṃ datvāti samaggena saṅghena cīvaraṃ datvā. Vosāsantīti bhikkhū paneva kulesu nimantitā bhuñjanti (pāci. 558), tattha cesā. Giraggacariyāti “yā pana bhikkhunī naccaṃ vā gītaṃ vā”ti (pāci. 834) ca, “antovassaṃ cārikaṃ careyyā”ti (pāci. 970) ca vuttadvayaṃ. Chandadānenāti pārivāsikachandadānena sikkhamānaṃ vuṭṭhāpeyya (pāci. 1167). Pārājikāni cattāri, bhikkhunīnaṃ saññācikakuṭiñca kosiyamissasanthatañca seyyā ca anupasampannena saha pathavīkhaṇanaṃ. Gaccha devateti bhūtagāmapātabyatā sappāṇakaudakasiñcananti attho. Mahāvihāroti mahallakavihāro. Aññanti aññavādakaṃ. Dvāranti yāvadvārakosā. “Anādariyapācittīti ca sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno”ti pāṭho. Payopānanti surusurukārakaṃ. Eḷakalomāni patto cāti eḷakalomadhovāpanañca ūnapañcabandhanapatto ca. Ovādo ceva bhesajjanti bhikkhunupassayaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ovādo taduttaribhesajjaviññāpanañca. Sūci araññakoti “aṭṭhimayaṃ vā dantamayaṃ vā visāṇamayaṃ vā sūcighara”nti (pāci. 517) ca “yāni kho pana tāni āraññakāni [V 0.0518] senāsanāni sāsaṅka…pe… paṭidesetabba”nti (pāci. 570) ca. Ovādoti yā pana bhikkhunī ovādāya vā saṃvāsāya vā na gaccheyya (pāci. 1055). Pārājikāni cattārītiādi dvīsu nagaresu paññattasampiṇḍanaṃ.

335. The particle `vā` is in the sense of accepting a statement; this is the meaning. Aḍḍhaḍḍhasatāni means three hundred and fifty. Viggaha means a human body. Atirekaṃ vā refers to the training rule concerning an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. Kāḷaka refers to the Kāḷaka training rule mentioned in the phrase “of pure black” (suddhakāḷakāna). Bhūta refers to the training rule on reporting a true attainment (bhūtārocana). Paramparabhatta refers to the training rule on eating consecutively (paramparabhojana). “And reviling among bhikkhunīs” refers to the rule: “if a bhikkhunī reviles or abuses a bhikkhu” (Pāc. 1029). Antaravāsaka refers to the training rule on accepting a robe from a bhikkhunī who is not a relative. Rūpiya refers to the training rule on monetary transactions (rūpiyasabbohāra). Sutta refers to the training rule on personally requesting thread and having it woven by weavers. Ujjhāpanaka refers to the training rule on being contemptuous and complaining (ujjhāpanake khīyanake). Pācitapiṇḍa refers to the training rule on almsfood arranged by a bhikkhunī (bhikkhunīparipācitapiṇḍapāta). Cāritta refers to the training rule concerning one who, having been invited for a meal, goes to a family's house without informing a bhikkhu who is present. Cīvaraṃ datvā means giving a robe with the unanimous consent of the Saṅgha. Vosāsanti refers to the context where “bhikkhus, having been invited, eat in the families’ houses” (Pāc. 558), and this bhikkhunī is there. Giraggacariyā refers to the two training rules mentioned: “if a bhikkhunī dances or sings” (Pāc. 834) and “should wander on tour during the rains” (Pāc. 970). Chandadānena refers to ordaining a sikkhamānā by giving the formal act of consent for a probationer (Pāc. 1167). The four Pārājika offenses of the bhikkhunīs, and the training rule on a hut built by request, and the one on a felt rug mixed with silk, and the one on sleeping together with an unordained person, and the one on digging the earth. Gaccha devatā means the training rule on the destruction of plant life (bhūtagāmapātabyatā) and the one on pouring water containing living beings; this is the meaning. Mahāvihāra means a large monastery. Añña refers to the training rule on evasive speech (aññavādaka). Dvāra refers to the Yāvadvārakosā training rule. The reading is “and the pācittiya for lack of respect, when being spoken to on a matter of the Dhamma.” Payopāna refers to making a slurping sound. Eḷakalomāni patto ca refers to the training rule on having goat's wool washed and the one on a bowl with fewer than five mends. Ovāda and bhesajja refer to the training rule on going to a bhikkhunī's residence for an exhortation and the one on then requesting further medicine. Sūci and araññaka refer to the two training rules mentioned: “a needle case made of bone, ivory, or horn” (Pāc. 517) and “those wilderness dwellings that are dangerous… should be confessed” (Pāc. 570). Ovāda refers to the rule: “if a bhikkhunī does not go for an exhortation or for communion” (Pāc. 1055). Pārājikāni cattārītiādi refers to the summary of the rules laid down in the two cities.

Catuvipattivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Four Failures

336. Ekatiṃsā [M 0.0567] ye garukāti ubhato aṭṭha pārājikā, bhikkhūnaṃ terasa, bhikkhunīnaṃ dasa ca saṅghādisesā. Sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇavasena aṭṭha anavasesā nāma pārājikāni. Tadevāti sīlavipattiṃyeva. Vitthārato dassetuṃ “pārājika”ntiādinā apucchitameva vissajjitaṃ. “Tattha yo cāyaṃ, akkosati hasādhippāyo”ti pāṭho. Duṭṭhullavibhāvanavasenāgatavipattiṃ ṭhapetvā pucchāpaṭipāṭiyā yāvatatiyakapañhaṃ vissajjitumārabhi. Ukkhittānuvattikā bhikkhunī aṭṭha yāvatatiyakasaṅghādisesā idha pucchitattā anantarapañhā nāma jātā.
